Astroneer. Another space survival sim in a sea of space survival sims, or so i thought.
From the beautiful low res poly graphics and colour schemes to the ingenious take on the survival genre this game kept me amazed for an extremely short amount of time.
And there in lies the crux of the problem with this title.
Great ideas implemented well leave the consumer wanting more and more.
However its not very long until you realise that this early access title needs more time in the oven.
Fact of the matter is that there is not enough content to allow me to support or reccomend this game.
I cant help but feel insulted by the lack of content that was released so far.
Streamers, youtubers and thousands of players alike picked this game up only to be left scratching their heads at the fifth hour, wondering what there is to do next.
Exploing the universe reveals a very limited amount of planets (all more or less the same as the starting planet) and there are no reasons as of yet to leave your starting planet. There is nothing to find out there in the universe and bar the starting location on the first planet there is barely any reason to explore the planet you start on.
Im sorry to say that this game, and others like it, have been released to early access with an insultingly low amount of content.
What happened to the days where games were released when they were finished?
This title flies so far in the oppasite direction that it really has ruined the experience for me, as well as my partner.
My girlfriend and i loved playing this right up until we realised there was nothing left to do within a day of playing it.
The developers deserve credit for crafting a solid base to their game but this cant keep being the model for these survival games. Releasing content peicemeal is NOT the way to reward people for buying this title.
Developers please read this and understand that the content that i experienced was smooth, almost bugless and enjoyable.
But please understand that the state that you have realsed this game in has left me, and many others, upset at the lack of content.
Survival games already get a bad wrap for never being completed and the fact of the matter is I will not give you, nor anyone else, the benefit of the doubt any longer.
Time and time again i have found these early access titles to be disapointing due to the lack of content.

I was a huge fan of Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, so I was very excited to play the next installment in the series. Did it live up to my expectations? Well...YES! Yes it did!
Not much has changed since Arkham City. The setting is almost identical, you get a lot of the same or similar gadgets (the glue grenades are a reskin of the old freeze grenades, for example), and the overall gameplay is very familiar. Which is GREAT! The gameplay was awesome before and it's STILL awesome! And while they reused basically the whole map from the last game, the addition of new story locations, new missions, and new Riddler puzzles makes the whole thing feel new.
Things that changed for the better:
-Those really frustrating Riddler puzzles where you had to find the perfect camera angle to snap a photo of the question mark? Those are gone. Good riddance, they were a pain.
-The sleuthy bits play a bigger role, which is cool because those parts are cool and show off a cool side of Batman.
Things that changed for the worse:
-I feel like there are more buildings and ledges that aren't compatible with the grapnel? It's a little more difficult and fiddly to get around as a result. Not by much, but a little bit. The bridge is also pretty annoying. Fast travel helps, though.
-No Catwoman segments. Those were neat in the last game.
-Higher percentage of D-list villains, because I guess they don't want to use the same ones every game and they're running out of good ones at this point. Although on the upside, maybe if you're a casual fan, you get to be introduced to some lesser-known characters you might not have heard of before, so that's cool. And a few big names like Joker and Penguin are still there, of course.
That's all I can think of. Not much has changed. But, again, that's good, because Arkham City was great to start with. The flowing beat-em-up combat is still awesome, there's still tons of secrets to explore, and I ended up enjoying this game just as much as its predecessors. I'm definitely happy I bought it. I would recommend it to anyone, even if you haven't played the previous games, since it's a standalone story.

This game does not reward gunplay skill. It very lightly rewards your ability to be able to kill a few people, then praises you highly with lots of points for being able to stand over them and activate an annoying animation with sound for a few seconds. You can be the best player in the world with 40 kills in a 10 minute game. But little jimmy can come along with not even half the kills and be able to pull off a few "PWNs" (as they're called) which will skyrocket him well above you to win a game.
It's a shame really because for what it's worth, the level design is great and the gunplay is tight. But should you decide to "PWN" you'll be blindsided 9/10 times by someone else and killed anyway. This is not an FPS if you're looking for a true competitive shooter with a care for KDR.. I wish I could say what Offensive Combat wants to be, but I can't. It's all a bit of a mess, and easy to see why it was a F2P title in the first place.
On top of all this, the community is abysmally small. Unless you're able to get on at peak times, you will struggle to find a game. Should you find an off-peak game, chances are you'll be fighting against another 1-3 players at most in Deathmatch. Team Deathmatch & Capture the Flag modes are pretty much dead on arrival. No one plays those anyway.
Half the reason I would say is the price. Those that play this game are the hardcore who have played this game religiously from the F2P days. As of time of writing, this game has never gone above 97 concurrent players and it shows. I'm just glad I never paid a dime for it, as I'd be feeling mightily ripped off!
You may be able to find something here if you're into the idea of a weirdly balanced slow non-competitive shooter. But I wouldn't bother until it's at least 66% off in a sale... Maybe then it might have enough players. But as it stands, it's not that great and is pretty much almost already dead on arrival.

While the video clearly shows I am rusty when it comes to competitive first person shooters, I had a blast playing this title so far. There's a ew off-line bot modes and your standard on-line multiplayer modes such as Death Match, Team Death Match (both of which I spent the most time with), and Capture the Flag. At the moment there's only a handful of maps, but the developers have assured me more is to come, which has also been pointed out in an update posted above at the time of writing this quick critique.
There's a number of different weapons you buy from earning in game currency, as well as various outfitd and costumes. While the weaponry does affect your in game stats, the aforementioned clothing does not and, honestly, that's the biggest downfall to that other than taking on different appearances like a faux Harley Quinn or a random alien.
Other than that, the game does have a pwnd option. It's cheeky and the most "offensive" part of the game. It's a bit childish overall, but strangely satisfying when you finally get revenge on someone who constantly takes you out and do a dance over their corpse or fart on it.
Overall, while not the most in-depth experience, it's far from a bad offering. Between expansive and restricted maps, decent variety to appearance, good amount of weaponry, and a great deal of traditional multiplayer combat reminiscent of Counter Strike, you are going to have a good time. There is room for improvement but with the devs looking to do more with it, Offensive Combat: Redux is a fun multiplayer combat title you can pick up and play that will only continue to get better as time goes on.

Note: As stated under the review posted date, "Product received for free," I did get this game for free (Review copy). Getting the game for free doesn't affect my review at all.

Auro's a rare gem of a game born out of Dinofarm Games' dedication to excellence and unparalleled modesty that truly echo who they are as a company. I've never known people to be more willing to workshop with their fanbase and engage in a dialogue with their beta testers, taking their criticisms to heart. Every spell, every rule change, every monster in Auro has been revamped and shaped a million times by not only Dinofarm, but by a team of steadfast fans ready to provide feedback. The art has been done and redone and redone again to meet the highest quality standards, also standing up to scrutiny and critique of those in the community. Dinofarm loves its fans, respects them, and incorporates them into the game-making process.
In going about things in this manner, Dinofarm Games has created a masterpiece with gameplay that's unique, fun, and bulletproof, an aesthetic that is charming, beautiful, and nostalgic, and a business-model that is more genuine and legitimate than any other indie-developer I can conceive of.
There is love in every pixel of Auro and it shows.

Disclaimer: I am currently a part time developer for Dinofarm games. I was lucky enough to fall madly in love with the mobile version of this game (where I player well over 1,000 runs) prior to joining the dev-team, though, and can safely say that I would enjoy this game tremendously even if I wasn't one of the programmers behind it.
Auro is a turn-based rogue-like that introduces two key innovations to the genre. The first is its ranking system, which generates levels for the player based on their persistent skill level. It cuts down dramatically on the stress you may experience in the first few hours of most rgue-likes, and helps make sure that you always have a fighting chance and that all of your runs will be exciting and dramatic.
The second key innovation is how you kill monsters. Instead of hitting them until their life-bar depletes, you simply "bump" monsters off of the board and into the water. This idea of bumping is at the heart of Auro, and just about every action you and your foes can take involves bumping in some form. This leads to characters consistently synergizing in surprising and delightful ways, like being bumped out of harm's way by a Slime, or setting up a charging Troggle to plow through your enemies.
They may seem like simple features, but they work together to create some of the deepest, most rewarding gameplay you're likely to find in a rogue-like. If you're a fan of either rogue-likes or strategy games, you should really do yourself a favor and pick this game up. I promise, you'll be glad you did.

I have been an avid Auro player since 2012 (nearly four years)! This game is a marvel, the closest thing to an evergreen game that you will find. The new 2.0 version is a cut above the previous mobile versions in both art and gameplay, and I can't wait to spend some quality time with it.
At first, Auro may strike you as a bit weird: There aren't any experience points or tons of cool items or achievements. That's because the game is fun and interesting on the basis of its core interactions alone. It truly doesn't need all that cruft to capture and hold your attention. You may have to spend a bit of time learning, especially with this new version--there's no tutorial--but put in the time and you will find the game more than pays you back.
This is the game that inspired me to make my own games. Incredibly elegant, fun, and strategically interesting for an extremely long time. One of the best games available period.

Auro is the only turn-based game I still play, and the only recent game where I don't feel awful when i'm in a tough spot and trying to find a solution by experimenting.  I also appreciate how Auro uses an 'ELO' system to encourage the player to keep playing and improving, instead of just a high score list.  The art style and music are very nostalgic; it feels like i'm playing a game on a sega genesis or super nintendo.  All in all, Auro is a very good game that feels worthwhile to play.

I'm one of those guys that plays games looking depth... real depth. I know I'm in the minority here, but things that are truly novel just speak to my soul. Because of that, I tend to drift from game to game, playing everything in my library at least once or twice, but hardly ever come back to them once I "get it".
Auro is not one of those drift-able games! I originally bought it on Android about a year ago, and have sunk hours and hours into it. This game offers true strategy, not the feigned depth of most strategy games out there. Most strategy games add tons and tons of complexity to their rule-set to keep the player from ever mastering the them. Auro keeps it super simple and elegant. After a hardcore year of trying to "get it" I keep being delighted with the emergence of strategies discovered through gameplay!
Seriously, out of every game I've ever owned, Auro is the game that has kept my adult brain entertained the longest.
Dive in, bump some foes, give it a solid chance. You'll be glad you dropped a few bucks on a game that rivals the simplicity and elegance of the greats like Chess or Go. A modern take on a true evergreen game.

More than likely I got my hopes up as to how fun this game would be or how much I would enjoy the premise.  At the end of the day I didn't like Unholy Heights and I don't think anyone is missing out by overlooking it.
The most unfortunate thing anyone can ever say of entertainment is that it's dull, bland and boring, which summarizes Unholy Heights pretty well.  Hell, I wouldn't even go so far as to say it's a game.  At best it plays out like a cell phone game.  The idea is that you're running an apartment complex for monsters and that idea seemed cool but there really isn't anything to it.  Monsters stop by and if they decide they want to stay, they will ask to move in, at which point you may either accept them or do nothing and just wait.  Eventually you'll fill up your apartment and start taking on 'quests,' where adventurers attack your apartment complex.  In order to defend against the attack you must knock on the doors of your tenants so that they come out and fight for you.  You have no control over combat, and each monster is either a ranged or melee attacker.
What kills this game more than anything is the amount of waiting it requires.  There isn't gameplay, you just sit and wait for events to happen and then they do and that's it.  The amount of waiting is also fairly ridiculous if you're not using the speed up button.  Between each wave of a quest, you wait about a full minute or two for the next to begin.  That just isn't necessary.
The only 'growth' that your tenants receive is iffy at best.  Sometimes they'll find a mate and that person will move in with them, doubling the effective strength of each house (due to having two monsters).  Wait even longer and these monsters might have a child, furthering their effectiveness.  Beyond that, they work jobs -- so they're not always around for combat when you need them -- and pay rent.  Well, sometimes they pay rent.  Sometimes they just stop paying rent and then ditch in the middle of the night.  If that happens, or the tenant dies, you need to refill the room.  The trouble with this is when you lose people during a quest it severely cripples your ability to finish it, as you are unlikely to replinish your ranks much during the downtime.  You can raise the rent on the apartment or get the tenants better stuff, which allows you to raise their rent a little bit more.  Other than that, the only direct control you have on the game is sending out units to combat or returning them to their apartment during combat.
The premise of housing an apartment complex for monsters sounded interesting but there isn't any gameplay to speak of and I felt very much like I was wasting my time.  As cool as the mechanics may sound, they don't hold up in any way due to a lack of control.  Further, the ♥♥♥♥ing waiting, man.. that's just all the game is.  Don't bother with this one.

Bought this game a while back, and i gotta say, it's no way a devil may cry game. (mostly just similar hack and slash combat system) But it's quite fun. Aside from all the non canon plot and backstory, there were acouple things i just didn't like: The story was mediocre at best, mostly predictable ending and plot points; how the game has times where it really plays its self; the distinct lack of puzzles, heck, i started the game hating the rebooted characters, espically dante, but over time, i grew to put all that behind me, that's only because i looked at this like like a different franchise all together. This game was actually challenging on average difficultly, which makes the many difficulties that more terrifying.
Some of the things i really liked about this game:
-The Music: the music in this game was all produced by one group, which gave it consistantcy. The music in the game really does a great job blending from combat music to ambience. But along with that, the music really did fit the style of the game, a little bit of edm, mixed with some metal. All the bosses had their own music, and the repeated music is really enjoyable. It really makes you want to take on every demon spawn that comes your way!
-The level design/overall art style: if theres one thing i love the most about this game, it's the levels, so much work went into this world (espically when you get to the tv place). It really feels like a unique experience every level, which was something a few of the original dmc games lacked. The artstyle was the real cherry on top, they really didn't try for realism in this game (original artstyle is one of my favorite things) they had a comicbook/western animation style, and stuch with it.
-satisfying gameplay and combat: this game was well cared for in the combat mechanics department, it feels so great to slash and bash enemies, and the combos are much easier to obtain (unlike in previous installments in the series)
The weapons in this game are also compelling, from powerfists to shurikens, you'll be wanting to use all of the weapons to get as high of a hit score as possible, and with a simple weapon switching system, you can pull of alot of diverse combos, and feel like a badass the whole time.
sure, some of the enemies are annoying.. but that just makes it all the more satisfying when you kill the last one and get that slow-mo money shot.
Overall: if you're a die-hard dante fan, maybe don't play this one (unless you're openminded) but if you like hack and slash games, like beyonetta, or god of war, that means you don't really give a damn about plot, and this game is for you.
If you really want to get started with this genre of video game, I absolutely recommend this game

If you're looking for a great tactics game with loads of replayability, look no futher than Auro!

The visuals and dialogue are full of charm and Auro is very inviting and easy to get into.
If you like tactics games, you won't regret picking this one up.

I played Auro a lot on my phone so I was excited to see it coming to my preferred platform. Auro is a game where you really feel like your decisions matter, one mistep could cost you your advantage and put you on the defensive, but when you get that perfect combo and watch your enemies sink it's incredibly satisfying. The pixel art adds an unmistakable charm and it's obvious that a lot of work went into art as well as gameplay, The deeper you look into this game the more you see what makes it great.

I started playing the mobile version of Auro during beta almost four years ago and am really excited to finally have it on my PC as well. After all this time and thousands upon thousands of matches, I'm still playing it almost every day. At this point I can safely say that this is one of the BEST VIDEO GAMES EVER.
While it may seem simple and like a typical "mobile game" at first sight, there is a LOT more to it. The emergent depth this game unfolds over time is quite incredible and puts at least 90% of all PC and console game releases to shame. Every piece, every single rule, in the game has been balanced and honed for years to make for one of the best examples we have of a well-designed gameplay system. Rest assured that you have never played a "dungeon crawler" like this before.
The laser-sharp focus on the core mechanism of "bumping" makes every monster and spell in the game work together beautifully. On top of that though, the "competitive single-player" metagame is nothing less than revolutionary in how it does away with pretty much every typical problem of match-based "highscore" single-player games.
Do yourself a favor and buy this game! And in doing so, tell the world that good gameplay matters more than audiovisual pomp and exploitative business models.

I played this game loads on Android last year, and they've really overhauled it for the steam version. The game never looked terrible, but the new coat of paint looks great and is definitely appreciated. The campaign mode, too, has been re-themed and reworked. I should warn the people thinking of buying - this is a tactics game through and through. If you're looking for an immersive story or buckets of content you should go elsewhere. But if you enjoy strategy games like Advance Wars, Final Fantasy Tactics, Outwitters, or even Chess then you'll get a lot of value out of Auro. The game starts simple, but put in a little effort and it rapidly ramps up the number of pieces on the board and becomes pretty deep.
I'll probably be putting as many hours into this as I did on the mobile version. I recommend it to anyone who likes tactics games.

Unholy Heights is a simple tower defense game. It focuses on you, as the devil, renting out apartment spaces to other monsters that just want to live a normal life but are constantly attacked by people. The art design really caught my attention when I decided to play this game. However, that alone was not able to sustain my interest.
-Lack of customization. It'd be great if you could change the aesthetic look of the apartment to your liking. It'd also be great if you can look into each individual room and arrange the furniture. Instead, we're stuck looking at the outside view of the apartment.
-Monsters grow stronger only if they are satisfied with their room. There should be more options available than this.
-Battles are random encounters with unsatisfying rewards.
-If you're being attacked and some tenants aren't there because they're at work or school, then it makes it more difficult for you. Without a lot of depth in monster growth and gameplay, it's frustrating.
-There needs to be a time system in game. I don't know when my tenants leave or when they come back. It would help greatly in planning when to do quests.
-Progress is random. You don't know when your tenant will get a spouse or a raise at work. Sometimes, it took long for me, sometimes it only took me a few minutes.
-Quests are very boring. There aren't any unique quests other than defeating enemies.
-There's no way to heal your tenants. When you get couples, they spend so much time doing "pillow talking" and it reduces their health. With this occurring randomly, it's difficult to plan out random encounters or doing quests.
-The siren is loud, annoying and unnecessary.
-Realistically, the more time you put into the game, the more successful you will be. Most of the game is random and there's no strategy to it like other tower defense games.
I'm disappointed because I expected a lot from this game. There was so much potential that was not utilized. If you enjoy casual gaming, then this is definitely a game for you. If you want a game that has depth in gameplay, I suggest looking somewhere else.

It is a roguelite action platfromer, that plays like Mega Man X. It has local, and online co-op. Three difficulty modes to choose from. One gives you lives, another one does not. And the hardest one adds modifiers much like the skulls from Halo, in addition to no lives.
You have two characters, one plays like Mega Man, (Long distance blaster shots) the other plays like Zero. (Short range sword blows)
There are also extra modes. One simply makes the levels much larger, another one is a endless mode. And you got your daily challenges, and seeded modes.
Overall, it's got some issues, and there are better games in the genre, but it's a solid game with a decent amount of content in there.
It's worth the money but at the time of this review the Co-op needs lots of work (it's still in alpha)

First off, I am, probably like most of you, a humungous Mega Man, Mega Man X, Mega Man Legends etc. fan. Anything Mega Man, I love. I saw this game and immediately wanted to buy it.
The clips I saw made it look incredible, but I was worried that it wouldn't play or feel as good as it looked.
Well, worry not. This game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. It is SMOOTH, the controls are tight, you rarely feel like you're not in control of your character (except with insanely high run speed - but I'm bad lol) and one of the best things is, every run is different. Sure, there are the same bosses, same levels (More hazards do appear the later you do the levels, regardless of order so they are always increasing in difficulty) but I've had runs where I can steam roll bosses AND levels due to an armor set bonus, jump height and damage, then I've had runs where I can barely make it through the last level !
I'm waiting for this to stop being fun, but it keeps getting better.
This game is not only an amazing homage to Mega Man X games, but it's an amazing game in general. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes Mega Man - but even if you just like platformers or "roguelikes" give it a shot.

All hail the return of Offensive Combat (Redux)!
TL;DR: Formerly F2P, bawdy FPS from COD devs gets resuscitated as a full game with real support from the developer. Offensive Combat Redux is frenetic, colorful, and fun, and was brought back by fans, for fans. It’s a fun and accessible game for those not interested in mainstream offerings.
What you get for your money: A full featured FPS multiplayer experience with enough “coins” at the start to let you buy the skin of your choice, and loadout two complete weapons. Unlike the F2P original, all weapons are unlocked at the beginning of OCR (better for noobs), but customization remains with an upgrade system of earned-in-game coins (no paywalls, no real money for keys to open loot boxes).
The shooting is (still) satisfying, with great feedback showing you how much damage each of your shots does. All the weapons have different strengths and weaknesses, so you can easily find a weapon that matches your play style. Weapon design is varied and well refined. Movement is good, and you can still stop on a dime and shoot someone in the face.
If you play a lot of shooters, OCR stylistically sits between TimeSplitters: Future Perfect and Loadout. It’s sassy, silly, and in no way takes itself seriously, while still delivering a solid, classic FPS experience. The game has a lot of modes, some of which you won’t play often, as classic death match is OCR’s strength. However, solo play with smart bots is still challenging for most of us, and a welcome relief if you are taking a pounding from real players all night. For me, the inclusion of a bot mode is a real gift for the game’s long-tail, ensuring OCR is playable for years.
This version of OCR is built from the code of the last playable version before U4iA imploded and the game went the way of the dodo. OCR is a passion project for the devs who loved the original and were able to buy the IP and last codebase in order to revive the game.
Some of the reviewers seem to reflect the content of the beta test rather than the actual release--in the beta everything was unlocked (how else are you going to test it?). Everything is not unlocked in the final version. As I mentioned, paying full price for a the game gets you enough coins to buy a complete skin for your character, and to completely upgrade two guns. All melee weapons have the same stats, except for the rubber chicken which gains you experience every time you use it--this is exactly like the F2P version. OCR devs unlocking all weapons at start means noobs actually have a chance to have fun instead of being fodder, and grind less. Also, unlocked weapons means you can swap out your guns and experiment with each one before going down the customization route. Player skins are cosmetic (as they should be).
For me, the only con (but not a dealbreaker) is the menu’s interface showing is it’s age--it’s a double-edge sword of preserving the original game’s character at the expense of modern interface design. That being said, the extensive customization requires an complex interface, and it get the job done. As an online PC game, it has online PC game performance. You are limited by your hardware, your bandwidth and the quality of your connection.
If you played the original Offensive Combat and loved it, you will be happy with Offensive Combat Redux. If you have never played OC before, OCR is a good way to get started--it's fast, it's fun, and it has plenty of content while respecting your wallet.
I played a lot of the original OC, I participated in the beta, but I bought OCR the day after release with my own money.

Okay, 12 hours and I've gone through the game with all characters and unlocked All achievements.  Time for a review.
Razenroth is a Binding of Isaac style game with unlocks and the "dark stones", a persistance mechanic that lets you upgrade your base of operations.  Controls are responsive and there are multiple characters to unlock.  As you kill monsters you level up and increase your stats and choose a new passive ability every 3 levels.  You find or buy gear and defeat stronger monsters to gain dark crystals and trinkets or get them by performing fetch quests.  The cons are that the game has a few odd design choices that can confuse new players.
You have 4 options in combat.
Boss design- Each boss looks fairly unique and requires a different strategy to take down.  Which can be a welcome change from brainlessly attacking.
Inventory- The number of combinations of gear you can have is very large, and all the boots, cloaks and hats change your character's appearance.
Passive items-While there are alot of bland, hp+ and mp+ items, there are quite a few pets and passives that make you feel quite powerful.
Explosives- Where Binding of Isaac makes using bombs in combat a difficult and dangerous task, Razenroth allows you to push them towards the biggest clump of enemies.  They freeze, damage and fear the enemies around the explosion.  That combined with the activatable potions can make for some interesting combat choices.
Shrines- while some are boring heals and minor stat boosts, there are also ones that allow you to freeze enemies, be surrounded by a windstorm and give you an extra life!
The ending- other than a text box it is the same for every character in every mode.  Which is disappointing for anyone trying to beat Hell mode (aka the hardest mode in the game) with every character.
"Freezing" enemies-Currently, enemies can attack a second before they stop being frozen.  If the ice slowly cracked over time until it "shattered" it would prevent confusion for newer players.
Difficulty modes- The amount of damage you take goes up by a large amount, making agility to increase your speed the best way of surviving the boss battles.  This limits your ability try different builds.
The final boss- Razenroth spawns fiery pits that launch homing attacks at you that heal the boss when they hit you.  The orbs expire but if you have a slower character, dodging them is very difficult.  This artificially lengths the final battle and adds a fake level of difficulty.
Design choices- okay there are a bunch of minor choices that, when taken together, undermine some of the fun of the game.  I would let these go but it would be sooooo easy to change them from a programming perspective.
Summary- I would recommend this game to anyone trying to be a game designer.  I think that the price-tag is reasonable, and the atmosphere, while not fully scary is unique to the game.  The number of design decisions alone are educational and the art direction shows that a lot of loving care from the developers.  Do I think that 12 hours is worth 43 more achievements?  That’s more a personal choice than anything else, but with luck, this will expand the market for Isaac-like games.

Strangely enticing. It has somewhat of an Animal Crossing feel to it, where the overall look and feel of the game is cutesy, and mentally engaging.
You play as the Devil, and you've somehow gone and blown all your money. So what does the ruler of the underworld gotta do to make a load of money? Naturally, it's become a landlord. Before long, you'll have monsters moving into your four apartment block, and you'll have to tend to their furniture needs whilst fighting off various 'good guy' types that come to try and thwart your money-making plan.
Eventually, things start getting a tad busy - you begin to have multiple floors in your block, and tougher invaders will start showing up. I found myself truly exploring my devilish side when this started happening - monsters that live in your apartments have the capacity to skip out on the rent you set for them, and I thought 'well, if they're not paying up I'll just send them into battle first. And they won't get the furniture they ask for.'. Not before long, you've got lavish rooms that act as bait for 'cannon fodder' monsters - ones that don't seem to do well. From then on, you're in between taking up various challenges from the quest board, and maintaining your monster's satisfaction, since they will gain power based on how happy they are.
The concept sounds simple enough, but beleive me Petit Depotto certainly did not skimp out on any detail of this game. Monsters can attract mates, engage in...er..'pillowtalk', have kids, go to work, do the housework, go for a walk, play outside...it's a very clever comedic factor when you click on a room and see one of your monsters are 'reading an erotic fanfiction' or 'sexually harrassing a pop star', and injects a very 'slice of life' feeling into the game: you see these monsters have lives, and fight, and love - you're the Devil, doing his everyday administration. The whole concept is a very cute, 'a day in the life of' thing, and is bound to put a smile on your face when you play it.
The music alone leaves me grinning at the monitor like an idiot.
Overall, this is creativity in indie gaming to the maximum - a solid, novel twist on the tower defence type game and beautiful to experience. The art is like it's straight out of a picture book and envelopes the player with warmth, but when the going gets tough, you gotta be prepared to flex your brain muscles. If you're a fan of action-micromanagement games like Plants vs. Zombies and Recettear, then this is for you.

Welcome to Unholy Heights, a cutesy 2D tower defense game with a lot of personality and charm. You are the devil that has just purchased a tenement. Just one tenement, there are no scenarios or anything, just this one tenement in the game. As time goes by, creatures will stop by to visit your apartment building, then they'll want to rent a room assuming you have free rooms. If you take them in, they'll take up residence.
This diverse array of creatures will then go about life. They'll head to work, sleep, eat, fall in love, have babies. You really have no control over what they do. The real game comes into play when at the end of the day and night cycle when a hero comes to your apartment to rob it and or kill your creatures. So what do you do to defend your building? Click on your doors to knock on them and they'll come out to fight. The only catch is will they might be at work and not in the apartment. Eventually, the creatures will come back from work and be able to fight if not start fighting when they bump into someone.
Each enemy has one of three types of attacks: melee, mid range and long range. Your foes will have the same style of attacks. Its a nice system and since each creature lives in a different room, you can wait for the enemies to get to the center of your building, then call the first and last apartment to pinch them where they can't run away. They can also do the same to you of course. If one of your creatures gets weak, simply click them again and they'll run away to their room, to your devil headquarters or away from the building.
These daily attacks are more and less a grind. They won't give you much gold. Instead your tenants will give you daily gold in rent. If you want the most gold, you'll take on quests by clicking the sign on your screen. These quests result in larger enemy amounts in usually 3 waves. These 3 waves take place in short amount of times, so make sure your creatures are healthy. Each of these quests has a star / difficulty rating and bonus gold for completing it. Some quests are mandatory in red, and others are optional, but the optional quests seem more like steps to the red quests.
If an enemy gets to the top of your building, they steal gold and try to get away with it. If an enemy makes it out alive, you'll fail the quest and can do it again. It is a very forgiving system that keeps you in the game with no real way to lose. You'll always have creatures wanting to move in if you have an empty building.
So what do you do with all of this gold? When you're not being attacked, you can click on a room and see the inhabitants of the room, along with everything in the room. The tenants will want specific things like CD Players, fans, playing cards, plants and so on. You'll need to buy them things and by doing so, your creatures will be able to gain defense, attack and so on.
You'll also be tasked with keeping your residents happy, which really seems easy enough. Every type of creature has different needs to become happy. Such as skeletons need to defeat enemies, one type needs to live amongst plants or it'll get sick and other creatures become happy or sad based on the overall joy of the tenement. Some of your creatures will become sad if there are creatures they hate living in the building. The bestiary shows everything.
You can raise or lower the rent, and creatures each have jobs, so if they can't meet the rent, they can fall behind. Then it is your choice, do you evict them? Lower their rent? Or just make rent free to keep the good creatures you've worked into deadly killers. When new creatures arrive you can see their job so you know if they're some deadbeat cigarette butt collector or just unemployed in general. That doesn't stop paying tenants from falling in love with unemployed creatures that do nothing.
Eventually, you'll be able to add more floors to your tenement, along with unlocking more types of creatures and objects for their homes. Not just that, but you'll see the creatures fall in love and later have babies. What does this all mean for you? When there are 2 creatures living together, that's just more attackers for you. Their babies will grow into adults and be able to fight as well. Creatures can only fall in love and breed with creatures of the same species. There are consumable items such as balloons that will help a resident find love, and erotic cakes that will help a couple make a baby. Of course there are less funny consumable items like health potions as well. Your creatures will gain health when they eat, so you don't really need to micromanage anything.
In all, this is a really quirky, one of a kind game that I can highly recommend. The only down side is there seems to be a lot of grinding before you can get through the quests. The game does a great job of explaining things especially compared to other sim games. The game also seems underpriced, but if they had different scenarios, I could understand them having a higher price. The game has the right amount of depth to keep me interested, without overwhelming me.

I've owned every single Devil May Cry game that has come out. Numbers 1-3 on PS2. Devil May Cry 4 and DmC for PS3 (Came with Vergil's downfall pre-order bonus and Samurai skin pack) and the HD Collection of Devil May Cry 1-3 on PS3.
Ohh...and I bought Ultimate Marvel Vs Capcom 3 just for Dante and Vergil bby!
So, even though I'm not a die hard fan, I may know just a little about the Devil May Cry franchise....just a little.
I got the Capcom Humble Bundle that included the Special Edition of Devil May Cry 4 (allows you to play as Vergil, Lady and Trish) and this game was also included in the bundle (So now, I have second copy of this game -_- ).
General:
The story in itself is completely from scratch and unrelated to the previous Devil May Cry series. This is a reboot of the franchise. So you don't have to worry if you haven't yet played the previous 'Devil May Cry' games. The characters are nothing like the originals, which probably p-is-sed off a lot of die hard fans. Since I'm not a die-hard fan, it didn't really affect me as much as it should. They creators do redeem themselves by adding a skin you could put on which pays homage to the original Dante.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very fluid and smooth, everything you could ask for in a hack and slash type of game. It delivers quite well, if I were to compare it to 'Metal Gear Rising Revengence' and 'Killer is Dead', DmC is definitely superior to the other two I mentioned in terms of gameplay.
Music:
The soundtrack is nice, there's some screamo type of music during battles, though I was hoping they added 'ONE OK ROCK'S - Nothing Helps' somewhere in here, even if just in the credits, because they did use that track to promote the game.
Pros:
- I do like the elements of the new take on Angelic and Demonic powers they added into this game.
- The combat system is great. If you were to take anything away from this game, be it at least that.
- For the fans for Vergil, the Vergil's downfall DLC allows you to play as him.
Cons:
- Story wasn't really that great. It didn't really draw me in but it was a nice attempt.
- Dante tries to hard to look and act cool, swears alot and behaves rude/rashly, completely alien from the Dante we once knew. But hey, some people might like this new character.
Overall it's a great game to play, I had a lot of fun and not just during combat but during other functions and action sequences of the game too. The story is really easy to follow.

This game is really good. It's something I keep going back to just for the gameplay, which is a good thing for a video game to have.
I don't really have a problem with the story, it's good enough, and I like the characters and the script well enough even though you might cut yourself on all the edge. It's not really good, just good enough.
But what really matters is the gameplay, which is really good. Is it easy to get that SSS rank on your combos? Yes. Does that make it any less fun? Nope, it's still really fun to knock a demon up in the air and bounce it on the ground until it dies.
The only thing I found myself annoyed with was the platforming. Thankfully these sections don't drag on for too long before you're right back in the action.
Definitely get this game if you like hardcore action games.

Let me start by saying that while I do say I would recommend this game, it's only because there are two options to choose from. I think saying I wouldn't recommend this game is a bit harsh but also I wouldn't recommend this to everyone I know either.
I have about 120 hours logged in this game. That includes being a beta tester from the second week of the beta launch. I have more hours than probably anyone else in this game right now. Here are my thoughts on this game in its current form. I'm hoping some updates will fix the issues but this is my review of the game as it stands now.
Pros:
The game is fun. Simple as that. It's not insanely complex and it does get repetitive after a while but the game has a certain charm that brings me back.
The game has a lot of neat skins with more being released constantly. In the last month or so I've seen them add at least 3 new character sets to the game. Their art team is working pretty hard on this stuff.
Anti-cheat system added to the game helps keep out the cheaters. Obviously eventually someone is going to find a way around it but it's at least something.
You can play with your friends fairly easily.
There are a lot of different guns. They all feel different from one another and have pros and cons. They are mostly all balanced for the most part.
The pwn animations are fun and you will want to do them when you get a really awesome kill.
Cons:
There are only 6 maps. Three are smaller and three are big. They are all pretty fun but the lack of variety will get a little boring prety quickly.
There are not many players. The game peaked at 45 players today and steadly declined form there. As of writing this review there are 2 players online.
There are still a few bugs in the game. Most are just annoying, some are really bad though. There is a bug for crouching that messes up a player's headshot hitbox for example.
Weapon mods are boring and don't require any thinking. You just buy the obviously best mod and you're good to go.
There is no mute/ignore/kick feature yet. This is said to be added soon, but it's still not there yet. So if a toxic player joins you, you just have to play with them.
There are only 3 multiplayer game modes. Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, and Capture the Flag.
Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch are not what you think. You can't simply kill players and win at those modes. Every kill you get awards 10 points. If you pwn the dead player though, you get an additional 20 points. This means that in order to win you either have to get 3x as many kills as the next best player, or you have to pwn to win. Pwn to win gives snipers a big disadvantage. It also forces everyone to pwn even if they don't want to. It's really not a very fun system and will end up just frustrating most people. Either you will try to pwn and get killed more often, or you will choose not to pwn and lose to a player with half your kills and was clearly not the better player. Also, pwns have different times they take to finish but award the same amount of points regardless, so everyone just uses the same short length pwn.
No one plays capture the flag.
The sound design is a bit weird. They are working on it though and hopefully it'll get better.
The game is pay to play and a bit overpriced for what it is. There are a lot cheaper or free first person shooters out there with more features and a larger playerbase.
Conclusion:
Offensive Combat has a special place in my heart. I enjoyed the game when it was free to play. I think the game in its current form still needs a lot of work but the basics are there. It is a solid, enjoyable first person shooter. It doesn't have a lot of content but it has a fun, fast paced gameplay that I quickly got addicted to. I think you should come in to this game not expecting the next Overwatch. It is definitely not going to win any awards.
The community, gameplay, and customization are what brings me back to the game over and over. I enjoy just hopping in for an hour or two and unwinding. If they removed the pwn to win system, added a few more maps, made an improved mod system that had pros and cons to consider, and also maybe added a perk system, this game would be solid.
I'd give this game a 6/10.

This game is so much fun.
It should go without saying that 20XX takes a lot of inspiration from Megaman, but that doesn't mean it's not its own experience. It provides everything you would expect from a Megaman game (cool character/enemy/boss design, awesome music, tight controls, carefully crafted level design, various powers, etc.), but puts its own ideas into the mix as well, resulting in something that stands out from other Megaman clones. For example, being a rouge-like game, there is less focus on level memorization and more focus on quickly assessing any difficult situations that come up. This needs to be done well by the the player, as they only have one life and no continues. There's no need to fret though, as the game compensates for this difficulty in multiple ways. Pits and spikes, which are typically instant-kills in Megaman games, only take one unit of health in 20XX. It also incorperates an augment powerup system, so though the game may get more challenging as it goes on, the player continuously grows stronger. With enough time and a good run, the player can eventually become a near-unstoppable juggernaut (or, since the characters are robots, I guess it would be a juggerbot).
If you like Megaman, or even if you like action platforming in general, you will love 20XX. This game is so much fun.

A true Hitman game. Unparalleled openness and freedom for every level and every objective. The map design is incredible. It is simultaneously gigantic and intuitive because how much the details resembles real-life scenarios.
Crazy replayability added by the devs with timed "illusive targets", user-made contracts and such. Even with the likes of Overwatch and DOOM in 2016, this was no doubt one of the best games of that year.
This was one of the most fun games I've played over the last year. I actually thought the episodic format worked well for Hitman.

I can no longer afford the DLC because all of it is tied in a costly expansion pack. I can't buy them individually, so what's the point? If I can't buy the other levels, then I don't want to play your game!

This is a yes, but a very reluctant yes. This iteration of Hitman is bittersweet and I would highly recommend purchasing
(and only parts) of the game. I've been a big fan of Hitman Contracts and Blood Money and, honestly, what Hitman 2016 gets right is incredible. In fact, I'd say that the Sapienza, Hokkaido, and Paris levels are
Hitman levels in the entire Hitman series. Better than Traditions of the Trade, A New Life, Murder of Crows, Beldingford Manor, and Meat King's Party. Partially this is due to the vastly improved game mechanics over the earlier games. Things like suspicion and stealth levels actually make sense from a player's perspective now (no more random cover blown events). The challenge system and opportunities are a big improvement, in my opinion, as it makes the worlds feel more alive and organic.
Despite singing this game's praises, there are a lot of really crappy things attached to this, otherwise, amazing game. The only reasons I didn't purchase this day one (like I did with Blood Money) was because of the episodic release schedule and always-online DRM. The latter being completely useless and absurd for a single-player game. The top of the leaderboards are obviously hacked playthroughs and, now that IO has broken off from Square, it's hard to say how long these servers may exist. The game can be played offline, but in a very crippled way.
More frustrating, depending how you look at it, is the episodic release format for this game. Not necessary and, I'd argue, was an overall damper on Hitman's success. If this was released like a Blood Money 2.0, a single package, it would have been a home-run, despite the lackluster middle levels.
That's why, I'd suggest, only buying these three levels and not purchasing the GOTY bundles. There are still legit sites out there that sell the levels individually. All in all, you can get these three levels for about $16 and can keep you busy for a good 30-50 hours by themselves. Frankly, I wouldn't pay more than that at this point, despite how good this game is, because of the uncertainty of this game's future and the abysmal online requirements. If and when IO decides to scrap the online requirements and allows this game to be completely functional offline, I'd be willing to purchase more content from them.

Well satan since you screwed up, you are being demoted to manager of a hotel in the middle of the desert congratulations!
Your hotel is called Unholy Heights, in which keeping the residents happy and defending against heros who dare to trespass is top priority. Heros will attempt to sneak in and steal your gold, to counter them you will use the monsters who reside in your hotel. You’re residence is perfectly safe as long as they reside in the room and don’t come out to face the heros. Resources will deplete as a result, though there is no way to game over.
+ Hotel Room placement matters
+ Monsters give clear indicators of needs
+ Monsters have families/jobs
Separating enemies by using the positions of hotel rooms is a good way to separate their forces and prevent tanks from protecting the glass-cannon type enemies. The monsters have a numerous weaknesses and strengths depending on how you use them, for example a long-range caster can be good for taking hits from magical spells with enough vitality since they have more magic resistance than your knights.
Monsters will get a bonus to their stats depending on their mood. Clicking on their rooms will provide you feedback on how to improve their residence. The amount you can tax them depends on the value of the room itself. The higher the room value the more you can tax without them feeling like they are getting ripped off. Once you hit a certain point you will notice that the monsters cannot afford the hotel with the job occupations they have, so you will either have to lower it, until they can get a promotion or find more prominent monsters.
Monsters can find lovers, and eventually make babies. Which also factors into how much they can afford apartment wise. So lowering it a bit after they make a baby until he becomes an adult and can hold a job is a recommended idea. Babies generally have superior stats to their parents so wanting to breed over and over again is recommended.
Gym equipment and combat both help increase the stats of your monsters. Increasing their happiness by fulfilling their needs and increasing the value of the apartments also lead to bonuses highlighted in blue that will give you big advantages.
The quests are arranged in 3 colors, red for main quest, green for unlocking monsters, and yellow for unlocking furniture. Only one quest will ever be red at any given time since its a single main quest, with various side quests you can accomplish. There are repeatable quests per hotel floor stage so you don’t have to worry about hitting a wall.

Fun game!
Addictive and a little challenging, this unique spin on a tower defense game/apartment management game will keep you entertained for hours. The tenants are all very quirky and quite endearing; getting to hear them ‘pillow-talk’ is also hilarious.
The game itself is pretty straightforward (the how-to-play section is very helpful if you get stuck), but in mid-late gameplay it can start getting a little muddled when it comes to choosing tenants. For example, if you choose to have demi-humans in your apartment, it would not be wise to put demons in there as well (they hate each other). Though this doesn’t deeply affect your game, it does kind of suck if you like having a variety of monsters living in your apartment.
Compared to some more traditional tower defense games, your tenants are the ones on the battle field and are likely to die. It’s important to keep an eye on them if there is a battle going on and get them to retreat if the opponent is too strong. One strategy I found helpful when fighting enemy casters was to turtle: attack (ranged), retreat into room (before unit gets hit), and attack again, etc. You do develop a bit of a play-style the more you play. Don’t forget to raise the satisfaction of your tenants as well, the bonuses are super helpful.
Quite an enjoyable experience.

As a guy who came up on titles such as Gran Turismo, Forza, Gran Turismo, GTR2, rFactor etc, I tried ETS1 and UKTS, craving a change of pace, but came away from it a little discouraged by the unnecessary constraints it would place on you (dumb time-frames namely, with no remit for exploration).
Enter ETS2. I had just came back from an episode at the hospital and couldn't go to work for a week or so, so I installed this at 10 in the morning and was still going at 6 in the evening. It has so many compelling aspects which may seem weird to the uninitiated, but make so much sense once you play.
Nice selection of licenced trucks, you bet! Massive scale map, check. Customisation options and a massive modding community, yep. A great sense of progression as a driver and eventually also a business owner, it's all here. They combine to make a game which rewards perseverance, provides a nice break from my otherwise fast-paced games and satisfy that need for a relaxing drive with ever-changing scenery. I'm convinced it has made my real driving better!
As for cons and caveats, I would love to see some new trucks from SCS, but the large modding community alleviates this for the most part. This game is playable with a controller (it's how I started on ETS2), but I strongly recommend you play this with a wheel which has 900 degrees of rotation (2.5 turns each way) to get the sense of control intended. DLC is a lil pricey but I reckon it's been worth it (I got the SCS collection then recently bought the Vive Le France DLC).
If I had to rate this out of 10, it gets a 9.5 from me!

Ori in the blind Forest is a excellent, difficult, and beautiful Platformer developed on the PC and Xbox. It tells the tale of Ori and a forest called Nigel as disaster strikes and everything gets covered in death and decay and your goal is to restore life in  forest.
That is the story in its most basic form and it developes as you continue through the different regions and collect life, energy, and abilities to make you extremely mobile and be able to traverse everything the games throws at you and it gets crazy toward the end. The difficulty in Ori is platforming and enemies but you are more likely to die to the obstacles and spikes. Theres a part of the game involving water that people dub as extremely hard even though I went through the event and found it very fun and easy.
The art in the game which makes up most if not everything you will see on screen, a fair bit of the art looks like oil paintings while characters and certain elements are in 3D like water and Ori might be but its hard to tell while playing.
The music is beautiful with many melodies that change per area you enter and during events. kind of reminds me of Dust an Elysian tail. actually there both really similar except Ori Doesnt focus on combat and Dust focuses less on platforming. There both metroidvania which means you gradually progress through the game and unlock items and abilities to progress with backtracking common and necessary to progress. there also littered with collectibles that help with either health energy or abilities luckily every necessary ability to beat the story is in your path. there are two or three abilities exclusive to the definitive edition dash and light grenades(thats basicaly what they are) are the only ones not necessary to beat the story. though the dash is nice and helpful it makes late game areas easier.
So for me this game is art litterally take a high definition shot of this post it on a mural and people can call it art. The story is intriguing and interesting though i have questions involving certain elements of the story, it doesnt make it bad at all. the music is extremely nice though i like lyrical music better, this might have lyrics it is very good. and gameplay is almost entirely platforming and puzzle solving so dont expect much other than that but that still makes it great since platformers arent that popular now a days.
I highly recommend Ori and the Blind Forest.

text:
This game originally failed because of core problems that existed in the game and the complete ineptitude of the developers (when they were Real Time Worlds) to fix or at the very least alleviate these problems.
Now on top of those issues you have an utterly broken cash shop system that will ruin  your experience 95% of the time.
To start I should address some of the original problems that plagued the game on it's original releaes, guns were (and still are) terrible to use and the application of modifications does not make that any better. The gunplay feels clunky and the recoil on most weapons make it impossible to hit anything less than 5 feet infront of you. that is unless you use specifc weapons.
Cars are in the same boat as guns, for a cops and robbers MMO, you think they would be able to get the driving down. This is not the case. The car physics are terrible and they don't control that great either.
The mission system is absolute garbage, you can follow through multiple objectives, winning one after another. but if you fail the final one (, you will instantly, ignoring the fact taht you and your side were dominating the opposition;; fail the entire mission (And I find this happens more for the enforcer faction than the criminal faction, in all my time playing). This is further problematic with the addition cash shop weapons.
Now your thinking: Wow, hopefully the new developer and publishers would of picked up this game up and would of tried to fix these issues, which while do not make the game unplayable, do not provide an enjoyable experience for prolonged periods of time.
Well, no. They ignored these issues.
And I haven't even mentioned the games instability, poor performance even with modern hardware. or the failure for the game to completely shut-down once your done playing (One of the processes used in the game will ALWAYS STAY UP).
What they did bring to the game. was one of the worst things they could of done. They added a cash shop for guns, no no, not cosmetics. these guns have an actual performance advantage over other guns that you can actually aquire through gameplay.
These wonderful items provide superior damage, little to no recoil in addition to some other effects they can provide.
This damages the poor mission matchmaking and balancing because if your enemy team has these weapons, and you don't well, your screwed. in laymans terms.
Now to be fair, the new devs have actually added some content in the game with the addition of the "Chaos district" and in game events. These aren't that great though, they aren't even the quality of the RTW content (Which isn't that great either), and the events are hampered by people rampantly cheating. Which I forgot to mention, is incredibly commonin this game (from outright use of hacks, to exploiting faults with the game or going out of bounds.)
the only positive thing I can say about the game is it's customisation system. and, unfortunately ,that hasn't seen any improvements since release of the ORIGNAL release. There is very little added to customise yourself since then (that that which is added is cash shop items -- go figure.) and while the emblem creator is nice and all that, if you don't have the ability to use it (since you cannot import emblems and pictures, you use geometric shapes to create them) thats just a wasted feature, and you will be dependant on the auction house to find anything you want. Which is ALSO an issue since people find it prudent to sell their crap for stupid huge amounts of money, and you can't filter or search by name of what your looking for. so if you want anything past "T" for example. be prepared for LE EPIC TROLL FACE MEME XDDD!!! for the next 40 pages.
To sum this up: If your looking for a GTA MMO, this isn't that. go play GTA instead, if your looking for a fun Free-to-Play game, this Definitely isn't for you. becuase this game is by no means "Free" and it's not fun either. I tried to cover everything I experience in my time playing this game, I probably missed something that would make me go for another 5 paragraphs. so it's best to stop here.
TL;DR: Games♥♥♥♥♥♥ p2w garbage. devs don't give a crap about the game and army of cheaters, go play some other game.

Just like I said about the original Borderlands, it's really hard to put this game into words. Borderlands 2 is Borderlands 2. There's really nothing it can be compared with. While there are some people out there who insist on comparing it with its predecessor, they are still two different games, no matter which way you look at it. In my Borderlands review, I praised it for its characters, humour and open world and even after playing Borderlands 2, I sustain to that. But this game builds on that
. While the first game was enjoyable, this game is
. It's just so much more polished and has taken the franchise to the next level. After playing the original, playing this was like time travel - and in a sense it was, as it takes place after the story of the first game. But what I really mean is that everything is just better. Better graphics, better AI, better inventory, better locations, better HUD, the list just goes on and on. That's not to say that the original isn't worth playing, I'm just saying that it would be difficult to play the first game after experiencing this. But if you start on the original and go on to play this, your experience will be enriched. Also, there are references to the first game and even its DLC, so I do recommend playing those first.
However, if you're not too concerned about the story and just want a great gameplay experience, I still strongly recommend this game. I recommend it even more if you have a group of friends to play with as that will greatly enhance your experience (and will allow you to get better loot, or so the game tells me). This game is just on point, right across the board. The story is awesome with its diverse charcters including one of the greatest villains
in history. The loot system is incredible and will end up being your primary motivation for playing this game as there are some pretty crazy and overly powerful weapons that can be obtained. The music is just spectacular and creates the perfect mood to appreciate the beautifully unique graphics, or in most cases, slaughter hundreds upon hundreds of enemies. The humour is unrivalled in the gaming industry, as you could almost call it a feature of the game.
Put simply, this game is amazing. It is definitely one of my favourite games of all-time and I intend to continue playing it, at least until Gearbox release the next instalment.

I left my base area on my recently fitted truck - just a seat and solar panel to save room for research items.  As a drove around the beautiful planet, I found many items to collect and loaded them on my truck.  Unfortunately I ran out of room so had to start leaving some behind with beacons next to them.  I also lost my bearings as to which direction my base was and took my best guess towards home.  As I ventured, I seemed to be going to wrong way but, glory be, crashed space ship wreckage began appearing and I decided to take items from the wreckage with me and leave behind my previously collected research items.
Still quite lost but not worried as the beauty of this vast planet was intriguing me.  I decided to make my best guesses towards home while still exploring and leaving beacons behind from later.
I was weathering storms and avoiding my truck from falling into vast caverns.  That is when it happened.  A hidden cavern suddenely appeared below me and my truck fell down and got stuck.  As I was trying to form the land around me to rescue my truck I fell further and died.
Incredibly dissapointed in losing all of my collected items and my truck in a cavern that I know not where it is, I decided to begin on my recovery efforts.
Instead of leaving my base blindly, I decided it would be best to try and find the direction of my own wreckage.  I built a tower - higher than the clouds by forming the land below me.  My tower was the highest point on the planet, I could actually see the curvature of the planet from the top but, alas, no sign of beacons or my truck.
Next step was to build a shuttle, and that I did.  Upon completion of my shuttle, I launched into orbit (with plenty of tethers on my person) and orbited my planet a few times before spotting what I believed to be the wreckage.
I landed my shuttle as close to the wreckage as possible and tethered over.  It was the cave, I could tell because my previous work on the land was visible but my truck was not in sight.  I decided to dig down and, after some time, I saw it.  My truck and research pods had fallen even deeper into the underground abyss.
I was able to tether and form the land around me to reach them.  I then began to explore the cavarn to find a way to drive my truck out.  Luckily, this was the easier part of my adventure.
And now here I sit, my truck next to my shuttle. I believe I'm on the other side of the planet at this point but I have confidence that I will prevail.  I am about to clean up my tethers and then begin the journey towards, hopefully, home.  Wish me luck.

As a guy who came up on titles such as Gran Turismo, Forza, Gran Turismo, GTR2, rFactor etc, I tried ETS1 and UKTS, craving a change of pace, but came away from it a little discouraged by the unnecessary constraints it would place on you (dumb time-frames namely, with no remit for exploration).
Enter ETS2. I had just came back from an episode at the hospital and couldn't go to work for a week or so, so I installed this at 10 in the morning and was still going at 6 in the evening. It has so many compelling aspects which may seem weird to the uninitiated, but make so much sense once you play.
Nice selection of licenced trucks, you bet! Massive scale map, check. Customisation options and a massive modding community, yep. A great sense of progression as a driver and eventually also a business owner, it's all here. They combine to make a game which rewards perseverance, provides a nice break from my otherwise fast-paced games and satisfy that need for a relaxing drive with ever-changing scenery. I'm convinced it has made my real driving better!
As for cons and caveats, I would love to see some new trucks from SCS, but the large modding community alleviates this for the most part. This game is playable with a controller (it's how I started on ETS2), but I strongly recommend you play this with a wheel which has 900 degrees of rotation (2.5 turns each way) to get the sense of control intended. DLC is a lil pricey but I reckon it's been worth it (I got the SCS collection then recently bought the Vive Le France DLC).
If I had to rate this out of 10, it gets a 9.5 from me!

This is an awesome rogue-like platformer that is both challenging and rewarding. It has some mega-man aesthetic with an art style akin to Brawlhalla. Platforming and movement controllers are tight, bosses get tough, and co-op adds another layer of chaos to a run. This game offers great incentive to come back and play more by offering permanent upgrades that are purchased using the harder to come by in-game currency (the longer you play the better permanent upgrades you can get) as well as allowing players to spend previously acquired currency on items to start the next run with. Since it allows you to start back at level 1 but maintain some upgrades that had been worked towards in previous runs as well as unlocking new items that will drop in the next run, the permadeath mechanic isn't so punishing that it would turn players away but adds the risk and difficulty that comes with a roguelike. Overall it is a great balance of generosity and challenge and offers smooth gameplay that works amazingly well at higher levels once the pace and difficulty begins to ramp up exponentially.
There are also various timed challenges you can complete daily, weekly, or at other intervals for more rewards and overall is a great package that allows for some of the most engaging roguelike platforming out there.

X3: Albion Prelude remains to this day a stellar paragon of development follow-through. Despite a publishing infrastructure that pushed this out into the world only "mostly" finished, for years afterwards this has been lovingly maintained and updated and honed and fine-tuned. The community surrounding it is a treasure trove of supplementary data to inform your gameplay and generally extremely pleasant. And the game itself, well, if you make it at least some way along the somewhat steep learning curve and the many options for free sandbox style play where you can choose and keep varying your occupations as a fighter, pirate, trader, empire builder, fleet manager and armada captain in a huge game universe that keeps evolving, then you will quickly realise just how many hundreds or thousands of hours of quality solo gaming time there is to be had here. Years in, it still looks gorgeous, the sound and music still do not grate on your nerves, and the atmosphere is still one to thouroughly immerse oneself in again and again. Luckily, I have mostly played with an offline (no-Steam) patch provided upon community request by the developer, so I must never admit to myself the thousands of hours I have enjoyed playing this! One of my all-time favourite games and still worth checking out today, especially the expanded, revamped version, X3: Albion Prelude, and to be preferred over X: Rebirth, its bold but ultimately disappointing sequel! Keep playing X3: Terran Conflict and/or X3: Albion Prelude until X4 Foundations comes out and has had a few years to mature!

SUMMARY
This game is one hell of a ride (pun intended). Has a few issues but otherwise it's well worth the purchase. I've had a great time with this game so far and I'm sure I'll be coming back to it in the future
PROS
- So much fun to play

- Has an amazing style that shows heavy goth and punk roots

- There's a surprisngly deep lore hidden in this game for those willing to look

- Soundtrack is fantastic
- The Vergil DLC is just as fun as the main game

CONS
- Camera can get annoying, keeps locking on to enemies even when you're trying to navigate
- Really short story - finished entire game in an afternoon
- The price of healing items increases after each purchase which means it's next to impossible to buy any near the end of the game when you need them the most
- Playing with a keyboard is... difficult. Strongly recommend using a controller instead
