Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is arguably the best in the series (also my personal favorite). This game follows Carl Johnson who returns to San Andreas when his mom is murdered. Throughout the story we learn about some treason in his gang, Grove Street Families. I won't go into details since that would spoil the story...
There are so many things to do in this "3D Universe GTA", swimming, gyms, hunger (yes, you can become hungry after a ridiculous amount of time and eventually die from it), stats (lung capacity, fat, stamina, muscle, weapon levels, driving skill, etc.), flying planes, flying helicopters, parachuting, and so much more! Each stat can be increased/decreased from its corresponding activity. For example, fat is affected by eating. The larger the meal, obviously the fatter you get, but you can buy salads for generally the same price as the most expensive food and not gain weight. Muscle is affected by cycling, weights, climbing, and other activities that logically bring up muscle in real life. You can lose muscle by not doing anything active or hunger, like fat...
Guns are also affected by this skill system now. If you pick up an AK47 and try shooting someone with it in the game, Carl will hold it poorly, be unable to move while firing, strafe slowly, and will be highly inaccurate. However the more you use this weapon, the better he holds the gun, he will eventually be able to strafe while firing, strafe faster, and be extremely accurate.
Driving skill is self explainatory so I won't go into detail.
Cycling skill affects the speed you can get a bicycle to, the higher the jumps, and the less chance that you fall off. Also, self explainatory.
I'm sure you don't want me to go on about the skills any longer, now we shall go onto the minigames.
You can play a wide range of minigames such as video games, billiards (pool), and go on dates (yes, dates). There are only 3 video games, but these can be fun to play with friends. Billiards is only single player. Fun fact, there was actually supposed to be a multiplayer billiards activity but sadly, it never made it into the game... And the dates... So there are multiple women that you meet throughout the game by story (like Catalina) and some you meet outside of missions and are sort of hidden. Each one has certain activities that they like to do and most have a specific body type they want you to have. One likes you to be a bit fatter than muscular, and another wants you to have no fat and max muscle. Good luck juggling them around because you have to do all that in one day. Yes, you have to go on dates all across San Andreas everyday, and switch your body type pretty much every time. Hope you have cheats active...
In my opinion, the story could be better, but it's not the worst in the series. I'd say GTA III had the least interesting story, but then again, I've yet to complete it. Anyway back to this, the story starts off as Carl being a gangster, but ends in him being one of the richest men in San Andreas. Don't ask me why, but he does. I'd rate the story about 7/10. Like I said, it's not awful but it's not great...
If you've played GTA Vice City or GTA III before, you know the controls can be a little hard to use at times. This game changed this for the most part... You can now orbit the camera around the character, climb objects, and most importantly, YOU CAN SWIM! If I remember correctly this game started the ability to swim.
Speaking of starting something, this game started and ended the legacy of the jetpack. It was the first game to feature it which was AWESOME! However, this easy mode of transportation has yet to appear in the "HD Universe GTA" games. There's really not much to talk about it, you fly up, slowly go down, move forward, sideways, backward, it's basically being able to walk in the air...
This game also started the car customization. Yes, almost any car could be upgraded, but bikes you couldn't. Also, though you can customize your car, it's mainly hydraulics, color, nitrous, paint jobs, and wheels. There's a radio bass boost feature but on PC, it really doesn't help. Don't waste the $100 it costs...
If you want to mod this, you might want to buy a physical PC disk and install it off that. Take this from someone who's tried to mod the Steam version, you can't. If you don't want to mod this and don't plan to in the future, then you should probably get this as it's the most stable version...
You're probably bored of reading this by now and I applaud you for getting this far because there's a lot of stuff in this review. But this game, is definitely worth at least trying. If you don't know how good it really is, you can look up stuff about it on the internet... Or of course, you could buy it and refund it.

The game that pretty much defined my early childhood. This is absolutely great and a classic game every PC gamer should own! Unfortunately, I have some bad news and good news. Firstly, this Steam version is not particularly great - it misses SA:MP - the multiplayer mode of which I made countless friends! Also, some songs have been removed, You can find out which songs have been removed here:
[
]
Thankfully you can add all of these songs again in the customizable radio station. My honest advise to you is that you follow a guide on the internet and legally downgrade this game to an earlier version, preferably versions in the v1.x range ('x' stands for random number/s). Also, some game physics are broken (such as the car physics and overall driving which is downright numb when framerate is manually unlocked) when you remove frame limiter. The game is otherwise capped at 25fps which is awful to say the least. However, that can easily be fixed with a downgrade in the version and a mod to patch the physics for 60fps usage. It all takes a while though, but it is all worth it in the end.
Of course this is a fantastic and hilarious game in its own right, even though it is aging now. I would give this Steam version or any unmodded version a 7/10 (because of technically glaring issues) and a fixed version a 9/10.
Getting it on Steam is a safe bet, but the best way to enjoy this game is to simply buy a retail copy as the downgrading process is not necessary.

Right off the bat, this is a great game.
It's a great spin on Megaman-style action platformers by introducing rogue-like elements.
Gameplay:
I love the amount of optional risk-and-reward type augments that players are given in each run.
I also think the crushing difficulty of the final area of the game is fair, it's meant to serve as an early run ender that players work towards both with skill and unlocks. This balance of skill and unlocks already puts it way over so many other current rogue-likes that feel too reliant on random chance to get a good run rather than skill.
I really dig the ability to turn off unlocks in each run to give a fun purist difficulty mode.
The weekly challenges, boss rush, and other modes are another really impressive addition.
I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, but that's just another bonus mode on top of this already solid game.
Art:
I might be a bit biased on the art considering that I spent a lot of time on Newgrounds and Flashportal growing up, so if you can relate to that you'll probably also dig the style here.
Music:
The soundtrack is a small list of tracks, but none of them have gotten annoying to me after 4 runs. It's a good megaman-fan soundtrack.
To conclude, I think this game is not only a really great megaman callback, but also a solid action-platformer in it's own right.

Despite not being the intended audience for these casual, physics-based puzzle games, Slash/Dots was quite surprising by how good of a game it is. Its simplicity of a concept doesn’t do the game its due diligence to the craftmanship behind how many small details were put into the design of its gameplay. Whether you prefer playing the game on your computer (as I have played 50/103 levels for an hour and a half) or on your mobile device like I have after work, Slash/Dots is a great little time-waster when you want something mentally stimulating enough to be a puzzle without being taxing enough on the brain.
At its core, Slash/Dots is very approachable for all ages. The simple goal is to get two colored marbles to come into contact by drawing lines to cut away wood pieces to make one marble or the other (or both) propel forward. Sometimes these levels will tax you beyond simply chipping away the level such as using various mechanisms like wheels or rotating arms; other levels may utilize the slowdown feature when drawing to time your cuts more precisely. These latter puzzles may not always feel the most rewarding to solve as the timing/physics can sometimes feel random; however, most puzzles often are focused around its other mechanics, the physics as a system and the new obstacles.
Perhaps the toughest obstacle when making a good physics-based puzzle game is nailing down the right amount of consistency as well as giving players leniency to solve problems. Slash/Dots manages to balance these two goals exceptionally well as I replayed every puzzle twice to make sure none of the solutions were flukes. If I found a process to solve it such as making specific shapes or a level of thickness/steepness, then it would usually result in a workable solution. Instead of making the marbles work a specific way or requiring them to be together when they stop, the game feels a lot more forgiving as you only need to maintain their inertia to get them into contact. This type of challenge makes for an addictive quality more so from the process of solving it than simply having the answer.
What makes these levels so enjoyable is their piece-by-piece nature that adds more and more complexity and new ideas to solve problems. Difficulty has a nice smoothness throughout levels, and if you failed to understand how to solve a given level you either need to learn something new or you need to build on what you learned previously. Sometimes the best method is to be playful with everything, seeing what parts will move or contort based on your actions, then making a solution from your observations. This is the kind of thrill I got from playing The Witness because Slash/Dots isn’t about solving (arbitrary) problems but learning how to use systems to make solutions.

While a level-editor would only make the game more enjoyable as well as foster a PC community, if the puzzles alone can excite you there will be plenty to sate an inquisitive mind. At roughly 3 – 4 hours, Slash/Dots offers enough to warrant its price-tag that its limited content is a minor concern. It’s simply good enough to leave you wanting more, and that is a good feeling to come away with when a novel concept doesn’t feel worn out by the end.

Physics puzzles are a tough genre, since many problems necessarily have several solutions. In
your task is to make two marbles touch each other. You accomplish this by strategically cutting wood pieces (by mouse click & drag). Simple enough?
Level usually (but not always) begins with a (meta-)stable scenario: cutting something will send the marbles or at least pieces of wood sliding, falling or flying. Optimally, a few cuts at strategic spots will beat the level and make you feel smart.
The physics is used cleverly. There are devices that sometimes act effectively as levers, or transporters, or flippers, or wheels.
At their simplest they push either marbles or other wooden sticks. The special items include couple kinds of perpetually rotating wheels, resulting in rather complex machines.
The best levels, in my opinion, were the ones in which one or several well-placed cuts would win the level.
However, sometimes levels have a timing component, like when a certain stick is rotating and a specific cut has to be made at the correct time. The time slows down while holding a cut, helping with the timing to a degree. With simplest puzzles timing mechanic works fine.
But with more complex ones, especially when combining two or more timing puzzles together or having moving pieces to cut, the puzzles grow tedious. For example, in a certain level a marble is rolling along a slide and one has to cut another piece to fall and catapult the marble with a lever to the other marble high up.
Without other guiding mechanisms, correct timing quickly becomes more luck than calculation, as the marble swings into every other direction but the correct one. Similar examples are abound the later levels. When challenge feels more luck even after guessing a proper solution (if timed correctly) with trial and error, there's a problem.
Thankfully, you can skip any level at any time with a cost of pride.
Despite being
game, the launcher has a rather short and obscure list of resolutions (1280x800, 1440x900, 1600x1024 and 1680x1050). Though the game ran fine despite.
More annoying was that the in-game options are also scarce: you can only disable (but not adjust the volume of) sounds and the hasty,
violin/string music that runs on the background (check the trailer for an example of the style).
I beat 95 of the 103 levels, while trying numerous times the eight (8) ones I ended up skipping because of their tediousness. This took me some 3.5 hours, so I'd guess that's the amount of content you'll be getting.
What would make it better? The length is appropriate for the full price but it would do well with more fun levels and less of those that require superhuman precision and timing, or luck combined with dedication. Also, unlike most games I review it doesn't have Steam achievements at this time: I would happily (with a pinch of wrath) beat the rest of the levels with that extra motivation.
Because of its flaws, I'd give it a mixed review if able, but frankly it's an alright puzzler for the most part. If you like physics puzzlers, I'd still wait for a sale of at least ~$1 (-50%).

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is arguably the best in the series (also my personal favorite). This game follows Carl Johnson who returns to San Andreas when his mom is murdered. Throughout the story we learn about some treason in his gang, Grove Street Families. I won't go into details since that would spoil the story...
There are so many things to do in this "3D Universe GTA", swimming, gyms, hunger (yes, you can become hungry after a ridiculous amount of time and eventually die from it), stats (lung capacity, fat, stamina, muscle, weapon levels, driving skill, etc.), flying planes, flying helicopters, parachuting, and so much more! Each stat can be increased/decreased from its corresponding activity. For example, fat is affected by eating. The larger the meal, obviously the fatter you get, but you can buy salads for generally the same price as the most expensive food and not gain weight. Muscle is affected by cycling, weights, climbing, and other activities that logically bring up muscle in real life. You can lose muscle by not doing anything active or hunger, like fat...
Guns are also affected by this skill system now. If you pick up an AK47 and try shooting someone with it in the game, Carl will hold it poorly, be unable to move while firing, strafe slowly, and will be highly inaccurate. However the more you use this weapon, the better he holds the gun, he will eventually be able to strafe while firing, strafe faster, and be extremely accurate.
Driving skill is self explainatory so I won't go into detail.
Cycling skill affects the speed you can get a bicycle to, the higher the jumps, and the less chance that you fall off. Also, self explainatory.
I'm sure you don't want me to go on about the skills any longer, now we shall go onto the minigames.
You can play a wide range of minigames such as video games, billiards (pool), and go on dates (yes, dates). There are only 3 video games, but these can be fun to play with friends. Billiards is only single player. Fun fact, there was actually supposed to be a multiplayer billiards activity but sadly, it never made it into the game... And the dates... So there are multiple women that you meet throughout the game by story (like Catalina) and some you meet outside of missions and are sort of hidden. Each one has certain activities that they like to do and most have a specific body type they want you to have. One likes you to be a bit fatter than muscular, and another wants you to have no fat and max muscle. Good luck juggling them around because you have to do all that in one day. Yes, you have to go on dates all across San Andreas everyday, and switch your body type pretty much every time. Hope you have cheats active...
In my opinion, the story could be better, but it's not the worst in the series. I'd say GTA III had the least interesting story, but then again, I've yet to complete it. Anyway back to this, the story starts off as Carl being a gangster, but ends in him being one of the richest men in San Andreas. Don't ask me why, but he does. I'd rate the story about 7/10. Like I said, it's not awful but it's not great...
If you've played GTA Vice City or GTA III before, you know the controls can be a little hard to use at times. This game changed this for the most part... You can now orbit the camera around the character, climb objects, and most importantly, YOU CAN SWIM! If I remember correctly this game started the ability to swim.
Speaking of starting something, this game started and ended the legacy of the jetpack. It was the first game to feature it which was AWESOME! However, this easy mode of transportation has yet to appear in the "HD Universe GTA" games. There's really not much to talk about it, you fly up, slowly go down, move forward, sideways, backward, it's basically being able to walk in the air...
This game also started the car customization. Yes, almost any car could be upgraded, but bikes you couldn't. Also, though you can customize your car, it's mainly hydraulics, color, nitrous, paint jobs, and wheels. There's a radio bass boost feature but on PC, it really doesn't help. Don't waste the $100 it costs...
If you want to mod this, you might want to buy a physical PC disk and install it off that. Take this from someone who's tried to mod the Steam version, you can't. If you don't want to mod this and don't plan to in the future, then you should probably get this as it's the most stable version...
You're probably bored of reading this by now and I applaud you for getting this far because there's a lot of stuff in this review. But this game, is definitely worth at least trying. If you don't know how good it really is, you can look up stuff about it on the internet... Or of course, you could buy it and refund it.

The game that pretty much defined my early childhood. This is absolutely great and a classic game every PC gamer should own! Unfortunately, I have some bad news and good news. Firstly, this Steam version is not particularly great - it misses SA:MP - the multiplayer mode of which I made countless friends! Also, some songs have been removed, You can find out which songs have been removed here:
[
]
Thankfully you can add all of these songs again in the customizable radio station. My honest advise to you is that you follow a guide on the internet and legally downgrade this game to an earlier version, preferably versions in the v1.x range ('x' stands for random number/s). Also, some game physics are broken (such as the car physics and overall driving which is downright numb when framerate is manually unlocked) when you remove frame limiter. The game is otherwise capped at 25fps which is awful to say the least. However, that can easily be fixed with a downgrade in the version and a mod to patch the physics for 60fps usage. It all takes a while though, but it is all worth it in the end.
Of course this is a fantastic and hilarious game in its own right, even though it is aging now. I would give this Steam version or any unmodded version a 7/10 (because of technically glaring issues) and a fixed version a 9/10.
Getting it on Steam is a safe bet, but the best way to enjoy this game is to simply buy a retail copy as the downgrading process is not necessary.

A delightful experience which seems designed for those who typically dislike tower defense games, like myself. While battles are certainly an entrenched element of the game, there is also an engaging sim management scenario spreading gleeful cheer to every Devil-infested corner of your complex. Monsters come to join your army, following the tantalizing odors of rotting flesh and cheap rent. Centaurs, demons, fish-people, and anthromorphic chickens are just some of the entertaining cast; over yonder succubi are speedily mating, and that pig-man may actually be Jack the Ripper.
After you get the tenants to settling in your economic housing opportunity, they start insisting on upgrades to their rooms, which is a marvelous opportunity to oblige and raise their rent. Money pours in, some tenants fall on hard times and are unable to pay, while others sneak off in the night to avoid their debts. It's all humorously presented, and the random enemies and quests you can send your nefarious, penny-penching residents on is just icing on the cake. Battles are usually relatively easy, with only a handful needing retrys.
All in all, Unholy Heights shouldn't be missed by those who adore catering to sims. Yes, hidden beneath the huggable chicken coating is a light, kinda tower defense game, but don't let that scare you off. This little gem is absolutely worth playing.

Right off the bat, this is a great game.
It's a great spin on Megaman-style action platformers by introducing rogue-like elements.
Gameplay:
I love the amount of optional risk-and-reward type augments that players are given in each run.
I also think the crushing difficulty of the final area of the game is fair, it's meant to serve as an early run ender that players work towards both with skill and unlocks. This balance of skill and unlocks already puts it way over so many other current rogue-likes that feel too reliant on random chance to get a good run rather than skill.
I really dig the ability to turn off unlocks in each run to give a fun purist difficulty mode.
The weekly challenges, boss rush, and other modes are another really impressive addition.
I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, but that's just another bonus mode on top of this already solid game.
Art:
I might be a bit biased on the art considering that I spent a lot of time on Newgrounds and Flashportal growing up, so if you can relate to that you'll probably also dig the style here.
Music:
The soundtrack is a small list of tracks, but none of them have gotten annoying to me after 4 runs. It's a good megaman-fan soundtrack.
To conclude, I think this game is not only a really great megaman callback, but also a solid action-platformer in it's own right.

Had the game before it hit Steam so you could probably triple or more the hours it shows.
The first game I got truely absorbed in, I'd research closed loop factories at work, printed out the sector map on A3 to make notes on what was where, made checklists of what ships I wanted for what based on their stats.
You can lone wolf it flying around picking fights and doing odd jobs, you can build up a huge armada and wage war on other factions, be a simple trader or build up a fleet of frieghters to carry out your trades for you, build your own stations to supply your forces or make money selling your goods off. There's also several story missions to play out that can net you some pretty good rewards and different starting conditions based on how much challenge you want to give yourself in the beginning. Personally I enjoy sitting back watching various ships coming and going from my factories, providing them raw materials or picking up the finished products that actually go on to supply other stations in the area (I'm also a fan of stealing the ships in retrieval missions, but don't tell anyone).
The game still looks good even by today's standards, all the ships and stations are highly detailed and crisp looking. The game maintains a great sense of scale with fighters actually being dwarfed by big battleships and massive stations, plenty of NPC ships around providing a bit of hustle and bustle to the empty stretches give you the sense of flying through the vastness of space rather than hopping about a tiny neighbourhood with everything next door.
Highly recommended if you're a fan of space games, you can keep things as simple as you like or really dig in and lose a few hundred hours.

I honestly don't know what it is about this game (which will likely extend to Albion Prelude, whenever I start playing that, possibly with the Star Wars mod), but whenever I load it up, it just feels... right. I know with my hour count (28.8, as of this review) I don't even have the right to say I've barely scratched the surface of this. Perhaps I've simply tapped the ground with a shovel at this point, given how little I've actually done. As a sandbox game, you get as much fun out of it as you're willing to put in the effort for, and this game does require effort to get started with.
Personally, I've been working on my own trade empire, though it's currently quite small (2 Mercury, 2 Caiman, and myself in a Caiman Super Freighter XL I bought off a Split), but I know my next addition to the fleet will work in Boron space. I just need to find the right market to tap into first. What I'm finding particularly nice is knowing I can relax on my own, flying my ships without worrying about some idiot trying to make me their content just for lulz (pretty much why I also play Elite: Dangerous in Solo), and just being able to enjoy a few hours of trade runs without having some PvP nutcase tell me I should quit and just play Euro Truck Simulator 2 if all I want to do is freight stuff around. Funny how those very same people get quite angry when told to go play EVE or a standard arena shooter if all they want to do is kill stuff, but that's neither here nor there.
When I get enough ships under my control, I honestly don't know what I'll do next. I could hunt for pirates/smugglers in my Asp (side note: I adore the Split's ship designs, hence why I've currently decided to make my Caiman Super Freighter XL my flagship, despite the considerably lower speed compared to the base Caiman to compensate for the much larget cargo hold), or maybe get a fast ship with decent cargo space and smuggle Space Fuel in Argon territory for some serious profits. I could also start making my own production facilities, selling my wares to stations that need them, or maybe I could run patrol missions for quick (though fairly small) mission payouts. Basically, I have options. My only current long term endgame goal is to complete at least one plot line before even installing AP.
Oh, and that GLORIOUS music! I usually prefer the EVE Online soundtrack when playing games like this, but I have no need to turn the music off here. It was quite the strange feeling, returning to Boron space and hearing that strange choir again after spending 12 hours in Argon, Teladi, and Split space sectors, also after a fairly lengthy hiatus.

It seems that there is a sentiment in most reviews (for this and some other games) that since it is so cheap, why not just buy it? Well, I think that's a fallacy. If you're not going to play or enjoy playing a game, then regardless of how little you spent on it, it was money wasted.
Now, Razenroth is not the worst game in the world. From a technical standpoint there's nothing wrong with it ― it even works fine on Linux ― it's not any sort of scam like some other games on Steam, etc. And it did let me kill some time, and considering I paid half a euro for it during a sale, I'm not mad or anything. But if you simply asked me whether you should get and play this game, I'd probably say no. There are better choices out there currently.
What is Razenroth? It's a top-down shooter slash roguelike. I would describe it as what you would get if Binding of Isaac didn't take inspiration from Legend of Zelda but DOOM instead. This game actually has some strong points. I thought the intro was neat and although the story is simple, it did introduce a bit of a Lovecraft-like atmosphere. Some of the art is pretty cool, especially the enemies, which look rather evil. Each level ends with a random boss fight and every one of those is unique and interesting.
So what's bad? Well, first, as soon as you start you'll notice very floaty controls. You can get used to them fast enough, but they're not good. Another very annoying thing you'll see are the trees. I mean, I guess one should expect them there since the game takes place in an evil-invested forest. But they're really such a pain since they basically constitute invisible obstacles. You never know when, while strafing and shooting at the enemies, you'll just plant your face into a tree trunk. That gets old soon.
The gameplay, in general, is rather lacking. I would describe the combat as neither fast-paced nor tactical. You just kind of float around trying to hit the monsters with slow-moving projectiles, hoping there's not a tree between you to stop your bullets. There are also issues with game balance; for instance, there is a secret item you can randomly find that pretty much wins a run for you. But I think the worst thing about Razenroth is the interface. There are no tooltips, no explanations, and no tutorial, so, for the most part, you have to guess what works how. For example, your "dark crystals" transfer between playthroughs but your money doesn't. The game never tells you this. Since you can exchange one for the other, after killing the final boss you should go to your hut and turn all the money in for crystals. You could figure that yourself ― on your second run after you wasted some already. There are many other problems too, but there's no point listing every little thing.
It took me 85 minutes to complete my first playthrough. The game is apparently designed to allow you to play for a while in short sessions, although there are auto-saves between the levels. At the time of writing this, I've played for 5 hours total and I'm something like halfway through 100-percenting the game.

I fully understand that this reboot "divided" the DMC fanbase and that some absolutely hate the new version of Dante. But as a dude who's played all the Devil May Cry games (my favorite is the third), I can't lie - I actually REALLY liked this. I think it might be one of the best action games I've played in recent memory. If that makes me not a "real" Devil May Cry fan, then so be it.
For me, the combat just feels so GOOD. Some people say that it's too easy or not as deep as the older games, which is possibly true, seeing that I regularly get SS or SSS ranks in DmC and rarely did in DMC4. But switching between sword, angelic scythe, devil axe, fiery gauntlets, heaven ninja stars and three different types of gun is such seamless fun, and I love the smooth way that Dante controls and the slightly simplified button inputs. This plus the fact that for once in a Devil May Cry I have almost complete control over the camera is just a dream to me, and a sign of what the old games could have achieved if they didn't have fixed camera angles. (Some people like fixed cameras; I kinda don't, especially when I'm trying to juggle an enemy and the dang view changes on me in mid-air.)
There's plenty of other solid stuff in DmC if you're willing to give it a chance - the game's colorful, with bright levels that change on you and some fun environmental traversal aspects that reminded me a little of Prince of Persia and Castlevania, since Dante's got a whip he can use to latch onto platforms. The story kept me engaged more than all other DMC games with the exception of DMC3, but I've seen some folks saying that they absolutely abhorred it, so your enjoyment may vary. Dante isn't as much of an "emo edgelord" as they say he is; he's really more of a punk than anything else, and by the end of the game he becomes more like the old Dante we know and love. (Yes, his hair turns white.) Vergil is quite different; he was your typical silent anime assassin badass in the past and they made him into more of a Julian Assange-sorta character here. I think a lot of people probably hate how much he talks in the game, but hey, he controls awesomely in his DLC epilogue.
In short, I dug DmC. I can completely understand why people despised it, since Capcom sprung this reboot on a fanbase that didn't think restarting the whole franchise was necessary. But IMHO, this has ended up as my second-favorite Devil May Cry, and I think it's a shame that we're unlikely to see a DmC 2 after the mixed reception this got. (Maybe I'm wrong. I hope so!)

The way they made this game free to play is by in-game purchases, those usually include anything from a modified starting weapon (STAR) to a P90 like gun (PDW-57). Weapon prices for each duration (3day=99G1C)(30day=499G1C)(Character Lifetime= 3,499G1C)(Account Lifetime= 4k)
G1C Prices= [400G1C= $5.00][800G1C= $10.00][2k= $25.00][4k=$50.00][6k=$75.00]

There are a variety of prices between all of the cars available, There are cars that you can't customize what so ever and then there are fully customizable cars.
Three slot cars that you are able to customize you can buy alone which can range from the lowest; under $25 or can get up to $35.
These three slot cars can come with a bundle deal thats gives you more customization options for about $10 more.

Ram raiding: is when you grab a car and slam into shop windows carry/put the items in a vehicle, turn the into a contact and then launder
Gamersfirst has tried many different ways on keeping elite players out of rookie zones... Most of it has failed.
One way of trying to do this is the threat system
: The threat levels go
Trainee: lowest lvl and rank possible
Green: Still pretty noobish nearly impossible to hit at high level if you do moderately okay at the game
Bronze: You are new to the game still and will still be looked at as a noob if you are low level and bad if you are high level.
Silver: This is the last threat level you can be before being forced into silver servers (more information will be told about different threat servers)
Gold: You can no longer join bronze or green servers and must play in silver or gold.
The second part to the threat method was adding different threat servers
Green: Almost never occupied (maybe 2 or 3)
Bronze: Second most populated servers on the game people who rank up to gold threat will purposefully "dethreat" to get back to silver so they can go kill noobies because they aren't good enough for gold servers.
Silver: This is where all the eilte gold players and confused silver players go this is the most populated server

The game is played through faction based missions, you will get a team of anywhere from 2 to 8 people.
These missions are always have a few starting missions then a finale,
starting missions can be "break into here" "burn this" "steal this car" "pick up this package" "guard this package from being picked up" then finale missions can range from anything like "kill/(guard) the enemy/(friendly) vip (it chooses the mvp from whoever's team got picked they can also not run in vehicles as they go really slow [vehicles can be pushed to speed up the vip's car])" "bring the packages you just stole/recovered and hold them here to gain points while the enemy tries to take it to thier base" "don't let them diffuse this bomb for a long pieriod of time"
Completing missions will give you cash and contact standing and maybe an item such as symbols, jewelery and emotes
Contact standing: Before you embark on missions you need to pledge to a contact giving all of the gained contact standing to them (winning gains more) and leveling them up giving you all types of items in the game.
Cash: Can can be used in many different ways, buying items from contacts or even buying off the in game markethouse that let's player sell thier custom creations or game premade items.

Character: You can change your character after you make it but not the name or gender

Prison Architect is such an interactive and humorous game. As a kid I can remember playing games such as Zoo Tycoon and Roller Coaster Tycoon, and this game gave me the same type of feel.
When you begin a sandbox you can create your very own prison from scratch: building holding cells, cafeterias, showers, solitary units, you name it. As soon as you open your prison, a truck will roll around with your first batch of inmates. Each of these inmates has a name, and if you click on them you can read a full biography on them and what they are in for.
You can also play a story mode, which if you are anything like me, you will enjoy collecting the polaroid’s which will give you insight on a background story that is unraveling within the prison. This is how you will receive the majority of your in game achievements. (They are my favorite part!)
From watching all of your inmates trying to squeeze all 100 of themselves in a tiny kitchen, to playing as an inmate in your own prison and trying to escape, this game has many MANY features that will keep you playing for hours!

I'm hooked!
Prison Architect is a fairly simple prison sims game where you build a prison slowly as accept certain grants and grow your inmate population. This is probably pretty obvious just from what you have already read so far.
I think the developers did a pretty good job at keeping things intuitive within the UI. The tutorial helps wonders for learning to use the more hidden research panels and nuances of controlling your staff.
The game was an interesting single player storyline as well. Even in the free build game type , they make it interesting by dropping photos and scraps of text to add a bit of a plot to collect.
The one thing this game really struck hard for me is my OCD with having to get everything perfect. I must have rebuilt my prison 10 times before I settled with something I really like, and even then I feel like I could restart and do much better.
Overall this game is addicting and I would recommend it to anyone!

I just love this game.
The gameplay elements are anything but innovative, granted; you've got a hero who can shoot bolts (or laser, or little daggers, etc.) and he goes around slaying enemies, and can pickup powerups and gain buffs and abilities as he levels up. Nothing new about that. It's maps and monsters and drops and bosses are randomized every time you play the game, which I really like; but that's not cutting edge innovation either.
So it's a traditional game, but don't let that fool you! It's done so well! I particularly liked the dark, bleak atmosphere, the minimal storyline, and the many, many ways the game can be played:
1. Increase your health and health regeneration and armor, to a point where killing you becomes virtually impossible (tank).
2. Increase your mana and mana regen and mana gain on hit, and forget about your primary attack: Keep spamming those magic attacks that deal huge damage (wizard).
3. Increase the chance of landing a crit and crit damage, and obliterate whole hordes of monsters in seconds (assassin).
4. Use a unique style in which you deal more damage but receive more damage (barbarian); shoot triple bolts and reflect things randomly at enemies, while running around crazy fast (ranger); focus on using potions and spellbooks (mage); etc.
Also, loot. Sweet, randomized loot. You have no idea what you'll get, and you can either choose to build on the buffs that your loot gives you, or complement them with your attributes and skills. You'll love it when you randomly get four pieces of matching armor! (haven't had that happen to me yet, I got three matching pieces only, which was really delightful).
I really like it. It's not a big game, but it aims at doing a specific thing, and it does it beautifully. And for the price, it's pretty good.
The only thing I would ask the dev to do, is maybe add a help section that describes different aspects of the game (for example, how exactly does armor work?)
10/10 would recommend.

I like this game. A lot.
It is what it says on the tin: Come expecting Mega Man X style of gameplay, stay for the rogue-lite randomness and item pools. There's a good bit of variety and learning curve in the game, and the items and weapons feel pretty good once you're used to them. Aiming a couple of the boss weapons is incredibly unintuitive, but this game lends very well to experimenting with differnent things to get used to how they work.
95% of my time so far was spent in the Beta, by the way (which was lovingly tended to for an incredible amount of time; This was a great example of Early Access Done Right even in the year of 2017). There's a lot of final touches I haven't seen yet that I'm sure I'm overlooking, but there's one particular pair of points I want to address.
By default, falling into bottomless pits won't kill you. This is good! It means you get to explore a bit and aren't heavily penalized for falling off of things. There's a lot of moving platforms, and a lot of enemies that fly, and you're not screwed just because something came on screen at the worst time. Falling into a pit seems to only ever deal 1 point of damage, and then resets you on the last bit of stable ground you were standing on. Fun!
...until you get into the final levels. These are the Wily Stage equivalents; Utilizing everything you know and your best reflexes to topple challenges that expect you to be able to respond to them. That's where my biggest problem lies with this game. At the risk of sounding like a scrubby scrub who scrubs, the final bits feels overly reliant on platforming over bottomless pits with no solid land "checkpoints." This isn't inherently bad, but if you're run didn't give you any kind of movement speed or maneuvering ability (double jumps, enhanced jumps, better dashes, whatever) you can feel unfairly penalized for not being able to move fast enough. I've had more than a few runs end because the spinning platforms were blocked by laser barriers flickering every half a second and my only way out was a series of temporary platforms (Mega Man WHOOOOOOMF blocks) that didn't match the timing on either the mobile platforms I had to maneuver through or the blinking laser barrier.
Losing a ton of health because of "difficulty" isn't fun, and the final stages aren't particularly short! If you're lucky you'll get the tools to help you, but it does feel unfair at times due to the random pools of platforms and sequences.
As mentioned, I like this game a lot. I'd like it a lot more if I didn't have runs end simply because I dared to pick up certain upgrades, and as an effect I made the final platforming challenges nearly impossible. I'll continue to work on improving my own play in the meantime, but the combination of "haha, you're too slooooow" sections is a bummer.

Trillion is not a game that will be to everyones tastes, it is unique and fun to play, but many players may find that it's trying to hard to be too different and therefore complicates itself, but if you're looking for a JRPG or SRPG with a unique spin then Trillion is definitely worth a look.

I like the part where you become attached to a character only to have them fight a hopeless battle, and you get to listen to their lamenting their weakness as they scream in agony when their bones are crushed and their body is devoured by a dimension hopping supergod.

Trillion is what I would consider to be "double-niche", as it is a mish-mash of (mainly) two genres: SRPG and Raising Simulator. About 80% of this game is navigating menus and reading the VN-style cutscenes as you train and raise Affection with the Overlord of your choosing (at least for the first 3, the rest after that are in a set order). The other 20% is mystery-dungeon-like gameplay where you navigate on a grid through the Valley of Swords for training or to fight Trillion; anytime YOU move, the enemies will make a move of some sort as well, each move you make being a "turn."
For your very first run, I'd STRONGLY encourage you to forego any sort of guides and just do it blindly, and take your best whack at Trillion that you can, because  while there are various ways to go about defeating him, there's a pretty easy way to do it that will suck all the fun out of trying all sort of different playstyles. I had originally played this on the PSVita and, after my first run or so, could no longer play it due to it crashing all the time. I picked it up again here on Steam and I'm pretty glad I did. In addition to the bugs from the Vita version being next-to-nonexistent, I thoroughly enjoyed the story and getting the 10 different endings. There's plenty of everything to go around here: comedic relief bits, fanservice, and heart-wrenching despair as you watch the Overlord, that you trained and who fell in love with you, get eaten like yesterday's leftover potato casserole. If you have the fortitude and willpower for grinding, there's a nice bit to be appreciated by 100%-ing this. That being said, if you just picked this up for cheap on a steam sale, I'd say just just play two or three runs, making your final run the True Ending run for good measure so you get the closure you, and anyone else playing this, would deserve.
Interesting fact about this game is that while it was developed my Compile Heart, quite a few Disgaea staffers were on board with the project, such as the director of Disgaea 4, Masahiro Yamamoto, and the composer for Phantom Brave and Disgaea: Hour of Darkness, Tenpei Sato. Sato's signature style is very present here, as just like in Disgaea, you'll find yourself humming the tracks that play in the menus, when fighting Trillion, etc. even long after you've been done playing the game.
I very rarely 100% games. I've only ever 100%'d three games in my life, but this one was worth it to me. Getting to see each Overlord's ending, and watch them die again and again and again and again all for it to culminate to the final chapter of the game, it's was QUITE satisfying to say in the least.

Bought this very cheap during the autumn sales but I have to say, if I'd known how good it was beforehand I'd probably have bought it at full price a long time ago. This game is quite underrated and I was pleasantly surprised to find a hidden treasure like this.
The concept itself is quite unique. Throughout the game, theres really only 1 real boss, which is the titular monster, Trillion. You spend a lot of the game just preparing your character to fight this boss, one at a time. Keep in mind also, that the game doesn't joke around when it asks "how many overlords will you sacrifice?" because your characters, upon dying to Trillion are dead for good for the remainder of that playthrough. This can be quite heartbreaking especially from your second playthrough onwards if you know you have to let a character you really liked die, but if you can stomache through it the overall gameplay, concept and story is quite good. It seems quite evident that its a low budget game, but I'm overall quite satisfied with the quality delivered and the sheer volume of content available. 15 hours in, and given how many endings and things there are to do I'm nowhere close to done with this game.

Just like I said about the original Borderlands, it's really hard to put this game into words. Borderlands 2 is Borderlands 2. There's really nothing it can be compared with. While there are some people out there who insist on comparing it with its predecessor, they are still two different games, no matter which way you look at it. In my Borderlands review, I praised it for its characters, humour and open world and even after playing Borderlands 2, I sustain to that. But this game builds on that
. While the first game was enjoyable, this game is
. It's just so much more polished and has taken the franchise to the next level. After playing the original, playing this was like time travel - and in a sense it was, as it takes place after the story of the first game. But what I really mean is that everything is just better. Better graphics, better AI, better inventory, better locations, better HUD, the list just goes on and on. That's not to say that the original isn't worth playing, I'm just saying that it would be difficult to play the first game after experiencing this. But if you start on the original and go on to play this, your experience will be enriched. Also, there are references to the first game and even its DLC, so I do recommend playing those first.
However, if you're not too concerned about the story and just want a great gameplay experience, I still strongly recommend this game. I recommend it even more if you have a group of friends to play with as that will greatly enhance your experience (and will allow you to get better loot, or so the game tells me). This game is just on point, right across the board. The story is awesome with its diverse charcters including one of the greatest villains
in history. The loot system is incredible and will end up being your primary motivation for playing this game as there are some pretty crazy and overly powerful weapons that can be obtained. The music is just spectacular and creates the perfect mood to appreciate the beautifully unique graphics, or in most cases, slaughter hundreds upon hundreds of enemies. The humour is unrivalled in the gaming industry, as you could almost call it a feature of the game.
Put simply, this game is amazing. It is definitely one of my favourite games of all-time and I intend to continue playing it, at least until Gearbox release the next instalment.

This game took some heavy hits in it's early reviews and many of those were justified but overall this is a solid game.
Technically it performs well. I have no problems running it on the highest settings or on my laptop with the lowest settings.  It actually runs better on my laptop than it's predecessor did and that is commendable.  There are a few notable graphis glitches but nothing that makes it unplayable.
The story was actually very good.  It was a nice change of pace compared to the other Arkham games.  The DLC story featuring Mr. Freeze was actually the highlight of the entire series for me.  I missed some of the notable voice talent and the animations and environment interactions were notably lower in quality but did not ruin the experience.
Play wise they had some fun new combat skills and some new gadgets but it did not feel out of place.  The fight dynamics suffered a little on the visuals over it's predecessors but only minimally.  The boss fights were actually some of the funnest in the series...even better than any of it's predecessors AND successors.  The online aspect was solid if limited.  Due to the age of the game and declining interest it is currently pretty hard to get a team together for some of the missions.  If you can though it makes for a fantastic multiplayer diversion from the main game.
I think it is a definite buy if you like the series and a must if you find it on sale.

I had a lot of fun building up my apartment. As my tenement grew, more monsters moved in, each with different stats, jobs, likes, and dislikes. I had to keep my tenants happy by fulfilling their special needs and buying them furniture. In return, they defend the apartment from invading adventurers and heroes.
Everything in this game has character; from the funny text descriptions of monsters and furniture to the cutesy 2D art design. Tenants will go about their day, some will go to work, others will hang around in their apartment; some monsters don't get along with others. I found myself chuckling often to the various activities of my tenants. Also, the soundtrack is super catchy and light-hearted, which fits the game perfectly.
There's something satisfying about watching your tenants grow; you might feel a peculiar attachment. They can get job promotions, fall in love, and eventually make babies! There's nothing like unleashing a family of Cheepies on an unsuspecting hero.
Unholy Heights is a very casual game; fun and enjoyable, easily worth the price of purchase. It definitely merits our attention.

What Rogue Legacy is to Castelvania, 20XX is to Megaman X. If you are a fan of the X/Zero/ZX series, don't let the art style deter you. You are missing out on some great jump n' shootin'.
20XX takes the fundamentals of the "X" series and puts it through the filter of a rogue-like. Movement, abilities, armors, bosses; it's all there. After about 10 minutes of playtime, veteran X players can rely on their muscle memory to make dash jumps and control their jump height. I was pleasantly surprised by how well they nailed the movement of the X games they are so clearly trying to emulate. The weapons the bosses give you have both applications in the stage and can be used as a weakness to a different boss. The armors that you find (I believe there are 3 total) rely on RNG to be discovered and purchased. They are not hidden away like the X games, but the abilities they give you are just as meaningful. It's almost like a "best of" armor pieces from X1-6, with a few new ideas in there as well. The bosses are also well designed and fun to fight. No spoilers, but, in particular, the final boss of this game in is fantastic. It really tests you on every aspect of the game in one fight, without feeling unfair.
The only deviations from the X formula are the tone of the story and graphical style, which may be a bit divisive. The story is rather tongue-in-cheek and the item and enemy descriptions are unabashedly self-aware. I'm not the biggest fan of this choice, but it conveys the love the creators have for the X series. Also, the graphics are.... different. Originally, the graphics were the biggest thing holding me back from purchasing the game back in 2015. They have definitely improved since then, but the bubbly look to the characters and their floaty looking animations turned me off at first. None of this translates to how the characters feel to control.
Frankly, this is much better than anything Inti Creates has put out since the ZX series. If you are fan of the X/Zero/ZX games, this is absolutely worth your time.

I'm not fresh on the old games. So this review might not contain the angst of the diehard fans, that being said it will be as objective I could give. When I first saw the teaser for this game and Dante's new look, I was in the outraged group of people. I remember swearing not to play this game and yet here I am. The main part of this game I feel will be remembered is its aesthetics. It's beautiful. And that's ultimately what's captured my interest after the failure that was the my introduction to this game. Distinct aesthetics mean good direction, and direction is what most games lack. But i digress. Despite the game's gorgeous looks, and this product being a port, the optimization is quite decent. It's not ideal, but it's more than passable. And the port itself was made not in a money-grubbing way. There are some problems here and there, but they do not really interfere with your experience. Production is really hit and miss. For example Dante and Vergil are voiced by one actor, and sometimes it really shows, breaking the immersion. Sometimes they even look too much the same and it doesn't help. Brothers don't really work that way. But then there are some props like graffiti art that warmed my heart and really did help with immersion. So that's up to you. In the process of the game you can unlock cool concept art too. But they show all of it in credits roll, so i did not really get that. Music is much the same techno sounding metal stuff, as in the last few titles, if a bit modernized, it felt fitting to this game overall. Gameplay wise there is not really much to tell. It's hack and slash, it's enjoyable. Honestly, i can understand the new looks too. It's not the long-haired flannel wearing grunge kids that are today's youth, right? Overall it's a must play. I haven't had this much fun in a while. I don't know about DLC, though. Production values are lower, most everything is rehashed. If you really enjoyed the original game maybe try the DLC. I wouldn't reccomend, though.

Batman Arkham Origins follows the early journey of Bruce Wayne through Arkham city on Christmas eve, acting as a prequel to Arkham Asylum, it is set roughly 10 years before Arkham Asylum. Batman is not that well established yet so a younger Bruce Wayne is portrayed. The voice is handed over to Roger Craig Smith, as opposed to Kevin Conroy but it doesn't dissapoint. Smith does a fantastic Batman, adding the gritty, stern personality to the Dark Knight.
The story is excellent, exciting enough to keep you playing and unpredicable plot twists hold their place. (Without spoiling it): Batman is still somewhat new to the vigilante life. Detective Gordon hasn't come face to face with the caped crusader and villains are meeting Mr Wayne for the first time. The villains are excellent. Having a huge contract put out on him by Black Mask, Gothams most notorious assassins are out for the hefty bounty. You encounter the likes of Deathstroke, Deadshot, Copperhead, Bane and more. Each villain voiced brilliantly and with cool combat encounters. The combat is as it has been after Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, the same brilliant freeflow counter based combat that remains fun and is always extremly satisfying to pummel villains into the dirt.
The down sides are minor and won't put people off. The multiplayer is dull, feeling like it was thrown in last minute to fulfill the whole "All games should have online multiplayer" criteria. It's just not worth the time, but doesn't detract from the excellent single player. The optimisation is slightly bad, feeling chuggy even on a powerful pc. Ultra settings make the game look beautiful, really capturing a christmas time Arkham city feel but makes the game run at low fps so high settings are recommended for powerful pc's and medium for less powerful pc's. It's not so bad as the game still looks good on high. The controls for PC in my opinion are quite bad. Clunky and hard to control on a Mouse/Keyboard it's screaming to be played on a controller.
All in all it's a surpisingly exellent "Spin off" game that is worth playing if you're a fan of the series. Pick it up cheap and you won't be dissapointed.

Potentially great game ruined by the game community/chaos and hostile environment.
In a gaming world filled with sci-fi and war-themed multiplayer games, APB seems like a breath of fresh air. It takes place in modern times more or less, in a city torn apart by criminals activity. You have the choice of playing as a Criminal (gang member) or Enforcer (law enforcement) and basically, have to carry out missions depending on what type of character you're playing. Often you will have to team with other players and take out "enemies" as you carry out your mission.
When you first play around with APB: R, it's actually kind of fun. It's like a lite version of GTA mixed in with a little Saints Row. As the action unfolds, San Paro's NPC citizens react to the action as it unfolds, sometimes crouching, screaming, diving for cover, or cursing, making the city come alive.
Your experience As a newbie is pure chaos, frustration, and confusion. Go on the PvP missions and you will get blasted again and again and again relentlessly by extremely high-level players or hackers/ cheaters. Slaughtered doesn't even begin to describe what happens.
"Teaming" isn't at all like co-op, where you and a bunch of people interact and help each other out. Usually, it's more like a bunch of random people thrown together with no sense of teamwork who just "do their own thing" while carrying out a mission and ignoring you and other teammates. Ironically, while keeping silent throughout the entire mission, they'll suddenly grumble in chat about how much the team "sucked" after the mission is lost, and then angrily leave it. Team leaders will similarly keep quiet during gameplay and not give any guidance throughout, then kick newbies off their missions when things go wrong. But as for now. gamers first has fixed this and you no longer get kicked unless you have a demerit medal.
Expect to be kicked/ abandoned during or after a mission a lot if you're a newbie. If you're not sensitive, you'll just become angered by the "kicking" because by being constantly dumped, you never gain enough experience to get better at the game or meet new friends who you can play with in the future. But if you're a sensitive player, the endless round of being dumped makes the game feel hostile.
The chaos is out of this world! You'll be on a mission minding your own business and suddenly a player who isn't part of your mission will just keep ramming the crap out of your vehicle over and over again or running you over. Sometimes even your own teammates will kill you by running you over with a car or shooting you for no reason.
This is exactly what the first few days for the newbie will be like-- slaughter, griefing, uncommunicative teammates, team leaders angrily kicking you off missions, teammates whining about how much their team "sucked, being abandoned by teammates during missions.
Regardless of all that. when it comes to me. having a lot of friends in the game and enjoying every moment having fun while we're playing and laughing and ignoring all the bad in the game community. it's all worth it.

I got this on sale for 39p so I’d have to be a real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ not to leave a good review but even at full price I’d say it’d be worth it.
At first the game seemed very basic and like someone had just bought a load of particle effect asset packs on the Unity store and cobbled together a game in a couple days. However it soon gets surprisingly fun.
Pretty similar mechanics to a lot of rouge-like bullet-hells just with... fewer bullets and a little less hectic and stressful gameplay but the large array of items makes it interesting. However whether or not you fail or succeed seems largely down to the items that spawn.
For instance the first play I got stomped by the first boss almost immediately as I was half dead and there were no health potions left on the map. Second time around I put more points into health and defence but still didn’t make it to the second boss.
Next run I almost immediately found an item that massively increased the drop rates of other items and then quickly found a passive healing item and about a dozen other things. Then I found a magic golden apple that promised to make me very powerful (doesn’t sound remotely suspicious) and was evidently rare enough to warrant an achievement...
As such I could just put everything in crit chance and ignore every potion I came across. The result was a 30% crit chance, twice as much crit damage, half the mana cost on spells and virtually no chance of actually dying. So even the final boss fell pretty effortlessly to the epic wizard I’d somehow become.
I incidentally love the fact that despite it having a backstory and voice over to tell said story it never makes any mention of why this guy and his grandfather are apparently both wizards. The assumption is that they gained magical powers upon being transported to this weird realm but they never seem especially surprised or perturbed by the fact that lightning is suddenly shooting from their hands.
After the end boss there is some further voice over (which plays loudly even though I’d muted the game and as such is more scary than the boss itself) but this still didn’t really enlighten me any on their wizardly ways.
It was slightly disappointing that the game just abruptly ends after the final boss so I didn’t even get the chance to try the items it dropped. Would have been nice if it could go to an endless or arena mode that gets harder until you die. Will be interesting to play it on the harder modes with the other characters though and see how hard that boss actually is if I don’t have about 30 items equipped...

20XX is a MegaMan Roguelike (or Roguelight) that, while yes, randomness is certainly a thing, it will really be your own skills and reflexes as a gamer that will carry you far into the game. While collecting random power-ups to make yourself stronger is useful, it's ultimately your ability to play that will decide whether you succeed or fail. Not if you were lucky or not.
Despite that, many level blocks that are randomly generated through level seeds, with random powerups and a large item pool to boot, each run will be a very unique challenge that you will have to tackle through and shouldn't get boring easily (I don't have over 300 hours for nothing).
Make no mistake, this game doesn't not have any (real) permanent upgrade system. There's a couple permanent upgrades to help you out, but ultimately it is you as a gamer who is the one who will be challenged. Not how many stats you obtain on Nina, the Megaman X-esque character who blasts her foes away with a giant arm cannon, or Ace, the Zero-like man, who goes in slicing in dicing with saber like weapons... or axes... or spears... or glaives.
The one who gets stronger with each one will be YOU. The player. As your skills become more and more refined, you will find that each death will get further apart. You may die on level 3. And then level 4. Then level 6. Until eventually you get to the final challenge -- and probably die a few times there too. But each time you get there, you will get a little bit stronger, as you increase your arsenal of items you can find.
And then when you finally beat the game, you look, to see all of these difficulty modifiers to challenge yourself even more, to make yourself even stronger as a player by handicapping yourself. And then when you've refined your skills up even more, testing your skills in the daily and weekly challenges to try and be #1 on the leader boards may not seem like such a daunting task to do afterall.

Also, there's two evade buttons, down on the D-pad does nothing by default, and  the Angelic mode (LT) vs Demonic (RT) mode mechanic does not feel as well implemented as that of Castlevania: Lords of Shadow's Light mode vs Dark mode, which is a game that came earlier than this one.)
As for the combat, it's alright; not terrible, but it's no where close to the most fun I've ever had. The enemy desigin is a bit boring since a lot of enemies are re-skins of others and have a broken doll motif; (it's very lackluster for a game where demons and angels are real.) Mentioned earlier, the binary mode mechanic feels better done in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. As for how the game fits in the action-adventure genre, I would recommend Castlevania: Lords of Shadow or God of War over this.

Do you like games that allow you to go AFK for hours while the AI does your grinding for you?  If yes, X3: Terran Conflict might be the game for you.
Okay, that's slightly unrepresentative, but it is important to note first up that it does take a very long time to do anything at the start of an X3:TC campaign, whether you're a fighter, trader or a bit of both.  Until you grind up enough credits to buy sector trader and later universe trader software, which allows your freighter pilots to go about their business making you money, you have to handhold them every moment to make good trades.  I have as of writing this 84 hours in XC:TC, all on one save, and I think about 35 of those hours were spent building my trade fleet up to a point where it could be left to go about its business, while completing missions in the background and hunting pirates and Xenon.  The latter is also something you can't jump into head first and expect to have quick results with, as your starting ship is often lightly armed and an easy kill for the larger roving bands of space marauders that one is likely to encounter.
Being able to accellerate time in-game by up to a factor of 10 helps a lot, especially once you have a sizeable trade fleet and you can just sit afk in an abandoned sector for hours while your autonomous trade empire goes about its business making you heaps of money.  I'm pretty sure that's the primary reason for the singualirty engine time accellerator existing, but it doesn't make it feel any less of a cheese.
This is a game that is all about patience, in many regards, and not just when managing a trading empire.  Anything larger than a heavy fighter needs a jumpdrive to get around the universe quickly, and with the exception of the ever-wonderful Hyperion frigate, which is a bugger to get hold of in Terran Conflict, all ships of M6 (frigate) class and above are nightmarishly slow in-sector.  This means that having abused time accelleration to get the money to afford to buy and then equip a fleet of warships, you find yourself abusing it even more just to get from A to B especially within some of the larger sectors, and they can be very large indeed.
That said, X3:TC does have a wonderful, and absolutely massive universe to explore, and its easy to lose several hours just flying about enjoying the scenery, seeing the sights of the universe such as Akeela's Beacon or enjoying the game's fantastic soundtrack, which has a unique theme for nearly every one of the 100+ sectors.  There are several races to ally yourself with or pit yourself and your forces against, and even factions within those races, who each have their own quest lines to complete for reputation, credits and other rewards, and thats all in addition to X3:TC's satisfying main storyline, and that's all to say nothing of the fact that the X3 universe's economy is constantly in motion, with a relative system of supply and demand that can make trading far more dynamic once you get enough in the kitty to start building your own factories and farms.
Fly anything.  Shoot anything.  Buy anything.  Sell anything.  Go anywhere, build anything.  X3:TC is the complete, and possibly greatest ever sandbox space sim, and I say that even with Elite:Dangerous on the market and Star Citizen looming on the event horizon.

Trillion is a pastiche of other (mostly superior) games - Disgaea, Makai Kingdom, Hyperdimension Neptunia, Etrian Odyssey, Demon Lord Box, Kengo - even Dark Half, an obscure Superfamicon cult classic. Trillion as an original title doesn't really add anything to the mix.
Trillion's problem is that it's simply a poorly made game. The controls are bad. The camera is bad. The combat system is bad. The skill development system is simplistic. The artwork and characters are decent, that's about all I can say.
A small but telling example is the MMO-style combat log - always visible, but the font is too large and every line breaks, so little text and even less usable information is displayed. The camera doesn't use the usual control setup for most isometric RPGs, which is seriously problematic since a core objective in Trillion is to see how far the eponymous antagonist is from a line on the far side of the map - a line the camera can't be adjusted to see from the other side of the field. Camera collision with Trillion's massive tail is a constant nuisance.
The worst part of the game, however, is the pacing.
Combat is glacially slow. A solo protagonist, simultaneous turn system, and DOTA-like creep spawns would seem to lend the game to fast-paced combat, but combat is slow, slower even than in a conventional tactical RPG like Disgaea or turn-based game like Dark Half. The slowness is worsened by long, boring animations where the boss seems to just stand there for a long period before doing something, and also by buggy combat where Trillion will just stand there while you wail away at his tail until you have to retreat for want of MP.
Some of the combat mechanics seem to suggest the devs never played through their own game (common in really bad, rushed China games). In the mini-dungeons, the turn counter ticks every time the character moves - but Charge (move two squares) can be spammed for almost no mana, with no cooldown. Opening the menu to chain-cast Charge, rather than just moving with the D-pad, is just another level of nuisance. Unlike most grid-based TRPGs, Trillion offers diagonal movement - but this can only be achieved by rotating the camera, one of many interface shortcomings resulting in choppy gameplay.
Trillion is made to be played with an Xbox controller. Do not even try to play the game with a keyboard, I'm not even sure if it's possible.
About 90% of the game is just training your Overlord through menus - which usually means just doing training wherever three other characters happen to be, which guarantees a necessary token to enter the mini-dungeons. Neither the mini-dungeons nor the Trillion encounters are particularly fun or rewarding.
The dialogue is exceedingly tedious compared to Neptunia games. You will often find yourself speeding through the dialogue, then checking the log to see what you missed. And most of the game *is* dialogue - Trillion is more visual novel than TRPG. Honestly, Trillion would make a better visual novel than TRPG.
Trillion is one of those many games with a lot of potential from good visuals and interesting concepts, ruined by poor and unimaginative implementation, bad functional design, and insufficient dev time.
I would agree with other posters that Trillion is not a $29.99 game. It's a $2.99 game. Maybe it's worth getting if it's 90% off on Summer Sale or something, you can mess around with it for a couple hours or something. Otherwise, yeah, there's just too much better stuff out there.

And you can always feel the adrenaline of escaping your known cities or returning to Los Santos (if you have been kicked out already). Even at the end-game you can hunt for the largest plane (I won't tell you where it is) and attempt to escape Area 51's airspace alive.
The biggest upside is that you can own more than 6 cars with your character, unlike GTA V. And you can safely store them into a garage, unlike GTA IV.
