I mostly got this game since it was on sale for 49¢, and looked decent. I was surprised by how much fun I had and am still having. It's sorta like the Binding of Isaac, where there are a bunch of randomly placed rooms with randomized stuff inside. The game takes place outside though, so the rooms have various props like trees, bushes, and other stuff to match the various environments.
Like Isaac, you go through the random rooms, killing enemies, finding various items to boost your stats, then finally finding the boss, defeat it, and move to the next area. There are 5 areas, each with a different environment. the first one is a forest, while the second one is some sort of Volcanic Cavern. I won't spoils the rest.
Razenroth IS different though. Instead of tears, your character is a Mage, and uses spells. First you have a Primary Spell, this does decent-ish damage, doesn't cost Mana, and actually restores mana on hit. Then you have your Mana Spell, which costs mana obviously, and does quite a bit more damage.
You have four button slots total, which are shown on the bottom of the screen. They are as follows:
The Primary Spell takes up the Left Mouse Button.
The Mana Spell takes up the Right Mouse Button.
The "E" Key takes up the Magic Book slot. Magic books do various things depending on the Book. Some boost stats like Primary/Mana Spell damage, range, crit chance, crit damage, and character speed/defense. Some do other things like summon tornadoes that damage enemies around you. There are a lot of Magic Books that do a wide variety of things I didn't list here, these are just to give you an idea of what they do.
The "Q" Key takes up the Potion slot. Potions do about what you expect: Outright heal or restore mana. Increase manage regeneration. Temporarily give health regeneration, increase crit chance, increase spell range, etc.
There are various characters as well. You start with one, the main character Charles, but you can unlock more. All characters start with a specific Primary and Mana Spell. Like Charles starts with the Magic Bolt Primary and Mana Orb.... Mana Spell. Potions and Magic Books need to be found. Characters all have 1 Passive trait as well, such as Charles having the trait that when you successfully hit an enemy with a Primary Spell, you have a chance of immediately casting a second time as well in quick succession.
You gain experience as you level, and when you level up you get a Stat Point to spend on Stats such as Health, Mana, Mana Regen, Mana Restored on Hit, Crit Chance, Crit Damage, Armor, and Speed. You also get 1 Talent Point per level, and when you have 3 Talent Points, you can buy a Passive Talent. Talents do things such as giving you a chance to cast 3 Projectiles instead of 1 when you cast your Primary Spell, Increase Damage while increasing Damage received, making you Mana Spell sometimes explode on contact which shoots some projectiles in various directions, and so forth. Honestly, I was rather underwhelmed by the Talents, I didn't find them as amazing as it would imply.
There are Items to find too, and they do various things, such as increasing stats, damage, Mana/Health, Mana Regen, Armor, etc. But they also have other traits too sometimes, such as occasionally summoning a meteor to strike the enemy, occasionally casting tornadoes around you, etc.
There are 3 types of Items. First are Gear, which consist of a Hat, Shoulders, Cloak, and Boots Slot, and you can only have one per slot. Secondly are trinkets, which you can have as many as you want. Then there are Pets, which are rare to find. All types carry the same types of boosts, like stats/damage and the like, and of course random bonuses. Pets, along with having those bonuses, also some times attack or debuff enemies depending on the Pet. You can have as many pets as you like.
There are a bunch of Primary and Mana Spells to find, with decent variety.
When you start a game or go to a new area, you always start in you house. The house starts out with a bench that will allow you to buy permanent upgrades to it. Such as Totems that permanently increase your Health or Mana. You also start with a bench that will convert 10 Coins into Crystals, which are needed to buy the house upgrades. The bench will also convert Crystals into 5 Coins. Crystals and House Upgrades are the only thing that transfers between games. As for what kind of upgrades, the Totems like I mentioned earlier, then there are benches that let you buy Keys and Potions, a Bench that will give you 1 Magic Item per game, a Kitchen Counter that makes it so you start each level with full health, etc. Bosses drop 3-4 when you kill them, and mini bosses drop 1-2. And like I mentioned, 10 Coins can be converted into 1 Crystal, so be sure to convert them BEFORE you die, or whenever you get enough.
There's also an option to change the color theme, which I really appreciate. It defaults to a dark color theme, but there's also a Bright Color Theme that I preferred, and even an option to mix it up. There's also a bunch of Mouse Cursors to choose from.
There are other things too, but that's enough explaining. For downsides, I found the Levels rather small, with not much variety in prop setup. I wish there was an option to make them larger. And while there are a decent amount of House Upgrades, I wish there were more. The Talents were rather underwhelming as well, I wish there were more interesting ones. And I found the Stat Points pretty useless overall, with only the Health upgrade being useful, with Armor and Mana being worth it afterwards. Health and Mana increases 10 points per stat point, while the other stats only increase by 1, making them not worth putting Stat Points into, seeing as Items are common enough and boost them far more.
Still, overall those are minor complaints. The game is definitely worth the $5 price tag, and I recommend you pick it up if your into a game Like Binding of Isaac with RPG elements and spells.

I have decided to write a review after approx 14hrs game time and 32 runs of this game. This game I will be honest at the start is hella fun, you have lots of things to find, abilities, weapons, armor, you name it, the levels are reletively short, followed by a boss at the end of each level.
But I will say this, on normal difficulty (easiest) the game for me became so frustrating I had to stop playing. Now the game in and of itself was fine, but it was the final boss of the game (Ragenroth) that is where I had the problems. And this boss even on normal difficulty was hard as hell. I can't even fathom what this dude would be like on the harder difficulty levels of this game. The boss spawns these things on the ground which shoot green projectiles at you and if they hit you, the boss heals. Ok fine, I can live with that, but even on normal difficulty and after my 1st time fighting him and approx 2ish hrs later, I had to just give up, because I was so mad, I was shaking. I didn't even die, I was so powerful from all the upgrades, abilies, armor, ect that I had, it was impossible for me to die. But because of this mechanic the boss has, I just could not defeat it.
I got too the boss a 2nd time, once again with pretty awesome stats and this time, I fought him for about 30min, before I decided, you know what? This is just stupid and I have had enough.
There is no set pattern on the boss stage, as too where he spawns the pads that shoot the green projectiles, you just have to run around endlessly trying to dodge these damn things and try to get hits on the boss, without those green projectiles hitting you.
People on the discussion forums were pointing out how easy it was to defeat the boss, blah blah blah, but in the end nobody showed either screen shots or video proof of them beating said boss, which makes me wonder of the validity of it.
Personally for me, I would not recommend this game and I will keep the game and follow the updates and hope that the dev does something to remedy this situation, as to be very honest with you all and the dev, the entire game is great, there is no doubt, I know it sounds stupid to just have an issue with the final boss and the rest of the game be great and maybe others are beating it like they say they are in the discusson forums but without any proof of this, screen shots, ect, I have my doubts.
Please dev, lower the difficulty level of the boss on normal.
I am not going to recommend this persnally, but by all means, play the game, it is fun, but I think it has some serious balance issues, especially with boss fights (mainly the final boss).
Cheers.

There are no reasons why Super Meat Boy shouldn't have been one of my favourite games, with a 5 star recommendation, except that the more I played, the more I found many of the traits it was lauded for, I actually found to be very sub-par, and I am hence going to rate this NOT RECOMMENDED.
BAD. Supposed to be one of the slickest Mario-like control surfaces available, but the dude just feels like he floats around, uncontrollably, constantly. I have played with both Xbox and Logitech F310 controllers and its the same feeling, I just don't like the feel AT ALL. I don't like the wall jumping feel. I dont like the landing feel.
In fact there is too much wall jumping. The game should be called "Wall Jump Boy" , you spend too much time doing wall jumps on a single wall, trying to control this unstable square that floats and slides around.
If a game is difficult then it needs to give a sense of growth and that you are building expertise. This game just feels like a constant cannonball run where you try to luck-out.
So rather than feeling like I'm building touch and skill , it feels like "Just try the level 100 times, repeat the same jump combo and eventually you might not get sliced and he might not bounce around and kill himself"
In a platform game like Spelunky, every death feels like it occurred for a reason, and next time you face that situation you can tackle it with a new level of touch and skill, which grows over time.
In Meat Boy, it just feels like I am hardly better than when I started, I still float and slide off platforms, my wall jumping is still random and manic.
NOT FUN
As you would have read, it is exceptionally difficult.
There are 2 reasons, the first reason is that it is hard to control the meat boy. This is not good.
The 2nd reason is that the level are designed to be very difficult. This could actually be good.
Do I like difficult games? Yes
I find this game difficult just for the sake of it. The levels are not particularly well designed, e.g. you will come to a dead-drop and have to just plunge down without any indication of what to do. So you die, and do it again. A truly well designed difficult game will give you a clue or a chance to act skillfully, but in Meat Boy expect to be punished and have to memorize things just because.
The repetitive level designs doesn't help and the challenges are rarely breathtaking, they just demand you to bash run and jump 100 times til you fluke a wall jump over 20 spikes between a bouncing slime ball and avoid sliding off a platform.
It's not fun and it's not in the spirit of hard games.
CRAP
The pallette is dull, the graphics are insipid, and lacking detail. Not to mention they are puerile (e.g. balls of snot/slime), but we are talking about poorly shaded balls of snot and slime.
Pixel art and retro art design can be beautiful but Meat Boy doesn't hit that , except when it does delight (briefly) the few hidden retro levels. (which happen to be obscenely difficult) e.g. The GameBoy inspired level. That was cool.
2ND RATE PLATFORMER. NOT REMINISCENT OF GOLDEN AGE. NOT RECOMMEND
Ultimately this game suffers from its own success, I expected it to be awesome, I didn't enjoy it (for reasons listed), and I gave it a rest. I picked it up again and tried to enjoy it again, and I just found more and more reasons that made me NOT ENJOY IT.
I don't like it, I don't appreciate it.
The game is 'OK' but when you're expecting it to be great, an OK game feels lousy.
It just screams out to me as a second-rate platformer, not at all reminiscent of Mario Bros or any great platformer.
This game was supposed to represent the spirit of the golden age of platformers , and it only represents the stink. It is like a bad clone that ended up on a Chinese pirate copy of a Mega Drive that some guy was seling at a swap meet.
In fact right now there are a lot better platformers on Steam. Go out and play them instead.

This game is adorable. A fusion of monster-breeding / tower defence, the cutesy graphics and quirky soundtrack add a touch of whimsy to the game. You basically spend your time managing your growing apartment, earning income to see to the needs of your population of tenants. Each race of tenants has their own demands and even ongoing racial rivalries that will require you to pick and choose who or what you want to stay and adds a touch of replayability.
As much as I enjoy the game though, it plays very much like a semi-idle game as some events like breeding, getting a house-mate and even a tenant you want are so random that you sometimes find yourself leaving the game running for hours. This would be okay if the game could run in the background while you do other things like surf or do your homework, but it does not. The feature of the game auto-pausing when the window is not active might ordinarily be a good thing, but in this case it only makes gameplay a little tedious since you become a prisoner of the window.
All in all, it makes for an interesting way to burn a few hours, but not if you like multitasking on your computer.

[Disclaimer: I am not an objective person.]
Conceived back in 2013 and successfully kickstarted in 2014 under the name "Echoes of Eridu", 20XX is an incredible action platforming roguelite. Based upon the gameplay of the classic series "Megaman X" for the Super Nintendo, 20XX procedurally generates levels based on level and biome. Each stage getting more difficult as you collect items that power-up your character.
You play as either Nina, a buster toting bombshell, or Ace, a blade-wielding melee fighter. Each character brings a different playstyle and quirks to the gameplay. The developer has expressed idea of more characters, but for now these two characters fill the roles of Megaman and Zero very well. The characters won't be lonely as you can also play couch multiplayer or online.
Now for my review of the game. I'll be honest, I'm extremely biased. I've played this game for over 2 years both multiplayer and singleplayer. I love the game and everything about it, but here goes:
20XX gameplays is just what you expect from a Megaman X game. Precise platforming with shooting and slashing. With the two characters you play as, both are extremely fun and rewarding to play as. They bring different playstyles as mentioned previously. Nina is safe with her ranged attacks but sacrifices damage, while Ace plays dangerously sacrificing safety for devastating melee attacks.
There are very few times you will feel that the game is unfair. The only times will occur when an enemy hits you off-screen. But, for the most part if you get hurt or fail, it's definitely your fault. The game has optional paths and challenges that rewards skillful play, and you feel extremely satisfied when you succesful navigate or blast your way through them.
Every run will be different from the last and you choose what you do depending on what the game gives you. Adaptability is a must with roguelike/roguelite games such as this one. However, 20XX is much more forgiving than games of the genre, such as "The Binding of Isaac" or "Enter the Gungeon". Although those play much differently.
Near non-existent. While the lore is extensive, the story isn't really there. It's as much of a story as the original Megaman X. However, from the cutscenes and encounters you face. You'll be able to piece together some semblance of a story. The story is just the right amount for a roguelike/roguelite game. Perhaps in the future there willl be more to read up on.
There's is however, a ton to look into. The lore for every enemy is written pretty well and gives good insight into them. Especially the bosses. There are currently 10 stages with varying difficulties, depending on how they fall into the run. The last two stages are always the same in terms of bosses, but the layout is still procedurally generated like the others. There are plans for more content in the future, however, what we have now is already a good amount for the price point.
While subjective, I really like the graphics style of 20XX. Very aesthetically pleasing, with a lot of small details you can notice (It's impressive if you do, considering how hectic the game can get). There are options to adjust the quality of the graphics in game, but it runs very well on almost all systems.
There are issues with stutter during instances with large amount of onscreen effects, such as explosions. But those instances are usually not going to cause you to make a mistake, as they are mostly cinematic. These small issues happen a bit more often than they should, but are actively being worked on. So be warned if you're on a lower end PC.
I love the soundtrack. It's amazing and fully captures what an action platformer like 20XX is. Cityfires, the composer of the soundtrack, has done a wonderful job. Each stage features a different soundtrack and does a great job of mixing the action and the atmosphere together to make you feel even more badass than you already are.
The community of a game can make or break it. Here, the community is great in my limited experience with them. I regularly read the steam discussion boards in order to get information on the game and most people are extremely helpful. They even have a discord for multiplayer and game discussion.
The developer is also very active within the community and responds to critique and suggestions very well. It's great to see a developer actually take part in discussions and actively participate with everyone.
It's a Megaman-esque procedurally generated action platformer. Yes, it's replayable. I've played it for the last 2 years. Wile not as expansive as something like "The Binding of Isaac: Afterbirth+". It's a lot less punishing and provides the same level of satisfaction. Every run is different and you need to learn and adapt to each situation differently. Every action you perform well makes you feel awesome, but that's probably because I have something of a hero complex.
Add on couch and online co-op. While the netcode is a bit iffy, it's still great to play online with another person and makes for a different experience from single-player. I originally played with my brother, who I grew up playing the X-series with when we were younger. The multiplayer really adds on another layer of gameplay for you and your friends to enjoy.
20XX is a great game with tons of replayability and content. While there issues, such as framerate at certain areas and instance as well as lack of story, 20XX shows a lot of promise for the future, but the current content is great for the price point as is. If you're looking to fill the Megaman-sized hole you tried to fill with "Mighty No. 9" or "Azure Striker Gunvolt", give 20XX a try, you'll have a great time, probably.

I bought this game during early access nearly 3 years ago. It was worth the money then, and it has improved so much since then.
20XX is an action-platformer in a similar style to the Mega Man X games for SNES. The twist is that the levels, powerups, bosses, etc are procedurally generated, providing greater replayability. There are also several features designed to improve replayability, such as online multiplayer, metagame progression (unlocks, etc), seeded challenges, multiple characters (basically, ranged or melee).
The procedural generation serves to keep things interesting, but it is not purely random. Difficult optional paths often hold stronger powerups. Stages get longer and bosses change their behavior based on the order in which you fight them. This means that on one run you may encounter the penguin boss first and defeat him easily, but on the next run he may be the 5th boss and prove quite challenging. Currency and shops also help give you control over the randomness. You can collect "nuts" and spend them on extra health, energy for weapons, or save up for new powerups/weapons.
After playing for a while, you will start to notice the recurring rooms used in the proc-gen, but most of them have multiple ways to traverse them. In some worlds, the levels are pretty clearly a series of rooms stitched together in random order while other worlds do a better job of creating a level that feels like it was created by hand. However, all the stages still have hidden paths to uncover. The challenge becomes how to adapt your playstyle to the powerups/weapons/enemy patterns you are given in order to complete a run as efficiently as possible.

The hardest thing about replaying the game on higher difficulties settings is the boredom. So many unskippable scenes! There's also parts where the game caps your running speed because shame on you for trying run away from dialogue you've heard before!
In addition to unskippable scenes, the game has the ridiculous habit of letting things "go on" as you wait for your screen to return from black. Repeatedly on mission 10, I kept coming out the cutscene only to find Danta having walked off a ledge. I don't know how they let that in. To a new player, it'd feel like they'd spawned you only to kill you.
As to a single playhrough, the voice acting or writing is just painfully awful at parts. (Things are either over-acted or have a unnatural word choice for a modern setting). The platforming is also a very annoying chore since Dante doesn't have much ups for being part angel, and his grapples (Demonic Pull/Angelic Lift) have odd targeting delays as you try to chain grapple movements together during platforming.
The controls on keyboard+mouse do not feel good, and the default gamepad controls go against the "standard" in actions games. (The left button is your gun instead of your standard melee, and the top button is basic melee instead of alt melee. Also, there's two evade buttons, down on the D-pad does nothing by default, and  the Angelic mode (LT) vs Demonic (RT) mode mechanic does not feel as well implemented as that of Castlevania: Lords of Shadow's Light mode vs Dark mode, which is a game that came earlier than this one.)
As for the combat, it's alright; not terrible, but it's no where close to the most fun I've ever had. The enemy desigin is a bit boring since a lot of enemies are re-skins of others and have a broken doll motif; (it's very lackluster for a game where demons and angels are real.) Mentioned earlier, the binary mode mechanic feels better done in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. As for how the game fits in the action-adventure genre, I would recommend Castlevania: Lords of Shadow or God of War over this.
UPDATE: Got all the achievements in the Vergil's Downfall DLC. It's even less fun than the main game since:
■ There's a bug where Vergil can't perform a regular rising strike.
■ His Devil Triggers offer less security than Dante's Devil Trigger.
■ The targetting on his projectiles is subpar since it can literally pick the wrong platform to materialize during platforming.
■ On the subject of platforming, Vergil doesn't have a regular double jump; (he still has a way to get high, but I don't know why they made it less intuitive).
■ A lot of his attack animations are slow and long compared to Dante equivalents; (it's especially bad for his standard melee).
■ His dodging is just awful compared to Dante's. The immunity window seems even shorter than Dante's regular dodge, and Vergil's dodge can be cut short if there's an enemy in his path.
■ You will take hits from enemies outside of your view. This happens sometimes in the main game (especially against harpies), but it's more common in Vergil's downfail since there's more harpies and enemies that like perfoming 2-hit combos.
■ The main boss fight in the DLC (mission 5), is a lot cheaper than any of the bosses in the main game. He has 2 attacks that are extremely hard to dodge; projectile swords which you can't destroy with your projectiles, and a dive bomb kick that interrupts Vergil's dodge and forces Vergil to take damage. There's also this annoying bit where he teleports away and you need to repeatedly have great timing in dodge a ring of projectile swords; it's a lot less forgiving than anything in the main game.

All in all, DMC isn't a good Devil May Cry by any standards except for overall gameplay, but its a DAMN fine game that you should try out if there's a sale or you have $30 lying around

This game is both a blessing and a curse, and here's why.
First of all, let me say that this is "Devil May Cry" for casual gamers. This is basically how DMC2 was, and is probably a lot of the reason behind the hate for this game. You will earn style easily by spamming a couple of moves or even by shooting, there is not much freedom of style later on due to specific enemies all having to die with specific movesets/grabs in specific ways, it's slow, and it all sort of falls apart from there. This is its curse.
Don't even get me started on the platforming, the simplified bosses, and that god awful camera.
Now before you !TRIGGER! and hit that NO button, please read further first.
From all the crap that they smashed together and ended up making another DMC2/Darksiders with, there is some diamond within the ashes. First of all, the combat is definitely more cinematic. I'm not talking about the bosses. I'm talking about when you're finished killing someone, the scene closes up on (Vergil/Dante) quickly glancing behind him, and bam, more demons. Cinematic transitions like that are just awesome. While the acting behind basically every main character was virtually garbage, the cutscenes were actually pretty great. The city felt fleshed out, the antagonist (both of them) did things in rather creative ways, and it was a breath of fresh air from the "Demon becomes God, then dies" plot that virtually every other DMC had.
The DLC (Vergil's Downfall) was a nice "return to roots" with a lot of the old Vergil's moveset, refining itself so well that even Capcom couldn't deny it when they used a lot of it for DMC4:SE's Vergil. ♥♥♥♥ Devil Mode, though.
As much as I hate this game and its cushiony, casual feel to it, I'm still going to recommend it for the same reason I'd recommend someone to play DMC2. It's not a gem in the series, but the mechanics implemented bring a lot of ideas that have and will evolve later entries, and it's worth taking a look at it for that reason.
Also because Combichrist is in it.

Este es mi primer Análisis de Steam, así que perdonen la poca profesionalidad.
Ori y el Bosque Ciego.
¿Alguna vez han visto una pintura muy bella y recordado un tema perfecto para ella o pensado en que música seria perfecta para la obra? Ori es un juego que soluciona esa pregunta, una verdadera pintura maravillosa con la música perfecta de fondo para crear una demostración artística en pantalla con la que muchos juegos solo podrían soñar.
Y no es que solo se vea bello y su música sea encantadora, es que ambas cosas y cuando consideramos la historia y el gameplay en sí, todo trabaja en una armonía para generar una sola experiencia de juego sobrecogedora en belleza, dificultad y emotividad, lo que provoca una buena pintura, una buena canción o un buen libro, Ori y el Bosque Ciego lo entregan en su totalidad, como una ola de sentimientos que comienzan con una de las más refinadas introducciones y luego mantiene dicho impulso de principio a fin en una historia, que sin grandes diálogos, solo con su arte, entrega mucho más que cientos de otros títulos en sus incontables líneas de dialogo.
Gráficamente el juego es sublime, la paleta de colores es variada, vibrante y profunda, las animaciones, efectos especiales se mesclan lo suficiente con el entorno para parecer naturales del mismo mientras que resaltan lo suficiente para mantener la atención enfocada en lo que es el gameplay, tan limpio es el trabajo en este caso, que: "es que no vi eso" no es una excusa válida para morir, cada escena es tan limpia como la anterior y el feedback visual lo suficientemente llamativo para cumplir como advertencia.
Las etapas del juego, para ser en su gran mayoría "un bosque" son increíblemente variadas, no repetitivas en lo absoluto y los estilos de las mismas dan una sensación permanente de un ambiente vivo, con pequeños detalles moviéndose en los fondos y al frente del plano de Ori, los colores distintivos de cada una, yendo de verdes vibrantes a purpuras profundos o grises y blancos, la paleta cambia al servicio de la sección y la narrativa de la historia de forma magnifica.
La música por su lado, y los efectos de sonido por otro, trabajan con el fin de crear esta permanente sensación de fragilidad expuesta por Ori ante la grandeza abrumadora y hostil del Bosque, la música es la voz del Bosque, de sus pruebas, sus peligros y sus ambientes, un permanente recordatorio de la lucha constante pero también de la esperanza y del cómo se pueden superar. Por su lado Ori, refleja fragilidad en todo sentido, su voz ya sea al ser golpeado o por ejemplo salir del agua, exponen a una criatura frágil y débil que sin embargo, es capaz de crecer y con esperanzas superar su viaje.
Pero hasta el momento, pareciera que el juego no es más que solo buen arte y música... Ahí es donde entra el aspecto del gameplay, que debe ser uno de los juegos de plataformas "metroidvania" más precisos, placenteros y desafiante de jugar en años, probablemente desde Dust: An Elysian Tail que no había un platformer tan sólido y cumplidor. Ori es ágil, eso se representa a la perfección en el juego, agilidad y rapidez es lo que el juego constantemente pone a prueba, con "un compañero" que hace la suerte de "ataque" Ori es libre de saltar, colgar, trepar, planear, evadir y desviar proyectiles y enemigos mientras ataca y combate, las secciones de plataforma y los puzles son casi indivisibles unos de otros, resolverlos requiere tanto ingenio como habilidad y reflejos, nunca se ponen a prueba por separado y vas a morir, varias veces, porque a pesar de su apariencia, no es para nada un juego fácil.
La exploración es magnífica, la cantidad de contenido es precisa además, con secretos que promueven la rejugabilidad, las mejoras de habilidades y los arboles de las mismas son variadas, Ori inicia su viaje como una criatura débil sin la capacidad de combatir prácticamente, termina el mismo con una diversidad de herramientas que le permiten enfrentar cualquier desafío que el Bosque le imponga. El progreso de Ori en la historia del juego y en la jugabilidad misma y los desafíos que la nueva área propone van perfectamente entrelazados, progresar en habilidades equivale a progresar en la historia y nuevos desafíos. Volver atrás para visitar nuevamente escenarios superados y conseguir mejoras es parte de la experiencia también.
Sobre la historia en sí, no mencionare mucho, es el elemento que conduce todo lo demás y la verdad entre menos de esta se sepa, creo que mejor va a todo, la pequeña reseña en la página de venta de steam ya me parece mucha información.
Sobre las deficiencias del juego, y no existe un juego perfecto ya que estamos, son realmente algo a "hilar fino". Quizá en ciertas etapas los puzles no son tan entretenidos, o quizá la voz del narrador no es la más apropiada a veces... Y con un trabajo quirujico que requiere esfuerzo realizar, podríamos encontrar falencias, pero cuando uno debe obligarse a buscarlas de tal manera, eso habla alto de lo positivo. Ori no es perfecto, podría por ejemplo, durar 100 horas... Aunque no sé si existe algún corazón con sentimientos que pueda tolerar tanto.
En neurofisiología, la Sinestesia es la condición de "confundir estímulos" permitiendo a los individuos por ejemplo "ver" la música en colores, o saborearla incluso. Ori y el Bosque Ciego es eso, un juego Sinestesico, que confunde de forma maravillosa los colores con la música, los conduce con una historia emotiva y poderosa y los presenta a través de un juego de plataformas sólido, refinado y apenas corto a ser perfecto.
Las calificaciones en números me parecen una pérdida de tiempo, pero si a alguien le sirven, 11/10. Es un juego que hace todo cuasi perfectamente bien, y el nivel de emotividad que destila le da un punto extra sobre la calificación perfecta. Ori y el Bosque Ciego es algo que todo desarrollador debería aspirar a ser capaz de producir. Muchos ríen cuando alguien menciona que los videojuegos son en parte, obras de arte, probablemente después de jugar Ori y el Bosque Ciego, esas risas se callen.

I read a lot of the reviews before buying and now having put a fair bit of time into it (900+ hours) I can appreciate both sides of the argument.  However personally, I absolutely love this game.
This is definitely the spiritual successor to the original Elite.  The initial trade runs to build up some credits evokes strong memories of the Lave to Leesti run for those old enough to remember such things.  Fortunately though the inhabitants of this universe haven’t felt the need to have their space stations constantly spin in order to make docking a nightmare…
Yet it goes much beyond that.  As others have mentioned, this soon morphs into an empire management style game.  This seems to upset some, but there isn’t anything forcing people to spend most of their time on this aspect of the game.  The various plot line missions encourage you to be the pilot doing most of the action (hub plot excluded) and there is always something to keep you going.
It’s not all roses in the garden though.  In the early hours of the game, the computer generated voices can grate a bit, but now they seem to fit quite well with the various races.  The UI is functional rather than pretty.  And the AI…  It’s quite the little tease.  You never know when it is going to get you, but it definitely will.  It’ll happily take you across the entire galaxy, dodgy asteroids, swerving around slow moving freighters only to ram you into the side of the space station you’re trying to dock at.  I’ve decided this is all karma for ignoring the game and letting it play itself at times.  Save often (salvage insurance).
The major criticism is that the learning curve is pretty steep.  That’s good and bad.  It’ll put off new players but means that you feel a greater sense of achievement once you finally wrestle control of that CAG script and work out what in hell it does.   Don’t judge the game until you’ve put a load of hours into it.
In short, if you want a fast paced space shoot-em-up, this isn’t it.  If you love Elite-style games and want to explore a universe with some gorgeous ships, a thriving economy and a good back story, this is it.

No More Room in Hell is a very well-executed Source engine mod. In NMRIH, the focus is on survival and escape rather than combat. It's a refreshing change from the arcade zombie shooters such as Left 4 Dead or Killing Floor. Gameplay is simple. Most games consist of defending a series of safe zones or completing a set of objectives. The game's difficulty sits in that sweet spot where playing with a group of random people can be difficult, but playing co-op with several friends makes everything much easier. Melee and ranged weapons take a little time to master, and finding ammo or weapons isn't always easy. NMRIH gets the atmosphere of a zombie apocalypse exactly right;. For example, you can't hear or see allies if you are too far away from them and the maps are very dark. This creates a sense of urgency and fear which few other survival games accomplish. For a free Source engine mod, NMRIH delivers a lot more enjoyment than current competitors such as Contagion or DayZ.

Razenroth is Enitvare’s second venture onto Steam following their popular debut, Stonerid, which was met with mixed reviews. The studio has put into effect the lessons that they learned from their first game and the result is more than a little surprising. Yet Razenroth remains a largely undiscovered gem by Steam gamers. This is a great pity as there is much to like about it. The game combines largely traditional top down shooting action RPG gameplay mechanics with roguelike elements to great effect. I found myself dying regularly and relatively quickly in my first few attempts. I was a little confused as to the best approach to take. However, once I finally began learning the nature of the game I found it to be a relatively quick study and one that is a joy to learn.
The opening several minutes long cutscene does a thorough job of establishing the storytelling of the game. You’re essentially searching for your grandpa in the Valley of Whispers  You start the game in your grandpa’s cabin and are free to explore the area and kill monsters who are ultra aggressive and hit harder than most early level game mobs do. You will not last long to get into a direct shootout with them so the first skill that you’ll need to pick up is that of quick movement and evasion. You can be attacked from mobs not on your screen meaning that you will have to become ultra alert to where attacks are coming from. Kill enough enemies and you’ll gain talent points. The culmination of each level includes a boss fight – each with its own set of mechanics. These boss fights can last several minutes giving you time to quickly learn their methods of attack and defense and then methodically taking them down. The boss fights were my favorite part of my time with the game as they genuinely feel like fair encounters that do not cheat but ones that are programmed well enough to be very challenging. The loot system is typical of most games within the genre. However, you’ll have to work for it as regular mobs seem to rarely, if ever, drop any loot. Boss mobs will drop at least one and there are chests and other special areas scattered throughout the levels that provide you an opportunity to find an upgrade.
In regards to the technical perspective of the game do not expect much. Both the graphics and the sound are rather bland experiences. Although the game is intended to be played in ‘dark’ mode I found the game more enjoyable aesthetically in light mode. Some may argue that this lowers the difficulty of the game but I found it to be a better experience this way. It’s definitely the type of game that I would recommend play while listening to a podcast. As I know that has become an increasingly popular thing to do I don’t necessarily argue that this is a weakness of the game but rather that the sound is just not memorable at all. Given that there is not much demand on the technical perspective the game runs extremely well. I was able to test this on a lower spec machine as well as my more modern gaming rig.
Razenroth has its shortcomings.  It is far from the perfect game however the gameplay resonated with me to make it an enjoyable experience. I’ve long been a fan of both roguelikes and action RPG’s. The top down action suited the gameplay and the boss battles were varying enough that it is well worth continuing on throughout the game. All in all, a very solid experience.

My first Batman game from the Arkham series. As such I cannot compare it to the others, yet. But this also works because it is first on the Arkham game story timeline. The combat is okay but gets a bit more clunky as new enemy types appear. This is coupled with keyboard controls that are not as responsive or well configured. I actually had to swap to a gamepad for the Deathstroke fight (and a couple of more times later in the game). There are lots of collectibles available (Anarky tags, Enigma data packs) and a TON of side missions. Plus 4 challenge ranks you can attempt while playing. But this all contributes to easily missable (and sometimes bugged) content, including some main assassins. Boss fights/levels are hit or miss. While some are great and engaging others become annoying really quick. Some examples - terrible fixed-camera Mad Hatter level and Deadshot hostage level end. A lot of people do not like Deathstroke, but once I switched to gamepad, the fight was actually good. Predator rooms give you options to either stealth or go in with a bang. Although this freedom is crippled by the challenges in Worst Nightmare rank. Because there is a limited amount of predator rooms you will want to do them according to what is in the challenge rank. After you finish up all of the content there is still challenge mode for some trophies but this mode became really annoying/boring fairly quick. Story is what drives this game and, while it is cheesy sometimes, I loved it. However, if you only go for the story the game is rather short. Even so it has glitches and crashed a couple of times. So get it for that nice Batman story or just to roam around Gotham ... but get it on a sale.

I bought this game during early access nearly 3 years ago. It was worth the money then, and it has improved so much since then.
20XX is an action-platformer in a similar style to the Mega Man X games for SNES. The twist is that the levels, powerups, bosses, etc are procedurally generated, providing greater replayability. There are also several features designed to improve replayability, such as online multiplayer, metagame progression (unlocks, etc), seeded challenges, multiple characters (basically, ranged or melee).
The procedural generation serves to keep things interesting, but it is not purely random. Difficult optional paths often hold stronger powerups. Stages get longer and bosses change their behavior based on the order in which you fight them. This means that on one run you may encounter the penguin boss first and defeat him easily, but on the next run he may be the 5th boss and prove quite challenging. Currency and shops also help give you control over the randomness. You can collect "nuts" and spend them on extra health, energy for weapons, or save up for new powerups/weapons.
After playing for a while, you will start to notice the recurring rooms used in the proc-gen, but most of them have multiple ways to traverse them. In some worlds, the levels are pretty clearly a series of rooms stitched together in random order while other worlds do a better job of creating a level that feels like it was created by hand. However, all the stages still have hidden paths to uncover. The challenge becomes how to adapt your playstyle to the powerups/weapons/enemy patterns you are given in order to complete a run as efficiently as possible.

With 1.0 FINALLY released, now would be a good time to highly praise this amazing title! 20XX delivers on bringing fans of the Mega Man X series a true spiritual successor, adding in roguelike elements to ensure that no two runs will ever be the same, complete with multiple armors, loads of cool enemies and bosses, with tons and TONS of awesome power-ups to keep coming back to try and unlock/find.
Story~: 20XX follows the adventure of Nana and Ace, the respective proxies of X and Zero, being hired by a pair of familiar looking scientists to wipe out eight rogue... Robot Masters? Mavericks? They never say what affiliation the bosses belong to, just that they're tearing the city apart, and you need to stop them.
Graphics~: Inspired by the days of classic gaming, 20XX harbors a rich 16-bit color palette, with plenty of lens flares and glowing, ambiant attacks by all characters, protagonist and antagonists alike.
Music~: The music is very catchy, although due to bosses sharing stage themes (equating to four main themes between the eight of them), you will have to listen to a couple themes a few times... more so when you inevitably die and do a new run. A good thing they're catchy and enjoyable to listen to, then!
Gameplay~: The bread and butter of the package. 20XX, being a spiritual successor to Mega Man X, has you running, jumping, and shooting/slashing at everything come your way, as to be aspected. However, with the roguelike elements in play, the layout of each stage changes between every run, ensuring that one simply cannot memorize a stage and its hazards, forcing players to build upon their reaction times and learn the ins and outs of their enemies and the weapons available to them. Nuts are the main currency within the game to allow you to purchase various augments (AUGS) or armor pieces to enhance your character and your odds of surviving the run. Every stage ends with a boss fight, and beating him rewards you with a large chest, which you can shatter to get some pick-up goodies.
Once a boss is slain, you then get the choice of taking their weapon, taking a large stack of nuts, or a random AUG. You may only hold onto three boss weapons at a time, but each is assigned their own button, and boss weapons can be replaced with new ones. Unlike traditional Mega man titles, your first stage is randomly selected at the start of the run, and completing each stage grants you the choice between three of the remaining seven boss stages, randomly determined before you get to the end. Holding true to Mega Man tradition, the bosses do have a weapon weakness order, although whether you are lucky enough to have the run allow you to make use of the weakness order is entirely up to luck. Due to the roguelike nature of the game, later stages get progressively more difficult the further you get, forcing you to improve your reaction times, and expects you to have some pieces of armor.
Armor upgrades come in four types: Helmet, Body, Arms, and Legs. In addition, there are four different complete sets; while you are free to mix and match what pieces you come across in your run, each armor set has a unique set bonus for completing the armor. The last thing worth mentioning in the core gameplay are the other two types of currency: Tokens, and Soul Chips. Tokens are used on the slot machine device that shows up randomly in the stages, usually in the hallway leading to the boss. Soul chips are acquired at the end of a stage and from random, uniquely glowing enemies. Unlike Nuts, Soul Chips cannot be spent during a run, and instead are saved for when the run is over (whether it was a success or not...), and are used in the main lobby to purchase new AUG's for future runs, new permanent passive AUS's that don't need to be collected, being able to start with a few AUGs, and buying Tokens to use in the run.
There are a lot of things I have ommitted explinations on, such as the various difficulty modes, daily and weekly challenge runs, seeded runs, and multiplayer. However, the core material mentioned in Gameplay applies to all of it, and that's what really counts here. Without naming.... another, disappointing title, 20XX honors and maintains the spirit of the legendary blue bomber, and will keep you coming back for more and more... and more... and more... and more... Did I mention no two runs are ever the same?

The weirdest thing about my review is that I suck at this game. I am absolutely terrible at Mega Man and games similar to it. But you don't need to be good at something to have fun with it, and that's been most of my experience with 20XX. Fans of Mega Man X will notice more similarities with that series than with the classic Mega Man, but you don't need to have Mega Man experience at all to enjoy what 20XX offers: a well-crafted, difficult, roguelike platformer experience.
You get two characters to choose between: Nina, who fires long-range blaster shots, and Ace, who has a close-range sword for melee combat. There are 10 levels to complete, but good luck making it that far, you'll find yourself having some hard times by level 3 or 4. Being a roguelike, this game allows you to improve every time you die through purchasing permanent upgrades or augments that you can acquire mid-run. Levels are generated randomly every time you enter them, and boss patterns will change depending on when you face them (Level 1 Kur is much easier than Level 5 Kur, for example).
The absolute best thing about 20XX is its presentation. My God, Battery Staple Games, do you have the entire cast of the original Mega Man games working for you? This looks exactly like what would happen if you took the platformers of old and gave them modern paint. The levels, the characters, the bosses,
, it's all an amazing treat.
The gameplay is entirely dependant on personal experience. Levels are randomly generated, after all, so one run through the Vaculab will be different from the next run through the Vaculab. For the most part, enemies and hazards are placed in spots that are easy to overcome, or will require a bit of quick thinking, but there will certainly be a couple of cheap shots against you. Historically speaking, the Agnisort level has been the poster child of difficulty, and for me it's still certainly an annoyance with some cheap fire hazards. That being said, I did open this review saying that I'm not good at this game, so your mileage will certainly vary. Keep in mind that the later levels in this game are not for the faint of heart; I've made it as far as level 6 or 7 before, and those were brutal. Levels 8, 9, and 10 apparently go even further, so be prepared for a challenge.
My last note is on performance. The game runs very smoothly, but for those of you on lower machines, you may want to turn down a few settings. Some levels and effects, particularly Agnisort, may slow your gameplay down.
and they've gotten way better since the game was in Early Access,
more improvements are hopefully coming down this line in the future.
All in all, if this kind of game is your jam, you've seriously got to give it a try. It's certainly better than Mighty No. 9, and for cheaper too. I absolutely recommend this to everyone who's interested in games like this. :)

The story, oh the story! As this is a review, I'm not going to post spoilers, but tied with everything else within the game, Moon Studios reminds us that when all elements of a game are balanced and perfectly matched, you are no longer making a game, rather a playable art.

Ori's controls are responsible, fun, easy to use and the abilities encourage positive exploration and creative uses to solve the puzzles of level design.

Chances are that you're looking at this game because it's developed and published by Idea Factory - the makers of the Hyperdimension Neptunia series.  Well, I'm happy to say that with a great history of success in that series, this game does not disappoint.
The majority of complaints about this game are that the characters are somewhat shallow, there's a lot more visual novel than RPG, and it's fairly repetitive.  In all of those regards, this game is actually better than the Hyperdimension Neptunia games.  This is because the characters here are *more* loveable than Neptunia characters, the visual novel side is generally more interesting and dynamic, and the repetitive nature is easily dismissed.
This is a standalone game with enjoyable writing and fun characters.  With Idea Factory, that means there's a bunch of different endings implemented just to give it a sense of being your own story, along with a really unique gaming experience.  Narratively, this game is comparable to Dragon Ball Z's alternate universe story where Goku dies to illness before fighting the Androids.  As such, you'll learn to love the characters on a *very* personal level, only with the knowledge that they're going to die soon enough and you won't see their dreams become reality.  You hope dearly that maybe, just maybe, this time you'll beat the boss or trigger an event to have a few more days, but you usually won't.  It is the epitome of morbid despair in gaming, but in a way that doesn't make you feel bad.  Eventually you'll win, but at what cost?

No More Room in Hell is a very well-executed Source engine mod. In NMRIH, the focus is on survival and escape rather than combat. It's a refreshing change from the arcade zombie shooters such as Left 4 Dead or Killing Floor. Gameplay is simple. Most games consist of defending a series of safe zones or completing a set of objectives. The game's difficulty sits in that sweet spot where playing with a group of random people can be difficult, but playing co-op with several friends makes everything much easier. Melee and ranged weapons take a little time to master, and finding ammo or weapons isn't always easy. NMRIH gets the atmosphere of a zombie apocalypse exactly right;. For example, you can't hear or see allies if you are too far away from them and the maps are very dark. This creates a sense of urgency and fear which few other survival games accomplish. For a free Source engine mod, NMRIH delivers a lot more enjoyment than current competitors such as Contagion or DayZ.

: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Razenroth is a top-down shooter with some rogue-like and RPG elements. It really took some time for me to warm up to this game. It starts a bit slow, with a storytelling cutscene that's several minutes long setting up the who's, what's, and why's of the game. Long story short, you are looking for your grandpa in the Valley of Whispers, a nightmarish region where all sorts of evil resides. Regardless of what awaits you ahead, you press on in hopes of finding your missing grandfather.
==========
As said above, Razenroth is a top-down shooter, meaing your point of view is directly over your character, giving you a nice view of your surroundings. Each game starts in a cabin that houses some of the unlockable features that become available as you collect Dark Crystals. When you exit the cabin, you are free to explore the surrounding region whilst fighting monsters and collecting items. Monsters can and will attack you from off-screen, just outside of your view. This means that they will often get the jump on you, and you will need to become quite evasive to survive. Movement is done with the WASD keys, and attacking is done with the Left and Right mouse buttons. Left clicking is your standard attack, firing a short ranged burst of energy towards foes. Right click is a more powerful, longer range spell that requires mana to use. Mana is regenerated slowly over time. The Q and E keys are used to activate various potions and items you find in your journey.
As you defeat monsters, you gain experience points. Like typical RPGs, once you gain enough experience you will level up, earning you a stat point and a couple of skill points. Stats include extra Health, Mana, Critical Hit Chance, and even Bonus Critical Hit Damage. All of these stats are equally important, but it's up to you how you spend your points. Skills have varying costs between 1 and 3 points, with most of them costing 3 point. Skills range from gaining mana per hit or firing a counterattack shot when damaged.
Perhaps the most frantic portions of this game are the boss battles. As you explore each location, you will eventually reach a portal on the ground with a skull symbol on it. Touching it tranports you to an enclosed area with a powerful boss. These encounters will test your skills and endurance, but mainly your patience. Each boss takes very small amounts of damage from even your most powerful attacks, making each encounter somewhat of a chore. Most also have alot of different attacks which require you to stay on the move and avoid certain patches of ground, as they have become home to poison gas, webs that slow you down, or even bombs that soon explode. Patience, persistence, and kiting are required to defeat pretty much every boss. When defeated, bosses will drop instant healing items, potions, gear, gold, and dark crystals...so they are well the challenge.
What RPG experience would be complete without gear? As you defeat monsters and open treasure chests you will find various pieces of equipment to boost your performance. Initially you begin with 4 main equipment slots and 6 accessory slots. Monsters drop gear very rarely, and bosses usually drop at least 1 piece. Sometimes treasure chests will contain 1-2 pieces of equipment, and at times you can find equipment sitting atop special altars waiting to be picked up. When you pick up a new piece of armor it automatically replaces what you are currently wearing. If you don't like your new gear's stats you can always pick your old piece back up and continue onward. Enemies also drop small amounts of gold very rarely, which can be used to buy items from merchants who also appear rarely. Gold can also be exchanged at a certain rate to obtain Dark Crystals in your cabin, which is where you start each stage from.
There are 3 different difficulty modes, and at least 4 unlockable characters to play as. Unlocking them requires you clearing available difficulty modes or defeating a certain number of monsters. These xtra characters have different spells and abilities, and are worth trying out to see how they differ. Even the lowest difficulty setting is quite challenging, so if you are one of those players who likes to tackle the highest difficulty of a game first, you are in for a treat!
==========
Razenroth is a very dark, bland game. The visuals are all dark hues, mostly brown, grey, and black. Not very colorful at all. The only things that are really colorful are huge amounts of blood from enemies and the pieces of gear and other items you find, especially potions. Monsters stand out from the environment pretty well, and are a tad bit brighter than everything else, making them easier to spot amidst other objects and action. Bosses are quite a bit larger than other monsters, making them MUCH easier targets than your standard monster fodder...who are alot harder to hit. Weird how that actually works out! Defeated enemies tend to explode into large pools of blood that persist as long as you are that stage. This is helpful for navigating each area and remembering when you've already been, even though there is a map.
One thing that some RPGs seem to not include is how equipping new gear shows up on your character. Razenroth has this feature! I was quite pleased when I discovered this, as I like having a dynamic character sprite. Looking at the same, boring character model gets very old after awhile. Changing it with new equipped gear helps keep things a little fresh and new.
==========
There really isn't much going on here in the musical department. The most I ever heard was in the intro sequence. Instead, the majority of what you'll be hearing are your own attacks. This can get old VERY quickly. You can also hear monster attacks, but they are usually drowned out by your own. Killing enemies is satisfying though, as most of them make a nice death noise as their corpse explode upon defeat.
==========
This game runs really well. 60 FPS in most cases, dipping down to maybe 40 or 45 at times. It loads fairly quickly, with minimal loading screens between stages and when starting a session. I didn't get any weird crashes, stuttering, or lag at any point.
The game only has mouse/keyboard support, so controller users will have to use programs such as Joy2Key or MotionJoy to play with a controller. Though honestly after playing a bit I realized that mouse and keyboard was the best way to play, as moving in this game would be a bit slow with an analog stick...and probably would not be handled correctly by the game itself.
==========
Interesting concept, decent gameplay, and frantic action (once you get a fair ways into the game) all come together to make Razenroth an enjoyable experience for those who can overlook it's shortcomings. Patience is definitely recommended, as it can get pretty difficult. But it you like difficult, this is one shooter/rogue-like/RPG you will enjoy.

The controls for the keyboard+mouse are absolutely terrible. For some reason everything is configured as if I am using a gamepad, which I was not. Even then, it was really hard to maneuver anywhere despite the vast emptiness of space.
The minimap was complicated and too small to provide any major key objects and destinations. Luckily, they had an autopilot that would've saved my time and effort to move around. That is if the autopilot actually works. In many cases, the autopilot jerks around and just circles around 'routes', like a GPS with a very bad signal; it keeps changing directions randomly.

To conclude, the game need serious fixing and further development to become a fully fledged game. It really has great potential if the developers actually listen to customer feedback and at least attempt to satisfy demands.

Really wanted to like this game but the more I played it the more I came to just be frustrated by it.  Some of the first problems I encountered were a GUI that isn't as well done as it should have been.  As an example, start a to jump somewhere.  Game does a long count down.  If you accidentally move your ship during this time while trying to use its clunky interface it cancels the jump (but still uses up the energy for the jump).  The autopilot acts like its drunk making dizzying turns in odd directions rather than smoothly navigating around objects (so letting the computer pilot your ship anywhere other than open space in a straight line gets -- nauseating).  Sometimes your ship crashes just trying to auto-dock.  Upon getting a Deimos I discovered fighter AI pilots seemed to love to try to park right in front of my ship... DURING COMBAT (um, you know, right in front of my main guns... poof, or with 6 GJ of shielding versus a tiny fighter just run them over; either way it was comically dumb).  Not to mention the number of ships that seemed determine to ram you (how does a small frieghter not see a Boreas destroyer that's 10x its size, flying in a straight line and moving slowly?)   IMHO the autopilot is the single biggest weakness of the game.
Your freighter fleets, once you start building your commercial empire are -- morons, there just no other way to put it.   You blacklist a sector and tell them DO NOT GO IN THERE... they go in there anyway because the black list tells them not to trade there, not to actually never enter that sector (so if they decide to fly through it on their way somewhere else... ALERT!  Pirates have blown up another fo your moron freighters.  Have a frustrating day).  They are not even smart enough to try an avoid pirates when they're spotted.  Instead your freighers will fly right up to a cluster of pirates or a Xenon Q if it happens to be in the path of where ever they're going (No, oh gee, I'm in a tiny freighter with paper shields and a single back facing popgun, there's a Xenon Q., oh well I'll just fly right past him.  Maybe he won't noti.... BOOM!   That's your automated freighters folks).  Your universal traders are even dumber, no only could I not find a way to get them to stay out of black listed sectors but even where I had advanced satellites out so they could see the pirates, or that big Xenon Q, before they ever entered the sector they flew right at em anyway.
Want a freighter just to shuttle cargo from one station to another, there's a script for that.  But again, it turns your freighter into a moron.  If its two stations in the same sector or adjacent sectors, that works okay.  But if it require jumping, you'll discover somehow your freighter with plenty of energy and a jumpdrive has suddenly forgotten how to use it.  Instead it stubbornly tries to fly the whole route.
As your empire grows you find yourself constantly chasing after pirates that spawn even in core systems and attack your freighters.  I can understand this in border areas, but when you have two groups of pirates marauding around a core sector virtually unchallenged and which kill two of your super freighters (there goes about 3 mil each plus cargo) you start to wonder why the local fleets aren't doing anything about them???  I found myself spending so much time swatting pirates I didn't have time to finish constuction of a new complex or finish missions.  If you can automate freighters trading, why can't you have a few corvettes or a frigate set up to automatically jump in and kill pirates attacking your traders?   Yes you can set them to patrol sectors, but its a little impractical to build a combat fleet big enough to patrol the entire universe!!!
An then there's some of the campaign missions.  They're a bit buggy and then sometimes they're just plain stupid.  I can ignore a mission that requires I use a TM to rescue some people even though I have other ships that will do the job better.    Or the silly campaign missions that force you to do something stupid.  Or the ones that do impossible things that leave you scratchign your head (forget how some guy got a colossus wreck at the back end of a Xenon sector, someone tell me just how did they cram all those Xenon ships in that lil cargo crate???)  But when you're presented with a sodoku puzzle which you must solve (taking 1 to 2 hours of real time) that's getting to be a bit much.  Oh an if your freighters get attacked while you're solving that puzzle.  Sorry but you you can't leave to help them or you have to start over on the puzzle (and that's not counting having my power go out just as I was about to finish solving the puzzle and had to completely start over... again).  In fact you pretty much can't do anything else while trying to solve that puzzle, which is bad in a game that frequently demands your attention.  Its just inappropriate to this type of game.
Its disappointing because in many ways this game came the closest of any I've tried to being a successor to Freelancer.  It did get a lot of things right.  Large universe to sandbox in.  Trade ships move to and fro according to real supply and demand.  The economy is functional (mostly).  Interesting ship designs and some flexible options to customize them.  But with the buggy and sometimes just plain stupid campaign missions (which also fail to tell a cohesive story, oh wow some sort of giant gate hub... but um... who built it, why is it here, why aren't the xenon more interested in it, what happened to the two people who originally discovered it... who knows, none of this is explained.), and the very glitchy autopilot, the game can become very frustrating.
If you've got a lot of patience and can live with those problems, there is some fun to be had.  But don't say you weren't warned about its issues and I wouldn't suggest paying full price.

Soon to come out of Early Access testing,
is a 2D platformer with Megaman-inspired gameplay, and with a roguelike twist anybody can dig into and enjoy.
To start off, 20XX is a game that demands more from you then to charge though guns ablazing. Moving platforms and tight jumps are the norm of the randomly seeded maps, and while health at first is more than enough to face off the many enemies you will encounter, one wrong move or poorly-timed jump too many will leave you at the mercy of the boss at every level's end.
It also does not help in your favor for the enemies to work together with the map, to bring you down and back to the hub level known as the "Ark". The game can always be played again, but so will the many colorful enemies, often in the likeness of common garden insects, and just as buggy and apathetic as you would expect from them. The good news is, many weapons and toys are at your disposal, and can ease in squishing your foes.
A basic blaster or energy sword, depending on your character, is standard issue and can be charged for more kapow. They are more than versatile, but often at times they can really feel lacking. Some power-ups can be obtained after vanquishing a boss, or buying them in the Ark for metal nuts, the universe's currency. They do require an energy supply, however, and are not to be depended on for longer battles.
Every map is always a new adventure, and almost certainly will never be repeated again. All the enemies will be positioned and waiting for you in different places, every time. Some set-pieces can be recognized, but with a ticking clock promising goodies, and you being shot at from all directions, one can never be allowed to get too familar with their surroundings.
And for those who may grow bored of even the randomly-seeded nature of the game, an easy solution is in play for those who are willing to use them. Various "skulls", each representing a new and deadly setback, challenges you to experience the game with the deck stacked against you in different ways. One may simply increase the damage enemies do, or perhaps it does something rather creative, such as making the clock eat away at your health if it hits zero.
Overall, 20XX is a solid title, and one that proudly represents what Early Access can really do. A great game in concept that is dragged down by repetitive gameplay and story elements.
Take 1 part Rogue-lite elements, 1 part Tomodachi Pet, 1 part Disgaea, and mix them all together to create something similar to this.
The main premise revolves around a God-like being (with a trillion health) threatening to destroy your entire dimension. Train up your challenger of choice over the course of two months and send them out on their way to death. As you train them you'll learn more about them which makes it harder and harder for you to send them off... or it should. Unfortunately the writing is fairly cookie cutter with no real twists throughout the entire journey. The characters, while all having very well defined characteristics, don't have that much depth or are just walking tropes. The way that you learn about all of the characters also follows the exact same pattern every time with no deviations. By the end of the game you'll have seen the exact same pattern of character interactions numerous times.
The training itself is simply clicking an option on a menu and watching the day go down by one with the possibility of a bonus RNG scene to play. After enough training you can go run through some mini-dungeons that are highly repetitive which grant EXP and items without costing any days. Alternatively you can let your challenger rest or spend the day with them which boosts their affection towards you. Basically, the majority of this game will be spamming your way through menus waiting for RNG events or story segments to unfold. Think of it as a Visual Novel and Pet sim with a slight RPG and perma-death twist. The actual combat is a grid-based affair where every move you make the enemies also move, but if you kill an enemy during one of your moves you get a free turn. When it comes time to fight Trillion you'll spend most of the battle dodging the massive field-wide AoE attacks it throws out while landing as many critical hits as possible. When your challenger dies, all their equipped gear is lost, but a large chunk of their EXP is transferred over to the next character you choose allowing you to always make progress.
The highly repetitive and cookie cutter nature doesn't mean that both the story and gameplay are so bad I can't recommend it by any means though. The interactions between all the characters are still an enjoyable experience to fans of the "Compile Heart" style of games. The gameplay, though highly repetitive and RNG based, can still feel relatively enjoyable. The premise also is a really interesting one that's good enough to follow to at least one of the many endings you could get. If you can pick up this game on sale I highly recommend it because, at the very least, it's a unique and weird experience.
Also, if you think you're doing awful, don't worry. The game is actually really forgiving with the amount of chances you get. Avoid looking at guides for help.

: IDEA FACTORY, COMPILE HEART, PREAPP PARTNERS
: Idea Factory International
==========
Trillion: God of Destruction is a difficult game to categorize, as it has prominent features from several genres. RPG, Rogue-Like, and even some sim elements are all a big part of this game. They mesh particularly well in this case, and create a somewhat unique experience. Let's take a look!
==========
The game begins when the Underworld is under attack from a revived God of Destruction, Trillion. The Great Overlord Zeabolos, current leader and protector of the underworld, is easily defeated and killed. However, a mysterious woman named Faust offers him a deal: great power, enough to defeat Trillion and destroy it forever...at the cost of his soul once Trillion is dedeated. Zeabolos gladly accepts and is brought back to life.
From here, Zeabolos realizes his body is not suited for literally anything, and assigns his other Overlords the task of fighting Trillion. Using a special ring Faust crafted from a part of Zeabolos' soul, the other Overlords can harness and utilize his power. From here, the sim element previously mentioned comes into play. You are given the initial choice of one of three different overlords to begin training. Basic gameplay is very simple and mostly menu-based for the majority of your time. You will be assigning and completing various training regimens to earn EXP for your Overlord, which you can later spend to permanently upgrade their stats and abilities. Each training regimen focuses on a particular stat, but also allows you to earn smaller amounts of EXP for the other stats. For example, completing the AUR training nets you the most AUR EXP, but you also earn a small amount REF, CHARM, and TASTE EXP as well. There are a lot of other options as well, including a blacksmith to improve your weapons, a shop to buy items, and another shop to buy Devil Envoys; these little critters assist you in battle on their own, oftentimes handling the rabble monsters while you focus on Trillion.
The rogue-like element comes from the Valley of Swords. Each time you complete a training regimen with a Great Success or higher, you earn a Training Medal. You can challenge the Valley of Swords once you have earned 5 medals. The Valley consists of small, randomly generated dungeons filled with loot, traps, and monsters. A lot of the items you'll need to improve your Overlord, as well as consumables, can be obtained here. Every so often during your training you'll be able to take part in "practice" battles against a being named Mokujin, who can sort of mimic Trillion's form and power. These battles take places every few days/weeks in-game time, and are a good way to gauge how well prepared you are to face Trillion.
==========
Similar to Idea Factory's other games, Trillion has a very anime-esque look and feel. The characters are all very well drawn and slightly animated in cutscenes. Each overlord is based on one of the Seven Deadly Sins, and this is reflected in most of their design. Ashmedia, Overlord of Lust, is clearly the best represented...for obvious reasons. In battle, the Overlords have a slightly chibi look, which actually works pretty well.
==========
For the majority of your time, you will hear the same song on an endless repeat loop. This gets a little tiresome after awhile, so the portions of the game where you are not training your Overlord will come as a big welcome. The other tracks in the game are fairly well done, especially the intro song before the title screen. That is by far my favorite part of the game's soundtrack.
==========
I didn't have any issues running Trillion. Framerate was high and stable, and controller controls were spot-on. I never experienced any issues like crashing or framerate drops, so that's a plus. I don't think many people will have any issues running this game.
==========
Even though Trillion is a very well designed game with great story and characters, it can be VERY grindy. Keep this in mind before you buy, but if you like games with grinding you'll have plenty to do. There are a few secrets that you'll uncover as you play, but I won't spoil those here. Trillion is worth a buy, and if you can snag it in a sale -- even better.

I was given a free copy of this game by the developers.
If you’d prefer a video review, have a look here:
In Networm, you play as a vigilante hacker, who’s trying to take down evil conglomerates. The gameplay consists of rhythm style movement without the rhythm. The music doesn’t go with the gameplay which, in my opinion is a shame because that would have added a cool element to the levels, instead you are, basically, avoiding obstacles on a circular plane.
The game was a bit of an eye-sore for me at first. It’s certainly not a style that’s going to appeal to everyone; with bright neon style colours peppered throughout a blue tube. But I do think it’s appropriate and relatively unique. I liked the menus as well; pretty much all of the presentation fit with the theme which is definitely a positive thing overall.
I really liked the mechanics of this game though, surprisingly enough. The actual gameplay of avoiding stuff is really simple; also, just as tip, I think switching to the camera that follows you is a good idea. The fixed camera was confusing to me. The thing that makes the gameplay interesting is that you can control your speed, and if you don’t go fast enough you’ll fail because of the tracer. You need to know when to speed up and when to slow down, and try to strike a balance between risk and reward. It gets another few layers of depth as well when you consider the upgrading system. When you get files you can choose to release them to the public and get the credibility currency, or sell it and get the credit currency. I just want to say that naming the two separate currencies: “Credibility” and “Credits” was maybe not the best call. It could be confusing sometimes. But both of these currencies are used to but lots of different things that can help make the gameplay a little easier. I have to say, without this system I’d have gotten bored pretty quick. I liked that you’re forced to micromanage what software you have installed because of your limited amount of memory too; which allows you to have different “builds” almost.
I really liked the theme of the game, and there’s a surprisingly cohesive story with a pretty sweet ending. It was an empowering feeling to release sensitive documents to the public, and you do genuinely feel like you're exposing something. Even if some of your hacks only lead to releasing information about a video game early.
All in all, this is a substantially good game for $7. There’s very little that’s negative to say; maybe it’s a little short, I finished it in about 3-4 hours, even then it’s pretty cheap. I absolutely recommend it; it could be frustrating at times, but in the end I kept playing because I was genuinely enjoying it, and not just because I had to release a review. It’s pretty addictive.
