I guess I am late a bit to this but better late than never, right? Moderate spoilers ahead.
While I am not one that has played too many VN-s, dating/raising sims or other IF games (only Megatagmension Blanc) I have read lots about the former and played the already mentioned game by the same company. Yes, from a change of Megatagmension (which I won't spoil) to this game, but I knew in advance it was going to be good. And yes it is.
I actually was on the lookout every few days or so for this game's webpage whether it will get a PC port as it was Vita only so far, but I am so glad it finally came true!
...Ehem. Onto the chase now. Trillion is a strategy game in which you must raise your Overlords to fight a colossal enemy approprieatly named Trillion, who has, quite literally a trillion HP points. No kidding with this one. If there is something that can ease your mind however is that you also deal ridiculous points of damage, even in the beginning 500k with normal attacks.
Gameplay-wise Trillion delivers but not as much as story-wise (will go on to that soon) but it's still pretty good. You select an Overlord to train with, you will have practice fights before the big boss himself (who is actually the only real boss in this game) in a huge arena, where gameplay is turn-based so there is no pressure. To balance out the odds, you can get extra turns when you defeat summoned minions, get skills which can move you around on the field, and, should it not go the way it should, unleash a final death skill. Yes, your Overlords can and will be defeated, and here it is permadeath : the story simply continues on, and, my Zeabolos...
....the story is simply amazing. The character development, the dialogue, the circumstances, the occassional hopelessness feeling... oh, and also the Overlords personalify (that's a word now) each of the seven deadly sins, for example, the sin of Sloth or Envy but you can read them up, and yes, you can actually see the characters exhibiting these traits leading to some humourous situations often, but I don't wanna spoil the story more. You gotta see it for yourself.
Now, Trillion isn't really a perfect strategy game gameplay-wise. In each battle there is a line which, if crossed by Trillion the battle will end instantly (as if you've retreated), and you get that "luxury" 3 times with each Overlords (retreat too), 4th time it happens you will be wiped out instantly. This frustated me a lot but I guess there had to be a time limit otherwise you can just poke at Trillion and wipe him out sometime at low levels. The Valley of Swords where you fight minions was quite enjoyable for me too, but some people might not dig the way the game handles the training : you just select an action every day : training, interact (a MUST if you go for good runs), valley, rest and so on. Valley doesn't take off a day however.
Affection points are very important and gained through giving gifts (you get them from a machine with tokens, 1 token per day) and interacting with the Overlords. Often you get events which give you a MASSIVE affection point boost (can be as much as 10,000k!) which are very important as affection points are basically MP and HP during battle. Oh, MP is very low if you don't get a lot of affection points, and evasion is the name of the game as getting hit by any of Trillion's attacks will either instakill you at low levels or deplete all your affection (which makes retreat unavailable).
Maybe this section will help getting a better understanding of what you are going to get with this gem :
Pros :
-Amazing storytelling, very lovely characters, and a few cool ones.
-Very nice soundtrack which only helps with the "atmosphere" so to speak.
-Sometimes good plot twists which add to the experience.
Neutral (things I liked but may not fare well with others) :
-The menu management system that includes training and so on.
-Valley of Swords is interesting to do from time to time and getting quick EXP.
-
-Interesting Trillion battle mechanics (for me at least).
Cons :
-Quite ironically there
-VERY noticeable lack of variety.
There is literally no point to play a tank (most attacks will 2-3 hit kill you at best anyway), mage (passives don't boost INT and
, only maybe hit and run or "assassin" build.
-There are no INT raising passive skills at all and there are some very useless passives (taunt, makes enemy close in in shortest route, don't they do that already?)
-Too many random events (there will be really many!)... I mean how often they happen, not their type. Sometimes you might get the same random event two times in a row! And random events (like the clock one) can give a LOT of XP which might be detreminal to the upcoming fight. Also they might fail so some may resort to "save-scumming" (saving and loading till you get a favourable event) to remedy this.
Phew! As for the final rating :
Gameplay-wise : 5/10
Story-wise : 10/10
Overall : 7,5/10
I recommend to give this game a go, it will be worth your time but the gameplay flaws might be a turn-off (slightly was for me at least.) along with the lots of random events/randomly working skills (Parry for example) but just for the feels and story there is no reason NOT to pick this up.

While I can see how there is potentially a lot of replayability in this game, there is not nearly enough core material. There are 6 episodes, each that I assumed had more than one mission. Wrong. So there are 6 missions. You could finish the entire game in an hour if you just ran in and killed your targets and everyone who gets in your way. I get that that is not what the game is about, but for people who are not die hard fans, or people that dont like to search every nook and cranny in a game for easter eggs, unlockables, challenges, etc, this game is pretty short. I even played some missions twice and only got about 7 hours out of this game. Sure there are different situations that you can do like going into a mission from a different entrance, escaping a different way, using different gear, different methods of killing, but that only lasts for so long. In the end I decided my time would be better spent elsewhere.
The game itself is actually fun though, it is just too short. If you can grab it on sale, it is a well put together game, with some very satisfying mechanics. Patience is a big part of this game, waiting for the right time so strike, or finding an opportunity is key to hitting your targets in satisfying ways. However, considering this game was originally released in an episodic format over the course of a year, and this is all the content that it contains, it is pretty absurd and disappointing.
Hitman is worth a play if you can get it on sale, but if you are looking for a story based game that keeps you on the edge of your seat with twists and turns this is not it.

mentions in their review the "three distinct gameplay types." They are one of the things about The Desolate Hope that make the game so entertaining, even with the farming and grinding involved. But they also are the reason why some players are fed up with the controls. The game doesn't tell you which key does what, and you have to figure it out for every gameplay type and interface.
But since I'm a nice person I'm gonna explain the controls ;)
1) the normal mode, prior to entering a simulation: walk with arrow keys. Enter a simulation or pick up items by pressing down. If you want to drop an item, use your mouse to click on the [x] next to the item's icon.
2) inside the simulation: walk by using the arrow keys, interact with merchants or virus by pressing down, purchase items from merchants by clicking on the item you want and jump/shoot by pressing x or y on your keyboard (x and z for QWERTZ-keyboards)
3) Boss battles: use your mouse to click on the attacks you want your robo-buddies to use. There is a combat-simulator for this right in the first room of the station.
4) Bonus: never ever hit ESC unless you really mean to end the game.
Now go and give this game a shot. It's awesome, touching and fun to play :)

Here is an apple pie recipe. Enjoy! :)
INGREDIENTS
1/2 cup sugar
1/2 cup packed brown sugar
3 tablespoons all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/4 teaspoon ground ginger
1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg
6 to 7 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples
1 tablespoon lemon juice
Pastry for double-crust pie (9 inches)
1 tablespoon butter
1 large egg white
Additional sugar
DIRECTIONS
In a small bowl, combine the sugars, flour and spices; set aside. In a large bowl, toss apples with lemon juice. Add sugar mixture; toss to coat.
Line a 9-in. pie plate with bottom crust; trim pastry even with edge. Fill with apple mixture; dot with butter. Roll out remaining pastry to fit top of pie. Place over filling. Trim, seal and flute edges. Cut slits in pastry.
Beat egg white until foamy; brush over pastry. Sprinkle with sugar. Cover edges loosely with foil.
Bake at 375° for 25 minutes. Remove foil and bake 20-25 minutes longer or until crust is golden brown and filling is bubbly. Cool on a wire rack. Yield: 8 servings.

I love and hate this game. As an art piece, it's beautiful. I love the world and the animations which are incredibly detailed, and the story will keep you interested.
However, the gameplay is where it falls apart. The game has two main large problems: lack of tutorials and wasting time. The main focus, the bulk of the game, and indeed the best part of the game is boss battles. These are broken apart with platforming segments inbetween. You'd be best off spending a lot of time in the provided battle simulator, which is the closest thing to a tutorial mode for the boss battles, which could've used more explanation but is ultimately not as hard as it looks to grasp.
Everything in this game costs a tonne of points, which leads to it becoming a grindfest. One particular world you'll be visiting is underwater and is very slow to navigate. The game has a day/night cycle, though during the night you basically just play a minigame to level yourself up in boss battles, so it really just distracts and takes away from the main game which takes place during the day.
In summary, there is good here, but it's buried under layers and layers of inconvenience. For a free download, there's nothing to lose, so I'd still recommend playing it to see all the worlds and cool 3D models if nothing else.
Also, the music, though just royalty free stock music, is well chosen and a nice listen.

Not a fan of platformers, but Moon Studios found a way to make movement and combat(the core of all action games) uniquely satisfying. Every time you gain a new power, it reframes how you view obstacles and fits neatly among the rest of your tools. The attention to detail and quality of life decisions by the devs impress me the most: Ori respawns quickly, saving is enabled almost everywhere(and with smart mana placement), backtracking is optional and always worthwhile, minimal hud elements, including the exclusion of text, means more immersion, a musical motiff that fits both dangerous escape sequences and tear-jerkingly tender moments, and the breathtaking visuals. This is one of those games where you play it for a couple of hours then say "I need to go to sleep/do shopping/visit family/eat", then you forget and keep on micro-managing your fledgling empire of station complexes, fleets & such; all while doing plot missions.
Pros:
-Massive Universe (Not Elite:Dangerous size, but it's still huge)
-Over 100+ different flyable/pilotable ships
-Multiple, optional, plots and story lines
-Lots of different missions
-Build your own stations and complexes
-Very good modding support and active modding community (even in 2016)
-Good replayability value. I've put over 300+ hours into this game
-Simple UI with lots of keyboard shortcuts, all of which are modifable
-Script Editor, spawn your own Tyr or D*ca and lay waste to everything...that's cheating though
-Game Director keeps things fresh
Cons:
-Prone to crashing late game, especially if you use Universe Traders. DON'T USE UNIVERSE TRADERS!!
-Unforgiving combat and punishing play (although this isn't a massive con, it adds a challenge)
-Steep learning curve to X-Series newbies (I was new to X with X3:TC, but I'm awesome at it now)
-Buggy AI scripts
-Game Director is silly at times. Make sure you dock a ship in every Marine Training Barracks if you want any good Marines
-Sector Invasions can mean you lose entire station complexes, fleets or such if 5 Kha'ak or Xenon destroys/carriers decide to just spawn in randomly. Avoid the North East part of the Universe Map (Getsu Fune etc)
-Laggy on low performance PCs, it does still run though. Just don't expect to "like" Terran sectors or those with lots of Nebula/gas in them
-Poor rewards at the end of some quests.
It is overall a decent game. 7/10, would be higher but AI and Bug issues are annoying & the Modding Community were left to fix them.

This game is my favourite in the series. It gets a lot of hate for reimagining a series so beloved by so many- but I am willing to bet none of those people have actually *played* this game. The system is exactly the same system we know and love- hack and slash, style combos, and a bunch of different weapons to test out on enemies.  Not to mention an amazing soundtrack.
And Dante? Dante is the exact same cocky jackass we know and love. In fact, even more so. He dives fully into the lifestyle of debauchery that was always hinted at in previous games, and yet, never fully shown. No such qualms here- his life is presented in startling detail. His character, of course, develops to have better morals by the end of the game...while keeping that cocky, snarky outlook on life we all know and love.
However, the story is really what shines, in my opinion. It is an antiestablishment story- a world controlled by demons, using mass-produced products and news. Sound familiar? In my mind, it's an artistic social commentary. The entire game is done up in this fantastic artsy grunge style.
TLDR: Buy this game. Especially if you're an unbeliever. It is fantastic.

This game is what I'd been looking for. Sure, there's a ton of bugs, but each time they patch the game (which happens every few weeks) it gets better and they are constantly adding new content. This game is quick and the levels ever changing, meaning you can never really tell exactly what you're going to get.
This is both the strength and weakness of 20XX. It's a strength since it's always testing you and pushing you with 'new' levels that have been generated. But it's a weakness because of the fact that unlike say a Mega Man title with a singular stage build you can't learn where challenges are and figure out how best to overcome them through trial and error.
This game has very little forgiveness which can be a serious turnoff for a lot of players.
But for someone who doesn't mind levels that keep you on your toes and having to use instinct to figure out WHICH powers you'll need and which ones you don't...
This is a game that will likely be right up your alley.

Thiss game is a mess, and as such is really hard to judge. It tries a lot of new things, but fails at many of them. If I had to analyse it coldly and rationally, I would consider it a bad game. But I had so much fun that I have to recommend it.
The concept of the game is very interesting : it's a giant boss fight and not much else. There are a few mooks here and there but they all get one-shot easily. And contrary to other RPGs, the boss isn't waiting in his castle until you've grinded enough EXP to defeat him. He's at the doors of your castle, killing your civilians, and you're sending your Overlords (classic anime girls) to slowly deplete his 1 trillion HP bar.
Despite its colorful cute anime graphics, the game explores extremely dark themes : despair, primal fear against a seemingly unstoppable predator, grasping at straws using the little time you have to train your Overlords and bond with them,  knowing that most of them will die before Trillion does - if he does at all. All this is well conveyed, and it's been a while since a game made me care so much about a character's death on an emotional level.
The story, visuals, music and writing are top-notch, with a very Disgaea-ish vibe (makes sense since it has some of the Disgaea staff). But it brings the usual Disgaea flaw in gigantic proportions : game balance is an atrocious mess. You allocate your EXP points in tons of different stats, passive skills, active skills, and most of them are useless, which you won't know until you've tried it and sent your Overlord to the death for nothing. You want a tanky biuld with high DEF and RES ? You'll get one-shot anyway. You want a magic build ? Useless, especially end-game (for reasons I won't spoil). It's Speed + Attack build or nothing, and since some Overlords have low base attack and high base magic they start at a huge disadvantage. On the other end, you can win much earlier than you're supposed to by combining some game-breakingly good passive skills. And why wouldn't you, when the life of characters you like is at stake ?
As a conclusion, I recommend this game, I enjoyed it a lot but it leaves a sour aftertaste to think how much better it could have been with some more polish on the game mechanics.

Edit: Now that I've finished the main story and side quests, I feel I can give a more detailed review.  This game has some good features, but also some baffling design choices.
+I thought the writing was pretty good.  The story may be stretched a bit thin, but the dialogue between characters really draws the audience in.
+This game reuses a lot of resources from Arkham City.  The game mechanics are almost all identical. The animations and models look the same, but with better textures.   This is a plus because Arkham CIty was arguably the best superhero game ever.
+I consider the Deathstroke fight to be the best boss battle since Mr. Freeze in Arkham City.  No button mashing, no distracting mooks, just a one on one fight with a character who can match or counter everything Batman does.  Sadly, I can't say the same for any of the other boss fights in the game.
+some new regular enemy types make the combat less repetetive, and force the player to be more adaptable.  There's martial artists who can counterattack, and chain together multiple attacks.  There's enforcers and venom users who can charge and grapple.
+The crime scene detective sequences have been considerably expanded and improved upon.
+The line launcher has been replaced with the remote claw, which can only be used for exploration in a limited number of areas, but now is hilariously effective as a weapon.
+New shock gloves let you effortlessly mow down large groups of enemies, if you get tired of fighting random mooks, and you will.
+At long last, you can reconfigure the controls while in game.
+No more of those puzzles where you have to break a vertical panel with a perfectly aimed dive bomb.
+I think the character designs look a lot better in this game.  Batman and Riddler's gadgets have sort of a homemade, prototype look to them.  Bane and Killer Croc no longer look like they'll accidentally pop their own head like a zit, if someone riles them up by asking them how they wipe their own butt.
+Fast travel with the Batwing means not having to deal with pair of gunman on every single rooftop.
-A lot of mediocre to bad boss battles.
is literally nothing but mashing whatever button prompt is on screen, and in the final battle, you're fighting the camera more than you're fighting
-Challenges are horribly designed.  Especially the stealth/predator mode challenge track.
-The city covers about twice the area, compared to the previous game, yet still feels like there's so much less in it.
-They spent time developing a multiplayer mode for a game franchise clearly designed around single player PvE.  That time would have been better spent squishing bugs, and fleshing out the stories of the huge cast of villains appearing in this game.  The multiplayer is getting shut down next month, and the only complaint I'm hearing from the players is they won't be able to get the full set of achievements when it's gone.
-You will get tired of fighting groups of random mooks, before the story is over.  Then the game offers you a huge number of challenge and training maps where you do nothing but fight groups of random mooks for trophies.  They could have made replayable predator rooms or boss battles instead, or even spent more time fixing bugs, but no.
-Control options have no slider for mouse sensitivity, which is pretty much standard in PC games and absent only in bad console ports.  You might be able to work around this by tinkering with configuration files.
Overall, I still believe the positives will outweigh the negatives if something is ever done about the bugs, but I can't recommend the game in it's current state.

OK before I get into this review I want to take a look at the DLC situation of it only being on PS4 and Xbox (which is not right). If this not changed at some point this might become a negative review. I will not support companies that deal with any catagory of shady DLC, and in this case it is not right to exclude PC from this new DLC since it was THIS PA community that supported the game all through development. I cant imagine that more people are playing this on console than PC, and I also doubt the game wouldnt have come as far as it had if it started on console (consoles arent as friendly to this genre of gaming since it is designed for us PC gamers)
Now on to the review of the game
( also please note that I have played this game mostly outside of steam so I have at least 20+ hours and I have come back to this game multiple times since purchase. I dont know if its still the case but once you buy the game here on steam you can register the game on the PA forum site and get access to download a non steam and DRM free version of the game.)
Prison Architect ( or PA as often refered to by the community) is a prison creation/ managment game set in the mid 1900s, when crime was high and mobs were still in business and in their prime, and when the justice systems of the world werent very nice places to be. There is a decent story for the game. its nothing too blockbuster worthy, but hey, this is a sandbox game, story should only be there to create atmosphere. In PA most time will be spent in sandbox mode creating your own prison. whether you want a calm prison full of reform programs (education, work, counselings, etc), a prison where you make a quick buck at cutting corners and using your prisoners as cheap labor ( having them do janitor/cooking work, making liscense plates, etc.), or have a cut throat prison full of high security prisoners and gang warfare where killings are commonplace and armed guards on every hall is a must. You play how you want to
This game can be very atmospheric and can really make you think things over. The first time you get a death row prisoner and actually commence the execution is...just..powerful ( in statement terms, not actual power, if this makes sense). It will REALLy make you think over what just transpired, even if only for a few moments. I would go into detail more but I do not want to spoil it, since it is one of the games climatic points
I do half to say though that the game can seem buggy at times. Its hard to keep people happy at times and they dont always seem to take full advantage of everything (such as not using common rooms all that much). The gang warfare aspect of the game also seems to take forever to take any kind of major affect, and I never really encountered any major gang events, just the average gang fights.
Overall 9/10

I have put more than 230 hours into this game. That has got to be a record.
Hitman is incredible. It's a puzzle / action / stealth game. I would consider it to be a mix between Groundhog Day (the movie) and something sneaky like Metal Gear Solid, but with a more mature tone. It's like Groundhog Day because every time you play a stage, the characters do exactly what they did the previous time. It's like a giant clockwork mechanism. You can expect x character to do y action at this point in time and exploit that. Once you know the stages and the character movements like the back of your hand you can get away with the wildest stuff. The story, while minimal, is intriguing. But the real star of the show is the level design. In short, these are some of the best designed levels in video games. It's difficult to describe how well-crafted they are.

This game is not easy, nor forgiving, however there is a little for everyone in the new installment of the Hitman franchise
Story:
I enjoyed the sort of episodic overview of the story, it brought a new light to a franchise that some might argue was dying. Although episodes cost money, they sort of stagger the player, and, on launch, didn't oversaturate the market. However that doesnt take away from the fact that Hitman is about Agent 47 killing people and leaving, and thats about it, but maybe that isn't such a bad thing. The game knows what it is and doesn't try to be extra.
Graphics:
Visually stunning, all levels are unique and have their own sort of personality. The hitman franchise has always excelled in this, with lots of locations and lots of enemies, always ensuring that the game is fresh and unique.
Gameplay: The gameplay has always been simplistic in the large scale of things, but extremely technical in the long run. Theres a PLETHORA of ways to complete every mission and every objective. This game provides an even more expanded version of this in the past, adding new and creative ways to defeat your enemies. Every mission is hard, but can be conquered. Your enemies are smart, but you are smarter. A briliant style of gameplay beautifully executed.
What did I not like? The amount of money I had to spend on this game. Just felt kinda wrong, but well worth. This game offers a mass scale of replayabilit'y. I ensure that no games are the same. Every run is unique
TL:DR
Pros-Graphics, Gameplay
Cons-Lots of money and simplistic Story
Overal: 7.75/10

I have enjoyed my time with Hitman, but I reccomend reconsidering a purchase, not because it is a bad game but because it has several notable flaws. The online DRM is nonense, this game is entirely single player. The online aspect is included only to discourage piracy. My internet connection basically never goes down, but Hitmans servers do, sometimes at the worst of times or for no reason at all.
When this happens all progress is lost, and the game kicks me out. This is a single player game, they're ruining the experince in the hope some pirate will be forced to buy it. The game does have a solid autosave and manual save system which helps, but I still don't like this.
Gameplay wise, the game is great, it's a return to the open ended style of the older Pre-absolution games.. Blood money namely, where there is a focus on non-linear creative assasinations.
Pros:Graphics are good, not ground breaking but they work.
Enviroments are well designed,very detailed and "lived in" and the amount of NPCs in some of the levels is very impressive.
Each level has many many ways to solve it, and there's always a way to get out of trouble if you haven't gotten yourself into truly unrecoverble situations. The ways vary from straight up murder with a sniper rifle, pistol or any number of direct assault methods, to more elebatorate accidents. Among other things. Unlike Absolution you will die if you try and shoot your way out, gun fights are dangerous.
The AI is, accetable. They will work together and are fairly observant compared to some stealth games, but as always they are easily defeatable when you learn the patterns.
Cons: The voice acting has almost zero vartiation. The Asian guards in Thailand sound like some Marines from America. This is a small thing, but for some reason it is noticable to me because of the detail of the enviroemtns, it sticks out as odd. They could do with some accents and variation.
Online DRM, it is useless, locks you out of content if you happen to want to play online and is a failure point for the game when the publishers decide to drop it. It is a terrible practice that needs to be shamed out of existence.
The game doesn't run very well. I have aging but still competent hardware and while it's accetable it runs fairly poorly with frequent frame dips. It is playable for me on near max settings, but it could be better, and the sheer amount of NPCs rendered makes up for that slightly.
The music is average, it just seems there to fill the silence, rather than to add to the game atmosphere for the most part. It's alright, generic. That's fairly subjective though.
I have enjoyed my time with the game, the gameplay is good, and unlike Absolution, it's a good Hitman game, but I don't suggest buying it for these reasons unless you're really commited to the Hitman franchise. If you do buy it, make sure to be ok with always online.

Amazing little free game about saving an automated research outpost as a walking coffee machine. It's got a number of different mechanics, including a platformer inside of virtual environments, a very simple top down zelda-like shooter inside of virtual environments inside virtual environments, and a fast paced rpg combat system for fighting the virus that's assaulting the simulations.
The graphics are somewhat primitive 3d, but with a style that makes everything look surprisingly good. The environments can be a little confusing to navigate in some places but the initial exploration of the simulations is still fun. I'm in some of the later game virus fights and the game is definitely harder than I expected, but I'm not as good at micromanaging the RPG combat. The turns come really fast and on top of that there are minigames which your characters can launch which build up bonuses but have to be played while still controlling all of your actions.
All and all I'm really impressed with this game, it's got a lot of charm and I've paid money for games that were much worse. Definitely worth a try, especially if you like fast paced micromanagement. I don't think I've seen any other RPG combat systems like it.

This renders the whole combo system refined throughout the series pointless, and rewards slow methodical gameplay in a fast paced action game.

A buyers guide from someone who has completed this game.
Note; A controller is realistically necessary for this game.
What you might like:
SMB is a great game. Possibly the best purist platformer I have ever played. To clarify; this game is fantastic because of the gameplay. It's hard - very hard - but fair. It's not random bs or rng (there is one slight exception to this in the dead meat boys, but even then it's minor). You win because you got good enough to win. The controls are tight, you have the ability to be incredibly precise.
It is suitable for any skill level, if you've never picked up a platformer before, you can still play this. You just won't get very far before you feel like you've hit a brick wall (as in, possibly under an hour of gameplay). But, if you enjoy the skilled aspect of this game, and you're reasonably competent with a controller (a lot of us PC gamers aren't after all), then you can keep making steady progress. You will feel very proud of yourself if ever you complete this game.
Personally I got stuck several times, but after I got a controller, and then subsequently got more used to using it (after feeling like I had two left hands initially), I could revisit the game now and then, break through those barriers and progress. Now, after finishing the light world and the dark world, I am hooked. I am at about 90% total completion and aiming for the 100% achievement. It's one of those games in which you EARN the win. It's not given to you like most story driven games (where you're expected to finish). You have to earn it. It's no surprise to me at all that only about 2% of people have "The real end" achievement. You have to get better, and when you make it, you know that you beat the game. It's an extremely satisfying feeling and one of the things I most love about gaming.
There is a huge amount of content and playtime in this title for a pretty small price.
What you might not like:
The story line is good, but pretty basic. Like, "your princess is in another castle" basic. Personally I think it's still great, but if you require a complex story experience, this is not for you.
This game doesn't give you pats on the head for trying. You won't finish it unless you get good enough to beat it at it's own game. If you need an easy game, this is not for you.
This game has some stability issues. They are really hit and miss. Either everything works perfect or you're plagued with issues. I'm only writing this review because I really want to play but it won't launch for me right now. Usually it works fine though, ymmv.
Again, to note:
You should be aware that a controller is needed. That's perfectly acceptable despite what many twits are saying in the negative reviews. A game on PC does NOT have to work well on keyboard and mouse (not just for being on PC that is. An FPS or RTS definitely should always work well for keyboard/mouse etc), but it should certainly be made very clear, as not everyone has every peripheral. After all, you wouldn't think a hardcore flight sim was a bad game because realistically you should be using a HOTAS, or a serious racing game was a bad game because you really should use a wheel and pedals. However, you still might not buy them because you don't have those things. If you don't have or want to buy a controller, this probably isn't worth your time. You will not finish it, that's for sure.
Tough but fair, not much else to say. If you want a more difficult game for your library, pick this one up. Goes on sale often and is pretty cheap.

This game absolutely scratched my Megaman X itch, and I am super excited to jump back into it and find out what the harder difficulty levels are like.

With so many early access games available these days it's nice to find a game which is actually finished.
Euro Truck Sim 2 was an impulse buy, but it didn't take me very long to realise that I'd got lucky and had found a great game.
As a simulator it's great. You need to know the basic road rules but you don't get bogged down spending lots of time stuck on inane tasks.
It has a lot of options for how realistic you want your gameplay to be too. You can choose the type of gearbox, whether auto or manual, and there's a further couple of modes for the choice of automatic or manual gear change modes.
The career is also full of options. Early on you start out drving other people's vehicles, but you get a choice for whether you want to just slog it out and keep doing jobs until you can afford to buy your own vehicle, or you can borrow money from the bank and purchase your first rig.
When you do buy a truck there are plenty of customisation options available, some of which are practical and others which are aesthetic. But you do end up feeling like you've bought a vehicle with an element of personalisation. Of course, you can opt to just buy an off-the-shelf rig and save a little money.
So far, I haven't spent a huge amount of time in ETS2, but this is definitely a game which I find myself looking forward to playing. The jobs I've done are long enough to make you feel like you've spent a decent amount of time driving, but they're not overly long and tedious. But that could all change: I assume there's a sleeper cab on my truck for a reason.
I'm currently playing with a joystick which seems fine. There's enough control over the truck in all situations. But I definitely think my experience would benefit from having a proper steering wheel and pedals.
If you're into fast action and explosions, this probably isn't the game for you. But if you like simulations with a strong element of strategically building up a business, I really recommend this game.

My character from scratch was one hitting most things, and obviously by 8 hours in, it is as simple as "drop aoe spell, move to chest, collect loot, leave dungeon."
The start of the game, has great potential, but it is like the other 90% of content is missing.  The writers finished their part, but the game designers went on vacation, and the game shipped while they were away, at least my imagination fits the product produced.

I bought this game a while back because the design looked interesting, though I didn't know what to expect, and sadly, it sat unplayed for quite some time because I didn't know anyhting about it.  By the time I got around to it, the game went free-to-play, and now you have no excuse not to play it.
The sci-fi premise here was a good one; without spoiling too much, a handful of AI's on a distant research station have a mission to run simulations to determine the habitability of a planet for human settlers.  Each AI has their own idea of how things will work best, and you get to experience each simulation through the course of the game.  A handful of intriguing twists are definitely what make this game worth the playthrough.
The visuals range from beautiful, to awesome, to ridiculous, to near-seizure-inducing.  The characters are interestingly designed and their simulations are fantastically imagined.  The research facility and simulations provide interesting contrast with the surrounding barren landscape under the quiet vacuum of a beautfiul starscape.  The battle sequences can be a bit much, at times producing effects fully intended to make them basically unplayable for a brief period.
Down to the gameplay, which was actually a lot of fun.  A pretty sizeable chunk of the game is presented in sidescrolling, platforming 2D.  You jump, shoot lazers, pick away at the story, and power up for your confrontations present in each simulation.  Those confrontations are frenetic turn-based RPG battles.  I must admit that even after completing the game, some mechanisms of those battles remain a mystery to me.  The battle display is a tad overwhelming, Information all over, attacks and effects constantly firing seemingly without reason, handful of minigames just doing their thing all at the same time.  There were a lot of neat design choices made here to make the battles seem very intense, while they really just boil down to most of the usual RPG elements served with great speeeed and clutter.
The soundtrack has some really cool jams.  While shuffling across the surface of the planet at night, I found myself just a little disappointed if I didn't allow the groovy bass parts to get heard before getting back into the station.  Each simulation has its own own sound that fits the AI's prodcued situation.
Above all the gameplay and art, If you can dig a good sci-fi, get this thing and enjoy yourself.

The Desolate Hope is easily one of my all time favorite games ever it's fun to explore, find secrets and the RTS RPG battles are just so addicting and fun
Pros
The art style I really like the way this game looks from the backgrounds to the individual character models everything looks great

Each character is distinct and memorable in design, battle capabilities and personality my personal favorites would be Malenz, Alphus, Mirad, Bio-Beta and Coffee. Yes I'm aware that that's the extent of all the main characters but their all just really well done
The gameplay it's pretty good and varied you have simple side scrolling platforming sections which are pretty good for the most part, overhead virtual dungeon crawler grinding hotspots which again are pretty fun especially if you can find all the secrets, walking while collecting stuff space invaders simulator is pretty relaxing and this part has a lovely background  and theme and finally the best part of the gameplay the RTS RPG battles! An over two-hour long documentary that speaks of the creation of the first video games in the technology wings of major U.S. Universities (Space War), to the development of the coin-operated and home video game markets by Atari from the mid 70`s to the early 80`s, as well as the development of Activision Publishing from disgruntled former Atari employees. The period of video game history covered in this film ends with the video game market crash of 1983. Not only very informative (told from the perspectives of many key `players` in the industry from this time frame) but also featuring a nice collection of archival footage (print and television media sources). Much better than any other documentary that I have seen to date on the subject.
Film is fully subtitled.

While this is a great* game, it is not a game I would recommend to most people. It is only reccomended for those that and insane enough to try. And try again. And try some more. Persistence is absolute key. You must tell your mind, yes I just lost 30 times in a row in under 2 minutes on this jump, but damnit, I am going to do it!. That is just my personal view. There are many positives to the game, but the average gamer will likely end up never finishing it (last 2 world's, last 2 bosses are a case in point). I'll list what I think are the pro's and con's. Again, this is  my viewpoint and does not reflect all gamers. After spending all morning beating the last 2 worlds and games, the game presents me the challenge to complete the game in the "dark world," which I understand is the "more difficult" version of the level/world. Will I play it? Most likely no. I am merely happy that I conquered Super Meat Boy. You also unlock the 7.x world for Cotton (the girl he saves). I may play those levels at some point.
* Feeling of joy and success when beating a level
* Shouting "**** YEA @(*&#^(*@&#^ LEVEL!" when you beat an insanely difficult level
* Music is great (though should be lengthier between repeats in the track)
* Controls are tight (if you understand them and the intended mechanics)
* The humor in the game is great, tongue in cheek at times and playful
* Incredible challenge, ramps up at appropriate pace
* Insane difficulty
* Games are often won when muscle memory overcomes pure frustration and insanity. Success is dictated by "resetting" your brain in a nano second when you lose over and over...and over...and over.
* Some boss fights are great (the boiling meat blood vertical climb against the giant Meat-boy), others (see: last battle against Dr. Fetus), are huge letdowns, driven by "see if you don't die here" vs. actual Boss battle pattern mechanics.
* Levels (much of them later in the game) are seemingly created out of 1 successful playtest, saying "yea, that's doable" and placing it in the game (vs. a game line N+).
* Gray Hair Simulator
* Definition of Insanity Simulator
* Rage Simulator
* Non-Alcoholic Addicted-to-tray-again-loose-3-hours-of-your-life Simulator

is a sidescrolling platformer with roguelike elements; their tagline alone tells you that, and is correct - if you like Mega Man and roguelikes, you should check this out.
Heavily drawing from the Mega Man X franchise, the game is led by two characters -
, the ranged X-like character, and
, the melee Zero-like character. Either alone or together in co-op, these characters have to make their way through eight stages of semi-randomized madness, with each level escalating in difficulty in terms of both enemies encountered and hazards to navigate. At the end of each stage, you'll fight a stylized boss with a unique power; each defeated boss gives you that power, which another boss will invariably be weak to.
Sounds pretty similar to the source material, right? Well, that's about where it stops. That's all the Mega Man you're getting, aside from a similar control scheme. Be grateful; it means there's room for so much goodness that wouldn't fit the Mega Mold, you won't know where to start.
Well, you'd almost never play a Mega Man game and completely eschew using the boss powers. You'd be denying yourself a vital part of the intended arsenal of the game. But in 20XX, you can (based on choice or by random luck) get pickups that make your main attack devastatingly powerful - at which point, you may decide to forego the powers the bosses give you, and instead take one of the two generic powerup augs that they offer instead, if they suit you. There are even special experimental augs that take this a step further and completely disable one form of attack, pushing the other form's damage even higher.
Though, by ditching boss powers, you're also denying yourself something else Capcom's blue hero doesn't get, at least not often - each power has a useful secondary function. One knocks over vending machines, giving you their contents for free. Several of them disable certain types of environmental hazards, to make traversal easier. One of them can be freely pointed downwards, and will provide upwards lift when done so, allowing for some spectacular saves on the literal fly.
The several different sets of attainable armor mods are each their own very complimentary entities, and collecting a matched set always has it's benefits - unless you pick up the augment that gives you massive boosts for being mix-matched, in which case you want whatever you can get.
The game almost always presents you, through the drops you get, with a different way to attempt to play. Got a lot of life, jump height and run speed? Try dashing your way through at high speed. Lots of main weapon power and the Scatter upgrade? Shotgun robot time. Lots of weapon power and more weapon energy than you'll ever use? Go nuts with the very satisfying boss weapons. Picked up an experimental aug? Prepare for
to change.
As well, the levels change their layouts every time; you'll grow familiar with certain setpieces, but the ordering and even presence of those setpieces is shuffled every game, along with the presence of loot crates, stores, and other bonuses.
And of course, death is final. There is no reloading a save after death, and you can only save when you quit. A nice touch is the fact that you will find fallen versions of the two playable characters lying on stages sometimes; the game will record when you die in a certain area/setpiece, and place a body there to be found and looted.
Like a dream. The controls are tight and responsive, allowing for some really technical tricks if you feel like learning them. The sensation of speed and control when playing this game is perfect, and in some ways even
than the source material.
The game is easy to understand, and every power-up (and there are a lot) explains what it does. The experimental augments are an exception, as they give cryptic hints rather than clear explanations, but a little thought can clue you in and of course, you'll know what it does if you pick it up.
There's a lack of a decent tutorial stage; the game kind of throws you right into an interactive menu, and you have to work it out from there. Anyone that's familiar with a MMX game will have no trouble, but a novice might get frustrated a bit before picking it up. (There, I suppose, is the roguelike facet again.)
20XX is like Mega Man X with a randomizer attached, and can be experienced in more ways than you're probably expecting. If you like platformers and want a game that will frustrate, surprise, anger, delight, and challenge you, GET THIS ONE. You won't be sorry.

A year later, install, play 20 min, uninstall.

The keyword here is DEPTH.

X3TC is a SANDBOX game, it gives you a universe, factions with characters, awesome ships, and a dynamic economy. It can be VERY action-packed, but not in the sense of run n' gun.
What does dynamic economy mean?
That means money doesn't come from no where, NPC actually have to transport products and materials, that means you can compete with them, find a potential market that nobody's aware of, trade illegal goods, establish a monopoly.
Nearly everything can be automated.
How cool it is to set up traders to trade around the universe automatically for you?
"But I don't care about economy!"
Then you have ships, big f*cking ships, small swarming ships, all of them are personally flyable.
You can sit on your I-win ship and crusade from sector to sector, or you can zip around in your lighting fast M5 and watch your big destroyers throwing out energy balls. You can board other ships with your marines, force pilots to bail and claim their ships, and even own a large fleet.
All of those, build upon one of the most versatile engine I've ever seen.
The stuff you want to do is 99% doable, you just don't know how yet. Ask.

text: This game does so well in making their characters likeable. You could be the devil himself (which you kinda are in this game), there will be someone you'll end up liking, someone who you end up growing very attached too, and someone who you will NOT want to see die. The time, effort, and affection you put in raising your favorite character, not to mention the connection you feel with all the NPCs that put their faith in you, will drive you try and kill/murder/destroy/annihilate the big, final boss who is making both your and their lives hell...no pun intended.

Coming to you live from the Underworld, the Great Overlord Zeabolos, Satan’s Grandson, faces off against Trillion: God of Destruction. Thrill at the of action of battling Overlords facing off against the insurmountable beast with one trillion hit points! Cue the montage music as we watch each of those Overlords train like their life depends on it… mostly because it does. That’s right, these are no holds barred grudge matches between Trillion and the denizens of the Underworld. This is a battle that will surely go down in the history books. Should the Overlords fail, the Underworld as we know it will be consumed by the ravenous Trillion!
Trillion: God of Destruction takes on the tried and true Idea Factory game format and there is not a darn thing wrong with that. For the most part, it’s a visual novel with light Roleplay and Strategy elements. You are Zeabolos, the current Great Overlord, who helps guide the preparations each Overlord makes before facing off against Trillion. How you prepare is left almost entirely up to you. Peppered all through your preparations are events which will either progress the story further or offer a bit of randomness to the game. The random events appear to be purely luck based. I believe it randomly selects one of the options presented to you as the correct one for that particular time the event comes up. Selecting the same option the next time the event appears will not yield the same results. There may be some way to tell which option is the correct one, but so far I have not managed to figure that out.
Speaking of randomness, one of the main things you should be doing to prepare for your battle against Trillion, is Training. Selecting the Training option allows you to pick the style of training you want. The style of training defines how experience points will be allocated. The one you choose will get the most experience, but you will also still get some experience for all the other elements. The training results rank appears to be almost completely random as well. I can tell Fatigue influences your chances, but you yourself have no real power over what the outcome of training will be. Your Training Rank seems to be randomly assigned to you each time you go so there is really no way to hone your skills there. Just select the training you want and hope for the best. Even if you get a poor rating, at least you will still get some experience and a gift token for your attempt. Scoring either the highest or second highest rank will also net you a medal that you can collect and then use to enter the Dungeon.
The Dungeon is really the more traditional gameplay element of the game outside of the boss battles. Once you collect five medals you can enter the Dungeon to find treasures, coins and even more of that valuable experience. The nice thing about the Dungeon in comparison to almost anything else you do in the game is the fact it doesn’t progress time. That means that you can run the Dungeon repeatedly without needing to worry about advancing the Doomsday (Trillion awakening) Clock. It also makes a nice change of pace to explore the small Dungeon. You can’t just rest and relax in there though, you are only permitted a limited number of moves before you need to escape the Dungeon or you will lose all progress made.
If honing your skills and exploring a labyrinth are not your style or you want a change of pace, you can also do various other things. For example, you can ask the citizens of the Underworld to help fund your war effort. You can give gifts to the Overlords to increase their Affection. Affection in this case is like a shield in battle. The more affection, the longer they can last in battle before taking HP damage or using their MP. As well, you can also spend time with the Overlords to raise their Affection a little. As mentioned earlier, for doing training or really anything in the game that progresses time, you get a gift token. These gift tokens are redeemable at the Gift Dispenser. It’s purely random what you get and you are not told who would appreciate what gift the most. You either need to get to know the characters a bit or just hope for your sake that it will be appreciated when you present a gift to one of the Overlords.
As for Character Development, this is a bit of a difficult conversation to have with you dear reader. Without wanting to spoil anything, I have to say that, for the most part, Experience is never really wasted. You should spend your Experience on whatever you think will make your Overlord the best Overlord they can be. If you discover something that is or isn’t working, just tweak your build on the next Overlord you train. The game lets you spend Experience in three different categories. There are the Traits/Stats that you typically find in these kinds of games such as Attack Power, Health, etc. There are also Passive (always on) and Active (select in menu when wanted) skills you can spend your points on. Each of these skills have multiple levels so if you find a skill you particularly like, you can always spend more Experience on it to boost it to its maximum level. As for your coins, it’s hard to make a suggestion here. The weapons each Overlord uses are locked to that Overlord. If you upgrade one Overlords weapon it has no effect on the other Overlords. Also, all Overlords take their gear with them to the battle with Trillion and once the battle is over, they do not give back the gear. Therefore, I would suggest saving your coins until you understand how exactly the game works before sinking all your coins into Character Development.
The Characters in this game, like most Idea Factory games, are all well designed and unique in their own way. Each has their own personality and character design. As you train each of the Overlords you come to know them better and you may even find yourself getting attached to some of them. That makes the reality of what is to come all the more powerful and moving. All your efforts in the Training and Development come to fruition once Trillion, the God of Destruction awakes form his slumber. Should your Overlord be successful at this point, the game offers up one of its ending sequences. Should that Overlord fail, Trillion will begin destroying the Underworld until its hunger is sated and it falls asleep once more. This gives the next Overlord a chance to train and prepare for their turn against the beast. Luckily, all the efforts of the previous Overlord were not in vain, the damage they dealt to Trillion remains. They also pass on some of the experience of their training to the next fighter.
The combat in this game has a bit of a learning curve but once figured out, it works quite well. You are snapped to a grid and you have to rotate the camera in order to help control where you want to go. You also have limited attack ranges; however some of your skills will help you attack things beyond your melee range. You need to be ever vigilant to the actions of your opponents and plan your moves in advance. If you just blindly run up to the boss and start attacking it, your fight will end as soon as it began. Lastly, this is not turn based. When you make a move, the enemy also makes a move at the exact same time.
So should you get this game? Idea Factory really went off the book when they made Trillion. It’s probably the most unique game I have played in quite some time. It seems to have taken elements from various sources and wrapped it into a package that works quite well. There are a few issues here and there where the dialogue and audio track don’t sync up properly, or there are a few typos but those kinds of things can easily be ignored. The training/development section of each Overlord begins to get to be a bit of a chore the further you progress but the random events help keep it fun and entertaining. All in all, Trillion: God of Destruction scores high as another wonderful Idea Factory game.

starts out like many of Idea Factory's anime themed games I have played, with the Satou Tenpei introductory music, along with the appearances of some of the characters that will be in the game.  The game itself is a hybrid style RPG reminding me a little bit of Disgaea and Neptunia in certain ways with a bit more of a strategy time management sim oriented edge to it.
You begin as Great Overlord Zeabolos, when the Underworld is attacked by the God of Destruction, and after a series of unfortunate events occur, you must pick between one of three Overlords to start with to try and defeat Trillion: God of Destruction, and must train them within a certain amount of time before it wakes up.  The prize up for grabs?  The Great Overlord's seat.  After a bit of reading and/or listening, you get some tutorials about the various options your character can do before God of Destruction (Trillion) will awaken.  There is a fatigue bar to watch for as you are doing your daily tasks, and you can run the risk of injury if this goes very high, penalizing you some.  If you put together three straight poor or excellent results, you will also get a certain bonus with further traininng.  One can always save during each day, but there are a lot of different activities you can choose between as you progress from day to day.
The main tasks that are used to progress through each day will impact various stats and numbers based on performance, and each one has importance.  You can trade these stat bonuses for passive and active skills as well, actives costing some mana to use.  The idea is to find out which ones and which types of activities you want to prioritize, and when, so you can be powerful enough to win against Trillion before it destroys Underworld's core.  You don't have to defeat this all at once, and you can remove yourself from the battle, or attack as much as possible before it leaves the designated area.  Just inflicting enough damage on it as you go is a key factor.

I like all the options and possibilities there are.  Too much to go over with Steam's 8k character limit, or whatever it is now, but the tutorial explains quite a bit in the game itself.  Most mechanics are either automatic or random, aside from when you actually fight something or move around at certain parts, which could definitely be a lot more, in my opinion.  That is my biggest contention with this game is that there is very very little actual activity to be done compared to other similar RPG games.  That being said, I do enjoy the fresh mix of varying concepts going on to keep things less boring and grindy than a lot of similar simulation style games I have played.  Nice tidbits of conversations and story.  Stats and abilities to juggle and spend points on.  Earning coins for entrance into a little dungeon to fight baddies and gather treausure in, and more!
A pro I always mention in a review, or con, is controller support.  I like to have the option when it seems viable and possible to use one.
There are a lot of different choices each day for you to work on.
The characters are interesting in the story.  I like their outfits, or in many cases, lack of, and the interaction and dialog is engaging.  Some of the voicing can be little bit over the top, but all in all they are tolerable for me to listen to.
I like all the random events that take place as you go.  There is a lot of reading and/or listening throughout to help with some of the mundane daily grind.  You may be presented with a choice to make that can make an impact on your game, like new skills for instance, some you can't get any other way.
The random gifts you can give the Overlord are fun, and it's nice to see what you will get each day when you use the vending machine, or whenever you check.
This game is very unique in my opinion.  The combination of types of gameplay elements is refreshing.
While it seems a little bit heavy on the simulation and strategy preparation as the days tick down to boss time, the addition of various random character interactions, as well as other optional events break up a lot of the monotony.
There are multiple endings in the game, which is always fun.  There is a bit of carry over into a NG+ mode.
While difficult, things are not always what they seem.  NG+ will net you some decent gains to get a head start on the next run, and also you don't (and I doubt you could) finish this boss in one try, due to several factors.  Progression is key.  You get several attempts at it with an Overlord though.
A bit of a grind, and the things you work on each day can get repetitive.
I had trouble with the battle mechanics at first, and I don't like having to change the camera angles to efficiently walk diagonally.  You won't do much grid walking on this game, but it is a vital skill for battles, and the turn-based dungeon.
I don't like everything moving each time I move.  One thing in particular bugged me: the easiest thing to do sometimes was to attack at the empty space in front of me when an enemy was one square away from a regular attack just so they would enter the grid area so I could hit them first.  I would have to take the first hit without doing this, generally.  AI is predictable.
A couple of the moves could use some tweaking.  Most are not very useful aside from certain situations, and others make you very overpowered with very little effort.  Experimentation or a little researching can significantly change the difficulty of the overall game.
I would have liked being a little bit more active as far as moving around and doing things in a traditional RPG sense.  There is a little bit too much focus on a daily routine, and making choices on that daily activity.  Not entirely bad the way it is done, but I would have enjoyed a bit more balance in a sense of third person movement, fighting, treasure hunting, etc.
The Steam page needs to show more actual gameplay related information.  You don't really know what you're getting yourself into by reviewing the page itself to a large extent.
I think this is a game that has taken a bit of a risk by mixing in the types of elements that are involved here, but it is a great choice for somebody that likes a decision-based system of time management and anime.  You're not rushed, but everything you choose to do or not do impacts what happens as you close in on the eventual boss battle.  There are traditional RPG and some light strategy elements with a grid-like battle system, abilities that cost mana, physical and magical attacks and resists, etc.  The game has a lot of visual novel and anime elements, being from Idea Factory, and is a pretty daring blend of a lot of stuff going on at the same time.
For somebody into a particular one of these genres mentioned, and mainly only that one, I would probably recommend other things before this at the current time, especially given its price as a brand new game on Steam. If you'd rather have something more action-based, the Neptunia games have much more, and they have some of the VN story element to them as well.  That being said, if you are an anime fan and you like hybridized games with multiple elements of gameplay, then this is really an interesting and awesome game worth trying out.

World 1-1 is a decent full-length feature documentary that roughly covers the beginning of video games through the mid-80s gaming crash (just before the NES came on the scene). It is comprised of a series of interviews that you have probably seen in other gaming documentaries, already, but presented in a less douchey hipster format.

If you enjoy video games and want to learn more about the history, then this documentary is well done and worth every penny & second of watching.  I will certainly be watching it again.
Words of warning though... it is all based on the pre-crash era of gaming.  No Nintendo, no Sony, etc.  It's mostly focused on the rise and fall of Atari - from Pong to ET.   And, it may be a bit 'dry', if you're not a devoted fan of the old school game years.   It's more of a history lesson that game documentaries such Indie Game, or King of Kong.
I personally really enjoyed it and am hoping the series continues.

A very nice documentary about the history of Atari, with the major selling point being the impressive number of Atari veterans interviewed. Many of the stories reviewed here have been covered in books about early video game history as well, but the real advantage
has is letting us see these stories told by the actual creators who lived them. This alone makes the film a unique and valuable account of the early days of video games. Some archival video footage and photographs, though limited, also help the viewer to imagine the atmosphere of the time.
It's important to note that the film is almost exclusively about the history of Atari. That's fine, but it's a little misleading that Ralph Baer is pictured right there in the store banner when the man himself is relegated to little more than a footnote. There is also a good portion on the birth of Activision, though, which is quite natural considering that Activision was started by former Atari employees.
The movie doesn't do as good a job as it could introducting its interviewees. For the most part, you have to figure out who each person is from the stories that they tell. This may have been intentional, as there are a few "aha" moments where an interviewee casually reveals the title of the game they are most famously remembered for. Still, a little more exposition on who these people are would have been nice.
But all in all, the story of Atari is fascinating, and makes for a fascinating documentary. You'll definitely get more out of it the more familiar you already are with the relevant history, though - or if you view it after reading through the Atari chapters of a good written account (like, say, Steven Kent's
).

It's a pretty straight forward documentary. I was hoping for something that captured the passion of the industry and the people who helped create it, but it's mostly people from the industry reciting facts about the business end more than anything else leaving it kind of flat. I'd rate this one about a 5/10. Worth watching for the info, but don't expect charm or nostalgia.
Better documentaries about the subject include Atari: Game Over (Currently on Netflix) and an older one about the History of Video Games that aired on the Discovery channel a long time ago which covers Pong to the first Game boy (which you can find on Youtube)

After you are done with the main missions, try challenges, assassinations, or feats you've not yet accomplished. Or even do it
.
So, let's cut to the pros and cons:
- Immersive gameplay
- You're a ♥♥♥♥in' badass
- hilarious at some points
- Wide range of difficulty
- No big learning curve
- I N F I N I T E    I N S T I N C T
- You never get bored because of the endless supply of challenges, escalations, and contracts
- Point system is much more forgiving
- Graphics
- Less linear, open maps (Blood Money style)
- And many, many more! I am probably forgetting some too!
- Glitchy (fun sometimes)
- Obvious cashgrab episodic content is obvious
- Voice acting is a mess
- Most bonus episodes take place in just smaller reskins of the six maps from the main campaign
- I was gonna say SquareEnix but they dropped IOI so nvm.
- Not much diverse content. For instance, maps just felt recycled with identical interactive objects and gags.
- Did I mention the episodic content?
- Glitchy (game breaking sometimes)

- No but srsly the story is blander than the love child of 007 Spectre and Assassin's Creed. It's ♥♥♥♥ing awful.

More X-Goodness.
Looks and plays great.
New players will find X3TC very easy to get into because of the tutorial missions.
However, experienced X-gamers will feel ahead of the class.
Mission icons are added for easily finding missions.
Good if you want it... but bad if you don't as it makes you feel like it's holding your hand.
Missions are now given by NPCs that can be found on stations or flying their ships.
Good because it makes those ships that flew around before have more importance.
But bad because they removed the BBS to do it.
Which means no browsing the news articles while docked, no missions from a bulletin board, no blackjack, no lottery...
So, while the graphics continue getting improved with each incarnation of X, it seems like there's a limit to the actual features they implement. And when they add something, they remove something else.
However, it's still highly recommended because those things you miss from the older games can be put back in by editing the game yourself or finding a script or mod already created at the official forums.
So... I give X3TC 4 out of 5 stars 'as is'.
But if they could keep all the features from the past games it would be a 10 out of 5.
The mod community may compensate, however.

Alright, now here's a game with a pretty sweet concept.
You're the head of the underworld when all of the sudden a colossal world-eating beast known as Trillion invades your kingdom and threatens to destroy everything with its whopping 1,000,000,000,000 hp (wow i wonder why they call it Trillion)
It's up to you, the player, to raise a herione from a select group of your friends (and potential lovers, wink wink nudge nudge) to slay the mighty beast with damage numbers that are unbelievably ludicrous.
It uses a dungeon crawling element to help train them for the fight against Trillion. (It's a pretty fun name to say)
Unfortunately, this is where the heart-breaking quality of the game sets in. Should your lovely lady friend meet her end at the hands of Trillion-- It's over for them, for good. They get consumed by Trillion in a rather grotesque manner... While you listen helplessly to their bones being broken and their bodies torn apart.
Decisions matter in this game, and if you make the wrong ones, you get punished hard.
You lose all items your heroine had equipped if they get devoured, with the only positive being a fraction of their EXP being transferred to a new heroine. The negatives include lack of items and the added extreme paranoia from being afraid that you'll mess up again and get this new girl eaten in much the same way.
As for the technical aspect, the port is rather nice, coming from the PS VITA to PC makes it run quite smoother. However, the glaring issue is some backwards controller mapping and keyboard mapping. There isnt any PS4 controller support, and its reported that keyboard controls are a little janky, but I'm using an 360 Controller and its working just fine for me, so if you have one of those you're golden.
Overall, Trillion is a pretty fresh concept (to me, atleast) that provides a gameplay somewhat reminiscent of half minute hero with the patented ''Countdown timer until the world is destroyed'' clock looming over your head, and pressure from potentially losing your waifu to a giant hungry god hellbent (heh) on eating, well, Hell.
For it's price I believe its worth the look into it, but noone will blame you if you wait for a sale (The one going on now is 40% off, so hey, now might be a good time)
I give it a 8/10 overall, and a super biased 10/10 if we're rating it solely by the soundtrack (Which comes with the deluxe edition, juuuust sayyyin')

Do you like typical anime girl tropes, such as the childhood friend, the super genki girl, and tsunderes?  This game is for you.
Do you like to knowingly send those same girls off to their deaths, as you hear their last pathetic mewlings as they're being eviscerated, and they sob softly about how they just want to go home, shortly before being decapitated? I sent my 10 year old exciteable niece off to die, just so I could get some information. That aside, game itself has a world like Disgaea, characters like Neptunia, and gameplay that's vaguely like a Roguelike.  Not a bad concept.
The main focus of the game--Trillion, the only boss, has 1 trillion hp.  You'll probably do something like 80 million with each normal attack at the start of the game.  As you get its hp lower, it gets tougher.. REAL tougher.  Tough to the point where I'm sitting on all max stats and it still obliterates me in one attack, making the game into a sort of 'run around and do a poke occasionally' game.
Would still suggest it, just for the pathetic mewling.

This game is fun. That's about the best word for it I suppose. The story is something else, you're the devil, and one day you decide to buy an apartment building to help fund your evil schemes and whatever. This game is sort of an apartmen managment sim mixed with a tower defense, you have to get monsters to move in and take care of their needs, while choosing which ones you send to fight the human menace!

The graphics are nothing to write home about, but I like the simplicity and think they add to the charm of the game, it's kind of like a Deviantart chibi fanartist's wet dream.  The music is also pretty cool, all the tunes (except the boss music) kind of remind me of the Animal Crossing soundtrack, simple and sweet.
The monsters in the game are all unique, they have stats, wants, and even jobs. It's definitely nerve racking to have to fight a boss when your main tanks are out on their paper routes. The monsters types are all unique as well, the Helmcheepies are melee monsters, but when they attack they shoot a projectile that passes through enemies. And the Zombies have a life-leech ability to keep them fighting.
Overall, if you want to buy this game, do. It's four dollars and has plenty of stuff for both casual and hardcore gamers, along with replay value that won't wear off until your third playthrough. If you want to buy it, happy apartment managing!

To be fair, not much happens in this game. You manage an apartment building full of different monsters, try to keep them happy, and then send them off to battle. Again and again and again. And they were so much better at coding, had so much better games, they were so much better at everything. Well, this might be true, some of the old games by activision is really good.
But at the same time, there were a big industry growing with many contenders, many good games made by many different developers and companies that is hardly mentioned in this documentary, but activision get their money's worth big time. And this, i do question. Did Activision pay for this documentary?
Today Activision Blizzard is the biggest game production company in the world. And they are known both for making good games and spew out sequels every single year, only to make more money. Well nothing wrong in that, because people buy it.
But they are portayed quite a bit in this documentary, without any of the competition being mentioned, exept companies that does not exist or mean anything anymore. Which i find to be sucpicious.
Other than that it was an overall good documentary, and i recommend it.

This is a must-play if you have even a passing interest in the stealth puzzle genre (games like Dishonored, Invisible Inc, etc.).
Don't be put off by there only being a few maps: each map is HUGE and intricate. What's more, there's a lot of replayability. There are anywhere from 80-130 challenges on each map, like killing people using only a certain weapon, or without the use of disguises, etc. It's a giant sandbox of stealthy, puzzley goodness.
I do wish it didn't have the always-online network connection thing (though you can play totally offline, but progress for each is saved separately). The menu UIs are also a little slow and fiddly, but most of your time isn't spent in them.
Tips:
* turn the Opportunities setting to Minimal or Off. The default setting spoils too much and interrupts too much IMO.
* I think the escalations are more fun than the main missions. The latter can be overwhelming at times whereas (most of) the escalations give you confidence on the early stages and gradually ramp up. They're more bite-sized.
* if you have stuttering (as I did, on my 970 rig that can do Ultra settings @ 60+ FPS at 1080p), try turning off DX12 before you launch the game. That fixed it for me.
Note: I played this game for hours on PS4 as well. My total hours played is much higher than shows here.

Now after playing this game a long time (and still not finished) I really have to write a review.
I always was a big fan of the HITMAN series. When I heard that the new HITMAN will come in episodes I was dissapointed and didn´t wanted to support this strategie.
So I also didn´t brought it when the first episode came out. But I was curious and watched some streams and youtube vids and one day my inner voices became louder and I brought it (all episodes together because they were already out at this time).
And what should I say: I was positivly surprised. I was never an achievement hunter but this game is leading me to search every hidden thing/type of killing the targets, etc. and even after half a year I am still not through every content.
They really did a great job on that game. The main story with the main targets, the elusive targets that come up from time to time so you have always new content, the escalation contracts, etc.
Each level is awesome. You have a really big "playground" where you can search for different solutions and ways to solve the task and I find them really detailed.
And even I am still not finished with the main episodes this week new content came up - a really new story with new targets. On the same maps - so I thought: Okay, some other people to kill - same same but different....BUT: No. Even if the maps are the same, they changed the settings in a really different way like they also did before + the whole play concept was different. It was a little bit more story driven and I liked it really much.
So in total I must say you get really a lot of stuff for your money here. When you are a person that prefers linear games that are only story driven then that game will maybe disappoint you.
For me it´s perfect. :-)
