I am a seasoned veteren of the X-Universe. Having seen the evolution of the platform from The threat to Rebirth, I can say that I am one of the lucky few who has been truly immersed in the universe.
A word of caution; this game is not for the general public, this game is NOT EASY. When i started off with X2 i was 13 years old. I could not grasp nor comprehend the power and possibilities of the game.
"THINK" that is the first word of the game motto. And really, if you cannot think, if you can not place yourself in the situations you find yourself being in. Do not waste your money on this game.
If you are patient, if you have a remarkable imagination and if you DO NOT mind failing and learning and failing again and again and again until you finally GET IT....GET IT!!!
This game is extremely rewarding when you finally succeed and grasp the concept. The story line from BTF all the way to Reunion is more or less linked. Playing them in succession to understand the story line is helpful but not necessary.
As you can probably tell, I am extremely biased. I have been rooting for this developer for more than 10 years  and i have seen the evolution of their child. This game is a work of art. Many may find it to be garbage... i dont blame them, i almost became one who felt the same. But through perseverence, thanks to my love of space and the unknown, i conquered this game.
I give this game a 10/10 in all fields.
Steam is a wonderful platform, unfortunately I lost my DVD copy of this game which i purchased for $49.00 CAD. I was very pleased to find the same game on steam for $17.99 CAD. It is well worth that twenty.
I have played a bunch of X-Rebirth. It too is beautiful, but it is still young and needs maturing. My PC is lacking the power to experience the full potential of the Rebirth.  But i can say, these two are very different creatures.

This is a game that you can easily sink many hours into and want to keep coming back for more. i think its a game that doesn't get old. The graphics may not be that great, especially looking at it now against more modern titles, but it is what i find emersive.

So far, I've put over 160 hours into this game, and I plan on putting many more into it. One of the mane reasons why I chose to purchase X3 was because of the fact that you're given a choice to pilot virtualy every ship in the game, rather than being forced to stay confined to fighters (and maybe freighters if you're lucky *sarcasm). The game dose have a steep learning curve, but there are excelent sets of tutorials put out by CdrDrive, and TheXPGamers that make it very easy to get past. Once you get past the learning curve, the game is a tone of fun, but also very time consuming because of all the research you have to do when purchasing and outfitting a new ship; the reason for this is because ships sold on the market come only with basic systems (and sometimes none at all) so you'll usually find yourself traveling to different sectors for all the ship systems you need/want. The world itself is very expansive and you're able to do anything from being a trader, selling goods to the highest bidder, to a warlord, building a large fleet and capturing sectors. If you like openworld sandbox games that are extremely in-depth that take time to play I highly recomend X3: Terran Conflict. If you want to play a fast and easy game that has little to no learning curve, or you simply don't have the time for such a game, then you might just want to hold off on this game for now (but I still recomend that you at least try it).

Opinion is subject to change during development.
Graphics - Clean and Colourful
------------------------------
Crisp, vectored, cartoony graphic style. Stages and their backgrounds are noise-free. Enemies stand out making easy targets for my blaster! Animations are fairly fluid, with main characters having a suiting slight robotic rigidity to their movements.
Content - Plentiful
-------------------
3 difficulty modes, including one which allows you to customize the difficulty, granting bonus rewards based on your choices. Daily and weekly challenges exist along with hardcore modes for those truly looking for a challenge.
4 sets of armor, a few different weapon types, and many passive items to discover.
2 playable characters with different play styles: ranged and melee.
Plenty of bosses to fight and steal powers from!
Controls - Super-tight
----------------------
Combat and controls are tight, responsive, and work very well with a gamepad (highly recommended). Not once did I feel the controls were the cause of my mistakes or deaths in game.
Sound - Nostalgic
-----------------
Combat sound effects, enemies blowing up, blasters charging, it all kept me in a state of nostalgia. The soundtrack is a retro-delight and is reminiscent of music found in games from the old Mega Man days.
Gameplay - FUNstrating
----------------------
20XX balances action and platforming well, rarely giving any lull in either for too long. There's always a secret chest to find at the end of challenging parkour platforming.
Each set of armor has their own slot (head, torso, arms, feet) with stats altering your character in some way: dash in the air, chance to gain health when killing enemies, etc. Weapon modifications changed the way your main weapon behave: 3 way split, shotgun style, and so on. Passive items are available to find during the game to boost your character's overall stats.
Bosses each have various and more difficult versions of themselves depending on when you face them in the game. Defeating a boss provides you the option of taking their power, which may grant you an advantage against a future boss. Each boss has a weakness to one other boss' power and it's up to you to figure the correct combo.
Online co-op in a game like this is a treat and for the most part worked fairly well. I experienced one bug that caused me not to see my partner's attacks, not a deal breaker, but visually jarring when enemies are dying around your co-op friend, yet all you see is them jumping around. Network lag was not prevalent, however I did see some syncing issues when spectating my teammate, again nothing game breaking. On the plus side, each player receives their own loot, while the in-game currency, known as "nuts", are shared. Yes, you share your nuts with your teammate.
Overall
-------
20XX is a great Mega Man style platformer fused with modern roguelike features. There are plenty of hours of fun here, especially if you want to find and unlock every item! Now grab a friend and charge up your blasters, it's time to pew pew.

This game is so excellent. If you like either Mega Man X or roguelites I would easily recommend it, but if you happen to like both of them then it's a no-brainer, it will probably become your favorite game.
Learning all the ins and outs of the different level pieces and enemy patterns is super satisfying. As you die run after run and make progress little by little you feel like you're really pushing forward and getting better at the game. And all along the way you unlock more upgrades and learn where more secrets are, until you eventually go into every run feeling like you can take anything the game can throw at you (particularly if you use the new permanent upgrades system).
The best thing about 20XX is that you can customize the experience to your liking. By default the game takes it easy on you in some of the areas where a proper Mega Man title wouldn't, such as falling into spikes or off ledges just dealing you damage instead of killing you outright, which is pretty necessary considering the permadeath aspect that isn't present in Mega Man. But if you don't want the game to go easy on you there? You can activate the corresponding "skull" in hardcore mode and you got it! There's a slew of these and they all can make the game more interesting and difficult.
But what if you're bad at video games like me and you need the game to coddle you a bit more than that? There's Reverent mode, in which you get three lives and start with three upgrades, and normal mode. Both of these modes have a permanent upgrades system where you can purchase stuff that you'll start every run with. Of course if that's too much then you can turn it off and on at will in between runs. The attention to customization is really so good.
The developer has been updating every second wednesday without fail for three years, and intends to continue to make the game better. He takes as much time as possible to talk with players on reddit, the steam community, and the mailing group and really sincerely cares about this game and its community,
Buy this game. It's worth it and it deserves your time if you're even remotely into this sort of thing.

I still remember when I saw the first screenshot for the original Devil May Cry inside a PS2 magazine. I already could see all the potential. I bought Code Veronica only for the Demo and couldn't stop playing it.
When the original game finally came out, I loved it. It was new, fresh and exciting. Dante was a cool dude, with quite a few hit and miss lines, yet very charming. I couldn't wait for the second one.
What a freaking' disaster that was. Still the gameplay had a few nice elements that CAPCOM would reuse in DMC3.
For me DMC3 had some of the best gameplay of the franchise, but probably the worst version of Dante. His charm was completely gone and his smartass lines became completely obnoxious. I was actually wondering if Dante had some sort of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, because he would yell and scream all the time. Barely paying attention the the things said by others. Often times his replies didn't even make sense in the context, making me question if the script was written by a native speaker at all.
Vergil completely outshines him.
Then DMC4 came out and by that time it became pretty clear that CAPCOM would not even attempt to use the ton of potential the franchise had. The backtracking was so ridiculous that I didn't even finish it.
Enter DmC: Devil May Cry, the Third game by Ninja Theory.
Demons are among us, influencing everything from the food industry, to media, to politics. Hidden in a parallel world called Limbo. You play as Demon Slayer Dante, a trailer park living punk, with godlike powers who aimlessly fought demons his whole life. His life changes when he meets Kat and Vergil, members of the Order, a secret society that wants to destroy the demons for good.
The premise has been seen before, yet the characters, environments and details are refreshingly different, especially compared to the previous games. The presentation and storytelling is something you might not have seen before. One particular boss fight actually uses the opportunity to give more background story about Dante's past and all that during gameplay.
The dialogs are not that great, often times even cringeworthy. But compared to the previous entries; it's Citizen Kane.
It still does a remarkable job of introducing you to the world, the characters and their motivation. I just wish Dante had a few more memorable one-liners. "Hey Succubus, suck on this!" is the best of the bunch.
Whenever Dante gets dragged into Limbo the vibrance of the colors gets pushed to its limit. The environments explode, stack on each other, split, etc. Each environment is unique, with it's own set of color palettes or details. It's absolutely amazing and is by far one of the best aspects of the game. The buildings have a very European architectures style to them, with a very lived-in feel, as they are covered in beautiful Graffiti or show signs of decay.
The textures are at times muddy, but the living and breathing environments with their wind, heat and other beautiful visual effects do a great job to hide those shortcomings.
Gone are the cheap garage bands of the old. Here comes Noisia and Combichrist. Noisia provides the music for the boss fights, cutscenes and quiet moments. Outside of boss fights, Noisia's trademark dubstep music takes a step back. The tracks become Industrial, with outlandish and unique elements. Giving the strange and incomprehensible world of Limbo an immersive touch. The "Poison Theme" is a fantastic example of that.
Combichrist is responsible for the combat music, often featuring one particular track per level. If you know Combichrist, you know what to expect. Fantastic examples of their craft are songs like "Never Surrender", "Feed the Fire" and "Throat Full of Glass". The dark industrial music adds another layer to the messed up world of Limbo.
The sound design is outstanding, with each demon having it's own unique sound, letting you know what's waiting for you around the corner. There is a nice sound balance with the weapons, with the demon weapon featuring a very heavy and impact feel to them. The angel weapon on the other hand sound exceptionally sharp, cutting the air with each strike. The environment has a character on it's own, with black ooze trying to stab, making a sharp, squishy sound while you run past it or walls building itself up to either crush you, or stop your progress. It's absolutely beautiful.
The combat is fast and fluid. With Angel and Demons weapons allowing Dante to push or pull enemies, allowing Dante the means to control the flow of the combat. Each enemy has his own strengths and weaknesses. Switching between weapons is encouraged, as Angel weapons very fast but have a low damage output, while Demon weapons are heavy and slow, doing exceptional damage.
The Combo-System is where this game shines. Each weapons has a rich list of movesets that can be further upgraded. You can string together combos, with several weapons. Starting a combo with an angel weapon and ending it with a demon weapon, even mid-combo. Throwing enemies into the air or smashing them to the ground. It's a beautiful system that encourages experimenting. Unlike previous entries you can do a lot without having to resort to jump-cancels.
The slow and out-of-place puzzles of the previous entries are completely gone, replaced by very intuitive and responsive platforming sections that break up the pace of the combat. These sections are short, yet still fun, allowing you to use the push/pull mechanics of the weapons to use the environments to your advantage. It's also here where you will be very thankful for the new free-form-camera. If you played the previous entries, you know how horrible platforming was in those.

Beautiful, surreal, engaging. The Desolate Hope is many things, including overlooked. This game is a fasinating blend of side-scrolling action, top-down shooting, and active-time RPG. The graphics is beautifully detailed and surreal pre-rendered 3D that puts FNAF to shame, the plot is very interesting so far, and the gameplay varies so often that it's hard to get bored.
It DOES have an issue with not explaining gameplay mechanics, but you learn things pretty quickly, and a big issue with constantly having to change hand positions between the mouse and keyboard - something easily fixed with alternate/unified keybindings between modes (having to select options with the mouse while moving with the arrows is a pain, when the side-scrolling sections have you using Z and X, which could easily be mapped to Yes and No).
The short answer is: this isn't like anything you've played before, and greatly deserves a look.

The desolate hope is a strange game.

HOWEVER, the boss battles alone are so different from anything I've played and so awesome that it makes the game really unique. The story is pretty original and the world building's good, I really wanted to know more about the derelicts and their story. The boss' designs are excellent too,
In the end its a very unique game that wont be for everyone. If you can go through the rough aspects of the game, go through the kinda grindy parts where you collect money to get upgrades then you're in for a very fresh experience.

I highly recommend this game for many reasons. This game not only has an enticing story that involves really awesome futuristic character designs, and a really cool setting, but the gameplay is very interesting because it changes the gameplay style in multiple ways. If you enjoy side scrollers, this game has side scrollers. If you enjoy RPG style boss fights, this game has RPG style boss fights. I honestly feel that this is one of the most underrated games that the online world has to offer. Now of course, the game does have some flaws to it that I'll mention just so I don't look like some blind follower of the game.
One flaw that the game has that I'll point out is that the game, while looking amazing at times, can have the occasional moment where something just looks really out of place, and it can take away from the experience if you are very picky about graphics, and art style.
Another flaw would be that sometimes the characters just keep talking for a very long time, and it can drive someone to just start skipping through a lotof dialouge that's very important if you care a lot for the story of the game like I do.
One final flaw I'd like to point out that can also be considered pro, it that a lot of the time, you're forced to start grinding the game's currency, and trying to find the merchants because at some points, the bosses become so difficult, the level of your characters don't matter, and what really matters is buying as much stuff that benefits you as possible. Now, you can either take that as a pro, or a con, I can see both sides.
So, that's my review on Desolate Hope, definetely in my top 5 for favourite games, and something I highly recommend!

Extremely cute game. You're the Devil. The Devil is a landlord of an apartment complex. Monsters and Demons are your tenants. Fight off the guilds and the heroes  and build your complex to the skies!

The story in this game can't really be called a story. Instead, I'd call it a "plot".
You've got the devil who has decided to open an apartment complex in "The projects". You start off with a delapidated, one story building with 4 apartments. Monsters and demons of various types and abilities move in.
Soon, local adventurers hear about this and decide they need to rid the world of the evil there. Defeating these adventurers gives you money to improve your apartments as well as unlocking different and stronger monsters.
The graphics are simple, yet charming. The game itself only has one setting - The Devil's apartment building. One would think that this would get boring after awhile, but it oddly doesn't. I think that's because things are constantly changing. Sometimes it's nice and sunny, other times it's raining. There's also a day and night cycle. These changes happen quickly enough so that you don't get bored, but not too quickly. Also, there are speed up time buttons which also help.

: The music is fairly decent and upbeat. The best song, in my opinion, is the one which plays during the end "credits" (which are well worth watching). The sound effects do get tiresome and annoying after awhile, but it's easily overlooked.
It took me about 24 hours to complete the game, though I tend to play games slowly as a personal preference. Others have finished the game in around 7-8 hours. Even if you only get 6 hours out of the game, it's still worth the asking price.
: After beating the game, a "Free Battle Mode" is unlocked in the options menu which makes the game somewhat replayable. There are also achievements which you probably won't be able to get during your first playthrough which helps add to the replayability of the game (assuming you like achievements).
Overall, if you like more "casual" games or are looking for a game which you can play in short increments and come back to later, this is definitely a game which you might like.
My advice: Try the demo and if you like it, buy it! :)

Have you ever wanted to be landlord so you could buy an apartment block and fill it with creepy demons? Well, wish no more because you can now fulfil that dream in Unholy Heights.
In Unholy Heights, you are the devil himself (think less horns and pitchfork and more fat middle-aged man) and you strive for world domination. How might you accomplish this? Well, what better way than to recruit demons to fight for you! They won’t do this for free, of course, and so you must provide a suitable apartment with livable conditions. In exchange, they will protect you and fight off any pesky villagers that try to take you down.
Part Sim Tower and part tower defence, Unholy Heights is a charming little indie game made by four-dev team Petit Depotto. Each demon have their own stats (sword attack/magic attack/magic defence/sword defence), can find mates and even have a baby. To keep them satisfied and rent paid, you must buy them the furniture they desire. Some are logical. Ice mage needs cold air conditioning. Some are just a bit silly. I mean really, what flower demon needs a $5,000 computer?! But this is part of Unholy Heights appeal. The demons are simple 2D sprites but the artists blend cute with creepy to make the demons almost lovable. The sky and mountain background look pretty although a bit boring and with the added weather effects, which have an affect on your demons’ stats, change the day and night up a bit, however not enough to really notice.
The look of your apartment block changes with each upgrade and eventually you can transform your shabby shack to a beautiful Japanese palace. These upgrade changes are a nice touch to keep you playing.
The background music is soothing enough to be mostly unnoticeable but when two demons are, pardon my French, making babies, there is a high pitched noise which made my ears bleed enough for me to mute the entire game. It’s probably best you listen to music while playing this game because those demons bonk like there’s no tomorrow.
The gameplay is simplistic and can become repetitive but you can often find yourself stuck in a bad situation when, for example, some villagers attack while your best demons are at work.
The Steam version has two interesting achievements which add some much needed challenges - one for not evicting any tenants and one for not letting any tenants die. Doing both of these at once made the game much harder, as you’d expect. However, there was a loophole in which you can simply raise the rent enough that your demons would just move out. This doesn’t get counted as evicting them and frankly, is necessary if you try to attempt these challenges. While demons get stat bonuses when they are satisfied with their rooms, they don’t level up and this makes it impossible to keep your original tenants to the final battle. That being said, over time new tenants come along and it’s just as fun trying to collect each set of demons as it is fighting waves of enemies.
For such a small development team, Unholy Heights is quite impressive. This blend of Simulation and Tower Defence is a combination that works well together. I would really have liked more career options or at least a way to see how much each demon was earning so I could adjust the rent accordingly and being able to see what rooms look like rather than just picking furniture the demons wanted would have been nice too.  I hope these features get added in an update or DLC at some point but that’s probably wishful thinking. Priced at $5 on Steam, Unholy Heights may not be the best value game out there but I got an enjoyable 15 hours or so out of it and I’d definitely recommend picking it up.

This 2 hour 11 minute documentary covers the birth of the videogame then focuses mainly on the rise and fall of Atari.  It is nice to have (mostly) the whole story in one film, and it IS a fascinating story.  Much of it is narrated by folks from IGN.
---------------
PROS:
1. STAR-STUDDED
You hear the stories from many of the very people who lived through the them.  Howard Scott Warshaw, Nolan Bushnell, David Crane, Al Alcorn and more.
2.  ENJOYABLE
It is an entertaining watch.  I expect I will put it on many times in the future and have it play in the background while I am working.
3. NICE MUSIC
------------------
CONS:
1. BARE BONES PRODUCTION VALUES
This is a sticking point for me as I am an animator.  But the "look and feel" of the presentation other than the music is very dry.  Almost no graphics and animation to give us a visual personality to the film.  The early videogame history captured the imaginations of most every child around.  There was so much that could have been done to create visual metaphors for the energy and creativity that was happening.  Instead, you get a fixed camera recording talking head after talking head.  Black & white titles using the classic font used on Atari cartridges.  That's about it.
2. VERY LITTLE VITAL INFORMATION
Next to nothing here that you can't learn elsewhere for free on YouTube by scouring through various videos that cover the history of Atari.
----------------------
CONCLUSION:
If you can afford it, it's a worthy addition to your library.  As for me, I am glad I bought it while it was discounted.  The spartan production values and not containing much in the way of new information do not justify paying the full asking price.  Look into getting Howard Scott Warshaw's "Once Upon Atari" before making your purchase decision.
As a young game designer (who has not done much yet) this really inspired me, and taught me a lot. If you are big into playing or creating games this is a must watch!

An amazing documentary on the rise and fall of Atari, the video game titan of the late 70's and early 80's. Although the interviews about the technical aspects of Atari games from the engineers who created them are fascinating, a more poignant and cautionary message about creativity versus capital pursuit is delivered when these same engineers take on roles as artists and philosophers discussing their work.

This is the documentary on video games that I've been waiting for.
We've finally reached the point in our world where the young engineers and programmers of the '60s and '70s have sufficiently become legends.  This documentary sums up so many of the questions I had about these early pioneers who helped create the very landscape of what has become video game entertainment.  If anything, this documentary helps showcase the pioneering technical and creative spirit that helped make video games what they are today.
What's wonderful about video games is that they seem so simple and yet are anything but.  Is it entertainment?  Is it art?  Is it just a business?  Is it fun?  Is it dangerous?  Oddly enough, the answer is yes; it is all of these things.  "World 1-1" explores that contentious history and how making games has run the gamut from being pure bliss to utter hell.
At the heart of this film, though, is you understand the pure love that these people have for video games.  They wanted to do something with the knowledge they had, and they wanted to make it fun, as well as challenging.  If making video games was pure drudgery (and I'm not saying the drudge doesn't exist.  It surely does), then video games wouldn't exist.  What illustrates the staying power of video games is that despite the fact that it's hard work, people still want to make them, and that's exactly what we get from this film.
What I hope is that we get more documentaries like this or perhaps even a continuation of this series.  What I find interesting is that this film is everything I wish Discovery or History Channel was like.  These were media outlets that used to thrive on this kind of documentary filmmaking and which could have made an entire series out of this.  But their loss in creative thinking is our gain.
Entirely propelled by face-to-face interviews with pioneers like Nolan Bushnell, the film never fails to be intriguing while telling us about what are basically the building blocks to early video-game engineering. Enough time has passed that many of the subjects have no trouble discussing their past, such as when Atari was bought up by Time-Warner, which some may say hastened the end of Atari, especially since many of them have gone on to bigger and better things.  Alas, we may have to wait another couple decades before we can get a truly detailed documentary about our current era of games, but I take solace in the fact that this documentary only scratched the surface of what the true substance of video games are.  Pay special attention to the post-credit interview in that I'd like to think it's a hint of things to come.  The eruption in gaming that occurred following Nintendo's rise to power would be amazing, especially if the documentary covered Japan's entry into the gaming field prior to coming to North American shores (though I imagine it would require a good bit of flying and some translators).
All in all, an excellent retrospective with a lot of great stories and thoughts, complete with period game artwork and personal photos, that fully explain the rise of the early games industry.

World 1-1 is an amazing video game history documentary movie created by the team made up of Jeanette Garcia and Daryl Rodriguez, two awesome, young but thorough movie makers from Miami. Although World 1-1 automatically might make you think of the world start screen from Super Mario Bros., the film is actually about what I call the rise and fall of the original Atari (I would have probably called the film The Rise and Fall of Atari). The film covers the birth of video games from their origins in scientific labs, onto games being played on what at the time were time-shared supercomputers, to the creation of arcade video game machines, and onto the rise and fall of early video game consoles (video gaming at home).

Let's nutshell this:
Pros:
-Incredibly survival based. You don't know how many bullets until you check your gun, for example. Your only indication of health is your vision.
-Realistic feeling of infection. Eyes will strain up. Your survivor will start to panic. All the way until he/she suddenly zombifies and goes after your friends.
-Good use of putting up barricades. Barricade animation could use some work, but is overall better than most other games.
-Unique reloading animations depending on gun used and how many bullets are left.
-Major focus on headshots. Torso shots are just not worth it.
-Incredibly challenging overall.
-Lovely soundtrack. Takes me back to NIN's Ghosts album.
-Amazing with friends.
-It's free. I'm not sure if HL2 is required, so consider downloading and starting it first to see if HL2 is required. If HL2 is required, then go buy HL2 as well. There's really no reason for anyone to not have that game anyway.
Cons:
-The L4D community is here. That means everyone joins a team-based game and does nothing but kill teammates, troll around, or lone wolf everything.
-Ammo is unrealistic. One example would be a house that has a sniper rifle sitting next to a big box that looks like the casing for said rifle. Guess how many bullets it has, despite looking like it's against a stash? Two. Yes. Just two.
-Mechanics are archaic. Weapon hits don't look as if they connect, as range of the swing and the actual range are incredibly different. This is also the case with zombie grabs.
-Similar to other horror survival games that aren't finished. Falling so much as a foot could probably kill you.
-Interface, servers, and pretty much everything in the game uses the same engine as Half-life 2, since it is technically a mod. That means that there is a huge lack in ease of use, and the overall gamepad use has a lot of work ahead of itself. This also means that even the "dedicated" servers are really just user servers. And yes. There isn't very much network optimization in this, causing terrible results with lag. In a zombie game, that is bad news.
-Graphics feel very unoptimized for this type of game. What would net you 80fps in Half-Life 2 will probably net you 40fps here. This really shouldn't be the case, as the graphics are just about the same, if not worse than Half-Life 2.
-I'm just going to list "L4D Community" here again, because literally everyone in the game has no clue what they're doing and will refuse to be useful.
-Ammo weighs way more than it should, which is bad considering that there is no help to indicate what ammo goes with what gun. I'm not kidding. Picking up three boxes of shells will literally take up 1/4 of your overall inventory.
-While I'm at it, let me emphasize that ammo is VERY PICKY in this game. Good luck finding the right gun for the right ammo most of the time. Keep a sledgehammer with you at all times.
So there you have it. Think "Dead Island meets Left 4 Dead....with an engine that might as well be from the late 90s."
...but when you create a game hell-bent on survival, or else death, and yet you have an entire community that is acting on just the opposite... This is just not a game worth playing with strangers, and (thanks to the impressive 8 player max) that's most likely what you'll be paired up with through most of the game.

This game has been sat, uninstalled, for a long time in my library.
As an avid fan of the original series I must admit I was dubious about this reboot.
Having said that I very much enjoyed this game and below I will try to cover it in detail why.
There were definately issues with the narrative & Ninja Theory were obviously trying to suggest a political undertone relating to today but the story was at least unique & it managed to keep me enaged for the duration. 'New Dante' is a common problem I see reported online & though he may be a little jarring to fans of the old titles, he did grow on me.
I won't comment on the graphics at this point in time as I had to resort to an old GPU not long into my gameplay.
I very much enjoyed the music in the old games, the combination of metal & classical scores suited the gothic theme they were trying to portray. This is not what you will find in this new iteration, but the new mix of heavy rock and drum & bass definately suits the new narrative.
The one area I think this game really shines is combat mechanics. The way you can switch between weapons & continue combo's is fluid & very satisfying. Ninja Theory did a great job of making the weapons feel unique & have impact when attacking enemies. They have very much captured the feel of the original 'hack & slash' series & in all honestly have improved on the gameplay of the old games.
In summary if you're a fan of the original series then this game is definately worth a purchase, if you're a little unsure then maybe wait for a sale. Either way if you're a fan of this genre of game then it isn't worth missing!
One final note: Having completed the title, could I see new Dante become original Dante?.....Sure....now you want to give it a try right?!

Trillion is certainly one of the most unique games I've played this year.  It's essentially a stat-raising visual novel where six characters each train in turn to fight against the titular trillion-HP megaboss. These character's lives are on the line -- if they die, they die for real and a bit of their stats are passed on to the next character. As to the combat itself, it's like playing against a cunning, evolving MMO raid boss with roguelike's combat system. As such, there's great emphasis on timing/positioning, the right passive skills, and most importantly movement skills. There's content besides fighting Trillion itself, but it's really scant and barely worth talking about.  (you basically occasionally get to explore one floor of a bog-standard roguelike dungeon for item pickups)
It's a game that will inevitably draw comparison to Disgaea, due to both being "Makai" setting games and the general levity and energy. But don't be fooled -- this one's story will break your heart. Many times, possibly. Probably my favorite aspect of the story is that it avoids being typical VN moe bait nonsense. It stars mostly adult characters who don't have typical communication problems or misplaced hotblooded hormones. That isn't the source of the main character conflicts. That... by itself I think is worth giving this one a look, much like another one of my favorites available on Steam  (VA-11 Hall-A).   I like to joke sometimes that Trillion is "Disgaea for grown-ups", though said affectionately as I love both it and many other Makai-set works.
Trillion isn't for everyone given some of its rougher qualities, but... if you really want something different: this one's characters, unique (if a bit basic) combat system, gorgeous visuals and music and willingness to take its audience seriously make it hard not to recommend. Just, you know, be willing to forgive some of its roughness around the edges and occasionally threadbare content.

Trillion: God of Destruction in a summary: Fight a Trillion HP boss, while you have a perma-death system, and training management/dating sim stuff. If Disgaea is familiar, or Hyperdimension Neptunia, this will be great too. Score: 1,000,000,000,000/10. (The game might not be THAT good, but I bought it three times, so that's saying something.)

The one other big downside is that the game has a twist...but it isn't hard to guess - the main thing keeping the twist hidden is that there are 4 or 5 other possible twists obscuring it.
However, the game ends with a very good finale - including a monologue so good, that I cried trying to tell someone about it afterwards. It's really quite good.  I won't spoil it here XD

This is a wonderful little game (clocking just over 8 hours) with a mixture of different gaming elements to please folks. We've got platforming, high-animation turn-based combat, fetch quests, and a nod to an old school classic alien shooter. The control scheme for most of the game is ridiculously simple, so it's very approachable, but it maintains its challenge in different ways. Some of the game play around the platforming and questing can feel repetitive, but it's never a waste of time, since you're on the clock. Boss battles are a spectacle, and though I wasn't exactly sure what each of my attacks might have been doing, that didn't diminish my pleasure at each victory. All these are held together by a compelling story and two unlikely characters who keep you motivated to see the ending.
The graphics were rich and imaginative, and they serve to reinforce the theme of the game's title. The soundtrack is also well-tuned to each stage of the game.
I was thoroughly pleased and impressed.

Within the first day of owning this game, I played it about 12 hours straight through just learning how everything works.  If you watch the trailer, you can instantly see how adorable this game is, although the trailer doesn't exactly show how perverted your tenants are going to be.
This game is an independant release from Japan, that got translated and ported over through steam.  It plays out like a silly tower defense game, as well as an apartment and romance simulator at the same time.  The happier your tenants are, the stronger their stats will be for you to fight through waves of enemies.  Battles in this game takes a unique twist as you can knock on your tenants doors to summon them to fight, which you can use to micro them to stop the people invading your apartment without getting everyone killed.
Unholy Heights actually has endless replayability as there are actually leaderboards in this game to challenge others in fastest game completion time.  The game only progresses when you go through the main storyline missions, and since there's repeatable quests, you can actually prolong any part of the game if you just want to breed monsters or customize rooms since you collect rent money.
The rent system is kind of dumb though, as a lot of the monsters will inexplicably run out of money, no matter if they are unemployed or have a job as a CEO.  You don't get THAT much money from rent, even at end game, but it does build up over time, and it does give a different method of earning money if the current quests are too difficult for you.
Either way, this game is a steal at $4 from its humor, graphics, music, and gameplay, and I reccomend everyone try it out if they want something cute and fun to play for a few hours! :3

San Andreas is a third game in "3D Universe" which was heavily based on real-life events such as rivalry between Crips, Bloods and Hispanic gangs, crack epidemic, Los Angeles riots and severe police misconduct in LAPD which involved unprovoked beatings and shootings, stealing and dealing narcotics, planting of false evidence, frameups and bank robbery. It is one of the rare games that features black character as main protagonist. Besides San Andreas, I can only remember that The Suffering and GTA V did it.
Map is almost four times bigger than its predecessor, and consists of 3 big urban areas Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas which are inspired by Los Angeles, San Francisco and Las Vegas respectively. Countryside in game effectively serves as a 4th area due to its large size and diversity. There are many recognizable landmarks (which are named different) such as Area 51, Hollywood sign, Hoover Dam, Golden Gate bridge and many others.
You play as Carl "CJ" Johnson, who returns to Las Santos after spending five years in Liberty City when he hears about his mother's murder. He finds his life very hard immediately upon arriving. Relationship with his brother "Sweet" is cold since he accuses him of leaving the family and friends. Crack addiction has affected many in his neighbourhood, and on top of that he gets on Frank Tenpenny's radar, a corrupt LAPD C.R.A.S.H. officer. Situation is grim, and he decides to rejoin his former gang, to get brother's approval and help making things better.
Whole getto vibe and jargon are omnipresent, they are delivered through excellently written dialogs and voice acting. Besides CJ's Groove Street Families, other gangs include their arch enemies Ballas, Vagos and later in the game Vietnamese Da Nang Boys, Triads, Russians and three families of Italian Mafia.
Gang wars becomes a thing later in the game when you need to defend your territory when enemy gang tries to take over. If you successfully do it, members of your gang will hang out in the area, and you can recruit them for helping you in missions. Stealth elements are also incorporated from Rockstar's previous game Manhunt; there are couple of missions which were specifically made with stealth in mind.
Role-playing elements are new part of the series. You can visit the gym and learn hand-to-hand combat, work on your stamina by running or driving bike and build up your muscles by lifting weights. It has effect on your appearance which is important because you can date girls, and not all of them love the same thing. Muscles will open you a way to some of them, while others won't appreciate it at all, so you'll have to visit fast food restaurant to gain some fat. You can customize your looking by getting different haircuts, clothes, jewellry and tattoos.
RPG elements that have effect on the gameplay are in driving and handling firearms. The more you drive certain type of vehicle or use specific weapon, the more you excel at it.
Swimming and diving are also introduced, so you don't have to be afraid of water anymore. You can even pilot a plane after acquiring license for it. Bicycle, offroad vehicles such as tractors and combine harvesters, even jetpack and using parachutes are now on the table. There are driving, bike, boat and pilot schools which will help you learn many tricks.
For those who love to hunt for hidden stuff, there is a plethora of it. Original 100 hidden packages are replaced with spray paint tags, but in addition to them there are hidden camera shots, horseshoes and oysters which will keep you preoccupied.
My favorite side activities in the game were definitely street races and trucker missions. There are over twenty street races and they include cars, bikes and aircrafts. You are given specific vehicle for each of them and you compete against 5 AI opponents. They are absent in aircraft races, they just consist of getting through checkpoints in a certain amount of time.
Eight trucking missions are separated into three types; delivering cargo within certain time limit, delivering illegal cargo whilst being pursued by a police with a three or four star rating and delivering a fragile cargo without damaging it. There are eight missions in total that successively become harder by having tighter time limits, stronger police attention or easily damaged cargo, all that by covering larger areas to reach destination. Last two missions are combination of fragile and timed objects as well as police attention, and can be quite challenging.
There are 11 radio stations in the game with over 10 hours of material. My favovite one is WCTR; Rockstar is always spot on with satire used in talk shows and advertisements, laughing is therefore guaranteed.
Voice cast lineup is led by phenomenal Samuel L. Jackson who gives voice to main antagonist. William Fichtner and Danny Dyer reprise their roles from Vice City as Ken Rosenberg and Kent Paul, while the rest of the cast include James Woods, David Cross, Peter Fonda, Wil Wheaton and many famous rappers.
Game has sold over 27 million copies by 2011 and remains best-selling PS2 game of all time. It has been remastered and ported to many other platforms. It is the last game in "3D Universe", Rockstar launched a new canon ("HD Universe") with GTA IV and GTA V.

Ignore the hate you've heard for this game. If you're like me and have played every single Hitman game since the start and loved them, this is for you. Absolution was a step away from the freedom gameplay. This game however has a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of freedom. I was always able to think of my feet whenever I messed up. Nothing felt linear. Game tried to get me to be creative with being undercover. Instead I grabbed a screw driver lured them into a room. You can go for extravagent plans, or do it your own way.

If you're a new player I'd say certainly pick this one up. It has a lot of hand holding if you want it. Not forced to have it though. If you're an experienced player, this game is for you as well. Plenty of grand kills available for you to perform. Those are always fun. There's also challenges that have strict rules for you to play with, and even targets that once lost, are gone for good.
Story wise the game is alright. I'd say it's enough to fit the type of game. The main focus is on the gameplay. It's not a bad story, just expect yourself to be ignoring it. Prison Architect is a 2d 3rd person building and management game in which you create the most efficient prison that you can manage. It’s easily modifiable and has a lot going for it.
It’s a waiting game but it manages to keep you occupied with things that occur within your prison depending on how you chose to set your prison up. Do you give your prisoners some room to move, or do you throw them into a two by three cell with nothing but a toilet and bed to save yourself some space and cash? Do you give solitary for breaking the smallest of rules or only for killing other inmates or trying to escape? There is so much to control in this game that it is one of the greatest management games I’ve ever played. It will appeal to more people than most others in the genre. There is so much to do and control in Prison Architect that it will keep you busy for days on a single playthrough – provided your prisoners don’t attempt a coup thus possibly getting you relieved of duty or stripped of state funding.
The game manages to keep you on edge and does not fail to keep one entertained.
First, the controls are the same as most games of similar type. It’s a good system and they didn’t try to make them anything different or really change them in any way. I’ll give the controls a 9 out of 10. They didn’t fix what wasn’t broken.
Second, the graphics are nothing special. They’re probably a step ahead of minimal placeholders. I’ll give the graphics a 6.5 out of 10. They aren’t bad but they aren’t anything special. They won’t be on your mind for any duration longer than you play.
Third, the gameplay is quite nice. You may play the game at your own pace completing objectives and stockpiling cash while you fine-tune your prison to your liking. I’ll give the gameplay an 8.5 out of 10. It’s a nice game to play and has A LOT of replay value.
I believe these ratings are relatively fair. This gives an overall rating of 80 out of a possible 100. It’s a very good game with a very high replayability that I think will entertain interested individuals for years to come.

I was scrolling through some Steam reviews and just had to say, they were all terrible so I decided to write one of my own. If you have something to add or would like to see something changed, leave a comment.
The game takes place in the modern-day city of San Paro where there is a constant battle between Enforcers and Criminals, and the player will need to decide to which faction they want to belong.
Gameplay typically consists of the two sides fighting one another in missions, where one side must complete a series of objectives with the other side attempting to stop them doing so. For example, several Criminal players may rob a convenience store within the game; the game will then seek out one or more Enforcer players of equivalent skills and other criteria and will issue an all-points bulletin for them to stop the robbery and apprehend or eliminate the Criminals. Players earn money for participating in these missions, which can then be used to upgrade weapons, vehicles, and their character appearances, all of which influence the game.
The game is played in the third person perspective. Upgrades, equipment, weapons, vehicles and clothing can be purchased from various contacts around the city (or can be alternatively bought through terminals in the social district), while ammunition is bought from vending machine-like terminals. Both the contacts and the "vending machines" are scattered throughout the main three districts of the city. Two of the districts feature their own fully persistent portions of San Paro, with their own pedestrian AI and a dynamic day/night cycle, along with certain contacts and missions. The third district acts mainly as a social component, being much smaller, having no pedestrians, restricting weapon and vehicle access, and featuring garages, auction houses, music studios, and several other NPC terminal shops. While in the third district, players, even if they're from opposing factions, cannot harm each other and may only interact through chat. In the other two districts, players are allowed to attack each other (so long as they are from opposing factions) during certain mission scenarios and/or if a player has a bounty on his head. When outside of these missions players can still draw and use weapons, but bullets, grenades, etc. will not work on other players, even those from an enemy faction. This prevents deathmatching and griefing.
There are also two other districts under the category of "fight club." These feature pure PvP environments for more experienced players and clans.
APB will provide you with many laughs and cries of frustration. What really stands out is the amount of possible customization in this game. If you have the mind of an artist you'll simply be amazed with the personalization of your character and vehicles. The graphics are still beautiful and the mechanics are quite enjoyable.
If you're only going for the combat, this might not be the game for you. There could be a few things that will be bothering you. The hit registration is a bit wonky and sometimes the game is terrible with lag. The matchmaking isn't that great, because there is a huge difference in skill. Either way it will be a challenging match for someone and it's definitely recommended to play with a team and communicate on Teamspeak.
It takes effort and time to become a great player in this game, but having a decent computer will grant you some advantage already. It's a rough learning curve and the community will not go easy on you. Incapable players will insult you and skilled players will mock you a lot. The key to survive in this game is to find decent people that will fit your personality so you may forget about all that.
Once you're familiar with APB Reloaded, you will learn to love it and it's going to be difficult to find another game that will meet your expectations. The game is unique and still has so much potential to grow, the staff is still working to improve the game with an upcoming engine upgrade "Soon™" to create even more possibilities, which will eventually and finally get rid of the limited game performance.
No! Let me start with taking away the illusion of the pay2win aspect. APB is a free2play game and gives you a slightly "limited" version if you're not willing to upgrade your account with "Premium". So what is this Premium Membership actually giving you?
Basically it means you rank up some faster and get some more APB$ while playing. The advanced customization is the only aspect you will be missing without Premium. So if you're a great designer, I'd definitely recommend upgrading to Premium.
The rest of the Armas Marketplace offers weapons, vehicles/kits and clothing. These available so called "pay2win" weapons are merely re-skins and have the same statistics as already existing in-game weapons. Some might have slightly different statistics, but can still easily be beaten by the standard weapons. Also some of these Armas weapons, vehicles and kits are also available at the in-game Joker Store for a period of time by the use of Joker Tickets earned in Fight Club or with Daily Activities. If anything this game is "pay4looks".
More information on weapon statistics etc. can be found here:

Most of the experienced players are even able to outsmart a cheater by using the environment to his/her advantage. I've now played enough to know that although this game is better than X3:Reunion, the interface is still poorly designed and they've made it even more annoying, hard as that may be to believe.
So it's still a game for people who have a lot of patience, who don't mind doing a lot of external research about things that should be in-game, and are satisfied playing poorly designed games with lousy user interfaces that go out of their way to waste the gamer's time.
The good:
Much better than X3:Reunion. A lot of the issues with that game were resolved here.
The bad:
Autopilot. At least in X3:Reunion is worked. Here, it doesn't. Which means that as you wait for your ship to crawl across the screen, even with a 10x speed-up (assuming you have it installed on a ship - WHY would it not be part of the game rather than having to be installed on each and every ship??), you can't trust the autopilot to do it right. At least in X3:Reunion I could read a book while waiting. With X3:Terran Conflict, you have to babysit the bloody thing all the time. So not only do they waste my time, they've made it so that I can't do anything ELSE while they're wasting it.
The more bad:
flight mechanics. The usual rant about THIS IS SPACE DARNIT!  It's not "3D cars in mud". If I stop my engine, I shouldn't just stop dead. I shouldn't have to loop around to get at someone behind me, I should just be able to kill my engine and turn around, still moving in the same direction I was moving in earlier. I'll put up with a lot of "let's play fast and loose with reality" for a game, but that one issue with space games is something I'll never accept. Freelancer got it right. So far I've not found another that has done so.
The ugly:
Nothing major so far. However, the game seems to revel in wasting the time of the player.  Where "waste of time" involves making me spend real, irreplaceable time doing things that end up having zero impact in the game, either because you have to reload or just accept that you've just spent the last 20 minutes for nothing. Over and over again.
Examples:
-- Still incredibly annoying, especially early game, as they make you pay (a lot) for the ability to save without docking to a station. This means that, early game, when you're weakest, you're having to start from much further back JUST as you thought you'd finished.  Once you can afford the "save any time" it gets easier. Until then, expect to be doing a lot of swearing. Or a lot of docking and saving, which is a massive time waster, especially on longer "timed" missions.
-- There are a lot more locals than in X3:Reunion, which means that when you take on a mission that requires you to fight someone else, more than half the time someone else will kill them for you, which wastes your time because they only count the LAST shot, not the total damage you did. So you bring then down to near zero and some local asshat pots the final shot in for you, aborting the mission and wasting all the time you spent doing it so far.
-- The autopilot in X3:Reunion only killed me once. That has changed in X3:TC, and the autopilot now will regulary attempt to ram you through a solid surface. Since ships that can take large amounts of weapons damage disintegrate at the slightest bump in this game, this, again, wastes time.
-- Don't bother with "covert missions". They seem to be bugged. No matter what distance you follow (5/10/15/20/25) you'll either be too close, or you'll lose them. Another waste of time.
Conclusion:
Waste of time, highly annoying, and just too many issues for me to be able to kick back and enjoy it. Still looking for a decent "space sim" game in the Freelancer model. Still waiting.

Ever wanted to be an Admiral? Command countless amounts of ships, all with their own fighters and escorts? Ever wanted to have multiple fleets at your disposal, jumping from sector to sector to crush your enemies from a moment's notice?
Ever wanted to actually
these capital ships themselves?
What about a space merchant? Make millions of credits, have countless amounts of traders working for you and have endless amounts of factories generating profit? Heck, who needs to ever work again?
X3 is one of the best single player space sandbox games out there. Although the learning curve may be steep, it is a game that is highly rewarding. Start off small, and slowly build up and have the space conglomerate/navy you've always wanted!

If you're looking for an open universe space game that lets you do what you want, this is it. However, if you're somebody that doesn't have the patience to learn practically everything by yourself, I would stray away. I took on the infamous "learning curve" this game has and I'm glad I did. I didn't think learning a game could actually frustrate me, but when I did learn, I started to have a lot of fun. There are very few space sandbox games that let you have this amount of control.
What little of a tutorial this game has makes up for it in variety and content. You can approach success in space by trading or by working for the military. You'll start out with a small spacecraft with hardly any weaponry or cargo space and are set in a galaxy with many avenues of approach. Your only obstacle is your ambition. 6 hours later of learning and I now have 3 trading ships in my fleet, including two extra large tankers which I use to transport energy cells from solar power facilities to space stations that need them. Almost every sector without a solar power facility needs these cells to operate and is a quick way to gain a fortune to expand your fleet and your success in being a merchant.
As mentioned earlier, you can also progress by working for the military or being a mercenary. The game starts you out with very little direction for this, but eventually you will find there is plenty of work to be done in the form of stations and military outposts looking for people to hire. Completing these jobs will earn you recoignition for your status as well as credits to spend on your ship or fleet.
In the end you don't have to do any of this, you are free to explore where ever you like as far as you like, attack anybody you want, trade with anybody you want, settle with any species you want. And I'm promised that's not the end of it. I'm very excited to really dig into this game on a day I don't have to work, I look forward to the expansions of everyones space empire, should they choose to purchase this game.

Whilst the game has a very steep learning curve, the reward is worth it!
3 Pros:
+ Expansive universe
+ Lots of different ways to play
+ You can have soo many ships!
3 Negs:
- The game forces you to use bigger and bigger ships until you need a whole fleet. At this point it becomes a fleet managment game and jumping a fleet becomes tedious.
- No end goal and enemies just respawn.
- Crashing into astroids/AI, it will happen a lot!
The amount of things you can do and the massive campaign means that it will be hundreds of hour before you see the negatives I listed, just exploring and trying new ships will takes hours and hours as the map is so huge. For me the positives far outweigh the negatives.
I also recommend a joystick for flying.

I'm in a situation where I passed 2h mark and therefore can't refund it, but also cannot persevere in getting to the end of the game. What was I expecting? Graphics caught my eye, and while most people would probably be completely turned off by them, I thought the screenshots had a weird amateurish MSPainty charm to them, so I was like "the person who made it doesn't appear to be a great artist, but they still seem to be dedicated to their game, so maybe it makes up in other aspects and might be pretty fun".
Somebody else called it "poor man's Ys", and on first glance it seems like a good comparison. You go from town to town, each town requires you to complete dungeons to move the plot further, until eventually you go to the next one. In dungeons, you move your character across the screen eliminating your enemies, whom you have to defeat to progress to the next screen. Dungeons are very short, at least up to the point I played; they are usually 3, maybe 5 screens long at most, not counting the boss. This makes it feel more like a beat 'em up or some other action based game than RPG, but hey, Ys
action based after all, so it's all good as long as the combat system is well made. Too bad it isn't, because most enemies move completely erratically trying to ram into you, and the ones firing projectiles are pretty unpredictable too. This brings me to another point, which is the schizophrenic difficulty: I played on normal mode and I never managed to die in this game, so it's not like I think the game is difficult, but it feels weird to go through the first dungeons with no effort whatsoever, then get to a part where I burned through large part of my supply of healing potions, then for it to get easy again.
I also have some other, minor technical complaints, such as the game allowing you to discard your potions to the point where you can carry negative number of them, very slow screen transitions in towns (maybe it's related to the 30FPS limit, and they would have been bearable if they lasted half the time), dialogues not allowing you to skip to the next line faster (useful feature in itself, it's there so you don't accidentally skip something important, but here it's annoying if you're not a very slow reader), or clunky UI.
Last, but not least, is the plot. From what I have seen so far, it's so full of clichés that I could probably give a relatively accurate guess as to how the story progresses further. There's a guy who finds a book which somehow takes him to another world called Venux which is under attack by demons, it happens there's a prophecy that somebody will defeat the demons, some girl helps him... Characters are really uninteresting and I really can't even give a damn what happens to them, I'm already starting to forget their names even. By the way, the most memorable scene in this game is when Yuri, the girl co-protagonist, is done with interrogating a baddy; when asked where he is, she responds "oh, he commited suicide ^‿^" with expression you can see in the logo in store page. The most glaring issue is the writing. It is incredibly obvious that whoever wrote the dialogues is not a native speaker, and the whole clunkiness of the story is not helped by poor grammar and typos.
I cannot recommend it, even with very low base price. It does seem that the dev works on fixing the game and uploads patches relatively frequently, but I have no idea how much they'd have to do to make the game good. I hope they find someone to proofread the script for them, at least.

I was several hours into my first game of Prison Architect when I found myself humiliated. I'm talking genuine, utter, red-faced humiliation, complete with a trickle of perspiration and a vaguely sick feeling in the pit of my gut. I've been humiliated plenty of times in online games, but this was an entirely new experience for me in single-player.
I'd been playing Introversion Software's prison construction and management simulator the same way I play any other sim, by slowly expanding my network of buildings—cells, rec rooms, storage closets, administrative offices—while keeping an eye on my finances, staff, and current goals. Most of all, I'd been doing everything I could to meet the needs of my ever-growing population of inmates. If they complained about being hungry, I'd expand the kitchen, serve higher quality meals, and allow more time on their schedules for chow. If they complained about hygiene, a lack of recreation options, or that they missed their families, I'd stop everything and construct new facilities or activate new prisoner programs to accommodate them. As a result of this close attention I'd experienced no riots, no fist-fights, no unpleasantness of any kind. Everything seemed to be going great.
Then I received a notification that an escape tunnel had been found. Five prisoners in adjoining cells had smuggled in tools and burrowed to freedom right under my nose (and right under the prison's exterior wall). I immediately felt betrayed. I'd been bending over backwards to meet their needs, to run a clean, efficient, and extraordinarily humane prison. How could they do this to me? That's when the embarrassment hit, because something important and incredibly obvious simply hadn't dawned on me until that very moment: meeting an inmate's needs isn't the same thing as making them happy. Prison Architect isn't like other management sims where you deal with a restless and fickle population. There simply is no happy state for your residents. Maybe they don't want to start fires or lay into a guard with a power drill, but that doesn't mean they actually want to be there. It's prison. It's right in the title. No one wants to be there! Lesson learned, too late.

Batman: Arkham Origins is an odd duck.
I first played this game the day it came out on the PS3.  I was super excited for it.  I played it and played it and played it... and ultimately decided that it sucked.  There were odd things that sucked about it.  The controls were a little off.  The had switched detective mode with the battarang quick throw for what appeared to be no reason.  Despite being an expert in the previous two games, I had difficulty fighting in this one.
And worst of all... the story sucked.  It was just bad and full of bizarre head-scratchy things like "This is at least 10 years in the past, why does everyone have a smart phone?"  And "Wait, Barbara Gordon is only like... 13 in this?  How does she have the time to grow up, become Batgirl and THEN manage to become paralyzed and become the Oracle we all know and love?  She seemed pretty experienced in the first game".
I actually hated this game so much I got ALL THE WAY to the end, and then I just stopped playing it out of disinterest.  About a year later I finished it up, and the ending did nothing to change my thoughts on the story.
Flash forward to this year, I got this game as part of a bundle (I think).  I decided to subject myself to my least favorite Batman game because frankly, I LOVE the damn Arkham games.  So I'm playing it... and who would have guessed it... I'm actually enjoying it!?
It turns out all of the technical items I mentioned at the beginning were problems associated with rushing a game out the door, and were fixed in subsequent patches.  On the down side, the story still sucked, you can't patch that!  But the gameplay is solid.  And there are some fun points as long as you don't pay too much attention to the story.
I also remember hearing that the PC port of this was terrible when it was first released, and I have to give credit to WB for fixing their messes post release- I didn't encounter any problems while playing it.  It still looks great (not so much when compared to Arkham Knight, but that's on a different level of programming).
If you like the Arkham gameplay, and you're forgiving with plot stuff, by all means, it's a good way to spend some time!

If you don't read the damn manual, or watch some kind of tutorial,
. There's no getting around it.
X3 has a REALLY steep learning curve, and it really is buried in menus. If you don't take the time to learn the game, you won't have fun with it. It's as simple as that. You can do an in-game tutorial, but it's nothing short of worthless. It'll teach you how to fly your spacecraft, but you can figure that out with the manual that you should read anyway.
But that being said... If you're willing to take the time to learn how to play,
. But it's not like Elite: Dangerous where you can more or less just jump in and go.
I will say that most of the game really is just flying from station to station and trading resources, so if that's not what you're into, you might want to skip this. Later in the game, you end up building up a mighty empire, and at that point you end up spending much more time micro-managing shipments to and from your stations, maximizing production of goods without expending too much of your profit, and from there you spend almost all your time balls-deep in a couple dozen menus.
I probably didn't make that sound very appealing, but that's because at face-value it really isn't. But there is something strangely captivating about the whole experience, if you can get into it. I spent about 5 and a half hours today flying from solar production plants to mining facilities, shuttling energy cells for maximum profit. That's basically all I did all day, and I didn't even realise how much time I had wasted. Your experience may vary, but... I recommend at least picking it up and trying it, if you've got some money to blow. You might end up getting a refund though, and if you do, try out something like Starpoint Gemini 2. As a master of the orginal MMX Series, 20xx Tought me something about the franchise that I'd never have know other wise. I am TERRIBLE at MMX (and 20xx because of it). I love the original MMX Series so muc, and played it so hard, so often that I have every level memorized across the orginal 6 games, enemy spawn locations, boss movements. Truely nothing touches me in any of the originals. That however doesnt mean I'm any good at them, Im just good at memorizing patterns, and teligraphs.
20xx on it's own merrit, is utterly fantastic. Every playthrough doesnt just remind me of the original MMX games that I loved in my youth, it reminds me that at one point I was ♥♥♥♥ing horrible at them. 20xx Just became the replacement for my SNES Emulator.
This game isnt just fan-service though. 20xx introduces procedurally generated levels, that are never impossible to pass. The bullet hell like sinerios are utterly satisfing to passthrough and they arent impossible by any means, there is almost always a way to get through it, (though sometimes you need to get REALLY inventive, and REALLY lucky).
Taking a chance on EA Games is something I do, fairly often, as I remember being "that indie developer" that no one wanted to support, so I love a chance to helpout new and upcomming IP's. And I was NOT Disapointed when I firied up 20xx and was greeted with an arcade style main menu, and chiptunes remicent of the NES / SNES age (as well as Arcasde machines).
The Controls are as tight as you would expect from old style sprite games. I mean they are RAZOR Sharp, and it feels perfect. The sounds and music are imersive, yet actiony enough to keep pushing you. Sadly the music also makes you feel a bit more invincible than you really are :-). The game play is incredible. The bosses are hard, and at high levels, are damn near impossible. (Twin Astrals, Deathlutus).
For us old mega man fans there's enough legacy refrences to keep us nastalgic. But if you know nothing about the original MMX games, you can still play and enjoy 20xx for what it is.
My ONLY complaints really is that there is (currently) only 4 tilesets, and I feel like there should be 8. Not because of the MMX games, but because each boss should have their own unique level designs. And do not attempt to play this game without a controller. Im sure many are capable, but if you're an old SNES MMX fan, keyboarding is pretty difficult. To be fair though, I dont know that games of this genre should be played with a keyboard.

The game controls very smoothly with an Xbox 360 controller, and the two playable characters are reasonably distinct - only the primary weapons are different (each also has their own four alternate weapons), but until late in the game you'll be using them heavily because of energy limitations.
The final level hasn't been implemented yet, but the eight bosses are present and accounted for. There are also several challenge options you can enable, such as Endless (which continues to scale as you go) and Lightning (which speeds everything up). You can apply multiple challenges at a time, if you so choose - my standard selection is Marathon (longer levels), Swarm (more enemies), and Destiny (cannot choose next level).

The first ten minutes of Ori and the Blind Forest depict a beautiful and soul-crushing story of friendship, selflessness, and loss. They recall the opening minutes of Pixar's Up! in their melancholy, and like in Up!, the introduction provides an emotional foundation for the life-affirming journey that follows. It is a phenomenal opening--a short and wordless tale, playacted by two expressive characters who move with purpose and demonstrate pure affection towards each other.
There's a certain elegance to the game's initial sorrow, and it translates to the way you move through this exquisite 2D platformer. Ori and The Blind Forest is, on a fundamental level, structured as so many other platformers are; It springs from the Metroid and Castlevania tradition, gating your progress behind doors that can only be opened once you have learned a particular skill. As the nimble, lemurlike Ori, you leap and flit about with fantastic grace, and as Ori's abilities improve, so do the joys of navigating his world. When you learn how to climb walls, Ori responds wonderfully to subtle movements of the analog stick, allowing you to finesse him into exactly the right place, such as a sliver of stone embedded within a sea of lava. When you earn your double-jump, Ori somersaults like an acrobat and reacts in mid-air to your aftertouch. What a delight to have such fine control over a character this agile.

I hated the new character design when it was first shown.. There, I said it!
DMC as a franchise is something I've always held close to my heart growing up. It was the first tv-ad I can remember showcasing a mature PS2 title and with a badass looking character. I got the game, loved it! Granted the sequel was vastly inferior but after that it seems Capcom has done well with the franchise. The one thing that's always been off with the series has been the lack of story. Much like Mortal Kombat, they actually went back and tried to fix that aspect in the reboot. Is it for the better or for the worse?
Better! With DMC4 they obv tried something more but it was for a character we were never attached to, one that never got well recieved and the story overall was a clusterfu*k!
This reboot completely re-establishes the DMC universe with interest and for the first time in the series it finally feels right. Gameplay has always been fun but the story was never too much for discussion. I'm thankful Ninja Theory took over this project.
Dante is back! Nero wasn't Dante, this one is for sure. The cockiness and attitude is back, the feel of DMC3 with a younger version of himself is at hand and we get to experience what made the character so great in the first place. Everything comes in place with this game. The best thing is, it feels natural and not forced!
Minor spoilers ahead:
So it's explained Dante is a hybrid and offspring of the love between a demon and an angel, as such he can wield powers between the two races. This is something I cant remember have been explained prior in any of the previous games, BUT it feels so obvious that it should have been! I never gave much thought about it before but now I can't understand how this wasn't part of the old universe! Ninja Theory got me hooked by mission 2 and I've never felt this excited going through the game for the story parts!
Gameplay is fine as expected as well, not even worth stating the obvious.
Final word from an old-school DMC fan?
Yes again the look, hated it when it was first released.. It does however fit with his younger self perfectly and honestly it felt natural within the first 3 missions or so. I have to say that if you're unsure because of the idea of the new design and reboot - TRY IT! I'd be surprised if you cant get attached to this amazing persona and gameplay.
This is handsdown the best game of the franchise yet with the exception of DMC3
Bosses aren't as memorable and overall the game feels easier despite me being rusty for not playing DMC4 in 5 years. I keep getting A-S ranks in first atempts thus far.
ALSO there's some random crashes here and there but its not destroying the game experience since theres now checkpoints during stage progress.
Overall I'd give this a pretty solid 4/5 - I hope this isn't the final entry as I want more of this greatness!

suffered some hate even before launch because of its departure from previous
games. The combat is revamped and the protagonist is aged down and punked up (also people really seemed to care what color Dante's hair was. Because that
influences the game experience).
is a shining example of the hack-and-slash genre. The combat is complex, dividing attacks into three categories (standard, angelic, and demonic), but this organization makes it easy to master. The more you play, the more competent you become with the system and the more complex and satisfying the combos become.
The story is a bit hit-or-miss, but honestly all Devil May Cry games have had lackluster stories. The ridiculousness of the series has been dampered, so you won't be skateboarding on demons and eating pizza with blades sticking out of you, and honestly it makes the game better for it. It's a much more serious take on what always should have been a serious game.
Aside from combat, the soundtrack is the best part of the game. Noisia and Combichrist provide heart-pounding beats to compliment your demon crusade. The music is well integrated into the flow of combat but is also pleasant to listen to on its own.
