I had never played any of the other games in this series, so I had no idea what I was getting into when I got this game, but I am glad I did. Yes, just like most of the other reviews I will say there is quite a bit to learn. I recommend looking at the guides avaliable (the X3 for Dummies guide helped me get a clue what was going on, while another guide taught me to salvage missles for early game income) the in-game "Flight School" isn't as helpful as i'm sure it was intended to be.
You start out at the very bottom of the bottom for ships and equipment and information on your surroundings which while for some this may be annoying, I personally found it makes progression feel that much more rewarding. Trading in that old Mercury for a Mistral Super Freighter was very sweet.
The music is rather mellow but fitting. Sound is decent, all the various beeps and zaps one would expect in a space sim. The voices are not terrible but not really very good either. Mostly you will hear the robotic female voice telling you the name of whatever you have just clicked on or various facts about said things, which is fine.
I have not experienced a lot of the fight system, being a humble yet cautious trader leads to following a lot of fighting around but not actually participating in it. That said even the small skirmishes are impressive to behold, there are a lot of different colored lasers and many different types of missile weapons all with various uses and effects I am sure.
The only notably terrible thing in the game is the auto-pilot which will at times crash you directly into things such as Gate frames or other ships. This can lead to your instant death if you hit something large enough or fast enough or if you're unlucky enough to survive hitting a military ship, war with an entire race. Embrace the save scumming unless you want to end up with your new suped up Split Elephant ramming into a fleet of the Argon Police force just because you forgot to leave the sector before telling its auto-pilot to place that Cahoona Bakery near Argon Prime, now you're roughly 20+ million credits down and at war with your own people. Despite this if you're careful with your own ship and not present in a sector while giving commands to the AI, it's an easily dismissable downside.
All in all I would say this is a good game if you:
1. Have a lot of time on your hands to play intense and involved space sims and enjoy doing so
2. Are patient with learning new things
3. Don't trust auto-pilots
4. Profit!

I really enjoy historical naval combat games and that was the reason I have titles such as Empire, Napoleon and Shogun 2 Total War Fall of the Samurai. Then, I had been researching about 19th century naval warfare but unfortunately there are not trully interest aside Totem Games and Fall of the Samurai DLC to make games set in this fascinating era.
Victorian Admirals is focused on 4 historical scenarios set in 1880s: Caroline Island Crisis 1885; Panama Crisis 1885; Marianas Incident 1887; Samoan Crisis 1889. The ships of the period are transitional between sailing ships and pre-dreadnought with steam powered engines. There is a great variety of ship models including gunboats, light and heavy frigates and monitors. The ship models are trully detailed, especially the damage textures, and the environment graphics look good as well with beautiful colors set in the Pacific and Caribbean. I also enjoy the engine and cannon sounds.
For those who complain about the lack of customization, the game is indeed customizable. Just go to Victorian Admirals and you will find a file Config where you can customize video settings and sounds settings, including music if you don't want to hear music while playing or to lower the volume of the music. I have this game maxed out and the graphics improve substantially, take a look at my video on youtube:
I am glad Totem Games has another games covering other conflicts of this era: American Civil War, Chincha Islands War, Anglo-Russian War among others. The next title of Ironclads II War of the Pacific will cover another new and exciting conflict between Peru and Chile. I Can't wait for the release!!

Another very poor offering from Totem Games latest in their "Ironclads" series.  The name may have changed but the game has barely evolved from 2010's Ironclads High Seas.  Even the in-game music sounds strangely familiar...
In this game you have a selection of about five different scenarios.  Each battle is a simple open-sea fleet action - no islands or other terrain.  The in-battle UI has changed a little, but the gameplay remains fundamentally the same - you can direct the speed and course of each squadron of ships and choose whether ships can fire at will or hold their fire.  And that's it.  You can't control individual ships, you just steer the leader and the other ships blindly follow.  If the second or third ship in a squadron is at risk of colliding with another ship, there is absolutely nothing you can do to avoid it.  You can't target ships guns, or choose different ammunition types, and there's no firefighting or damage control functions.
To put things in perspective, I'm a tabletop wargamer and history buff.  I love the Ironclad naval era.  I was absolutely bored to tears by this game, and resent having paid full price for it.  Even if it's on sale, don't bother.  However cheap it is, you won't get your money's worth.

ASTRONEER. Although the adventure sandbox game has not even been out for not even two weeks, I think of it as a success in a gaming industry with a lot of failures. While it does borrow a few features from similar games, it does what most of the others fail to do: create an environment where patience is rewarded. This may seem like a negative aspect of the game, but don't be fooled. While you may find small joy in the "jump-in-and-go" mindset many other adventure titles have offered, you probably get bored of that gameplay very quickly. ASTRONEER manages to integrate a unique and refreshing take of survival, crafting, and gameplay-progression ino its world. I would highly reccomend this game to any newcomers of the exploration-sandbox genre and even to the veterans who think they've seen it all.

The game hasn't been out for long upon writing this review, so I'll give it some slack. I played through it and basically did everything there is to do in the game -with friends- in about 10 hours (most of my hours are from save files being corrupted and having to restart) So here is what I came up with.
The following is based off a game that I know is very new, and I'm sure there will be improvements soon.
Pros
+Very fun to play overall
+Visually exciting
+Exploration is lots of fun
+Drop in and drop out multiplayer works mostly well and removes hastle of setting up servers
+There is quite a bit you can do when it comes to expanding how you want
+Simplistic inventory system
Cons
-At times a simple bug will ruin a whole moment
-Crashes pretty often
-Confusing to start out
-Resources start to get really thin and hard to find making expansion and exploration difficult
-Long and sometimes frustrating loading times
-Practically impossible to find key resources on other planets
-Long deep caves are usually a waste of time and lack resources
-Needs more content
-Only has one visual setting and that's view distance
Why am I recommending the game? I had so much fun playing this game, enough fun that I went through it a second time with 3 other people. All it needs is more content and less bugs, I should have a reason to go exploring to other planets without getting screwed over. Personaly the experience of this game isn't worth the price, but I know for a fact that it has the potential to live up to the 20 dollars I spent on it. With patience I will come back in about 6 months.

A really addictive game that feels like it will never end. The title might be a little misleading, as I found myself worring about management a lot more than about architecture, especially since the player can't even build a multiple floored building and that he doesn't have to worry about the mathematical complexities that come with it. Despite the title, the amount of time you can spent with it is amazing. It has lots of mods and downloadable maps, a short but great campaign that functions as an excellent tutorial, an escape mode and it provides a lot of player agency in running the facility. It's simple enough for casual play, deep enough for the more dedicated players. I found myself going between playstyles, where I left the game open while I ran a video or podcast next to it.
However, the bigger your prison gets, the slower your system will run it. I've a 3,3 Ghz CPU and by the time I almost had a thousand inmates, the game ran definitively slower than before (though it was perfectly playable). The game also suffers from numorous glitches. Some experienced some severe bugs where parts of the area was unusable because the game said a building is standing there eventhough it was clear grounds. I noticed that workers don't reliably lay down powercables, where parts of it are missing by the end of the contruction. I saw the same issue with some maps I downloaded from the workshop, meaning that other players must have experienced the same. There are also a lot of glitches involving the behaviour of your employees, which often get fixed with a quick restart or reload of the game. Luckily, the devs continue to update the game with fixes.
I got this game for 5,60 euros, which (looking back) was a steal.

In case the title didn't give it away, in Prison Architect you build and manage a virtual prison. Whether you want it to be a profit-driven hellhole of recidivism or an idealistic place of relative peace and reform is up to you - you can always sell one and go on to create the other (or, you know, opt for an in-between).
I began my journey as a prison architect as most presumably do - by working through the campaign. As you'd expect, this introduces you to the basics of building and managing a prison, with each campaign building on the last. There are also optional goals within each campaign that offer you a little bit more (and some achievements if you're the hunter type). For the most part I found the campaigns entertaining and spent a good amount of time on these alone. But they are designed to prepare you for the task of constructing and managing your own prison, which is the meat of the game.
Prison Architect gives you a good number of options for starting your sandbox prison - land size, whether or not you want trees, lakes and derelict buildings on the site, whether or not you want to have to deal with weather (warmth will become a need for your inmates), gangs, emergencies and the like and staff needs, and cash - if you want to just build and not worry about cash there is an option for that.
As for your actual prison - there are plenty of choices to make as you go along. Despite having played for awhile I feel like I've barely scratched the surface. I haven't touched (ha) pressure plates or timers or switches with different conditions or segregated my inmates by security level. There's really a lot you can manage/control if you feel so inclined. That said, once your prison is running well.. there's not a whole lot more to do (but sell it and start a new one, aiming to touch those elements you haven't yet..)
On top of all of this, there's also an 'Escape' mode/game, where you play as an inmate. In this mode you gain reputation which you can use to increase your stats and recruit other inmates to your cause. Then, using stolen implements, you either dig or attack your way out. It's a fun addition to an already full game.
I'm not sure I'm going to play much more Prison Architect myself, but it would be very easy to. If you're looking for a construction and management sim and the idea of a prison appeals to you then you can't really go wrong with this one. :)

This is a decent free game, with with some bright spots, but also with some flaws. This is my take, good and bad, on this title.
Good
1- Having up to eight players can be a lot of fun, especially with everyone communicating properly.
2- Guns seem to respond fairly realistically, with good feed back and sound effects.
3- No UI. I personally find them to be annoying in some games, and this game gives you the bare minimum.
4- Ammo mode makes the game more realisitic, forcing you to save shots and rely on melee more often.
5- Latency in lobbies seemed pretty good.
6- It's free.
Bad
1- Graphics are sub-par at best. Some of the zombie models look like card-board cut-outs, with floppy movements.
2- Lack of varied environments. Every grass area looks the same, as does the buildings and streets. Also, what's with the lack of color, are the tree's and zombies dead as well?
3- Lack of mode types. Just two, objective and survival, and survial is definately the weakest of the two.
4- Lack of knowledge. I don't mind a steep learning curve, as it sometimes makes things more interesting. That being said, what are points used for? Why are the default controls all over the keyboard?
5- Lack of haste. Your character moves rapidly enough, especially while sprinting or jumping fifteen feet in the air, but why on earth does he reload at a snails pace? Granted, I am not expecting Flash type speeds, but move with a little bit of haste, yeah?
All in all, a decent time waster. It's free, so it's always worth a look, but they have a lot of work to put in to keep my interest.

Being both a ship fan (both naval AND sci-fi) and a steampunk fan, I smiled at the idea of this game and quickly slapped it onto my wish list, which then my friend got for me for Christmas.  I really should have looked at the reviews first.
Graphics:
The ship models themselves look nice, but that's it.  The skies all look bland and the water has no real detail except for the reflection of the ships and sky.  The damage the ships take only amounts to brun marks, tattered flags (the flags that ALL point in the same direction ALL the time) and fire.  There are no break models, so when a ship is destroyed, it just sinks.  Also, there are NO graphic options.  No resolution choice, no graphics scailer, nothing.
Sound:
The sound seems fine except, for me, it is tied to where the camera is in relation to the ship, and if you're off center, the sound ALL comes from one speaker.  The music quickly gets boring.  Also, THERE IS NO VOLUME CONTROL TO SPEAK OF!  The sound literally jars you unless you turn your computer's sound down!
Controls:
You don't get to actually DO anything except control the game speed (slow, less slow), ship speed and ship direction.  And it takes several seconds for the game to repsond to those commands.  I am not sure if this was an oversight or intended for more realism, but it does this game NO favors.  Also, having NO control over your weapons ensures that you will just sit there, occasionally toggling controls and waiting for something to happen.
Gameplay:
WHAT GAMEPLAY!?  All you do is pick a battle, pick a side, see a little paragraph about it, and then you are thrown into the battle.  NO ship or fleet customization, no weapon setups, nothing.  You get what you get and hope that you move just right for ships to think about firing.  And then you play the waiting game until soemthing happens.  Most of the time, it's either your ships or the enemy ships running away.  I have no clue what triggers this, but it happens often.  You lose control of that ship and watch it run off to do God knows what, leaving you do fend for yourself.  One by one, your ships flee.  I would guess it is because of damage, but since there is no way to fix damage or anything, it's just a matter of praying that more of their ships flee than yours; and also praying that they don't decide to stay around and keep shooting, which they are prone to do.  Your ships MAY also come running back, but will more often than not, just sit sail by and give your the middle finger.  Most battles take the ENTIRE hour and a half time limit (if not most of it) and after it's over, you feel like you just sat there, screaming at a movie and not a game.
All in all, avoid this game and ALL of Toten Game's lineup (reviews on this games mirror the sentiment of this review).  There are battle naval combat games available on Steam.

Most modern character-driven games are either/or propositions. Either your avatar is perfectly capable of murdering hundreds of people without flinching, or it’s some kind of narrative exploration. Hitman’s Agent 47 can’t take much fire, doesn’t talk much, and can’t fight very well unless it’s planned out in advance and goes off without a hitch.
The assassinations never go off without a hitch, it’s just not really possible for 47 to use a gun and clear out a room of more than three people without getting dropped by security guards.
Last week I was playing one of the elusive target missions where you’ve only got one shot to complete the mission. No saving, no loading. It took over an hour to figure out how I was going to assassinate the target, and I did, but then I had to complete the second mission objective and use the key the target was carrying to open a safe and retrieve a flash drive with information the client wanted.
One problem: The safe was in a hotel security office brimming with guards and military. All armed, and because there were two types of personnel I couldn’t just have an army costume on and open the safe. The regular Hotel guards would freak out and shoot me.
Bewildered, I cheated a little bit and read on a forum for Hitman players that you could pull the fire alarm and the room would empty out. Great idea!
Of course, no Hitman plan survives contact with the game.

As a long-time fan of Hitman, I am happy with this game and wholeheartedly recommend it. The gameplay is extremely satisfying: never before were we provided with such multitude of options to neatly and perfectly eliminate targets. The locations are absolutely beautiful and diverse. The replayability is insane.
However, the game feels terribly, inexcusably undercooked in some aspects. The most obvious one is voice acting. It is abysmal. There are a couple of actors with very prominent american and british accents, and they voice ♥♥♥♥ing everybody. NPCs in France, Italy and Japan all will speak with the same goddamn voice with no hint of respective foreign accent. The only character with great voice acting is 47 himself, and maybe some of his targets.
Dialogue writing is similarly terrible half of the time, though quite good the other half. Some NPCs' reactions to game events are so overdone that it will make you cringe. Also, every other NPC passing you by will try to react to you disguise: if you are walking around dressed as gardener, random NPCs will greet you with "Hey gardener!". People don't act like that. It might sound as a minor issue, but it immensely damages the immersion.
The other thing that feels undercooked is the way the NPCs move around and interact with the environment and with each other. Their movements look awkward and just don't feel seamless as they walk toward the object, then align themvelses with the object, then start interacting with the object. You would expect much more smoothness from 2016 videogame.
All this considered, the game is still a masterpiece. Better suited for seasoned Hitman players, but great for newcomers too.

This is a decent free game, with with some bright spots, but also with some flaws. This is my take, good and bad, on this title.
Good
1- Having up to eight players can be a lot of fun, especially with everyone communicating properly.
2- Guns seem to respond fairly realistically, with good feed back and sound effects.
3- No UI. I personally find them to be annoying in some games, and this game gives you the bare minimum.
4- Ammo mode makes the game more realisitic, forcing you to save shots and rely on melee more often.
5- Latency in lobbies seemed pretty good.
6- It's free.
Bad
1- Graphics are sub-par at best. Some of the zombie models look like card-board cut-outs, with floppy movements.
2- Lack of varied environments. Every grass area looks the same, as does the buildings and streets. Also, what's with the lack of color, are the tree's and zombies dead as well?
3- Lack of mode types. Just two, objective and survival, and survial is definately the weakest of the two.
4- Lack of knowledge. I don't mind a steep learning curve, as it sometimes makes things more interesting. That being said, what are points used for? Why are the default controls all over the keyboard?
5- Lack of haste. Your character moves rapidly enough, especially while sprinting or jumping fifteen feet in the air, but why on earth does he reload at a snails pace? Granted, I am not expecting Flash type speeds, but move with a little bit of haste, yeah?
All in all, a decent time waster. It's free, so it's always worth a look, but they have a lot of work to put in to keep my interest.

Know lets go over why I graded this game the way I did. To start off, The graphics in this game aren't stunning, but they really don't need to be in my opinion, my main gripe is unless you are playing higher than 1080p the antialiasing settings aren't enough to take the edge off of the geometry in the word.  The audio is simply not the greatest. Although it wasn't a big problem to me personally I think if someone that drives real life trucks played this then they would notice that it doesn't sound the most realistic.  The content in this game can take months to fully complete even after my 80+ hours in the game game I have discovered a mere 40% of the map, giving me many roads and cities to explore in the future.  If you have a low end PC, and wanna find a sweet spot were you won't spare graphics for performance that you are simply out of luck, the low amount of configuration in the settings won't let you find that perfect sweet spot where you can get a perfect 60+ frames per second with okay graphics. If you are a high end PC gamer and are looking to push your system to the max then this game is not for you either, because the max settings on a high end PC will be able to push out at least 80+ fps. So instead of putting that extra 20 fps to better graphics you may as well just put on v-sync. Enough of ranting on optimization lets get to the map itself. While the map may be very large and time consuming to explore, there is sadly not much variety in the towns, one day your at Luxembourg and then you are in Paris, and you can't really see anything that makes the cities stand out from each other, and the cities are very small and don't allow you to go sightseeing. Road terrain gets very repetitive too, while going through the map it feel like the whole time you are going on the same road for hours and hours, sometimes I've gotten confused and thought I've been to a certain area before when I had not. So just keep all of this in mind before buying this game. If you want better graphics, and map design go with American Truck simulator, if you want more content then buy this game. Have a good day/night guys/gals. If you can ask a friend to share the game with you before purchasing, because it is definitely not for everyone.

This game is super dope. It feels like you're playing Megaman X in terms of how tight the controls are and how precise you have to move your character to got without damage. As a fan of Rogue like games, this is up there for one of my faves.
You start the game normally (without any items) and as you play you get more powerful. However, one of the cool things is that as you play, there are tougher enemies that drop currency for when you start a new run. That currency is then used for buying new items that you get to try right away! Imo that was a really sweet move because in a lot of rogue like games, ala Boi or Enter the Gungeon, you don't get to even see how good the item you just unlocked is until you randomly get it in a run.
I also really like how the implemented the weapons and equipment into the game. As I said before you start out with nothing (aside from your purchase before a run) and as you go you get items. However some items are part of your equipment that give you sweet powers like hovering, lifesteal, quick dashes, other stuff like that, but those items are part of a set of armor so if you want a chestplate, you have to get rid of the old one. Think of the active items in Binding of Isaac, except they're passive.
Which brings me to my next point. The boss items are really cool. They are your activated items that you use energy (NRG) to use. This is a game that could be everything, yet is ruined by its own errors and exploits.
1. The matchmaking system makes new players face of against pros with the best of the best more or less from the get to, due to an exploitation of "Dethreating"
2. P2W system makes it almost impossible for a free player to get anywhere in this game as those willing to spend the $ on it quickly overpowering all others.
3. Matchmaking APB 101. 3 Threat classes, Bronze, Silver, Gold. Threat levels from 1-255 matchmaking is based on k/d ratio, meaning a Silver Threat level player with a rating of 255 can join all three server types easyly overpowering everything and farming rep and creds. This ruins the game for new players, as there are no safe zones from them where they can slowly level up and gain better weapons, mod and vehicles.
Threat classes are made the way that the better k/d ratio the higher threat level so an new player can soon be locked to gold servers with a rating of 50- against others with max ratings. just getting pwn´d completely for little reward and alot of frustration.
Unless the matchmaking system gets an complete and utterly needed overhaul facing players of the same rating against each other instead of by Threat Level i will not recommend this game to anyone and will advice people to boykot the game entirely.

And the music is fricking amazing!!!

Despite being a game built on repetition, it's hard to get tired of HITMAN™. Each level is meant to be played several times and the developers have gone lengths to make sure that there is enough content in all of them to keep players occupied for quite some time.
Your first run of each level will probably end up being messy and chaotic. You might get spotted by a group of guards and end up having to hide in a cupboard for a minute, or you might have to knock out half the kitchen staff to stop them from finding the unconcious body of the chef whose clothes you needed to borrow.
But as you play through it again and again you become more aquainted with the levels. You memorize where to find useful tools. You learn which disguises are useful in which parts of the level. And before long you're setting up complicated schemes to kill your targets in the most ridiculous ways possible, all while feeling like an absolute badass.
The overarching plot of HITMAN™® is mediocre at best, but that's okay because where the narrative really shines is in the smaller stories contained within each level. The missions are full of intrigue and features a cast of colourful villians for you to assassinate, amongst them; a fashion mogul turned spymaster, an eco-terrorist with severe OCD, and what appears to be a fictionalized version of former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt. All of these characters are made out to be reprehensible to the point where killing them feels not only justified, but also good.
HITMAN™®© offers a series of sandboxes filled with dark humour and tons of possibilities for murder in the most creative ways imaginable.
It also offers always-online DRM, which is kind of sh*t tbh.

My second fav X-game, Albion Prelude being my first...
While Terran Conflict did have it's intial game breaking issues when first released, Egosoft quickly fixed the issues that caused the game to be unplayable at the start; After they released the patch, correcting the issues, the game quickly became my 2nd fav game.
My only issue with Terran Conflict is that the Asteroids and some of the structures were too large, and caused me frame rate issues when going into particular systems.  Theres no way your going to mine all those asteroids, so I didn't feel that they needed to add so many, and so many big ones at that, just as eye candy.  Some times too much eye candy can affect game performance, and it's because of this that the game will restrict you to smaller battles unless you have the optimal system that can handle large battles, either way, it's a 32-bit application, so having more than 4 gigs of ram will not really improve your situation, as it wont' utilize any more of that ram, no matter how generous you've provided yoru system with it.
With that out of the way, the game is quite fun, and rewarding...  And some game glitches were often fun to exploit, such as the time when I waped into a system, to see a Capital ship colliding with a jump gate, and slowly exploding, leaving it's valuable cargo floating in space for me to collect, not a bad haul near a fresh start of a game if I may  add.
I tend to stay away from the campaigns as much as possible, and often times will look for a save game online, of someone who has completed the game, because to me, some of the missions were too challenging, and I just want to do what i want to do, and not be told what some other alien wants me to do for them.
All in all I give this game an 8.5/10

Fun game for a little while! I got a little bored after finding every useful resource and building every structure on my starting planet. I'll explore the other planets and see if there are any new discoveries.
Some of my exploration adventures.
-Slid down a mountain too fast and died.
-Found a shallow cave, fell in it and died.
-Recovered my dropped items but suffocated before I could get back to base.
-Found a crashed ship and a chair, but it slowed my move speed and I suffocated before getting back to base.
-Figured out that Tethers are a survival gear, and built those to extend my range!
-Didn't bring enough tethers and then got lost in a cave. Suffocated and died.
-Brought more Tethers, then got poked by a spiky plant in the cave and died.
-Took revenge on the spiky plant, and the nearby gassy plant gassed on me and I died.
-Debris hit me in the head during a wind storm and I died.
-Dug towards the center of the planet, but didn't bring enough tethers and suffocated. This happened four times until I got there. Then it took about twenty minutes digging a ramp up to get out.
-Drove my truck to the north pole, and couldn't find home again. Drove up a snow-capped mountain to get a better view, and found a giant solar panel sticking out the side. Started digging it out, slipped and fell off the mountain, and died.
-Respawned and went into orbit in an attempt to land nearer to the lost truck. Landed and started a new base...and attached my habitat to it so I couldn't fly home again. Oops. That's where I'm at now.
I have enjoyed:
-The first planet is colorful and large! The landscape is nice, the mountains tall, the occasional wrecked debris items are interesting the first few times.
-Figuring out how the game works, and how to survive, and finding new things.
-The user interface is creative! The auto-snap attachment points work well for building everything.
-Shift-clicking items to put them on my backpack, so convenient.
I have not enjoyed:
-The camera. I have trouble getting the camera to rotate if the cursor is close to my character, either close to the feet or near the middle of the screen. It feels annoying to have to move the cursor to the edge in order to right-click rotate, then back to the middle to interact with something. (Is there a camera rotation key?)
-The Rover and Truck are so bouncy when driving. Going over a small mound or rock is enough to flip off balance. I can pretend it's a really low gravity planet, but I must be more massive than a fully-loaded truck because I don't bounce nearly as much.
-Running out of buildings and vehicles in ten hours. I enjoy construction and progression, so I feel like I ran out of things to build. So I'll pretend it was a ten-hour demo.
I look forward to how this develops!

I remember in my youth days playing the first ever game of X series (can't remember the name). It was awesome in its own way. It had an open world, trading aspect, dogfight, construction and an interesting plot. It buried into my mind as one of these games that kept one coming back.
Several years later we got X3, which brought back memories and made me glee with expectations. Unfortunately I was deeply disappointed.
One would expect that after so much time the series would improve significantly and draw some of the best solutions from other successful games. This here has not happened. It seems the game have stopped mentally in early 2000 but went on graphically to current gen. The world is VAST, gigantically OPEN, enormously FREE, pleasingly NEAT, and you are free to do as You please, in every aspect of this word. But before You do, there is a discouraging amount of things You first need to learn.
One would expect to learn some basics of trading, exploring, upgrading, before even trying to comprehend the advanced forms of play. This here does not happen. What You're introduced to, is bare basics of ship control, and that's all. Looking at key configuration I had the feeling that someone outsourced tutorials to a player that had the game for 30 minutes. You're just thrown into the universe and be like "oh, You're here, follow me into this sector we've got some bad guys to kill". That's just an insignificant fraction of what the game has in store.
X3 has almost nothing to offer in terms of introducing You into the world, apart from opening cinematic, and because of that it is unenjoyable from the beginning. You ask what's later? I don't know - I've been disappointed by game design to the point that I didn't want to find out. And believe me, I tried two times already in span of 2 years.
There are other games worth Your time in terms of space exploration, trading, fights and empire building. Games like EVE, Freespace, Freelancer...
IF You have time - take it at Your own risk. Otherwise - seek other solutions.

AO always manages to polarize the community - some people love it for it's gritty, angry Batman, it's more realistic suit and for referencing past comic tidbits (like Bane being rather cunning and clever). Others don't even want to consider it part of the main trilogy (and if you pay much attention to the Arkham City skyline in Knight you'll notice that Rockteady pretty much deleted WB's work. Adios Diamond District and the bridge.)
Story wisel, it's okay. Some of the massive success behind Asylum was that it didn't push the history of the characters on you - it assumed you knew them already. Origins tries hard to introduce some key members of Batman's rogue's gallery but it's a sub par effort. It's esentially the only bit of lore that Rocksteady didn't do themselves. If nothing else it's fun to see Batman be more of a person - there's no cape-and-cowl chill when he's doing the nut, smashing computers and spitting when he growls.
Oh - and counters are harder to pull off. I tell myself it's because Bruce is still too "angry and inexperienced" like they kept reminding us.
Multiplayer mode isn't worth mentioning. I played it on PS3 and it was just broken. If you've got some friends or people who owe you, you can at least get all the achievements in private matches.
All that aside, you've got a decent story, a larger Gotham space to play in that City and the Cold, Cold Heart dlc is quite good. Snag it on special.

Forget what they say about this game. Most of the bugs are fixed.
The only that still exist is:
Gliding makes batman go up and down (just dive for a sec and it stops).

I gotta say (unlike others) this must be the best Batman game till now.

Most epic cinematics.
The combat is reaaally better. Plus the Shock gloves are epic.

The story may seem a bit dull at first but seeing how age affects every villain and Batman (if you compare them to the other Arkham games) and how some came to be the ones we know is just amazing. (Probably cause i'm a sucker for origins :X)
Not to mention how i haven't yet finished the main game with 18+ hours (haven't even touched the Dr.Freeze dlc yet).
Also the side-quests introduce more villains and or inform you about how Batman got his friendly relationship with Barbara etc. (And there are more than the other Batman games).
TL:DR I harshly exceed the minimum requirements but this hasn't stopped me for loving the game which shows a lot.

Before I begin, I must tell you all that No More Room in Hell can be abbreviated to nmrih. It is also easier to pronounce the two syllables Nim-Reh rather than the entire game title.
My Experience :
Nmrih was one of the most adrenaline rushing zombie game I could play for free on steam (granted you have some form of Source Engine SDK files installed already).
The concept of having limited ammo and the introduction of teamwork was new and exciting. Though it was very hard to get used to the game at first, a few rounds of the game should help you ease into the playstyle.
This isn't a shoot-em-up zombie survival game. This is a holding-onto-dear-life sort of gameplay. Guns and weapons are hard to scavenge, and the zombies can easily swarm the whole team, even though 80% of the zombies can only limp. The other 20% are runners, they run like marathon runners and you do not want to be near them unless you have a surefire shot with a gun or hit with a melee weapon on its head. I don't want to spoil the gameplay too much, so the rest of the game features can be yours to discover.
Pros:
-Plenty of maps and custom maps
-Has survival mode and objective mode
-FREE (if you have the source files)
-Great co-op game
-Still in development
Cons:
-Still in development (I repeated this because when a game is in development, it has things to be worked on, but it also means that the game's dev team isn't dead)
-Hitboxes can be pretty weird (when the zombies change directions, their heads jerk too fast for the player to catch up with)
-Doesn't give me free Cake for my birthday
That is the overall review of the game, I would highly recommend you get this game, so click That Green Button below to download now! Have fun surviving...

It feels definitively amateurish in terms of gameplay
*The platforming segments have nice backgrounds and soundtrack, but they are dull (little more to do than spamming your shooting and collecting chips that are just laying there), the enemies have cool designs but all of them just have one form of attack which is shooting pathetic energy balls at you, and since the simulations are actually pretty small it gets really repetitive in the late game
*The wireframe top-down segments are even more bare, its just looking for hidden corridors while shooting down mostly static enemies, it is somewhat more challenging than the platforming tho since bullets are harder to dodge and healing is not as easy, but overall they feel more like a tacked-on feature that was added onto the game to make it a little more varied rather than an actual part of it
*The boss battles are definitively the best part of the game, they are fun, challenging, and confusing in a good way that makes you interested in learning better how they work, but I think they are unbalanced, enemy moves are disproportionately stronger than yours even taking in account it's 4 vs 1, sometimes the bosses destroy you if you even drop your guard one second, sometimes you destroy them 10 seconds into the battle if you get a little too strong for them and late in the game hacking chips practically become mandatory in order to beat them
*There is little to do on the base other than go look for stuff on the outside and bringing it back to the Derelicts, it would have been nice if this part of the game was handled in a more interactive way
It might just be suited for people looking for something unusual and up to tolerate the clunky gameplay for it, but despite all it's shortcomings I think it was pretty good and ambitious for a free game made by one person, it makes me wish Scott did more than endlessly milk FNAF because this shows a lot of promise

This game is not something you can casually pick up for 20 minutes.
If you buy it, be prepared to commit some time to it.
A true 4X game.
The draw of the game is its complexitiy. Yes it has a steep learning curve and you will probably spend the first 10-15 hours wondering what the hell is going on and how can I get that gun onto my ship.
It is a richly detailed, highly functioning economy simulator with many hours of plot stories/missions and an unlimited number of side quests. And unlike EVE or Elite:Dangerous, it doesn't feel like you are grinding.
You start out in either a trading ship or a small combat ship. From there you can complete increasingley complicated missions such as:
- Assasinate someone
- Courier this person/parts/goods from A to B (but watch out for pirates)
- Supply a station with xxx units of this trade good
- Build a station in this location
- Follow someone without being seen
The higher your respective trade or combat rank the more difficult the missions. Distances get bigger, trade orders get larger, targets get bigger guns and escorts.
But, after that you can set up automated traders or stations to generate credits. While they're busy making money fly around the galaxy and discover new trade routes, hidden sectors and rare trade goods. Then buy a frigate, fit it out with some big guns and go shoot something. Collect some bounties, expand your empire.
Each race manufactures its own ship for each class, with varying strengths.
Low shields but fast - Split
Slow with armour - Teladi
Really good but compatible with only their races weapons - Terran
Completely useless but look pretty - Boron
On another note, the developers Egosoft have a good relationship with their community and have included some player created mods into official patches.
Tips
-Learn how to use autopilot
- Use 'J' to speed up the game while in autopilot
-Aquire a jumpdrive ASAP, makes getting to known sectors an easy task.
- Set up a few Universal Traders to generate income
- Go view the forums at egosoft for some tutorials

First, let me say that I really hate having to leave a negative review for this game. It actually has all the elements in place to make it truly great -- a huge, explorable universe, a complex economy, a huge variety of ships that each have their own use, a nice backstory, good graphics and music -- but it has some really critical flaws with playability that make the overall experience extremely tedious.
This is really three games in one: In the early game, it begins as a 3D space combat and flight simulator, and succeeds quite nicely at this. But in the later game, as you accumulate more resources and ships, it becomes more of a economy/trading simulator and fleet command style of game.
The critical problem is that the entire interface is designed around first-person navigation and combat, and controlling groups of other ships involves absolutely enormous amounts of navigating through menus for even the simplest task, like "move here". Secondly, ships move *very* slowly in this game, even with the built-in option to speed up time by 10X. Thirdly, trading ships, even the upgraded ones that are supposed to be self-sufficient, are stupid and require lots of hand-holding. The net result is that, once you have a large economy and fleet of ships, you will spend 30% of your time in menus, 69% of your time waiting for ships to move from point A to B, and 1% of your time actually doing whatever it is you intended to do in the first place. To build, equip, and move a medium-sized fleet into position to attack something is the work of several hours (not counting the time needed to get money for it), which is just absurd.
What this game *desperately* needs is a way to toggle between first-person cockpit style view and a third-person, RTS-style, "fleet commander" view to ease management of large numbers of ships.
Other minor criticisms are that the voice "acting" is generally terrible (major characters are often voiced by obvious computer-generated text-to-speech), and the quests are pretty simple "go here" or "deliver this to there". The different sectors start to all look the same after awhile. Also, there aren't many capital ship battles, a problem that was fixed in the expansion, X3: Albion Prelude. However, none of these are major problems in what is essentially an open-world game. The only critical problems are the interface and speed of doing anything, but these are enough to make the experience really frustrating.
All this said, if you have lot of patience and a lot of time to burn, I would actually recommend this game. For others, no.

Personally speaking, I was a bit put off by the intro... OK, a lot. This world of excess and corruption disturbed me, and I wasn't sure that I would be able to stomach the game. Happily, there's only one other scene in the game that really bothered me.  As a side note, I L-O-V-E-D the sequence where Dante was "getting dressed." SO funny! Should I link it? Oh yes, I must!
So if you watched that video above, you might have noticed three things:
- Language (there is a LOT of cursing... Oh, and innuendo... and disgusting imagery sometimes, too)
- Psychedelic lighting (Seizure warning! There are a lot of locations without it, but one in particular is INTENSE)
- Grunge (Oh yes, that music is peppered throughout the game)
The primary thrust of the game is the combat. There's definitely more to it, but I'll come back to that in a bit. You can slice, you can dice, you can absolutely pulverize your enemies in the most stylish ways imaginable. I'm not being flippant; this game truly has some of the most beautiful battle mechanics I've ever seen in a game. I cannot imagine how the game could be played without a controller, as there are so many moves and combos that I'll only touch on them here. I gathered from the intro that two of Dante's weapons are standard: His sword, Rebellion, and his guns, Ebony and Ivory. In addition, there is also a demon axe, an angel scythe, a gauntlet, a pair of shurikan-type weapons, a shotgun, and more! You're not limited to one or two weapons at a time, no no. You can switch between them at a touch of a button (or several :p), and ALL of them have multiple upgrades!
So how do these upgrades work? I'm glad you asked!
Every time you defeat an enemy or take out possessed scenery (like lampposts, motorcycles, etc), you will get
, which are used to buy items such as health stars, gold orbs (to revive if you've died -- won't lose progress in the fight if you use these), health crosses. TIP: This isn't an RPG, so if you want to increase your maximum health, save up for the health crosses! They increase your maximum by 10%!
renew a portion of your health, and can be obtained from green pods and killing enemies (though you won't see them very often.)
come from slaying enemies and by completing levels. Each level is scored, so to speak, and gives you a white orb bonus based on the total points you've accumulated during the level. These orbs are used to purchase ability upgrades, both for yourself and for your weapons.
There are two ways to access the shop & upgrades: Through the menu between levels, or by finding Divinity Statues during gameplay. Here you can not only upgrade and buy items, but you can also practice your moves... You can even try out new abilities before upgrading! Not only that, but unlike other games I've played, the upgrades are not permanent... If you decide that you'd rather put that upgrade point somewhere else, just take it off and reassign it; it's that easy~
During each level there are multiple items to look for. Finding them will not only give you more orbs, but will also earn you some achievements and increase your level score. Things to look for:
- Destroy them to release their souls
- There are multiple kinds to look for: Gold, Copper, Ivory, and Argent.
- You'll need one of the hidden keys to unlock its corresponding door (ie. copper key for copper door.) Behind each door you'll find a secret mission, which will gain you orbs, extra combat, and achievement progress.
There are 58 Achievements to be had, ranging from things as simple as acquiring new weapons to completing the game on the hardest difficulty.
The story, while not earth shattering, was very enjoyable, and the cutscenes are just beautiful (although not all of the content was! lol~) Our character Dante is cocky, but somehow lovable, whereas the antagonist is not just evil, but manages to evoke the purest disgust possible. *shudder*
If you're looking for a game of exploration and discovery, you'll find some here, but if you're looking for some righteous, kick♥♥♥♥♥combat, Congratulations! You've just hit the jackpot!

I'll preface my review by saying that before this I had only ever played Devil May Cry 4, so I'm certainly not a long-time fan of the series, but I did play dmc4 pretty thoroughly. Anyway, on to the review!
DmC: Devil May Cry reimagines the series from the bottom up, and essentially chronicles Dante's transformation from an edgy dude who can see demons and enjoys killing them when he finds them, but doesn't quite understand who he is, into the full-blown Nephelim badass who is now killing demons with understanding (perhaps that he's not just crazy?) and purpose. The game in a smaller part also basically tells the story of Vergil and Dante's relationship develops (I'll leave it at that), and how the world becomes a place where a demon hunter would be necessary.
The story really doesn't take itself too seriously, for better or worse. Dante, especially during the earlier parts of the game, is an angsty hot-head, which definitely rubs many people the wrong way, but there's defenitely a level of character development that takes place in which he becomes more of the Dante I remember seeing in dmc4, both in attitude and appearance.
I don't understand all of the hatred on Dante's look. Dante's hair starts turning white as he realizes his true potential, when he first starts devil triggering his hair starts turning white. Beat the game and you can play through with white hair. I personally thought this was a nice touch, as when you start the game Dante doesn't know that he isn't human, hasn't realized his demonic powers, etc.
Gameplay is (in my opinion) far improved upon from devil may cry 4, there's about the same variety of combos and weapons (not including the variety presented by pandora) but the difference is in the ability to chain combos and attacks together between weapons. This was certainly possible before, but now it feels like almost every combo and attack can be chained together to create a lot of potential variety in how you approach each battle.
Also, love them or hate them, this game has zero quick time events
This has quickly become one of my favorite hack and slash games to date, the story has pretty consistently good voice acting (crazy from a Capcom game) and an entertaining story that's funny, full of over the top action and told well with the help of the aformentioned voice acting but also fairly organic movement and gestures from the characters within the game. The main game took me about 20 hours to beat playing on the hardest difficulty that you initially have unlocked, but I started a new game+ the second I beat it, and the next difficulty up gives all of the enemies new and remixed move sets that have kept the game fresh and have forced me to develop new strategies to deal with old enemies.
All in all, I would highly recommend this game.
Oop also I played with a controller, I don't know how the combat would be using mouse and keyboard, but I can imagine it wouldn't work as well.

TL:DR 20XX is basically Mega Man, but a Rouge-Like, and it's really good.
20XX is a lot like Mega Man, but is a rougelike and is procedurarlly generated. It plays really well even on a toaster(check the specs), especially if you turn it onto Less High.
The gameplay is basically jump and shoot, like Mega Man, but it also adds a dash. On the ground, the dash can be cancelled by dashing again for jumping, which is like normal jumping but with increased air mobility, and is almost essential, especially in platforming segments. Luckily, this doesn't matter too much. The enemies all have a predictable pattern, and you must learn these unless you want to risk taking damage, which you need for the bosses. The flower things, for example, shoot a spike at you, and then they are stuck for a bit.
The bosses are really well done, and even though they don't do their attacks in a specific order(I think), You can still figure out the individual attacks and dodge those. After you kill them, you can choose between 3 items: The boss power, 10 nuts(money) or an Aug(more on that later). The boss power is a weapon they use, which in turn you can use, 10 nuts is literally just 10 nuts, and the Aug is a random Aug.
Augmentations (or Augs) are power ups. Some only do good things; take Contractor Plus, for example. It raises every stat by one. Some are tradeoffs, like one that increases damage and health but costs speed. They are almost needed but you don't need to stress over getting them, you'll just die.
If you beat a level fast enough, you get a prize. This could range from an Aug, to nuts and health, to a new weapon, such as a shotgun. Everytime you win, you get a random number of soul chips, which can be used to unlock new weapons and Augs when you die.
There are also things strewn about the levels, like vending machines that give health for nuts, or the occasional "Very Safe Laboratory," or even shops. The shops give you stuff for nuts, and have a health vending machine in them. Very Safe Laboratories give you a prototype aug. I won't spoil what they do, you can just find that out yourself.
There are things you can do at the Ark, the place you go when you open the game and the place you go when you die. You can unlock Augs, or buy already unlocked ones with Soul Chips. You can also buy Tokens for a slot machine, which appear in levels. There are other modes too, like Casual and Defiant. Casual lets you have 3 free Augs, while Defiant lets you make the game harder. Both aren't eligible for leaderboards.
You can play as Nina or Ace. Nina has a gun while Ace has a sword. They both have very different playstyles and Augs can have different effects with them. There is also multiplayer, which is basically 2 players playing at once.
The level generation is very well done, and I like how it all works toghether.
The music is great, and I love the graphics. But there are still some problems. For one, there are a few glitches, and a few explotable problems with the generation (i.e.: Skipping whole areas because of an insane jump stat, or double jump). But I expected that, since this game is in early access. I can't wait for the game to be finished, because it already feels complete, and since there are going to be more updates, I'll love to see what happens. I know I didn't even cover everything, but there is so much to cover. Thank you for taking the time to read this and have a good day/night.

TLDR: Don't buy it. Amazing game but eventually all savegames will corrupt and there's no way of getting them back forcing you to start over from a really old savegame or scratch.
Actual review:
First off, I love this game and have spent most of my game hours directly off of the non-steam version. I have all starts unlocked and have finished all the major plots. I only switched to steam because I thought it was more stable. Boy was I wrong. I would totally recommend this game if not for one major flaw: Save game corruption. Every save I've had eventually corrupts without fail and Egosoft's support forums are littered with reports of the same thing. The general response has been to either verify your game cache or to reinstall updates. If that doesn't work then guess what? You're screwed. Most players respond with statements such as. "Oh you lost a few days? I lost weeks of gameplay, so it's not that bad." Moderators always respond with "it's one of your drivers/your system's fault." So how do you prevent it? There are 3 possible ways that are in no way garunteed to work at all :
1 . Some people recommend turning off anti virus software as it's known to corrupt saves. I won't even go into how ridiculous this is...
2. Not doing the main plots -as they're known to cause glitches- so goodbye player HQ and personal hub as well as special ships and access to new sectors.
3. To doing what's called a rolling save. Basically saving in all of your save slots for one game and saving 1-2 slots that you only save over after the end of each play session. This still has a chance of causing corrupt saves, most people have to use a mod to save their game. So goodbye steam achievements. Not to mention the fact that autosaves are known to cause savegame corruptions and any ship larger than an m6 can't dock at a regular station, so you're forced to buy salvage insurance to even save. At 3k a pop and having to save at least 3 times every hour this depletes your hard earned credits fast.

The plot of
is a refreshing departure from that of its two predecessors in that it resembles a bad Hollywood movie instead of a bad comic book. The game completely dumps its primary plot point early on for a tangential mess of disjointed, QTE-heavy fights and villain-hopping. There's literally a point in the final act where the main villain is imprisoned and Batman just goes and fights some side villains to kill time before his inevitable escape. There isn't a proper reason for
to have so many seemingly random subplots because not a one of them is any good, and none of the villains are at all as compelling as they were in
, with formerly interesting takes on comic book tropes replaced with super-fancy death battles between martial artists ending with one of them being defeated and saying something edgy like "What are you?" entirely unironically. Between this type of writing and lengthy, misguided attempts at forensic criminology,
is a hot mess of narrative shortcomings and gameplay blunders that amounts to an experience with the equivalent fun factor of
if it had been marinated in warm vomit instead of being play tested.
Truly the cruellest part of
is that it doesn't even have the decency to simply be a bad game. No, this is the evil twin of
that was accidentally dropped as a child and promptly forgotten, and has spent the subsequent years watching its predecessor flourish in the spotlight of 9/10 ratings from mainstream media outlets and honed its skills for the moment it would release and prove to all that W.B. Games Montréal - a studio renowned for timeless classics like
and the Wii U port of
- was as valid a developer as any other, and completely capable of releasing actual games as well. Except while
grasps the very basics of what made the series successful, (it needs combat, stealth and arbitrarily hidden  pickups), the level design, writing and pacing all got lost in translation, winding up with what is essentially a twelve hour trot through a truly diabolical parade of suffering for
fans.
Set on Christmas Eve,
depicts a young Batman in a city ravaged by rampant crime and a police force so corrupt that when influential mobster Roman Sionis - called Black Mask after his black mask - puts a $50 million bounty on the head of our brooding vigilante, the Gotham S.W.A.T. team is involved as quickly as the eight assassins privately contracted to do so. These assassins don't cooperate at all with one another, nor do they learn anything from their previous encounters with Batman, exemplified in the Electrocutioner, who is knocked unconscious by Batman in a single punch and then continues to pursue him, apparently believing he has a shot. The Electrocutioner is one of only a couple of these assassins who actually want the money. Bane in particular is established as being interested only in getting revenge on Batman for wronging him in some way. This is mentioned in passing a few times, but it never progresses past being a piece of exposition to squeeze into cool-sounding dialogue about justice. This is the primary motivator for most of the dialogue. In a tense scene between Batman and
, the former demands that
free a hostage now that he has arrived.
responds with "you're just a distraction, compared with what I've got up my sleeve". In the end, of course, all the
wants is
, which he could, logically, have accomplished several times over in this story, but he chooses not to. It's the little things that really annoy me about this story. I can look past an overarching plot that's generally meaningless - this is a superhero game after all, but it's hard to tolerate the way
repeatedly sacrifices believability and common sense for cool-sounding dialogue. Combined with controls that feel like more of a suggestion than a command and a myriad of game-breaking bugs that are still mostly alive and kicking after three years, the crappy writing drags the whole thing down, providing such a wealth of things to criticise that I won't even go into a detailed analysis of its gameplay shortcomings. It would be fruitless to do so, seeing as the core product is so fundamentally misguided.

The 90s were a special time. The International reputation of the USA was more closely aligned with baseball, basketball Disney and a naughty President than the decidedly militaristic and dark cloak it would come to adopt in the coming century. The internet had not made information instantly accessible and the world therefore felt so much larger, so much more varied and unknowable. NWA, gangsta rap in general and various news stories had suggested the dangers of gangland Los Angeles, among other places, but these things were all distant, almost mythological.
Poking above the waves in the late 90s however was a series of top-down crime simulation computer games known as GTA which would eventually bring this entire world of crime right to your TV or computer screens. A catchy title, the first two installments (and an expansion or two) had the players navigating a city viewed from above, running their little sprite around shooting people, stealing cars, jumping bridges and delivering bombs. Addictive gameplay was given an edge by a high degree of polish, vaguely black humor, outlandish micro-plots and satisfying - if unrealistic - vehicle gameplay to be enjoyed alongside some hilarious radio channels.
When GTA 3 came out at the turn of the century these things were translated more or less directly into a 3D world, meeting with huge success and revolutionising the public concept of exactly how much we would be able to expect from computer games going forward. An entire, full scale city was rendered for us in seamless 3D (a short draw distance not being noticed as there was no real precedent to hold the game up against) Beyond the graphics, the gameplay was every bit as darkly fun and raunchy as it had been in the 2D games, only this time in full 3D with a distinctive visual style - and of course the car driving was still there, satisfying as ever, with those radio stations becomming a core feature of the game - ah, Lazlow.
The exceptional expansion GTA Vice City had come and gone - arguably staking a solid claim to being the best game in the entire series with the quantum leaps the game offered in terms of gameplay and, if less noticably, graphics - and before you knew it a new title had been announced: GTA San Andreas.
Things were different this time around. Consumer commitment would be tested by a huge change in tone from the white trash east-coast earlier games to a Gangsta Rap-inspired west coast rendition of Los Angeles gang warfare, headlined by an African American protagonist, and radio stations which would be booming out rap classics. Rockstar by now was building a third title for the ageing PS2 system, and the technological bottleneck which meant that the graphics in this game were only separated from Vice City by aesthetic margins - more polygonal detail on cars and most other objects, more vibrant colours, a more evocative set of terrain types - meant that a huge amount of attention was fixed on shoehorning more and more gameplay innovations into the package.
Looking back each GTA title released on the PS2 was a quantum leap ahead of previous titles in terms of gameplay. GTA IV would arguably buck this trend - perhaps they ran out of ways to innovate, perhaps the power of the new system was too potent for them to focus on their other obligations - but San Andreas really was a bigger, badder, better game than any previous title. As such this review stands as a solemn assurance:
Don't let age fool you, San Andreas is a lush, vibrant, jam-packed world of crime with half-forgotten gameplay tweaks and additions that will out at you out of the shadows of the past and cause huge grins to break out on your face.
You play as Carl [Williams? I forget], an African American man returning home from the East Coast to bury his mother and - exactly to what extent this was part of his plans at the outset is unclear - reconnect with his initially grudging former gang bretheren and wrestle control of the San Andreas region from anyone else who might wish to stake some claim to it. Small fish prevail at the start, as a corrupt cop, double-dealing gang member, pathetic music artist hopeful and a few other similar characters have you running the kind of jobs that are best accompanied by NWA or Cypress Hill, but after a highlight of the game has come and gone - an all-out gang war in which you are free to dominate an entire city if you can be bothered - you are ejected out the refuse pipe of the starting city and sent scurrying across the redneck alpine regions between the SA towns, ending up in a different town full of different crooks and continuing on your quest for relevance and power.
The game is long, the missions varied and often challenging, the vehicles more varied than ever and great fun. The list of characters is endless, and the gigantic environment offers hours upon hours of entertainment even when it is cordoned off into smaller regions at the start.
Buy this game! It is guaranteed to be good value no matter the price, and it is a holdover from a time in gaming when things like the console wars persisted and the idea of single companies like EA or UbiSoft holding sway over vast spans of offered products was, while emryonic, merely background noise to the single-player offerings being offered for the iconic gaming platforms of the day. Of those offerings, GTA: SA is without a doubt in the topmost echelon.

While The Book of Desires looks astonishing for its time, it is also a prime example on how good graphics alone cannot make an enjoyable video game—even in a casual genre like hidden object games.
Beautiful but shallow: these are probably the two most prominent words I can use to describe The Book of Desires. While it is undeniable that its hand-drawn scenery looks gorgeous for an early 2012 hidden object game, it has almost no positive qualities beyond that.
Well, okay: there are tons of hidden object scenes, especially towards the end; and, for the most part, they are quite decent.
The problem is, there are other parts to this game, not just these scenes, and those parts are terrible: the adventure game mechanics suffer from horrendous item placement and the puzzles are almost insulting.
As for the story, it is supposed to be about a little girl trapped in a magical book that is supposed to fulfil secret desires, but it is an unsalvageable mess that lasts barely an hour and a half, hitting the final nail in this poor game’s coffin.

The Desolate Hope at first glance will seem like a very strange game, but after playing through it for a bit the game really shows how much of a gem it really is. You play as a coffee pot tasked with removing a virus from 4 robot's internal systems in order to keep the station running. While inside the robot's programming/system the gameplay functions as a platformer while you look for the virus to fight. The platforming is pretty fun giving you plenty of mobility allowing you to explore the numerous environments. When you encounter the virus the game changes to a rpg style real time turn based fighting system. The boss fights are super fun and very fast paced which can be great and enjoyable, or very deadly if you are not paying attention. There is a time limit represented by a day/night cycle which does add some tension, but more time can be added on during the night cycle if you find battery packs. The night cylce is when you can leave the hub world and search for items to level up the robots which are the memebers of your party during boss fights. One of my favorite aspects of this game are the graphics, the robots look great and really look intimidating while also looking somewhat cartooney. The Desolate hope is a great game that you can enjoy even if you dont like the five nights at freddys games, and the best part? Its FREE.

This game was a pleasant surprise. I actually don't know why/how it managed to sneak itself into my game library. I think I must have bought it on sale. I prowl the steam store every day for good deals, and even when the game doesn't look interesting but it's, for example, 75% off and under 10 dollars, there's a good chance I'll buy it.

You don't just simply put up walls and call it a building. You have to build a foundation, set up the lighting, set up the water, etc. You don't just hire guards, you choose their equipment, choose their shifts, their patrol routes, etc. You don't just take prisoners in, you have to assign their cells, their cellmates, their level of security, make sure they have access to toilets, food, showers, fun activites, useful courses to help them assimilate back into society, etc. Again, the level of depth is incredible, and will have you tinkering EVERY LITTLE BIT for HOURS.

So this is like many other management sim games, you have a bunch of uncontrollable little dudes you build stuff for, with a major difference being the fact majority of them would rather be anywhere but here and would rather flee or get killed by guards than just live their lives, so, instead of keeping out external threats like monsters or bandits, or trying to create a sustainable economy before everyone dies from hunger, you're trying to keep them inside.
Well, actually, not just inside. Also feeling just good enough or suppressed enough not to start a riot or something. As a matter of fact, there's a massive laundry list of needs, including laundry. There's basics like bed, bathroom, shower and food, and then there are things like leisure, religious needs and desire to meet their family. And these things, they don't just help prisoneers lay off some steam, they also bring more problems to handle! Relative visits? Contraband! Workshops? Excuse to make shivs or tools for digging tunnels. And when you have a whole load of rooms and facilities, from laundries and libraries to shrink offices and security armories, you gotta make sure those are all monitored well enough so no con would snatch anything or murder anybody.
Now, obligatory visual and audio quality mention! It looks simple but functional, despite being simple stylized shape-people the lil' dudes still have butt cracks, which is quite a feat of game design. Sound design is alright with some nice ambiences in the mess hall during lunch and such, and there's no music. Also there's a secret 3D mode but that's just an experiment in visualisation that probably won't be as convinient or nice as you'd want to.
As for more personal takes: It's more fun to set the game to infinite money, or give yourself immense funds with some notepad magic, than to try and transform a shoddy detention center into a proper prison. Sure it's fun to start from basica and try something different in design every time, but designing prisons to ensure maximum ultra-violent riot carnage or proper order and safety is way more fun than handling routine trying to build u the budget for it. There's this "grant" mechanic which kinda alleviates the fund earning problem, actually - you can get a couple of grants with a load of cash for fulfilling conditions like expanding the prison block or starting a new rehab or education program and letting enough prisoneers pass it. Still doesn't excuse the fact you'll need way more than that to build a proper prison, stiff funding means stiff planning. Another thing I miss is something I briefly mentioned in the beginning - external threats. Like, here in Lithuania, there was this problem with gang members using penumatic cannons to paradrop cell phones to their convincted buddies, which only ended when prisons started using communications jammers. Wish there was something like this in the game too - as in, more active involved outside world like suspicious strangers walking around that may either be accomplices or lost strangers and could use investigation from guards, arsonists, tunnel diggers, maybe even a whole bunch of mafia soldiers trying to free up their boss with an assault.
So, yeah, this game? It's nice. I wish it had something more and modding scene doesn't seem to be in a rush to deliver it, but it's hard to deny game already has plenty of things to do in it. It's just quite likely you'll spend more time playing in unlimited funds or the bonus escape mode (where you control a single character and must escape a prison, own or anyone's else) than the "default" game.

The 90s were a special time. The International reputation of the USA was more closely aligned with baseball, basketball Disney and a naughty President than the decidedly militaristic and dark cloak it would come to adopt in the coming century. The internet had not made information instantly accessible and the world therefore felt so much larger, so much more varied and unknowable. NWA, gangsta rap in general and various news stories had suggested the dangers of gangland Los Angeles, among other places, but these things were all distant, almost mythological.
Poking above the waves in the late 90s however was a series of top-down crime simulation computer games known as GTA which would eventually bring this entire world of crime right to your TV or computer screens. A catchy title, the first two installments (and an expansion or two) had the players navigating a city viewed from above, running their little sprite around shooting people, stealing cars, jumping bridges and delivering bombs. Addictive gameplay was given an edge by a high degree of polish, vaguely black humor, outlandish micro-plots and satisfying - if unrealistic - vehicle gameplay to be enjoyed alongside some hilarious radio channels.
When GTA 3 came out at the turn of the century these things were translated more or less directly into a 3D world, meeting with huge success and revolutionising the public concept of exactly how much we would be able to expect from computer games going forward. An entire, full scale city was rendered for us in seamless 3D (a short draw distance not being noticed as there was no real precedent to hold the game up against) Beyond the graphics, the gameplay was every bit as darkly fun and raunchy as it had been in the 2D games, only this time in full 3D with a distinctive visual style - and of course the car driving was still there, satisfying as ever, with those radio stations becomming a core feature of the game - ah, Lazlow.
The exceptional expansion GTA Vice City had come and gone - arguably staking a solid claim to being the best game in the entire series with the quantum leaps the game offered in terms of gameplay and, if less noticably, graphics - and before you knew it a new title had been announced: GTA San Andreas.
Things were different this time around. Consumer commitment would be tested by a huge change in tone from the white trash east-coast earlier games to a Gangsta Rap-inspired west coast rendition of Los Angeles gang warfare, headlined by an African American protagonist, and radio stations which would be booming out rap classics. Rockstar by now was building a third title for the ageing PS2 system, and the technological bottleneck which meant that the graphics in this game were only separated from Vice City by aesthetic margins - more polygonal detail on cars and most other objects, more vibrant colours, a more evocative set of terrain types - meant that a huge amount of attention was fixed on shoehorning more and more gameplay innovations into the package.
Looking back each GTA title released on the PS2 was a quantum leap ahead of previous titles in terms of gameplay. GTA IV would arguably buck this trend - perhaps they ran out of ways to innovate, perhaps the power of the new system was too potent for them to focus on their other obligations - but San Andreas really was a bigger, badder, better game than any previous title. As such this review stands as a solemn assurance:
Don't let age fool you, San Andreas is a lush, vibrant, jam-packed world of crime with half-forgotten gameplay tweaks and additions that will out at you out of the shadows of the past and cause huge grins to break out on your face.
You play as Carl [Williams? I forget], an African American man returning home from the East Coast to bury his mother and - exactly to what extent this was part of his plans at the outset is unclear - reconnect with his initially grudging former gang bretheren and wrestle control of the San Andreas region from anyone else who might wish to stake some claim to it. Small fish prevail at the start, as a corrupt cop, double-dealing gang member, pathetic music artist hopeful and a few other similar characters have you running the kind of jobs that are best accompanied by NWA or Cypress Hill, but after a highlight of the game has come and gone - an all-out gang war in which you are free to dominate an entire city if you can be bothered - you are ejected out the refuse pipe of the starting city and sent scurrying across the redneck alpine regions between the SA towns, ending up in a different town full of different crooks and continuing on your quest for relevance and power.
The game is long, the missions varied and often challenging, the vehicles more varied than ever and great fun. The list of characters is endless, and the gigantic environment offers hours upon hours of entertainment even when it is cordoned off into smaller regions at the start.
Buy this game! It is guaranteed to be good value no matter the price, and it is a holdover from a time in gaming when things like the console wars persisted and the idea of single companies like EA or UbiSoft holding sway over vast spans of offered products was, while emryonic, merely background noise to the single-player offerings being offered for the iconic gaming platforms of the day. Of those offerings, GTA: SA is without a doubt in the topmost echelon.
