This game has a great concept but poor execution. You have to go several menus deep to do most things, and I find myself spending most of my time repeating the same series of clicks over and over again. Maybe there is a better way to do it, but the game gives you no help in finding out what that might be.
I watched several videos, and read tutorials online before playing, and even then I was expecting a steep learning curve. Which is fine. That's not the issue, the issue is the poor design of the game. The game gives you the option to trade lots of different goods, but in reality you can only trade energy cells and ore at the start. The others never vary enough in price to make them worth trading. The "dynamic" trade system results in the AI traders contently supplying factories with everything they need so the price never changes. The result is far from dynamic.
I found my greatest goal in the game was to get an automated trader so I wouldn't have to do the mind numbing, and painfully slow trading myself. You know something is wrong when the goal of playing a game is to make it so you don't have to play the game.
Another guide I read said you can build cash with missions. So I tried that. Except when you start out you can't do most missions. My slow trading ship can't do the trade missions fast enough. My discover can't haul enough, or fight well enough. A lot of missions require special equipment. So you fly around to 5 sectors looking for 1 mission you can actually do, then make a few thousand or tens of thousands or credits. I don't mind low rewards starting off, or hard to complete missions. The thing that gets me is having to tediously check 10-20 missions before you can find 1 you like. And it's not like you can fly into a sector and access all of the missions available in an quick, easy way either, no just get ready to mindlessly click through more menus.
Even with all of that, the game has potential, and I can see where it could be fun once you get the hang of it. But if you don't have hours and hours to sink into a game, and a lot of patients to slog through the learning curve, you're going to get frustrated with this game. Maybe once you're an expert the game is fun enough that you can ignore the poor deign, but I can't.

I am a big fan of the Arkham series. Of them all City was probably my favourite. It's one of the best games ever made.
Origins is very similar in gameplay mechanics. It adds a couple of new features that were also added to Arkham Knight. It introduces a few new types of enemy and features some very good boss showdowns.
If you count Arkham City as one of your favourites I think you will like the experience of exploring Park Row and Amusement Mile before the city fell and was turned into a walled prison. It's familiar yet has a very different ambience. A freezing cold Christmas night with the few good people of Gotham hiding inside due to a police curfew.
Batman is younger and angrier. Most of the goons on the streets have never seen him and have only heard stories of the unstoppable Bat. Legends and relationships are built as the night wears on.
Technically the game doesn't have the same polish as Arkham City. I experienced some minor bugs but overall the game ran well. If you have a fast GPU there are some nice visuals and effects like APEX turbulence for the snow flurries and tessellated tracks left behind you. There are some cool locations and the world is larger than Arkham City - you also get to explore the Batcave.
Well worth playing for Arkham fans.

This feels like a game made by people with all the right tools at their disposal, but possessing insufficient ability or care to get enough out of them.
The tone is set from the very beginning, with juddery intro videos, and the glitches persist from there. The game is riddled with little glitches, like unconscious enemies remaining standing, or hitting an invisible floor when cut down from gargoyles so that they float in mid-air. It also suffers from sharp framerate drops even on a 1080.
Aside from consisting of a B-list of villains, the boss fights are often badly designed. The first in particular sets a poor tone by being badly unbalanced and frustrating, while later ones are ruined by the grossly overpowered shock glove weapon which renders them ridiculously simple.
The detective scenes offer a glimmer of hope as an interesting new concept, but the game tells you, audibly and visually, exactly what you have to to every step of the way. There is no skill or thought required. They are glorified QTEs. Indeed, much of the game feels this way - it is constantly telling you exactly what you have to do.
It has its good moments - a few strong cutscenes, some decent voice acting, generally decent graphics - but is not in the league of its two predecessors.

For as long as I can remember back, I have always loved Megaman. From start to finish. All it's titles and even the less great ones seem to have held a special place in my heart. Megaman X in general though was the one that I grew up playing the most of. I grew up always asking why it was never 2 player Co-Op and I can't be the only person who felt like it was such a missed opportunity on capcoms part for not having ever allowed it to be Co-Op. I have only owned this game for 2 days now, I have played the hell out of it and the nostalgia rating is 10/10. But set aside nostalgia and look at this game as a stand alone game that simply takes what megaman always was and builds up on it to make itself unique. It is still early access and already has an incredible amount of potential to be one of my favorite games of all time.
The inputs are flat out amazing, I did have to change the bindings so that B on my Xbox controller was my dash, I couldnt handle the default RB being the dash, but set aside that..I have changed nothing and love everything. I recently got to play it with my friend who I grew up together always saying "Why isn't megaman 2 player co-op" it was literally like getting ina time traveling device and warping back in time to play megaman as we thought it should be. (Not to diss megaman, I am such a huge fangirl of megman lol) This game exceeded my expectations for being a game that isn't even complete yet. For the price especially. It seems steep at first until you realize that this game has near infinite replayability (Especially if you read up on the forums as to what the devs plan to do with the game in the future, such as a creating your own stages and such that get shared with the community and put into the actual game.) I not only enjoy the game as it is right now at this very moment, but the updates I hear that are coming are exciting to hear.
Most of these other reviews will go into way more depth than I will, for me I realize the selling point was the Co-Op gameplay. There is never any lag, I've had no issues thus far, no bugs that I have found, And trying to play the game in lightning mode is hilarious when you have a friend who mashes dash and can't control his character. Watching him slide off the edge to his death about half a million times while I wait at the top was priceless. I recommend this game for anyone like me who grew up playing megaman and wanted to play WITH your friends instead of taking turns on stages.
This is a beautifully done game and a far better one than that of "Mighty Number 9" which wasn't at all that mighty. This game instantly succeeded where that game fails. The soundtracks good, the gameplay is amazing, the challenge is incredible but starts off easy for the new players who would just enjoy casual gaming. The items seem fair and pretty balanced (for the most part at least, I always feel OP until suddenly I'm at 2 HP and wondering wtf happened to my life)
Over all, I came here to put this review here with 2 days into the game because it has ALREADY exceeded my expectations and I know I will enjoy this game in the days following. I may even come back to add more to the review later when they add things for updates. This game is just too good. 10/10 already, and its unfinished. The reviews for this game do not lie. :)

The TL;DR of my impression of this game can easily be summarized as: "Holy ♥♥♥♥-sticks this is amazing."
Checklist of awesome:
- Fantastic controll: jump 'n' shoot, wall jump, and dash. The movement system is fine-tuned to excellence.
- Rogue-like elements implemented fantastically: Power-ups can significantly alter different playthroughs by modifying movement, durability, weapon behavior, and other upgrades.
- Additional upgrades can be unlocked which adds an enjoyable progression system.
- Level and boss order is shuffled, more dangerous enemy variants show up at later levels. Bosses also gain more difficult abilities/behaviors as you progress on each "run" you make.
- Optional modifiers increase difficulty in multiple ways: Increased enemy speed, stricter time limits, restricted item drops, and longer levels to name a few.
- 2 characters, each with different weapon behavior power-ups, and a different approach to combat
- Shared-screen multiplayer done extremely well. Camera does a good job of zooming out when you get further apart. (Online is available as well but I must admit I havent tried it.)
- There's more but you really need to see it for yourself. It's been a long time since I've played something so satisfying.

It says that I received this game for free but I did not.
As a player who did not wait for the actual releases in real time, purely taking the games by themselves for what they are....  well I know that WB Games Montreal did not found this feast, in my opinion this is one of the better games in the series.
I absolutely love the combat in comparison to the other games it feels much more visceral, involved and directional.  I love how they took the formula from Arkham City and expanded it across a larger Gotham.  Each game has something that sets it apart from the others, but this game feels in my mind like a Perfection of the original concept.
Arkham Knight had a bigger more detailed City but it also had a Batmobile which to drive around....
And it's severely lacked in good boss fights.
Arkham City arguably had better boss fights but Arkham Origins had far more of them.
What prompted this review was my decision yesterday to take on some of the challenge maps that I hadn't before.  I really love the challenges in this game more than any other.  The initiation/rite of passage campaign is fantastic.
I found myself motivated to play through all the challenge Maps because I was having fun.
About some of the gadget changes in complexity from Arkham Knight this game supplied more takedowns from what we loved in Arkham City and Gadget features in general...  while this doesn't chronologically fit with the series, I think WB Games made a good decision to say "f**k it" and allow the inclusion of some anachronistic gadgets.
I love the added height and range for Batman's flight capabilities vs. Arkham City.  The cinematics in the set pieces in this game are absolutely wonderful.  I feel that the challenge level has been stepped up over Arkham City, leaving plenty of Headroom for an average player like myself.
I can't tell you how many times while playing Arkham City I wished to have fast travel, when an objective force me to have to fly to the other end of the map, and I wasn't in the mood for what was arguably an enjoyable part of the game (map traversal).
I love that in this game you see the early bat caves and interact with Alfred.
The cold cold heart DLC is absolutely fantastic as well, expanding on both of the previously mentioned goodies.
Yeah the Batmobile in Arkham Knight was great and might have been nice in this game, but I feel that Arkham Origins stands well on its own home without it.
Arguably Arkham Knight was a bit too much of a driving game.
I've also recently discovered how amazing the multiplayer on Arkham Origins is.
I feel that WB Games missed an opportunity by not setting up PvE Batman and Robin versus computer Co-op.  Which arguably would have extended replayability a great deal and removed the need for people who are willing to play the role of Joker and Banes bugs.
I've heard people say that multiplayer was unnecessary in this series but to be honest Batman and Robin work together all the time, and I think that the multiplayer maps on this game are really really spectacular.  And I wish there was more options for their use.  As I am normally only a single player sort of gamer.
Many people have talked about the portrayal of Bane in this game, and I must pile on with the Applause for this version of Batman's other nemesis.
Bane Begins the game as Batman's most physically and mentally formidable enemy, and out of desperation and hatred makes the somewhat tragic decision to mentally injure himself in order to physically best Batman.
The origin story for mr. Freeze in Cold Cold Heart is also done heartbreakingly well...  a Worthy origin story for his heartbreaking roll in the later series.
I've played all the Arkham games multiple times.  And if you love the series as much as I do I suggest that you try an experiment.
Throw out any previous biases you've had it take the games as a whole.  Start with Arkham Origins then play Asylum, City and Knight.
Just run through the story modes in order without having to Great a gap between the games.
I found it to be a blast.
Even the reduced gadgetry of Asylum didn't feel too out of place, as the smaller scale of the event didn't leave you feeling overmatched by what you had in the game...  Arkham Origins was a larger-scale event as was Arkham City...  and Arkham Knight needed the Batmobile.
If you do this I highly recommend collecting all the stinking Riddler trophies in Arkham Knight that way you get the lock Em Up after the boss fight he's deserved through all the other games.  And at the risk of too many spoilers, you also get some Nifty closure with Catwoman.
Don't count this game out people.  It might not be made by Rocksteady, but it's a great game.  An excellent origin point for all the other Arkham games.
Roger Craig Smith is fantastic is Batman and Troy Baker bring the maniac Joker to life wonderfully.
Go for it.

I maintain to this day that the 'Bash' ability is one of the most, if not the best,  novel and satisfying abilities I've seen before or since. Cannot recommend highly enough.

A young girl is scared that her parents are splitting up after a nasty argument. She dreamed about a book that can grant wishes. However, the next day, a strange man gave her this item. When she wrote her wish, she finds herself stuck in a nightmarish world, where she has to defeat the Guardian of the Book if she wants to come back to our world...
The Book of Desires is putting you in the shoes of a child, in a nightmare world... However, she's confronted to skeletons, ghosts and anything else that can scare easily a kid, but our protagonist isn't at all scared of where she is. Everything is written as if it was an adult and not a poor girl scared about the future of her family.
The gameplay is the standard one: find objects, use them, clear hidden objects scenes, solve puzzles. Apart the fact that you will speak to people that will help you and the little twist at the end, nothing is really extraordinary. But I must say that everything is polished and well-balanced. There is just one or two bad translations (like compass translated as "boussole", used for finding North, South, East and West, which is a right translation but in the scene, it was the tool to draw a circle, which is "compas" in my language) and a puzzle that seemed to be broken as I couldn't do anything about it apart waiting for the skip button to be active.
The graphics are really fitting to a creepy world: everything is dark, filled with scary entities. I appreciated them, As for the soundtrack, I didn't really pay attention to it.
What really bothered me is that I didn't feel like the child was reacting as a child. If I can take Clementine from The Walking Dead and make a comparison, I would say that Clementine was more reacting like her age, even if she was in a post-apocalyptic world and had to grow up quicker than planned. However, in the game, it's like you were controlling an adult and an adult that doesn't seem to frightened despite the circumstances.
In the end, I would consider The Book of Desires as an average casual game. It's not too bad but it's not as good as other titles out there. If anything, I find the price a little high, it's better to wait for a bundle or for a big discount. As for me, I won it during a giveaway, as it was a bundle leftover from Groupees. I'm giving it a positive review despite being mixed about it.

What is The Desolate Hope?
It was one of Scott Cawthon's earlier projects before he struck it big with FNAF, and is a spiritual sequel to an even earlier game of his. It's genre is hard to describe, but if you're asking me it is a an RPG with some Metroidvania and Time Management elements, but the real meat comes from its turn-based boss battles (even Cawthon admits to this).
You play Coffee, a sentient percolator on board the Lun Infinus space station. The space station is home to four (technically five, though one has since broken down) robots called Derelicts, who were tasked to create the ideal colony for humans by running simulations. Unfortunately, the Derelicts have been running far longer than expected, and a virus has started to worm its way into the simulations and wreak havoc. As Coffee, your job is to go to the simulations and locate the viruses, and the Derelicts will fight the virus off (the aforemented boss battles).

This game feels like a real step backwards from the previous DB title. It seems like the devs were more focused on delivering a game where you can alter every aspect of your career player's appearance or building your own cricket ground rather than an enjoyable cricket simulation. The difficulty has been ramped up for this iteration (no bad thing as cricket is a very hard game to master). This however has perhaps gone a little too far for back foot shots, as they seem near impossible to perfect. The AI for field settings is much better this time, it feels a bit more reactive and a bit more like the opposition have a 'plan' against you. However the AI for fielders is so bad; random slides, unnecessary throws to bowler's end, peculiar running around the ball, might be a simulation of club (or rather beer match!) cricket, but international fielders do not usually get up to such shenanigans. The commentary is truly awful. Lacklustre voice work that does nothing but sap your immersion in the game rather than bring added colour (if audio can do such a thing!?!) The wicketkeepers exhibit peculiar behaviour, flitting between being incompetant clowns to displaying superhuman athleticism (in one instance dismissing me by having me caught behind with a one handed catch in the position of a second slip, therefore diving fully across the guy at first slip!, to a spin bowler from a fierce back drive).
If you want a fun cricket sim buy DB14, for all its flaws its still a superior game. If you want a frustrating and in the end unrewarding cricket sim then you've probably been on the staff for Big Ant and were part of the development team so therefore won't have to buy it. Otherwise don't buy this buggy mess of a game.

If you start a new game, this is a great RPG. Several expansion DLC's are worthwhile and the reviews are accurate. As I wrote in the beginning, stay away from the Ultimate upgrades, both 1 and 2. The base game has good scaling and great humor. The Ultimate upgrades changed the scaling so that you will be killed by one shot or your vehicle will be destroyed with one shot. Weapons get stronger, but enemies get MUCH stonger.  Obviously, the Ultimate upgrades changed the game to require you to play on-line with multiple players just to survive. The Ultimate upgrades should at least inform you that you are required to enter the multi-player world. That is not why I buy RPG games. Play the base game, and after you defeat the Warrior. This is a really good game for something Steam would make Free To Play. I enjoy how it's set up, just raw hardcore survival. I say hardcore literally. This game throws lines and lines of "Zeeks" at your weakly fortified hideout. You and any other survivors you may be with have to constantly watch your backs, keep a gun - and crowbar - handy at all times, and be ready to switch from flashlight to rifle in a split second. However on the downside, the game could use some improvments. I never liked how Left 4 Dead looked, it was too "common". This game looks a lot like it and if not that - exactly like it. Another matter is the ammo deal. I can't tell what ammo goes with what gun, and that's a problem when you're running, gunning and scavenging. My final concern is that this game could be better with less "pick a person and get thrown into the fray" gameplay and more immersive gameplay. It needs a character creation, the ability to name your character and some sort of level format.
Aside from the entire game, this would make an absolutley awesome free-roam apocalypse game.

It's a game about the good ol' jump n' shoot / slash (wo)man doing their thing with some elements you might've seen in Rogue Legacy or other similar titles. What more do you need?
XXX
- Procedurial generation might limit what the dev team can do with stages in terms of unique looking locations or secret placement somewhat, but the advantages in replayability may very well outweigh that.
- I found the way this game does its difficulty curve interesting, even if it tends to kick my butt 100% of the time so far. It appears to expand enemy movesets and stage layout combinations not only for the duration of the current run but also as you gradually unlock items in the shop.
- Music and sound effects didn't particularly left an impression on me, but they are informative and do not irritate.
- I found the color palette pleasing to the eye despite all the explosions and energy blasts constantly happening on the screen. Some animations look like they could use a little bit more detail when compared to others, but overall it seemed quite smooth. I've liked the idea behind Ace's plasma cutter thingy and some other little details and have yet to come across anything that I actively disliked or that looks like it doesn't fit. Although some stages could perhaps benefit from some more doodads in thier 'building blocks'.
- Despite struggling with the difficulty, I did not find the game frustrating. The way the characters move and control are the major reasons why. Big kudos to the dev team!
- Humorous, tongue-in-cheek poking fun of what is happening on the screen starting from the intro and all the way to the run result comments add to the atmosphere in a nice way.
- On the technical side of things, I've run into some visual artefacts only once so far. UI scaling doesn't appear to alter the size of text popups of characters talking, item descriptions in the pause menu or skull selection screen. Some walls are prone to stopping the characters' sliding down them unexpectedly repeatedly at the same spots.
XXX
Overall impressions:

As a pretty huge Mega Man fan, I was always on the fence with buying this because I was very nervous about jumping into this and being disappointed by what seemed like a promising concept.  Ended up being very, very satisfied with the game (at least, in its current state, since it's an Early Access title).  It really scratches that Mega Man X itch (despite the intro obviously referencing MM2, the game is overall trying to replicate the X series more than anything) and then some.  Controls feel really good (using a PS3 controller, with the actual in-game controls tuned to my liking), gameplay is fast and quite fun, music is very catchy and enjoyable to listen to, and the Defiant settings let you turn up the dial with some difficulty spices to season the game to your liking.  Even when I can recognize particular segments (it's not possible to have an unlimited number of set pieces for a stage, after all), the different combinations still feel fresh and engaging to tackle.  My one real complaint lies with the visuals and animations, which I personally feel are a disservice to the cool character designs and give the game a kinda Flash-like appearance that might turn some people away from an otherwise really great game.  The game also currently lacks a proper end-game (ending after the eight bosses, assuming the Endless Run defiant setting is turned off), though from what I can gather, it's something that's currently being worked on among other things.
Overall, I think if you're longing for a solid Mega Man game (X series in particular) and the idea of a Mega Man-esque rogue-like game sounds like it might be your cup of tea, I'm confident that you'll end up very much enjoying this game, even in its technically unfinished state.

So a friend watching me play this game totally engrossed asked me where the fun was, and I looked up from my laptop long enough to think about that question and realize that I didn't really know. Was the fun in the trading economic parts of the game? No, sending your trading convoys from system to system to try and hawk off those Teladi Sun Flowers is more tedious than "fun" by any conventional means. Was the fun in exploring the galaxy and flying from system to system? No, ships are too slow and most of the time you'll be flying to system on autopilot while your SETA (a device that speeds up gameplay) does all the work there. Is the fun in the combat? At least that's fun, right? I hate to break it to you, but the combat can get wearily repetative real quick, and the intense dog-fights of the early game disappear as soon as you get a corvette class ship.
In all honesty, I have no idea where the fun is in this game, but it's there, alright. It's gripping, frantic, and you'll be so invested in your little ships that you'll be crying at the screen once you see a Xenon Q drop into the sector and blow one of your trading ships back to whatever year this game was made in.
That said, this game is by far one of the most difficult that I have played in a while and I wouldn't recommend it to just anybody. X3 drops your right into a hostile universe of intergalatic trade and warfare with little explanation of what to do, how to do it, and very little to do anything with. How are you supposed to survive, let alone succeed in this universe? The same way you do in any capitalist society: pull yourself up by your ♥♥♥♥ing bootstraps you lazy, entitled, leech. The previous generations of spacefarers didn't have anything when they made a go at it so ♥♥♥♥ you for thinking you're going to get off so easily. (Said previous spacefarers also didn't have anywhere near as many challanges to face as you will, but just try explaining that to them).
In all seriousness though, newcomers will have a serious learning curve thrown at them and some unfortunate bugs to worry about. For example, X3 has one of the most realistic functioning economy's in any game, but it often works too well. GoD (don't ask me what that stands for) will spawn and remove factories based on supply and demand. Makes sense, right? Factories that move product obviously stay in business in the real world while those that don't get shut down. Where's the problem with that? Well, a few of the races don't HAVE the infrastructure to maintain a functioning economy because the devs didn't think it through enough and so the factories that produce the only compatible missiles and ammo for your ship might just one day disappear and leave you high and dry. Veteran players figured this out a long time ago and have their work arounds; new players, however, beware.
If you get this game, make sure to consult the forums for advice, tactics, and warnings (disappearing factories aren't the only bugs to be mindful of) from those more experienced capitalists.
Have fun.

First off: This is a game that is Early Access (A finished product shouldn't be expected)
I love early access games. I know I can wait a while and get a more polished product for a lesser price later on, but as a developer, I would like to help with development. This game is awesome! I have really been into survival/crafting/exploration games (i.e. Subnautica) and this one has a particular sense of calm and tranquility that I really appreciate. It's all too easy to get involved in dungeon diving to slay creatures and grind gear, but in Astroneer, you are rewarded for your curiousity and not really burdened by monsters pecking at you every chance they get.
Some things I really like about the game:
* Fluidity of the terrain shaping tool
** Wow! For being in 3d, this tool works well and renders well. There are a few quips when using a controller but that is to be expected. Grade A stuff!
* The customization of your base
** Your base will truly be one of a kind, every time! You create your base and expand as you see fit!
** You have many options for power sources which are quite intuitive
* Soundtrack
** The music is just like the game. Calm and serene
* Platforming Aspect
** Great controls and physics in regards to scaling up the new chasms you create with your terrain former.
Some things that need some polish or nice to haves:
* Need a way to deconstruct modules on your base. Once it's done, it's done. If you improperly set up your base, seems like you have to start over.
* Need a way to respawn/unstick your character (even if it means leaving your collected items behind).
* If you use the terrain former too fast, you can wind up falling forever between the walls of a cave.
* There should be an optional tutorial that get's you up to the point of at least creating your first extension of your base.
** For those (like me) who struggled with understanding that compound and resin are not the same! ^_^
* The scenery for the first world is very cartoony (could just be this planet).
* The controls for the terrain builder for controller could use some tightening. Perhaps a way to lower the sensitivity.
Overall, I like what I see. I get to explore in peace and try crafting new items! Please, if you make changes and introduce creatures, remember the experience that you have been giving your players all along. Subnautica made a few changes and now the game doesn't feel the same. I hope this continues to be the awesome experience it is!

Let's start with the main bad point because I really want the developer to do something about it.
The fielding in this game makes it almost unplayable. The AI is shocking, with fielders not diving for edges, or turning their backs on balls hit straight to them that then run away for 4. But by far the most annoying thing is their seeming obsession with throwing the ball to the bowler whenever a shot has been played. Whether the batsmen have run, from all over the field, they throw the ball to you. This means if you haven't had a chance to run back to the bowlers end, then it usually goes for 4 overthrows. The overthrows may only happen in 1 out of every 10 matches, but why the fielders think it is a good idea to constantly throw the ball to an unguarded end rather than the wicketkeeper is beyond me. Please, please, please sort the fielding out.
Other than that it is a good game. The graphics are an improvement on DB14, as is the career mode with the options for creating a player and career progression both improving massively, though you start at 19 rather than being able to start at 16 as in DB14 which I would have preferred.
As mentioned at the start you will need a controller for this game, and I think if I had a do-over I would have got this on console rather than PC. The Steam controller isn't quite there for batting, with the touch pad used for shot selection meaning, ironically, that is isn't as smooth as if it were a joystick. I am considering getting an Xbox controller for this, so if I do I will update this if it is an improvement. With bowling the touch pad is used for timing the jump and aiming the ball, so there are a few times when it doesn't register the pull back to start the jump and the bowler runs through, but other than that it isn't as bad as the batting.
This game has really mixed reviews, with people either loving or hating it. Personally, apart from the fielding, this is a solid upgrade from DB14 and they have produced another decent game. Download the demo if you are unconvinced and judge for yourself, but I like the game and I have already started to think of excuses to get me out of social events and back home to play it...

What a FANTASTIC achievement. I'm a huge cricket fan and student of the game, and didn't think a video game would capture the subtleties of cricket, but, it does, it so does. 14 was playable but flawed, struggle to find the flaws with this one. The minor ones that come to mind include frustrating field changes by ai, the strike changes with some stumpings which is weird, the women seem to have super thin arms and and could use some more designing work. Biggest flaw is the field resets, especially in competition mode. Some, behind the scenes (news clippings, buzz on the circuit over a performance, maybe someday clips from cricketers) would be AWESOME in the career mode but it is incredibly cool as it is.
Now for the good. In listing the jumps from 14, leg glance dominance is gone, edges are now a thing, run outs are more intuitive (keep rt and nothing else pressed, otherwise the runners do wierd things), the super-fielder problem is gone (great work done wrt problem) but best of all. SPIN IS THE WINNER, it is artistic and varied, though you need to figure out how to add a quicker one in there. The commentary is exponentially better but little things like speaking of overthrows like shots, anti climactic last ball commentary etc (ideally you should add specific commentary/lines for the end of matches).
This ended up being longer than I planned but these are my thoughts of the top of my head. I'm not a gamer per se, just very into cricket and I'd recommend learning this for any lover of the game.

When I first started playing Super Meat Boy I liked it, but I didn't think I would stick with it as the difficulty increased.  And I certainly didn't picture myself replaying levels just to get a slightly faster time or to unlock everything.  Oh how wrong I was...  This game is a platformer where speed is everything.  Thankfully the controls are rock solid, so when you die (and you will die a lot!) you know it's because you screwed up.  It might sound ridiculous to keep playing a level over and over just to keep dying, but the levels are short enough that you don't get bored with the repetition and it's oh so satisfying when you finally conquer a level.  The good news is that no matter how bad you are when you begin, as you progress through the game it basically teaches you to be better at it.  After playing the game for a while, revisiting those earlier levels that you had trouble with suddenly becomes a breeze.  The levels are cleverly designed, but quite often you can find shortcuts if you think outside the box.  I've never been a fan of speedruns or replaying levels for a high score, but Super Meat Boy hooked me in a way that most other games haven't.  Although this game can be frustrating at times, it's because you are frustrated with your own performance and not the game, which usually motivates you to try again.  8.5/10 for this great game.

This is my first and only review I've ever made about anything, but this game truly deserves one. Yes, it is hard to learn to play it, there are so many different things you can do that you will basically use your entire keyboard to organize it all. But if you ever wanted to travel the stars, seek out distant planets, interact with different species, have a fleet of ships at your command, (ships that you yourself can fly) build stations in space, and/or build a galactic empire, hijack ships with trained marines, become a merchant/trader, a pirate, war hero, or simply not be known, watch entire fleets trading fire, use a turret while the ship attacks another, fire a barrage of missles at targets, destroy entire space stations, watch an assortment of people/NPCs live their lives all around you, fly thru asteroid fields, or just blow them up, then this is the game for you.
There is a lot I could say about this game, but in short, it's like nothing I have ever played, and I have been gaming for most of my life. I go on to speak about a few things on X3 Terran Conflict, but to be honest, there is just so much to say about this game, that it would take a heck of a lot of space. But here are a few bits, hope they help.
Nearly every ship in the game you yourself can pilot, from tiny fighters to large warships. You can travel the stars in on a large well defended ship, and then take out a fighter in your bay for a quick spin around the sector. The game itself is beautiful, from the stars to the ships down to the stations. It is all a sight to see.
I've played many space games in my time, but none come close to X3. It does have missions you can take on but at your leisure, it is essentially an open ended game; do what you want, when you want. It will take time to learn everything, but little by little you will pick it all up. You will start slow, no money, a poor ship, and lost in the sea of space, but in no time, you will have the money to improve your ship and its armament, and ofcourse you could always come across a abandoned ship in space.
The sad thing about Terran Conflict is that, dog fights are out of the question. All ships have some or the best weapons in the game so you are stuck flying a larger ship with better defenses. Not that you can't use a fighter class, it's just that you will die often, so make sure to save often. For this reason I would recommend you start with X3 Reunion. While dog fights in Terran Conflict are almost suicide, in Reunion they are a must; while also being fun. I myself played Reunion first and learned the basics thru that game, and that made Terran Conflict much easier to learn. Terran Conflict is just a much faster paced game.
I highly recommend this game to all space lovers, for I never felt closer to space than I have while playing this game. The mechanics are hard to learn but great once you get the hang of it. The visuals are a sight to see, and the ability to almost do anything you want is great. As I told a friend once, you could be flying to a far off place, while out of no where your trade ship is being attacked, while one of your stations is also being attacked, while your sector is being invaded, while your patrol fleet is being ambushed, all in a split second. It is truly something.
These few points and explanations do not do it justice, only playing it will.

I've put about 4 hours into the game, and have, with the help of a friend in co-op, managed to go spacebound and land on a couple of other planets.
This game is a very chill play experience. On the starting terran world, there are only a few threats to your survival, and those that are there can be avoided with some planning and forethought. This allows you to carefully explore the world, enjoy the soundtrack, and have fun.
About the game's aesthetic. The game is cartoony without being garish. Animations are smooth, colours are bright, and models are, for the most part, well crafted.
Crafting is simple, but limited. I expect this will expand as the game continues through development. Even so, there is more here in this early access game than I expected.
There are still many bugs, most of which I experienced while using vehicles. They seem to have no weight to them (physics are off), and can bounce around and can be a pain to handle. They do get jostled around by wind storms, which is fine, but I did experience some problems mounting items to them.
Resource collection on foot seems solid. Using a vehicle-mounted drill is clunky, especially when partially-collected resource nodes attached to your vehicle cannot be moved or removed. The only way to remove it is to finish filling the node, but very often that will begin a new resource node that cannot be moved or removed. I would like to be able to move partial resource collections, or delete them entirely.
Overall I am very impressed with the fit and finish of this game, and I am excited to see what is to come.

Let's face it, this game has some flaws, balancing issues being the most prominent. Seriously, I was able to just mow over every boss in the game by simply unlocking all the conditionals and setting them all to stun the boss for one second. Except for one conditional, which I set to "Charge Tweak" the boss every ten seconds. However, when trying to play the game with a diverse set of conditionals, I found myself being constantly mowed over. So yeah, there are flaws.
I will admit that there is a lot of room for forgiveness here because the game is completely free to play, no signup or anything. You simply download the game and play. I feel like I would probably still recommend this game to people if it cost money, but only if it didn't cost more than $5.
So what exactly is "The Desolate Hope"? It is a game made by Scott Cawthon, who is best known as the mastermind behind the "Five Nights at Freddy's" franchise. He made this game two years before the first FNaF was released, but it apparently didn't get onto Steam until 2014.
This game is a blend of three different game genres: 2D platformer, top-down dungeon-crawler, and JRPG (kinda). You start in the "real world", then gain access to four different digital worlds to explore. The "real world" and the four digital worlds are the "2D platformer" part of the formula. While you are within these digital worlds, there are terminals scattered about that you can access. When you access them, you are dropped into a digital world within the digital world where you can farm for money and unlock conditionals for boss battles. This is the "top-down dungeon-crawler" part of the formula. After speaking to a respective digital world's Derelict, you can find and confront the boss in what is basically a JRPG-style battle, but without the turn-based element. This is the "JRPG (kinda)" part of the formula.
Since I've only played through it once, I'm a bit unsure what I would have to say about the game in terms of replay value. While I'm not eager to jump right back in and play through it again, there isn't anything preventing me from playing it again.
Also, let me just say that the demonstrational videos on the store page don't do the game's aesthetic justice. Seriously, this is actually a very pretty game. And that soundtrack! Tasty!
The story is suprisingly engaging, regardless of the fact that you are kept in the dark about what is actually happening for pretty much the entire game, right up to the final boss. The ending is definitely interesting to say the least.
So would I recommend it? Yes. I would definitely say this is something you should at least try. No money changing hands, no signup, nothing to make you regret downloading the game if you don't end up liking it.

The bowling's fine, for the most part, and I like that I can add extra bounce or flight (I've only bowled spin, I didn't care for being a quick in DBC14 and that is yet to change) to my deliveries, but the batting is poor. The amount of times I've gotten out because the batsman and I have alternate interpretations of where a cover drive is supposed to be hit (and I have this issue for other shots, but I seem to experience it the worst when playing off the front foot, though occasionally when attempting a back foot shot, the batsman will just not bother) makes for a very frustrating time.
I can understand a game being difficult because it requires skill, DBC14 did that just fine. This has the same level of difficulty, and it adds crummy batting controls on top. Adding grade cricket was a nice touch, and letting me assign skill points like an actual RPG was the right move, but they messed up the gameplay. You know, the bit that makes up 90% of the game.

UPDATE
OK so my initial review although expresses how great I feel this game is, it didn't do justice for how great the game really is. As I continue to play this game today, the developers have continued to bring the game to an even higher level with each new update. I feel that my review should evolve a bit to give the game the proper credit that it deserves.
If I had to pick three tags that describe my gaming preferences they would be RPG - MANAGEMENT - BUILDING
This game encompasses all of these for me; although it is definatley hard to really categorize this game as an RPG in the traditional sense in normal play mode, it does contain the Escape mode which I have spent many hours stabbing away and causing total hell across different prisons that people have made and uploaded to steam.
Although I have been a pretty hardcore gamer for many years, this was really one of the first games that I got so into that I felt there was some sort of learning curve (definatley before I ever got into HOI or KSP etc ) - looking back now I would say the learning curve was somewhat small compared to other games I have played since, but it is there so don't expect to just pick it up and start building prison systems that will really be successful until you have read a little bit of wiki and user advice.
Some games in this genre (building, management) are just a little too easy and streamlined for too many people to play IMO - although this game offers different settings as far as adjusting difficulty levels( temperature, gangs, etc), there really is no EASY MEDIUM HARD setting, because the game is going to be as difficult as you make it for yourself. If you enjoy building/management sims that offer truly unlimited possibiliteis for achieving what you may percieve as perfection and allow you to control the speed and difficulty as you see fit throughout your progression, look no further.
If you are considering buying this game - I don't care what type of games you like, you just should. This game is truly special, truly different, and when I found it I felt that it was something that I had been really yearning to play for a very long time. Thanks to the developers to creating something so special and so different.

This game is outstanding. It does a lot of things right. I said before that Arkham City built on Arkham Asylum and made it bigger, well, Arkham Origins builds on Arkham City and makes it bigger and taller. For a guy who likes to glide with Batman, let me tell you, that is a lot of fun.

Firstly, Batman: Arkham Origins is most definitely one of the weakest games in the series, but that doesn't mean that it's certainly a bad game. It's a solid Arkham game which is rather enjoyable for what it is.
The story is interesting enough to keep you playing, but the gameplay feels too similar to Arkham City.
In my opinion, one of the best things in the Arkham series has been how every installment to the series has had the similar kind of a feeling while being actually very different from eachother at the same time, and that's one thing where Arkham Origins failed.  It was a somewhat bland copy of Arkham City, even though it did have it's own things as well.
Overall Arkham Origins is a good game, but a rather weak entry in the Arkham series.
So despite being one of the worst Arkham games (in my opinion), I do recommend you to give it a try, you might even prefer this one over the other ones.
If you find it during a sale or something, do consider buying it.
Here are some pros and cons;
Pros:
- Mediocre, but still interesting enough story.
- Troy Baker's Joker is really good (even though I do prefer Mark Hamill's Joker myself).
- Good looking graphics.
- Some lesser known Batman villains finally receive a slice of all the attention they deserve.
- Lots of content.
- Interesting multiplayer mode.
Cons:
- Even after all this time, it does have quite a lot of small bugs.
- Often feels like it's lacking something.
- Half of the map is pretty much just a slightly modified version of Arkham City's map.
- Game feels and even looks a bit too much like Arkham City.
- Animations are awful from time to time.
- Pretty much dead multiplayer mode.

The story is well-crafted and meaningful -- from a narrator using a beautiful-sounding fantasy language to deaths of main characters to friendships and changes of heart to morals of the story to be gleamed to twists and turns. The challenges are real -- such as the escape from the Ginso Tree and several of the puzzles. The game mechanics are well-integrated -- the game uses every ability you have acquired up to that point which makes for a challenging and well-integrated game. The typical infuriation of a platformer is alleviated -- since you can oftentimes save wherever you are, provided you have the energy to do so. In short, the game is a masterpiece. Play it.

A worthy successor to X3: Reunion. With more ships (including bombers, which are a powerful addition for anti-capital ship combat). But lets not forget the biggest deal of all. You can play as a Terran!  At long last we have seen our Terran brothers again, and can even play as them!
+Great Story! (You'll need context of the other games to fully understand it though)
+Wide variety of mission types
missions alone include assassinations, defend a station, patrols, escorts, and even convoy hunting,
missions have you supplying or delivering wares to stations, or buying used ships (can be a great way to turn a profit when you repair it yourself).
missions to have you build stations for the universe (thats right, get PAID to build stations. Last type of missions are the "
" missions, which have you transporting passengers, scanning asteroids, returning stolen or abandoned ships, tracking ships, etc.
+Randomly generated missions
+Vast options of ships/equipment to choose from. (Scout ships, interceptors, heavy fighters, bombers, transport freighter normal/heavy/super freigther, "Transport Large" (capital ship sized transport ship), corvettes (like a small frigate), frigates, destroyers and carriers.
+
(when unlocked) can reverse engineer ships (possibly jump beacons if you can get enough!) build ships, and house many ships,
+Living breathing universe. All those ships you see flying somewhere are doing things around the universe. Be it supplying a station somewhere, patrolling the sectors for hostiles. (Dont worry, escorts and the various ships respawn over time ... stations on the other hand ... dont (exception being shipyards and equipment docks)
+Reputation system for factions (how friendly/hostile they are to you, your clearence from shipyards, trading discounts, etc.)
+
. Game can run autonomously in trade/exploration/combat aspects. Just buy the ships, buy the ship software from military bases and equipment docks. And you can have self sufficient fleets that can even automatically do trading across the universe for you (with Trade software MK3).
+Build your own stations. You can contribute to the universe and turn a decent profit when built on the right spots. Especially useful for obtaining some of those harder to obtain wares.
+Piracy, you can steal from freighters, capture capital ships, and smuggle illegal goods accross sectors.
- Starts off a little slow. Because it takes a bit of time to work your way up (more from finances than from reputation; which is slightly hard to raise, easy to destroy).
-A little buggy. two story missions can be rather difficult, and can break if you arent careful (Mission six of Terran Conflict can break, so make a special save before you start it). and Mission seven can be annoying because you have to try to board and steal a capital ship (but dont worry, after a time your allies do it for you). Other than that, its pretty much bug free!
- Autopilot can be clunky sometimes. Such as when navigating around the massive Terran stations, or when flying the  bigger ships.
- Relatively steep learning curve. This is for those who havent played any X games. If you havent, I suggest doing the tutorial (which only teaches you how to fly and communicate. Then reading up on the basics of trading, or of things in general (could learn even helpful basics in combat)

rly gud megaman x love letter
The roguelike element does add to replayability, picking up where I thought the Mega Man X games lacked. I've never been one for speedrunning and "mastering" a level, so the levels rebuilding themselves between plays makes just picking this up and playing it for half an hour exactly what I want, just different enough to be new, but still similar enough to not require much focus. Though it's worth saying that, at these state, the "randomly generated" levels are a bunch of "room/zone" types that get swapped out and plugged in in different orders, with what appear to be different possible enemy encounters in them as well. So, say a level you see has "room A, room B, and pit A". Your next playthrough in that area will likely still have rooms A and B, and pit A, but in a different order. I haven't seen much variation between the same levels and replaying, and while I don't find that to be a problem yet, it would be nice if there's more to come.
The two biggest problems it has, completely subjectively, are art style and the very roguelike element that I think saves it.
The art is very plain. The whole thing looks like an early 2000s Newgrounds flash game, and all of the character designs are very boring. This is going up against Mega Man X, whose early years had some very beautiful sprite work. I know sprite art takes time and I'm not complaining that it's not a pixelated game, god knows there's too many of them out anyway and variance is nice, but the characters themselves don't lend to the style either. Plus I just don't like the protagonist designs - rather than having to pick Nina or Ace, just give us a plain GUN or SWORD selection, and then some very basic character appearance customization with heads, colors, and simple accessories like hair or whatevs. I wanna be a s0rd girl.
And the roguelike weakness, I feel that there is very little sense of progression. I'm not sure what can be done about this without going against the entire point of being a rogueplatformer, but something about it just doesn't make me want to play again after I die. I get that starting over is the point, but it really feels like I've accomplished nothing. At least Rogue Legacy leaves you feeling like you've put a dent in the game, with your ever growing weapon/gear inventory and stuff.
Still, it's worth picking up and worth going back to. In the current state, the co op works fine, and it feels very fluid with an Xbox 360 controller. Probably better than Mega Man Xtreme.

UPDATE
OK so my initial review although expresses how great I feel this game is, it didn't do justice for how great the game really is. As I continue to play this game today, the developers have continued to bring the game to an even higher level with each new update. I feel that my review should evolve a bit to give the game the proper credit that it deserves.
If I had to pick three tags that describe my gaming preferences they would be RPG - MANAGEMENT - BUILDING
This game encompasses all of these for me; although it is definatley hard to really categorize this game as an RPG in the traditional sense in normal play mode, it does contain the Escape mode which I have spent many hours stabbing away and causing total hell across different prisons that people have made and uploaded to steam.
Although I have been a pretty hardcore gamer for many years, this was really one of the first games that I got so into that I felt there was some sort of learning curve (definatley before I ever got into HOI or KSP etc ) - looking back now I would say the learning curve was somewhat small compared to other games I have played since, but it is there so don't expect to just pick it up and start building prison systems that will really be successful until you have read a little bit of wiki and user advice.
Some games in this genre (building, management) are just a little too easy and streamlined for too many people to play IMO - although this game offers different settings as far as adjusting difficulty levels( temperature, gangs, etc), there really is no EASY MEDIUM HARD setting, because the game is going to be as difficult as you make it for yourself. If you enjoy building/management sims that offer truly unlimited possibiliteis for achieving what you may percieve as perfection and allow you to control the speed and difficulty as you see fit throughout your progression, look no further.
If you are considering buying this game - I don't care what type of games you like, you just should. This game is truly special, truly different, and when I found it I felt that it was something that I had been really yearning to play for a very long time. Thanks to the developers to creating something so special and so different.
Build and run your own prison!  A great simulation, resource-management game that doesn't make it easy.  More depth and strategy than I expected it to have.

This is a great game, and however it still will need some work to be a truly awesome game, it will occupy most of your gaming time!
# What are the +'s? #
- You can build your prison however you like, in any shape you like.
- It is really realistic how riots arise and how inmates start joining them.
- You can determine the difficulty yourself, by adding different options. Like adding the gangs and Wheater and temperature options.
- Contraband is very realistic to be found in a real prison.
- Escape mode is a great addition.
# What are the -'s? #
- When in escape mode, you can't trade contraband for money, which really brings the gamemode down.
- You need to have 20+ deaths to even get a warning, which is a lot if you even want a challenge.
# What could be improved? #
- Escape mode lacks the things your prison in sandbox mode does have.
- Make a easy, medium and hard difficulty button, so that if you REALLY want a challenge 5+ deaths in a day can give you a warning.
# Conclusion #
A game to have and, if there are going te be some big changes, a game to look out for!

This game is beauty.
Its graphics are utterly beautiful. Vibrant, bright, colourful. Different areas have different 'overtones' - green, yellow, purple... The foreground, 'main platforming layer', and background occasionally merge. The animations are very fluid. But, really, all these words wholly fail to capture the beauty of Ori. It reminds me of Rayman 2 brought to 2017 (I know, the Definitive Edition of Ori was released in 2016, but hush :P) - but then better.
And the graphics wouldn't be complete without the sound. From Ori's adorable sounds - that fit perfectly with the animations - to the music of the different areas. Sometimes, Ori uses certain tunes and re-uses them in different styles, which is actually - or so I think - how some of the best soundtracks work. Regardless, Ori's music (and sound effects too) is 'emotional' and adds a great deal do the experience. To the beauty.
The most important thing of a game, I suppose, is the gameplay. Ori is a platformer, with a relatively unique twist; the entire world is as it is. No fancy world map with levels on it, no, Ori is one gigantic level. Which deserves a lot of respect; the creation of this world - blocking off all the paths you should only visit later, mostly through the variety of abilities you can unlock - must have been a great puzzle. But the result is amazing. And beautiful - see a trend here? The gameplay is fully interwoven with the story, which I can't really explain but which is a very good point... But, for example, the Mario games have a flinter-thin story that are an excuse for gameplay.
But actually, I think the most important thing of a game is the experience. Which is an integrated whole. The story is... You guessed it, beautiful. I will say one thing of it; each prominent character goes through a similar narrative cycle. Of loss and grief and how to deal with it. That realisation is probably a huge spoiler, but I suppose some people might never have that realisation, and if so, they would be missing something absolutely vital of 'the Ori experience'.
Many say that Ori is a hard game, but, there I disagree. Ori is probably at the perfect difficulty level, not too easy, not too hard, requiring both some platforming skills and some mental skills, to figure out certain puzzles, usually by using your abilities in new ways. Many say that the Ginso Tree is the hardest area of Ori, and many give up here - don't. It's perhaps the single best platformer 'level' I have seen. In graphical beauty, musical beauty, and gameplay - from first traversing various areas the ordinary way, to using a new ability to traverse similar areas with similar challenges in a new way, to an exhilarating escape sequence that is one of the high points of a very high game indeed.
Go forth, and experience Ori now.

UPDATE: After some deliberation I have reversed my recommendation, because: while I probably will not return to the game for a while, it wouldn't stop me from recommending it to others who are looking for this type of game.  The game is solid enough on its own accord to appease those (IMO) who enjoy this type of game.  For those that like rogue-like games with challenges and what not this game has a lot to offer. It isn't replete with bugs that are game breaking and further development is, as of right now, pretty much guaranteed. It's just not what I was looking for, which is why I originally would not recommend.
--Original Review--
I consider myself a big fan of the original Mega Man series, especially X2/X3, and was very hopeful to try out something new after the massive failing that Mighty No. 9 was.  I ended up picking this up on sale, but I still found it hard to justify the price of what I paid for it, because while this panders to the Mega Man fans, it sadly, is not Mega Man.
Pros:
-It does sort of capture some of the Mega Man feel with the platforming and some of the character designs.
-It incorporated newer elements such as daily and weekly trials, as well as speed run options.
-Has a timer for updates on the main screen.
-It tries to add a new type of element (rogue-like) to try and keep the game fresh. (Also, see explanations)
-You can switch between "Mega Girl" and "Zero" at the main screen without meeting some predetermined type of requirement.  It's a free swap.
-There's mini bonus missions you can do in a level, gaining a benefit if you "don't dash," or complete the mini-level with other set requirements fulfilled.
-It has a multiplayer option, though I did not get to test it.
Cons:
-The stylized animations were not to my liking.  They appeared almost childlike at times, overexagerated, and sometimes annoying.
*Update* For clarification, the items in this section are removed from "Cons" in order to better explain my opinions on the matter. This section has been renamed to:*
"My personal opinions because I have an opinion about things and people get butthurt when I don't kiss the golden butt of their digital god, which may or may not be offensive to some so if you get butthurt then just skip this part:"
-It is NOT a Mega Man clone, for those looking to fill that desire. If you want Mega Man, go back and play the older games, that's the only way to get this anymore.
-To the Mega Man purist, the rogue-like element is a killer.  There's no way to run through the levels in a specific, orderly manner.  You take what is given.  I was given an ice level once, and a platform heavy sky level about four times.  These are the only two levels I was given.  Maybe something to do with the early access part.
-To the Mega Man purist, the rogue-like element is a killer.  There's no way to run through the levels in a specific, orderly manner.  You take what is given.  I was given an ice level once, and a platform heavy sky level about four times.  These are the only two levels I was given.  Maybe something to do with the early access part.
Things to further expect:
-This still needs a lot of polishing.  This is excusable since it is an early access game, and this is to be expected.
-Landing on spikes/falling into pits was not an insta-kill like some are used to.  This is a good thing considering that death is weighted much more heavily in this game than a simple "level restart."
-Boss mechanics were very easy to understand, though at times ridiculous.  They ranged from simply jumping over the telegraphed charge to bullet hell.
-Future updates may warrant another attempt at getting involved in this game.  Right now though, I'll continue my runs through X2/X3.
If you're looking for a game to "do things" in, that has platforming/shooting styles similar to the blue bomber, this will probably fit the bill.  If you're looking for something specific to replace the hole in your heart known as the Mega Man franchise, then, well... this may not be for you.  For me, unfortunately, I'll have to keep waiting.

This review is for local 2P Co-op which is the only mode I've played. Bottom line: this game is a total riot.
I bought this game because I love Megaman X, expecting the roguelike mechanics to be negligable. My biggest gripe with roguelikes is that I usually feel as though the randomly generated stages and items do not significantly affect how I play or force me to adapt. (I love Risk of Rain and Torchlight, but itemization has never affected my playstyle).
20XX uses RNG and roguelike mechanics in a meaningful way. For instance, the playthrough where we got a dash shield vs the time we somehow rolled 3 mario hats and jet boots felt way differently, and even guided how we approached levels.
What I liked:
- Excellent visibility. Screen stretches SSB style so if your buddy screws up a segment or is way ahead of you, it's not disruptive to either of you.
- Option to downsize the UI. The UI blocked me and got me killed a few times but once I downsized it to 75% I never had a problem. (I don't think this would be an issue 1P Solo)
- It's fun to choose different boss rewards and strategize item and power build with your partner!
- With four different character combos (as in, which of you is playing which character), there's a lot of game replayability in a way that 1P Solo might not have. Asymmetric co-op is exciting.
So even if you're not a big Megaman X fan or are disillusioned with Mighty No. 9, if you want a badass 2P co-op, this is a real gem with heaps of replayability.

PROS: It has an interesting plot. The predator sections work pretty well.
CONS: Where do I begin?
The combat is buggy and does not work well. It often seems like the game is designed to make you break your combo. Counters don't always work. In fact on the harder difficulty you have less time to counter, but the counter indicators stay up – meaning you can think you can counter when you can't. Or Batman will just refuse to counter. Or your combo will just drop for no good reason. I've run into other glitches as well, where quickfire gadgets will just not work, causing the combo to drop. The camera also tends to be too close to Batman, meaning characters can hit you from off-camera and give you no opportunity to counter or even know they were there. Brutes do unblockable attacks and can't be taken down with special combo moves, and you'll often be fighting them in a narrow space with barely any room to dodge.
The combat locations are also frequently badly designed, as fights occur in closed-in spaces that give you little space to maneuver and plenty of space for the camera to get stuck. In one case I think I was fighting five guys, one with a shield, in a space the size of an elevator.
The abilities tree is also annoying. Many of the most useful special abilities are locked off until later sections of the game and require the completion of entire separate sidequests. For example, disarm and destroy – one of the best ways to deal with shields, guns, and stun batons – cannot be obtained until completing a sidequest that does not appear until the game is three-fourths completed. The grapnel disarm is also locked off until at least halfway through the game.
The 'challenges' are also extremely annoying because they, too, are tiered. And worse they don't 'stack' and several special abilities are easily lost forever because they require grinding out challenges that can ONLY be completed in a few areas that do not respawn. If you want the sonic shock batarang, better get Worst Nightmare Rank 6 completed in the bank during the first time you are there or you'll have to do it during the Deadshot mission. You get two chances. Enjoy. If you want to unlock the Dark Knight skin you will spend a lot of the game grinding out challenges.
The checkpoints are also badly located. If you need to restart a predator room, for example, it won't save when you begin, so you will often have to spend a minute or two to get back to the room and probably go through an unskippable cutscene, which can be annoying when you need to redo a room to try and complete something very specific and easy to mess up (like knock three people down with one propane tank).
I should discuss the boss battles as well. Many people seem to enjoy them but I did not. The Deathstroke battle was really a glorified QTE in terms of how it worked. The Firefly fight was a mixture of QTE, dodging and using the same quickfire gadgets over and over. And the Bane fight was a more annoying and less-good version of the fight from Arkham Asylum. I felt the Mr Freeze fight in Arkham City was by far the best Arkham boss battle and nothing here is close.
I find this game immensely frustrating. I've played the other Arkham games – Asylum, City and Knight – and I just cannot like this game. The plot is interesting. But the actual gameplay is so irritating I find myself screaming in rage. Play the other games. Skip this one.

The soundtrack is intense and heavy, taking inspiration from Metal and Neurofunk aspects and a handful of work from the iconic NOISIA.
Overall, a great time was had, and I find myself coming back to polish a level and hunt some achievements long after completion.

UPDATE
OK so my initial review although expresses how great I feel this game is, it didn't do justice for how great the game really is. As I continue to play this game today, the developers have continued to bring the game to an even higher level with each new update. I feel that my review should evolve a bit to give the game the proper credit that it deserves.
If I had to pick three tags that describe my gaming preferences they would be RPG - MANAGEMENT - BUILDING
This game encompasses all of these for me; although it is definatley hard to really categorize this game as an RPG in the traditional sense in normal play mode, it does contain the Escape mode which I have spent many hours stabbing away and causing total hell across different prisons that people have made and uploaded to steam.
Although I have been a pretty hardcore gamer for many years, this was really one of the first games that I got so into that I felt there was some sort of learning curve (definatley before I ever got into HOI or KSP etc ) - looking back now I would say the learning curve was somewhat small compared to other games I have played since, but it is there so don't expect to just pick it up and start building prison systems that will really be successful until you have read a little bit of wiki and user advice.
Some games in this genre (building, management) are just a little too easy and streamlined for too many people to play IMO - although this game offers different settings as far as adjusting difficulty levels( temperature, gangs, etc), there really is no EASY MEDIUM HARD setting, because the game is going to be as difficult as you make it for yourself. If you enjoy building/management sims that offer truly unlimited possibiliteis for achieving what you may percieve as perfection and allow you to control the speed and difficulty as you see fit throughout your progression, look no further.
If you are considering buying this game - I don't care what type of games you like, you just should. This game is truly special, truly different, and when I found it I felt that it was something that I had been really yearning to play for a very long time. Thanks to the developers to creating something so special and so different.

# Conclusion #

The concept is good but the execution is atrocious.
The tutorial holds your hand with a deathgrip, instructing you what to click on and where, and doesn't even allow you to click away the tutorial pop ups -- those just float there, forever, the entire rest of the game interface disabled, until they are obeyed.  The game manages to maintain the same feel well into gameplay, which I found startling and impressive.  The two primary types of gameplay seem to be solving music puzzles (described below), and find-the-object search-and-click.  Whenever you've found enough objects to unlock a puzzle, the interface will "helpfully" switch screens for you, and you are going to be solving that puzzle whether you want to or not.  There are no settings in the options menu to control this behavior.
I like casual games, but this game manages to make casual painful.  Interrupting the player's train of thought and forcing them to shift from one style of gameplay to another is a recipe for tension, not relaxation, and it has no place in a game this slow-paced.
Railroading and pacing/transition issues aside... The puzzles remind me of a cross between simplified base 4 sudoku and tetrad-based fill-in-the-shape puzzles.  You get tetrads built out of different colored pieces, each piece having a portion of the melody on it, and being color-coded to match a particular instrument.  You want there to be one block of each color in each column, and you want the parts of the melody to go in the correct order, and you need to arrange the tetrads to do that while fitting in the given shape.  It ends up being very simple, but it COULD be fulfilling and interesting -- if the game would let go of my damn hand and let me do anything on my own.
All in all, I would primarily recommend this game to ten year olds, people who have never played with either puzzles or games before, and recovering stroke victims.  I suspect that most other gamers will find the structure to be chafing, rather than a helpful source of direction.

Astonishing. A work of art, both visually and story-wise. This game features some of the best visual work I've ever seen, with a real '90s hyperfuture feel. Gorgeous. I was thrown at first by the simplistic gameplay. You derp around on rails to access the main platformer levels and eventually do some goofy top-down goofing. I eventually figured out the roles of these parts of the game: Basically you need to earn FAT STACK$ and buy hella upgrades to have any chance of winning the game, and you gotta do it fast-like before the landlord flips the breaker and things go dead. Yeah.
But you're here to fight a virus, and that's the main draw of the game. The battles are intense, complicated, and unforgiving; they're the only serious or difficult parts of the gameplay. You need to derp around the research station to access all the simulated worlds and to level your characters for battle. You need to explore each simulation carefully to find upgrades for your fine robo-dudesmen to use in battle, and to actually locate and challenge the manifestations of the Virus to initiate battle. You gotta enter the source-code world to get sweet conditional buffs for your battles. You gotta GIT GUD to beat the living hell out of robotic cyber-nightmares. IN BATTLES.
Found a little glowing fireball? Activate it. Pull up your big boy pants.
...
And yes, you have to fight THAT. No, don't slam the escape key. Not that you can beat it first time. Haha, no.
You gotta GIT GUD.
It's time to micromanage four different characters with different move sets JRPG style, but *in real time*, trying to out-murder a terrifying robo-devil of some description while he is continuously jacking up yo boys with MIND LIGHTNING. Like a good frantic multitask in the morning? The final moves of each of your characters start little minigames *to be played at the same time* on top of the main battle in order to get some powerups. All this, and the virus is no sissy either. The difficulty ramps steeply, and the game is unforgiving if you are too slow or waste a move.
Fortunately, you get a practice arena in which to learn the ropes and PLENTY of fights in which to hone your skills. And failing a fight only sets you back in time- no resources are permanently used up, and you can try again. It's a good implimentation of super-crazy death challenges.
It's astoundingly addictive. Loads of fun.
P.S. I note how most other reviews have either fewer than 3 or more than 10 hours of play. I reckon a first-time playthrough would take ~9 hours, so there's how you tell if somebody actually finished the thing. I definitely took a full hour to get familiar with the game, but then I was hooked good and firmly.
The ending is delightfully bittersweet. I hope you enjoy the heartfeels.
P.P.S. Malentz is my favorite character. His outlook on life is eerily similar to my approach to College. I like how he's the biggest, spikiest, spidery-est robot, but collects toys and spends his time tinkering in his Farmville-style hermitage. He's also got the best moves, though there's competition from that big loveable teddy bear Alphon.

I've got a lot of hours into this game.  I keep coming back to it for the same reasons that others do.  It's an incredibly complex, wide open sandbox.  Each of the dozens of sectors has its own unique look and accompanying sound track.  A constantly changing background world with a dynamic economy.
Some people have commented on the very steep learning curve.  It can seem overwhelming when you look at all of the stuff that you can do.  The good news is that you don't have to try to do it all at once.  In fact, I would strongly advise against it.  Instead, pick one of the starting characters and focus on just one facet of the game at a time.
I think the Trader start in Albion is the easiest because you're not dumped into a series of firefights right away.  It'll give you plenty of time to slowly build up some skills just flying around getting to know the various ship classes.
Once you've the hang of it and you've built up a steady stream of income, you can go ahead, buy a relatively powerful corvette and go pirate hunting.  Get your Combat reputation up and you can start buying carriers and other capital ships and start challenging the pirates and the Khaak in a big way.
If, OTOH, you want to dive right in and start shooting stuff I would suggest the Fight start in the Terran sector.  You'll get plenty of opportunity to fine tune your combat skills fast.
