The worst in the entire franchise. So frustrating. Controls sticky or unresponsive in certain fights. The menu system is janky. The idea that he meets so many of his villains for the first time in one night is ridiculous. Events take place that contradict information provided by the earlier entries in the series (not major, but lore continuity matters to me). Larger play area, yet it feels emptier than Arkham City. The map from Arkham City remains for the most part. The multiplayer is dead, but that's to be expected. They reuse a lot of assets from earlier games, some of which don't make any sense the way they are used. Example: There is a photo frame with a picture of Aaron Cash and his family from an Cash's desk in one of or both of the earlier games. In the photo, he has his hook hand, meaning Killer Croc had already bitten it off while incarcerated in Arkham Asylum. This photo frame is used repeatedly in Arkhm Origins, basically anytime there is a desk and a photo frame is needed, it's Cash. Doesn't matter where, police station, bank, radio tower, all Cash. Doesn't matter that Origins takes place before Cash or Croc are at Arkham, thus Cash still has his hand. Honestly, at times it feels like this game is just a cash grab riding on the coattails of Rocksteady's success.

As annoying as it can be, I still had fun. Buy it on sale with the DLC bundled, don't waste your  money buying each piece individually.

I have only a few hours on the PC version, but I have beaten the 360 version 3 times. So far, the silky smooth 60 fps and high resolution are enhancing the experience even further.
An excellent, genuinely underrated game. While I don't like this incarnation of Dante as much due to his lack of clever dialogue (opting for more of an in-your-face, "♥♥♥♥ you" type speech than 1-4's more snide and humorous banter) I think pretty much every aspect is equal to or better than the main series.
The art style is an absolute pleasure to look at, with carefully chosen colors and architecture. Limbo is a very unique setting and feels very oppressive, which is what they were going for.
The music is very high on my list of best ost's, though it's definitely not for everyone. It is a mixture of Combichrist's aggrotech/death metal and Noisia's bass-heavy electronic music (Dunno exactly what genre, but it ranges from Drum 'n' Bass to Dubstep). A testament to the ost's quality (and to the quality of the musicians composing it) is that I actually am not a fan of the genres in general. All in all, it feels very appropriate to the gameplay and pumps you up as you lay down some sick combos.
Which brings me to the gameplay. Some criticize it for being less "free" than the originals, and I see where they're coming from. DMC4 in particular has quite a lot of stylish freedom in what you can do, and you can perform a buttload of crazy combos with cancelling and tech and all that. However, the grappling system and the ease of switching weapons in the heat of battle make it a very smooth and skill-intensive experience. The multiple melee weapons allow you to tailor your approach to battle on the fly, using a scythe or shurikens to take out a mob of easy enemies, an axe or knuckles to deal some heavy damage to high profile targets, or your trusty sword which is good in any situation. But the thing that makes combat so ♥♥♥♥ing fun is the aformentioned grappling hook. Depending on whether you have angel or devil weapons equipped (by holding the left and right trigger, respectively) you can either pull yourself toward the enemy or pull him to you. This opens up all sorts of "CUHRAYZEE" juggling shenanigans.
And the bosses. Oh, the bosses! While they are somewhat easy, they are extremely fun encounters with unique mechanics. I don't want to spoil anything, but they're some of the highlights of the game.
And so, I wholeheartedly reccomend this game. If you like hack 'n' slash games, this is one you should definitely try out!

This Review focuses on DMC: Devil May Cry as in
, rather than one attached to the previous Devil May Cry series created by Capcom.
Personally, I like the old series better, however I had to try my best to stay impartial when giving this game a review.
I personally enjoyed the games updated graphics and texture features. The textures on the enemies and spawns fit the demonic theme of the enemies perfectly. The detail in the environment added to the overall emersion of the game and the missions, making the plot easier to get dragged into. My only argument about the graphics and textures is that in some points,
, the backgrounds can be somewhat distracting and disorienting to the fight at hand.
The mechanics fit the game quite nicely, however on a PC the controls were a little bit whacky. It is hard to make these types of controls for the PC, and I think the game creators did a good job of trying to make it so that you could access all of the skills and combinations for all of the weapons you acquire with this game. It can be hard to remember all the massive amounts of attack combos, but they make it so that the game doesn't require every single combo in order to succeed. Some of the combos are just clicking patterns with your mouse, but others require you to knock an enemy into the air.However, if you’re not good with aerial combos, the game creators made combos and chains on the ground that are just as strong. I know that I survived the game without even realizing that I was using certain combos that I’d unlocked. However, if you’re picky about combos and chain attacks, the game gives you plenty, if not almost too many, combos to practice and learn from, and the game doesn’t make you practice them in the middle of the story, and you are able to revisit them in training mode. Lastly, if you’re big on combos and chains, you can earn additional points toward your missions overall rating. (D-SSS), through your chains and combos.
The addition of "style points" and rankings based on impressive chains and combos makes it a goal to hit combos, and not a necessity. I personally enjoy all the different chains and combos that they made possible with the game, even if they are tricky to remember. It gives the game a bit more flavor. The best part of this, in my opinion, is that the combos are optional, meaning that the game doesn’t make you learn and master every combo on a dummy a million times, to be able to continue with your game. You can do that on your own time.
The unlocking of these skills and combos with rank-up points is also another thing I think that adds to the games flavor. Being able to unlock combos that you think you'll use, and the option to chose not to unlock ones that you don't think you'll use adds the feeling of customization to the game. Even though you'll probably need to unlock everything by the time you finish the game, there are several combos and skills that I didn't know I had prior to visiting the training area. The training area allows you to practice different combos and chains, and I like that as well about the game. It came in handy for me to figure out which set of skills works best with my fighting style, and which ones to avoid.
The music choice was a bit edgy for my liking, however the old DMC games contained heavy music similar in style to that used in this game, so I can at least say that element is consistent with the previous series.
The character development for the main characters is solid, and you get to know the main characters the best-as in any game. However, the development of the supporting characters wasn’t as strong.
The development of nemesis characters and boss characters is solid, in that you get to know why you’re trying to kill them, why they are against you, and how you get to the point of facing them. I think this is very important in a game and it’s character development, because why spend the time fighting a boss if it doesn’t have a purpose?
In some games hordes all look the same, but some enemies are stronger than others with different skill sets and stats, and it’s important to make stronger Horde enemies stand out. DMC does a very good job with this. The horde enemies have different looks based on their attacks, and the stronger a Horde enemy is, the bigger and nastier the creators made it look. This made it easy for me to tell who to focus on first, and who to shred through at the end. The last aspect of the horde that I think that DMC did a good job of showing, is that each part of the horde is important. If you forget to kill something in the air, it will continue to hurt you and make itself noticeable to you until you get around to it. Nothing really goes unnoticed in the horde, and I appreciate that every enemy has a purpose.
!Spoiler Alert!
In general, I give this game a positive rating, and on a scale of 1-5 I'd rate it a 4 as an individual game, but in comparison to the old DMC series, it would be a -1 (again, that's my bias talking).
The mechanics fit the game, but can be tricky to master, and some mechanics must be mastered in order to complete the game. The game gives you some degree of customization with skills and perks, but since the main characters are set, the lack of player customization is appropriate. There are DLC packs and unlocking features that allow you to change the appearance of Dante and Vergil, however they don’t add much to the game, nor take away from it. The plot development is solid, but sweet and short, and I wouldn’t say this game has much replay value. There are a variety of difficulties, making it so that you could focus on the mechanics and battles, or the story. But in all game modes, if you can handle it, the story development is worth playing through. The main character development is solid, but the supporting character development is a bit

This is a genius idea made into an exceptionally enjoyable game. Tetris-like blocks contain bits of a musical score and are colored according to what instrument you'll hear when clicked upon. Fit them all together in the correct way to play famous songs. Out of all of them, there were only two I didn't know by heart. But even if you don't recognize a single one, a bar on the bottom of the screen will play the whole tune for you, as many times as you like. The catch is, you'll only hear each score from ONE instrument. That instrument normally plays the main tune so it's usually not too difficult to figure out what order those blocks go in. But then you have to place all the other instruments and make sure the blocks fit together correctly. For those who love both puzzles and music, Musaic Box is a real gem. My only gripe is that the game isn't long enough. I could have happily played for many more hours.

An inventive and unique little puzzle game.
In this game you find pieces of paper, in the style you would in a hidden object game, and you use those pieces to unlock new music, therefore new levels, for you to play.
The levels consist of famous songs, you’re given a preview to listen to and must reconstruct the music with the blocks you are given.
It was fun having a puzzle game that relied mostly on sound. I say mostly because not only did you have to sus out which notes go where from listening to the preview, but you have to think logically about how to make the Tetris style blocks fit into the outline you are given and them still be in the right order.
The music is fun, it takes classic and well known songs and adds instruments into the background. Some sound really odd, seeing as you end up with something like Mozart with drums and a little tambourine going off in the background, but it’s still fun and inventive.
The game is a little short, but it’s unique and I like the more unique kind of puzzle games.
If you enjoy music (especially classical) or puzzle games in general, I think this one is a good way to kill a few hours. It took me 8 hours to complete it entirely, but admittedly I did get stuck a few times and wondered away from my PC a few times. A normal human being probably wouldn’t take as long.
All in all, I like it. It’s not the best puzzle game I have ever played, but it’s not the worst either. Not by a long shot.
TL;DR : A fun puzzle game based around music. Mostly classical stuff, with a modern twist of instruments added into the back for depth. It’s a little short, but worth a try in my opinion.

The game itself is really good. Once you actually get to do something.
Unfortunately it also involves a lot of backtracking. During which you basically select your destination, hit "autopilot", hit "time-compression" and then still have to idly wait several minutes to get anywhere. After which you get to do something for 1 or 2 minutes until you backtrack to where you started.
Which is actually the one single reason why I can't really recommend the game.
Seriously: I wouldn't even mind if they had built in an animation, showing the pilot leaning back, picking up a game of Sudoku and asking you if you want to actually play something to pass the time while you wait for your ship to reach the next sector. Or randomly show the pilot spilling coffee over the controls after which you have to rewire the control board before your oxygen runs out. Unfortunately they implemented neither of those options and just made a game with built-in coffee and bath-room breaks.
However! If this is actually a non-issue for you. If you enjoy open world exploration games in space, you love figuring out complex game-mechanics, you don't mind spending app. 50-70% of your game-time (depending on how you play the game) in transit, can forgive a game some hickups here and there, don't mind if you have to repeatedly do similar actions over and over again to earn cash and you got tons of spare time to sink into X3, then by all means! Get this game! You can spend weeks - months even - of time playing! Slowly building your empire! If that's what you are looking for then just hit the "add to cart" button NOW! This game is for you!
Otherwise: if you don't have much time to play. If you don't really like it when a "new" mission is giving you this strange deja vu feeling that you've done all this before. If you prefer a strong story and a more linear way of telling it. If you want the game to just cut straight to the chase instead of leaving you hanging in there. Then just skip X3 and look elsewhere. Because this game will feel unrewarding if all you can spare is an hour or two every once in a while.
Thus I think: X3 is a good game with a great and loyal fan-base.
But it just isn't equal loads of fun for everybody.

TL;DR;
-Slow game pace (Even for a space game I consider the pace too slow)
-instanced space pockets = Vast universe now apparently (Wth are people smoking)
-Game mechanics don't make sense (Repairing costs more than buying a new ship)
-Misions are too random and unbalanced meaning you wont be able to do most of them.
-Cannot save game on the fly, you must dock which is a tedious task (even with autopilot).
-Buggy autopilot, basic controls, camara and UI makes this game less appealing.
I heard someone say on a forum something like "The game is long, not slow". That of course is wrong. Skyrim is long. This game IS SLOW.
The game like many other space games fail on one simple thing; Travel time. Due to this, you spend about 90% of your time traveling from destination X to Y to Z. And in this game it does little to take away that factor. You may as well be watching a screen saver.
You cannot save the game until you are docked. Which only reduces yet again the pace of the game. If you dont save your game, you littlerly have to start again if/when you die. This means, yes, more traveling and doing the same♥♥♥♥♥♥you just did an hour ago. (Oh and docking aint fun in this game, there is no "click and dock" you have to either wait for the slow♥♥♥♥♥♥autopilot or manually dock yourself)
The game is not vast despite what you might hear. You go from sector to sector via warp gates. It's just a load of instances linked together. Oh and you cannot interact with planets in any way. They are just background art.
The controls, camera and UI are very basic. Giving commands to your other ships is executed poorly. You can give limited quick commands when targeting other ships (Or rather I should say command) which is attack. Thats it. The autopilot is also buggy, a lot of the time it will just throw you about makiing you puke from motion sickness.
Some other things that don't make much sense: its cheaper to buy a new ship than to repair the one you have (And yes ships cost A LOT). Misions are completely randomized meaning that you wont be able to do like 90% of them near the start of your game. They are also unremarkable from what I've seen; "Do this and get credits" everytime.
Glad I tried this game on free weakend. I won't be buying it and will not recomend it to anyone, one of the most boring and unbalanced space games I have played to date.

After playing some more, I've decided that this game simply isn't for me. Moving around is slow (even when the acceleration SETA active), and navigation is pretty complicated. Worst of all -- the game only saves when you dock at a station, so after I spent 20 minutes chasing a pirate through four systems, his buddies killed me and I had to start all the way back at the first system.
Maybe I've become spoiled by modern autosave features, or maybe I just prefer a more arcadey style. It's possible that I'll come back and give this one another try, but for now I'm going back to GoF.

20XX is an excellent homage to the Mega Man X series. The controls are tight, the sounds are rewarding, the items make sense, and the level generation seems to be working decently. There are many particular configurations of levels that repeat, so there is much familiarity in each level, but the layouts are different enough to keep things from getting too stale. However, the levels each retain fairly distinct personalities, so you begin to get a sense of how each level will play as you get more experience in the game. As the difficulty increases, the platforming becomes much tighter, and hazards become more challenging, but the competent and responsive controls keep things from being unnecessarily frustrating. The movement is insanely rewarding and  enjoyable, especially with movement boosting items and augmentations.
The bosses are well done, and all fairly different. There is some cheesy damage that doesn't seem fair, especially as the difficulty increases, but it leads to a sort of good kind of frustration, like the pain and pleasure from wiggling a loose tooth.
This is one of my favorite games right now, and I would gladly pay for DLC with new levels and new bosses. However, it could be very easy for new levels to feel bland in a game like this, and just as easy for new levels to feel like remixes with no new personality if they're just new tilesets with the same old hazards. 20XX has a very large resource of inspiration to draw from for level themes. A couple I can think of now are water themes (ala Bubble Man), or desert themes with shifting sands (like Super Mario Bros. 2) that players can sink into.
One appeal of Mega Man was having levels that had various mixes of standard hazards, and very particular types of enemies in particular spots on the map. If 20XX lacks anything compared to Mega Man X, it's pacing. The game feels like a frenetic & frantic time trial with pseudorandom enemy generation, and so loses some of the stop-and-go pacing from Mega Man games, such as minibosses, special enemies, and even vehicles & manned armors.
This is an excellent game in its current form, and if it seems like I want more, it's only because there is so much that this engine could provide. People grow up with particular game serieses, and for me, Mega Man/Mega Man X was pretty high up there. I don't really care for the leaderboard features, and I don't care for the lore, either. What I would prefer is to have many different types of hazards, puzzles, level themes with distinct play styles, and a good variety of bosses.
If the developers can find some way to make the creation of bosses, levels, hazards, etc. available publicly, I think this engine could serve as the standard for the Mega Man/Mega Man X genre.

May be my expectations were too high, but after suffering this game for 10 hours, I just cannot recommend it.
- The graphics is gorgeous, but it looks like artists did not communicate with game designers at all. The art rarely conveys a message of what to expect, gets in the way by hiding your character and generally is wayyy too rich for a metroidvania
- Music is fine, but sound effects are poorely integrated into a gameplay
- Level design - this one's easy, cause there's NONE. Game feels a lot like a mobile game with separated levels. You finish one level, save a checkpoint and go on with the next one. There's no reason for you to learn the specifics of a level in any way.
- Story is meh, Lore is non-existent. This was quite a surprise not to find any lore elements in a game. I mean the forest is gorgeous from art perspectice, but it feels so shallow without any lore.
- Controls are just plain bad. Character feels laggy, it's  hard to be precise when jumping on narrow platforms, especially when combined with double jumps and wall jumps. And then there's myriad times when you perform unwanted actions, like instant double jumping from the walls, dashing down while floating and so on
- Enemies are a mockery of a game design. There's probably like 5 different enemies in a WHOLE game with slightly different variations. Meaning ice version will shoot icycles, and fire version would should red blobs. Wow, much work on that.
- The game is super easy with totally unexpected few hard spikes. Maybe it's because I only played it in hard mode, but it does feel  a lot unbalanced in this way
- Overall, the game has no depth whatsoever. It's a casual platformer, which will infuriate you during hard spikes and will hold no replay value. There are masterpieces right now in metroidvania genre, go get them, this is just bland.

Some of the positives are the freedom it gives you, even if it is a bit much for a beginner. The variety is also a nice touch, many different ships from different civilizations. Being able to just trade, just bounty hunt, or be an imperialist are all right there. Much like a single-player EvE but without the overly aggresive die hards playing it.
Would I recommend this to anyone I know or in general most people? No, but for some it would be something they love. That's what it seems like though, you either love or hate the game. I started to enjoy the game after the long initial grind but eventually lost interest because it didn't hold my attention like most games in my library. This is my single favorite game in my game library.
I got this game recommended to me by one of my friends and back then I wasn't a fan of simulator games and unfamiliar with space games.

I started this game not knowing what to do, even with some newbie help from my friend.
After that, the manual was (barring a few errors) pretty helpful, but even then doesn't apply to even a quarter of the game.
the game has a steep (massive) learning curve, combined with the vast amount of time you have to spend in game to actually become a sizeable entity makes this the most rewarding game I have ever played.
I haven't bothered much with it's sequel (X-Rebirth) or it's brothers of the same era (X3-Reunion & X3-Albion prelude), but I can tell you this game is worth it, though I can't possibly tell you which is better.

The game isn't without flaws though, for starters the auto pilot or auto 'pilok' as it is often referred to, because it is notorious for crashing your ship into rocks, other ships or sector gates.
While for me this is extremely rare, it does happen.
Also, this game has a GOD.
GOD is actually part of the game engine and calculates which factories do not produce (enough) profit and deletes these, potentially risking important factories of rare weapons to disappear.
While most (if not all) factories can be built yourself, some factories need to be unlocked by getting further into the game, but this problem is certainly not insurmountable.

Right now I don't have any more negative things to comment on this game, the things mentioned above being my biggest ''issues'' with this game.
I say "issues", because they can be easily overcome with some effort on your own part.

I hope you enjoy this game as much as I still do.

It's obvious that everyone's first thoughts about this game generally compare it to FNaF, and that's understandable. As a big FNaF fan (now Scott Cawthon fan) I did the same thing, and I still do occassionally as I'm going through. However, I think it's important to note that this is not FNaF and FNaF has nothing to do with it.
The Desolate Hope is an amazing game, and even though it probably will never be as popular as FNaF, I hope that someday Scott can turn out another game similar to this one (assuming that developing games is something he wants to do for a long time). The visuals are amazing, I've actually just set one of the scenes from the game as my wallpaper. The characters are loveable as hell, each having unique and interesting traits. Gameplay is, foor the most part, very fun. Music is well done, fitting to the atmosphere and easily getting into my head for hours (in a good way!). I'm a sucker for this old but beautiful graphic style, and sci-fi settings, so this game is like a little slice of gaming heaven for me. (Also I would die to have a game visually and atmospherically similar to this one, but have it be a hidden object/puzzle game rather than an RPG~)
My only complaints with this would have to be some aspects of gameplay. The nights drag on, and are pretty much just a lot of holding down the left arrow key, especially after you've gotten the wrench and have no incentive to care about how efficient you are in your nightly collecting. Another thing I took issue with was the real-time combat with viruses. I often find myself flustered and frustrated, which makes strategizing difficult. Lastly, if you want more upgrades, there's a good chance you'll be grinding in those little terminal worlds for money for quite a while, which I find really annoying.
tl;dr : this game is freaking awesome and beautiful, but the gameplay can be frustrating.

Before I turned to Saints Row 2 for my fix of devilishly criminal fun, I played APB.  And boy, was it nice.  You had the option to be either the Authorities or the Criminals, and that right there is fun in and of itself.  It gives you two character slots to start with and right there, I already knew I wanted one character for the Cops and another for the Crims.
The game plays out fairly laid back; you go around doing your own thing until you put yourself onto a list for receiving missions.  Each mission is divided into several parts, and participants will be from both sides of the law, so the Criminals are going to try and complete objective A while the police try to stop them from completing it, and vice versa.  Each mission is also heavily team-oriented so you'll always have someone watching your back as you complete certain tasks, or the other way around.  You score in-game money and you can buy new weapons and ammo for use for a few days at a time, so it gives you a reason to keep earning money in-game.  In general, this game's a fairly sandbox Cops-N-Robbers kinda game, and that's fun.  You can also customize your character to an impressive degree, so you'll have a lot of options to choose from, which, also gets you to use up your money, as well as buying and customizing your own vehicles.
My only issue with this game is the sole fact that it is very much so "Pay-To-Win" after a certain point.  Sure, you could save up for this neat gun that you'll only be able to use for, let's say, a week. Or, you could drop some real money and buy yourself a rocket launcher that you can keep forever. thereby breaking any sort of balance between players.  I mean, how do you defend against something like that?
All in all, the game is fun and if you don't mind the occaisional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a pay-to-win weapon, chances are, you're going to have a great time. 8/10,

Hitman is a game that makes you feel like a professional Hitman.
There are wonderful options for completing levels in creative ways, and there is something very satisfying to thinking up the perfect strategy, playing it and everything working out perfectly.
Of course, there's also the tense moments where you aren't sure whether something will work, or you make a mistake. Those only add to the experience.
The only drawback of this game is that, while the levels are great and lovingly crafted, there are only few of them. This, however, also contributes to the experience: The levels are extremely replayable, and you are encouraged to play them again and again in different ways. Then, finally, when you know a level inside and out, you can take out one of the elusive targets, where you only have one try to take them out. Having no plan going in, making it up on the go with the experience you have on that level, is incredible.
Take note though: You have to be ready to replay levels, and to do things over and over again. on't expect something new at every corner, rather just expect to do things again and again in new ways.
This game is a lot of fun, and I really recommend it. Unless you are a fundamentally impatient person, then this is probably not the game for you.

So, this is basically a point-and-click adventure title, where you take control over this cop girl from Chicago, and you have to find this serial-killer who kills women and remove their guts. I think it's fair to leave it like this when it comes to the description of the plot, in order to avoid spoilers.
Anyway, the graphics aren't bad, I just think they could highlight certain items that you need to find sometimes, because everything seems to be blended at the background. The sound effects and music are simple, there's nothing really special about them. The voices of the characters are awful and cheesy; I assume that it won't take long for anyone to notice that. Since we're at it, you'd better keep the kids away from you while you're playing it, because the protagonist sure loves to curse everything for no apparent reason. Then again, who would actually let their children play a game with that sort of dark premise? Oh, ok, they can actually do even more horrible things while playing GTA 5. Moving on...
The gameplay is rather fluid and intuitive. It's easy to access the inventory, to combine items when needed, and you can also browse for previous chat logs, in case you don't remember anything you heard about before. You can also get to move your character quicker by tapping the mouse button two times. Another thing that I really liked about this game, is that there aren't really many places to visit, and if you don't have anything to do at a certain location, it'll also automatically prevent you to return there. Besides the traditional elements, there're also some puzzles to solve, but some are really tedious, so I didn't feel any guilt by reading how to solve a couple of them in a walk-through.
Overall, I don't think that this is one of the most memorable adventure games ever, but it's not a bad choice also. The only thing that I'd advise you, is to stay away from the sequel (you might thank me for that later).

Time to review one of my favorite games here.  I'd actually tried to write this up before, awhile back, but Steam went "HERP DERP DURRRRR" and wouldnt post it.  It does that, sometimes.
Anyway.... 20XX.   The most basic way I always describe this game to people is: "This is the game that Mighty No. 9 wishes it could be".  Frankly, some of the actual Megaman series wishes it could be this one, too.
So what exactly is 20XX?  Overall, it's a platformer that's extremely similar to the old Megaman X series (on the SNES), with alot of roguelike elements, and even more general brutality than the old games were known for.
Starting things off, you choose from one of two characters:  Nina, who uses ranged attacks, and Ace, who uses a sword (they sound a bit familiar?).  When you begin a run, the game's first stage is chosen at random... you dont know which of the game's 8 bosses you'll be going after.  The old idea of being able to always choose between the full 8 is gone, to prevent players from always choosing an "optimal" path... you cant do that now.  When a level ends, you are given a choice of 3 randomly selected bosses to go after.  Since, as you'd expect, each boss is weak against a specific power, this gives the choice of order some weight.  There's more to it than just that though... but we'll get to that in a bit.
The first thing you're likely to notice (other than the excellent graphics) are the controls.  They are, frankly, perfect.  This game just outright FEELS like that old series did.  You have the same moves, too... running, the sliding dash, basic jumps (right down to the same height), and clinging to, leaping off of, and generally scaling walls. And of course, your weapons... you can fire normal shots, or you can use charged attacks.  Also like in the old X series, there are various suit enhancements; these can give you additional special abilities, such as the ability to double-charge your weapon, or the ability to temporarily fly in any direction for about a second.
There are also boss powers to use, of course.  You have quite the array of attacks to choose from, and they all have their unique uses.  You've got things like the boomerang blade, which can be thrown in 8 directions, the shockwave, which can smash enemies and cancel bullets in an area around you, or something like the power I call the Death Pixel... you'll see why I call it that if you try it out (it can be charged, give that a try).  Each power is both useful and satisfying.  But not just that, each has an additional special function.  For example, remember those nasty vanishing and reappearing platforms?  Yeah, they're here too.  If you're having trouble with them, and if you have Eternal Star's power, you can smack them with that to lock them into place.  Something like the Death Pixel can smash up vending machines, giving you some free money.  Each of the 8 powers can do something special in addition to it's main function.
Now, this being part roguelike, the different levels you go through are randomly generated, being made of tons of possible "chunks".  These are all very well made and they work well together... but the difficulty is very, very high here.  A gazillion traps and nasty foes await you in the horrible hellholes that the bosses call home.  Fortunately, again, this is part roguelike, which means you have a bewildering array of powerups that can help you.  All sorts of ideas, both basic and very unique/creative, can be found as items in this game.  You'll find them in chests, in stores, or as rewards for defeating a boss.  Some of them get pretty quirky, and the more powerful ones almost always have a downside:  Something that gives your basic attack a huge boost might also lower the damage of boss powers, for instance.  Some of them get pretty complicated.  As with many games like this, knowing when NOT to take an item is just as important as anything else.  There are even special weapons for both characters that entirely replace your basic attacks.
Between runs, you'll be able to spend Soul Chips (granted from special enemies with massively-buffed HP) to unlock new items, or buy a couple to take with you into your run.   The game has a nice sense of progression, as there are LOTS of items here.  So many.  There are also a variety of modes and difficulties to choose from, including dailies.  You have a ton of stuff to do here.
And did I mention the enemies?  There's lots of them, of course, and they can get pretty devious.  Learning their patterns, and also knowing when/how to use boss powers to your advantage, is very important.  It's very easy to die in this game.  The bosses in particular are extra difficult, and WHEN you fight a boss determines how hard it is.  Death Lotus might seem like an easy win if he's the first boss... but if he's number 8, he'll drown you in flowers and horrible exploding things... good luck with that.
Overall, while the difficulty means this isnt for everyone (there IS a "casual" mode though), the sheer fun of it, and the incredible amount of polish, make this the "Megaman" game I'd always wanted, one with endless replay value and stuff to do (and powers that are actually useful).  Even in it's EA state, I'd absolutely recommend this to anyone.

X3: Terran Conflict put one, very important thing into perspective for me: space is astronomically huge. (Pun so very much intended.) It also taught me something very important: it takes way too damned long to fly anywhere in space. Let’s do this.
I – Story [5/10]
X3: Terran Conflict is an open world, simulation game from Egosoft. There are multiple stories for the player to choose from, but I will be dealing specifically with the first one, “Terran Defender”.
The player assumes the role of a Terran pilot who is out on a routine patrol in the solar system when, suddenly, they are summoned to aid in a battle at Neptune. Xenon pilots, using special beacons, were able to jump deep into the system; bypassing the usage of a jumpgate. During the ensuing chaos, a drone steals information from the Terran station at Neptune and delivers it to an Argon ship near Pluto. After the battle, the player is given the task of investigating the hostile activity of the Xenon, who are suspected to be under the influence of a hitherto unknown source.
Xenon and various pirate factions are discovered to be coordinating raids on ships for valuable resources. New ships begin to appear, which resemble Terraformers (Boron warships). The player assists in the delivery of Terraformer wreckage to Terran scientists who are able to deduce that the new ships are counterfeits based heavily upon commonwealth technology.
Robert Pearle (an undercover Terran operative) has information concerning the origins of the new Terraformer ships, but he has been taken into custody by Argon forces. The player meets up with a fellow Terran agent, Patricia Heywood, and the two set off to rescue Pearle from the Argons. Following Pearle’s extraction, he accompanies the player on a mission to Split Space where it is rumored that the new Terraformers are being built. A mobile factory is discovered and taken by Terran forces and several Split scientists are taken prisoner as well. During interrogation, one of the scientists mentions the name Aldrin. (Aldrin was a Terran colony that was established long before the Terraformer War. The colonists at Aldrin managed to shut down their jumpgate and protect their Terraformers from the software error. Aldrin had been presumably lost during the war.)
The Terrans launch an offensive; reverse-engineering a jump beacon to get a fleet to Aldrin. A fleet of Xenon ships joins the battle against the Terrans, defending the Terraformers. A boarding party successfully takes control of the Terraformer CPU ship and the player is tasked with escorting Aldrin dignitaries to the Earth Torus, thereby opening Earth to the player.
Had I played the previous games in the series (which I was unaware was a series until I started into this review) I probably would have enjoyed the story more than I did. That being said, the story was still okay (and very reminiscent of the opening mission of the first Mass Effect).
II – UI [7/10]
Once I figured the user interface out (for the most part) it was a great system for the game. There was a “tutorial” (for lack of a better word), but it was not all encompassing. I felt a bit on my own to figure out the more advanced functions of the game. There was no minimap, which put quite a handicap on navigating. Aside from this though, the user interface, as I said, worked great for the game.
III – Gameplay [7/10]
Gameplay in X3:TC was really fun. Learning how the UI worked took some time, but the gameplay itself, was very unique. It is all first-person, whether you’re nestled safely inside your vessel or ejecting into the merciless void of space. It was a great way to explore and I sincerely hope we see things like this much more in games that are yet to be released.
My biggest complaint about the gameplay, however, is that (aside from combat) it is incredibly slow paced. If travel time had been done in relation to how long most people can stare into the abyss, it would have been okay. With the exception of the Grinch and sociopaths the world over, travel times can become extremely boring.
IV – Content [10/10]
There is a truly massive amount of content in X3:TC. There is a huge universe to explore (and exploring it fully could very well take you the amount of time it would take a real astronaut), tons of missions, over 100 ships, ship classes, and weaponry. If you can stay interested long enough to discover it all, more power to you.
V – Visual [7/10]
The graphics in X3:TC are decent. Taking into consideration that immense scale of the game, the graphics are about what you’d expect. While they’re not bad, they’re not outstanding.
VI – Audio [5/10]
I was rather unimpressed with the music of X3:TC. The soundtrack can often make or break a game (or salvage it from a gruesome end) but the music felt uninspired and pumped full of space-y noises. The sound effects weren’t bad and the voice acting was alright as well.
VII – Overall [6.8/10]
Overall, X3: Terran Conflict is an alright game. I didn’t like it as much as the rating I gave it, but, that’s that.

This is by far one of, if not the most beautiful side-scrolling platformers ever made. From the stunning visuals, to the blissful and moving soundtrack, this is a powerful game.
I am generally not one for side-scrollers. I tend to dislike the simplicity and the lack of any real progression. Ori and the Blind Forest is so different than anything I have ever played though. It captures you within the first five minutes of gameplay, and keeps you wanting to come back for more.
This is not an “easy” game. By no means is it anywhere near the difficulty of say things like Dark Souls, but it can be challenging. All the same, no matter how frustrated I got, I just kept pushing because I wanted to know more about the fascinating world.

The progression is fairly steady, starting you off with fairly easy concepts and patterns. But by mid game, well you get really good at contorting your fingers (if you are using a keyboard) to get just the right combination. I don’t know how many times I raged at the game, just to come back an hour later and realize what I had been doing wrong. The satisfaction from finally beating that sequence that you keep dying on is glorious.
Seriously though, this game is well worth the money, and time. Even beyond platformers, or side-scrollers, this is one stunning and compelling game. Buy it, and enjoy the journey.

Most my game time has been re-listening same audio dialogs and traversing the same screens while trying to progress, I didn't really know what to expect but I still feel this isn't what's supposed to give the game lenght.
As a puzzle game, puzzles are too few and they're very straight forward making waiting for animations the hardest part. Some puzzles can take time but even then it's because they are tedious to solve. Personally I got the notorious cookie puzzle right on the first try with little analysis and educated guesses.
As a story game the characters are too one dimensional and stereotypical and the game lacks any suspense save for few moments. I mean you can't exactly expect Telltale level writing from such a game but I must absolutely protest the store page advertising the characters 'rich'. An as a player I would appreciate it a detective game actually let me come up with my own theories and experiment on them instead of progressing 100% linearly through the set course of discoveries I am 'supposed to make'. I feel like I'm pushing a train forward and I'm struggling to finish the story but I hope the destination will be nice at least.
As a point and click game the hardest part is actually finding the interactable objects, so it's actually more of a hidden (mystery) object game. There is a journal that gives you a good idea on what to do or where to go next but it's not there on the screen, you have to dig it open from the menus.
With a bit of wandering and trial and error I could live with but the biggest gripe for me are the controls and the UI. This is an old game but let's face it, these gameplay mechanics have never been hard to make. I mean this 2004 game will leave your brain screaming "Heureka!" when you return to controls and menus of the 90's Resident Evil games.
On the other hand it's nice they support both keyboard and mouse (point and click) controls but why are you forced to pick one? There are times when I'd like to scout the environment by moving through it and sometimes it's nice to scan an area by hovering over with mouse. But switching the input type is tedious and I've only done it handful of times.
UI is dated even considering the games age but wouldn't mind it if it wasn't also slow and unintuitive: everything has a dedicated area in one of the boxes and you need to navigate a lot to get to places in the UI. Some programming could have moved the interaction menus next to items where the cursor is, some more programming could have made obsolete the 2-3 menu screens for every time you wanted to match a photo to a scene.
I feel like there's definitely something there that this game just has but doesn't execute properly. I wanted to love it but the gameplay is just so boring. I wish this game did better in it's time, it might have blown the lid off this genre so we might have gotten bigger and more polished games instead of remaining a niche category.

You start up the game for the first time and breeze through the tutorial missions (they basically just told you what to do and you did it). Feeling confident, you start the first real mission: Paris. You have some random guys to kill with names you can't remember and it's gonna be during a show or something. You walk in the front door, look around find the bar and load of places you're not allowed into. You are completely lost.
But then you start again. You find a staircase to the basement and using your super sneaking skills, grab a disguise from someone in the changing rooms. The map opens up. You get more disguises, more items, you even find some oportunities. You follow one of them to the end after several failed attempts and barely make it out without the guards at the exit shooting you down.
You check your score and, to be honest, it's pretty bad. But you also completed some challenges? You find the full catelogue of challenges and it compels you to start again and try some of these awesome set pieces. "You can drop the lighting fixture?" you find yourself wondering. So you go again, starting in the new location you just unlocked. You find some new rooms with new stuff. You kill the targets with the new opportunities. You finish the mission. You go again.
Soon you know many of the guards' patterns, where and how to get the best disguises, and you even know the names of the targets: Viktor Novikov and Dalia Margolis. Then, when all of the opportunities have been found and completed, you feel satisfied and you head to the main menu to reflect on what you have learnt and there, staring you in the face, is a button to take you to the next mission.
Hitman is one of the coolest experiences I have had with games and it has introduced me to both the Hitman series and the Stealth Action genre as a whole. I would definitely recommend picking it up. Maybe not the whole thing at first, but at least trying the tutorial levels and, if you can justify the purcahse, Paris. Well worth the money.

I'm so glad to see people agree with me. Let me just give you guys my opinion on this sad little potential wasted game. On the outside, this game looks pretty good. It's true, you get to customize your character, do some fun things around the city and play games in teams with different objectives. Sounds good right? Nope. This game will constantly pester you to become a "premium member", and if you do that, you get more money in game, and even get things like more tattoos. Premium members can have up to 50 tattoos. Guess how many normal players get? 3. THREE. And even if you do pay for premium, there are still other things you have to pay real money for if you want to enjoy the game, for instance, guns. The most important thing in this game. You'll find the guns you are given to start off are awful, but fair enough. You can buy guns with ingame money and "joker tickets", which are a pain to get hold of, and the gun expires in 7 days after you've bought it, so you'll have to collect the funds to buy it again! You could buy guns with real life money of course, which are overpowered and very expensive. I thought this game is decent enough to maybe pay a little more, so I decided to check out the store. I found this gun I liked for £5. I thought, maybe as a one off. Then I looked and it said I'd only have it for 30 days. There IS an option to keep the gun forever, but guess how much that would be? £25! You could buy a whole new, better game out of that! And this is just for 1 gun, out of the wide variety of guns you can get. And the thing is, this game is not "OUTSTANDING". It seems like it could be a decent game, fairly fun (if you weren't getting constantly killed by those who do buy over powered gun), and worth playing, and maybe paying a little for. But it's just ridiculous how much you'd have to pay if you wanted to have a good time with this disappointment. Thank god GTA 5 and GTA Online is coming to PC.

If you like cricket, then you will love this game.
To veterans coming from Don Bradman 14, the changes in this game will be immediately noticeable. The bowling feels so much more compelling than in the previous game, edges are satisfying to watch, and the AI batting is much improved. When batting, the increased range of strokes makes it so much more fluent to play, and more of the shots feel useable, unlike in the previous game.
The graphics are a letdown, whilst jarring at first, with character models appearing somewhat more cartoony than the previous game, the improvements to the animations, environments and lighting engine overall give it a nicer and realistic feel, though somewhat lacking compared to other triple A sporting titles on the market.
The improved career mode is a godsend, injecting so much more life to playing as your own pro, with the introduction of dynamic teams and club cricket. It feels satisfying to work your way up from the bottom to the top, and the difficulty adjustments you can make on the way allow you to tailor the game to your liking.
Some bugs do persist though, with AI fields in first class games to reacting quick enough to your shot placement, allowing you to continually score into vacant gaps and not reacting and plugging them. It’s easily possible to score very quick runs with low skilled batsmen into these gaps. This was a bug in the previous game, so it’s frustrating to see it carry over to this game, three years on.
Overall, it’s a great cricket experience. The best cricket game ever made, and well worth a look.

Coffee saves the day in this bizarre RPG-sidescroller hybrid, The Desolate Hope. In it, you play a small video game program tasked with exploring several unique worlds and battling viruses within as per the orders of a coffee machine tasked with maintaining the extra-planetary colony of Lum Infinis. To aid you on your quest, you have the help of four derelict robots each running their own simulation for you to explore.
Gameplay is split between a megaman-style sidescrolling jump and shoot, a top down shooter where you explore cyberspace within cyberspace, and RPG-style 4 on 1 battles vs bosses. TDH features a really bizarre artstyle that I can only describe as “uniquely Scott Cawthon” and if you’ve played any of his other games (especially FNAF) you’ll see why. Another interesting feature of this game are the day-night cycles. During the night, you are relegated to exploring the surface world to scavenge for items to improve the derelicts, increase power to the station, or score a few extra credits playing a space invaders style mini-game. Daytime is considerably more busy, requiring you to dive into simulations powered by each derelict in order to seek out and destroy the viruses located within. Once you encounter a virus, you are thrust into a high speed active-time RPG battle where quick thinking and careful planning are required in order to survive.
On that note I have to say that, while most of the game was a fairly interesting experience, the boss battles are incredibly confusing and I managed to clear each one without really understanding what was going on. There is just so much happening on the screen in any given moment and the bosses will interrupt everything very frequently to do a full-screen attack. In any case I won, but I have no idea how or why.
Chaotic boss battles aside, I still really enjoyed The Desolate Hope and you probably will too if you like eccentric hybrid RPGs. Plus, it’s FREE (can’t beat that!)

Definitely the most polarising game in the series as expected from the initial response to our "edgy" Dante. I'll try to keep it short and each section will be two sets of numbers. The score on the left is for newcomers to the franchise while the right is for the veterans.
Story
6/10   6/10
The DMC franchise isn't really known for it's story and focuses heavily on the gameplay as expected. The story in this one however is definitely more detailed and structured and the idea of Limbo being a living city trying to kill Dante is creative. However, everything else feels meh. It's your typical "enemies have taken over the city" story, albeit done in a better way. In this one, the demon world of Limbo and the real world are basically on top of each other but Limbo cannot be seen by humans. The media is run by demons and is basically a long joke pointed towards FOX News and Bill O' Reilly. However, there's not much to really talk about sadly. There is definitely some character development with Dante I'll get into later and it is seen.
Characters
6/10   5/10
The characters in the game are mediocre for newcomers but are terrible when compared to the ones from previous DMC games. Let's start with Dante. Dante is such a tryhard at being the character that isn't supposed to care about what's going on around him and he doesn't get out of his teenager phase for a while in the story. Thankfully, he does become more caring and a decent person by the end of the game but it takes too long for him to start caring in a more visible way. The old Dante was more carefree and smart mouthed, always taking the chance to hurl jokes but always gets serious when he has to, Also, the new Dante curses for no reason to seem cool. Vergil is another story. In the original games, mainly DMC 3, he was more respectable and craved power from the start. In this DmC, he's more humble and willing to do what he can to save humanity from the demons. It's quite a contrast that does have a payoff in the end, at least to me. Kat on the other hand feels like a filler character, similar to how Lucia was in DMC 2. She really had no purpose in the story.
Gameplay
8/10  5/10
This is where the game is very divisive as well. For new players, the gameplay is streamlined in a good way. It makes it easier to land combos and to keep the combo meter up, giving a feel of satisfaction to those new to the series. You end up unlocking Angel and Demon weapons that have a color that corresponds to enemy colors. Use Demon weapons on Red and Angel weapons on Blue; very simple. There aren't too many weapons and you'll end up sticking to what you prefer the entire game along with his main sword Rebellion. In the old DMC game, the arsenal was bigger and offered more combos and included different "styles". Think of like switching classes in FF5 where you have different abilities unlocked with different styles, except in an action form. DmC doesn't have it. The style meter dropped very quick in previous DMC games, forcing the player to adapt quickly to keep the meter up. The difficulty has also dropped quite a bit in DmC but there's always the other modes such as Son of Sparda and Dante Must Die.
Soundtrack
8/10  6/10
This one is very subjective. I was a fan of the original soundtracks and the new one. DmC's soundtrack is mainyl done by Combichrist and the electronica and industrial feel definitely works in the game, especially in FOX News stage. The older games focused more on heavy metal and symphonic as well. This is up to you guys really if OSTs are that important.

A short, but sweet experience that doesn't need a heavy investment in time.  Musaic Box is a puzzle game at heart with a very basic story to it.  Find outlines hidden about your grandfather's workshop.  Doing so succesfully will allow you to uncover your birthday present.  Once you complete an outline you'll be able to piece together a musical melody that starts in pieces and needs to be assembled to complete the final work.  As a layman,  I found the music enjoyable and sometime's nostalgic.  The difficultiy varies with a few pieces being somewhat hard to solve.  Luckily there's a hint option that makes the process a bit easier by shading out misplaced pieces.  Even though I favor this game it could have been much more than it is.  There are only five rooms to explore and about a dozen or so melodies to solve.  There is a Creation option at the end of the game, but it only allows your to rearrange previously solved melodies.  I wish they would have gone into depth explaining the history behind each piece and possibly extending the experience with other areas to explore.  Personally, I wouldn't pay full price for this game, but that's just me.  Wait for it too show up in a bundle or a sale and you won't regret the few dollars you spend on it.  Kid friendly, but your child may struggle with no prior knowlodge of the music in the game.  I played in Big Picture Mode and had a problem with scaling.  The screen was stretched off screen on all sides.  If you encounter the same problem keep in mind that 3-4 of the outlines or solutions to outlines are hidden a bit off screen.  That's what gave me the most trouble.

I'll be honest; I was really excited about this game: the idea, the story, the overall execution. I was intrigued and then I saw fairly positive reviews so I bought the game (and its sequel which I have yet to play because I wanted to give this a true review for the game itself) on sale.
I have been misled, bamboozled, tricked. Because I fell for the positive reviews and spent 10 hours of my life playing a game with no conclusion and honestly I feel so blindsided and empty--I have honestly never been so upset at the ending of a game and I have played "Life is Strange."
Let's break it down: Victoria was supposed to be a relatable, "stick-it-to-the-man," edgy, "anything-to-get-the-truth" main female protag, but honestly I agree with her boss in that she acts and sounds like a rich little girl not getting her way. It's not that she wants to find the murderer of henious crimes; it's that she's bored now because she's so far behind the chase. Her humor in regards to crime scenes, while at first charming, quickly lose its touch and her lack of genuine concern, shock, and sadness make her seem apathetic.
While, because I went into the game blind except for the description on the Steam Store page, the switch to her grandfather's story was a shock, I found myself prefering him to her in almost every way. He was more genuine, sympathetic, seemed to have friends and family he truly loved outside of his work. They tried to parallel Gus's and Victoria's behavior with each other, but it came off as her trying to copy her grandfather because it was "cool" and "the right thing to do" to get out of the "system."
Onto the puzzles: they sucked! I mean, some of them were okay, and I even truly enjoyed a couple. And I will be the first to admit that I have very strong feelings about certain puzzles (those puzzles where it's a bunch of slide-y squares and there's one missing and you have to slide the squares around until the picuture is correct, then add the last one, yeah I hate those. A lot. And this game had one), but a lot of these puzzles were just straight hard, not challenging. I know I'm kind of impatient when it comes to puzzles so I never really actually critique a game on them, but I actually tried for this game. I was stuck on one of the puzzles for over an hour--not joking you. That lockpicking minigame sucks so much; it's the absolute worst. When I finally broke down to find a walkthrough of it, the first three I tried were wrong! Then I came across a Steam community page for it because everyone agrees this is the worst puzzle! It's a fun idea, but the WORST execution. The most difficult puzzle I've ever come across in a game before hands down.
This game was made in 2005 so there are things I'll automatically give it a pass for: horrible jogging animations, no autosaving during certain puzzles that would have been nice, the sad but simultanously hiliarious jaw-flapping that happens every time a person spoke that, at times, made this game worth the puzzle struggles and the unrelatable characters.
Then we come to the end of the game. Dues Ex open ending, sequel baiting, no conculsion to the 10 hours I just poured into this game from my life. And this weird little tidbit for the next game they give you to say "hey Victoria is going to LA buy the second game" but let me tell you buddy her going to LA does nothing to close the freaking wide-as-hell plot hole you have in the ending because she's looking for evidence of someone who was an adult in the 1930s-1940s and BUDDY BOY IT'S THE 1990S AT LEAST BECAUSE SHE HAS A CELL PHONE IT WON'T LEAD TO THE IDENTITY OF ANYONE ALIVE RIGHT NOW.
So basically everything a sh!t show and Victoria is a dumbass because why didn't she call for backup/the police like 80 times throughout the game and everything she did was so freaking Extra(TM) that it hurts.

X3 TC is probably my favorite of the X series. It feels much more fluid than any of the other titles in the series. Its the epitome of a procedural ope world space/economic sim. You can go through the whole game with no story plots, or you can utilize the story plots to your advantage. Build, conquer, trade, do all of the above. Its all up to you.

A fanatic in games related to anything space, I find myself blown away by X3: Terran Conflict and the amount of sheer possibilities this game offers. I have searched and played a wide vareity of space strategy, arcade combat and simulator games over the past 20 years and X3 is by far one of the richest and well made games I have ever played to date. Its beautiful, ruthless and endlessly vast.
To start, I will say that this is a very deep and heavy space simulator. You will spend more time setting up keys and shortcuts aswell as getting used to the interface and HUD before actually trading and fighting. That being said, once you have your keys set up and got comfortable you can easily start highlighting other ships and taking on missions. Whether those are escort, enemy take out, trading, rescue, scouting...the list goes on or just plain messing around in space it will leave you busy not for hours, but days, months, even years.
The Terran story is the easiest to get into as you start at Uranus, neptune, pluto, mars and then out to the alien sectors. During those missions (3 main story missions or 2-3 hours into it) you start to get ships as gifts to either sell for money and then use to upgrade others given to you. This is a perfect example of how the game plays out, it takes a bit of time learning what to do and where to go but once you start chipping away at the surface you learn more and get more. The game snow balls the learning experience always teaching you something new once you get new ships or get to new areas but then opening up even more doors to things you did or didn't do before you can now do better or differently.
As it may take you a little while to learn the ropes, you start to realize if you want to avoid the main story entirely you can. You soon discover you can be a pirate and steal your own ships and make your own evil empire, be a master trader and send automated convoys throughout the 200+ sectors in the universe and have your own military escorts. Be your own military (well for the leading race you are with).
Graphics! Oh my the Graphics. It was released in 2008 and this game has aged well! When it was first released it was a monster of a game to run on PCs. Even low graphic settings it looked good but required alot, but with todays tech for PCs 7 years later this game can be easily pushed to high on mid end gaming pcs and can be maxed effortlessly with your average PC for games today. And when it is its breatless. The detail and scope of the game is mammoth, everything is so complex and intricate. A small space station in the distance can become a hulking megafort. Docking alone is a treat as you see upclose the details and raw size of the game. A true work of digital engineering mastery!!!
The final conclusion is that it plays like anything you want it to be, even to go so far and say mid to late game it can be a strategy game in the same vein of civilisation, but at the drop of a dime become star wars and rock your world. I bought a few other games on ps4 recently and thought I would be playing those... yea forget those games.The gameplay, graphics, open world, the story, the polish and loving patches made to fix the bugs. It deserves a 10/10 and rightfully so.
Warning : If you intend on flying small fighters all the time and have epic space dog fights then tune your mouse skills up or get a gamepad/ joystick. You can buy Autopilot upgrades for combat early on but anytime you are in a mid to heavy fighter and they are in a light scout fighter you will go in circles shooting like crazy if you don't have a joystick or have your mouse sensitivity maxed. You can fly classic without those too, you just switch alot between auto pilot and manual fire mode. All that being said, its minor and is for early game. Once you get given your first few ships, you can simply have them follow you and intercept anyone while you pick and chose your targets.

First, let me just say that this is my first Devil May Cry game. That being said, I thought this game was GREAT.
I don't know much about the original story, but I definitely liked this "modernized version". It's not a very complicated story: Dante wants revenge on the demon who killed his mother (and who is pretty much controlling the world). But honestly, that's enough for me. I really liked the look of the game and how the world was portrayed - especially "limbo", the hidden "demon world" around us.
Looking through the other reviews it seems like some people think that Dante is too "cool", and yes, he sure is confident and maybe a bit smug, but honestly, I liked him. Despited his "flaws" he seems like a good person, and he made me laugh several times throughout the game. And yes, he is cool.
My favorite character was probably Kat, a human who helps you out on your missions. I really wish we could have gotten to know a bit more about her, but sadly we probably never will as a sequel doesn't seem to be coming any time soon.
Vergil, Dante's brother... He is the smarter sibling, while Dante is the stronger one(?). I knew before starting the game that some things would happen between them, but I don't want to give away too many spoilers.
Then there is Mundus, the demon god. Decent bad guy although I would have liked to know more about him as well. Especially regarding his relationship to
.
I can't remember the last time I had this much fun fighting in a video game. The fighting feels fast, smooth and kick♥♥♥♥♥ All of the weapons are really strong in their own way, and while it is easy to get into the game it takes some practice to slash and bash through legions of mobs without getting a chainsaw in your back.
Apparently this game is quite a bit easier than the previous Devil May Cry games, and I agree that putting a check point before
fight was a bit too much. It sometimes felt like, especially on the harder difficulties towards the end of the game, instead of starting a fight with 10% health you might as well just suicide and respawn with full health (at the cost of a lower score, of course). It doesn't really give you that "I gotta try my best to survive!"-feeling. On the positive side, having check points before each fight means you can try to chain attacks and pull of amazing combos evey fight without worrying too much about screwing up.
The only part of the game that I didn't really enjoy was when you have to run around helping people in the real world, since you aren't really able to fight while doing this. Luckily most of the game takes place in limbo, which is where the fun happens.
The game looks good to me. I really liked the style of the game, and although the game is fairly linear, the world around you changes all the time, making it feel like you are actually part of something more open and bigger. The first time you move around in limbo you will most likely have a blast.
The music in the game is heavy metal/heavy rock-ish(?) stuff, which is not really my type of music, but it sure makes you feel like a badass when you fight through hordes of enemies with that music playing in the background. It really suits the mood of the game, and the fights would feel way less epic without this great soundtrack.
I also really liked the voices of the different characters. In my opinion, pretty much all the voices were spot on. The one liners from Dante were perfectly delivered, making even the bad jokes funny. Well done.
Again, this was my first Devil May Cry game, and it seems like most of the negative reviews are from people who have played the previous games. For me, this was a great introduction to the series, and I'm definitely going to play the originals as well. If you want a really good fighting game with a decent story that looks and sounds great then look no further. This is the game for you.

This review is not only going to give you my personal feedback about The Desolate Hope, but is also going to shut up all the people who think that Scott Cawthon is a terrible game developer.
Before Five Nights at Freddy's, Five Nights 2, FNAF 3, and "The Final Chapter", there was a little splendid title called The Desolate Hope, made by everyone's favorite cryptic, Christian, 3DS Max and Clickteam Fusion 2.5 game dev, Scott Cawthon. ;)
References aside, this is a game that everyone should play at least once in their gaming lives, and if not then maybe thrice; especially because this game is FREE! Additionally, if you know someone who hates Scott Cawthon just because of Five Nights at Freddy's, let them try out this indie gem to have them rethink themselves.
Gameplay.
The best part about this game is hands-down the gameplay. It actually combines three types of gameplay styles; top-view, Zelda-like shooting games; Mega Man style, non-linear platforming side-scrollers; and Turn-based RPGs with a unique blend. The RPG style is what I really want to talk most about. The first two gameplay styles are fairly self-explanatory (that is if you know what I'm saying), but Scott has added a very creative twist on turn-based RPG battles. Unlike traditional RPG battles, attacks come seemingly automatically, meaning that you need to react fast to initiate an action. It's a little hard to explain, but I'll try to proceed. Furthermore, there are nice little "microgames" that play during the battles which provide benefits to your party. I apologize for my poor explanantion, but its quite hard for me to put this into words.
Graphics.
I personally enjoy the visuals of this game, then again I also personally enjoy mashed potatoes with ketchup. The game's graphics use 3D images as 2D sprites, which in turn give it a strange feeling of playing a 3D game from the early 2000s, while in reality it actually isn't. Now this feeling, this is something that I like, as it practically tickles my spine with nostalgia. GG, Mr. Cawthon.
Music.
While I'm under the impression that this game's music consists of royalty-free songs, they're still quite catchy and enjoyable. Scott really knows how to direct his music, even if he didn't compose it.
Overall, I reccomend that everyone play this game, especially because it's free and you have nothing to lose. It's a charming and unique title that'll make you enjoy game design and almost wish you could do the same. At least, taht's what it did for me. ;)

I thought this was a fun game, even though it's fairly short; I finished it in ~2 hours.  The goal is to solve a series of musical puzzles, but to do so you have to find pieces first.  That first part seems like a standard "find the hidden object" kind of game to me (and it will give hints automatically over time, so you shouldn't get too stuck), so it's the second part that's interesting.  In the musical puzzles, you have to arrange a series of blocks in a grid so that the grid is completely filled and the blocks allow the given piece of music to be played properly (in the correct order).  Most puzzles offer some guidance by providing the main melody for you to listen to, and there's a hint system you can use if needed that will tell you which blocks are incorrectly placed in a full grid.  It may be a little hard to explain in words, but I think it's easy enough to learn and fun to play, so if you like these sorts of games, this one is worth a try.

DBC 17 comes nearly three years after DBC 14 broke new grounds in creating a fun yet challenging cricket game for all platforms, something which the biggies of the gaming industry *cough*EA*cough* had considered too demeaning for them to take up. DBC 14 was a genuinely fun game, but it had its issues, some of which were never resolved. Of course, the success of DBC 14 meant that the next iteration had to be big enough to live up to the high standards set by the studio.
Sadly, I cannot give a convincing thumbs up to this iteration of the game. A lot has improved - batting is much more fluidic and realistic, especially at the tougher difficulty levels (if you are a DBC 14 veteran, don't be afraid to crank up the AI), bowling is tougher than before, but much more rewarding, once you get the hang of it, and fielding has been pushed up a couple of notches for the good. The interface remains simplistic, and focuses on getting you in the game as soon as possible. There are still no licensed players, but the fledgling community should take care of that. The career mode is much more comprehensive now, and slightly less frustrating than before (again, this depends on how it is evolved during the game's) life cycle.
However, the improvements end here, at least for now. For a game priced at par with AAA titles, DBC 17 lacks production flair. A little more colour to the presentation would have done wonders, especially in the moments leading up to or after a match. Commentary is abysmal - there is no other word for it - with drab voices, unexcited commentators, and frequently messed up lines. Over time, you will realise how the bad commentary actually kills half the fun to be had out of the match. Animations could have been spruced up much more, and the fluidity could have been worked upon. It's not that the end game is bad, just that three years and a AAA price were enough for anyone to expect all the previous issues ironed out, and substantial improvements put in.
While I can easily recommend this game to a DBC newbie / cricket enthusiast (assuming you are okay shelling out this kind of money), I will be hard pressed to do so to anyone who has played DBC 14. The game needs a couple of updates and major patches before it deserves that credit. I will be sure to update my review if and when that happens.

How to even start? I can't recommend this game at all, and I'm writing this review as an outlet for my overwhelming disappointment more than anything else. If it helps you decide about this game: bonus. I understand it's part of a trilogy, but honestly, I played this one first and I'm never going to bother with the other two for the bad taste this one left.
Short Version: Don't. The puzzles aren't good and the characters are bad. The story is disappointing and it doesn't end. Not even a little; so no satisfying victory for you.
Long Version:
If you're into point & click, puzzles, mysteries and crime, this game is going to look like Christmas until you actually start playing it. I picked it up because my gf and I like all of the things it was supposed to be, and it had so many good reviews! Reading over those reviews now, I feel like I must have played a completely different game.
If you're still reading, here are some of the reasons I recommend you look elsewhere for whatever it is you're after:
Pace - This game is slow even if you play it as quickly as you can. It will not let you do anything out of order or sooner than it thinks you should. You will have solved most of the puzzles before they've started, but often you'll have to talk to a specific person, or look at a specific thing before the main character will go 'oh, I should do blah' and only THEN can we proceed. So really, the puzzle is trying to get to start the puzzle?
Puzzles - They're not hard, some of them are tedious, and they're not really story relevant. Also, there aren't very many of them, so it's less of a puzzle game and more of a walk around simulator. There isn't any outside-the-box thinking here and when I say story relevant I mean the puzzles you complete to progress the story don't make sense within the story itself. Which brings me to the third and most serious offender
Story - Dear. God. Okay, so this is the part that broke the game for us. Somewhere in this game is a really interesting story about some disturbed people killing other people all tied together with art and family. It should be awesome, but you don't really get to be a part of that story and the best parts of the game are when you're reading journals and speculating on who the big bad is.
One of the characters you play as, Gus, is actually pretty interesting. He takes you along through his section of the mystery and he makes sense as a character. He's a private eye, not a cop, and he does some not exactly legal stuff to get ahead of the killer before more people are hurt. People he loves are being directly impacted, so you get his urgency and interest. We could get behind that; it wasn't always great, but it made enough sense for Prague in the 20's.
The other character is Victoria. You're with her most of the game, and she might be the single worst federal agent in the history of terrible representation of the FBI. At the beginning it's not so bad: she clearly has a lot of personality and not a lot of respect for authority, which is a staple for cop characters, fine. But that lack of respect leads her out on a ridiculously elaborate and illegal adventure that should land her in jail except SPOILERS: she off-handedly blackmails her boss. It becomes ridiculous and farcical that she could carry on the way she does and not face criminal charges.
