Microsoft's very own Moon Studios outdid themselves with this metroidvania style 2D game.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a 2D metroidvania with a heart and soul. The story features Ori, a nimble and feeble spiritual creature whose days of joy in the forest of Nibel come to and end when the great spirit tree loses its strength. Ori's foster parent, Naru, dies, and Ori is tasked with restoring the forest of Nibel back into its former glory. Accompanying Ori in its journey is Sein, an Ocarina-of-Time-esque spirit, but much less annoying or in-your-face. The story evokes strong senses of loneliness, bitterness, and forgiveness, and will definately make you feel more than your average adventure game. Ori and the Blind Forest is a fairy tale for adults; it has many lessons for you, but none of them feel spoonfed or forced.
Graphics and presentation are some of the best to go around. The game has a cartoony outlook and dreamy sound design which further enhance the feel of a fairy tale world. The locations vary from lush forests to dreary caverns and darkly-lit marshes, usually containing hidden secrets to find. There are no technical issues, either, as the game runs at a solid 60 FPS all the time.
You can play the game with a keyboard and mouse, a keyboard, or a controller. I played the game with a keyboard and did fine, but a controller is a safe bet as well. Ori and the Blind Forest looks like a game for kids, but this could not be farther from the truth. The game is very hard at times, requiring you to perform exact jumps and mastering the full set of your skills from very early on. You'll unlock the ability to dash, double-jump, glide, scale walls, and many other throughout the 8-10 hour campaign. Certain sections at the end of each dungeon can be particularly challenging, but they never feel drawn out or unfair. The game is well balanced and feels fair even during the most hectic of times.
The Definitive Edition gives you the ability to visit all the previously completed dungeons and places and collect all the hidden collectibles. The regular edition does not support this "feature".
Ori and the Blind Forest: Definitive Edition is a masterpiece, a first-class game which reportedly took 4 years to make. This is one of those games you don't want to miss.

+ Great support for all combinations: keyboard, keyboard and mouse, and controller
+ Definitive Edition gives you access to previously completed areas to gain a 100% completion

Okay, two years after I had bought this game as a part of the X Superbox I feel obliged to write a few words about it. Simply because X3: Terran Conflict (and other X games) are some of the best games EVER made. I would actually hesitate whether to still call this a game. It will steal your life.
First things first. It's probably gonna be easy for veterans of previous X games to get into this one, few slight changes but the same mechanic in a nutshell. For the others though, be warned! This game has one of the steepest learning curves I've ever experienced in a game, yet it is also probably the most rewarding. You start out with one ship in a vastness of space and you can virtually build a galactic empire with hundreds of ships, factories, and resources at your disposal. It's not gonna be fast, it's not going to be easy, but it's going to be fun! And you can really do it! No MMO has ever come close to the level of freedom and complexity of all the mechanics in this game. No other sandbox game provides such a beautiful playground for making all your dreams of becoming an overlord come true. It's a gem, an absolute beast of a game, so patched and so loved that even when the developers provided little to no tutorial (very extensive manual however), you can get all the information you need to become great relatively easily.
It's difficult to recommend this game to just one group of players. You can get a lot of fighting experience in this one, which I personally enjoy very much, but it's not a simple grabba shipz and go pwn everybody rite nao. No... You have to work on your reputation with a faction, you then get to buy the ship of your dreams, then you have to take it and slap dozens of upgrades on it to make it really shine and then you go get yourself some kickass weapons. I love maintaining all these little details, you can change your weaponry on the fly and tear all kinds of enemies apart. There are limits of course, but lemme tell you... I did destroy a class M6 bomber with about 150 MJ shields with a little M5 ship that only has 1 MJ shield.... I did take out a Kha'ak corvette with my M3 Mamba thanks to an insane firepower provided by Mass Drivers and their non-existent energy consumption. This might not mean anything to you now, but trust me, when you get there and live it... you will remember ;)
Ooooor you can pretty much just ignore the whole shooting thing and become a filthy rich and successful trader and buy everyone :D The story isn't important, you write your own. The graphics are very good in my opinion. Music and sounds are more than adequate. Mostly you won't even notice the music, which makes those rare moments of entering a sector that's different than all the others that much more enjoyable.
This game is about options, freedom and passion for honing all your skills. And I love it.
Personal rating 10/10

20XX is, in many ways, the Mega Man game we wish Mighty Number 9 was. The gameplay is smooth and fast, it brings something new to the table by being a Roguelike instead of the standard platformer, and there are upgrades that stack on top of each other.
20XX borrows a lot from the Megaman X series, which was ultimately the greatest series in terms of gameplay, barring X7. It has two playable characters, Nina and Ace, who play just like X and Zero. I kind of wish they had included a third character similar to Axl, but, as it is, the variet is nice.
The game has a number of levels, each of which with a boss at the end. Unlike the Mega Man games, however, you start on a random level, with the difficulty increasing as you beat more bosses. After defeating a boss, you can gain their ability, an increase in health, or some money, all of which are useful. The skills are varied, and I've never found myself considering them copies of the various boss abilities from the Mega Man series, which is a plus. Each boss is weak against one skill, and strong against another. This is once again an improvement against the Mega Man series, and forces you to not depend on a single ability.
Health and Weapon Energy are rare, and, in later levels, it can be easy to never encounter any. Though you can find them on enemies, they are mostly found in chests, which also usually contain an upgrade. Upgrades have a variety of effects, including increasing your maximum health and increasing your weapon damage. They also usually stack, allowing for large boosts. There are also armor and weapons- the armor functions much like the X series armor, but the weapons are the most interesting. They modify your standard attack, which can be very useful. For example, Nina has a shotgun weapon that has greatly reduced range but fires a spread of shots that together do much more damage than Nina's base weapon, and Ace has a spear weapon that greatly increases his range.
Lastly, by doing runs, you gain money, which can be used to unlock new upgrades
My only issue with this game is that there is no 'endgame', no reason for doing runs aside for unlocking new items, and once that's done, there's not much reason to keep going. Other roguelikes, such Enter the Gungeon and The Binding of Issac, have a story that keeps you coming back, that keeps you going through the game even after you've unlocked every item. 20XX does not.
So, my final score: 8/10. It's lacking that all-important ending, but everything else is wonderful.

Oneday maybe they'll make a game called "Batman in Atlantis."  Or "Batman on Krypton."  Or "Batman in Metropolis."  But everyone knows Batman spends his nights in Gotham.
When Rocksteady made "Arkham Asylum," it was the best Batman game ever.  It was the closest thing to "being Batman." The only downside was that you were being Batman somewhere other than Gotham.  Can you imagine a Batman game on the moon?  It wouldn't be the same, would it?  Batman walks the rooftops and swoops down on dark alleys.  He doesn't spend 365 nights a year in prison corridors.
He guards Gotham City.
"Arkham City" took that into account.  But the aesthetic of an abandoned city district turned into a live-in prison is not the glass mountains of the financial district.
It's not Gotham.
"Arkham Knight" finally brought us the giant metropolis of Gotham City, rooftop by rooftop, high-rise by high-rise.  With the Batmobile itself to fling around corners in fiery abandon.  Batman: Check.  Batmobile: Check.  Gotham: Check.  Everything was finally in place.  It's a masterpiece.  The summation of decades of Batman stories and runs.  But between "City" and "Knight" lies "Origins."
"Origins" was the game that first left Arkham behind, with it's crazed lunatics and asylum setting.  It's prison decor and cockroaches.  There was good stuff there.  But it was a Batman story on the edge of canon.  With "Titan Joker" it simply walked up to that edge and jumped off.  And it's that very plot point that is integral to the entire Arkhamverse.
"Origins" left behind the ever more insane antics of villians from "Asylum" and "City," and boiled Batman down to his essence.  A crimefighter.  A detective.  You know, DC, "Detective Comics."  It's got more "police procedural" in it than any of the others.  Rocksteady made games about Batman losing his sanity.  "Origins" is about keeping a cool head and following the clues.  All while the mob has a contract out on your head.
"Origins" left the asylum behind.  It paved the way for "Arkham Knight."
It brought us Gotham City.

This is a very simple music based puzzle game with an eye spy front end. The mechanics are done well, but the game lacks any significant puzzle complexity. The musical pieces include familiar classical tunes...Old MacDonald, Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, Auld Lang Syne, etc...pretty boring stuff. Keep your expectations low and you won't be disappointed spending five quarters on it, but you can play this on the web as a free java game all the same.

What a great game, I didn't really know what to expect, especially for a price this low. I expected some sort of old school point and click adventure, but got a nice music/rhythm puzzle game instead, with point and click elements. The goal is to search rooms for parts of music sheets and combine these together to create a full sheet. You then have to recreate the music by forming a puzzle. You do this with several blocks, each with their own instrument(s). The example is listed in the lower center so you continually have to listen to the example and try and fit the puzzle together. It starts off easy but gets more difficult in a matter of minutes. It's a nice challenge, and I enjoyed it very much, because I'm an avid music listener. It's, so far, all classical music though, but most of them are well known.
Even though the music fits the style, it would've been nice if there was a game around (sequel maybe, someday ?) with more modern music or where you could load your own music.
[Rating: 77/100]

Short at 2 hours long, but compelling. I finished it in one sitting (well I would have if I didn't have to go to sleep), and there is a sure sense of gratification with successfully putting together each musical piece. The 'searching' sections are mostly trial and error, and some parts are way too easy, but it's a nice relaxing little puzzle game with, of course, some great music. It's probably not worth $5, though, so maybe wait until this one's on sale.

Musaic is a musical puzzle game. It's all about clasical or traditional music that was made throughout the ages. It also has a bit of a hidden objects game too. I surely suggest it for whoever likes music and puzzles!

Musaic Box is half hidden object game, half music puzzler. Finding enough objects takes you to a puzzle screen where you arrange blocks of different shapes that have parts of the melody, harmony, or rhythm on them, so that they form the whole song when played beginning to end. This game only uses classical, public domain songs, but the tracks are definitely pleasant to listen to if you can enjoy orchestral music (with a few exceptions, most of which are at the start).
The puzzle quality is decent. Most puzzles aren't hard. Some are a little tricky, but the hard ones are only tough because the harmony sections will repeat a few times and you won't have enough info to know which is which. That said, there's a hint button that will reveal misplaced blocks, which makes that a bit easier.
I finished it 100% in 2.5 hours. It's a short game that was worth the time and money I spent on it. I spent $1.25; don't pay much more than that.

I personally loved this game; the light adventure-style gameplay coupled with some amusing puzzles as a vehicle for a nostalgic trek through a handful of classical music pieces reminiscent of some happy memories made for a very pleasant experience.

I absolutely love this game! I am not a regular reviewer of games despite gaming a lot and having a lot of games, so please stick with me if I ramble a bit.
I finsihed with 994 hours of playtime on DB14 and I am sure I will clock even more playtime on this.
I was really nervous buying this game with the mixed reviews that are on here but I decided to buy the game anyway as I remeber how good the dev team were at fixing issues on DB14 and my passion for cricket.  I needn't have been worried about anything.
The batting brings a new challenge without changing too many of the things that made the last game so good.  I am still getting used to it but I get  a bit better with every innings, despite getting frustrated with myself for playing stupid shots (a lot like real life!)
The bowling is a lot more rewarding than on DB14 where I felt sometimes it was too easy on the lower difficulties and was a bit of a boring slog on the harder difficulties, on this version I feel like I really get into the battle between batsmen and bowler. I read that the controls are a lot more difficult, but I have found them to be absolutely fine.
The whole Career mode has had a revamp and it is fantastic, you earn SP points which you can use to level up certain batting/bowling/fielding attributes as you go along. You start off playing for a side local to the county you choose to play for and play in t20 matches for them until you are good enough to be selected for your county, you can also choose the batting and bowling difficulties independantly which is a fantastic idea.
CONS
I have only found two real negatives at the moment which are;
1. The game randomly crashes when loading up a match (averaging once for every 10 hours of game time so far)
2. The wording in the game, you can use shorter or longer pitch bowling. This annoys me everytime I see it, obviously longer is the opposite of shorter but in the context of cricket it should be shorter or fuller pitch bowling!
PROS
1. Graphics - smoother, better and easier for the PC to handle than DB14
2. Batting -  more challenging and rewarding, you get yourself out playing the wrong shots
3. Bowling - more rewarding and more fun
4. Career Mode - Everything about it, brilliant ideas, brilliantly executed by the devs
5. James Taylor on commentary - nice touch and hasn't got too repeatetive on me yet
All in all I fully recommend this game for anyone. Cricket lovers, DB14 lovers and people new to cricket will all love this game and it is fully worth the pricetag.

Simplistic with complex expansion.
This game is absolutely addicting to play when you aren't faced with major bugs. Anyone wanting a survival/space exploration game will absolutely love this. This is not overly complex which makes it great for gamers new to the survivalist experience while still featuring complex expansion for more advanced users. I won't go too much into detail but learning how power, oxygen, and mining worked in the game was very simple and allowed more time to focus on playing the game rather than trying to figure out how the game is played. The planets are fun to explore and are very diverse.
Important Note: There are lots of bugs, especially with rovers and trucks. Don't let these bugs discourage you too much as the game is in pre-alpha and I don't doubt the developers are fixing these with updates.
Pros: Exploration options, simplsitic and easy to learn layout, unique user interfaces for fluid gameplay, terraforming simplicity
Cons: Needs more uses for resources, no server based multiplayer (hosted by player's world with invites), needs better optimization (lag spikes occansionally),
Overall Review: Entertaining with a lot of room for expansion and improvement. Playing with a friend was lots of fun for me but there were synicing issues which caused lost items and chunk loading glitches. This game is worth the $20 price tag. Some may disagree but the game will be worth it in the end when bugs are fixed and gameplay is better optimized.

This is an early alpha game, so there are bugs galore. However, it is a very promising and charming game already. This review is based on my impressions of the game in its current state.
+ Very addictive gameplay
+ The terrain tool offers limitless creativity
+ The right balance of exploration, survival, danger, and awe
+ Great aesthetic
+ Co-op is a lot of fun
> Minimal UI
> Curvature of the planets can get you lost if you aren't paying attention
- Might be too easy, could use difficulty slider
- Lack of interface options (for multiplayer, graphics settings, etc)
- Random people can join your game uninvited (and ruin your base, interrupt your progress, cut off your tethers so you die, etc)
- Structures cannot be removed once placed, base expansion can sometimes be unpredictable (nodes will rise and drop in unexpected ways when they project forward)
* Loses FPS very quickly when you expand base. I go from solid 100 FPS to about 15-20 FPS after a couple hours of gameplay
* When in co-op, leaving a rover/truck will disable the engine of the other player's vehicle
* When a player leaves your game, their terrain tool is stuck in the air where they stood
* When you join a player's game, sometimes you are unable to pick up resources on the ground
This game is absolutely worth getting if you are into semi-casual survival/exploration games and sci-fi games. The forums are abuzz with activity, the developers push updates very often, and there is a long life ahead of this game. It is exciting to see all of the suggestions made by the community and how the developers are taking them to heart in adding content to the game. This is definitely my "main" game for the foreseeable future, just as Minecraft was a few years ago.

One very strange and huge game.
If you like the thought of a slow paced sci-fi universe simulator with the potential for extreme micro-management, then this is probably the game for you!
It has a few flaws...
The start scenario I went for dumped me a mere 21 sector jumps away from the start of the main plot line. There is no in game help / hint to guide you on this one. I only found out because eventually I looked on the wiki to see how to start the main quest line.
I clocked up around 50 hours of game play before I even knew how or where to start the main quest line, and I only found that out from a wiki. Just pause on that one for a second and try and think of any other game that happens.
The game will happily offer you missions you can't complete because you don't have the equipment for them. Occasionally you don't find out you don't have the right equipment until you've reached the end of the mission, at which point you may as well load the last saved game and try something else. If you just followed someone across many sectors at <100m/s to find that out .. you may not want to play x3 for a few days.
The auto-pilot is a little derpy. It's not too bad in the smaller station systems, but probably can and will kill you trying to get around the massive Terran stations. In fact the massive Terran stations are so big (and the auto-pilot so derpy) that I've managed to entirely miss combat scenarios because by the time my ship had got around the space station, they'd all been shot down. It takes that long.
In most start scenarios, you start in a pitifully underpowered ship. It's so bad that to begin with, even completing the easiest combat missions is tricky, and you can ignore 99% of the other missions because you don't have life support cargo or the money needed to do them. I can see that aspect putting a lot of people off. The beginning is just a horrible grind with none of the upgrades to make it more bearable, and not enough cargo space or cash to make trading profitable.
So what do you do? Go wiki hunting. Find some abandoned ships, get them, sell or equip them, and begin to get a slight grip on the game. Noteworthy: This is a game you will almost certainly give up on if you don't read the wiki, and if you consider grabbing a few abandoned ships via the wiki as cheating .. then you will probably give up if you don't cheat.
If you ignore all that, there is a vast, complex universe out there waiting for you to spend hours and hours carefully constructing your own empire and fleets of ships. That's your basic deal with this game. Flawed & slow vs. a lot of potential for detailed (slow) space empire building.
I'm not sure if I like it or not, but I do load it up from time to time and get a little further.
Note: My hours look low on Steam for this game, because I don't run Steam to play it.

(Note: this is a joint review of both the Terran Conflict and Albion Prelude variants of X3; thus, I'll post the same text to both.)
I **really** wanted to like this game. I *really* did. Let me explain why.
I'm a veteran video game space cadet. I played the original Elite and Wing Commander on Commodore 64, and lots like them, since. I've played EVE Online off-and-on since Trinity (~ 2007). I ***LOVE, LOVE, LOVE*** spaceflight games that are "sandbox-y" for almost as long as I've been playing video games, and that's been too long a period of time (I'm now 41).
The Egosoft team was obviously ambitious. And, in some core ways, they succeeded. But the whole thing ultimately feels rushed.
In the end... At minimum, there are five things keep me from recommending this game.
(01) - There's no clearly-evident, gradual-slope difficulty ramp, and what you see is not always what you get. One minute, you're doing something that you percieve is very easy, is in fact very easy, and you are succeeding quite well... And the next minute, you're doing something that you percieve to be (very) easy, is in fact very difficult, and ends up being effectively suicidal as a consequence. One ends up having to revert to game saves frequently before gaining a good feel for that the *real* difficulty of various things are, as trial-and-error appears to be the only logical path towards mapping out a successful long-term course of action for oneself.
(02) - The accelerated time mechanism... Isn't accellerated enough. 600% of real-time is the max; in fact, it should be variable, with max *at least* %1,000, given the distance between various objects of interest, and the max velocities of the majority of craft in the game (esp. in the early game). Expect to spend LOTS of time simply staring at your screen whilst you travel from place to place. For me... It got *really* old after a while. Asteroid mining in EVE Online came to mind - a great "second screen" experience whilst your primary focus is on something else (work-related?)... But boring-as-hell if you have nothing else to do at that time. Or, at least, it *would* be a great second-screen experience, if the next line-item wasn't true.
(03) - The auto-pilot is borderline suicidal. It's certainly borderline schitzophrenic. At minimum, it's not consistently reliable for what one would expect to rely upon an autopilot for: performing the mundane, common tasks associated with piloting a craft, without harming the vehicle or its contents. Simply put... It's difficult, if not impossible, to "trust" the autopilot within confined, or crowded, space... Which means its use is circumstantial... Which erodes the value of such. (IMO, anyway.) It results in lots of time "babysitting" the craft when (IMO) one shouldn't have to. If this one thing were fixed... I would borderline-recommend this game for use as at least a "second screen" experience (as described above). But, as it presently stands, I would distrated too often by my "babysitting duties". :-(
(04) - The tutorial sub-system is *far* from complete. I appreciate the fact that Egosoft respects their customer base enough to deliberately avoid "hand-holding them" through everything... And I actually *like* the idea, in concept, of forcing the player to learn the majority of the game through actual experience. But there are better ways to do the latter - EVE Online provides some excellent examples. For a game this complex... Just teaching them how to move around, and them leaving them to their own devices, with one having to traverse the majority of their local solar system in order to learn enough subsequent basics to gain an idea as to what their options are (much less decide upon a course of action in the direction they wish) is a bit ridiculous, IMO. It's as if the game's creators expected anyone buying the game to have prior experience with a variety of similar-genre games in the past, such that they would "just know" what their options are, thus lessening the tutorial/ training burden. It's pretty lame, in this respect.
(05) There's no context-sensitive help to speak of (that I could see), beyond short descriptions of various items/ entities. I could forgive (04) if there was strong (05) present... But there isn't. I shouldn't feel obligated to alt-tab to/from my web browser to search the web for basic how-tos, as I play along, to make up for the lack of available in-game documentation.
In short... This game feels like it was the work of a small, highly-ambitious, highly-skilled development team... Who hit a budgetary/ deadline wall before this could be fully baked... And, like many rushed programming projects... The documentation is the first to be sacrificed at the altar of timelines and budget constraints.
Again... I would *really* like to recommend this game... But, as I've played it over the last few days... I just can't. And that makes me sad. :-(

Though this game isn't developed by Rocksteady, it's still really damn good! It overall captures the spirit of the previous two titles, even with the new voice cast (who actually did a really great job at sounding like younger versions of the characters we know from Asylum and City). They story is also really solid and it's cool to see how they met Batman for the first time. They also really stepped up the whole detective element of the game, and it is now really awesome and ties in a lot better to the story than it did in the previous installments. It does have it's negatives though. For example the camera angles can be really annoying in a few of the missions, but it's still playable. The controls can at times be unresponsive, but then again, nothing game-breaking. It also has a few issues regarding the pc version. To make the game playable, you have to sacrifice the extra details by disabling anything that requires DirectX 11, because it causes a number of issues. If you do that however, you are left with a smoothly running game (except for the saving icon which at times can cause a second of stutter). Other than that, you have yourself a very good game that is worth picking up, even if it isn't on sale!
Pros: The most badass batsuit to date, great voice acting, really awesome storyline, solid and flowing combat, better detective elements, good graphics.
Cons: DirectX 11 will make the game unplayable, saving icon can cause a very slight stutter when shown, controls can sometimes be unresponsive, a few of the missions have some really stupid camera angles.
9/10

Don Bradman Cricket 2017: a review......
The game has now been extensively patched and gameplay really is the best a cricket game has ever been. If you bought this game and have put it to one side, take it out again and give it a new chance with the latest patches. it really is a whole new ball game: get it? :)
Don Bradman Cricket is the worthy successor to Don Bradman 14. The attention to detail and the depth of gameplay is quite amazing. The fact that you can now choose to play either as a female or male cricketer is fantastic.
I myself have been playing the game the last week and can quite clearly say it is the best cricket game ever made; ever! And I have played them all and always been thoroughly dissapointed.
Everyone is entitled to their own opinion and of course eerything depends on wha you are hoping or looking for in a game and whilst DBC still needs some tweaking and polishing it has all the ingredients present to make it a classic and I have full confidence that BA wil do jut that.
The Don Bradman series is different because it caters to such a wide range of tastes: want a quick fire 5 over bash? No problem. Want a five day test match? Done! And both variations give a realistic and satisfying game.
The level of editing now available is mind-boggeling and thanks to the talents of many in the community you can download your favourite players, kits, teams, bats and even stadiums.
I myself am setting up my own custom league and making a number of small town stadium to go along with them. I would never have thought that that would be possible in a cricket game.
Another great addition are the game play modifiers so that you can now tweak every aspect of gamkeplay so it suits your own needs: need more time to judge the pace and length of the ball? That is now possible along with a whole array of other modifiers such as bounce, friction, front-foot anticipation....the list goes on!
Cricket is a complicated game consisiting of many types of cricket and each area of discipline (batting, bowling and fielding) has its own dynamic and skills: these are really well catered for in DBC17 and you really have the sense of being part of a bigger picture where everything matters down to the tiniest detail.
Another plus is that the team making the game are themselves very passionate about the game and have listened intently to to the community, striving to bring the game both the hard-core cricket fan and the casual gamer can enjoy.
I think they have done a really good job in presenting players with the possibility to find there own particular niche within the game.
They are committed to bringing tweaks and patches where needed and listening for feedback as to where the game needs some good old spit and polish.
Having already spent many hours on this game i can highly recommend it to every cricket lover: yes it will take a little bit of learning: but thats what you want out of a game: the satisfaction of developing your skills and seeing that pay-off in the field of play. On the other hand there are so many modifiers and custom modes that you can just strap straight up and bash your way to glory as your favourite cricketing hero.
Conclusion: should you get this game? If you like cricket: yes! The game oozes cricket in all it's infinite subtleties.

If you come into this game expecting cricket 2K17 or EA Sports Cricket then you will be disappointed, with more games than just this one.
What I have found playing so far:
Positives
1. Batting is challenging and fun. It requires actual timing and skill.
2. Bowler AI is much improved over DBC 14 and is constantly changing it up.
3. My Career mode, player creation is much improved and offers greater depth.
4. Visually better than DBC 14, yes the lighting is different but is more natural. (Grass blades people, grass!)
5. Pitch variation: The pitches are much more dynamic this time around. Without saying much, you should pay attention to the pitch report as different bowler types will be more effective than others.
6. Getting singles is much easier and more natural this time around, fielders are effective (most of the time - club cricketers are meant to be fairly average =) )
7. Ball physics are much enhanced, although there are times where it bounces more than a tennis ball lol.
8. Stadium creator is neat, could be a bit more robust but heu - Stadium creator!
9. Customisation is quite remarkable from logos, teams, kits etc to setting up your grade league in my career (I reccomend creating a few rural type grounds for this part of the career as the defaults are proper stadiums. I don't recall my local team playing at the MCG lol.)
Cons:
1. Commentary is pretty bad, and by bad I mean horrendous. Fortunatly, if you mute it, the sound effects and ambience make for quite the relaxing time.
2. A few visual bugs that I have encountered: namely, stuttered animations in fielding and replays. Not a biggie as I'm sure this will be fixed later.
In Summary:
If you like cricket and cricket likes you then DBC 17 is a fine game. Just for the love of god don't expect a 2K or EA game.

After the disappointment of Post Mortem I was relieved to find this game is as great as I had been led to believe.
In comparison to Post Mortem, this game still has a hard coded 4:3 aspect screen resolution but crucially it does not crash all the time when the game loses focus. The horrible first person camera is gone. The annoying branching dialogue that could result in you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a character so you miss out on crucial information has been replaced with a much simpler system. The interface is generally much better all round. There are no randomly appearing items in this game which makes things more satisfying as instead of back tracking across every location you can just remember where you saw a suitable item.
The story in this game is excellent, it really engaged me and kept me wanting to play on. The split between the two interconnected murder investigations was very well done.The puzzles are also very good, they are all very logical and don’t feel arbitrary. Most of them are quite simple but the more challenging ones take a bit of thinking about but are very satisfying.
I did encounter one bug though. The mouth movements didn’t work properly, the characters either kept their mouths closed or they rapidly flickered open and closed. This is only a very minor thing and in no way detracts from this excellent point and click adventure. I don’t think you are going to miss out on anything significant if you entirely skip Post Mortem and just start with this game.

I'll start off by telling that Still Life is the second game of a trilogy. Post Mortem, introduces one of the protagonists, Gus McPherson but playing the prequel is not mandatory to understand what's going on, although it can help in understanding some of the background story. This game itself ends in a cliffhanger, so playing Still Life 2 is necessary to complete the story.
You play as Victoria McPherson who is a young FBI agent in Chicago with a reputation for ignoring procedure. She's investigating a series of brutal murders. When visiting her father during the holidays, she has a peek into her Grandfather Gus's trunk. He was a PI in the 20's and it seems that one of his last cases bears an eerie similarity to the one Victoria is investigating now.
The game allows you to use forensic tools such as dusting for fingerprints, using a revealer spray to show cleaned up blood stains, taking photographs and looking for bits of clothing or hair left on the scene but it's used sparingly. Some of the puzzles definitely require the use of a walkthrough and keep in mind that the game switches protagonists on occasion between Victoria and Gus.
While it may not be one of the best or innovative adventures ever, it certainly is one of my personal favorites.

An odd 2D, or turn-based RPG in an even more odd setting (a science fiction, real world-based one where you fight viruses, in this case), which sees you enter metroidvania type worlds with several stages and a boss at the end of each stage, through a melancholic, sad hub, in order to avert an incoming crisis which will affect you and the other characters. Also, the game doesn't let you save your progress at will, and instead auto saves most actions and forces you to deal with failure. Yes, it does sound like Demon's Souls, and while there are no gameplay similarities, I felt it was worth mentioning how similar the atmosphere and pacing of the game was; the difficulty, too. Even if I didn't consciously acknowledge it at the time thanks to all the differences in gameplay, the atmosphere, pacing and structure of the game are basically identical to Demon's Souls, and that similarity really drew me in, and might draw you in. Anyways, the gameplay is unique, in that there are three sorts of gameplay (and small Zelda 1 dungeon style mini-dungeons); the solemn management and searching of the hub world night time management, when you enter a robot's simulated world, with the ruleset of a metroidvania shooter, and when you enter a boss battle, where you go into a turn-based RPG battle where accumulated, I guess I'd say, 'stat tokens' which you've picked up in the metroidvania gameplay add to the stats of all your characters during the fight. I have to say that the story, pacing, atmosphere and enigmatic nature of the game drew me in at the start, but I think that the game escalates the difficulty carelessly. You get some fast-paced challenging fights early on, but the game quickly makes literally every RPG battle consist entirely of one-shot attacks very quickly, ruining the chance to have a more sensible difficulty curve, and also making some boss fights simply too unforgiving.
I would have liked this game, but the boss fights feel far too difficult. Seriously, it feels like you have to do things perfectly to win some of the mid-game and late-game fights, and it feels like the sort of design that is only intuitive to the developer.
In conclusion, I really, really wanted to love this game. The bleak atmosphere and story, the spectacular characterisations of the Derelicts (the robots), their virtual worlds, and their fall from grace, the surprisingly great, if odd and idiosyncratic presentation, set in a world where humans have already died out, the combination of several genres, the lack of hand holding, and the very compelling story. I just think that the game's too hard, and personally, I can't say whether I recommend this game or not. I think I recommend it, solely because I want a sequel to the game so badly; just, hopefully next time, the boss fights aren't so ridiculous, and the metroidvania areas slightly more distinguishable and less maze-like.

Note: This game is in Pre-Alpha This reveiw will be updated over time as they add new features.
What is it? Astroneer is set during a 25th century gold rush where players must explore the frontiers of outer space, risking their lives and resources in harsh environments for the chance of striking it rich.
On this adventure, a player’s most useful tool is their ability to shape their world, altering the terrain and extracting valuable resources from planets, and moons. Resources can be traded or crafted into new tools, vehicles, and modules to create everything from massive industrial bases to mobile rover bases.
Gameplay is interesting and engaging. The typical starting scenario goes as follows:
Choose your astroneer from the Exo Dynamics launcher and press launch. You will land on a random Terran planet. At this point you will explore the surrounding area and start building up your base using various materials around your lander.
As your base grows you will unlock more and more features via research. This includes Rovers, trucks, Spaceships and all kinds of other stuff. Some of which isn't even in the game yet. Building your own vehicles and spaceships is quite rewarding and taking them to different planets is also a very intriging feature.

Comparing this game to Arkham Asylum (AA) and Arkham City (AC). Prior knowledge of these would be preferable if you want to get the most out of this review.
Combat:
Pretty much the same as AC. If you liked that improved version over AA then you're pretty much golden. I think the overall number of enemies you fight at once is a bit lower though. The downside here is that the base game offers also exactly the same types of enemies (standard, armored, gun or melee weapon) and the same ways to combat them. It's pretty much 100% the same game in terms of combat, which might have been a bit of a missed opportunity.
Gadgets:
Same as combat. You have access to pretty much the same gadget as in AC with 1 notable exception: The line launcher is gone and replaced by a different version. You can now only use it on certain anchor points but you can also use it to do takedowns, etc. Apart from that cryo bombs are glue bombs, but work exactly the same. Again, no improvements or differences.
Graphics:
Also no noticable differences to AC.
Setting:
Even the setting is basically the same as AC. The map seems to have been expanded a bit and some land marks in my opinion are at another place than in the AC map, but apart from that you're still going to see the Church, the Courthouse, the GCPD, the Steel Mill, etc. Of course this Gotham has not been turned into a prison yet, but even Wonder Tower is there, but not accessible. The most notable differences here are the Gotham Bridge and some in building areas like the Hotel. Of course it's winter again...what's nice though is that there's no more maze like underground complex. Overall it's ok, but not ground breaking.
Collectibles:
This might be a plus for some, but a negative point for others. Personally I like that the number of collectibles has been SIGNIFICANTLY reduced compared to AC. More than AA, but not too many. You're also not going to have too much of a hard time collecting them all, because as in AC you can interrogate Riddler's men to get the location of the "extortion data" (no trophies this time) and most are quite easy to spot when you know where to look for. Some require some rudimentary puzzle skills, but if you've played AC those won't pose any kind of problem. The informants are also conveniently placed on your map and by the time you have acquired all gadgets you will only have to backtrack to like 3 inside locations (or 4 perhaps) and you know you'll have them all. It's more convenient than AC. There's also some "tags" to scan for Gotham story information. And you can scan some "plaques" for a short side quest. These are however not displayed on your map, so it's up to you to find them all. Gone are the riddles though, which is kind of a shame, since those very quite fun. Overall you will still have to invest a few hours to "catch them all".
Crime scenes:
These are also back again, but have been improved over AC. There's still not much player input or thinking required, but they're well presented.
Side missions:
These are this time centered around 8 "individuals", small quest lines so to speak. They're a nice distraction and give you some information into the up and coming bad guys for the most part. One of them can only be started after the game has been beaten.
Story (possible spoilers below):
The story is overall good I'd say. Some characters don't get to shine enough, some are "different".
Boss fights:
Initially the story revolves around you being targeted by 6 Hitmen (Electrocutioner, Deathstroke, Shiva, Firefly, Bane, Copperhead plus Killer Croc as an added bonus). The boss fights are for the most part rather boring and badly executed to be honest. More below:
Overall the game is ok, but not brilliant. It also still has quite a few bugs. Thankfully those could all be resolved by reloading a check point...but still.
Multiplayer:
Just the same as AC really, but you get to fight as Deathstroke for whatever reason as well. Why not the other bad guys too? And make them a bit more different...Deathstroke feels different. He's weightier. Apart from that there's just Bruce Wayne as a DLC character...yay
DLC:
Apart from Cold Cold Heart it's forgettable, unless you want to heavily dive into MP. One DLC adds Bruce Wayne as a playble character into the MP game...yay. He plays a bit like Catwoman from AC, but I had honestly hoped this would be about Bruce Wayne becoming Batman as the title suggests...nope.
Cold Cold Heart:
This DLC puts you up against Mr. Freeze. It's actually quite enjoyable apart from the increased difficulty. I have no idea why it's not possible to change the difficulty of the DLC in Arkham games, because if you just want to enjoy the game you're out of luck. The DLC is definitely not on "easy", meaning you die with about 4 gunshots and somehow countering is also less forgiving. The overall story is nice, the presentation as well, but it drags on a bit. The final boss fight, however, is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ It is reminiscent of the fight against Freeze in AC, but not nearly executed as well...missed opportunities.

The first Batman game I owned was Arkham City, which was a total disaster, even though there were many good reviews of it, and from there I deducted that the whole Arkham Series is just really terrible, but Arkham Origins proved otherwise. A really great game, Arkham Origins brings you back to way before Batman became the crime-fighting vigilante we all love today. If you have not played any of the Arkham Series before, and want to get Arkham Origins as your first, I would totally recommend it, as it has a better graphic quality than the other Arkham Episodes, and it is filled with rich detective work, and crime fighting as well as the storyline is very captivating, a must have for any Batman fans.
However, this game is like all other Batman games, really confusing & dark. Many times, this game will just give you a dead end, and unless you are Albert Einstein, you will take ages to solve it, and end up consulting an Arkham Origins guide online. After enabling hints in the game, I realised that it barely helped at all, it only tells you when to 'Counter' or 'Strike', the hints does not help you solve the puzzles. The few things I've learnt from playing this game is that you should make use of your surrounding, and check every corner as well as please use your damn Batman Sensor (Press 'x'), as it will tell you which object can be interacted with. It also taught me to read every conversation and do not skip it, as many clues are hidden within it.
This game is definetely worth the price it was put up for ($20), and I'm lucky to snatch this game for a cheap $5, even after the sales, anyone hesitating to buy this game should just buy it, as it is filled with many difficult puzzles to solve, a good open world environment, many side quests/missions & lastly a really good community that will help you at all cost to solve any problems you might encounter.
Do take note, however, if you are playing on Windows 10, you need to disable DirectX 11, if not the game will seriously bug out & crash. Learn how to do so in the Arkham Origins community hub.
Overall a really good game, and the best in the Arkham Series, I'm rating it 8/10

I didn't write a lot of review, in fact this may be my very first one, but I think this game deserves it. For at least 6 months, a friend told me repeatedly to play Ori, which was in his opinion one of the best game of those last years. I had a lot f game to finish/play first, so I didn't play it for a while. Then, after finishing my last one, I wondered why not giving Ori and the Blind Forest a try.
Well, I'm glad I did.
I'm not a huge fan of platformers (for example, I never finished trine), but I found the journey with Ori to be really pleasing. I consider myself as a serious gamer, and this game was able to mix story, music AND challenge very well. The game slowly requires to use more and more of the tools you've at disposal, and you'll need reflexes AND a brain to finish the game (I played in hard, no idea if the timers are different in the other difficulty levels.
To sum up :
Pros :
-> Story simple yet very effective, without the usual "bad guy evil because he's the bad guy".
-> Music really, really good (one of the game you don't want to "press any key" because of the menu song). I'm gonna keep an eye (and ear) on Gareth Coker
-> Gameplay challenging
-> Good set of skills at disposal
-> Graphics are beautiful
Cons :
-> Pretty short. I did the game with 100% exploration (yeah, I REALLY liked the game) in about 12 hours in hard difficulty. You can do it in way, way less, since more than half of that was to look for those very last % of exploration.
Long story short, Ori and the Blind Forest was as a great journey.

This is gotta be one of the worst, most poorly designed games i've ever had to suffer through (right next to Metroid Prime, Last of Us and Bubsy 3D). The worst offender being how sluggish and unresponsive character is and how utterly awful and devoid of any talent the level design is. For the specific example - the water escape part of the tree level. That was the absolute worst level i had ever  played in my 20 years of gaming.
Aside from that:
Game looks pretty but distinctly lacks a good style, masking it beneath the shining effects (which is cute for the first 5min and after that you start to realise how extremely tacky and distasteful it is). More than that, "artsy" visuals make it hard to see what's actually going on on the screen half f the time.
Buttons for the controller are non-remapable (ok, peasants don't need that - but we're on PC right now, so what the hell?).
Game loves to put combat in your face. Sadly, the "combat" in this game consists of nothing more than mashing the attack button. The rest is up to your auto-targetting projectile over which you have no control of.
Main character may seem small, fast and agile, but don't be fooled! Play has hitbox about 1.5 size of the sprite, you move like a pregnant snail and jump about as well. And don't hold high hopes for double jump. You know how double jump in most games either gives you a second full fledged jump or at least half of one? In Ori it's more of a gentle nudge that gives you *some* horizontal momentum and that's about it. No vertical one - at best it slows down your freefall for a moment.
Skill tree. Why the ♥♥♥♥ is it even there? You only have 3 paths (so forget about any non-linearity) and upgrade costs jumps from 1 to 2 to 3 at the equal intervals along all of them meaning you're gently but firmly encouraged to just stick to buying all of them gradually. More than that, most of those skills are just awful (design-wise): one whole tree is dedicated to doing slightly more damage with your attacks (see above), that's it. The other one is mostly consist of shoving you collectibles on the map. And it's not a single upgrade - oh no, it's split into 4 or 5 separate ones - one for each thing being shown. OF the remaining last branch half of the skills are unlocks for slightly upgraded versions of your abilities, THAT  YOU CAN BUY BEFORE YOU GET THE ABILITY ITSELF. I'm not ♥♥♥♥ing joking.
To say nothing about the fact that you have to sit/"play" through a 10min (i'm not kidding) long interactive cutscene to get to the gameplay.
And speaking of gameplay - wouldn't it be fun if enemy and hazard damage scaled with the amount of health you have, meaning you could never take more than 3 ma-aybe 4 hits? Yep. What's the point of collecting health upgrades then? Beats me.
And the cherry on the cake? You know those awful stages in platformers when there is an insta-kill screen-wide threat moving from one side of the screen and you have to run for your life in the opposite direction through the various obstacles? Wouldn't it be great if the threat was rubberbanded so it no matter how good of a progress you make it would instantly catch up to you so you could never slow down even for a moment. But not the opposite, oh no - slow down for a moment and treat gets you - no rubberbanding in this direction.
In conclusion, if you want to play a good metroidvania - play Hollow Knight. Avoid this piece of rubbish at all costs.

Nuke Town is basically just the Nacht Der Untoten of this game, a map that people can just play on and have fun, but the randomness of the perks and PaP ruins the map mostly. I think the elevator system in Die Rise to be odd, plus the lack of PHD Flopper makes the map annoying. Buried is obviously awesome, with the Raygun Mark 2, Round Infinity, and the Remington New Model Army (which should have been in Origins, but isn't for some reason). Origins is just Origins, we all know it and love it, and it was the beginning of Primus. Now for Mob of the Dead... it's obviously the best map in the game, just the atmosphere nails the map, the Hell's Retriever, the Blundergat, etc, etc, I love it. There are somethings I do hate about this Zombies though. For one, the two hit system, I can just never get used to it after BO3 and WW2. Two, the horrible weapon ports, the M1911, Galil, etc, they're awful. The 1911 is way too big and too loud, and why does everyone try to port it in custom BO3 maps? The one from BO1 is better. Three, the lack of PHD Flopper just ruins everything, the Mustang & Sally is ultimately useless now and I just hate that.
All in all, this game gets a 7/10, it's not perfect, not by a long shot, but it's still pretty good.

I wanted to like this game.  The game uses an open world with a very deep level of intricate trading to draw you in, but when you get there, you begin to notice a few annoying hampers to the fun.  1) Quests are given by NPCs.  The randomly generated quests are indicated by a small icon beside the station name.  Since more than one quest can be simultaneously given and these quests are divided into types which are represented by icons, you never get a correct indication of all available quests.  This is because only one icon will be displayed while multiple quests could be generated.  If on your computer you were trying to find out your Wi-Fi signal strength and all that was shown was a Sun Java update, you'd get the feeling of this annoyance.  2) Sometimes an open ended game is a good thing.  This is not one of those times.  Many of the given quests are unaccomplishable without prerequisite hardware, and this prerequisite hardware seems so vaguely indicated, so whisperingly hinted at, that it's not possible to know -- that multiple failures are the only way outside of research out of game to discover whether you'll be able to glean your needed profits from a quest or finish it at all.  This leads you to feel as though a quest is probably going to be a discouragement rather than a step towards your goals.  Again, I cannot overstate the literal impossibility of doing some of the quests.
If you can get over those qualms, and you might, you'll find an interestingly designed space-trader with a plethora of ships from drive-enabled space junk starters (we're talking PT boats here), to multiple gunned, AI piloted capitol ships which can be organized into floatillas, (we're talking the Pacific Fleet here).  Despite some unfortunately difficult hurdles, a very intelligent person with a lot of free time might have a chance at this, and the game itself has a lot of content and a lot of promise.
I give it a 3/5 for Content, Concept, and Quality minus Ease and Clarity, but no reccomendation.

Note: This game is in Pre-Alpha This reveiw will be updated over time as they add new features.
What is it? Astroneer is set during a 25th century gold rush where players must explore the frontiers of outer space, risking their lives and resources in harsh environments for the chance of striking it rich.
On this adventure, a player’s most useful tool is their ability to shape their world, altering the terrain and extracting valuable resources from planets, and moons. Resources can be traded or crafted into new tools, vehicles, and modules to create everything from massive industrial bases to mobile rover bases.
Gameplay is interesting and engaging. The typical starting scenario goes as follows:
Choose your astroneer from the Exo Dynamics launcher and press launch. You will land on a random Terran planet. At this point you will explore the surrounding area and start building up your base using various materials around your lander.
As your base grows you will unlock more and more features via research. This includes Rovers, trucks, Spaceships and all kinds of other stuff. Some of which isn't even in the game yet. Building your own vehicles and spaceships is quite rewarding and taking them to different planets is also a very intriging feature.
There are some major holes in the gameplay that become apparent later in the game. You can however expect all of this stuff to be ironed out before release.
All in all this is a VERY solid pre-alpha. I would recommend buying it if you enjoy sandbox games in the spirit of minecraft with its own unique game engine and scifi themed gameplay.

I just bought this game last night Dec. 26th in pre-Alpha V 0.2. and started playing it more today Dec. 27th. I have only played it in single player and have clocked in almost 4 hrs. worth of game play.
So far the survival and exploration elements work well together. With only having to worry about oxygen and power to live is super helpful in being able to do what you want most. Being able to wonder aimlessly and discover wreckages, find resources or materials is already a fun time. In addition to keeping and eye on thoes two meters, there seems to be a slight weather element. On the planet I spawned on there was a wind component which varies from a slight breeze to an intense dust storm that rolls by. Never knowing when the next storm comes, and what the storm may bring in, helps add additional boost of adredaline and tension in hoping none of your equipment, or yourself, blow away.
There is already a bunch of machinery you can craft and resources to collect, so this game has lots of content for you to enjoy. Among the machines there seems to be a shuttle you can build to explore the other planets that orbit yours in the sky. Although I have not yet gotten there it seems to be available. Also I have built a little rover which is fun to drive around and is super easy to maneuver.
As far as criticisms go, the game isn't optimized yet. So my decent laptop has a low frame rate. And occasionally there would be a resource in the planet's ground that there would be a portion you can not pick up. Not sure if it is picked up and the game is having a glitch or that part is just never collected. Also while driving around, the way you steer is where you look. So trying to take in the scenery around you becomes a little more trickey without stopping the car. Lastly with the driving, the vehicle seems to slide around a lot when I'm trying to stop, but there is also a possibility that it's just my planet.
BUT since this game is in the EARLY pre-alpha stages, thoes kinds of things were expected and I'm sure will be fixed by the time the game fully launches. My final thoughts is that none of the game's early problems effect it on a large scale. The resources are plentiful, the art is beautiful, and is loads of fun!
Considering this game is still being developed it is very detailed and I enjoy it a lot. Can't wait to see awesome updates in the future!

I HIGHLY recommend this game -- even if you're not into FPS, zombies, shooting, gore, or cooperation. Why? Because it's FREE. There is no payment model in this stand-alone Half-Life 2 mod even though after playing for dozens of hours, I think it deserves some monetary compensation. So what is the game about and why do I recommend it?
Well for starters the atmosphere is both gripping and exciting - trying to navigate your away through dark city streets dimly lit by burning car wrecks and the countless hordes of the undead forces the players on their heels. The game's varied soundscape, which includes such noises as the skull-splitting crack of a zombie's head from a powerful swing by fire axe, to the grumble and gurgles of nearby zombies that have yet to detect you... and from the frightened voices of teammates heard through fully-integrated in-game voice chat, to their cries for you to help them as they are mercilessly being eaten alive. The range of emotions and claustrophobia tense the player, eliciting such panic and fight-or-flight response that it may put you in danger, and cost both you and potentially others their lives.
This isn't just a concern of running and gunning - which it sometimes can be - if you have enough ammunition and want to move at a faster pace, or are at risk of being completely surrounded and devoured by the shambling masses of rotting flesh... But above all the shooting and gore, this game's also about methodical teamwork and calculated risks that serve to not frustratingly overwhelm the player, but to deepen their immersion and enrich the scope of the game into a wider breadth of enjoyment and quick-thinking.
Each element working in tandem with the next - brings both the individual player, and team together as a cohesive whole into confrontation with a vast array of challenges and threats to overcome. There's so much fun and excitement to experience in this - let me emphasize one more time - FREE GAME, that it takes a few deep breaths at the end of a successful (or perhaps unsuccessful) mission to collect one's thoughts and comprehend what in the hell just happened!
Even after playing one of the many multitudes of varied maps and gametypes - which will keep you busy and entertained dozens of play-throughs each, you will inevitably run into something new and unexpected that will give you cause for hiding in a well-lit corner to reload, rethink, and take on the masses of walkers (and some sprinters) yet again, even while bleeding profusely, or slowly losing consciousness to infection, hoping - wishing - you find the necessary medication somewhere along your travels just in time before turning into one of those... things.
The developers in my mind have literally given the PC-gaming community a gift... by both making this game, while also making it free for us all to enjoy together. Masterfully crafted and downright scary, forcing one to be quick-thinking and quick on their feet, using both teamwork and individual contribution to the misson's goals, this free stand-alone zombie survival mod, that took 7 YEARS to create is worth every second, and every penny... if pennies were involved.
Try. This. Out. Highly recommended!

I never really noticed the music save for one level, otherwise the sound design was just OK.
The game world and level design is absolutely gorgeous. For every seemingly mundane setting there was a compelling altered version of it that the game pulls you into. One memorable time was starting off in a night club that turned into a tron style hellscape featuring music based arena hazards.
Story is kind of meh. The villains were fairly simple and anyone with passing familiarity with the DMC series will know the 11th hour twist at the start of the game.
The Virgil DLC was alright but Virgil himself lacks the depth of his Brother's comabt system. Definitely needs multiple playthroughs as there are roughly 5 or so levels with one mechanic introduced in each. While this was forgivable in Dante's story because you recieved most of your tools before the halfway point, Virgil only gets one level to really use his full kit before his story ends.
Overall, worth it. The fun gameplay is the most important thing and the beautiful levels are a nice bonus.

This is gotta be one of the worst, most poorly designed games i've ever had to suffer through (right next to Metroid Prime, Last of Us and Bubsy 3D). The worst offender being how sluggish and unresponsive character is and how utterly awful and devoid of any talent the level design is. For the specific example - the water escape part of the tree level. That was the absolute worst level i had ever  played in my 20 years of gaming.
Aside from that:
Game looks pretty but distinctly lacks a good style, masking it beneath the shining effects (which is cute for the first 5min and after that you start to realise how extremely tacky and distasteful it is). More than that, "artsy" visuals make it hard to see what's actually going on on the screen half f the time.
Buttons for the controller are non-remapable (ok, peasants don't need that - but we're on PC right now, so what the hell?).
Game loves to put combat in your face. Sadly, the "combat" in this game consists of nothing more than mashing the attack button. The rest is up to your auto-targetting projectile over which you have no control of.
Main character may seem small, fast and agile, but don't be fooled! Play has hitbox about 1.5 size of the sprite, you move like a pregnant snail and jump about as well. And don't hold high hopes for double jump. You know how double jump in most games either gives you a second full fledged jump or at least half of one? In Ori it's more of a gentle nudge that gives you *some* horizontal momentum and that's about it. No vertical one - at best it slows down your freefall for a moment.
Skill tree. Why the ♥♥♥♥ is it even there? You only have 3 paths (so forget about any non-linearity) and upgrade costs jumps from 1 to 2 to 3 at the equal intervals along all of them meaning you're gently but firmly encouraged to just stick to buying all of them gradually. More than that, most of those skills are just awful (design-wise): one whole tree is dedicated to doing slightly more damage with your attacks (see above), that's it. The other one is mostly consist of shoving you collectibles on the map. And it's not a single upgrade - oh no, it's split into 4 or 5 separate ones - one for each thing being shown. OF the remaining last branch half of the skills are unlocks for slightly upgraded versions of your abilities, THAT  YOU CAN BUY BEFORE YOU GET THE ABILITY ITSELF. I'm not ♥♥♥♥ing joking.
To say nothing about the fact that you have to sit/"play" through a 10min (i'm not kidding) long interactive cutscene to get to the gameplay.
And speaking of gameplay - wouldn't it be fun if enemy and hazard damage scaled with the amount of health you have, meaning you could never take more than 3 ma-aybe 4 hits? Yep. What's the point of collecting health upgrades then? Beats me.
And the cherry on the cake? You know those awful stages in platformers when there is an insta-kill screen-wide threat moving from one side of the screen and you have to run for your life in the opposite direction through the various obstacles? Wouldn't it be great if the threat was rubberbanded so it no matter how good of a progress you make it would instantly catch up to you so you could never slow down even for a moment. But not the opposite, oh no - slow down for a moment and treat gets you - no rubberbanding in this direction.
In conclusion, if you want to play a good metroidvania - play Hollow Knight. Avoid this piece of rubbish at all costs.

This is the game for the space nerds. It's looking a little dated these days and god knows, there's more menus and options than you can shake a stick at but for the time invested, you get a huge reward. If you're a fan of space and the idea of fighting, building and trading in a reactive virtual economy, X3 Terran Conflict will blow your mind. Literally if you're not careful.
Personally, setting up my own major trade empire and exploring the farthest regions of space in my ship is an absolute joy, especially when there's something illegal burning between two fingers on my left hand and Planet Caravan by Black Sabbath playing in the background.
X3 Terran Conflict is a huge game. Although there is a "plot" or quest, you can choose not to follow it. I see it as a huge, open space sandbox that I can sink hours of blissful time and purpose in one sitting. Once you've broken through the learning curve and are used to the menus it's a real joy.
Although it does support the Xbox gamepad, it's best played with mouse and keyboard in my opinion. Don't buy this game unless you're willing to sink literally hours of your time in to the immersive universe and be prepared to do some learning ebfore you can play it properly.

This is undoubtedly the best indie game I have ever played, continuous updates and visible progression. 20XX brings back all the megaman that Mighty No. 9 failed to recreate. This game has been worth every penny I've spent on it and the co-op functionality, although finicky, has been a pleasure to play. I look forward to a few fixes regarding the boss door in co-op locking the client out, and the addition of a final boss/ boss level for after all the stage bosses. Can't wait until this game is fully finalized.
FULL RELEASE EDIT (POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD):
Final Stages:
Damn, the game has gotten so much better since this review was posted, with the inclusion of two additional stages at the end of the run, it brought a whole new challenge to the table, the final boss was quite honestly one of the most tense moments I've had in games for a long time and the musical additions with the last two stages are so sublime, the final boss especially. With the Deepstation stages, the elements of all 4 areas you've been to before are mashed together into a gruesome trek to the two new bosses, stage hazards and enemies all band together to make your life a living hell and at the end of it all are two boss fights that take everything you know and force you to apply it all at once in their own unique ways, this was incredibly well done.
Graphics/Art Style:
Aside from that major inclusion there is also a lot of smaller changes that bring the game to life. The graphical changes with the enemy designs and items look excellent, and distinguishing enemies from each other is very easy because of how colourful they are. Each projectile also has a distinct look to it and in turn it makes it easy to spot and dodge. The artist also changed up some of the level tiles and its a decision I completely agree with, seeing Perforator Alpha and Rollster Beta having different looking stages is a nice visual change and keeps the art from getting stale too quickly. One thing I'm unsure about (because of bad memory) is if there have been graphical changes to Ace and Nina since Vile Visage took over as the permanent second boss in  Frostor, BUT the two of them look a lot better than I last recall and whether thats placebo or accurate.
Online Co-op (With my friend from Peru):
The co-op netcode was also polished down so well, my co-op partner and I have run into only one netcode issue since the full release where they got stuck in the boss room ceiling, but it was easily fixable with the newly added TELEPORT TOOL and thank god this is a thing because when you're playing across continents with high latency values it serves as the duct tape for cooperative play. Don't get me wrong though, the netcode is vastly improved, before the teleport tool hit the scene my partner and I ran into netcode issues quite often and now it's only once in a blue moon so good on the developers for improving the online co-op and giving a solution to pretty much every netcode problem.
Permanent Upgrades:
Now, one thing that was also introduced was the addition of permanent upgrades which I personally don't use but I appreciate the inclusion, for the more casual player, there are upgrades you can purchase in the hub that apply to every run you start, stuff like item drops on certain levels, some chests to get you started, it's a nice way to be able to include any audience not as keen on the challenge of roguelike gameplay. The permanent upgrades of course have to be earned by playing before hand but they're some nice training wheels to get you earning soul chips for new items in future runs.
Gameplay:
Although largely unchanged, the gameplay is extremely responsive and tight and it only hiccups a bit when you're walljumping with leg powerups (mainly the hover). Ace and Nina both have their situations they do well in and do poorly in, I personally think Ace is the better character but they are both very usable! There were so many times where I couldn't get close enough to attack an enemy only to have my partner back me up from afar with Nina's buster and there are times when enemies would approach from awkward angles where the buster just can't aim towards, luckily though Ace's saber can hit above himself by a bit so it can help against Flapps on Kur and Eternal Star's stages. Which brings me to another important gameplay element, the stages themselves. The stages in the game are highly defined both visually and mechanically, Ace does better in Skytemple and Deepstation One and I find that Nina tends to do better in Deepstation Two and Vaculab just because of how they are structured. The game doesn't deter you from playing who you want in that sense but no matter who you pick, you gotta be ready for downs just as much as the ups. Jumping and dashing work excellently and wall jumping is mostly smooth (again I'm looking at you Armatort's Momentum). If I take damage I feel like it's my fault for not playing well enough, or not making the right desicions by picking up boss powers (or getting bad luck in my run). However, when you get better at the game, you notice it and it feels satisfying to get better, sure you get bad luck sometimes and sure you start out without the really good powerups but you notice your improvements as a player more than the improvements of the item drops.
Story:
I'll be the first to admit, I did not care about a story in this game I was here for the gameplay from way back when the Vile Spider was a thing. I was plesantly surprised to see an interesting story in the game. The data lore is rich and intriguing and reading up on characters like Brighton Sharp and Arlan Flat was fascinating. I was only prompted to do this though once I got through to Deepstation Two. Again, this is not a story-driven or focused game, but the little bits of story they threw in was immersive and it felt like it belonged, I really do feel attached to these characters because of this. So way to surprise me with this element I didn't think I'd see much of.
Music:
The music in the game didn't particularly stand out at the time of posting the early access review and it remains largely unchanged, I liked the Vaculab theme but there wasn't any extremely memorable track other than the menu theme for me at the time. But (as mentioned earlier) the release of the Deepstation stages and bosses, bring new tracks to the table and I LOVE them Arlan Flat's theme (which I am listening to as I write this review) is the best thing about the soundtrack, it fits the mood perfectly and keeps the action tense, the same can be said about the stage tracks but Arlan's theme honestly just blows the rest out of the water. Despite the outstanding endgame music, my opinion on the tracks from the earlier levels still stands, they aren't that memorable to me, but the music is amazing in the most important areas so it helps make up for the stages prior.
Side Notes for Devs:
So there's a bit of a thing that had me laughing I don't know if it's intentional but I just want to point it out for the devs in case it's not intentional. The wallspook power-up completely ignores Vile Visage's shield whether this is intentional or not, it kinda defeats the point of the fight if I can just sit in front of him spamming my saber and ignoring the enemies he spawns. This also happens with Arlan Flat's Omega Model (although it's a lot less gamebreaking).
Final Thoughts:
I bought this game about a year before this edit which is happening on October 29th 2017 and I have gotten so much more than what I thought I was going to get, I absolutely love this game, it showcases how to do early access right. Buy this game, enjoy all that it has to offer and show your support for the developers they worked so hard on this hidden gem of a game and I will be looking forward to any work that they do in the future.
I loved almost everything about the game, I just feel like the game needs some more memorable musical additions, that's all. Cheers Batterystaple!

Band of Outlaws is a simple 2D action platformer. You jump across several different stages in order to fight a boss at the end  whilst shooting enemies in your path (very mega man esque). This game is pretty short, but it can be replayed over and over if you want to put a speedrun aspect into it, or if you didn't pick up all the collectables throughout your first playthrough. The multiplayer is even pretty well done, it works like a deathmatch between the players and turned out to be a lot more fun than I anticipated. It's definitely worth the $5 the developer is asking.

As someone who both enjoys side-scrollers and loves Robin Hood, I really enjoyed this game. As soon as I saw the Fox Hood skin option I was desperate to unlock it (hitting my nostalgia there). It was a pretty short game; I totaled about an hour and 20 minutes of playtime by the time I completed the final boss, though that includes some backtracking after the game crashed.
I had a bit of trouble figuring out the controls at first. WASD and Space were intiutive, but it took me forever to figure out that you use the arrow keys to shoot your arrows. There was nowhere to look up key bindings, so I was just poking at different keys for a while.
The graphics and music are bright and fun, and the controls handle well. The levels have plenty of baddies to shoot (some with more spite than others- lookin' at you, OWLS) and lots of money bags to loot, while the bosses offer a nice challenge. I expect to play through the game again in the near future, and consider my money well-spent.

Batman Arkham Origins is one of the best cinematic batman games ever. Note that I said 'cinematic'.
