On the surface, Still Life is just another modern rendition of the Jack the Ripper mythos, told on two timelines. Under it hides one of the most engaging serial murder thrillers ever written for a point ‘n’ click adventure game, completed by a bit cruel, but somewhat realistic puzzles.
I’ll be honest: Still Life is my favourite adventure game. It was developed by Microïds, a French company known for their unique titles, and uses the same gameplay system that was introduced in Benoît Sokal’s Syberia. This system is also its main drawback, since it is designed for very slow play. Everything will seem sluggish, even for this genre: walking speed, dialogues, even the user interface. It’s not as bad as the old FMV adventure games, but it’s up there.
On the other hand, all the other areas in game design are almost flawless. The main character, Victoria is a little bit clichéd tough-girl FBI agent stereotype, but she quickly evolves into an interesting character. Throughout the game, she is placed into a lot of neo-gothic scenery that just oozes atmosphere, all to emphasise the urban fantasy theme of the Jack the Ripper style killings she is investigating.
The story has another side though: we learn that these killings copy events that already happened in the 1920s in Prague, and Vic’s grandfather (the protagonist of the quasi-prequel, Post Mortem) was involved in them. His segments not only offer insight, but serve as a contrast to Vic’s world with its washed out tone and almost cruel grittiness.
The plot may have sort of a fantasy vibe to it, but the gameplay doesn’t. Progressing feels quite natural and realistic, but not without obvious adventure game puzzles like the clock at the morgue or the cookie recipe. Some of them may be a little too cruel, but the reward is always worth it… even if the ending won’t give the satisfaction of closure one may expect– unless they are accustomed to modern French thrillers.

It's no coincidence that Super Meat Boy shares its initials with Super Mario Bros. This is a pure platformer that boils gameplay down to nothing but running and jumping. Meat Boy's goal is always the same: he must reach Bandage Girl, who is ever in another castle. Doing so is never an easy task thanks to the numerous dastardly traps in the way. One prick from a buzzsaw, spike, or monster's jaws will splatter Meat Boy's bloody pixels (which remain as a grisly reminder of your failure during your next attempt).

This game is an absolute masterpiece. Everything about it is flawless. The controls, artwork, music, level design, humor, and on and on. Yes, this game will punish you for your mistakes and you will ragequit, but you will come back for more. You love the pain. The pain is so worth it.

After all these years, Super Meat Boy's still a prime example of fun mechanics, airtight controls, and killer challenges all coming together to make a rock solid platformer.
Meat Boy's a simple guy with a simple mission: save his girfriend Bandage Girl from the Nefarious Dr. Fetus. He'll need to wind his way through several worlds full of saw blades, deadly salt, fireballs, and all sorts of monstrosities to come out victorious.
Meat Boy controls like a dream, with the precision physics necessary to navigate the treacherous worlds he encounters. He's fast, he can wall jump, and he leaves a juicy trail that lets you see all the paths you've taken and the unfortunate ends you've met. Some of the stages involve a number of puzzles that will have you racing the clock or collecting keys to make your way safely to Bandage Girl. The main game, while never unfair, is a considerable challenge, and if that's still not enough for you, there's a series of dastardly Dark World stages that will gladly teach you the meaning of pain. You just might discover a few warp zones here and there to mix things up too...
Super Meat Boy's got plenty of difficulty for even the most seasoned veterans, while still being straightforward enough for new players to enjoy--though the later stages may prove very difficult. Worth taking a look if platformer-puzzlers are your thing.

In it's current state, I can't recommend this game. Saying it's riddled with bugs would be hyperbolic and somewhat misleading but serves to warn the consumer as to what they're walking into upon purchasing this title.
So far, the building and resources are pretty barebones. If you've played a handful of survival games before, you know what to expect: gather resources, build things to make gathering and surviving easier, avoid environmental hazards, etc. If I'm being honest, I'd say the building is somewhat barebones.
There are enough resources in the game that you could count them on your hands and have some fingers left to sum up the things you can build. You have items that can be crafted to extend how far you can travel from your base to refil your oxygen, build solar panels to recharge your backpack to use your terraforming tool, or extend the life of either of these things. That is if the game doesn't crash on you...
Something you should know before purchasing is that it has it's share of bugs. Because of the terraforming tool you're given, there is a good chance that you'll clip your character through the floor and fall between the cave systems below and the ground above. If you plan on playing with friends, expect a crash after about 20 minutes or so. If it seems like I'm giving this game a hard time, it's because I am, but because I think this game has the potential to stand up to the likes of Don't Starve.
This game has a refreshing aesthetic coupled with a minimal art style. The game just looks good. The modular aspect of building your base is nice and simple and a good way to easy one into the survival genre. No food meter to worry about here!
TL;DR - The game looks nice, it has good mechanics, not enough stuff to build, and gamebreaking bugs.
P.S. Stop forcing me to reset the sound settings every time I boot the game up and please make it easier to join a friends' game other than through Steam! Also, it would be nice if selecting fullscreen or windowed from the launcher actually did something other than launch in windowed mode every time, no matter what choice I pick.

The game uses roguelite progression where you go between randomly-generated levels and fight bosses that are weak to eachothers powers, but when you die, you're kicked back to the Ark and have to start your run again. The progression comes from Soul Chips that certain powered-up enemies drop, which you can then spend on additional item and weapon drops that will appear in future runs once you return to the Ark.
The gameplay is very solid, especially for an early access game. It should be said that if you like Mega Man but are wary of 20XX because it's both early access and a roguelite game, it's still very much worth your time. The levels, while largely randomized, very rarely feel unfair and it's possible to clear large portions of the game without taking damage if you're skilled enough. That said, the generation isn't perfect and you can still take unnecessary hits from time to time, and the platforming sections are generally either ridiculously easy or borderline impossible without much in between.
TL;DR - 20XX is ♥♥♥♥ing great, gets constant major updates and overhauls, and is totally worth the price.

This is the game for the space nerds. It's looking a little dated these days and god knows, there's more menus and options than you can shake a stick at but for the time invested, you get a huge reward. If you're a fan of space and the idea of fighting, building and trading in a reactive virtual economy, X3 Terran Conflict will blow your mind. Literally if you're not careful.
Personally, setting up my own major trade empire and exploring the farthest regions of space in my ship is an absolute joy, especially when there's something illegal burning between two fingers on my left hand and Planet Caravan by Black Sabbath playing in the background.
X3 Terran Conflict is a huge game. Although there is a "plot" or quest, you can choose not to follow it. I see it as a huge, open space sandbox that I can sink hours of blissful time and purpose in one sitting. Once you've broken through the learning curve and are used to the menus it's a real joy.
Although it does support the Xbox gamepad, it's best played with mouse and keyboard in my opinion. Don't buy this game unless you're willing to sink literally hours of your time in to the immersive universe and be prepared to do some learning ebfore you can play it properly.
Pretty difficult game to get into as there really isn't any tutorial and it is extrememly complex.  Oce you get the hang of it you will have a blast creating and manageing your growing space empire.

Although I am reviewing Terran Conflict, I have approximately 200hrs in between it and Albion Prelude.
Simply put, if you like space shooters / simulation / strategy, this is the game you want to play, period. The gameplay is whatever you want it to be. You start off as either a merchant or mercenary, and decide what to do from there. The most impressive thing about X3 is scalability. I don't know of an example that compares to X3: Terran Conflict or Albion Prelude. There is no endgame, as you can grow yourself out to whatever lengths you like. Mods also make this game infinitely better - Terran Conflict allows for the XTM 2.0 mod, which doubles the amount of area in-game, as well as the number of spacecraft, weapons, and opportunities.
The battles in the game can go from tedious to downright impressive. The largest engagement I've been a part of was a 3-way battle between Xenon, Argon, and my own mercenary squad. Approximately 500 ships were engaged in real time, spanning from scout based fighters to massive carriers and battleships - all resolving itself in real time. No other game, no matter its pitch, has managed to do what X3: TC has done in a single player game. Given the price, it's worth a try if for nothing else than  seeing how much it can remind you of Privateer or the old Tie Fighter games. At best, it'll consume hundreds of hours while you build a galaxy-spanning trillion-credit empire with your own starship factories. So fun!

I'm thinking of doing this whenever the game I had is on sale. Maybe push someone who's on the edge on whether or not to fork out that little dollar they have or make them have a second thought of buying it. Mild spoiler ahead.
Just like other Arkham games, the combat is enjoyable and can be addicting. It's like playing rythm games but with violence and bone-breaking.You need to push the right button at the right time. With variety of enemy, you'll need to adapt to their different patterns. The additional ranking system, where your combo is judged and marked is a nice additional feature for me.
There is also more buildings you can get into compared to Arkham City which I think makes the game feels a bit fresh and new rather than feeling you play Arkham City all over again.
The predator challenge where you have to take out enemies one by one is challenging enough. Throughout the game, enemies are more adapt to your techniques. If you keep taking them out from above, they'll mine the gargoyles or ledge. Take them down from below too often, they'll throw bombs. Taking your time to knock them all out , they'll put mine traps.
You can also explore the Batcave. You can gain XP by having cheek-in-tongue conversations with Alfred who complains about bats in the Batcave. You can also have virtual combat challenges and training in it.
Though debatable, Origins might have the best story compared to other series. It has more emotional side to it. It explores Bruce Wayne as a man full of rage rather than just as his inexperience as Batman and learn what it takes to be Gotham's Knight. He learns he can't challenge Gotham alone. The villains feel really fleshed out. Great rouge galleries. Especially Bane
The story alone is enough reason to play this game. It really felt different out of all the entry in the series.
If Arkham Knight suffers from bad port, this game suffers from questionable game design. I'll nitpick the little ridiculous bit first. Why Batman, master of combat can't break thin wooden plank. That's like the first thing you break if you learn martial arts. In the game, you have to explode it with the explosive gel.
The map design to say controversially, is lazy. A big part of it is literally a revised copy of Arkham City. They do make it bigger by adding additional area but that only make travel through the city feels more like a chore. This has to do with Batman's navigation ability. Batman can grapple boost to a building to travel faster. Problem is the speed of his glide and grapple boost is the same in Arkham City. Batman's navigation mechanics and the speed may work in moderately sized, condensed map as in Arkham City but not when it's big as in Origins. I think it needs to be faster.
To be fair, they had relatively little development time. And the publisher, the infamous WB more or less wants this game to be made just to keep the hype for the franchise alive as Arkham Knight took 4 years to complete.
The nygma challenges and collectibles is such a drag as you have to backtrack anything you missed in the huge empty buildings with nothing to do as you had cleared the enemies earlier in the game.
The story is great. IMO, the strongest out of all the series but I can't help but feel it was just a retold of separate stories that had been written in the comics which was tailored together perfecly. The man who laughs, The Killing Joke, it's all there. Tailored together and was changed here and there. The other two series Asylum&City, though inspired by the events in comics, their story stands on their own.
Was this game worth your time? Yes, definitely but I suggest you play Arkham City first. I think it will give you a feeling of an expansion from the previous game. Deathstroke's fight is great, Anarky's a great philosophical fight and the DLC is the best out of all Arkham series's DLC. The cold,cold heart and Bruce Wayne's training in Korea/Japan(I don't know. I think there's a cultural mix-up in the dlc).

Still Life introduces you into a crazy serial killer case that went on for several centuries leaving bloody traces in different parts of the world recently leading to Chicago…
You are playing the main character “Vic” who is an FBI Agent leading the investigation of the recent Chicago murders. She soon gets personally involved as her family seems to be connected to the investigation from the past. Here it is going to get really interesting. You are jumping back in time and witness some elaborated places in Prague in the 20’s playing Vic’s granddad who was the former PI in a very similar case. While stranded in the past and finding out how everything started you get interrupted by reality, just as new information comes up for our present investigation. While talking to possible suspects and witnesses, doing usual detective work (including going rogue after an argument with the boss, being suspended and facing the bad guys on your own), you will also discover some brutal murder scenes.
You will be presented action scenes, outstanding storytelling and good character development. The gameplay requires some getting used to, especially the use of the inventory. While playing, you can easily miss out on objects, but you do not carry a lot of things at the same time, so putting everything in a useful combination is pretty obvious, but it did not bother me that much. And, like a typical point-and-click game, you also have to solve some puzzles (most people say this is unrealistic and dull, but I always like that most in such kind of games…).
At first I thought it would be just a usual point-and-click adventure, but afterwards I would say it is one of the best games I played in a long time. The case you have to investigate is getting under your skin - I seldom played such a thrilling point-and-click adventure. Released in 2005 the graphics are not the finest, but it is still enjoyable. The amount of settings is enormous and I praise that the story kept its mystery elements until the end. The sound acting was really good, even though not always in sync. In contrast to the second part (I have not bought it yet, but it has lots of negative reviews, so…) you cannot do anything wrong with this game - especially if it is on sale.

Since i saw A TON of overly polarized reviews on this game, im gonna try and give a critical one on this game
Lets start of with the worst: the story of this game is mediocre to cheesy, the characters are rather shallow and flat and the dialogues are boring at best amd cringeworthy at worst. Which is realy sad since there are a lot of good ideas, they simply arent worked out (the "transformation" of dante as a bad boy to an upstanding person, the demon society-thing as a form of social criticism, vergil becoming the bad guy... you get the idea) I have not played the original DMC-Games, so i can not comment on the development of Dante as a character coming from this point of view (although the "not in a million years"-scene kind of looked like a slap in the face to older fans IMO) All of that said however i think that this game ABSOLUTELY doesnt need a good story.
Now to the atmosphere: this game has one of the most imaginative and beautifull leveldesigns ive seen in a long time, my personal favourite being the mirrored demon-prison on the bottom of the lake. Enemies and bosses blend well into their "habitat", the way to the end of the level actually makes sense gameplay-wise and the secrets are mostly well integrated.
The biggest + in my opinion is the soundtrack: OH MY GOD, i would die to see combichrist live and i had no idea that noisia is that ♥♥♥♥in good. That big plus however can turn the game into a nightmare if you dont like industrial and DnB tho, as the music is heavily integrated into the gameplay. In my humble opinion however something like this is much more fitting than classical music a la Final Fatasy or Legend of Zelda
NOW TO THE CORE: THE GAMEPLAY
Im a little torn with this: the controls are very good, responsive, fast and i even think that its not always required to have a lock-on (but thats up to you). The melee-weapons are all strong and usefull at some point, the main-weapon being the best IMO and combos are very fluent and diversable. Ranged weapons however are mostly garbage, only the shotgun has some uses as safety-net AOE-knockback. The enemies are just a tiny bit to easy and the bossfights are not realy THAT challenging (except for the final fight.One of THE BEST bossfights ive had in a hacknslash). Big - is how fast the game hands out S rankings. Its realy darn easy to get SSS-rankings in fights and S rankings at the end of the level.
Summary:
One of the coolest soundtracks ive heard, great atmosphere however little replayabilty, rather easy and very boring story
Recommend it for beginners of the HackSlash-genre or if you just feel like slicing up some demons to a beer in the evening

This is the coolest game I've ever played. I'm a big fan of stylish, intricate, fast paced and varied combat, but often combat like that is difficult to perform in video games - requiring you to master some kind of clunky weapon changing system. DmC does a great job of making a plathora of weapons and an even larger plathora of combo moves for each one very intuitive and accessible. This means you can get wrapped up in the story and illustrate it with beautiful fights without the frustration of a "learning curve" for controls. I looked at the list of moves available and thought I would never be able to use them all, but before I knew it I was handling a mob of enemies with 5+ different weapons at once and looking like a badass. Maybe some hardcore players will find it too easy, but you can choose the difficulty setting and then unlock even more difficult settings.
I highly recommend using a gamepad like the Xbox 360 controller to play.
Combat is definitely the central and most impressive feature of this game, but there are other great things to be said of it as well. It looks great; it's gritty and bloody but doesn't feel like a boring gorefest because fo the imaginative "limbo" world where the streets split apart before your eyes and chunks of the world become floating platforms. The story isn't legendary but it fits the gameplay perfectly. The voice acting is good, and although he starts off as a brat I came to like the nuances of Dante the main character. He's pretty easy on the eyes, too..
The story doesn't take long to get through but you are encouraged to play the missions many times over to find hidden items, increase your score, and try new difficulties. Since the controls are intuitive and accessible, you could easily put this game down for a while and come back to it to keep working on your scores. I didn't have any complaints as I played it. Some people pointed out that the boss fights were a bit of a let down, and maybe it's sort of true. But for whatever they lack in challenge, they sure make up in imaginative and horrifying creepiness.
I highly recommend this game if you want some fast paced action, and you don't have to be a hardcore gamer to enjoy it.

A very charming multi-genre game with beautiful yet surreal enviroments and a nice soundtrack. You play as a coffee machine named Coffee (or rather, a thing in the body of Coffee) in a space station named "Lun Infinus". You enter the rooms in it to find the "Derelicts" (giant robots). In the rooms of them you can also enter a simulation in which they are also present. Simulations are the 2D platformer sections of the game. Each simulation has different goals and upgrades you can buy from the robots.
In some more hidden sections within these simulations are sub-simulations (a simulation within a simulation). Sub-simulations have wireframe graphics and work similarly to the original The Legend of Zelda (and look kinda like FNaF minigames). You and your rabbit (which only appears here, may I add) go from room to room until some monsters start appearing. Defeating a monster will make a cabbage patch appear which your rabbit then eats and you get some bits for it (bits are the currency of this game). There's also a place to buy upgrades here but I won't go too much into it. The main goal of sub-simulations is actually to unlock conditionals for battles.
Speaking of battles, they're probably the best part of the game! Within these JRPG-like battles, your creepy Derelicts fight against even creepier viruses. I won't go too much into getting to battles because I don't really want to spoil much. If you want to level up your derelicts for said battles, you'll need to go outside during the night phase when simulations are disabled and find some items they happen to collect.

Fantastic fun and very much the Megaman X-X4 reboot you've wanted.
Nitpicky cons:
The levels lack that handcrafted elegance that the X games achieved, chiefly in X4. There are times that the procedural pieces are so big and unintegrated that you'll see them every other playthrough, and some so small that the level starts to feel clunky and inelegant.
The powerups leave you less with a sense of progression and more a sense of some number variable going up. You can easily give yourself way too much or too little speed to survive. This is, I think, a part of the charm of the game but it's a stark departure from the lands of Megaman X past, where a powerup is a powerup.

DmC: Devil May Cry is an EPIC, dark fantasy slash-everything-you-see game with some awesome personality to it. Personally, I have not played the original Devil May Cry games, so if you are a fan, I can not guaruntee you will enjoy this as it seems to be quite different, but from the perspective of a newcomer, this game is purely epic.

This game was so much fun it's redick. Let's start by saying, I have never played any of the Devil May Cry games. My opinion is based soley on THIS game. The story isn't as bad as others made it sound like. It was not terrible and I'm okay with saying I actually enjoyed it. I only skipped one cutscene by accidnet. The voice acting is not bad, it's just the writing at times can be a little corny. But I'll always remember what my mom taught me, some of the best science fiction has had some small amount of corny there. Fiction and fantasy require you to open up your imagination. Which is a good transition for the level design and art work. It is amazing. The scenery is super cool and it really drew me in. The fighting, oh my, the fighting! The movement and the combat is unlike anything I've ever played. It reminded me like a mix between God of War and Prototype. But better. Extremely better. I only wish it was longer, but that's always a good sign. I would recommend this game to anyone that likes a good old hack 'n slash. It's fluid movement and compelling combat will make you wonder why more games weren't this good. I will be looking out for more Ninja Theory games coming to PC.

Despite all this, on its own terms, DMC is a fun hack'n slash with a cool setting, tons of weapons to play with, mostly smooth and fluid controls (though the camera and auto aim can be more deadly than the monsters sometimes), and an appropriately rockin soundtrack.  Reboots are always gonna be met with resistance, but this one, I think, did it right. I saw this game in my discovery queue one day, saw that it was free, so I looked at the screenshots to see if I should get it. It looked interesting, so I said to myself "eh, why not" and downloaded it. I started playing it and was very pleasantly surprised. I expected a crappy little Mario rip off and got a cool little game with a witty attitude. I fell in love with the game in the first section of dialogue, to tell the truth. The gameplay itself is a bit wonky, but I've forgiven it for being so much fun. Anyway, after I had been playing for a little while, I loaded up the game and got another little surprise. This game was actually made by Scott Cathon, the same man who made the Five Nights at Freddy's series. This was the biggest surprise that I got because this game is extremely creative and takes little to no inspiration from popular opinion like the FNAF series does. For those of you who don't know what I mean by this, a TON of people are scared of anamatronics, so it only makes sense to make a horror game with them as the main antagonists. While this isn't a horror game, you can see some creepy-looking things in it. There's actually a simulation where you can see something that looks a bit like Freddy Fazbear in structure.*
PROS AND CONS
Pros:
-Very creative
-Humorous
-Witty
-Interesting
-Well-written
-Lovable characters
-Beautiful pseudo-3D environment
-Interesting 3D design (there are 3D areas inside simulations)
-Made by Scott Cawthon (if you like his work)
Cons:
-Wonky control scheme
-A bit confusing
-A bit slow
-Difficult
-Made by Scott Cawthon (if you don't like his work)
So final verdicts? This game is AMAZING and would be worth a cheap price. However, it's free, so no one has an excuse - you NEED to play this amazing game. An honest 10/10 for this game.
*This game was made before FNAF was even an idea, so I know it's not an Easter Egg, but it's still cool to see how his skills in modeling has developed

Nowadays, the same cannot be said.
The only real reason you should be playing this game is the character customization. There's just simply no other game that actually has a detailed character editor that lets you put custom symbols on your character/character's clothing. Symbol and car customization are pretty weak on the other hand, due to the high limitations of the editor (Up to 100 layers for a symbol, annoying customization bar for cars doesn't let you place more than a couple of complex symbols without preventing you from saving). However, to get the most out of the editors, you'd have to buy premium otherwise your customization options are extremely limited (25 Layers for a symbol/3 symbols for clothes and character/7 symbols for cars). Also, a good amount of clothing options are locked away unless you pay a certain amount of money for them (Some things cannot be bought seperately and requires you to buy things in packs that can go up to 2099 G1C/US$26 because it includes a 30 day gun).
APB's gameplay is horrid. Most of the weapons work most effectively in one area but work poorly in other areas, which means you'll be spending half the match switching guns(which takes forever because you'll have to firstly go to an inventory area, then click a bunch of things to change your weapon, then wait to restock the weapon's ammo completely) to suit the situation that you're in, The driving has input lag for people with high ping, and most of the cars drive like their on ice (skidding everywhere and poor traction), The matchmaking is completely horrid, APB uses a "threat" system for matchmaking to show a player's skill. In late 2011, the threat system was changed from 30 threat levels(Bronze 1-10, Silver 1-10, Gold 1-10) to 4 threat levels(Green, Bronze, Silver, Gold). With the new threat system, it just throws in random people of different threats and gives the losing team the option of backup (
), which means that missions will normally always be one-sided. There's also not that much to do in the game, the only game types you can play are missions, fight club, and social. Missions are normally 4v4 objective based matches that lets you level your character's rating level up that takes place in different parts of the map, Fight club is a fixed section of a map (Waterfront's Baylan Shipping/Asylum (Beacon was removed for some odd reason)) that's more focused around killing people instead of doing objectives, social is where you go to customize things/use the marketplace/go AFK for no reason. The missions are really repetitive, mostly either involving you defending an area, or go to a place and press the action button, the placement for objectives is another thing that causes missions to be one-sided, as objectives can sometimes spawn in easy camp spots.
One of the things I dislike about APB the most is the cash shop. Before anyone makes assumptions, No, the cash shop guns are not overpowered, as a sheer amount of the cash shop guns are just re-meshes of a gun that's available for free. Most of the things in the cash shop will cost you a lot of money, with prices going up to US$50+ just for a pack containing one car with kits, one outfit and one gun for one character. The cash shop even goes to selling ludicrous items such as a "friends and ignore list extender" which adds 50 capacity to your in-game friends/ignore list for a hefty US$12.5. Sure, the devs have added a F2Per's option for obtaining cash shop items via the Joker Store, but the prices are pretty expensive. It will cost you 1000 Joker Tickets to buy a 3 slot cash shop gun for 7 days. However, the maximum amount of Joker Tickets anyone can earn within a week is around 1000, which means you will have no Joker Tickets to spend if you want to save up for something neat on the Joker Store.

REVIEW UPDATED: 09-29-2017
This is kinda early, considering I said I would update this review when I managed to beat the game, and I haven't yet.
I've been playing on normal mode, and as of the time of writing this, I have managed to beat 4 bosses, only to die in stage 5. And I have to say...
... Y'KNOW WHAT THIS ISN'T HALF BAD.
Anyone who's seen the previous iterations of my review may note that my real only issue with this game was the difficulty. For the record, I have always played in Normal mode. Not hard, not easy, just normal. I always consider this to be the "intended" experience of a game, so when I make a review I base my review on the Normal setting of any game. Not easy, I don't need my hand held. Not hard, I don't need my face bashed in.
That said, my problem was normal felt too HARD on normal. Which, for you hardcores out there might sound like I just needa git gud (but we all needa git gud really. It's how and why that differ). But for a game inspired by MegaMan I was expecting to have MegaMan style fun, and I just wasn't.
I also mentioned in my review that this could easily be remedied by adding a bit more health pickups. Now enemies occasionally drop health, and nuts are a bit more plentiful (which also adds to your survivability since you can purchase health with them).
Now I'm managing to get all the way to stage 5 and I actually have confidence that I can beat the game.
I should note that prior I was playing with a friend in co-op m ode. I was having trouble getting to stage 3 with a friend to help me. Now I can get to stage 5 solo. That is a VAST improvement in the game's balance and one worth tweaking my review from a not-recommend to a yes-recommend.
Now this game feels like a fun MegaMan tribute.
... OHP, I guess I should also talk about other things I like about the game instead of just yammering on about it's past faults and how they got fixed.
Aside from that one flaw, I never really disliked anything else about 20XX! It's got nice music, nice artwork.
I think the only music track I dislike is the boss theme. It sounds kinda lacking compared to the stage themes.
Fun weapons and powerups. Good music, decent stage design and no instant death-traps like Mighty No. 9. We have a winner here!

I, for the life of me, cannot understand why all the reviews are positive so far!
I cannot stress enough, this game is a downgrade from Don Bradman Cricket 14!!! It would have been more appropriate for the developers to release this as an early access title considering its current state...
Every single aspect of this game, aside from its lofty aspirations, is worse than its predecessor!!
When my wife played this game for the first time, she stated "It's as if they took all the parts of Don Bradman Cricket 14 that needed fixing, failed at fixing them, and then broke every other part of the game while they were at it"...
I have never been so disappointed with a $65 (AUD) purchase in my whole life!
A few of my favourite issues with this game are:
1) The physics – one of the highlights of DBC 14 for me was the realistic way the ball came onto the bat - fast!! DBC 17 has destroyed this feeling, it feels as if the ball is more inflatable beach ball than cricket ball!! This seems partly due to the speed of both the bat and the ball, which are both far too slow to accurately represent the game of cricket... or physics in general!!
2) The bowling controls are in fact less dynamic and allow for less control than DBC 14 (While requiring twice as many buttons to be pressed) - instead of controlling the length of the ball with the timing of the thumbstick movements (A great system which actually required skill to bowl the ball where you wanted to), you simply press a button to choose a length, and a modifier to move it foward or backwards a little... meaning there are 12 exact lengths that can be bowled, and no skill is required to achieve the same length delivery ball after ball...
3) While the graphics and lighting may in fact be "improved/running on a better engine" from the previous version, they do not look better overall - its hard to explain... everything is just too rounded and shiny looking, to the point that IMO, DBC 14 looks better, as it captures depth and shadows better.
4) The system for setting fields is massively overcomplicated, as is the UI experience in general!
5) There are things wrong with almost every part of this game, fielding, batting, bowling, the UI, the academy... Some of it major, some of it minor, but its guaranteed to annoy the hell out of anyone who enjoys the sport of cricket!!
So I will end with this suggestion:
- If you are the sort of gamer that is prepared to pay a AAA price for a low-budget indie game, and say things like "quality doesn't matter, I want to support this developer, regardless of how unfinished their games are" and "This game has the potential to be the greatest cricket game of all time!! Who cares if its going to take another 3 years of development to realise this dream!!" and "I am happy to spread lies about the quality of this game" - This is the game for you!!!
- If however, like myself, you prefer notions such as "value for money", "honesty" and "Calling a spade a spade", then avoid this game like the plague, as it is unfinished, sh*te, and a complete and utter downgrade from its predecessor!!!

This game has everything that a fan of point&click games would desire and is an absolute must-have for those who are into the genre!
It focuses mostly on an intense story with a great atmosphere, that is only accompanied by random puzzles here and there. The game makes the player actually think about what would be the next logical step to do, instead of just hinting to the next location or which object to click next. And it actually always is logical! As opposed to so many other point&click games that just drive you crazy because the actions are just so stupid and random.
It generally emphasizes on an actual realistic feel to the whole game, which goes from random character interactions, over cut scenes to animations for waiting for the elevator, getting inside your car or walking. Looooots of walking in this game.
You switch between two playable characters that are bound by plot (and blood as well!).
The female protagonist is very likeable. She's smart, devoted and the player can always relate to her actions. Also she has a great fashion taste (...them bunny slippers).
The male protagonist is just as clever, and his story is even more horrid and disturbing.
The realistic feel of the game and it's characters authenticity are surely thanks to the great voice acting. Bad voice acting can really ruin a game for you, but that's absolutely not the case here. The voices fit the characters and they also emphasize the words just perfectly, always fitting the current situation. (That's usually a thing that really pisses me off with other games).
This game has an overall intense and authentic feel to it which is also thanks to the very interesting setting we have here.
The story takes place in a modern Chicago with 'flashbacks' to the Victorian Era at Prague. There's a moderate change of scene in the game and you can switch through all the detailed locations at will at any time. What really makes the game interesting is the great location scenery with very detailed graphics in variation with animations as well a lot of cool cut scenes, which really make it feel like you're watching an action movie at times!
The buildings and some of the rooms are made in a futuristic style which is interesting as well (a brothel that looks like it's taken from a sci-fi movie and her house just looks like a giant church.)
So, there is not a lot of actual puzzles in this game. Maybe 10 or so, I'm not sure, but it wasn't that many. Which wasn't neccesarily a bad thing, since they really have what it takes. Maybe they're too hard even, but I eventually all figured them all out, except for one where I had to use a guide.
Like I already said, the game focuses more on "logical" puzzles as to where to go/what to do next, more than actual puzzles.
So. Here it is. The reason why I could give the game only 9 points and in my opinion it's only flaw.
Right at the beginning of the game I was totally unable to figure out the item menu and it took me a while to understand the functionality. It wasn't explained anywhere. There were a few other moments during the course of the game, where it still made me some troubles.
And then there's the walking. Like I already said, looooots of it. You have to change locations quite a lot, especially if you're not sure on where to go next, and just randomly want to check out some places. See if you missed something. That's when the frustration starts. First there's the animation of getting into your car, then the animation of you getting out of your car (and walking a few steps). The characters can actually run, by double-clicking somewhere. But you can't "speed travel" to the next room, by double-clicking on the door for example. So you have to watch your character walk all the way to the end of the screen. Then walking to the elevator. Then the animation for pressing the elevator button. Then the animation of the character inside the elevator. Then the animation of getting out of the elevator... and so on, you get where I'm going with this.
I get that they wanted to make the game seem "realistic", but that's just too much, it's still a game after all. Also, the whole game seems to take place in one single night! (which doesn't really fit to the story at all).
They never mention her going to sleep or anything, she's a freakin zombie! So much for realism.
Great game with great characters, a great atmosphere, challenging puzzles, but bad controls.
I hope they fixed all the negative aspects in the 2nd game, that's next to play for me.

Still Life is a sequal to the Post Mortem set 80 years later focusing on Vic McPherson, granddaughter of Gus McPherson. A young female agent working for the FBI in Chicago who stumbles upon a series of murders that are all connected to a case Gus was involved with 80 years prior. Unlike the Post Mortem game, this entry of the "Still Life" trilogy is done differently. There's no series of multiple dialoge choices so it's a more linear storyline and the cast of characters are what make this game a real joy to play. I did enjoy the characters from Post Mortem, but the cast of Still Life takes the prize on that category. Vic is a cool heroine full of attitude, humor, and spunk. She's the type of woman I would ask out on a date. While the background designs are much more elabrate and the music score is very top notch than what was present in Post Mortem. The Chicago masked killer is more memorible than the Paris masked killer with the whole motif of Jack the Ripper meets the Phantom of the Opera. Overall the game is a living form of art that will please the eye of art lovers or video game designers.

The fact that it is Rogue Lite makes every playthrough randomized to some extent, which adds a lot of difficulty at times. I wish there were more enemy types as it can be a bit repetitive. It would also be nice if they added more bosses to more guarantee a new set of bosses every play through. New level types would be nice as well.
Would I recommend it? Honestly if you like Mega Man games getting this should be a high priority on your part. This feels so much like Mega Man X while being different simultaneously that it is really hard to put it down.
Looking forward to seeing how it further develops.

Overall, probably one of the best CoD campaigns, though the multiplayer and zombies are meh.
Campaign: The campaign was definitely the most ambitious for the series at the time (maybe of all time? I've yet to play any past this one), adding customizable equipment loadouts with unlockable special gear, a choices-and-consequences style semi-branching storyline, optional missions with more Spec Ops-esque objectives and minor RTS elements, and overall having the campaign be more focused on actual shootan gameplay instead of nigh-impossible-to-screw-up scripted "pilot the thing" moments. Even when it -did- have those moments I found them far easier to screw up/far more interactive than previous CoD entries.
Not to imply that it's perfect though, as the character writing is a bit iffy. At one point, a character murders a civilian in cold blood, then another character murders an unarmed military dude, only for the first character to go "Hey! I thought you said no uncessesary killing!" Like, dude, you just murdered a defenseless civvy, you're not one to protest.
Still though, probably in my top 3 CoD campaigns.
9.2/10
Multiplayer: It was pretty disappointing to see the Strike Package system replaced with just the generic scorestreak setup.
Likewise, as seems to be standard for the Treyarch CoDs, gun balance wasn't the best and most of the people I played with were using the same four or so rifles/smgs. The Wildcard and Loadout Point systems were neat tho.
I also didn't see a barebones playlist but this may have been me being blind/not looking hard enough. I uninstalled before the realization hit me and I don't really feel like reinstalling to check, sue me.
7.3/10
Zombies: Full disclosure that this review is based entirely on the base game's zombie map as there's no way in hell I'm paying Activision's over-the-top prices for the map packs.
So first off it was pretty greedy of them to only make one zombie map, then split it into subsections so they could pretend you had more maps to play with than you actually did. WaW had the excuse of the mode originally just being a cheesy bonus inclusion, and Blops 1 at least gave us two distinctly unique and fully fleshed out maps.
Tranzit is honestly pretty "meh". For starters, the game does a pretty bad job of explaining that the Turbine is used to power things. I actually thought at one point that it might've been a zombie-slowing field or somesuch because they never bothered to give any indication of what I was meant to do with it.
Also, the segmented map takes claustrophobia to entirely new levels and doesn't mesh well with the standard Zombies balance of "run laps around the map if you're getting swarmed so that you can group them up and deal with them without being surrounded". And god help you if you go down and need to re-get perks because your teammates will -not- be happy if you take the bus for a loop without them.
It certainly didn't help that gameplay wise the only real change from Blops 1 was the equipment/trap/turbine system, and overall that isn't exactly a notable change.
6.3/10
Overall Game Score: 7.6/10, though don't let that deter you if you're only in it for the campaign, cuz it's p good.

If you are prepared to spend at least around 15 hours to learn this game (youtube, documentation, experimentation), then this is a very good game.
It is not an arcade space shooter - but a combat and trading simulator. Not fast paced. Don't even bother with using a gamepad - learn to play with the keyboard and mouse and it is a lot better that way.
During my roughly 100 hours of gameplay, I experienced only a handful of crashes and corrupted save games. Other than that, the game is rock solid and looks great.
There is so much to do here, and progression is really balanced - you start with only one ship and very limited scope, but eventually are able to build factories, set up automated trading ships, mine asteroids, buy large combat and commerce ships...it is great.

As stated by a lot of players, this game will eat up a lot of time. But for clarification, it is not exactly in the same way as one might picture these quotes in the context of a game such as Civ.
Think of this game as being more like FSX or what I have heard of Arma. You will spend a lot of time in transit, especially if you don't know how to use SETA or your ship doesn't have it equipped. At least in FSX that is kindof the point of the game. For me, this is 75% downside, 25% bonus. At least it gives a sense of realism.
The physics are a bit arcadey and un-Newtonian, though this is not unlike many games. If you stop applying throttle, your ship simply stops. Feels basically like driving a car in 3D, which certainly isn't bad. Once you find the controls, it isn't too bad to get a handle on the flying in-and-of itself, though I have always had a problem with aim in pretty much all games, but you do get an aiming point if you so choose.
The real "depth" that the other reviews refer to seems to be in ship customization, base building, and otherwise interacting in the universal community. So many different races (many looking sadly little different from humans, but others being more interesting), so much regarding reputation and stuff. My last game I got murdered by a swarm of pirates, so I haven't yet fully fleshed this part of the game out yet, but it looks cool.
This game, for reasons that are now more obvious, doesn't talk a lot about exploration. As far as I have discovered, it doesn't seem like you will ever "go where no man has gone before." There is plenty to explore, that is true, but there seems to be a significant population almost everywhere of the major races (of which the number is truly staggering). If you like diplomatic, intrigue, trade, and combat elements to space games, this should be great for you! Only real weakness seems to be exploring the outer reaches.
Of course, I could be wrong and it does take a long time to learn this game. But if you are willing to spend a long time getting to a location as the tradeoff for a deeper economy and customization, it should be great!
Finally, get a joystick. I can't honestly say I would have enjoyed this game at all without one.
Right now, I am really on the fence as to whether to recommend this. There was some excitement, and the story was interesting, with so many races. Most of the game, however, is getting to the action not in it. Then again, I might not be using SETA properly.
Will hopefully update this review with more gametime.

I'm one of those people that have been following the Devil May Cry series since its debut in 2001, that loved the first game to the point of obsession and that, in the following years, have been more and more disappointed with the way Capcom managed the franchise and let both the characters and the basic plot of the series go to waste. Hence I wasn't surprised when this reboot was announced, and I have to admit that at first I was amongst the screaming mob that instantly dismissed this game as utter garbage, resulting from a sleazy marketing operation. But instead of stubbornly clinge to a first impression I wanted to try it first hand so that I would've been able to express a complete and reasoned judgement. And well, after watching the credits the overall verdict that I can give to this DMC is actually quite positive.
Let's say first of all that the protagonist is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ it just has to be admitted. Instead of the good ol' Dante we have this teenage prick that tries hard to be edgy and acts like the typical street thug, spitting out lines that sometimes are really cringe-worthy, especially in the early parts of the game. But if you think about it, it's not so different from the young Dante that we had to bear in Devil May Cry 3. And guess what? Contrary to the latter, the kid we see in this game actually experiences an hint of character development. That's because the plot, while obviously not particularly remarkable in terms of depth, is still written decently and is surely much more consistent than the awful mess we saw along the years in the various sequels of the original Devil May Cry. Even if don't personally like much the more "urban" aestethics of the setting, I appreciated the fact that the developers tried to give it a bit more depth with the whole "New World Order" mood, which is not exactly the top of originality (it's actually clearly inspired from the movie They Live) but it suits well to the purpose. So pros to that.
The gameplay, which is the primary aspect for every DMC, is pretty solid, level design and platforms are not particularly remarkable but are still well made and the different interactions with the surroundings made possible by the new weapon system are an interesting and fun to use addition. Those who are familiar with the series will notice that the difficulty is rather below its standards, but thanks to the aforementioned new weapons making combos is still fun and the new game modes add an extra challenge to everything. Of course you don't have to expect anything nearly as hard or deep as Bayonetta, which IMO has set the new standard of excellence in this genre. However, If you never played a DMC before and you're not very accustomed to action games this one is an excellent entry point.
The biggest flaw I've found in this title is the enemy design: they look dull, unimpressive and generally lack diversity. I don't recall a single boss battle that really troubled me or that left me with a strong impression, except maybe the final battle. That is a big lack for an action game and doubly so for a Devil May Cry. I also felt the abscence of enemy lock-on during combat: to attack an enemy you have to face towards him with the left stick, it generally works well but sometimes you can't hit the precise enemy you want to at the first shot, and that can be really annoying. Aside from this couple of things, this DMC is a good action game that can certainly be considered way above the average of similar titles. Could have been even better if it wasn't for the flaws I pointed out, but it's still good.
On technical level the PC version looks flawless and runs perfectly smooth, always still at 60fps without a single hiccup while running at maximum settings (on my rig I currently have an i5-2500k @3,60 Ghz with an AMD Radeon HD 7850). So for once, we don't have to complain about the porting - yeah yeah I know, there are very few graphic customization options but I don't care, considering the average quality of console ports that I've seen during the last years I absolutely cannot complain about this one.
A side note about the "Vergil's Downfall" DLC: I don't recommend buying at full price, it's very short (only 6 missions) and the story adds very little to the plot, it looks more like a tentative to include a playable Vergil due to popular demand and nothing more. It's not all bad, though: I appreciated the fact that Vergil has its own combat style with some features directly inspired by the Nelo Angelo boss (aka Vergil himself) in the very first DMC as well as the whole atmosphere of the levels, much darker and oniric than the ones from the base game, which fits very well to the completely different personality of Vergil and sometimes makes it all look like a whole different game. Playing with Vergil is also harder than Dante, partly due to the limited move set and partly to the very "technical" (yet extremely powerful when mastered) combat style, so expect having to swear a bit if you plan to get an SSS on every level on every difficulty mode. So all considered I suggest to buy this DLC when it's on sale, buying the complete pack on discount would be the best option.
As a final and personal note I have to give my congratulations to Ninja Theory, because having to deal from scratch with a series that had such a troubled background and that always brings extreme expectations is not easy, and managing to do so while at the same time giving a new consistence to its plot and characters is a proof of talent. Not many people could have done that. Bravo.

I have been eagerly waiting for this game, and have got to say, im not disappointed!,  the game looks amazing, and with the addition of the community created stadiums/kits and faces, the game has the realism i was after, i played a test match and have got to say for the first time, the AI batted realisticly, playing smart leaves, defensive shots and placing the ball into the gaps, I also like how you're able to find the batsman's edge, which in other games has been very uncommon, the gameplay its self is great, the batting allows you to play 360 degree shots around the ground, and to pick holes in opposition fields, i have found the running between the wickets quite delayed, and when sliding the bat after a quick single, just too late, rather than sliding the bat in, as the batter runs over the line, the bat is grounded after the batsman crosses the line, i hope that is fixed in a upcoming patch, its not game breaking but quite annoying when you are unnable to do a quick single because your batsmen will not ground his bat until hes over the line, but so far from what ive played this game is amazing, its a big step up from DBC14, although there is no major additions, everything has been improved. i definatley reccomend this game to anyone who is interested in cricket games, and for any hardcore fan, this game is a must!!

The most obvious and game changing improvement from DBC 14 is the bowling. The ai bats more realistically and is more engaging to bowl at, and I've seen some handsome shots and some satisfying dismissals.
The biggest change to batting is that you now have the option to see the delivery hud marker earlier, which is ideal for anyone who felt they were too rushed to pick a shot when batting in DBC 14.
Another change is the addition of gameplay sliders, with which you can fine tune various parameters - the pace and bounce of the bowling, lateral movement, batting footwork or timing difficulty, and so on. I haven't explored all the possibilities yet, but I've been able to adjust the gameplay with very promising results so far.
The dev team have a track record of excellent support for their games, and they continued to take user feedback and refine gameplay and modding options for DBC 14 for a long while after release. I'm expecting the same thing with DBC 17.
As I understand it the PC version has fixes for some issues that drew criticism in the console release, and while I expect future patches and community mod content to improve gameplay further and smooth out some rough edges, as a keen follower of the sport I think it's a pretty good game right now, and the best bits are excellent.

The PC version of DBC 17 is a sure winner. Graphics are smooth and crisp, lighting is absurdly good and although Big Ant are a small developer on a tight budget they have made every effort imaginable to make this a cricket game for cricket lovers.
Gameplay has definitely come a long way with AI being more tactically aware than in the predecessor DBC 14. They judge chases more efficiently and tend to play better cricket all round. Cricket can now be played 360 degrees around the field and shot making is intuitive and fluid. Edges are clearly way more evident with catches through to the keeper a regular occurance. With 3 different settings and customisable sliders for your own personal preference anybody can pick up a controller and enjoy the game of cricket despite you level of play.
With a lot of negative feelings towards the initial console release, the developers have made every effort to listen to the customer and fix what they wanted fixed.
Customisation in the game is unrivaled with the academy for users to create and share teams, logos, bats, stadiums and players.
With literally hundreds of ways to edit and customise every gameplay, match types and tours etc including Day/Night Tests and every other format imaginable, it certainly has enough depth in its modes. Career mode has been deepened and conitnues to be my favourite.
Although a lot easier on the eye than DBC 14 the initial screens and UX are not always user friendly and at times can be long winded when navigating, BA have however made steps towards making it easier and I am sure will continue to do so.
Commentary is still sometimes one dimensional and repetitive, but James Taylor is a breath of fresh air and a major coup for the game.
- Graphics         8/10
- Commentary    7/10
- Gameplay        8.5/10
- Customisation  9.5/10
- Modes             9/10
- Customisation 10/10
In my book a big step up from DBC 14 in many and a good sequel. Definitely worth it.

I waited for a long time before playing this game. I felt like it was just a 'cash in' because it wasn't made by the original developers. Now that I've finally played it, I admit that I was wrong.
Arkham Origins is a decent game and I have enjoyed playing it. The graphics are an improvement on Arkham City and the story is very good. The developers seem to genuinely care about the character too. As the game is loaded with really cool Batman related content.
Of course it uses the same engine, as the previous games in the series, so that helps. However the game also creates it's own powerful athmosphere with it's Christmas Eve setting. The snowy Gotham City, great music and some really cool attention to detail, sucked me in to this take on Gotham.
The game can be a bit buggy though and it crashed on me a few times. I was still able to enjoy myself and it looks great running at a mostly stable 60FPS. However there are occasional FPS drops in some areas of the open city.
Origins is definitely worth playing as part of the Arkham Series. It's filled with cool content and is often on sale for a rediculously cheap price. However if it's a choice between this and one of the other games in the series. I would choose the others, simply because Rocksteady games were the innovators of this type of Batman game and their titles are more interesting and more fun to play.
Arkham Origins probably was made just to 'cash in' on an already successful series. Thankfully though some people who really care about the character got on board and managed to make a pretty good game.

I last played GTTOD back in April, and it was a mixed bag. It had some promising ideas, but really awful level design and some really buggy mechanics.
TL;DR:  While the game still has issues, it's a lot of fun, and I'd say worth 10 dollars, especially given how active the developer is.
So, while the game is described as a first person shooter, I feel like it plays out more like a bullet hell. That is, all of the weapons in the game are either melee-based or projectiles, meaning that you can dash around to avoid them. Your dash also has no cooldown and you have infinite ammo (you still need to reload, though). This means that aiming is far less important than dodging, as you can eventually kill an enemy as you're dashing around (the bullet time mechanic does help give you a few precious seconds to do some precision aiming).
Thus, the core gameplay loop turns into a ballet of bullets as you dash around like Titanfall's pilot on crack and slow down the game to a crawl to pick off enemies. In this sense, it really reminds me of Vanquish, but far faster-paced and without cover.
The game is pretty short as is, though. There are 10 main levels and you can beat the game in about an hour or two. That said, there are a good variety of weapons and the game is highly replayable (you can shoot for a better score, which, admittedly, isn't implemented in a very satisfying manner right now), so you can stretch it out past that.
The soundtrack by Wolf and Raven is really nice, and my only major issue with it is that the game's audio mixing isn't great, since the bullet fire tends to drown out the music (and there's no slider for sound effects).
Performance is a mixed bag as well. Up to level 8, I had no issues getting 60 FPS on my GTX 1080, but from that point on, it tanks hard, to the point where I was getting 20 FPS on Level 10. And in a game that's so fast paced, that kind of ruins the game (so I wouldn't recommend levels 9-10 for now).
It's a good game with a lot of potential. The story style mode while short is enjoyable. Collision needs work but outside of that its a solid game.

Truly a diamond in the rough, this game was my own personally much delayed introduction to the X series. X3TC is now among my favourite games ever, and it is as of this writing my most-played game on Steam. It's a space trading/shooting/exploration/storyline sandbox at its core, like many other great games before it, but simply leaving it at that is not fair, because it smashes its way out of that mold and into something vastly more interesting.
A key element is its emphasis on starting and growing a largely autonomous fleet above and beyond your own personal ship. What starts out as little more than having a second ship you can give remote commands to fly to various stations for purposes as basic as checking the prices there, will eventually grow into configuring a completely unattended merchant fleet of small freighters buying and selling commodities automatically.  But trading alone can only earn you so much, the game lets you take it to the next level with construction of factories, stations, and starbases and static defensive emplacements. Later still you may end up with defensive battlegroups patrolling sectors where you have assets, groups of combat carriers with huge wings of fighters and other huge capital ships and smaller escorts to protect them. It opens up a wide array of gameplay possibilities and late game can become more like a Space 4X RTS where you control a sprawling manufacturing and military empire as you vie for economic and sometimes violent dominance with rival factions. But it is ultimately your own sandbox, so this is only one possibility.
If that's not your style of play, nothing will force you to do it that, although some missions will be very difficult without having remote controlled ships or in some cases your own factory complexes. If you'd prefer to have a fleet of mining ships tearing up asteroids instead, or a fleet of combat ships following you around to help you kill pirates, or scout ships to explore the galaxy remotely, or if you just hate the idea of automation completely and would rather fly every ship personally -- you can! Yes, even the capital ships are fully pilotable and fully functional. And it is nothing like simply flying a huge fighter. They are incredibly slow but well armored and well armed, and generally bristle with turrets (which can themselves be set to automatic or controlled manually).
I don't know why it took me so long to get around to trying this game. I think I was turned off initially by a few fairly subtle things: The map of the universe was very grid-like and shaped vaguely like the periodic table of elements, with gates and routes generally corresponding to north/east/south/west. This isn't realistic, of course, and I was afraid it would break my immersion. It doesn't. It's mostly just a layout choice for a totally abstract concept. You'll never really know it unless you *are* in fact looking at the map ingame, and even then it's not immediately obvious. Once you've planted your butt in the seat of a spacecraft, there is no up or down or north or west, it's just space. There's a gate over there, let's go to it. Oh, it goes to Akeela's Beacon. Is that north? What's north? I don't care, all I care is where it goes. It's no different than any other jump-gate based universe and it's just as immersive, interesting and enjoyable. Secondly (and again for some reason this relates to the periodic table of elements) is the names. Some of the race names are pulled straight from elements, like Argon, Boron, Xenon... as a non-player, that just seemed lazy and uncreative and distracting. Some of the system names seemed really goofy too, and I wasn't looking for a comedy. "Ceo's Buckzoid"? Well, as it turns out this is all just part of the story and the lore. These things actually do have explanations, and it's not a joke. Patience, grasshopper, it will make sense in time.
There's so much more to the game beyond those minor complaints, that they cease to even be a thought in my head when playing the game now, but in case anyone else had similar concerns, I wanted them to know that those concerns are unfounded.
The game is certainly not without its actual flaws though, it's rough around the edges in many areas including UI usability and complexity (which rivals Dwarf Fortress), poor weapon and ship balancing, AI, and the much-hated suicidally stupid autopilot. The way combat and movement is handled when you are watching or participating in it is vastly different from how it is handled when you are not (when your automated ships are running in the background in different sectors, not rendering onscreen). In fact it is so much different, that different equipment loadouts are required to be successful the different situations. Some minor differences in combat outcomes could be forgivable, but letting in-sector and out-of-sector become two different and incompatible metagames is extremely frustrating.
But despite these flaws, it still manages to be a powerfully enjoyable sandbox to play in, and if any of the positives I've mentioned sound appealing, I guarantee you will be able to overlook the flaws.

Well, we've made it to release, so it's time for a new and improved review.
20XX is pretty good, we'll get that out of the way quickly. Don't let the weird Newgrounds flash aesthetic fool you; this is a solid and genuinely fun game clearly made by people that actually understand and care about this weird little jump-and-shoot-man "subgenre". It already beats Mighty No. 9 in that regard because it's faithful AND it's new mechanics don't clash with the gameplay. Like Beck's dash does. But this is a 20XX review, not a MN.9 review.
Speaking of the Newgrounds aesthetic, it really is pretty rough. It's not necessarily bad looking, but for the most part it's nothing really spectacular or gorgeous. I might be biased because I dislike puppet/Spine animations to begin with, but the animations in this game tend to come across as rather stiff. The art direction of the cutscenes and some boss portraits also clash heavily with the ingame art, and don't really connect very well to what's actually going on ingame. At least it gets the job done, though.
As I've said in my previous review, the overall balance and difficulty of the game is pretty mixed but leans towards being too easy most of the time. As of the time of writing this I'm on a 5-win streak, and I've done 6 runs since the game released all in the span of 4 hours. It's kind of difficult for me to say though why this is, because I'm genuinely not sure if it's because I'm really good or if the level and enemy design is a touch too easy, because some other reviewers are claiming it's extremely difficult after a certain point. Maybe RNG is on my side as well, who knows. You could say "well, why not play the harder difficulty with optional modifiers?" and my answer to that is "because it's artificial difficulty, that doesn't change the fact that the underlying game is still a touch too easy".
The music on paper is pretty good, but as a budding musician/composer myself the instrumentation is extremely repetitive and almost doesn't change at all from track to track. Cityfires/Brandon Ellis is a great composer and the compositions themselves are also really great (I can't stress this enough), but the overall theme of the soundtrack is just far too repetitious. It's the same few recycled drumsets and modulated chiptune leads throughout, and it needs more variety in instrumentation. I'd like to point to Tee Lopes' Sonic Mania soundtrack as an example of having an incredible amount of variety in your soundtrack, as every track sounds unique even if it's for the same act.
Really though, there isn't anything in this game that screams "terrible" or "don't buy/don't buy at full price". I don't really know how to end a review properly, so I'll just say that it's good, fun, worth your time and if you're feeling pensive, at least get it on sale. It's a great game for people that like roguelites, Megaman X, or both.

Overall if you enjoyed the previous Hitman games (though maybe not if you enjoyed absolution, as it is quite different to this) then you'll probably enjoy this too. It's also a perfect starting point for newcomers, especially if you like stealth or sandbox game. Or if you're a psychopath who enjoys murdering people. Or both.
HITMAN is a sandbox game about drowning, stabbing, burning, shooting, strangling, smothering, pushing down an above average height and [insert hundreds of deaths here] in a sandbox environment.
You play as 47, an agent in mysterious organization, tasked with killing various high profile targets in different environments.  The game is all about replayability, and while finishing a mission once will only take you about an hour, you can have a lot of fun by replaying it. This is helped by the numerous challenges, which task you with killing targets in creative ways, or with specific restrictions. HITMAN differs from other stealth games because you're supposed to hide in plain sight: hide in a crowd, pretend to be a customer in a shop, disguise yourself as the chef of an hotel and poison the food while everyone is looking at you, it takes a lot of patience to achieve the rating of "silent assassin" or to complete some hard challenges, howewer the game manages to be accessible to new player by featuring a customizable HUD, the option to turn on and off helps like instinct, and the opportunities, which are guided assassinations to help the player learn the layout of one of the six incredibly complex locations. In HITMAN every location feels alive, and i personally had a lot of fun simply walking through the maps and looking at the NPCs, or at certain detalis. Most importantly, you get total freedom when approaching a mission, and you can kill the targets in many ways, both scripted by the developers, and improvised by the player. The game also features various bonus modes:
The player made contracts, which are, as the name suggests, made by other players and are set on one of the various scenarios.
The escalations, which are a set of missions of increasing difficulty made by the developers.
And the Elusive Targets, which are special targets that can only be killed in a specific period of time (think of it as the timed events of some mobile games) and, most importantly, you only get ONE attempt at them, though i don't really like the idea of them getting locked up if you start playing too late, or them disappearing after an attempt, it could have been solved by making your score and the unlocks count only on your first attempt, or if you tackled them in time. There really aren't too many negative points for this:
I don't like how everyone in every location speaks with the same language and accent (english), previous games had different languages based on your location. Also the GOTY upgrade is a bit overpriced, howewer they still gave us some nice updates for free, and the content in the GOTY isn't even important to the story, so we're really only missing out on some secondary content whose only reason of existance is probably to fund the next IOI games.Overally if you enjoyed the previous Hitman games (though maybe not if you enjoyed absolution, as it is quite different to this) then you'll probably enjoy this too. It's also a perfect starting point for newcomers, especially if you like stealth or sandbox game. Or if you're a psychopath who enjoys murdering people. Or both.
