It is so disappointing to see the state of the simulator section of the gaming industry. It is filled to the brim with cheaply designed, terrible looking and awfully working excuses of games. It is very rare to finds a really excellent simulator game on steam and that is a letdown. But when you do find a gem it is absolutely amazing and to a certain extent revolutionary. Euro truck simulator is one of those games. This game excels in many ways, some are almost incomprehensible. This game truly redefines the category of simulator and takes it to another level. In this review I will be examining the aspects of the game that I really like and dislike.
It is obvious from observation that many aspects of this game have been carefully and professionally crafted. In particular I love the economic aspect of the game. The ability to create a trucking company (Or empire if you like to call it that) and to manage it is really fun. I love being able to hire employees, purchase trucks for them and buy garages and garage slots for them to park their trucks. I would recommend that the developers would allow you to choose how much you can pay you employees and how that would affect their attitude towards work, them choosing to leave and the quality of work that they would strive towards, thus the amount of income they produce for you. However considering the complexity of economics it would not matter if they implemented my suggestion. I also love the fact that you can take out a loan. No matter how annoying this sounds it is almost a necessity for beginners to take out a loan to buy upgrades for your garage and buy new trucks for you and your workers. It is a massive convenience for the player. I love the sheer size of the world that they have recreated. It will take the player days, if not weeks for them to navigate the stunning scenery of Europe, from the mountainous landscape of Scotland to the flat plains of Poland. Another aspect I deeply enjoy is the need to discover the world and explore outside of work. To be able to freely roam around the world is very fun. I love the variety of trucks and dealers there are to discover.
This game is not completely flawless however. There are some features that need urgent addressing. One of the most agonisingly annoying things in this game is the Artificial Intelligence or as I like to call it Artificial Idiocy. Some people suggest that the AI does not think in a way that a human would. I beg to differ. I say that the AI just doesn’t think in general. It is just atrocious. It is just like it is programmed to go in a direction strait and then turn when necessary and slow down. No consideration as to of whether I am there or not. I have had many accidents as a result of the AI’s idiotic programming. For example I was going from Bern to Genève, this truck was wanting to go into my lane because that was the only way he could get to his destination so what does he do? Forgets that he has cargo and doesn’t give a damn. He just merges into my lane way slower than me because truckers are apparently old women and I get stuck in the railing as a result. AND GUESS WHO GETS FINED?!!! ME!!!! Me of all people. I wasn’t even in the wrong!! Even worse. When it should not give way it does. Even when I am not on the
For Example there is a T intersection that leads onto a freeway. Imaging a line that is about 5 or 10 meters away from the intersection. I cross that line by just a fraction; all the cars and trucks are giving way to me even when I am the one that has to give way. It is SOOOOOOO INCREDIBLY ANNOYING I RAGE TO DEATH SOMETIMES. Sometimes when I am turning right (This is in the UK of course) the AI even stops right in front of me thinking it is giving way to me but all it is doing is blocking my way. When it does that I rage even more then when it even properly gives way to me. I would recommend completely reprogramming to Artificial Idiocy. Put the Intelligent back into this Artificial intelligence. I would make it think, not only that but make it think like a human even if that means they will have some accidents. Overly long rant about the AI over, There are some minor things I would adjust. I would like to be able to make my own custom paintjobs and symbols and put them on my truck. I would like the cities to be much bigger.
Overall this game is amazing but it could use some improvement, particularly in the AI department. I rate this game 8.5 out of 10. -1.5 points for the terrible AI.

Short Review: If you think graffiti looks cool and want to make something like it, you might like this game. If you're 'meh' on customization and love shooters, then there are better shooters which you're probably already playing.
APB is a fun game for a certain niche of players. While it is a shooter, you will only love it if you can dive into the customization, which can best be described as making graffiti. It's a simple system of manipulating colored shapes, and is easy to dive into for new players and incredibly deep for the experienced ones. The players who can really get a handle on it can make some truly incredible creations and even the novice players generally come up with something cool that makes them stand out in the crowd. If you can dive in and get hooked on the creation system, you will love this game, but if you can't, then you'll probably hate it because the rest of the game won't carry the experience on its own.
The shooting mechanics are decent, but it's nothing to phone home about. If you're new, you won't understand why you're dying, you'll rage, and you'll call this game pay to win. I know I did. Eventually though, you realize where to stand and how to move around the environment and what guns to use in what situation and to crouch and you can have a good time.

Old School Memories:  This is a side-scrolling beat ’em up game. These were the absolute bees knees when I was a younger gamer. The fond memories of the genre came flooding back to me from the very moment I began playing here. That, of course, means that games such as Double Dragon, Golden Axe, Final Fight, Altered Beast and Renegade were on the top of my mind. The answer I would immediately ask is how does The Ables: Freepoint High stack up against the classics? Surprisingly for an early access title not too badly. Qiwi Games acknowledges the roots of the title’s genre by implementing 90’s-esque graphics with a soundtrack to match. However, they’ve also recognized today’s standards and are working hard to implement modern expectations. It’s a balancing act but one that they’re well on the way to meeting.
Almost perfect gameplay: This will be one of those reviews that tracks back to the first point throughout. However, that’s because everything meets such a high level of consistency throughout the game that it’s impossible not to. The game play is tight with one caveat. I’d really like to see the double jump feature improved immensely. It’s going to be pivotal to defeating a number of the challenges throughout the game yet it’s not quite as tidy as it should be.
Based on a book: The game is based on the best selling book, The Ables, by Jeremy Scott. Admittedly I have never read the book but the game already has encouraged me to pick it up. I would encourage fans of the book to pick up the game. Jeremy Scott is also the co-creator and narrator of CinemaSins, one of the more popular channels on YouTube.
Awesome soundtrack: I would be remiss if I didn’t make a specific point about the soundtrack. The score has been created by Ronald Jenkees. Jenkees started out as one of the most talented musicians on YouTube but his rise to fame can be tracked directly to Bill Simmons. Simmons, the famous sports commentator hired Jenkees to create the theme music to his popular podcast. That particular theme is titled ‘Derty.’
A lot of work to be done: Currently only four of the seven levels are complete. However, what is available is super fun to play. I’m a big fan of the tutorial level which demonstrates what all of the super powers will enable you to do once the game is feature and content complete. That’s not to say that the price is high for the value that you get at the moment just that there is a lot more content to come.
The Ables: Freepoint High has the potential to be the very best side scrolling beat ’em up in recent years. It may even be on par or ahead of the classics but at this stage as a gamer it’ll be a very tough ask for it to be considered better because of just how much sentimental value those games hold. But for someone who treasured those games I couldn’t ask for much more than what Qiwi Games is offering me. They will raise the price prior to release but the $9.99 is a fair price for what the title already offers.

I am a big fan of Jeremy's work. I really enjoyed the book, so when I first learned about this game, I knew I was going to buy it. These are my unbiased thoughts of the game so far.
Pros:
- Good looking graphics, somewhat reminiscent of Mega Man games.
- Beautiful background music.
- The gameplay works well, starting off fairly easy, then sending you into a real challenge quickly.
- The boss fights are a nice challenge, taking me a few tries to beat them.
- A wide variety of powers at your character's disposal.
Cons:
- Lack of customization for characters.
- Only half of the levels are currently available.
- You can't control where the fireballs go. There are times where you want to hit a certain enemy, but they will go after a different one.
- The hand blasters can only fire directly in front of you. I wish you could control the direction in which you fire like you do with the laser eyes.
- I never like it when enemies in a game follow a pattern, preferring that they react to the player. Some of them do that, but a good chunk of them don't.
- During the boss fight in the Beach Cave, there is a point where it's impossible to avoid taking damage, that being after he summons the mini Supernovas then uses his powers to fly to the other platform at the top of the screen.
- During the Transportation Center level, the difficulty seems to suddenly spike too high out of nowhere.
- Also during this level, the game will start lagging when a lot of enemies spawn at once.
- As you're entering the boss fight of this level, there is a glitch where sometimes the screen will leave without you, automatically killing you.
Sins:
- What's the point in having super strength as an optional power if punching becomes obsolete once you obtain the hand  blasters? There should be a way to switch between blasting and punching.
- During the first level, why is it that none of the other students are doing anything? Why do they just stand there until they see me, then give me their powers so I can do all the work?
- Where were the teachers during all of this?
- During the Downtown level, why is the player running in the middle of the street instead of on the sidewalk? They could avoid the cars a whole lot easier this way instead of jumping over them.
- Game does not contain a lap dance.
Overall thoughts:
This game has a lot of potential. At only $9.99 (though I bought it during the holiday sale) it is a definite purchase. It does have quite a few problems that need to be fixed, but I'm sure that once they are, this game will be all the more enjoyable.

I recommend this game... but not for everyone.
I would recommend this game to any fan of the space-sim genre (who has a LOT of time on their hands and is willing to learn) BUT... buyer beware, there are some major flaws (I will ellaborate) and it is almost a necessity to mod the game to make it accessible and playable.
There is a MASSIVE learning curve (anyone who says otherwise is talking *&%$), I am about 200 hours into my first playthrough and I feel like I have barely scratched the surface of what you can actually do in this game. Any game with an instruction manual that is over 100 pages long is going to require some serious patience. I even found EvE-Online more accessible than X3TC. Some people will find these to be plus points but for those who want a game they can just pick up and play... buy something else. Don't listen to anyone who compares this to Freelancer (Freelance was much more of an arcade game), if you enjoyed Freelancer there is no guarantee you will enjoy this game.
First I will list what I though were the good points :
-Graphics are pretty good for a game of its age.
-Reasonable sound with great music.
-A HUGE universe to explore.
-A plethora of different ships, space stations, weapons, ship equipment, etc. (the vast majority of which the player can own themselves).
-A bustling trade universe with many resources and end products which the player can trade in.
-Great sandbox feel to the game, you could play for hundreds of hours and build a huge trade empire or combat fleet without ever touching on a "Plot" mission.
-A very helpful and dedicated fan base who are more than willing to help out new players (dont think i have ever seen the word "noob" on any forum/thread), there is a huge resource of info about the game on various websites/youtube and there is a large modding/scripting community.
Now the not-so-good :
-The game interface can be pretty cryptic and is not very intuitive at all. It took me a long time to figure it out (in fact I still dont think I have it figured out fully). A lot of the fans of the X series will praise the interface but I think they are comparing to previous X games (which must have had a truly aweful interface).
-The AI can be pretty dumb, flying ships into stations or something simmilar. However i think this has been mostly sorted out in the later versions of the game.
-Missions directives can sometimes be quite confusing and it is easilly possible for a player to accept a mission that they are vastly under-equiped for, which is just poor game design IMO.
-Some of the plot mission requirements are absolutely insane and from what I have read, many players opt to mod the game to lower the requirements (because they really are that rediculous, requiring the player to amass huge amounts of resources) which feels a bit like cheating to me. But remember, you don't HAVE to do the plot (sandbox).
-Very little in the way of in-game tutorials leaving the player to figure out most of it on their own. I for one, dont mind having to sift through the manual or read the wiki to figure stuff out, but for some this will be a deal-breaker.
-The need to mod the game.... you really do have to. The vanilla game is sadly lacking in certain areas and without some of the mods the vanilla game feels like a beta.
-The NPC voices are incredibly anoying!!!
In conclusion this is a game with huge potential so long as you are willing to put in hundreds of hours of gameplay (its like having a second job!!). It can be very rewarding and incredibly frustrating at the same time. The interface can be very irritating at times but if you can get to grips with it, there is a lot of enjoyment to be had. If you are looking at buying this game I would highly recommend having a look at the available mods and what they do BEFORE you start playing, because some of the mods require you to restart the game from the beginning before they will take effect.
A vast, deep game with huge potential so long as you are willing to put in the time and can get past the steep learning curve.

I'm pretty late with this, considering that I bought the game a week after its release, because I had to look at DmC with quite an ambivalence.
After giving it some thought now I decided it's time for my take:
This game is for you if:
-you like the devil may cry franchise and are not offended by this being a reboot
-you can stomach juvenile personalities and  a not-so-ambitious story about a "...schizophrenic world that is being continuously corrupted by the corporate big boss and his lackeys, where you play as the cool guy with super powers that tries to save the world with his fancy weapons and never misses the opportunity for a witty(?) comment."
-you actually know what this game's story and characters are like and don't mind/care
-you like fast paced action, a lot of room for creating cool combos and all that with fancy graphics (they really are fancy)
-you like to squeeze every last drop out of the provided gameplay mechanics and spend hours and hours to master the game AND feel rewarded for it
-you just want to hop into a game, not having to care about anything that is being said, and simply unload on monsters
-you like combichrist and noisia (or that type of music in general)
-you played the other DMCs and had issues with their difficulty (this game is VERY forgiving)
This game is NOT for you if:
-you really care about a well written, original story/characters/dialogues  -  feels like a stereotypical teenager's take on DMC
-challenging boss fights are a must for you (there are 6ish bosses that feel like recoloured/textured versions of another - except for the very last one, that one is really good)
-you expect a similar skill cap to DMC 3/4 and combo variety of that level - DmC is infinitely easier and the difference between 100 hours and 1000 hours of gameplay/practice is marginal
-you want a built-in turbo mode (there is a mod for this tho)
For a diehard DMC fan like me it was really difficult to give this game a proper review.
I've spent more than a thousand hours on DMC 3/4 on multiple platforms and versions and have yet to master them.
DmC has nothing left to show me after the 100+ hours I put into it - good 100+ hours I admit.
Unlike with the former two games, I'm done with this one.
Conclusion:
This game is good and you should buy it.
Do not expect D'M'C, this is DmC - keep that in mind and you will have a great time.

Wow! I really wanted to be able to sit here and say that I loved this game. Having not played other games in the series I was not blinded by nostalgia or a bias for the older versions of the characters, and I genuinly found it, as a property in its own right, to have characters and plot that, whilst not original, was developed well enough and satisfying and I genuinly looked forward to coming back and seeing what would happen to them next. The combat was fun and surprisingly deep and challenging and I enjoyed all the weapons and combos and unlocking new abilities.
The enemies are well designed for the most part, varied, interesting, and exciting to fight. Some are better than others, of course, but by all counts its a solid show. The exception are the boss fights, where both design and mechanics are sadly incredibly tired and cliched for the most part with only a couple of exceptions.
The level designs are pretty standout, with amazing skyboxes and interesting secret areas and agility trials. There are not really enough puzzles for my taste, but oh well. That is not a big thing really. There are a couple of very memorable levels, including one in the opening sequence of a TV News programme, and that was clever and appropriate, and original too. Unfortunately I don't think enough was done with it really.
The graphics are good, considering, although the textures do sometimes take a long time to load, especially in cut scenes (and this is running on a machine at least three times as powerful as it needs to be).
Now we get to the big point...the negative...the thing that ruined the whole deal for me...the one issue, so large, that it singlehandedly earned the game this negative review and my undying hatred after a considerable amount of swearing.
The final, piece of a*** bossfight.
It started off interesting enough. For the record, to challenge the fanboy morons who would say "You just cannot play the game", I lost less than a quarter health before I got to the final, last stand, part of the boss' routine. So clearly I can manage well enough. This last stand consists of summoning a double who defends from all attacks. The boss is crouching, healing, and is totally untouchable due to their double's defence and attacks. I expended all my healing and regeneration items on trying to figure out the secret, only to have to reload. And guess what. Your items do not reload with you. What kind of shoddy, dreadful, gut-wrenching design is that! But I managed. But I could not figure out the secret. I was getting really cross and fed up with this lazy repetitive nonsense, and I finally broke my sacred rule and looked up a walkthrough.
The secret? A contrived use of an ability that, at no point before, had been used for this use, nor said to be useful for this use, nor hinted at in the bossfight. I would NEVER have worked that out on my own, and perhaps that makes me thick, but I maintain it is lazy and shoddy game design to introduce a new gameplay mechanic, which in essence it is, in the last boss fight as the only way to make it tough, because otherwise it was not.
And even WITH that advice, it was a matter of sheer luck as to whether or not the ability, which requires items or grinding attacks to build up to a useable level, would actually perform as needed when activated and drained far too fast!
I cannot begin to describe the amount of bad language I used and how close I came to rage quitting, which is rare for me. Every example of poor design in a boss fight is present in this final, extrenuous encounter.
And if that wasn't bad enough, the ending afterwards was not even worth the effort.
I am genuinly upset that I cannot recommend this game, but it would be hypocritical of me to recommend a game with so many flaws even in just one fight that I would crucify any other game on.
Disagree with me if you want. Say I cannot play it if you want. I can play it. I did play it. I was playing it on medium difficulty (ok, so not the toughest, but it wasn't the easiest either!) and I managed to achieve a lot of high scores in other levels and as I said I did really well to begin with against this final boss and did not find it hard to hit them, dodge their attacks, or otherwise fight them. It was purely this execrably poor mechanic that foiled me, and at the same time sapped all my goodwill for an otherwise enjoyable game. Play it, don't play - it is your choice. It has its fun moments, but the plot ended up lamely and the final boss fight was a joke of bad design. I would recommend DANTE'S INFERNO as a game before this!

After the crushing disappointment that was being a backer of Mighty No. 9, 20XX shows what you can do with a team and a budget a fraction of the size, when you have incredible talent.
20XX is a combination of Mega Man and a Rogue-lite. It's a game that's designed to be done in runs and played over and over again. The levels are randomly generated, your health is persistent between them and when you die, you die. However, you can purchase items that you can carry forward into future runs, hence why it's a Rogue-lite instead of a Rogue-like.
Unlike Mega Man, while there are many different bosses and each have weaknesses you can exploit with weapons from other bosses, you don't get to pick your order from the get go. Instead, you get to choose one of three bosses to be the next one when you complete a level. In addition to the main mode, there are weekly and monthly challenges, both in standard and hardcore flavours, in which you can compete for leaderboard position.
While the controls aren't always quite as tight feeling as I'd like, this plays like a traditional Mega Man game in many ways and I say that as a compliment. Since the levels are randomly generated, you are subject to the whims of the RNG gods a little bit and some levels will be easier than others. However, they always feel well designed and rarely like something the computer put together with an algorithm.
20XX looks, runs and sounds amazing and again, it's incredible that such a small team did so much better a job than a large team with millions of dollars crapped out for Mighty No 9. The colours are vibrant, the character and enemy designs looks great and the game performs very well. It also has an excellent, chiptune inspired soundtrack.
I normally avoid most Early Access games and while 20XX is one at the time I write this, it already has tons of content and I'm still playing it regularly. The developers are updating it every 3 weeks and are providing great communication to the community. This is an Early Access game I can wholly recommend in its current state and I can't wait to see it finished up. Don't buy Mighty No. 9, buy this.

Astroneer is a space exploration game that also offers 4 player co-op if you don't feel like exploring alone. Astroneer, in its current state, has quite a bit of content for a pre-alpha game. That being said, the game has and does seem to have great potential ahead of it. I tuned into the Developer Podcast on December 22nd, 2016 and found the roadmap of this game. The developers seem to be listening to their community very closely and are considering adding things into the game that they might not have thought of prior.
That being said, the co-op in the game has more bugs easily noticeable than if you play alone. The multiplayer aspect has more glitches than if you play alone. For example, the trucks/rovers are completely broken in multiplayer. The game has been updated 3 times before the podcast on the 22nd, the game released on the 16th of December.
In my honest opinion, if you enjoy exploring or just even like the art style of this game - Buy it. I rarely play exploration games, but the art style of Astroneer drew me in faster than any other game on the Steam store has. I bought this game expecting to put upwards of 5-6 hours at first for it's pre-alpha state. I've now noticed I've put 17 hours into the PRE-ALPHA alone.
TL;DR - If you enjoy exploring and the art style, buy it. If you want to see more content, wait to buy it. Check out their website for the roadmap of this game's future (It looks very promising!)
extremely promising in alpha.

Astroneer shows a lot of potential for being a Pre-Alpha Early Access Game. So how is the game in it's current state?
Pros:
-The gameplay is pretty good. Very Simple.
-The design and graphics are very pleasing to look at, the low polygon style fits the game perfectly.
-Multiplayer (Only with Steam)
Cons:
-Lack of content (Pre Alpha). After a few hours of playing solo or with friends you have done pretty much everything the game has to offer.
-You have no control of your spaceship. You can only launch it and land it.
-Lack of graphic options, The only notable thing you can change is drawing distance. No options for AA, AO, Texture quality, Foliage density, Effects etc.
-Bugs and a lot of glitches.
-Not optimized, FPS drops when you start to explore and load more of the planet.
If you want to support the game the 19.99 price tag is worth it.

There's nothing really wrong with X3 honestly. It's a solid easy to use interface and has some pretty epic dogfights. All it really lacks is a better interface for larger, slower cruisers to fight and maybe a lil more fluid inventory system (like EVE Online) but other than that it's the best out there for single player space sims.

This is the best title in the series! It has the most content of all of them in it with a very vivid modding community. There is not much of a story there like in X2, but it keeps you entertained for hundreds of hours. I'd describe it as the singleplayer version of Eve Online. X is not a game like Freespace! It's more almost exclusively focused on economy and management. The combat is fine, but just not complex enough.

If you are a space sim fan and have run out of titles to choose from, then this game is worth a go. There is a lot of depth and many different ships to fly within a huge open universe. That being said, there is a huge learning curve to go with the depth. I found myself browsing the web for answers on how to do even the simplest of things far more often than I would have liked.

The tutorial is...well, you on a search engine because the developer felt as though only people who had played their previous entries would be playing this game.

The graphics are nice but there is no getting out to explore planets or space stations. You are limited to being in or around a ship throughout the entire game. In fact, you will never be planetside at all.

The AI is horribly broken to the point that it could frustrate Ghandi, assuming that Ghandi would have been a video game nerd (I'm not sure he'd be a space sim fan if he was), which constantly gives you the ultimatum of either losing large amounts of money or reloading your previous save. Choosing either option causes you to feel as though you have recieved the raw end of the deal since you will never get back the time spent.
If you are not like Ghandi the space sim fan and prefer action to trade then you again shouldn't bother as you will indeed be bored. There is action but there is far more travel-time than action and when it does break out, the enemy A.I. is not very bright and the outcome is based on a numbers game (who has more firepower). I personally don't mind travel-time in a space sim game but I'm sure it is only because I like the genre and the exploration that comes with it as opposed to enjoying this particular franchise. Sadly, there is no cockpit view to enjoy the exploration with and the camera is rather limited as well. There is a couple of outside views available but one of those views cannot be used to navigate intuitively and the other view is a camera stuck directly behind your burners with no allowance for deviation so you cannot really see your ship anyhow. It's possible there is an option somewhere to move this camera but it seems that will be another research topic for when I play the game next...which would be whenever I'm bored of poking myself in the eye with a stick.

Even in Early Access this game shows so much promise. I can easily put many hours into the game without realizing it due to so much adventure and fun to be had. I'm so excited for where it is going and cannot recommend it enough to others who enjoy an open world adventure game!

Well, after 300+ hours in I just might give a positive review :)
I'll start with not-so-good stuff:
- missed a few classic features, like human shields, weapon customisation and briefcase for sniper rifle. There are alternative decisions to rectify that.
- too gamepad-friendly interface: oversized tiles in the menu, weapon wheel, etc.
- lack of dark and grim atmosphere that I loved in Hitman: Contracts, for example
- soundtrack is forgettable.
BUT
Right now, after numerous updates, it's definitely the best game in Hitman series (and like the only good AAA game in last couple of years)
- In terms of sandbox and variative gameplay it's like Blood Money cranked to 11. Seriously, guys, sandbox is great over here.
- In terms of difficulty it has normal mode that is optimal for experiments and fun, and a Professional Mode that will remind you about your butthurts in Hitman 2: Silent Assassin.
- Player contracts mode is a huge upgrade on contracts mode from Absolution. Well, mainly because the maps in this game are actually designed for a Hitman game this time.
- Tons of content. 6 main missions, 4 bonus missions, 4 missions from GOTY campaign, about 60 escalations (new game mode), 26 elusive targets, challenge packs, player contracts...
- While the game is looking good but not very stylish, cutscenes in main story are amazing.

Pros:
- Huge, open world maps.
- Endlessly re-playable. I have over 443 hours in game, and still have a lot of fun.
- Regular new content and challenges, both from the developer and the community.
- Make your own contracts, and try and beat them. Then try to beat the people who beat your score on your own contracts. Then try and beat other people's scores on their contracts.
- One of, if not the best, stealth games ever made.
- Beautiful graphics and production quality.
- Lots of surprisingly clever humour and easter eggs hidden everywhere.
- Play any way you like, or try them all. Silent assassin, targets only, make your own targets, or kill them all. Or make your own challenges, e.g. using only melee weapons, only explosives, only poison, only accidents, never change disguise (suit only). You are limited only by your imagination and a huge range of weapons, physics and NPCs, main targets, and environmental combinations.
- Episodic release. I know many thought of this as a bad thing, but it turns out this is one of the few games that it's perfectly suited to. It forces you to play each level over and over, in a way you wouldn't if it was released all at once. There wasn't a single month where I ran out of things to do in the previous map before the new one was released. All the episodes are extremely high quality, huge, and endlessly re-playable. The end result was a game that felt fresh, new and fun for well past the six month release schedule.
Cons:
- Always on DRM. The only reason the game doesn't get 10/10 from me. That said, it has never actually affected the gameplay, but it's not a good way to do things. When the servers one day go down permanently, you will lose all of your progress in game, in my case 443+ hours of it.
- Not much of a story, and what there is, is hard to follow. That said, you pretty much make your own new stories on each level playthrough, so not a big deal.
- Timed elusive targets are fun, but playable once only, whether you succeed or fail. I get what they're going for, but it can be very frustrating if you fail the mission because of a bug or glitch, and can't redo it - ever. It's also a lot of good quality content to lock people out of permanently.
9/10. My game of the year for 2016, and one of my favourite games ever. 10/10 if they ever remove the always-on DRM in a way that allows you to keep all your progress offline.

It amazes me how an early access title is already ten fold better than a certain other Mega Man imitator with a budget hundreds of times larger than 20XX...
This really feels like how Mega Man would have evolved. Don't be discouraged by the rouge-like genre. This game still features tight design, so I never was screwed out to a lack of decent items. Speaking of those items, it's amazing how different you'll play based on what you items you acquire. Everything is unique with its own pros and cons. The amount of tactical decisions you make in this game add a deep layer of depth. Decisions such as:
Should I take the boss weapon of aug?
Should I purchase health, an aug, or save?
Is it worth it to try traverse an optional part of the level for the item?
Which boss should I fight next?
Should I trade this weapon for another?
The only two negatives I can think about are the lackluster K&M controls (then again, it is a Mega Man inspired platformer), and the game can get repetitive if levels are played in the same order each consecutive run. If played in a random order, levels will contain different enemies, hazards, boss movesets, and challenges for the player to overcome.
I haven't even encountered a single bug yet either, nor any problems with performance. Just amazing how much a team with a hundredth of the budget, of a certain other Mega Man inspired kickstarter game, can match and even exceed the quality of the Mega Man titles from 20+ years ago.
BTW, the art style of this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.  Manages to be more detailed than many other 2D games, even ones that had a kickstarted budget on $4 million.

TL;DR at bottom
Found this gem at PAX Prime. Walking past it I had to double back because it looked jsut like Megaman. One of the devs (Chris) Approach me as I was sayign to my bro "This looks just like Megaman." "That's because it is, a megaman roguelike." Played it and immediatly bought it. He promised a megaman roguelike, and that's exactly what we get.
The classic rock-beats-scissor boss style that defines the megaman series can be found here, even going as far as having certains powers help with certain levels.
There are hidden power-ups that you can find off the beaten path that feel right at h ome with the megaman gameplay style. From air dodging to blaster power-ups, I've yet to find a power-up that did not feel native the it's inspiration.
The big selling point is that this is all set in a roguelike! The levels are never the same, and will be filled with different challenges, including challenge rooms that will come upgrades for a reward.
In addition to the standard game on three different difficulties, the devs run daily and weekly challenges, and two difficulties for said challenges. They also offer a couple different game modes: a speedrun mode and a boss rush mode.
The replayability for this game is insane, add in that it can be done co-op on the same screen and it will be easy to sink hours into it with a roomate.
Cons:
-The character art designs could be better. They aren't bad, but they're off. I actually think it would have looked better to have nina take on the zero role and Ace take on the Megaman role. There are a couple animations used that stuck out as odd for me too. One that comes to mind is the charge up animation for ace. Ace swings a sword, and when he charges up his sword blaster(?) opens up and you see this circle charging. There aren't any big flaws in the character art design, but rather small thigns here and there that stick out in an otherwise fairly polished game.
-Throughout all of PAX, my friends and I were very excited about the game and talked about it a lot, but we called it megaman. None of us could remember that it's name is 20XX. This isn't really a con for the player, but I can see getting the name out there and remembered being a possible issue for the company.
-No static single player campaign or straight forward story, yet. The game is still in early access, and it's possible that an actual story is made and will be added on release. I don't know, and forgot to ask. I doubt it though as this is a roguelike. For fans of true roguelikes, this isn't a con.
Pros:
-Very true to the spirit of Megaman
-Great use of having two different genders for characts, but not putting it on a pedastal or drawing unneeded attention to it.
-Lots of upgrades to choose from and power-ups to collect, Progression has longetevity to it, and getting your perfect loadout isn't neccesarily easy or quick.
-Very high replay value, leaderboards, multiplayer, multiple game modes, and daily/weekly challenges really extend the lifespan of this game.
-controller keybinds feel great. One of the highpoints of Megaman was how much finesse a player could accomplish challenges with, and that's present in this game's control scheme.
-True Roguelike, you get one life when you play, and that's it. You die, and you start all over. For easy and normal you can buy power-ups to start with, but they're lost after that run.
TL;DR Conclusion:
Great blend of megaman with the roguelike genre. Expect the game to be true to the genre and not have a campaign or driving story. Lots of gamemodes, daily and weekly challenges, difficulty settings for all of the above, and co-op both online and same screen will keep you more than content for hours. If you're a fan of megaman or a fan of roguelikes, I can safely say you will enjoy this. It's a unique roguelike thanks to the megaman influence, and for megaman fans it feels like a never-ending game.
All in all: 5 star game.

This game captures the spirit of Mega Man X.  The controls are silky smooth and tight as can be.  The two main characters you play as are obvious mirrors of X and Zero.
The differences lie in the procedurally generated levels with increasingly difficult bosses.  As you progress through the game on each run, the levels and bosses at the end of those levels all get harder.  And at the end of each level you make a choice on who you want to fight next from three options.  There are small and short challenge rooms which often unlock powerups.  There are four main slots for character powerups that a Megaman X fan would expect:  Helmet, Boots, Chest, Arm.  There is a large range of discoverable powerups in each slot.  For example, some boots might give you a double jump, some might give you an air dash, some might let you hover, or fly.  There is a nice variety of these for all of the different upgrade slots on the character.  There's a LOT more items and basic upgrades to be found for your health and damage as well.  Plus of course you can grab a defeated bosses power if you wish.
The enemies and bosses are fun to shoot and kill.  It's all challenging. No run is the same.  There are leaderboards for daily and/or weekly challenges.  This game has a very nice amount of content for its relatively small price tag.  This game is absolultey recommended for almost anyone and I highly doubt any fan of Megaman X wouldn't love this game.

Essentially two games in one, The Desolate Hope combines familiar gameplay elements from vastly different genres to create something greater than the whole of its parts. While clunky at times, it feels refreshingly creative despite doing little new.
Normal levels play out like a simple sidescrolling platformer where you collect resources and unlock & upgrade abilities. Every map has one boss that you have to beat four times; although it sounds tedious, they mix things up by moving the boss entrance around the map and drastically increasing the difficulty of boss tiers (which essentially forcing you to play through other levels and then backtrack). This helps breaks up the flow and promotes exploration, instead of just steamrolling through the maps one at a time.
The bosses that you are preparing for during the platforming segments are the crux of the gameplay; it is really refreshing to look forward to a boss battle in a western game. These play out like JRPG battles, with your party of AIs on the right throwing their "spells" at the boss on the left. It took me a while to get used to it because its very fast and click-happy, with bosses often acting faster than your whole party can. Eventually the combat gets so fast that you have to use special abilities to automate certain functions (trying to avoid spoilers here!). Herein lies my biggest complaint because once the combat gets truly challenging and gives you all your tools & toys, the game just plays itself.
While I really enjoyed this game, I don't see it getting a sequel anytime soon considering how it ends. Hopefully once the devs are done milking FNAF we will get a spiritual successor because The Desolate Hope is a very creative and colorful take on a futuristic apocalypse.

This is not your regular Five Night's at Freddy's game everyone has so lovingly fell in love with
The Desolate Hope still has its weird art style everyone has fallen in love with in the FNAF series but it has a very compelling story to follow with and very lovable characters.
The game offers memorable yet some weird and scary characters along with a very compelling story which will hook you in no matter what. The atmosphere is just stunning, it take you a minute to admire the beautiful atmosphere, a few times I stopped and looked at the art style. The combat system is very unique, a bit confusing at first but you get the hang of it after a few tries and the combat music is so much fun to listen!
However this game does have its fair share of problems, however none of them are game breaking. The gameplay may get repetitive, collecting chips at night and finding viruses during the day. Walking is very slow and their is no option to sprint or run a bit faster. There is a lack of tutorials to introduce you to the mechanics, which can leave you wondering for quite a while and asking yourself what on earth you have to do next.
But, this game is a gem of a game and I congratulate Scott Cawthon for making such a beautiful indie game very different to his widely successful FNAF series, and hopefully this game may be given so more love, care and attention and we get a series just like FNAF fans are getting right now.
The only thing I am sad to say is that although this game is very good, it is a lost gem piled from Scott Cawthon's other successful game series, which is a real shame :(

If you liked Hitman games prior to Absolution, you will love Hitman 2016.  It is the best in the series by far.  There are only a handful of maps, but they are huge and full of opportunities to try many different strategies.  The replayability is fantastic.  There is always something new to try.
Just when you think you've mastered a map, you get a whole new challenge with user created contracts.  The map may be the same, but just trying to eliminate a different target changes the whole dyanmic.  The additional Escalation contracts keep things interesting too by introducing an increasing number of parameters to follow, which again, changes the whole dyanmic of the maps.
The episodic release of this game makes sense to me.  I bought the game just prior to the last map being released, so diving in at that point was a bit overwhelming.  I wish I had bought this at the beginning with only the first map because it would have encouraged me to explore the map more before moving on to the next.
The graphics are great, and it runs pretty well on my system (GTX 970 and i5 6600k).
I'm very much looking forward to Season 2 of Hitman!

This game's a whole lot of fun to play, and that's pretty much the bottom line. It controls really well, the level design feels sort of fresh from playthrough to playthrough (though you will start to recognize pieces being reused). The powers you can take from the bosses are all really helpful for a wide variety of situations, with some even carrying extra special effects like Kur's weapon allowing you to loot a vending machine for free. Music is really good too.
There are a feq minor quips here and there though. The enemy placement can at times be obnoxious, which is due to the nature of this being a roguelike. This is most noticeable in late level versions of skytemple where it sometimes feels like enemies are crammed into sections of the level. The little flying bat things also seem to be way overused and become something of a chore to kill. That and Eternal Star fought at a late level is honestly a bit too much in terms of difficulty compared to all the other bosses at that stage in the game. some bosses later on also feel a bit *too* tanky to where I feels tedious to kill them (I'm looking at you late level visage).
Regardless of the quips this is a game that's a whole lot of fun to play for people who are into the megaman series and even for those who aren't. I've never played a megaman or megaman X platformer before in my life, but damn if this game doesn't make me want to give them a try. There's also challenges worked into the game to tighten up the difficulty if things start to get too easy for you vets out there, and a casual mode if you're having too much trouble. I managed to win on the normal mode on my fourth run, I'm hoping to get a streak going and maybe crank up the difficulty soon to get a better feel for the challenges worked into the game.

There's a lot to familiarize with, and it's is not from the sheer difficulty of the game, but from the quantity of content to explore i.e the command softwares, ship equipment, weaponry, sector information (e.g supply and demand, production, wares), factories- the list goes on. Patience is probably needed, and it's not going to be from the speed of the ship relative to the average distance to travel (there's time compression and jumpdrives for that).
Surmounting this, you get a game with features analogous to ones in real-time strategies (e.g units, control groups, invading sectors) and empire building (e.g production, fleets, personnel), in addition to what's obvious: shooting, trading, objectives from NPCs in a toggle-able first/third person perspective viewing stunning scenery coupled with unfittingly reused NPC avatar assets from 2003.
The odd ding of the game is the UI and menu interaction (without community mods/scripts), and even for a game like this, there isn't the convenience of command queuing. It's usual to navigate sub-menus and sub-menus within sub-menus- making some functionality hard to find at first or tedious to navigate to. Another is how [player owned] AI ships can get that one surge of stupidity or suicidal tendency then bump into objects until they crash and die, or try to fly through a Xenon sector then die.
The main attraction of the game is in the freedom and possibilities in player defined goals. Don't expect tense emotional moments, flashy cutscenes, or iconic characters with funny and quirky lines- is not part of what mostly goes (or what will ever go) on. Some of the plot lines available (9 in total) aren't so great with some missions including ~5 seconds long unskippable scenes (fortunately infrequent) that show redundant information that the HUD shows already, and [being told to] follow(ing) a ship flying at 56 m/s for a 60 km or so journey, though the end rewards can have a massive effect on the universe and what's available to the player.

In an effort to buff up on the different genres of games I've experienced, I bought Still Life during the Summer Steam Sale of 2013. Since it is currently the Autumn Steam Sale I figured I write up a review for those currently looking to buy it.
Still Life is a 3D interactive puzzle adventure that follows a single muder mystery case that unfolds from the perspective of two different characters, FBI Agent McPherson (In 2004 US Chicago) and her PI Grandfather Gustav McPherson (In 1920s Czech Rep Prague) . Neither of these two characters interact directly with the other; Gustav McPherson's story is told through diary.
In general there's not much difference in gameplay that occurs during a switch of characters as it is mostly done for narritives sake. In terms of gameplay Still Life's is fairly weak. Much of the interaction in the game mainly comes from chosing the correct person to talk to, using the right items/objects and solving a few puzzles. The puzzles themselves are actually very well thought out and surprisingly difficult! I actually found myself at wits end on a puzzle and am ashamed to say that I actually had to find help online!
Graphics wise Still Life looks quite dated now a days. A lot of the lip synching when a character speak looks incredible jarring. Mouths on some characters look more like nutcrakers when they talk.... On the flipside character models themselves are well designed and look quite decent too! Where Still Life really shines though is in the Pre renderded enviroments. If you're a fan of early Resident Evil games or like looking at background art in general, you will enjoy the look and immersion of the enviroments that the visual departments in Still Life offers.
Though honestly the main reason anyone should really play Still Life would be for its story and characters! Over all I feel like the characterization of everyone in Still Life is done very realisticly. A lot of the dialouge does a very good job explaining the lives and personalities of the people they are suppose to represent. It's been more than a few months since I've played this game and though I can't recall completely by heart all the names of the characters; the use of the voice actors and the roles the characters played in the story themselves are embedded quite well into my mind.
Also mild spoiler alert but I have to point this out as it's a slight♥♥♥♥♥♥move on the developers part. The story ends on a cliff hanger! You don't catch your murderer. You have to buy part two to wrap up this case. Because of this I recommend that if you want all of your monies worth that you buy this game when it is on sale. While it is a good game at telling a story and presenting convincing and unique characters, Still Life fails to completely maintain any interesting gameplay. The story doesn't suffer from it but sometimes you feel more like you're watching movie.
I recommed this game but only buy it as the part 1&2 bundle and on sale.

Still Life follows the trail of a gruesome serial killer in a classic thriller/mystery style. You play as detective Victoria McPherson who is investigating a string of prosti tute murders, all of whom's bodies were found badly beaten and mutilated. The atmosphere is well done and each crime scene is quite graphic. The style of this game is a classic point and click adventure. As far as game play is concerned, adventure games tend to be vague and it can be difficult to figure out what you are supposed to do next, but that rarely happens in this title. In fact, in Still Life, it is usually very obvious what you are supposed to do - but that's the hard part. The puzzles in this game range from rather simple to frustratingly demanding. While the puzzles do become immensely complex, the puzzles are also very logical. I personally spent about 30-40 minutes trying to figure out one of the difficult puzzles in this game. So if you are going to play this title, you need to have patience and a strong penchant for puzzle solving. This isn't a title you can just rush through (unless you look up all the solutions, but that seems kind of silly). The graphics are a bit dated and the voice acting while good/ok, isn't top notch. About 8-10 hours playtime.

This game is a fast-paced platform/RPG about a CoffeeBot and his artificial Intelligence D-Co 9 trying to stop a digital Virus that is destroying 4 robots simulations, until they get tha the virus.... Well, play by yourself :P

Before Scott Cawthon had everyone cowering in terror from creepy looking robot things, he had them assisting and being assisted by... creepy looking robot things. In The Desolate Hope, you are a computer program originally designed to run video games. Coffee, a walking, sentient coffee maker, activates you and explains that you are to take over his body and use it to fight off a virus that is attacking the simulations maintained by the other robots of Lun Infinus. Coffee would do so itself, but it's far too busy maintaining things and flagging the viruses for you. And with that, you're off on a very unique adventure.
There are four working robots running simulations on Lun Infinus, and you will have to enter each one and defeat four viruses within. Do not be afraid. They may look intimidating and even dangerous as you enter their respective chambers, but they're all on your side, and they're all quite friendly. Their simulations, on the other hand, have gotten a little... weird. Originally sent out into space to run these simulations for five years, they've now gone thirty years without contact.
The gameplay is rather varied. Although much of your time will be spent wandering and shooting. In reality, Coffee's body can't do much more than walk around and pick stuff up. You'll use the real world to walk between the robots' chambers and collect knick-knacks to give to the A.I.s within. Inside of the simulations, the game plays out as a sidescrolling jump-'n'-shoot game. You'll shoot enemies, find secrets, collect eggs which will help you against the virus boss fights, talk to things, and hunt for the viruses. You can find computer screens which will dump you into some sort of sub-simulation, an overhead wander-'n'-shoot game. Here you can collect resource chips (The Desolate Hope's currency) and destroy the rift-looking whatsit that's hidden away in one of the rooms to unlock a new conditional for later. Then you have the virus fights.
The fights against the viruses are where the game really shines. These are flashy, fast-paced RPG battles. They are turn based, but with an active time system (think PlayStation-era Final Fantasy). Your party consists of the four A.I.s that you've been helping, each of whom has a unique set of skills. Every time one of their menus pops up, you can use one of these skills, or charge. What skills you have access to depends on that A.I.'s level of charge, and keeping them charged is an important part of the fight. The viruses get tougher as you go, and you'll need more tricks up your sleeve to see this game through.
The A.I.s don't level up with experience. Instead, each trinket you bring back from your nightly expeditions outside will convince one to devote more of its resources to your cause, which is represented by the A.I. leveling up. You can purchase a variety of useful abilities from various robots within the simulations. And then you have those conditionals I mentioned. You can set one of a number of useful actions (healing, for instance) to occur when certain other events (like opening a mini game or getting a combo) occur within battles. The catch is, while you have the entire list of "then"s from the get-go, you have to find and unlock the "if"s yourself.
So, let's talk quality. The review part of the review.
The art in this game is really weird, but in a good way. You can tell it was created by the same guy who did 5 Nights at Freddy's. It's the way things are modeled and some of the textures, and it's also some of the weirdness and the robots. There's a giant robot in the background of one of the simulations that reminds me an awful lot of Freddy Fazbear. The way Coffee walks down the hallway of Lun Infinus seems like it probably directly inspired the shot of Foxy hauling♥♥♥♥♥down the hallway in the first 5NaF. The simulations all have different looks and feels to them. The sub-simulations look completely different from anything else, and the virus battles are flashy and remind me a bit of anime, only without the... y'know, anime. Even wandering outside at night is lovely and mysterious.
A major contributing factor to that lovely mysteriousness is the gorgeous music. I can't give Scott credit with creating it, as he says he bought it all through a website called NEO Sounds. But I can absolutely credit Scott with taking the care and effort to find, purchase, and use the perfect tracks to complement each scene. I have no complaints about the music.
The story is one that kept me paying attention. The core plot isn't
complex, but it's presented well and supplemented with backstory and information about the world and A.I.s. As with everything else in this game, the story's got that air of mystery that draws you in.
As for the gameplay, I like it. The jump and shoot sections aren't exactly Mega Man, but they're not boring and they offer exploration and an engaging way to get from point A to point B. The overhead sections are neat if you're just trying to find the rift thing and destroy it, but if you wind up grinding for resource chips the game becomes pretty boring. Good news is, you don't
to grind. Bad news is, intentionally or not, you're kind of encouraged to. See, the entire game operates on this day/night cycle, and the days and nights go by pretty darn quickly and you only have so many of them. You have plenty of ways to get resource chips as you go about your ordinary business, but the overhead sections are the only place where time doesn't pass (other than dialogue windows, I believe). Add to this the fact that you can buy the ability to earn resource chips even faster in these sections, and you'll probably decide it's easier to just grind for awhile rather than waste time.
This brings me to the time limit itself. It does add an element of pressure to the game, which is nice. But you'll need to figure things out for yourself, you'll have no idea what order to fight which viruses in, and if you're like me, you might waste a couple days trying to explore simulations which are open to you, but which you can't actually do much in until you have the right items. That said, even if you do wander aimlessly for awhile, you will probably eventually hit a stride where you can take out two or three viruses a day, making up for lost time. I still wound up completing the game like six-ish days ahead of schedule. And I hear you can find items outside which will grant you extra days, once you start cutting it close.
As I said before, though, the active RPG virus boss battles are where the game truly shines, and they'll be what you're striving for. Not the shooty bits, but the flashy, fast paced (the RPG battles are actually faster paced than the shooting sections, can you believe it?), try-to-even-begin-to-keep-track-of-all-this♥♥♥♥♥♥at-once-lol sections.
With the sort of creepy but mostly cool art, the fitting audio, and the sweet battles, I recommend The Desolate Hope. I don't know if it's free forever, but it seems like it probably is. And free is more than generous for a quality game like this.

I haven't written a review for this yet?! OK. Here it goes:
Absolutely recommend this game. More than a year after its release and conclusion, IO Interactive keeps updating the game with new contracts and missions. They've recently started reactivating the "Elusive Targets", the unique and limited-time "one shot, one opportunity" missions.
Now the game is not perfect by any means, but the price of entry is relatively cheap now, and there's a ton of content available at this point. The diabolical hooks of Square Enix still show themselves, such as a mandatory internet connection for this primarily single player game. Hitman is out from under SE now, however, so it's worth supporting the devs as they try their best to deal with all the moronic business practices SE enforced.
The game itself is along the lines of an "immersive sim", something like Deus Ex or Dishonored but without RPG elements. It is all about player agency and gives you as much freedom as technically possible to accomplish your goal. You can customize the amount of help the game gives you, so if you want to be led by the nose and just experience the set-piece kills and the story, you can do just that. You can also fast-track unlocking all the weapons and turn it into a mediocre third person cover shooter, if that's your thing. The choices are there.
TL;DR, get HITMAN, f**k Square Enix.

Astroneer is a space exploration game that also offers 4 player co-op if you don't feel like exploring alone. Astroneer, in its current state, has quite a bit of content for a pre-alpha game. That being said, the game has and does seem to have great potential ahead of it. I tuned into the Developer Podcast on December 22nd, 2016 and found the roadmap of this game. The developers seem to be listening to their community very closely and are considering adding things into the game that they might not have thought of prior.
That being said, the co-op in the game has more bugs easily noticeable than if you play alone. The multiplayer aspect has more glitches than if you play alone. For example, the trucks/rovers are completely broken in multiplayer. The game has been updated 3 times before the podcast on the 22nd, the game released on the 16th of December.
In my honest opinion, if you enjoy exploring or just even like the art style of this game - Buy it. I rarely play exploration games, but the art style of Astroneer drew me in faster than any other game on the Steam store has. I bought this game expecting to put upwards of 5-6 hours at first for it's pre-alpha state. I've now noticed I've put 17 hours into the PRE-ALPHA alone.
TL;DR - If you enjoy exploring and the art style, buy it. If you want to see more content, wait to buy it. Check out their website for the roadmap of this game's future (It looks very promising!)
extremely promising in alpha.

Astroneer shows a lot of potential for being a Pre-Alpha Early Access Game. So how is the game in it's current state?
Pros:
-The gameplay is pretty good. Very Simple.
-The design and graphics are very pleasing to look at, the low polygon style fits the game perfectly.
-Multiplayer (Only with Steam)
Cons:
-Lack of content (Pre Alpha). After a few hours of playing solo or with friends you have done pretty much everything the game has to offer.
-You have no control of your spaceship. You can only launch it and land it.
-Lack of graphic options, The only notable thing you can change is drawing distance. No options for AA, AO, Texture quality, Foliage density, Effects etc.
-Bugs and a lot of glitches.
-Not optimized, FPS drops when you start to explore and load more of the planet.
If you want to support the game the 19.99 price tag is worth it.

I have spent countless hours designing, building, managing, and simply watching the bustle of my prisons. What I particularly like: While many other games of this genre lack interesting mechanics for the late-game, Prison Architect always keeps you on your toes, be it
: Not even your Super-Max-Prison is super safe!
Due to the huge amount of details and the mechanics within the simulation it is somewhat deterring to begin with, yet satisfingly complex when you gained experience and master all the different challenging aspects. For beginners, there is a variety of options to reduce the level of complexity, by simply deactivating some of the simulation's advanced layers.
If you are in for challenge, you can also slip into the role of one of your inmates and try to escape your own (and other's) prisons. Talking about this, the workshop and mod support is great and the community has developed a huge amount of new and alternative content.
While I do enjoy the game, I think it costs a tad too much. I bought it during alpha phase, when they had a steam sale, which lead to a more reasonable price.

Prison Architect is a real time strategy game similar to city builders. You are in charge of building and running a prison. You get to design the daily regime, customize room sizes and contents to your specific likings, control what types of prisoners get in and out of your prison, and try to stay in business.
The gameplay of prison architect is what you could expect from city builders. You can designate a certain amount of tiles to a room, place objects in that room to help it function and try to find the perfect size for each room and distance between them. You also have to design your travel-ways, as letting prisoners travel through tiny hallways can lead to a lot of angry shoving and death. Add customizing and caring for your own staff to that, taking care of scheduling, and dealing with gangs? You have a pretty in-depth simulator here. Not to mention there's another game mode where you get to play as a prisoner and try to escape. That game mode is admittedly lacking and completely lacks a tutorial whereas the main game has an entire campaign that serves as an over-glorified tutorial. Overall there's a lot to do in this game. And with all the options? It's very fun and very addicting while you're doing it. This is one of those games where you start up your first prison at 8pm and look up, realize it's 2AM, and think, just 5 more minutes...now oh look its 6AM.
The story of the game is actually rather interesting even though it is just an over-glorified tutorial. Unfortunately it suffers because the game also has a lot of bugs, which surprised me for a game old enough that the developers have stopped regularly patching it. The third mission in particular has a nasty one where you have to move riot police around, and if you go the obvious closest route you fail the mission because your riot police get stuck in a doorway and stop moving, defending themselves, and just generally responding. Other than that though, the whole campaign was well written and really tied together nicely while teaching you what you needed to know for sandbox mode.
The graphics and sounds are both really lacking. The graphics don't bother me, but the sounds do. This game lacks a lot of specific sound effects and opts for ambience effects based on where your prisoners are and what they're doing based on the regime. That's why the cafeteria clatters and reverberates with silverware and voices during dinner but you'll find your prison woefully quiet during free time and lockup periods. This all does a lot to take away any immersion the game could have had, which is unfortunate, but not the biggest deal for an title in this genre.
This game is an amazing simulator, and it doesn't suffer from the same traffic issues most games in its genre do where you build bigger and bigger and suddenly you can't get everyone where they need to go because they all want to take one route instead of the many available to them. It DOES however have it's own critical late-game issue I think you should all be aware of. It's the fact that once you have one of everything and a prison population that suits it, you get to a point where all you have left to do is repeat what you've already done. There's no expansion of districts or ability to connect distant places to make this easier like in city builders though. You are after a certain point of expansion, basically forced to start over in one of two ways. You can continue to expand the same prison by doing the same thing over again in some other chunk of free space you have left, which then brings in the hassle of assigning certain rooms to only service certain parts of your prison and all your funding will come from your own original profits since you've already used all the grants that help you build your prison. Or you can sell what you have made and start in a fresh empty lot with the value of your prison in your pocket, sort of like a new game plus and with all of the grants once again available to you. This process is what eventually had me quit the game. I think this is one of the biggest flaws all district-less builders suffer from though.
Overall though, Prison Architect is a fun game. It's definitely above average, but it's not the indie gem everyone says it is. This gets a 6/10 from me. I definitely recommend you buy it if you enjoy this genre when it's on sale because $30 for something you can experience all of within eight hours is not a good price for your money. If you really love this niche, then you'll love this game, and with modding support and the ability to save and share your prisons, it even has it's own little community of builders you can become a part of.

----
I had to play this game in short bursts because it was just too much stimuli being thrown at me every second. The game constantly throws flashing colours and photoshop filter swaps around like confetti and it gets really exhausting really quickly. On top of that a lot of the visuals are kind of disturbing. The player experience is a bit like going through Dante's Inferno yourself - like some sort of club music infused drug induced kaleidoscope nightmare.
I think I finished the game in about 10 hours total, but in reality it took me about two months of playing an hour or so a week. It was just too much for my poor brain to handle.
Which isn't to say I didn't enjoy it, quite the contrary! The set pieces were kind of jaw dropping and the ending I thought was particularly awesome, but you may find that you grow numb to all the spectacle if you play it over the course of one or two sittings.
If you're a Devil May Cry veteran, I'd definately recommend cranking the difficulty up to maximum for the best combat experience - I played it on the middle difficulty setting and found everything just a bit too easy and forgiving, and I am really not very good at fighting games at all so that says a lot.
Once you finish the game once on any of the standard difficulty settings you unlock another higher difficulty setting to play through with different enemy spawns, and once you finish that there are two or three more to do if you're into that sort of thing - so there is longevity for completionists and challenge lovers.
Overall, a good game worth playing if you've got the mental stamina for it, though be warned it contains very adult themes throughout.

I love platformers, so I quickly took a liking to the first part of the game which is to shoot enemies for colored eggs (which I found out much later give you power ups during boss battles) while dodging or shooting down enemy attacks and passing obstacles.

All in all, this is a very well made, very unique game bringing two very different gaming elements together into one very strange, very addictive game.

This is a curious little title, with unusual characters, setting, premise, among other things. You play as an AI from a video game system being repurposed for exterminating digital viruses, and you have a physical body on loan from a space station's coffee machine. The stated goal is to purge the viruses springing up in the simulations some of the robots on the planetary outpost/station which other AIs before you have generally failed. To do so, you need to work on numerous layers of your surroundings. As fair warning, this game really doesn't hold your hand, but does give you some room to experiment and learn what it is exactly that you need to do and how.
As for genre, it's pretty hard to classify this as any single genre as it's a mashup of several, while not feeling particularly broken. There's meatspace (physical space, rather), where it's closest to an adventure title similar to King's Quest, in that you have direct control over a character with limited actions rather than click and point like, say, Monkey Island 1-3. In simulations, it's more of a platformer/shooter, to sum it up. When you get into the source code segments (I don't recall the exact explanation to what these are, though I'm sure the game mentions it somewhere early on) it's more adventure/shooter like the original Legend of Zelda. And when you fight bosses, it's sort of an Active Time Battle RPG but also upwards of 5 or 6 games going on at once, and this is where the game may be completely overwhelming while also being an amazing spectacle.
It's almost beyond words to describe boss fights, I suppose the closest is what 80s movies predicted games in the 90's to be like? Either way, very unique, in a positive way. Character designs are also wonderful and range from beauty in simplicity to visually overwhelming and I love them all, honestly. The audio is pleasant and mostly appropriate for each area and segment, the game also does a great job of setting up just how grim the situation is without explicitly stating it.
For criticisms, the game has pacing issues similar to a roller coaster, slow build up before going extremely fast until the bottom of the next hill. As for graphics, very subjective to whether folks will like them, I find em charming personally, but some may not enjoy the mid 90's-style pre-rendered sprites and animations akin to Donkey Kong Country. Difficulty for each part of game is also VERY drastically different, which can cause a little bit of whiplash. I apologize in advance if there is a manual that explains everything somewhere, but there's parts of the game and characters that feel as though there's probably context given in something extraneously, such as in a manual with a little blurb about the character and maybe backstory, but there's quite a few NPCs who seem to just be there with the only context being "Hey, this NPC performs function X or sells Y or sells Z for a small fortune."
Overall, it's a rather unique experience and I'd suggest folks give it a fair shake. I've enjoyed what I've played thus far, and hope others enjoy it as well!

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is one of those games many people initially would not buy, as it kind of seems boring, and with the entire genre pretty much plagued by terrible games.
However, ETS2 is one of the few massive exceptions. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a great game, even for those who normally don't play these types of games. Even though the whole game revolves around seemingly boring work, it manages to make it incredibly entertaining and fun to play.
A lot of the game's fun lies in its simple but engrossing gameplay. Drive from A to B without damaging your load or taking too long. But as soon as you turn on your own background music, podcast or stream, the game becomes a whole lot more immersive and incredibly relaxing. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a great way to relief some stress after a long day. You will often find yourself spending hours in the game even though you only intended to do like one or two deliveries. The variety in landscapes, roads and driving experiences combined with the excellent presentation prevents the game from getting too monotone and boring. Especially with the expansion DLCs.
In addition to being a great game overall the Modding community for ETS2 is massive. There are mods of all kinds, whether they add more realism, new paintjobs, better graphics, or entirely new maps with a more challenging approach. ProMods, a mod that expands the map by a massive amount is one of the best mods for any game out there.
But what is the best mod then, you may ask? It's an easy question to answer; Truckers MP. Truckers MP adds a multiplayer mode to ETS2 and ATS, giving you the ability to share your passion for driving with thousands(!) of other players at once, adding a completely new experience to both games. It's almost a must for everyone who decides to spend some more time in this game.

Sonic 4 Episode 2, is a sidescroller platforming game featuring Modern Sonic and Tails. People have really mixed out opinions about this game, and it is time to give mine.
SPOILER ALERT! CONTAINS PART OF THE STORY.
Story is easy to understand. Let's start from Episode Metal, I guess.
On Stardust Speedway M.Sonic lies on the road defeated by Sonic. Eggman suddently brings him to life, and tells him to fly to his base. When he's here, Eggman fixes him and M.Sonic blasts off.
In new Zone, M.Sonic finds a weird artifact giving him power. The place is falling apart and Metal escapes.
Nothing happens till the last zone. At the end, M.Sonic sees Sonic and Tails fly on Tornado with an unknown mission. He finds somekind of rocket and he flies it, to get to the Tornado. This is where Episode Metal ends.
Sonic 4 Ep. 2 main story starts when Sonic and Tails are landing, and they land in Sylvania Castle (original first level Sonic Team).
Let's now take some rest from the story and focus on gameplay.
It's like a normal, classic sidescroller, but Tails follows you, and he is more useful. When your partner is out of the screen, you can press a button to get him back. As always, Horming Attack returns, but its better than in S4EP1. First time, Tag Actions are introduced. They take huge part of the levels, and make Tails more useful. Controls feel nice, visuals are beautiful. You can get 50 rings, to enter special stage at the end of the level. But here is a minus. H A L F  P I P E  H E L L. Let's continue the story.
After 3 Zones nothing interesting happens. Just at the almost last zone, Sonic and Tails are chasing Eggman, he escapes, and then our heroes found out that Metal has found a plane, and he's determined to destroy our heroes. He fails, Sonic and Tails get on the airship, and they try to stop Eggman. Another Metal fight at the end, and we got another cutscene. Eggman and Metal escaped from exploding airship, and there looks like there is no escape pods for heroes. They eventually find the less working ones, but they get them to the final zone, Death Egg mk II.
Some platforming, we enter in the boss with Eggman and Metal Sonic and after that, we get glorious but short Metal Sonic race. We win, we move on. Platforming, and then we fight with the Eggman final creation that looks like a heart. Boss is mostly luck based but it's easy. Heroes defeat Eggman, Death Egg explodes, and heroes escape.
The end.
Final Verdict: Sonic 4 Ep 2 is a fun game, but it's not perfect just like in story, or some bosses. It's really good. 8/10
