APB: Reloaded is a game that combines 3rd person over-the-shoulder shooting within a sprawling MMO world that is always changing. After a rough start with RTW (being a retail game with monthly subscription) it was closed and sooner or later picked up by K2 Networks. Formerly known as GamersFirst; K2 Networks set out to turn APB into the "Free2Play" game it is today, complete with a Cash Shop *ridiculous prices.* Overall a decent game. The customization will keep you busy for hours. The balancing could use a little work and the server is straight up horrible at times. "Hackusations" are common in every other match. Although actual hackers play, it's not as common as the game-chat would have you believe. Some people will tell you it's pay2win. I disagree. Get a friend, and use a mic! While I think Mega Man is still better, there's no sighn of a new Mega Man game coming in the future. And, since it's randomly generated, this is the perfect game for anyone who's a fan of the Mega Man series or just platformers in general!

This is such a good game. I've played hours on top of hours of this game. I paid about $20 for this game, and got over 360 hours of gameplay that I have mostly enjoyed (can get a bit stressful but that's part of the game). I have started so many prisons, sold many prisons, scrapped new prisons. There is so much you can do, and you can have your own unique prison. For example, you could have a prison with the worst of the worst inside of it and not too many cells, or you could have a huge facility that is filled with low security prisoners. The choice is yours, dormitories or cells, reform or heavy punishment, death row facilities on the side or no deathrow facilities. There is a lot you can do with this game, and the developers have made a masterpiece. Below are the pros and cons:
Pros:
A lot of the of choice on what you do, you don't have to build a specific kind of prison.
The developers put a lot of effort into this game unlike some other games which the developers kind of abandoned.
Hours of fun gameplay, complications and learning from your mistakes and improving your prison to make it the best.
Lots of options you can choose before you start a prison, for example, if you can see throughout the prison with guards/camers or not.
Haven't tested this, but where it says the price, it has an Apple logo and a Windows logo, which I assume means it can be played on both types of computers.
Cons:
A few mistakes here and there, for example, the common room which prisoners hardly ever/never use (at least in my experience).
A few mods that can ruin your game, one which was supposed to fix something but ended up creating another problem and I had to sell and start another prison as my prisoners wouldn't feed. (I may be wrong and it might've not been the mod).
You should most definitely buy it if you are into architecture games, and I believe it is also an Indie game so you would be supporting a small company. I highly reccomend you get this game.

As much as some may disagree on the reboot and its right to exist, it definitely deserves to be played. For new DMC fans, it's a good starter to the universe. The story has more depth than any of the previous games, and still holds true to the character's personalities, with some interpretation. It's not as lighthearted as the past games, but if one would recall  Devil May Cry and Devil May Cry 2, glib wordplay and stupid jokes were not always the norm for our hero, Dante (and I quote "I wanted to fill your dark soul with light"). The gameplay is very smooth and the combat system hasn't changed much. You still obtain weapons of differing styles and the Stylish meter is still in play, albeit with new vocabulary.
For the old DMC fans, if they wish to play, this game is a nice nod to the old franchise. The camera work is smoothed out (hallelujah) and all the weapon actions have been universalized, button combo wise. It's still a hack slash, and it's even incorporated the grab and pull mechanic from DMC 4. Secret missions are still a thing and money becomes obsolete after you buy all your health upgrades (just like old times). All the achievements are nods to the original franchise and it's fun to try to catch them all. The only problem I have is that, for the old crowd (and possibly the new) this game is way too easy. Compared to the time I spent on the old games, I felt like I breezed through on my first try. I don't know if that is because they streamlined the weapons or smoothed out the camera, but it didn't feel like a challenge.
TL;DR - They fixed a lot of weird mechanical quirks from the old games, but it may have made DmC too easy for some.

Most point and clicks deal with fantasy and sci-fi subjects and puzzles that would not be in real life. This is a point and click for adults if there ever was one. A serial killer with a twisted sense of art is on the loose and you are the agent who is going to stop him. This game does not shy away from gory details. Get ready for autopsies, visiting gory crime scenes, and delving into the mind of a lunatic. If thats not enough, get ready to visit some sketchy locations such as a house of ill repute with a serious S&M complex. Without spoiling the story, the game feelis like you are playing two games, since this game spans two time periods, and you are playing as two detectives. I love the look of the game. For those familiar with Syberia, expect the same level of excellence, just a completely different atmosphere. The cut scenes can be very exciting to watch. Some of the cut scenes can be gratifying to watch while others can be difficult. I believe this game is one of those overlooked gems that seriously needs more press.

If you enjoy adventure/point'n'click games like Syberia, this is absolutely a game you should check out. The game offers a nice atmosphere and an interesting story. The puzzles are on the simple side and the game itself is very short, so it is very suitable as a nice little break from your of course oh so busy life.

X3:TC starts out as a space trading / combat game.  It's not a hugely exciting specimen of that genre, either; for example, combat tends to be a little too formulaic.  But where it really shines is when it turns into a sort of first-person fleet / empire building game -- i.e. when you start buying more ships and building your own stations.
X3 lets you pilot every ship in the game, ranging from the largest destroyers and cargo lifters down to the tiniest scouts.  You can even just fly around (slowly) in your spacesuit.  Plus, it lets you own as many ships as you want, and remote control them all, or even automate them to some degree.  Want to fly a carrier and launch a fighter attack?  Want to join the fighter attack and let the AI handle the carrier?  Everything is possible.
On its own, with no mods, it makes for a decent but not terribly long-term space game.  The features are there, but a lot of them have subtle problems or tricky UIs that make them tedious to use long-term.  The mods are what make it really shine -- some of them are pretty amazing, like MARS or CODEA.  The downside is, although each mod does neat stuff and takes the game in interesting directions, the mods rarely interact with each other -- this isn't like Minecraft, where mods build on each other and seamlessly plug into each other.  So you might find yourself wishing mod X (e.g. an auto-trader AI) took advantage of useful feature Y (e.g. an advanced point-to-point jumpdrive) from mod Z, but unless you go in and edit the code yourself, it never will.
If you like slowly building up your space empire, X3 is a brilliant time -- up until the endgame, when some of the cracks start showing through.
For example, although you can go anywhere and destroy anything, you can never eliminate some of the annoying persistent threats to your growing merchant / station fleet -- Kha'ak clusters and corvettes, pirate raids, etc.  Blow up their shipyards?  Ships keep magically spawning anyway, and the shipyards themselves reappear after a delay.
Another problem is that the piloting AI isn't the greatest, particularly when dealing with larger ships and/or faster speeds.  You're liable to crash into an asteroid if you autopilot through a field of them.  In a large firefight, your giant AI destroyer might work so hard to avoid plowing through smaller fighters (which would be barely a scratch on the shields) that it ends up destroying itself against an asteroid / station / enemy ship instead -- or it just never gets where you told it to go.
Out-of-sector combat (i.e. any sector you're not in) is safer because it's more abstract, and doesn't include collision detection.  But this also leads to discrepancies between your ships' combat capabilities in-sector and out-of-sector.  You might choose a perfect weapons combination that makes your ship a nigh-invulnerable powerhouse in-sector, but send it to fight out-of-sector and it could well find itself outgunned by (what ought to be) an inferior enemy due to basic math.
Eventually, even this game does wear itself out, at that point when you realise you're doing increasingly tedious things just so you can say you conquered the game.  That's probably the time to stop.
None of this is to say you shouldn't play it.  I've sunk almost 400 hours into X3:TC, and probably 100 hours of that was before I started modding it.  Be sure to grab the Bonus Pack from the official site, which will give you a bunch of little features that don't count as modding the game (and disable scores/achievements/etc.).  But eventually, do check out some of the more impressive mods, like MARS, XRM, etc.

Yes, Freddy. You're good at what you do and you have an enormous fan-following. But I think I'm gonna step aside for a sec and admire Scott's lesser appreciated work, and a game which has quickly become one of my favourite games of all time.
Sadly, I cannot remember if I came across this game by browsing "Games under £4" or if I only heard about it through Five Nights at Freddy's. But I'm so glad I found this game either way.
So what's the thingy happening, then? Well, you play as the re-programmed CPU of a video game controlling the body of a feisty coffee-pot with legs. You're stranded in a space station an unknown distance from Earth with 4 (once 5) super-computer robots who are trying to find a way to perfectly colonize distant planets for humans. Viruses are starting to take their toll on the simulations and the space station is on it's last shred of power, so it's up to you (and the AI of the coffee-pot) to gather as much resources as you can to take out the viruses before they ruin the mission.
Just like FNaF, this is a really original concept.
The gameplay is broken up into several segments, all being from different genres of games, and you're constantly under a time limit; something you don't see in a lot of games. It's very reminiscent of Majora's Mask, in a way. This kind of gameplay mechanic would work in so many games which ignore it, like all the games where a big event is about to happen, but you could do a lap of the world before it even begins.
Some may argue that the gameplay gets very repetitive after a short while, and I'll admit there are a few places that get rather tedious, but fortunately it's much more engaging than FNaF. Also, just like FNaF, it's feels amazing to beat the game because of how much work goes into it.
And as for Scott's signature art-style, this game is
Scott captures the creativity, the vision and the desires of the Derelicts perfectly in their simulations. And as for the space station and surrounding area, it's awe-inspiring how lonely it feels. Don't even get me started on how good the soundtrack is.
You get all this, and a ton of depth and story, for just £3.99. It's a longer game than the Freddy Trilogy as a whole, and it's perfect for what it's trying to acomplish. I just finished this game clocking in 7 hours of gameplay and I can't wait to play it again. Tenaouttaten

The Desolate Hope is a game on a timer. You, the game program turned hero then put into a coffee machine (coffee still included) are on a mission to defeat a virus that's been wreaking havoc on a space base populated by 4 giant robots called Derelicts so that they can continue their mission to create a habitat for humanity. You enter into virtual worlds constructed by the Derelicts, root out the virus, and then delete it. You have 2 weeks to do so. Broken into three parts, The Desolate Hope's main draw is the RPG battle segments and Scott's signature "♥♥♥♥♥♥ 90's CGI" look that you'll love or hate. I love it.  The other parts of the game, a platformer and top down shooter, sadly lack the energy or even entertainment of the the battles. They're honestly kind of boring, but are necessary since Battles (They're such a large event in the game that they deserve a capital B) don't give EXP or money. The platforming is slow, isn't particularly challenging, and occurs within small, separate maze-like areas where you travel around and gain upgrades that let you explore further. The different areas are designed differently enough, such as one area being almost entirely vertical, which helps makes exploring a bit less tedious. The top-down shooter is accessed within the platformer, and is used almost exclusively for farming money which is used to purchase upgrades for the RPG segments. There's honestly not much to say about these segments, they're average at best and tedious at worst. The game follows a routine: platforming segment, talk to an NPC in the area, then go find the boss and engage in Battle. This allows the player to fight them whenever they want. Players confident in their ability can jump right in and fight, while others can grind a bit first.
However, it's such a wholly unique experience once you're playing the Battles that it's worth playing the game for them.♥♥♥♥♥♥s flying everywhere, there's a racing minigame in the corner and it's making little squares appear, the music is remarkably unlike anything heard for an RPG about giant robots beating up another giant robot, numbers are popping out of everything, and the enemy just turned into a spring-y toy, only to come back and kill everything with a vaguely defined laser light show with names such as "Intense Intensity". I want to get into the game mechanics more but I feel that the Battles are best when you discover everything on your own, with the confusion you feel mimicking your character's as they slowly figure out how to  utilize the power of the Derelicts, who you control in Battle. The Battle system feels like the (il)logical conclusion to the Active Time Battle system, which is an RPG system where players take their turns, but only when their Turn bar has filled. You need to move as quickly as possible, make snap decisions, and deal with everything the boss can throw at you. It's the most active a player has ever needed to be during a turn based RPG, and it's just incredible at that moment when the entire battle system clicks into place and then you're that guy from The Matrix reading those green screens of gibberish. TDH follows after Shadows of the Colossus and as such the only enemy you'll ever face in a Battle are bosses, which is a double edged sword. It makes every Battle weigh more, since they're so limited, but they're also really fun so you want to keep playing them. If you needed a visual representation of how great the Battles are, this paragraph dedicated to them is more than 50% of this review.
Oh yeah there's also night-time segments since the game actually runs on a day-night cycle. Anything I've described up until now can only be done during the day. At night, all you can do is play a training machine for mock Battles, and walk to the left and pick up various items that are extremely useful and play the occasional Space Invaders clone. What the ♥♥♥♥
Game clocks in at around 9-10 hours, possibly more or less depending on your completion. It's short, a wholly unique experience, and only 5 bucks. Maybe Scott'll make a sequel if he's done riding the furry porn market for millions.

A woodland doomed by mysterious forces seeks a champion to restore its former glory in Ori: The Blind Forest: Definitive Edition, a metroidvania featuring a young forest spirit named Ori and his sidekick Sein.
For what its gameplay is worth, Ori :TBF is your typical side-scrolling metroid-like containing the usual combination of hunting for upgrades, discovering secret items, fighting enemies, and generally watching the completion counter  in the pause menu gradually tick up to 100%. New areas are “locked off” by abilities not yet found in dungeons or the open world area. You also have an XP meter that fills up by finding spirit energy (or by killing creatures) that grants you an ability point once filled. Abilities are split into three trees each offering very useful enhancements. You can also expand on your health and magical energy by finding their respective upgrades. Unique perhaps to this game is Ori’s ability to create a spirit link at any given time away from enemies or unstable/dangerous areas by holding B. This link serves as a sort of quicksave for Ori to warp back to on death as well as the only means of accessing the ability system and spend ability points.
I was a bit surprised to not have any real boss battles in this game. It’s very common for a metroidvania to have them but to be honest the substitution of mini-boss and special event “boss” went over very well (it’s a bit of a stealth-action hybrid). Also Ori’s method of attack being focused on an auto-targeting sphere meant spending more of my screen watching time on where he would land after jumps; Quite useful since one particular enemy type and its variants shoot harmless projectiles that sprout into dangerous obstacles.
What may end up as a consequence of the Definitive Edition is the overall marginalization of the ability system and the lazily attached extra area. Unfortunately due to how the game manages ability XP and the new area’s added ability points, you will almost certainly end up with a surplus of ability points that cannot be spent. Moreover the new area is not tied directly to the storyline and only serves as a sort of “flashback”, making it very easy to miss or forget as I did when I beat the game without even setting foot inside it (thinking the plot would take me there eventually). However, the area itself is very well made and the abilities you find there are quite useful for speeding up your run through the game so I have mixed feelings about the whole expansion.
Ten hours later I decided to finally hang up my hat on Ori: The Blind Forest. Not because of frustration, but moreso because I had seen all the game had to offer and didn’t feel like 100%-ing it. It’s a very pretty game with a soothing soundtrack, heartfelt moments, and an unexpected level of challenge. The fun factor is definitely there for what it’s worth, I only question the reasoning behind implementing the expansion so awkwardly when it could have been much better. Regardless, it’s definitely worth picking up, especially on sale, for anyone fond of platforming and exploration games.

Casual where you can either choose 3 power ups to start with rather than nothing or what you can buy from the shop.

I used to love this game to death, I stopped playing for a few months and when I came back the game was completely different, but not in a way that I enjoyed. They added a bunch of bloat to the game that made it more random, and less fun overall. The difficulty curve is all over the place and I no longer feel it was the game I purchased. It's completely different now.
You'd think adding more items, and challenges to the game would make it more interesting, but no. The game can go from really challenging to absolutely bananas difficult without warning.
Why are there 3 different health upgrades now? Nearly every stat boosting item in the game has been given at least 3 different versions, you'd think this would make the game more interesting but it only adds more randomness.
They changed just about every single boss in the game, a level 1 boss used to be a really straight forward affair, with the difficulty ramping up with each successive level completed. It was really fun to try bosses in different orders to see how the progression effected their attack patterns and strategies. THIS IS NOW WHAT A LEVEL 1 BOSS LOOKS LIKE AS OF THIS DATE.
This is absolute god damn nonsense. This is not hard mode. This is not some weekly hardcore challenge. This is the baseline difficulty for a level 1 boss.
The game used to have an absolutrly DELICIOUS difficulty scale. It was almost perfectly tuned.
This is just a small sample of what the game throws at you now.
Notice the gamefield behind the game over screen, and not the Game Over screen itself. The right and left wall, and ceiling are covered in spikes, when you pass directly in front of these spikes, they will launch an icicle at you, dealing damage, the three beehive looking enemies in the middle shoot mines that track the player and stick to you, If you do not enter the green spheres before the 3 seconds are up the mines will explode and deal damage, if you do, they are disarmed. Notice, now, the black bar looking objects in the room. The objective is to touch all  of these objects to activiate them, and unlock a piece of armor. Are you a bad enough dude to do all of this in less than 15 seconds, without dying, or taking so much damage the reward is no longer worthwhile, because you still need all that health you lost trying to defeat the boss in the earlier screenshot?
The point I am trying to make it that at no point was this game EVER so outrageously difficult. On Defiant, or hardcore, with skull mutators on? Yes. Absolutely. Challenge accepted. This is the normal difficulty now, though. Normal. Baseline. It only gets more outragoeus from here. These examples are from the first 3 levels of the game. This is not a case of getting better. The game is so frustrating to play I DO NOT WANT TO GET BETTER. I want to eat my arm in rage. It is frustrating as hell watching one of my favorite games ever to play and relax with get turned into something akin to Cloud Berry Kingdom, or Rogue Legacy. I do not find those games fun at all. If you call a game Sonic the Hedgehog 4 then you will expose yourself to heavy scrutiny especially as such a game will always be compared to the classic 2D Sonic games from the 1990s. Unfortunately, I don't feel this game is anywhere near as good as Sonic 3 & Knuckles, however, when I looked past the name of this game, I found it to be overall a pretty good Sonic game.
I played the PC version of this game using an Easy SMX controller (which controls pretty much like an Xbox One controller).
Gameplay:
I thought the controls and the physics of the game were good. Sonic plays well and it is fun to use the homing attack. The standout feature of this episode is the classic Sonic & Tails partnership - Tails is less of a hindrance and a lot more of a help as you can activate flight mode in midair, swim underwater and launch a spinning combination attack to increase Sonic's speed and bash through stronger walls. The only annoying thing is Tails might steal Sonic's air bubbles when you start to drown.
Levels:
The graphics are excellent for a 2D platform game although sometimes they look so detailed that you don't always know if a platform can be used by Sonic in the foreground or if it is part of the background scenery. The zones are a lot more original than in Episode 1 although Oil Desert Zone is quite a pain in the backside, make sure you stock up on plenty of lives because there are a lot of instant death scenarios and bottomless pit areas to navigate.
Some sections are very reminiscent of the original Sonic 2 and my favourite level has to be Act 1 of Sky Fortress zone - this is a much enhanced version of the original Sky Chase level with new obstacles, longer gameplay and even a section involving Metal Sonic! In fact I would go far to say I prefer this act compared to Mirage Saloon Act 1 in Sonic Mania.
The game though is a little on the short side for a 2D platformer.
Boss Battles:
I found them to be quite challenging and very original concepts where you had to make use of Sonic & Tails's combined moves to take a hit on Dr. Robotink/Eggman. It's great that Metal Sonic is back and you get to face him a few times. Ironically the easiest boss seemed to be the Final Boss, maybe I got lucky that I beat Robotnik on my first attempt but I was a little deflated at how short that boss battle was.
Music:
Arguably the weakest area of the game. Normally Sonic games have great music but overall I thought the execution of the soundtrack was poor. They tried to go for a slight contemporary Megadrive/Genesis vibe but it doesn't sound good, it is a shame because some of the melodies are good but the synthesizers used just don't do them justice, I'm sure if someone like Tee Lopes remade these tracks they would sound much much better.
Storyline:
It's a simple Sonic storyline, practically the same as the original Sonic 2 but with Metal Sonic involved. The main strength of this game is the dynamic between Sonic and Tails which is perhaps one of the best portrayals of this duo's relationship in any Sonic game. The animation is great particularly in the Special Stage, watch the emotions of the characters as they get closer to the Chaos Emerald, win the gem or even just fail to clinch it. Metal Sonic is a really good secondary villain although I wish the final race with him was a bit longer, his final defeat just felt a little too rushed.
Conclusion:
If I had to give this game a rating, I would award it 7/10. There are quite a lot of very good elements with good gameplay and graphics plus the right level of difficulty but it falls short of being a truly great Sonic game worthy of the title Sonic 4.

If you're a fan of classic point-and-click adventure games, you should try Still Life.  The plot revolves around an agent investigating serial murders in Chicago and discovering that her grandfather investigated the same type of murders in Prague decades ago. While the dialogue is pretty campy, the story is amazingly gripping at times and the pre-rendered backgrounds are extremely well done and atmospheric.  Smooth transitions between the Chicago story and Prague keep the game interesting as you uncover clues from the past and present, playing as both Victoria and her grandfather. Nothing can hurt your character but there were a few moments of dread as she searches through some intensely disturbing areas of the game and gets uncomfortably closer to finding the killer. Movement is a bit clunky though and there are times when you feel like you're waiting endlessly for her to reach her destination, even when can run (more like brisk jog). Also, lack of true ending - glad there is 2!
Out the entire series (Post Mortem, Still Life and Still Life 2) this has the best story.

A morbid adventure game that is a great pick for anyone who likes CSI or has fantasized about being a police detective.  Although the graphics are a little dated, the chilling plot is guaranteed to keep you playing.

3/5 stars. This game was originally released in 2004 and has aged well. It's a standard graphic adventure game wherein you walk the protagonist around various locations, collect items and solve classic puzzles.
Pros: Good story/characters. The graphics are still acceptable. Puzzle difficulty increases as the story progresses. Gameplay length is acceptable: You'll get a minimum of 4 hours from it. A PDF walkthrough is included with your purchase.
Cons: Can't play in windowed mode. The resolution is locked at 1024x768, making the graphics a bit grainy on a 1920x1080 desktop. 95% of the f-bombs and exposed breasts are gratuitous and exterraneous to the tale. A couple hiccups in the French-to-English translation (re: the cookie recipe uses metric tools but gives you imperial instructions.)
Microids "Syberia" series is far superior so buy that instead. If you've already completed those, then pay around $5 for Still Life and you'll be happy.

As much as some may disagree on the reboot and its right to exist, it definitely deserves to be played. For new DMC fans, it's a good starter to the universe. The story has more depth than any of the previous games, and still holds true to the character's personalities, with some interpretation. It's not as lighthearted as the past games, but if one would recall  Devil May Cry and Devil May Cry 2, glib wordplay and stupid jokes were not always the norm for our hero, Dante (and I quote "I wanted to fill your dark soul with light"). The gameplay is very smooth and the combat system hasn't changed much. You still obtain weapons of differing styles and the Stylish meter is still in play, albeit with new vocabulary.
For the old DMC fans, if they wish to play, this game is a nice nod to the old franchise. The camera work is smoothed out (hallelujah) and all the weapon actions have been universalized, button combo wise. It's still a hack slash, and it's even incorporated the grab and pull mechanic from DMC 4. Secret missions are still a thing and money becomes obsolete after you buy all your health upgrades (just like old times). All the achievements are nods to the original franchise and it's fun to try to catch them all. The only problem I have is that, for the old crowd (and possibly the new) this game is way too easy. Compared to the time I spent on the old games, I felt like I breezed through on my first try. I don't know if that is because they streamlined the weapons or smoothed out the camera, but it didn't feel like a challenge.
TL;DR - They fixed a lot of weird mechanical quirks from the old games, but it may have made DmC too easy for some.

This is going to be one of the hardest reviews I have ever done. The reason is because I don't recommend this game. I have never not recommend a game on steam before and it breaks my heart to do it with this game. The reason why it's so hard for me is because I love this game! In Arkham City and Arkham Assylum, there seemed to be something missing from the game play. Like the mechanics were sorta off and I just couldn't put my finger on it. Don't get me wrong, I loved those games. They are my top 20 favorite modern games. Well when Origins came out for sale for $5 on Steam, I just had to buy it and see how it all started, and boy, this story is just amazing! I love the origins of the Joker and how Alfred confronts Batman, telling him that he's going to far. This game just makes Batman seem more realistic and more human instead of the emotionless Batman we usually get (which there if nothing wrong with it, it's just nice to see something different). The cinematic scenes are downright beautiful, voice acting is spot on. I was actually scared not to see Mark Hamill in this game but Troy Baker does a tight job with him, adding his own version of the Joker. I mentioned the controls, yes, the controls more fluid in this game. I love the more complex fighting styles and whenever I am fighting hand to hand in this game, it seems like I'm always on the edge of my seat not trying to die while in the originals, i didn't have any worries about dying at all. The stealth mode is better, there are more interactive areas where I can use fire extinguisher to create smoke, there are more vents to hide through and the NPCs seems to be more alert making it harder to take them out one by one. Origins also tried to do a dectivie mode where you slowly piece together a crime scene using your technology, which is a pretty cool aspect to the game but I just wasn't a big fan of it personally. It just seems awkward using for it. The other big thing that I love about this game over the originals is the more open world part. I always wanted to fight in Gotham City and whenever you watch a Batman movie he's always out in the open instead of just only be in Arkham and I want to play a Batman who in Gotham over Arkham. That, and it always seemed kinda claustrophobic in the other two.
Now why would I post all of this great stuff for a game that I am not reccomending? In fact, it seemed like I liked this game better than the other two right? It's because of the damn bugs. The bugs are often and the bugs are bad. Game is constantly crashing and getting stuck in one area. I often have to shut down the game and go back into just to fix it. For some reason when I went into the game one time all of my controls  were literally bound to the left mouse button. Just completly out of the blue. The odd thing is, this game has been out for nearly three years now and we are still having these bugs. It doesn't quite ruin the game yet for me but it can easily do that to you. If you don't mind the bugs and are patient then I say pick up the game when it's on sale. But I just can't reommend a game that has been out for three years that has bugs that a early release game shouldn't even have.

So... yeah, just read a plot summary or watch a playthrough unless you are ready to spend money on a bet as to whether you will even get to see the whole game.

If you're looking to get a Mega Man game, 20XX isn't one.
Mega Man has always had this heavy difficulty balance between the player's resources like weapon energy and HP, 20XX just lets you dial those up to breaking the meter.
Mega Man has finesse to its bosses, 20XX makes you feel like you're building a tank. At some point dodging becomes impossible from the sheer number of projectiles on the screen and your health-to-damage ratio just makes it more viable to tank stuff with your face.
It's not a Mega Man game and I don't see any reason to compare it to Mega Man other than the structural similarities. It's just a good, fun, shooty platformer on its own robotic legs.
The game would do well to just keep distancing itself from Mega Man and being its own thing in the future as well. Tying it to Mega Man would make 20XX just waste its own potential.

Sonic the Hedgehog 4: Episode II is a massive improvement compared to Episode I. Whereas Episode I featured largely unattractive visuals, hit-or-miss level designs, and boringly easy boss battles, Episode II proudly boasts attractive visuals, consistently good level design, and challenging boss battles.
Pros:
- The level design is consistently enjoyable and creative
- There are hidden items in each level, incentivizing repeat plays
- An extra Metal Sonic zone that connects Episode I to Episode II
- Sports surprisingly good visuals (especially when compared to Episode I)
- Each level is accompanied by great music (there isn't a single track I dislike)
Cons:
- Boss battles tend to stretch on too long
- There are walruses in one level that cause you to consistently drown if you're not quick enough
TL;DR: Episode II is a good game—a huge step up from Episode I—and I highly recommend playing it.

I will be reviewing this game in three categories:
Gameplay - How are the controls? Is the gameplay fun? How about difficulty?
Presentation - Is the sound cool? Does it look nice?
Other - Miscellaneous details
Gameplay: 6/10
If you've played the first episode then you should be comfortable with the controls and game engine by now. However, there are two differences. First is the physics and momentum. I don't care too much but it's nice to know that they try to fine tune it a little bit better. (Though I still think that they nerfed the spin dash...) However, the controls feel stiff to me. Second is the addition of Tails. Sonic's buddy can team up with Sonic to use cool maneuvers. On the ground, you can use a SUPER ULTRA CHAOS TURBO CHARGED spin dash to go insanely fast. In the air, you can have tails pick you up and fly you through obstacles for a period of time until he gets tired. And in the water, he can propel you in the direction you choose, making water levels bearable for the first time in 2D Sonic history. (jk, Hydrocity ftw) It's a great addition and is utilised enough to shake things up in stages. Speaking of, the stages are alright overall. The best are the first two, then it gets worse afterwards...Even the special stages are fun, since they are far easier to go through. (But why the halfpipe AGAIN?)
My biggest complaint is the length. There are five stages consisting of three acts and a boss. For reference, the very first sonic game had 6 stages with three acts and a boss. This is a very short sonic game! And there isn't too much replay value unless you're a score junkie. And the difficulty is pretty easy overall, even for casuals. Disappointing.
Presentation: 8/10
It's a Sonic game... the soundtrack is bound to be glorious. More accurately, though, the soundtrack has lots of synthesised genesis-ish music that is catchy and feels like it belongs in the classic games. My personal favourites are White Park Zone Act 1 & 2 and the Metal Sonic Boss Fight. The graphics are great, though the models do seem a little bit uncanny at times. (Eggman...*shudders*) The locations are fantastic to look at and it features some great scenery. Nothing mind blowing, but it is more than servicable.
Other
- For those lucky (or unlucky) enough to own the first episode of Sonic 4, you get access to Episode Metal. In this mode, you play as Metal Sonic and go through 4 stages of the original game. It's neat, if a little lazy.
- The bosses in this game are not fun. They drag out for WAY too long... Though Metal Sonic is incredibly cool to fight.
- Just like Sonic 2, you and a buddy can play together in Co-op. Just like Sonic 2, Tails can never keep up. Unlike Sonic 2, Sonic can bring Tails directly to him. Tell me the evilest things you've done with this feature.
Result: 14/20
A throwback sequel to a throwback game that while fixing the little flaws of the original and adding in new stuff, still has some core problems intact. If you're a modern Sonic fan, you'll probably like it. If you're a classic fan, you might not like it. As a game on its own, I'd recommmend waiting for a big sale. All in all, a good sequel but only an alright game by itself. I do wish to see an episode 3, but please make the game big if you do SEGA.

Game design- wise The Desolate Hope is pretty woeful, as much of the challenge comes from guessing which walls you can either break or just pass through in a janky platforming gameplay mode, and the other half of your time you spend mindlessly walking in one direction and picking up power-ups as you go, occasionally playing space invaders for a bit.
Having said that the backstory is appealingly grim, the artwork is great and you play as a coffee-maker that is possessed by a game logic AI, so for the uniqueness alone I'm compelled to recommend.

Game is separated into distinct parts where the gameplay is different. There's the platforming to navigate the world,  4-direction top-down shooter in a mini-game to get unlock upgrades, and real-time turn-based hybrid RPG-like combat as boss fights. The platforming and the shooting are simple while the boss fights can pose a challenge and look intimidating, but there's a reasonable learning curve from the first boss to the end of the game.
There's no restriction or linearity to dictate where and when to progress; so, some trial and error to find which boss is the party as is, is equipped and upgraded enough to handle.
Aside from the aspects of gameplay, The Desolate Hope strays a bit from the standard with user interaction. Pausing is bound to unconventional keys (F2 or ALT) [while ESC immediately closes the game]. The manual makes no mention of this; minor-ish issue, but more significant than usual as the game is under a time limit, ticking down in most areas of the game.

This game was described to me as 'a pot of coffee goes into the dreams of depressed robots' and it's pretty spot on, though falls way short of what I got in the end. An amazing story hidden beneath a deceptively simple shell, equal parts XBLIG platformer and ultra busy fast paced RPG combat [yeah, I didn't even know it was possible to make an active-time battle thing this damned hard], it's worth an evening to barrel through to enjoy some mad AIs rambling about their new hobbies, and to see just in how many ways you can break the combat concurrently.
It also has a spider in it.

With a name like The Desolate Hope, you'd expect a dark, depressing game.  And then you realize you're playing as an Autonomous walking Coffee Maker... Don't get me wrong, there is definitely a feeling of desolation and despair in the story, but there's also a lot of the title's hope too. It's a platform game with minor Castlevania elements, and boss battles in active-time-mode like a Final Fantasy Game (except way more frantic). It's charming, and unique, and has moody interludes and just works really, really well.  All the more so considering it was entirely made by one person.  It's fascinating, sweet, thought-provoking, fun, and frustrating; I took about 7 hours to finish it, with a little bit of grinding.  All of the boss battles are challenging - I thought I'd be playing the final one forever before I noticed a trick that made it much easier (and came out of the game rules).  The biggest problem with the game is that it doesn't document how to do things well - I stumbled across something 2/3 of the way through the game that would have made things much easier having known about it upfront. But that's a minor quibble for what turned out to be a much better game than I had expected.

An in depth single player space simulation that has hundreds of hours of playability. As a sandbox the game is great and there is a lot to it. However there is a large downside that is an unavoidable price of this immersion -- the learning curve is precipitously steep.
As with many things in life, "good things come to those who wait":
The patient should be prepared to spend a lot of time researching on the Egosoft forums for advice and assistance on how to perform what should be simple tasks. Alternatively masochists such as myself can dive in and work things out themselves the hard way, which is rewarding, but painfully slow. Those seeking instant gratification or pew-pew action need not apply.
I have been playing this game on and off for nearly a decade now, and probably would have spent more time playing it were it not for Eve. To be fair Eve and X are not directly comparable genres, but both fit the mould of a space-themed game that will yield large economic rewards to those that are prepared to invest a large amount of time. I would describe X as the more 'casual' of the two games as it is single player and therefore the economy does not respond to human factors, which makes it somewhat more predictable.
One final thought. The plot and missions are weak, and almost a sideshow. This potentially poses the question, "what is the goal of the game?" To answer that I would simply borrow the answer that the explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes gave to a journalist when asked, "Why explore?" ... "For every person that needs to ask that question, I am glad that there others who feel the answer and never need to ask".

I'll keep this review a short as possible with a list of pro's and con's and a conclusion:

- This game delivers to your expectations on what a Batman game should be
(minor, IMHO)

- This game delivers to your expectations on what a Batman game should be, which could make it unoriginal and somewhat predictable (but, overall, I liked it)

Decent yet flawed Arkham game. The idea of an open-world Arkham game based around the less-fantastical aspects of the Batman mythos (detective work and crime-solving) is refreshing enough to make it worth a playthrough, especially if you get it on a deep discount. If you've played Asylum and City until you've memorized them, then this makes a solid change of pace. Be aware, though, that the combat is not as tight, nor is the stealth as tactile. Everything in the game could have used another six months of polish. The boss fights are inventive, but since many of them rely on those less-polished mechanics you often encounter challenges that, rather than fair (as in AA/AC), come across as annoying. Moreover, the combat scoring is far more granular and rewards a precision that simply does not exist due to the looseness of the controls.
Worth the ride for the main story, the bosses, and the crime scene sequences. Just don't expect it to be as endlessly replayable as Arkham City.

Well, basically you drive a truck and deliver trailers to your destinations across Europe. This game is from the people of SCS who made other Truck Simulator games, as referring to
It sure seems like it does, I honestly thought when I first saw this game it seemed boring when I saw this. I gave the first Euro Truck Simulator a try and loved it. This game soul purpose is meant for people who want to kill the time that's worth it and love driving.
Actually, yes it is. It may seem like an easy task to do, but it's actually a challenge.
You start off small as you drive for other companies and build your way up. You start with the very small tasks that you can get done within the first 20 minutes of your gameplay with the short trips. Eventually, you gain skills and level up as you go. You can use those skills to help you for traveling the longer distance and get higher payment as you complete the tasks. Eventually, when you get that steady income, you can own your own truck and make even MORE money. You start off with a small garage, and you'll be able to upgrade it and hire drivers as you go! Even yet, take the shortcut way taking out a loan! You pick on what to do!
Yes, and no.
It's really how you look at it. The Physics on this game isn't 'Top Notch' but it get's the job done. For example, you hit a vehicle you'll just hit each other and no physical damage would be done between the collision. If anything, you'll just get a fine. Speaking of fines, there are laws you have to follow. Such as speeding, Red Lights and Green Lights and so on. The weather system is alright to my standards as you can change the settings of how often you want it to make it rain as you're on the road. Gas and time is a big factor too. It's important to keep track when you need to complete your delivery and keep your Fuel up at times! Sleep is also needed!
The game alone is more focused on the single player aspects. Although there is a mod where you can download and be able to drive with your friends and other people!
Heck Yes!
You can find a lot of mods, such as custom trucks, map mods, Graphic Mods and more!
Although alot of these mods aren't off the steam Workshop, you would have to try to find these mods somewhere off a ETS2 Mod Page
Yes and no
There's a lot of DLC's shown off this game off the page, but half of them to me aren't worth getting. Most of them are for Paintjobs for your trucks.
The important DLC's are the Map Expansions. These are the four Map Expansions you would likely want in the future
- Euro Truck Simulator Going East
- Euro Truck Simulator Scandanavia
- Euro Truck Simulator Vive La France
- Euro Truck Simulator Italia
All of these Expansions alone will give you hours of fun for every single DLC. I have over 500 hours on this game, and only explored 67.32% of the map!
There hasn't been that many issues in the past for me, I had rare crashes that happen here and there and stuttering problems, but that's likely my CPU bottlenecking my performance. The AI traffic can be brutal at times, making sudden stops ahead of you, or cutting you off simply. But this is a rare occurrence. Although take care as you put Mods into your game, some mods will crash your game at times, but that's often rare in that case.
if you love driving, this is a must have! I never had interest into trucks until I played this! The scenery all around you while driving is just..breathtaking. Enough where you just want to stop and admire the scenery around you! There's a wonderful Day/Night Transition, weather effects, going 90kmh in the UK is just great!
ProMods is very reccomended also if you have all the map expansions!
For a Simulator, I'm giving this a 9/10. There has never EVER been a game like this before!

Not sure how to say this. It was a pretty good game, but in *MY OPINION*, I did not enjoy it as much as others. That does not mean you will not like this game. I am just not a big fan of third person shooters. The story was pretty good, probably the best part. The shooting mechanics, ehh, again I'm not that wild over.
What I disliked the most, however, was what seemed like they padded the game down to extend the playing time by having infinite enemies spawn until you reached the next objective. Okay okay, I know i need to move there, but give me a dang couple of seconds before i move that doesn't require you to spawn 50000 more enemies.
And secondly, while I totally understand the decision and accept it as it's logical, I don't like that you are constantly having to switch weapons. Every wave of enemies uses different weapons, and ammo from one gun doesn't work on another. So, if you have a favorite gun, you won't use it since you can't hold much ammo, and will need to trade it out for a gun you like less 5 minutes later. And 5 minutes after that, you'll need to switch to another gun. But what if you don't NEED a sniper rifle since you're in close combat? Well, you should not have used all the ammo in your medium range gun. But what if you need a sniper rifle and all the enemies are dropping are shotguns with 4 rounds and a pistol that doesn't have much range?  Well, you just push forward and try to not get killed so enemies stop spawning.
I mean, okay, i did enjoy the game, it had a good story and great graphics. But do I recommend it? Yes - if you like third person shooters and don't mind being forced to constantly change your weapons, sometimes ever few enemies, it's a great game. If you are like me and prefer first person shooters, but still can enjoy third person shooting games, I would still recommend it. It just wasn't for me.
I'd give it a solid 6.5-7/10. As far as my ratings are concerned, a 6 is for fans of the genre who will definitely like it. If you do not like third person shooters, then do not buy this game, as it will be unlikely to change your mind, UNLESS you are into a good story.

I walk around outside the space station at night, my coffeemaker robot silouetted against a starry sky. A somber tune plays. I'm looking for items. No platforming in this area. Just left and right to move and down to interact with a sparkle on the ground. Suddenly, the game turns into space invaders. Green aliens appear above me and the game prompts me to press "x" to shoot them down. Why? Why here? I don't know. It just happens randomly. I feel like this scenario sums up my experience with The Desolate Hope fairly well.
The items I'm searching for are given to other robots. Our cause is to destroy a virus that plagues our space station. These robots are extremely intelligent and were designed to simulate human life on this unnamed planet. It makes sense that they each robot fondly collects particular human items given their mission. One hoards clocks, another stashes paintings. They "devote more of their resources to the cause" the more you give them objects they like -- in other words, they level up.
I like games that bewilder me. I like games that are surreal. Why am I a coffeemaker? I don't know why I'm a coffeemaker. With a full coffee pot, at that. Coffee sloshes around in your pot with each step you take. You'd think such a fragile thing would make a poor protagonist in the platformer parts of the game, what with enemies shooting at you, but I guess it's made of reinforced glass.
There's platforming, RPG battles, and more. Take the ATB system from Final Fantasy games and inject it with steroids. That's exactly what you get during the RPG virus battles. They're probably the most frantic, explosive turn-based battles I've ever played. It's hard to really grasp what's going on at times, but I found myself doing well enough to win most of the time. The game isn't harsh if you fail; it simply kicks you out of the simulation you were battling in.
The game is somewhat dragged down by the lack of an options menu, long loading times, and choppy gameplay during the RPG bits of the game. The thing that I find most baffling is that the escape key exits the game completely. It's such a standard way to pause computer games that I accidently exited out of the game twice. As far as I can tell, there's no way to pause the game.
Do the game's wildly disparate gameplay types coalesce well? Probably not. But I think the "throw things at a wall and see what sticks" approach works for this particular game. I definitely recommend the game if you want something unique and with good character and environmental design. The platforming aspect of the game is pretty standard, but the rest of it is not.
Play this if you like a great atmosphere coupled with palm-sweating 100 mph combat.

The Desolate Hope is a unique, non-traditional RPG that's really great. Sometimes. Okay, a large portion of the game is pretty meh (platforming, mundane fetch quests, and overhead adventure) but the RPG battles... They're absolutely insane. You have your standard buff/debuff/attack/defend/etc but then there's things like minigames you have to play during the battle that help you if you do well, by providing buffs, attacks, etc. On top of that, you can store different moves, such as attacks, heals, revives, and even one that auto-plays the minigames for you for later use upon click. I will say again, the other parts of the game are pretty... meh. They get less painful with upgrades, but the RPG battles are what makes this game memorable. (Also, avoid anything that talks about the meaning of the game until after you beat it if you plan on playing it. It ruined the story a bit for me, but other people may feel differently about it.)

X3: Terran Conflict (and the X3 series in general) is difficult to write a recommendation for because I'm not really sure why I love it. In fact, every time I try to talk about it, I inevitably get round to a laundry-list of complaints, particularly about the interface or the AI. But paradoxically, not being sure why I love it is exactly the reason I love it, and the reason X3:TC is my single most-played game.
I've never been a fan of the nostalgist's lament that games were better in the old days, but one thing that a lot of modern games are is predictable. Sure, I like them, but I know exactly why I like them, because they've been risk-aversely designed to be obviously enjoyable. X3:TC is enjoyable, but not obviously so, and in that, it recaptures some of the magic of an older generation of games.
If you like games where polish has been sacrificed for depth and vastness, and games where your own personal goals become more important than the embedded storyline, then definitely check out X3:TC. Be warned, though: it will eat your life.

There is simply no other single player space simulation out there that even comes close to the depth and complexity of X3 Terran Conflict. A series high point as many improvements to the older X games can be found here in X3TC. Improved interface and UI gives way to full keyboard and mouse control with a new and improved flight model. A much more polished sandbox experience provides a larger and more detailed universe complete with a fully dynamic supply and demand based economy that you can exploit, support, and or decimate on a small scale or faction wide.
Improved combat from small fighters and scouts to massive capital ships and carriers. Different variations in ship types with upgradable engines and thrusters. Travel by stargate or use Jump Drives to instantly travel large distances through space. Varied assortment of ship systems and upgrades for specific roles that can all be created by NPC and or players complete with logistics and supply lines. Jump Drives require fuel and larger fleets will require support ships and stations to rearm and refuel.
Play to whatever style you favor the most at any time. From small scale skirmishes to large scale epic fleet battles. Traders, explorers, pirates, bounty hunters, mercenaries, haulers, miners, police, military, industrial, and civilian. Micro manage everything or automate it with RPG based NPC fleet and corporation controls. Industrial mining operations and station construction. Name your player, corporation, ships, and all of your assets. Fully simulated sandbox complete with a full array of terran and alien factions. Your actions will effect your reputation around the universe with each one. Play the story at your own pace with full 3D open world space flight where nothing is scripted and anything can happen, even full scale invasions.
The universe is alive with friendly, neutral, and hostile NPC's. Some will even offer you random jobs and trade. Fly any ship in the game in first or third person. Hire wingmen to fly your ships and protect your assets. Train soldiers for 3rd person boarding operations and defense. Deploy satelites to create a network for tactical and economic information in realtime. Explore the universe to find hidden stations and derelict ships. Perform spacewalks to claim and or repair ships. Keep track of your thoughts with the captains log as your experience unfolds. The only limitation is your imagination.

I love this game overall BUT there are some bugs, big bugs, & some annoying bugs. Some things I noticed were doors getting stuck open and the animations stopping. Usually happens when building too quickly. Priosners in a large group hardly move when unobstructed, this is more than a large number issue, rather its more as though the logic for movement is excessivly recalculating. When I watch this event happen it appears one prisoner in the group is causing everyone else to hang up. Not a bug but an annoyance - construction workers demolishing walls, or disassembling item will leave the item in a box and walk away. Another worker from across the map will come and take it to storage - why not just have the worker who disassembled the item just finish the job and take the item to the storage? VERY VERY annoying issue is building a building. I can only construct foundations in squares. If I have a room Im building thats got a few different angles I need to place cement walls and then put cement floors down the issue, is, lets say I designate this as a domatory - put a few poopers in, make a shower put some doors on, it will tell me the structure needs to be enclosed. It is! So I have to make several square foundations just to demolish the walls so it fits right - why not mark up an area with a foundation and have an option to 'Build Foundation' so Im not wasting money tearing down walls?! Theres defently an issue and Im almost wondering if I manyally place walls and floors the logic in the games thinks its incomplete (eg open roof). But I dont know! I just want to place walls and select the area to finish the foundation or something so the logic dosent think the room is not enclosed. This drove me CRAZY! Water pipes - good LORD! If I have an applicance that needs water and I have a water main nearby I wish it would just auto connect so I didnt have to micromanage down to the last foot to connect it becaue I have too many things going on to mess with this. Same with power. Which is another issue - YOU CANNOT HAVE 2 POWER PLANTS on and connected to the same grid at the same time! You need SEPERATE grids (UGH!) Another reviewer said the game only uses a single thread on the CPU, I have a i7 4930k with 12 threads (32GB ram + two RX480's in Crossfire) and I noticed 6 of them lit up when the game was running with nothing else going (I was specifically monitoring the game). But I would on ocaasion notice lag spikes when the logic for pathfinding of the prisoners was bound up in the first issue I listed.
The animations and art were fantastic! Sound effects were also good. I rarly went under 100fps (100Hz) on my 3440x1440. BTW this game is friendly with odd-ball resolutions. Windowed mode works well too so you can watch YouTube or whatever and play without issues.
Some reviewers said that after you build a prison and have done everything theres nothing left. Well yes and no. Challenge yourself to see how many prisoners you can get is the goal. And stay profitable. THINK AHEAD when designing! When starting a new game plan your GRANTS! Always check to see what grants are available and tacticly plan on those because starting is one of the hardest times.
The future of the game? I almost wish there was a DLC that allowed you to make a prison based in the 1930's. When a lot of the reabilitation thats available is not present. Breakouts were more common and prisoners did more naferious things (think Shawshank Redemption).
Overall its addicting. VERY addicting. If your a perfectionist - this game is for you. It has that feeling that SimCity 2000 had for me years ago. You'll run into the bugs and issues but if you just learn to plan ahead being aware of the shortcomings youll blow past them most of the time. There's lots of micro-managing to do if you like that. But it does get tireing at a point.
Even with the issues I reccomend it (Grade B+)

A steadily improving, lovingly created "this-is-what-it-should-have-been" title. Beautiful graphics, actual gameplay (which is still being fleshed out at the moment) and even multiplayer support (though still pretty janky).
You pick one of four cartoonish astronauts about to drop on an uninhabited terrestial planet right in the middle of a 25th century gold rush. Gather ressources, build your base, deal with the hostile environment. Slowly work your way up the "tech tree" until you manage to build a spaceship which allows you to explore the other planets in the system you are located in.
All in all this doesn't sound very promising, other games achieved the same. But the game is just... good. The developers put a lot of thought into an intuitive inventory system and a very slick user interface. They licensed the Unreal Engine 4 instead of resorting to cheaper alternatives or even trying to reinvent the wheel. Performance is great as of now, with a few hic-ups here and there which are being worked on. Feels like these dudes listen a lot to the players and are very eager to improve their product instead of just calling it a day and moving on with a handful of early access bucks.
If you decide to buy it now, don't spoil yourself by watching dozens of let's plays beforehand. There is not much content as of now - if you've already seen everything in some Youtube video, you might feel cheated looking back at that 20€/$20 pricetag.

It really captures the reality of life, and upon this opening of the eye; you really wish you hadn't found it. Once you complete the game, you realize you as the player had been the fourth squadmate of your team; and acted on the choices as well. You're not the player in this game, you're the victim.
(As for gameplay, the cover system is great, enemies die to around 3 bullets so it feels satisfying to mow your way through. Although the entirety of the game is just repetetive wave survival; lucky its not a long game. Its more for the story, although the gameplay isn't bad. I'm going to go sit in a corner of darkness now and try to process the ending which still has be shellshocked).

This is the best Sonic game since the 90's.   TLDR at bottom
I'll be clear: Episode I was awful.  This is a Completely different game.
Level design is very well-done.  Unlike Episode I, these levels feel like they were actually tested.
The physics are almost completely perfect.  It is strange having the homing attack in a 2-D sonic game, but the later levels prove that it can be a LOT more useful to jump normally and tap the D-pad, just like in Sonic 1-3 and CD.  My only complaints are minor, such as the fact that you don't roll faster than running and that you can't roll between two springs facing each other.
The team-up mechanic works really well for single-player.  Sonic can call Tails for help flying or swimming.  He can also call him over for a combined-spin dash that is more powerful than your normal attack.
I wish the animation was a tad shorter, but it gave this game a few sonic-heroes like places where you had to use the ability to get through.  But they're not just gimmicky, the team-up abilities REALLY are useful, and saved my life quite a few times.
The zones start out a little bland, but they get awesome as they go on.  Take a little time to sit and admire the backgrounds in each one, they've got plenty of detail (The desert zone has some beautiful detail).
My biggest complaint about Episode I was that the boss battles were terrible.  These boss battles are totally awesome!  I haven't had this much fun figuring out bosses since Ristar on the Genesis.
The only one I would complain about is the final battle, just because there is an animation that plays after you hit the boss each time, and it takes 10-15 seconds before you get control again.
The music composition is great, but I really wish they had used actual instruments.  Personally, I'm not a big fan of chiptune.
These melodies could have sounded waay better on actual instruments.
That said, the Metal Sonic fight music was epic.
A tip to PC Players: back up a few feet from your screen.  In high definition, all the colors are quite overwhelming and hard to process.  Back up 3-4 feet and the game looks a lot better.
I know it sounds ridiculous, but would you play Sonic 2 with your face ten inches from your CRT TV back in the day?   (hint: it hurts)
TL:DR: Don't go in looking for reasons to hate it.  Play it with an open mind, looking for a good time.    You'll have fun, just as you would with the old Sonic games, and you'll enjoy it as much as the old Sonic games.

I don't recommend supporting Sega. Even buying their good games supports bad practices but Episode 2 still isn’t a good Sonic game.

At the time it was more of a sidestep than an improvement from Episode 1. The physics seem slightly better but are massively reliant on scripting and the game's key new tag gimmicks are a greatly inferior version of something Dimps tried back with Sonic Advance 3, only serving to rub in the comparative lack of variety.
The rest of the game is still very keen to push the homing attack, to its detriment.
Although the graphics are a significant improvement on the first episode much of the music is even worse with the Eggman boss theme and Oil Desert 2 being particularly infamous. Metal Sonic's theme is neat though.
The 10 second loop used for Eggman’s boss theme isn’t helped by bosses which can easily last over 3 minutes. I’m glad that the bosses are original this time but they feel like they belong in Sonic Rush or its sequel rather than a classic Sonic game whose bosses tended to be much faster paced.
Episode Metal, the reward for installing both episodes of Sonic 4, is underwhelming. It consists of modified versions of one level from each zone of Episode 1. Metal Sonic's mechanics feel like a halfway house between Episode 1 and 2 but he's otherwise a Sonic skin. The 4 levels haven’t changed much but now there’s a lot more spikes & pits. I could say it’s kaizo placement but in reality it’s nothing overly difficult.
The one compliment I’ll give the game is that its system requirements are lower than you’d expect. As long as I set it to 480P my laptop can mostly run it at full speed & it’s extremely weak hardware.
The ability to run at resolutions other than 720P only exists because fans spent weeks complaining to Sega about its absence. They never bothered patching Episode 1.

Unfortunately there isn't much difference in this game and episode I which I also gave a negative review to.
Episode II tries far too hard to imitate Sonic 2 (from the Genesis). From the introduction of Tails with no story given whatsoever (seriously, why is he suddenly here? Isn't this supposed to be the second half of Sonic 4?), to levels based off Sonic 2 and even the bonus stages for collecting enough rings when finishing a level. Unfortunately this game isn't a remake of Sonic 2, it is supposed to be the second half of Sonic 4. At least episode 1 modified the bonus level to be a new take on the gameplay from Sonic 1 (rotating the level and letting Sonic freefall, rather than just moving Sonic himself). The gameplay in the bonus levels of Episode 2 is identical to Sonic 2.
A quick reminder of the issues that plagued Episode I. Unfamilar feeling controls and physics, poorly designed levels, extremely frustrating boss battles and for PC specifically, a terrible port.  All of these are present in Episode II unfortunately. The introduction of Tails doesn't detract from the already existing negative gameplay. Ironically, the addition of Tails introduces new problems that didn't exist in episode 1. There are tag team moves that are now possible such as flying throughout levels, a super spin dash and quicker swimming. However, these mechanics aren't explained at all. Instead all that is given is a prompt to tell you that pushing a specific button will perform an action. There is no explanation of how you may only "jump" whilst flying with Tails 6 times before he will automatically begin to land. There is no explanation of the benefits of super spin dashing and the uses of this mechanic are extremely limited. The two mechanics also clash with each other frequently. With an Xbox controller you engage flying by jumping and pushing X. To super spin dash you simply push X. In a game as fast paced as Sonic, it is far too easy to instinctually push a button expecting a certain action to happen and a different action actually taking place. It would have been much simpler to assign the actions to different buttons. B and A both produce jumps. Couldn't B have instead been used to super spin dash? The dual swimming also isn't explained which led to many frustrating level attempts.
Another irony is that the ability to fly with Tails also allows a lot of the existing platforming to be bypassed. Why bother to attempt to use springs or maneouver over platforms that go up and down when I can instead just fly straight to the top?
There are a handful of levels and bosses that are extremely poorly designed mechanically. There are situations in which you will find yourself dying repeatedly due to no fault at all of your gaming ability. There were far too many times in which I found myself shouting "bull♥♥♥♥♥♥" at my screen. This isn't Dark Souls. This isn't Super Meat Boy. I'm not supposed to get this frustated at this type of game, especially when the problem is how the level or boss is set up, rather than the challenge of the gameplay.
I rage quit the game more than I'd like to admit. If not for the completionist in me, I wouldn't have bothered to finish at all. The fun that is had in the acceptable levels is undone by the frustration of the poorly made and designed game. If you are a fan of classic Sonic and wish to experience a modern take, then Sonic Generations and Sonic Mania are leagues better. If like me you just want to experience and complete the game for the sake of doing so, then prepare yourself for a lot of frustation and contemplation of nostalgic feelings for better Sonic games.

They allow more open reign on exploring the stages. And the adventure is topped off with a final boss which is truly spectacular. That being said, there's still some level design issues, and the music is repetitive and occasional downright bad. But Sonic 4 Episode II isn't bad at all.

The Desolate Hope is a difficult game to both explain and recommend, but I fully recommend it. I only know of The Desolate Hope because of Cawthon's work, Five Nights At Freddy's. I didn't care for that, but I'm sincerely glad that it was made just so I was able to play this fantastic but flawed game.
Flawed is even an understatement, it doesn't have a shortage of problems. The gameplay is split into 4 sections and 3 of them are boring to actively horrible. The levels are short and it takes only a few hours to explore them thoroughly. The game's progression is about grinding for currency to purchase every upgrade in the game - and every upgrade is needed.
Gameplay sections in this game are neatly split into the following:
• A ATB (Active Time Battle, think Final Fantasy VII) system used to combat a total of 17 enemies (18 if you count the training dummy)
• Platforming levels used to navigate each Derelict's simulation and gain access to each of the battles, as well as purchase items from vendors hidden and not
• Overhead battle arenas that are also hidden in the platforming levels to various degrees, but no less vital
• A mandatory side-scrolling collection minigame in order to level-up your party members
Coming to grips with each section requires experimentation and exploration. Unfortunately the game's own (largely forgiving but still present) time limit works against this, but without experimenting and trying new things constantly you can find yourself going around in circles unable to do jack squat.
The ATB sections naturally steal the show, despite their relatively small amount of gametime compared to the other sections. There's a fantastic amount of depth, even taken on its own merit -  the buff/debuff based strategy means blitzing your way through the battles just isn't an option, and experimentation is forced to the point where I was coming up with cascading choices the likes of which I hadn't seen since Shin Megami Tensei: Strange Journey.
Constant meter management lends the pressure needed to keep things hype, and the pacing between battles is ramped up perfectly - with the final boss requiring a ridiculous amount of strategy that incorporates everything that you've learned so far (and then some, it's a right ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). Despite the game giving you every skill from the get-go, the pacing manages to thrive in spite of that, an impressive feat. The combat is just fantastically-designed overall.
The rest of the gameplay is boring. Even actively bad at points.
Platforming sections are simple scrolling events. There's no difficult or demanding platforming, no interesting or particularly varied enemy types, the movement itself feels slow and clunky with minimal animations and stop-n-go momentum. Even the upgrades that affect the platforming just alter it so you spend as little time as possible there.
Overhead battle arenas are even worse. There's 3 enemy types, no interesting formations, and the mechanics themselves are horrible. More so if you don't find the hidden vendor. You shoot in the direction you're facing and move at the speed of a snail - it's not twinstick, it's not shmup, and it's not fun.
Finally there's the collection minigame which isn't anything. Moving in the one direction and collecting token items.
It's difficult to recommend this game because for most of it, you'll be slogging through one of those 3 terrible gameplay modes. You won't be coming to grips with the hectic, insanely indepth ATB system, you won't be admiring the fantastic art direction (which is the best art direction I've seen in an indie game, period), you won't even be stopping to admire the layered plot and the well-defined Derelicts, who make for interesting, distinct and likable characters.
But if you're even slightly willing to force your way through those slow parts to get to the meaty core of this gem, then I wholeheartedly recommend you buy The Desolate Hope.

tl;dr - Imagine if Mighty No. 9 didn't suck. You might get a game like this instead.
20XX looks like a simple Mega Man clone at first. You run, you shoot forward only, stages have the usual spike-and-pit-dodging platforming culminating in a fight against a boss whose power you can take with you. But unlike the classic games, the levels in 20XX are procedurally generated. Every run will be different, not just because you may or may not get certain item drops, but because the very levels themselves will play differently each playthrough. And yes, there are a ton of item drops, ranging from simple stat buffs to replacements for weapons to mobility tools that make the platforming incredibly fun.
Difficulty: The game starts off pretty easy compared to the classic Mega Man games. However, each stage ramps up the difficulty a fair bit, complete with bosses getting different patterns if you encounter them later in a run. The decision of what boss to take on next (you'll have a choice of three after each stage) might be influenced as much by the difficulty curve as which weapons you have. If you find the game too easy for your liking, there are optional difficulty mods you can turn on; much like the idols in Bastion, you can pick which parts are too easy and make them more challenging.
Replayability: Given that the levels are generated anew each time you play, you'll unlock more items the more you play, and that there are daily challenges available, this is the sort of game one could easily put a lot of time into. There is a lot of game for your money here. And given that runs of the game aren't too long, you can play multiple times in an afternoon.
Definitely would recommend to anyone who enjoys Mega Man style games, or even platforming games in general.

20XX is a fantastic game that genuinely captures the old Megaman spirit.  Every run feels different, and it's enjoyable honing your skills from one run to the next.
If there's a problem with the game, it's that the roguelike elements detract from the simplicity of classic action.  Things that you take for granted in most games, like a consistent running speed or jumping height, are extremely variable in this game thanks to the different powerups you can obtain in a run.  Compared to a game like Megaman X, where I'm extremely comfortable in knowing exactly how fast I can go and how far I can jump, in this game there's an element of uncertainty that prevents me from ever being completely comfortable controlling my character.
Nonetheless, this game is so unique and so well designed that it would be a sin not to try it out for yourself.  There are tons of different weapons, really cool level geography, and lots of interesting choices you have to make.  I highly recommend it.

Let me put it simply: This is a great, must play game you should get if you have any intrest in the subject matter. It is the final polished version of 16 years of Hitman games.
Take for example disguises. In the second game they were bad. Even on the earliest levels they were easily seen through. In the later levels they were totally useless. Meanwhile in Blood Money they were too good. Nothing short of opening fire caused them to fail. Here they are, again, basically infailible... except that certain people in the same "pool" of disgusies can see through you if given long enough. They see through is faster if they're closer and if they see through it but you're not close you have a chance to hide and run away. Likewise the game is very clear on what zones your current disguise gets you into and forgiving if you accidentally wander in. Indeed it gives you a nice clear status on your hud which varies on disguie, location and actions.
This is just one example of how everything has been improved. Sure there are only six levels but the options within those elvels are amazingly varied. Furthermore it gives you greater leeway in screwing up so there's a middle ground ebtween eprfect stealth run or total massacre.
