Update: Now that the game has been officially released, it's time to update my review.
TL;DR This game is good, but a little of an acquired taste. Get it. The hours you'll get from this way outweighs the cost.
Let's get the obvious out of the way. This is a much better Megaman X game than Mighty No. 9. I got into 20XX after MN9. While MN9 is not that bad, it's a very infuriating game, mostly because of the dash-kill mechanic and because of the extremely cheap level design. I didn't like the graphical style at first and ended up almost returning the game. But once I got used to the graphics and understood the systems, it became very fun.
While 20XX plays very similarly and has its roots in the original series, it is by no means a Megaman X game clone. It takes parts of the formula it likes and assimilates it. The rest, it blends up and either throws out the window, or is presented to you in another form.
In terms of combat, 20XX has a large diversity of weapons. You have the traditional abilities that you can absorb from the bosses (or you can forsake the abilities and choose to either gain 10 nuts, the currency in the game, or for a random upgrade), and a bunch of different weapons for both characters. That's right: Zero isn't the only one getting new weapons like in X8. X also has a bunch of weapons for you to find.
Movement feels the same as MMX. You have double jumps, hovers, air-dashes, wall-clings, wall-jumps and sticky ceilings. Players familiar with the MMX series will be right at home here.
Level design feels more challenging than cheap in most situations. There will be many enemies, and many crevices and traps to fall into. Hell, on high enough levels, you'll feel like 20XX also has some element of bullet hell built into it. In that situation, the game can be a little cheap, but at that point, you're likely to have enough health to be able to take some cheapness. In fact, your armor pieces themselves are also very cheap, so it kind of evens out a little. What is striking is that all instant-death situations in MMX instead take life from you. In that sense, 20XX is more accessible.
If that sounds too easy for you, the game has many different "skulls" that you can enable to make it more difficult. No upgrades? Enemies do way more damage? Enemies last longer? You never run out of stages to run through? Sadists who find the fixed difficulty of MMX too easy will be delighted at the skulls system.
20XX follows the MMX formula very closely, but mixes things up by introducing a roguelike element to the game, making it very replayable.
Levels are procedurally generated through sets, and a level editor is currently in the works to allow players to create their own level sets for use in the game.
You will come across many different pickups in the game, and what was done away in terms of exploration (which rewarded you with armor pieces, tanks and hearts in the original series) was replaced with a multitude of mechanics: Glory Zones in every level past the first level which reward you with 1 of 4 armor pieces (collect all 4 of this to feel like you're cheating), and a simple upgrade system which lets you increase different aspects of your character through upgrades called Augs: attack damage, power damage, speed, jump, maximum health, maximum energy, armor, and a bunch of other cool things like sucking in pickups when you charge your attacks,
On very rare occasions, you also come across a Prototype, which gives you a massive boost on one end, and a massive debuff on the other end. For example, you can find one that lets you do massively increased damage, but take double damage.
Prototypes are the embodiment of decision-making, which is something you will find abundant in the game. Do you pick up the power? Do you need nuts (the game's currency)? Is this Prototype going to be good for my current setup? Do I want to gamble and hope I get a System Restore (another Prototype that removes all debuffs but lets you retain all buffs from whatever Prototypes you pick up)?
There are many permutations of such decisions that you can make in a game, and they all work towards making the game insanely replayable.
Music is presented to you in a chiptune fashion, so older gamers may really like the nostalgic element it lends the soundtrack.
Music is very upbeat and has a similar uplifting style to the soundtrack in the original series which will make the most cautious players want to rambo their way through the entire level (and die in the process).
My personal gold standard for the soundtrack in the original series would be in MMX3, specifically Blizzard Buffalo's stage. Careful use of droning synthesizers conveyed a feel of, and I paraphrase a quote from a random Youtube comment (because everyone on the Internet is a music expert), "The sadness as Blizzard Buffalo's city ended up being frozen."
You don't get that here, because, frankly, who has the time for introspection? What you get is awesome, catchy and epic-sounding soundtracks. It is a little repetitive though, especially given the replayability of the game, but nothing is stopping you from putting on some of your music, or even some of the themes from MMX. I suspect the developers knew this even before players got their hands on the game, but the alternatives would be to have either no music (which is ridiculous), have such a large soundtrack that players don't get bored, or to have music be generated on-the-fly. The latter solutions are too costly, given that the game is still so young.
20XX is good, great fun. If you're a fan of the MMX series, you won't regret picking this up. Many changes have been made to the game since its inception. The most striking for me is that Glory Zones which could be impossible for a certain setup (such as encountering one where you had to use only powers; this made it imperative you always picked up the first power you came across to prevent this from happening) to complete in the past have been removed. Positive:

Negatives:

You can also get stuck on some platforms if you accidentally jump too high (which is another bug)
- Combat and movement. Hard to tell when to block enemy and you cant for example go up a ladder while jumping.. generally the movement is just too jumpy.. its like you are controlling leaping frogs from that board game
- Some of the music is too tingly

- Some of the setting/rooms not being very fitting
- Lack of coin drops from enemies and other things and only being able to get a few coins at a time from things like bosses and breakable objects. Because of this you won't even have much money for upgrades and might have to grind (I'm not sure, because I'm gonna stop playing after getting cards).

ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW THE DIVIDE:
I gave this a negative review first because bugs made the game near to fully unplayble at first.
I promised to wait a week for the dev to bring out fixes and look at it again then.
I just did that, here's what I conclude from that.
It seems the window/fullscreen bug that got the displayed area of the game limited to one corner of the actual screen it should show got fixed.
Same for the lockup of keyboard and controller input that made me stop attempting to play previously.
This is a plattforrmer game with a story, you are a wind type fighter but you wont notice that much at first since you work in the library.
The control scheme is seemingly oldschool and awkward at the same time.
You press up to jump by default which makes jump dashing somewhat tricky, especially when using a joypad.
More about the controlls and the problems I found with them below..
If you explore a lot between story bits like me there is a chance that you will run into the first monster while having no way to defend yourself beside running.
Some messages that are supposed to give tutorial hints vanish  too fast to be of much use.
Graphics are okay for this type of plattformer, but have some weaknesses which are appearent while changing rooms/maps. The scrolling isnt as smooth as it could be especially when you are in a smaller room, which usally results in the map moving a noticeable bit before the room/map actually changes.
Controlling your character can be harder then it needs to be, since my xbox controller somehow uses all keys from all control shemes in the options at the same time.
As in, once I got a certain item that was supposed to make it easier to reach places previously not possible it did that, but at the same time brought the pause menu up.
Which.. made it a lot harder. Changing the controlls in the menu did have an effect, sadly still overlayed all controll shemes. The control display GUI in the upper right corner of the screen also reflects that after I kept an eye on it, it keeps changing back and forth between keyboard and controller button lables.
I assume this will be fixed later on, if I could give this a neutral review I would. Unfortunally steam does not have that option. I played plattformer games since the original gianna sisters was new.
I still play lots of them. This has some potential but awkward default controls make it hard to enjoy unless one is into that extra challenge caused by that.
Graphics, solid for what the game tries to be, music and sound effects? Similar.
Fun, maybe for you, not so much for me. I stopped a bit after I got the third Item which caused me to notice the problem with current controls.
So, did I actually try this? Now that I could, I did for as far as I could stand right now.
Which isnt that much because of the problem with control shemes overlaping.
This tries to be a plattformer with story and metroidvania elements, it falls short for me personally.
So, I repeat, neutral review, this got good and bad parts. Decide for yourself.

I'll try not to spoil too much because this game is simply something that needs to be witnessed first-hand rather than explained.
On the surface, it looks like your typical Third Person war shooter with not a lot going for it in terms of narrative and perhaps for the first few chapters it seems like a boring slog through Dubai... Unless you know what to look for. In truth, the meta-narrative starts within the opening credits of the game and the deeper you dive, the deeper and darker the plot becomes and by the end of it you'll be wondering just how messed up of a person you really are.
I thoroughly enjoy this game but that's not to say that it's perfect and doesn't deserve criticism. The controls are clunky and pairing this with playing it on the higher difficulties can mean you having to go through an entire sequence again because your character seemingly moved out of cover when you didn't want him to. There are some several issues with the plot in the sense that it'll force your hand in a scene that everyone has probably heard about at least one time or another and the fact that once you've witnessed it once the shock of it wears off. That said, despite its flaws, I can't recomend this game enough simply for the narrative and the story you'll be dragged through, it's something I think everyone should experience at least once.
Look past the shoddy controls and drag yourself through the horror, it's worth it.

I love this game. The narrative, voice acting and story carry this game by itself. If you're simply looking for a shooter I can't really recommend this game, as it isn't really a strong shooter with extremely well flashed out mechanics. It mostly boils down to duck behind cover and try to shoot everyone in the vicinity before you get killed. Some weapons handle differently from others, but the game mechanics in and of itself aren't especially good or bad.
But Spec Ops is not here to be the standard generic shooter, ala Call of Duty or Battlefield. The story is downright dirty, as you slip in the shoes of Captain Walker, that is sent to Dubai which had it pretty bad these past months as Sandstorms hit the city pretty hard, swallowing it almost entirely. You try to investigate the ruins of Dubai in search of the Batallion that requested your aid, as you slowly descent into the maw of madness.
Honestly, I can't tell you a lot about the game without spoiling it and I don't want to spoil it, as the narrative is this games strong suit. If you like Story heavy games, with a lasting impact on the character you're playing and seeing consequences to your actions this is for you. Even though it's a relatively short game, I played through in about 6-8 hours when my Internet went out recently. It still is an experience to be had, can only recommend it.

Sonic the Hedgehog 4 - Episode II is a 2d platformer developed by SEGA and released May 15, 2012. As with Sonic the Hedgehog 4 Episode 1, these games are basically a revisualization/reboot of the classic SEGA Genesis Sonic Games.
Dr Robotnik /Eggman is back at it again, Sonic needs to go kick his robo-butt again
, This time you're joined with tails, and Robotnik has Metal Sonic.
Yeah no, there's nothing else to say here, you've danced this dance. There's no voiced characters, just gestures and good old fashion 2D platforming. Some people will like it, others will hate it.
The new thing brought to the table in this game is the addition of using Tails. He's basically going to be your Yoshi in this game, and just like in Sonic 3 he can be beat up with no real consequences.
You can rebind the keys to what you want, but the default keys I used for the whole game were WASD for directional movement, and JKUI for the buttons... so J is jump, U is to use a tails power, and either K or I were to activate Super Sonic after collecting all 7 chaos emeralds.
I really liked to be able to use the tails team power to get out of Super Sonic mode, so that's nice... Originally you couldn't stop super sonic mode unless you died or ran out of rings.
But I digress, Tails has two uses: If you're standing on the ground sonic and Tails will make a big spin-dash-wheel which can destroy objects in the way. And if Sonic is in the air, Tails will fly with him, btw hit J to go up, if you hit U again Sonic will let go of Tails.
Again, This game has pretty much what I'd expect and want out of a Sonic Game. I got really discouraged and bosses and bonus stages, but I successfully beat the whole game, got all the chaos emeralds, and yeah... to most people that's the sign of a fully beat sonic game.

Update: Now that the game has been officially released, it's time to update my review.
TL;DR This game is good, but a little of an acquired taste. Get it. The hours you'll get from this way outweighs the cost.
Let's get the obvious out of the way. This is a much better Megaman X game than Mighty No. 9. I got into 20XX after MN9. While MN9 is not that bad, it's a very infuriating game, mostly because of the dash-kill mechanic and because of the extremely cheap level design. I didn't like the graphical style at first and ended up almost returning the game. But once I got used to the graphics and understood the systems, it became very fun.
While 20XX plays very similarly and has its roots in the original series, it is by no means a Megaman X game clone. It takes parts of the formula it likes and assimilates it. The rest, it blends up and either throws out the window, or is presented to you in another form.
In terms of combat, 20XX has a large diversity of weapons. You have the traditional abilities that you can absorb from the bosses (or you can forsake the abilities and choose to either gain 10 nuts, the currency in the game, or for a random upgrade), and a bunch of different weapons for both characters. That's right: Zero isn't the only one getting new weapons like in X8. X also has a bunch of weapons for you to find.
Movement feels the same as MMX. You have double jumps, hovers, air-dashes, wall-clings, wall-jumps and sticky ceilings. Players familiar with the MMX series will be right at home here.
Level design feels more challenging than cheap in most situations. There will be many enemies, and many crevices and traps to fall into. Hell, on high enough levels, you'll feel like 20XX also has some element of bullet hell built into it. In that situation, the game can be a little cheap, but at that point, you're likely to have enough health to be able to take some cheapness. In fact, your armor pieces themselves are also very cheap, so it kind of evens out a little. What is striking is that all instant-death situations in MMX instead take life from you. In that sense, 20XX is more accessible.
If that sounds too easy for you, the game has many different "skulls" that you can enable to make it more difficult. No upgrades? Enemies do way more damage? Enemies last longer? You never run out of stages to run through? Sadists who find the fixed difficulty of MMX too easy will be delighted at the skulls system.
20XX follows the MMX formula very closely, but mixes things up by introducing a roguelike element to the game, making it very replayable.
Levels are procedurally generated through sets, and a level editor is currently in the works to allow players to create their own level sets for use in the game.
You will come across many different pickups in the game, and what was done away in terms of exploration (which rewarded you with armor pieces, tanks and hearts in the original series) was replaced with a multitude of mechanics: Glory Zones in every level past the first level which reward you with 1 of 4 armor pieces (collect all 4 of this to feel like you're cheating), and a simple upgrade system which lets you increase different aspects of your character through upgrades called Augs: attack damage, power damage, speed, jump, maximum health, maximum energy, armor, and a bunch of other cool things like sucking in pickups when you charge your attacks,
On very rare occasions, you also come across a Prototype, which gives you a massive boost on one end, and a massive debuff on the other end. For example, you can find one that lets you do massively increased damage, but take double damage.
Prototypes are the embodiment of decision-making, which is something you will find abundant in the game. Do you pick up the power? Do you need nuts (the game's currency)? Is this Prototype going to be good for my current setup? Do I want to gamble and hope I get a System Restore (another Prototype that removes all debuffs but lets you retain all buffs from whatever Prototypes you pick up)?
There are many permutations of such decisions that you can make in a game, and they all work towards making the game insanely replayable.
Music is presented to you in a chiptune fashion, so older gamers may really like the nostalgic element it lends the soundtrack.
Music is very upbeat and has a similar uplifting style to the soundtrack in the original series which will make the most cautious players want to rambo their way through the entire level (and die in the process).
My personal gold standard for the soundtrack in the original series would be in MMX3, specifically Blizzard Buffalo's stage. Careful use of droning synthesizers conveyed a feel of, and I paraphrase a quote from a random Youtube comment (because everyone on the Internet is a music expert), "The sadness as Blizzard Buffalo's city ended up being frozen."
You don't get that here, because, frankly, who has the time for introspection? What you get is awesome, catchy and epic-sounding soundtracks. It is a little repetitive though, especially given the replayability of the game, but nothing is stopping you from putting on some of your music, or even some of the themes from MMX. I suspect the developers knew this even before players got their hands on the game, but the alternatives would be to have either no music (which is ridiculous), have such a large soundtrack that players don't get bored, or to have music be generated on-the-fly. The latter solutions are too costly, given that the game is still so young.
20XX is good, great fun. If you're a fan of the MMX series, you won't regret picking this up. Many changes have been made to the game since its inception. The most striking for me is that Glory Zones which could be impossible for a certain setup (such as encountering one where you had to use only powers; this made it imperative you always picked up the first power you came across to prevent this from happening) to complete in the past have been removed. This is a game made by gamers, for gamers.
I give the game nine wrong armor pieces dropping from a Glory Zone out of ten.

Beforehand: The game is already good at it what it is. If you like MMX, "platform puzzles" and roguelikes this is the game for you. If you expect a Mega Man X/Zero/ZX game with a "endless" mode, you'll be heavily disappointed. Also I'm writing this review from the point of view of a extreme hardcore MMX/Zero/ZX fan.
About the Devs: Extremely responsive, care about the reviews (ask whats wrong with the game on a negative review etc.), listen to players, release regular updates. Thats exactly how early access should work!
-----------------------
Review:
Oh what was I excited when I saw 20XX for the first time. Finally a worthy successor of the Mega Man X heritage? Not exactly. The controls are great, the "shooting" feels also great and the game itself feels really like MMX but then... there are the stage designs and some other things. You probably think now "Of course the stages are a bit strange due to the procedural generation etc." But no, thats not the problem. The problem is that the stages are basically a concatenation of "jump on small platforms" parts, they're basically everywhere which is really annoying. Yes of course, this stuff was also present in MMX but not as much as in this game. You encounter more or less difficult "fallpits" every 5 seconds.
Another point is that I don't like the rogue like elements very much. One of the coolest thing in MMX was that when you couldn't beat a boss, you could come back later with some nice upgrades and beat him. Now if you die, basically all your stuff is gone. However, this doesn't effect the rating of this review, since I knew from the beginning what kind of game I had to expect.
I would really love to see a "traditional" mode that would allow you to keep the stuff you've collected in stages/runs. Probably balanced by having multiple lifes for the whole "game" - if you run out you have to start over. I also suggest to add a function to turn off Nina's hairstyle. It's just a minor thing but somehow the hair bugged me (although it's nicely animated). Would have prefered a "classic MMX helmet hairstyle" (Ciel or Zero).
So can I recommend the game? If you're "just" a MMX fan: Not really, maybe, I don't know to be honest. On the other hand, if you're a MMX fan who likes rougelikes then this is probably the game you always wanted to play. But for me it's sadly not the holy grail I expected it to be on first sight.
Another note: I have to disagree with the comments about the music. It's not at all like the music of MMX (it's good but nothing really special imo). The music in the game are mostly chiptune like tracks which were never present in any MMX game as far as I recall (except for the secret boss/mode in MMX8 and ZXA). The music in Mega Man X has always been inspired by the music of 80s (for the most part, excluding MMX2).
Edit: The game is rather difficult if you don't have a certain upgrade early on and you maybe fail in one of the next stages if you have some bad luck or the rng gods don't smile on you.

Hey.  You.  Lookin' at this review.  Let me ask you a question.  Do you like AWESOME things that are AWESOME?  Then you gotta play this game, dude.  It's friggin' cool, and CRAZY addictive.  Like popping BUBBLE WRAP addictive.
20XX is a Mega Man X inspired roguelike, and unlike another recent Steam release that takes its inspiration from Mega Man, it won't make you cry like an anime fan on prom night.
This game comes with two playable characters, Nina (X) and Ace (Zero).  Each has a standard weapon, but new ones can be acquired in stages, and more can be unlocked through play.  When a boss is defeated, you can choose to take their power (Which another boss is weak to!) or an enhancement or the game's currency to buy things in stage shops or vending machines scattered around the stages.
As the game begins, you start in a random stage with weak enemies and a fairly small amount of set pieces.  As you progress through stages, enemies get tougher, stages get longer, more items and abilities drop, and you can acquire armor pieces that, when a complete set is formed, gives another bonus!  Once completing a stage, you're given the choice of up to 3 stages to progress to, until all 8 bosses have been defeated.   Once you defeat the last boss, the final teleporter ends the game and gives you a score/recap.
If the game gets too EASY for a PRO like you, you can enable Skull modifiers, that do things from make stages longer, start stage generation at level 5, increase enemy count, remove drops from the game, remove specific bonuses from the game, make pits/spikes instantly kill you, speed the game up, double enemy damage, etc.
If the game is TOO HARD for a CASUAL like you, or you feel like dicking around being overpowered, you can begin a casual run with 3 of the items you've unlocked.  It can be cathartic to tear through enemies with a ton of power bonuses.
If you really have an itch to scratch for a Mega Man X game and can't wait any longer for MMX Corrupted, I cannot reccommend this game to you enough.

Riddle me this, when is an Arkham game not an Arkham game? When it's not developed by Rocksteady of course. What you get with Origins is a game from WBM Splashdamage which does a pretty good impression of the Rocksteady brand of Batman game we all know and love.
The story is pretty decent but the script is a little leaden. There are preformance issues, with a few rough edges here and there such as the camera occassonally flipping out, Batman unable to jump some small objects, getting stuck or not responding which of course can ruin the combat. There are a few confusing sections where progression is hampered by poor game design rather than difficulty.
The boss battles are little more than trial and error pattern learning quick time snore-fests and worse still the same bane boss fights are repeated more than once..sigh. The core exploring, fighting, leveling up and puzzle solving elements of the game play are enough to carry the gameplay experience and will keep you coming back for more.
Oh, they did try to too "improve" the fighting system making the thugs attacks faster than Batman thus making fights boringly counter biased. Which gets very annoying after the 8-9 hour mark, as it stifles the players choices in combat, the very thing that made the Rocksteady system unique  (-_-)
When all said and done Origins is still fun because it apes the Rocksteady games so closely unfortunately it is seriously short on any ideas of it's own, not to mention messing up the core combat mechanics which is the very foundation of the series. Worth a play through if you can get it cheap as there is a lot of content here. A solid 6/10 experience.

(Context: Hitman lover from way back, hated Absolution)
This installment is pretty good, and a huge welcome leap away from Absolution. It really does try to get back to the sandbox style of the older (better) games. However in this game everything revolves around "achievments", if you want to unlock anything (Even basic things like a sniper rifle or poisons) you have to get enough achievements. So instead of replaying missions because they're fun af, you're loading old saves and killing the targets etc in slightly different ways because you have to in order to unlock basic stuff like explosives. To be honest it kinda ruins the fun for me. Maybe when you're waiting two months between missions you don't mind replaying it a bunch of times, but if you're playing it in one go (like me) you want to have all the equipment unlocked so you can actually use it in the next mission, it just becomes a bit of a chore to replay the mission straight away only to kill the target in a slightly different way so you can get a new achievement and unlock a whatever. So if you're mainly intending to play this game offline, DON'T BOTHER as you won't be able to unlock and use even basic equipment.
Apart from that criticism above, the missions are still mostly pretty good though; very large, very sandbox-y, numerous ways to get things done. Great graphics and gameplay, music not too bad, thankfully they have enough little things (Contracts, escalations, etc) for you to♥♥♥♥♥♥around in and it not be boring. So this is a good game! 7.8/10 from me.
Other little things that annoy me tho:
- Everyone speaks in American or English accents despite being set in France, Morocco, Japan, etc
- No sniper briefcase, if you want a Sniper you have to carry it around in plain sight!
- Sedative is now pointless since you get the same effect from choking someone out/whacking them in head
- Can no longer take hostages :(
- I miss Jesper Kyd even though the new composer has some alright tracks
- To experience the multitude of elaborate assassination paths, you're going to basically need to be guided step by step for half of them using the in game clues (I had it on minimal mode, so it told me what to do, but didn't show me where anything was, leading to me spending a long long time running around the map hoping to find something and giving up/reading online...); and if you have to be guided step by step, it isn't as fun as naturally figuring it out yourself like in earlier Hitman games.
Anyway, would recommend

You start off small as you drive for other companies and build your way up. You start with the very small tasks that you can get done within the first 20 minutes of your gameplay with the short trips. Eventually, you gain skills and level up as you go. You can use those skills to help you for traveling the longer distance and get higher payment as you complete the tasks. Eventually, when you get that steady income, you can own your own truck and make even MORE money. You start off with a small garage, and you'll be able to upgrade it and hire drivers as you go! Even yet, take the shortcut way taking out a loan! You pick on what to do!
Yes, and no.

For example, you hit a vehicle you'll just hit each other and no physical damage would be done between the collision. If anything, you'll just get a fine. Speaking of fines, there are laws you have to follow. Such as speeding, Red Lights and Green Lights and so on. The weather system is alright to my standards as you can change the settings of how often you want it to make it rain as you're on the road. Gas and time is a big factor too. It's important to keep track when you need to complete your delivery and keep your Fuel up at times! Sleep is also needed!
The game alone is more focused on the single player aspects. Although there is a mod where you can download and be able to drive with your friends and other people!

My relationship with APB: Reloaded has been like how an abused spouse comes back to her partner. You come back hoping everything has changed and the game has gotten better over the past year or so, but all in all it's still just a bad game deep down inside. Bad analogy? Let me explain why.
APB: Reloaded is fun but extremely hard to get into due to the fact that when you start out you get paired with people WELL beyond your skill level, and not even the tutorial city can prepare you for the assraping you recieve once you get into a real server. Going into a Bronze server? Prepare to get rekt by recently upthreated Golds and on-the-border upthreating Silvers as you get called a noob and eventually booted for not knowing what to do. Sure, Golds are banned from Bronze threat servers, but the only thing they have to do is de-threat to silver and it'll be no time before they start pounding your innocent virgin pucker back to submission. The thing that really shines in the game, however, is customization. You can customize your character to your hearts content to make them look like the baddest flipping cop or the finest looking criminal, but unfortunately that's where the positives really end. Missions are tedious "capture the flag", "hold the point", and "team deathmatch" modes, weapons that are way too overpowered to be in the game are easilly obtained throughout the first few hours of the game, and "pay to win" elements are painfully obvious. Furthermore, the community and social aspects of the game are absolutely horrible. The only thing you'll see someone type most of the time in-game are either insults or hacking accusations, and most of the time your teammates will be doing solo kill runs while rarely focusing on objectives, inevitably resulting in loss, and consequentially, more rage. Compared to the last year, opposed from previous reviews by others, hacking has (almost) been abolished by Reloaded's new anti-cheat engine, named "FairFight". Whether hacks for the game still exist or not are unknown, but you'll rarely find a person using a script in the game nowadays, lest they get caught, publicly shamed, and banned by their automatic anti-cheat program.
I've installed APB two times, and tried my hardest to get back into it. It's a great game, don't get me wrong, but unless you've got some balls and a good trigger finger, or a team of friends backing you up, it's not worth the download. Overall, APB: Reloaded has not aged well since it's initial release.

text: After being disappointed with Sonic 4: Episode I, I wasn't expecting much out of Episode II, but you know what? It's not a bad game at all. The physics still aren't as good as the classic games, but Episode 2 feels better to control. Sonic has faster momentum, taking less time for him to build up speed. Episode II improves upon the original in every single way. The visuals look much better, the level design is MUCH BETTER than Episode 1. Less cheap enemy placement and no gimmicky puzzle elements. The tag-team elements between Sonic and Tails are used very well, especially with the final boss. The music is good, too, again, much better than Episode 1's. Overall, I'm glad SEGA looked at the issues with Episode 1 and got rid of them in Episode 2. I'd recommend just skipping Episode I and just go right into Episode II.

Now this is more like it. After the relative dissapointment of Episode I, I didn't even originally bother checking out Episode II. Sonic Colors and Generations were the future of Sonic at the time, why go back to something inferior when those games, and other classics were still a ton of fun? Recently however I decided to get both episodes of Sonic 4 during the Steam Winter Sale. Episode I was still quite meh, but I was surprised how much I enjoyed Episode II! That's to say, I didn't think it was great persay, but it was a solid experience while it lasted. First off, the graphics are MUCH better this time. I didn't realized how plastic-like Episode I looked until I saw the beauty of this one. Some of the environments were quite stunning, not a whole lot of 3D sidescrollers stand out as much graphically like this one did to me. The physics have also improved, essentially gravity and momentum have returned. I thought Tails may be a fairly unnoticable partner as in Sonic 2, but instead he was a big help and a welcome addition! His new maneuvers added and interesting and fun twist to the game! Although I did feel cheap a few times using his flying ability to get out of bottomless pits... The game also adds Red Rings to the levels, though only one per stage. I felt this was a harmless addition, it added a bit of extra challenge but also felt a bit shallow. On the negative side I still don't like how short the game is, or how unoriginal most of the settings are, and I still found the game to not provide much of a challenge. Still this is a perfectly solid Sonic experience. While I hastily recommended Episode I to Sonic fans only, Episode II I feel could be a good introduction to new players. It won't overwhelm them, will charm them with some of it's visuals and set pieces, and provides a simple balance that is easy to adjust to. You won't be missing out on much if you only play this part of Sonic 4, buying both only adds the rather pointless copy and paste Episode Metal. While I still recommend quite a few other Sonic games on Steam before this one, it's worth checking out given the right mindset. This may be the first Sonic game I use to introduce my nieces to the Sonic franchise.

I wanted to try this game out because one of my most anticipated games, Hellblade, is being made by the same creators of this game. I am very happy to say that there is so much fun to be had in this game. The gameplay is fast-paced, but rewards players for taking the time to study all the combos. The boss battles in this game are some of my favorite, and really do see who took the time to learn all the moves. It's also very fun to compare your score with friends after beating certain levels. Coming in, I wasn't expecting much from the story, but I was very pleasantly surprised by it. The game builds a very interesting world and concept, with character developement from both Dante and Virgil. It even has a great and shocking end bossfight which makes me hope that when the developers are done with Hellblade, they'll get to work on a sequel to DmC. Unfortunetly, the campaign is very short, but it'll make you want to replay levels again on higher difficulties to get the best possible score you can. Theres also a "Bloody Palace" mode that has you fight off against hordes of enemies, which can be fun and is a great time killer. The voice acting most of the time is good, but there are sometimes where it tends to get a bit sloppy. The music is also very fitting for the character of Dante and the situations he is in. You'll mostly be hearing Rock, Metal, and Dubstep. Something else I really liked about this game was the platforming. Platforming is fast and fun, but it isn't mindless. In the end, DmC Devil May Cry is a game that provides alot of fun especially if you know a friend who also owns the game and wants to compare scores, but the storyline is very short.

A quick and sweet rogue-like with intense platforming and shooting that'll leave you in a hilarious scramble.
It seems to be in a cared for early-access program.
It's got some pretty intense platforming that starts gently and ramps up to become pretty challenging.
The simplistic shooting reminiscent of Megaman leads to an entertaining combat dynamic that can lead to a hilarious sort of frustration as a small flying robot pokes you from an awkward angle as you scramble to get the angle to shoot it.
The boss and enemy design feels relatively creative, with a wide variety of enemies and varying tiers within those enemies. The bosses get harder the later you leave them, allowing the game to feel like it always has a steady difficulty curve no matter how you play.
With the bosses, enemies, and platforming in mind, there is an interesting mechanic to try and set up a route of play where your skills are best expressed at a particular time. If you have troubles with platforming, you may try to set up some bosses and their environments earlier, or if you have troubles with a particular boss, you may try to face those bosses as soon as possible.
The items all feel good to use, and I rarely feel like an item has ruined my game without me knowing it could. However, there was one time when my friend and I were playing two-player and he killed me by picking up an item that increased offensive power but decreased health. We were able to laugh it off and avoid it in future. The cumulative nature of normal items allows for potent builds focused on attacks and powers, or fun builds that just jump really, really, really high and make the platforming become easy (or even challenging for dumb-but-fun reasons).
The item unlock system doesn't feel grindy and does feel pretty progressive... until the end, when it may be prone to that because it may reach a situation where an item is very expensive but there may be multiple items remaining and you cannot spend the rest of your currency on it. It's also nice to see that an unlocked item will grant you use for your next run so you can test drive it, and that there's an unranked mode where you can test items by starting with a few.
The item unlock system and the item system go hand in hand where the unlocking currency can be spent instead to improve your chances with the next run by buying you items for that run.
The two characters add fun ways of playing. Nina's ranged tendencies versus Ace's melee tendencies allow for very different kinds of games to be played, and the combinations of them in two-player add lots of variation.
Overall, I'd say it's a fun game and feels very polished for an early access game, doesn't seem like it will burn out, and will have a pretty strong launch, and I'm excited to see where it goes.

[Review from Early Access Stages]
When I first saw this game in Steam's store, I was a little skeptical - to say the least.
The idea of a "Megaman X" style of game, with procedurally generated levels seemed to be an insurmountable task, in my eyes, mostly due to the fact that the formula for the "X" series was based around fast-paced action platforming. Something that procedurally generated levels could have very well killed, due to the random nature of such a system. However, I was pleasantly surprised, once I got this game. For - not only did it keep the fast-paced action platforming alive and well - but it actually improved upon the formula, by adding in a decent amount of exploration and randomly spawned power-ups that could be found!
Now, this game wasn't as fleshed out as it is now-a-days, when I bought it - as I made sure to snag the game pretty early on in its life. A time when there were a few aspects that kept showing up in stages pretty repeatedly, giving away where secrets; traps; and enemy placements would be (though, the sprite-work was always amazing - and has only gotten better with time). However, even back when that was going on, I still found myself playing the game most every day, because of how addictingly fun the gameplay was! So, now that things have been DRASTICALLY upgraded - with new boss rooms; stage pieces; challenge rooms; and more - I find it harder to put down, than ever before. Constantly going through multiple runs, to see if I can find new secrets, or possibly even unlock a new power-up!
That said, while the game is mostly good, there are a few things that do need a little bit of work done to them. The main things being the online multiplayer and level biomes.
With the online functionality, I've often had a hard time connecting to a public lobby - and when I did, 4/10 times there would be a glitch that disconnects either of us. Which, is to be expected with early access versions of online multiplayer, but still something that's in need of "a little" tweaking. As it's almost to the point of being spot-on.
Another aspect - that would be nice for the multiplayer - is alternate skins/colors for the characters being played. I say this because I always play as Nina (the X counter-part), and find that most prefer to do the same. Making it somewhat confusing as to who's who, sometimes - when on the same screen. Which is why I suggest having a few new skins or colors for the players to choose from, when they pick a character. One of the ways this could be easily completed, would be by having the option to play as the different sprite versions of each character (ex: Choosing to play as modern Nina, or classic early access Nina). And, the developers could even add special functionalities to each - such as having the classic variations be naturally more powerful, but unable to use replacement/upgraded parts (ex: the torso replacement, that can cause you to heal when you bust an enemy). This would make it more of a challenge for those who play as the "classic" versions of the characters, but keep it fair at the same time.
Now, as to what I was saying about the level biomes. The main issue here is that there seem to be only four different ones (or maybe I'm just unlucky and only ever get the four same ones?): Grass; Ice; Factory; & Sky. And, while these are really nice, they start to feel a bit repetitive after a while. So, adding in a couple more - such as a desert and city biome - would help make things feel a bit more varied. Though, this is more of a nit-pick than a problem.
In the end, I would HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who likes the "Megaman X" style of action platforming. It keeps everything fast-paced, without feeling too streamlined. It's gameplay is addicting. And, it feels like this could have truly been a "Megaman" game, if the developer had contacted Capcom.

I wanted to try this game out because one of my most anticipated games, Hellblade, is being made by the same creators of this game. I am very happy to say that there is so much fun to be had in this game. The gameplay is fast-paced, but rewards players for taking the time to study all the combos. The boss battles in this game are some of my favorite, and really do see who took the time to learn all the moves. It's also very fun to compare your score with friends after beating certain levels. Coming in, I wasn't expecting much from the story, but I was very pleasantly surprised by it. The game builds a very interesting world and concept, with character developement from both Dante and Virgil. It even has a great and shocking end bossfight which makes me hope that when the developers are done with Hellblade, they'll get to work on a sequel to DmC. Unfortunetly, the campaign is very short, but it'll make you want to replay levels again on higher difficulties to get the best possible score you can. Theres also a "Bloody Palace" mode that has you fight off against hordes of enemies, which can be fun and is a great time killer. The voice acting most of the time is good, but there are sometimes where it tends to get a bit sloppy. The music is also very fitting for the character of Dante and the situations he is in. You'll mostly be hearing Rock, Metal, and Dubstep. Something else I really liked about this game was the platforming. Platforming is fast and fun, but it isn't mindless. In the end, DmC Devil May Cry is a game that provides alot of fun especially if you know a friend who also owns the game and wants to compare scores, but the storyline is very short.

Officially my new favorite "button masher" game ever. Why did I put "button masher" in quotes? Because that is what it tricks you into thinking it is. If you go into this game mashing buttons, don't expect to get good scores, and you may even be punished in some fights. The skill involved in perfectly executing attacks between 8 different weapons with 10-20 learnable moves each and 3 different key toggles for switching in real time (normal, angel, and demon) in the most effective way possible makes this game extremely challenging. Besides the awesome moves, I never expected such a large range of enemies (most of these games rehash the same 3-4 monsters and get dull quickly, and while DmC reuses the same 10-20 demons throughout, DmC never got repetitive for me at any point).

Loved the game, tracing back the first version (not Definitive), and very few issues really arose to my awareness at the point of annoyment, but very few to unbalance my enjoyment, even considering dying 470 times, as I did in my first playthrough.
The game presents wonderful visuals, coupled with pristine sound track, some smart traps, tension-building unknown turns and challenging levels.
Controls, even using gamepad, may be a bit tricky, especially when you needed to jump about, or dash or else, and you accidentaly stomped to death. These were the few occasions that got me annoyed.
For a first timer playing the game, one may find the difficulty level curv a bit too punishing, as some have pointed out, the game goes on smoothly, then you have a escape sequence that's fairly harder than anything else until far. However, differently from many that started feeling frustrated not to be able to finish the game flawlessly (which would then make them say the game would be 'too easy'), I felt challenged and kept trying. Most of the times I died due lack of attention, but controls would be a tad irritating every now and then.
The fact we can now fast travel up and down, to and fro, helps wonders, to retrace and reach places or things we couldn't access at first, and the new two levels are elegant, sort of hard, if one is not used to the difficulty mayhem presented in the game.
The fact we can choose safe places to save is also very useful and I do understand the necessity of not having them in the escape sequences. Given people often complain about controls, I wonder how would they feel, if they accidentaly saved the game 1microssecond before dying? It wouldn't make much sense to me either, if we had checkpoints in a 1-2 minutes sequence; it would completely kill the feeling of urgency and threat of getting killed.
All in all, the new abilities make the game fast paced, helps avoiding death easier in certain occasions and also helps reaching places you couldn't reach in the original game earlier in game. Nothing really feels overdone or missing, imho, so I can recommend the game if:
- You are not bothered by sudden surges of hardship
- You like platform games
- You like fantasy settings with good visuals and original soundtrack
- You are not bothered by casual accidents caused by controls
- You have a mild to moderate level of patience
- You pay attention to details
- You memorize what's taught to you; and you can combine these teachings into gameplay
- You remember 'Dash' may save you from almost anything
I still need to finish the game with the "No Dying" achievement. That's part of the fun.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is that rare thing, a strong sim tethered to a strong game. Where other vehicle-obsessed devs seem to take player motivation for granted, Czech studio SCS understand that a pleasingly modelled steed needs a pleasingly modelled environment to shine.
On this occasion that environment is a swathe of Europe stretching from Plymouth in the west to Wroclaw in the east, from Aberdeen in the north to Milan in the South. The tangle of motorways and major roads is stylised and condensed, but feels massive. After a splendid week of non-stop trucking the stats screen tells me I've still only seen 50% of it.
There's satisfaction in exploring new routes, seeing new golden been-there-done-that squiggles appearing on the in-game map, but it tends to be the promise of cold, hard cash that gets you out of bed in the morning. Like Farming Simulator, ETS2 has a simple yet resonant economic sandbox at its centre.
You start as a low-skilled, truckless lorry jockey, forced to take work from established haulage companies. Slowly (or rapidly if you go to a bank) you amass the funds to buy your first rig and rent your first yard. Then the fun really begins. Contract perusing, truck pimping, skill upgrading, driver hiring... this is Eddie Stobart: The Game in all but name.
Spending 90 minutes ferrying a tank of propane from Sheffield to Prague could (should?) be tedious. The fact that it isn't is largely down to good-if-not-quite-OMSI-standard physics, and varied road layouts and scenery. Periods of smooth, almost soporific motorway motoring nestle between passages of edgier wheelwork. One minute you're cruising along contemplating the sunset over the central reservation, the next you're on a rain-lashed country road at night, waiting for the right moment to pass a painfully slow pantechnicon. Tiredness can't kill in ETS2, but it can leave you jack-knifed in a ditch, feeling awful with a substantial repair bill to pay.
The only time when the game itself loses concentration is when attempting to evoke certain regions and sounds. The further you get from central Europe the less convincing the landscapes become. No one seems to have told SCS's countryside crafters that rural Britain features long green things called hedges. Cities are often depicted with the shortest of visual shorthand – a few warehouses, the odd landmark if you're lucky. Don't expect to see a favourite local roundabout, slip-road, or speed camera in this highly-recommended HGV-driver RPG.

When I think of a "sandbox" game, I think of X3. It's a space flight sim, but what really gets me is the economy. It's a HUGE universe, and every area has it's own living economy that will change over time. You can build your own factories and hire more ships to run around the universe making money for you. You can even get your own capital ship, with fleets of supporting fighters and assault ships to invade whole systems. The world is yours to do whatever you want!

The 'X' series of space games have always attempted to push the boat, and generally got it right. X3 in its various iterations is the best of this and is what the Elite games would be if they were around today. While not the best when it comes to combat or missions, it does have the most in-depth trading and space-station building/owning system which provides the bulk of the gameplay. It's not perfect, but certainly addictive and well worth the money. It always feels like with a little bit more work (and admittedly a fair bit more modern polish) it could be the best in it's genre, but it does a great job none-the-less :)

This is the best I've seen in an open world (galaxy really) space simulator that is detailed and micromanaged to the extreme. This is not an easy game to just jump into. Once you learn how to make money (and get your ships upgraded to do automatic trading, you can then focus on building your fleet of ships, to trade, explore, build, and conquer.
But this game, as I said, is not easy. When flying, your auto-pilot can collide you into an asteroid, or a space station, or another ship. You only can fly so fast, so auto-pilot is a must. But you still must be there to take control should you need to dodge something.
If you don't upgrade your ships with the most powerful lasers, missles, and have proper shields, and you get into a fight. Expect to be destroyed. You can only save your game when docked in a station, but you can buy SALVAGE INSURANCE to save any where.
It's a graphically pleasing game and the music is mellow. Play this for the journey and the attempted realism.

I'm sure we all now that there are a lot of zombie games out there, but this one just might take the cake. I get that this isn't an open-world type game like "Nether" or "Infestation: Survivor Stories" or "DayZ" , but this one has things to it that those do not. Let me just start with the controls. When I first got this game I wasn't sure how to pick things up, but I soon realized how. The controls are fluent and make you feel like you are almost actually there,  because of how fluent and easy they are. This game is pretty hard to play in the fact that when it comes down to the fact where you are getting chased and you have to press 1 to open up the Weapon Inventory and choose a weapon, gets your heart racing and gives you the "Oh No" feel that not many games have at this point. If you're looking for a game like World At War where you can just go out shooting 100% of the time and get random drops, than turn away because this game is no for you. let me just run down how it starts off for you. You and possibly 7 other players start of in an area, that varies depending on the map you choose, while some areas are objective based maps, and some are wave based maps it all depends. You spawn in and you see meelee and weapons and maybe some guns in the area while you see maglite flashlights, and if you're lucky, some first aid. I tend to like to use the M16a4 even though you need to conserve your ammo while searching for more clips and rounds. For Meelee weapons you can choose anything from small hitting kitchen knives to sledgehammers and shovels. Like real life, the heavier they are, the longer they take to swing. I prefer to have the Fire Axe, which is up high on damage list, while having a sharp edge to chop their heads off, or a medium weapon like a hatchet or a machete. Something that is fresh in this game is, how much you can carry all depends on weight of objects. You could carry a bunch of small weapons, or a few medium weapons, or like one huge weapon and one small weapon. So overall this game is a fresh take on survival, that will get you jumping out of your seat and your heart racing for more. For a Free Game this is a sure as hell download for much love zombie fans.

Gameplay feels amazing and intuitive, if you die its only your fault (and you may die a lot as in over 300 times like I have and yet it doesn't feel like you died a lot). As you progress through the massive interconnected world, full of secrets and hidden areas, you begin to find new skills scattered across the map and abilities so that your options of what you can do increase. The game increasingly becomes more fast paced though this depends on the time you spend backtracking and exploring rewarding you with more abilities so you are able to explore areas you previously could not - and you might just find certain cool eastereggs and references too!
Ori has the best abilities I have seen in any platformer all of which feel fluid and can be linked together for fast-paced dynamic action. My favourite is 'Bash', allowing you to push off projectiles and enemies while sending the projectile opposite way to where you propell yourself. The only thing that could change is add more different of enemies, though the somewhat limited selection doesn't hinder the game in any way since you never getting past the same 8 or so enemies.

I dislike driving games in general and I have no interest in vehicles what-so-ever. But there's something about this game, that makes want to keep playing it - especially when I'm offline, which happens frequently.
EDIT:
After racking up a few more hours in the game, I've found two points of critique that I thought are worth mentioning.
1). The AI. I'm don't exactly obey the rules of the road. I especially tend to drive way too fast. But when I come roaring down the road at 130+ km/h in a truck with a trailer attached to it, it doesn't mean it's a great idea, to turn out right infront of me in a vehicle, that's doing about 80 km/h at the time. Even if I'm slamming the brake immediately, I still crash into the vehicle infront of me. I wish the AI acted more sensible (or human) and would check their damn mirrors before cutting me off.
Another noteworthy problem with the AI, is how it functions inside the city centres. If you need to cross the road in the opposing direction, and there's oncoming traffic, which you'll have to wait for to clear before you can make the turn, the AI will sometimes stop in the middle of the road, waiting for you to make your turn. However, they do it right infront of you, so you can't make the turn without crashing into them. They also tend to not give you enough room when you have to make tight turns (mainly outside towns), which also causes you to crash into them.
In general, I'd wish the AI was more sensible.
2). Signs. Primarily signs that indicate the speed allowed on the road. The GPS indicator does not provide the top speed you're allowed to drive to avoid getting tickets, when speeds of more than 80 km/h are allowed. It shows (presumeably) the speed trucks are usually allowed to drive on that specific stretch of road - or what the designers recommend - whichever it is, I'm going to drive at the top speed I'm allowed, while still (for the most part) avoid getting tickets. The problem is, there's a lack of speed signs. Often I find myself having to guess what the allowed top speed is on the freeway - sometimes it's 90, sometimes, 100, 110, or 130 km/h. I've found myself driving hundreds of kilometres without seeing a sign that tells me what speed I'm actually allowed to drive at. It's a minor gripe with the game, but it's still an annoyance to me, which is why I'm mentioning it.
These are the two most annoying things I've found with the game so far - I have a few more minor issues with the game, but I'll get back to those if I'm bored some day.
Anyway, still a fun game, and I'd still recommend it :)

At the moment of writing this review, 20 hours been put into the game while still being in early access. Keep in mind some things might have changed by the time you're reading this.
This is my longest indept review so far and I hope it helps out for those still deciding whether to get this game or not.
TL;DR: Great game, fluent controls (as long as you have a controller), awesome music, replayability with enough challenge, constant development. Might take a while for a casual gamer to get into, needs some tweaking on class / power balance and has RNG (which you decide is either bad or not).
Pros
- Awesome Music
- Fluent Controls (controller recommended!)
- Increase in player's skills
- Lots of replayability
- More then enough challenge, even for the hardcore gamer
- Constant updates
Cons
- Might take a while for a casual gamer to get far (a long run)
- Classes and items need more balance
- RNG (not per se a con)
Awesome Music:
Classic 8-bit music which fits right into the game. Different audio tracks have been created for certain areas and they all feel very natural to the environment. Might get a little repetitive for some, especially if your RNG and newbie skills make you do the same levels.
Fluent Controls:
Despite the fact the controls might take a while to get used to, and that you need a controller in order to play properly, the end result is that it feels GREAT. Controls can be customized completely to the users will, which was the first step for me since the standard control layout didn't feel very natural to me (in case you want to know my controller layout, I am using xbox 360, let me know in the comment section of this review). Once used to the controls the second step is to know what to do at certain situations. For example, holding the dash button (vs not holding it) + a quick tap on the jump button vs a long tap on the jump button. This might be frustrating at first, when you come at that one point on the map, killing you with full health by making the same mistake over and over. But once you understand what to do, it just feels very fluent and natural.
Increase in player's skills:
A lot of this has already been noted in the previous column, to add, that by time you get to learn how certain monsters behave, what kind of places to avoid, what powers / items to get, which maps to choose first and last (considering you're playing regular mode) and ofcourse, how the bosses work.
Lots of replayability:
Starting off with the learning curves, also mentioned in the "fluent controls" and "increase in player's skills" column, which make you feel more like a badass the longer you play. Every time you finish a run you earned points during your last playthrough with which you can buy artifacts for the new run (artifacts give extra bonuses, like health, damage, pets), you can choose between a few cheaper ones which are already unlocked into the game versus a few more expensive ones to unlock them for the rest of your playthroughs (please keep in mind that due to early access this progress might be wiped eventually). Aside of this there is a daily and weekly challenge + hardcore mode, which I'll go explaining deeper into the next column.
More then enough challenge, even for the hardcore gamer:
So you won the normal mode, and unlocked most of the artifacts, what else is there to do? First off, the daily and weekly challenges. The daily challenge can be done once a day while the weekly can be done repeatedly until the weekly reset.
Simply put, those challenges are the same for everyone, so the same infrastructure, same mobs, same loot.There is supposed to be leaderbords but I completed the weekly once and I didn't see any, so either my score was to low or this isn't implemented correctly yet. Next to this there is hardcore mode, which adds certain mods to your playthrough like; monsters having more hp or doing more damage, everything going faster and even things like no more artifacts and one single hit being instant death. Those are chosen by the game for the daily and weekly hardcore challenge (to clarify, those are seperate from the normal daily/weekly challenge) but can also be added when playing the regular mode, in which the player can choose which mods to add.
Constant updates:
I'll keep this one brief, since I don't own the game that long for myself. But there is a timer which counts down every 2 weeks for the next patch. And so far of what I'v read from the community and previous patch notes, the game is in constant development.
Might take a while for a casual gamer to get far (a long run):
Due to getting used to both controls and how to use them properly in the environment, combined with the learning curves all mentioned in the previous columns, this game might feel to hard for a casual gamer. Ending in the result that one might be stuck just doing the first few maps over and over. Although this is still randomized it takes away a lot of the fun factor, not being able to build up your character and getting stuck on tiny points in the map due to not knowing what to do. There is an option to add 3 artifacts before beginning a run but this doesn't prevent the points I just mentioned.
Classes and items need more balance:
There are two classes, Nina and Ace, Nina shooting lightning bolts from a distance while ace uses a melee weapon. I currently find Nina way underpowered versus Ace, due to slower movement and more clumsiness when meeting face to face with a monster, Ace can rush through the maps a lot easier. There are different weapons to pick up during the game which might make Nina better suited + maybe mixing some powers but I haven't tested this to much, and even if this would be the case, it would mean you need to be lucky with the RNG. As for the powers (which are magic spells) I find a lot of them to be rather bad compared to others, for example, a blue square which moves very slowly from left to right (or right to left) while just hitting them normally seems easier. I currently just focus on one spell (a lightning shockwave) which disrupts a lot of enemy attacks, while otherwise only picking up artifacts. Which made me finish the game a couple of times by now (also while playing Ace). This is ofcourse early access, but definitely needs to be worked on. As for the artifacts itself, this has a lot to do with RNG, which is my next point.
RNG:
Random Number Generator, it is what defines the present-day term of roguelike combined with permanent death. If you don't like to die and start over, or having randomized maps and different items each playthrough. Then I would suggest not to look any further into either this, or any other roguelike games. But if you don't mind this, or even like this a lot, like I do, then this game fits right in. Not all the items are equally good, but this is to be expected from a roguelike game, and I enjoy finding that awesome boots which make you fly for a brief second, or that penguin that accompanies you (yes I love Penguins!) to either come really far or lose it a few moments later due to some blunder you just made. So RNG, I mentioned it as a con since this aspect might not suit everyone, but to people like me, this is a pro.

+ Especially for the price, a fair amount of content that will keep you busy as you find every secret there is to be had.
+ Outstanding world design, with seamless transitions between very distinct and unique "levels." The levels are designed to make you use every power in your arsenal as you acquire them.
+ Phenomenal story. Although in this game it isn't exactly needed, the story is well worth the price alone.
NEUTRAL:
+- The ONLY one there is, and it is minor: a good portion of the secrets require a fair amount of backtracking to previous "levels." However, you will have to use powers you didn't additionally have, thus making the revisit a new-ish experience.
CONS:
-None
Definitive Edition Differences:
While the graphics remain the same, as they should, the definitive edition does offer a few new things over the original version.
1. New powers not seen in the original game.
2. Some levels are changed very minorly to accommodate usage of these new powers, which is a good thing. You won't be experiencing a new game playing one version and then the other.
3. Expanded theater mode, which if that's your thing, then another bonus for you.
Overall Score: 9.8/10

"It's better than the first game." ... That's it, that's all it really amounts to. As a game itself, Sonic 4 Episode 2 is still awkward. You get Tails this time around and don't have to get a second controller or anything of the sort to utilize him, which is honestly brilliant (as is the multiplayer feature with him as well!). He can now join you in a high speed rolling attack, or fly underwater which seems to give him infinite flight.
... Aaaaand then there's the rest.
It's honestly a genuine step up from Episode 1. The graphics don't look as if Sonic is pasted badly on shopped scenery, neither does Tails. Music is... well, there's more of it. You won't hear the same boss theme over and over and over. In my opinion, however, it definitely isn't "better". The biggest problem with the game is its frustratingly cheap level design. For example, when bouncing up on a spring, there can be an enemy atop the platform you're trying to reach, but you have literally a millisecond to react or you take the hit. Or, for Christ's sake, trying to fiddle with Tails' flight in a pitfall-heavy section only to get on a platform and Tails randomly lets go of you, thus causing you to fall backward off the edge to your uncalled-for death. Sky Fortress is definitely on my list of most hated stages in the franchise.
The plot doesn't really matter but it meant a ton to me. When I read that Metal Sonic returns and Little Planet from Sonic CD is back, on top of Tails being here, I got irritated. "Oh boy, Sonic 2 + Sonic CD!" However, it was actually really okay and different. That's the one major plus I'll give Sonic 4 if nothing else. It's not a nostalgia cashcow like the first, it is instead its own game with its own final boss. They threw in the Metal Sonic race remake, but it was still different because you had Tails with you and it was done differently from Sonic CD.
Aside from cheapness... gameplay is far tighter, bosses are way more interesting, special stages are actually fun (UNTIL THE SEVENTH), level design is still meh but better than Episode 1, and Tails saved this game.
It's really not that bad if you just want to drop money on a Sonic game, especially if you enjoy Classic Sonic gameplay (with a homing attack to help). A vast, vast improvement from the first, and leaves the story at a good place to encourage an Episode 3.

Sonic 4 - Episode II actually does a lot to improve on its predecesor, though it's still somewhat flawed. This time, the physics are a bit better, as Sonic does have inertia, but they still don't feel like the originals, especially when Sonic is curled up into a ball. However, this time around it feels more intentional. When you're curled into a ball, you go slower but are less vulnerable to enemies while freely running lets you move faster at the cost of being easier to hit. It doesn't feel like the original Sonic games but it does stand up fairly well on its own. Tails is also here, giving you an arsenal of team-attacks you can do, which does add some depth to the game, albeit breaking the pace up at times. The stages are more creative this time around as well, as they are totally rendered in 3D and combine stage ideas from previous games. The music still has the weird instrumentation from the first one, however, and towards the end of the game they start getting more lazy with reusing tracks.
That said, it feels like a much more competent Sonic game than the first episode and I'd like to see a conclusion, but that's probably not happening.

While the most glaring issues of Episode 1 were fixed in this follow-up, the game is still marred by incredibly janky and cheap level design, repetitive music with horrid instruments, and just a lack of soul. One of the prevailing issues reviewers described about the Arkham Origins game was that it was 'more of the same'. I liked the previous two installments of the series and so I decided to hold off on playing the game for a couple of years, let it age like fine wine. Really, what I got was vinegar.
My initial playthrough was fine, I knew I would be a little bit awkward as I got used to using an Xbox controller over keyboard and mouse, but once I got to the first boss fight, I couldn't help feeling like the controls were unresponsive, or at least the attack indicators didn't match up with my window to avoid the bosses attacks.
Next came the open world and it felt kind of empty. Scattered pockets of a very small variety of thugs and pickups to acquire. I figured that maybe if I pushed on and got through more story things would fill up. This is where I was starting to get annoyed with the gameplay.
Since I played the previous games I had a little bit of previous knowledge as to how the game worked, stuns, dodges, takedowns, etc. But this didn't gel with the fact that I was playing a prequel to the Arkham adventures. As a result, there were several points where I was confused and frustrated that I didn't have X ability yet. I couldn't grab thugs or pickups with the batclaw, I didn't have a faster means to fly across the map, even combat felt janky when I successfully dodged a knife attack only for Bats and the thug to awkwardly pose and then not know what to do with themselves. I knew I should be able to punish the thug and perform a takedown, but the game didn't. Even when I got the knife takedown upgrade it didn't seem to work.
My frustration doubled when I tried to find how to get my abilities back and saw the upgrade menu. I don't recall the Arkham City upgrade screen very well, but this one was really obtuse, especially when it felt like upgrades were hidden behind achievements and didn't explain themselves well, like "Get to Dark Night achievement level 10 to unlock". Was that my character level? Did they mean Achievements with a capital 'A'? The headers didn't match, it felt disconnected and I wasn't grasping anything. Now I was lost in regards to gameplay as well as the story.
Then this morning I decided to give the game another chance, switching over to KB+M since mashing the X button on the controller was starting to become painful. Lo and behold, crash on title screen. Application was stuck open and was causing Task Manager to become unresponsive and pretty well blacked out one of my monitors. Restart, try again, same song and dance. Spent the better part of an hour troubleshooting, verifying integrity cache, reinstalling, restarting, and deleting my save which seemed to have been corrupted. No dice.
If you got it working on your machine, if you haven't played Batman since Arkham City and wanted to try it, be my guest, but I don't have time for this sort of quackery.

Spec Ops: The Line is a diamond in the rough: though it has many virtues, it doesn't enjoy a lot of name recognition or popularity, and that is a shame. On the surface, the game struggles to stand out from it's contemporaries, so it's easy to "judge it by it's cover." The gameplay is solid, but a little generic. The cover-based, 3rd-person combat works well, and comes with a simple mechanic for ordering your two squad-mates to prioritize targets. It's modern setting as American soldiers fighting in the middle east is arguably a bit TOO familiar (though this famliarity arguably serves a greater purpose). The artists do a wonderful job of contrasting a once opulent city with rapid chaos, destruction, and decay, though the graphics aren't technically amazing.
So why recommend it? Because beyond that, it is a profound and haunting experience. Spec Ops is a story rich 3rd-person action-HORROR. The choices and insights it presents will linger with you long after you exit the game. The downward spiral of events imbues what would otherwise be a generic experience with a message that keeps the player pushing forward to see what happens next.
Spec Ops is set apart by its story, and a POWERFUL story it is. Set in Dubai, a huge sandstorm has wrecked the city, and ravaged the populace. Of all the civilian and military aid originally sent to help, only Colonel John Konrad and "The Damned" 33rd Battalion remained through the worst of it, disobeying orders and deserting to do so. The 33rd promised to evacuate the city and get the refugees to safety beyond the Stormwall; the evacuation never came. You play as Captain Martin Walker of Delta Force, sent in with your team to figure out what went wrong. What you find is a situation that mutates from bad to horrifying the deeper into the city you go.
Beyond that isn't for me to say. You have to see the details--and the devil within them--for yourself.
Bottom line: If you like a dark, introspective NARRATIVE, or want to experience a subversion of the typical military shooter story, this game is worth buying. On that basis, I can't recommend it enough.
