While not as shockingly bad as Episode 1, Sonic 4 Ep. 2 really doesn't improve upon the formula all that much. It's a tired retread that doesn't come close to any of the Genesis games. There are positive qualities: The storyline is non-existent, a Hedgehog isn't revived by a kiss, the music is bland but okay, and um...yeah that's about it. More than anything else, I appreciate Sonic 4 simply because it makes the previous games look so much better by comparison.
Once again, the first major failing of Episode 2 is the level-design. Everything feels cramped. It's a combination of the camera being zoomed-in too much, a lack of anything note-worthy nearby, and a general absence of "flow". All of the stages have this boxy feel to them. It's like they were slapped together by some sort of map-maker and the results are really unnatural. Good levels are supposed to be sketched out before-hand, like a storyboard. It allows for the designer to develop a specific theme. In this game, it's more along the lines of: we'll have some jumps, then a ramp, and here's a loop, oh and another loop sounds good, then we'll follow up with some rings, and then... The levels are stretched out enough to fill some allotted amount of time (2-4 minutes), and that's it.
Every zone in the 2D Sonic games has a different tile-set. Imagine if for Sonic 1, every zone looked like Green Hill. Spring Yard would look like Green Hill. Labyrinth? Green Hill. Starlight? Take a wild guess. Even though every zone looked like one another, they would still be very different, because they have concepts and themes unique to each of them. Every zone in Sonic 4 Ep. 2 is visually distinct, and yet they all feel so similar to each other it doesn't matter. There is the standard array of springs, ramps, traps, and enemy robots. Nothing really changes beyond "Hey you gotta go fast here".
When Episode 2 tries new ideas, the results are middling at best. Tails is along for this trek, and the BFFs can perform team-up actions. At practically any moment you can get an assist from Tails to reach higher areas, create a super rolling attack, or swim. The system is implemented awkwardly, as most of the flying sections are forced. Also, due to the poor level-design, it never feels like you've discovered a shortcut or a secret when flying around. This I attribute to the claustrophobic aspects of the level-design. Since you can never see too far in front of you, nothing looks out of reach. Part of the appeal of finding secrets like 1ups and red rings is that you can see them, but you have to consider how they can be collected. In this game, if there's something you can't get to, it's probably because you took a different route. I guess this is to encourage replay value, but it's at the cost of exploration, which isn't a good trade-off.
Another issue with Tails and - by extension the level-design - is the mechanics. When flying, you have to be careful when approaching cliffs from below. If you press against the wall, what will happen is that Tails will step onto the cliff, and Sonic will fall to his death. This doesn't crop up very often, except for the sections where you're forced to rely on Tails to fly. As with Sonic 4 Ep. 1, the hardest part of any act is towards the end. To put it another way, these parts are the only time where death is a real possibility. They can involve a lot of traps, stupid pet tricks, or other gimmicks. The unbalanced difficulty makes the rest of the act feel like padding. Sonic The Hedgehog games tend to be easy, but there is still some sort of balance, with the later zones being more challenging than the early zones. With this game, all of the difficulty is in these end-of-act sections.
The boss-fights are garbage. Metal Sonic makes his less-than-triumphant return for this adventure. I've always liked its design, and the Sonic CD "boss-fight" was really cool. In this game, he's ran into the ground. Every other boss-fight involves a duel with Metal Sonic, and the encounters all have this samey design to them. You're constantly running, trying to get a hit on the hedgebot, but an invisible force pushes you backwards while he performs various attacks. You'll fight Robotnik (or was it Eggman?) a few times as well. These fights just run way too long. Some of them start with an interesting look or a cool visual, but then they drag on and on for several minutes. I especially dislike the third boss. It's far too easy, but then in order to get the last hit, you have to awkwardly lure him to the right spot, just to land a super rolling attack.
As a "bonus", if you own both this game and Episode 1, you get to play a shortened version of Episode 1 starring Metal Sonic. Apparently it takes place shortly after Sonic CD, but I don't care about that. It adds an unnecessary convoluted twist to a storyline that didn't need it. All that really needs to be said is that Robotnik is back, and so is Metal Sonic. It's a freaking robot! Eggman probably just rebuilt the son of a ♥♥♥♥♥, or made a new one. Your best bet is ignoring Sonic Team's attempt at tricking unsuspecting gamers into playing through Episode 1 again. Yes it's a shorter and re-arranged version of the game, but the level-design is still absolutely wretched.
Jon Rooke, the European Marketing Director at SEGA, recently had this to say: “Sega has publicly apologised to the fans as the quality of console games in the Sonic franchise hasn’t been acceptable over recent years. It’s been tough translating that iconic side scrolling 2D experience from the 90s into 3D but Sonic is still huge for us so the new games will be more inspired by how it played in its heyday." It's a nice gesture. However, I can't shake the feeling that we'll end up with Sonic 5. I'm certain that it'll star Knuckles, every zone will be a half-hearted throwback to Sonic 3, and it's going to be a thoroughly miserable experience.

This game has come a long way since i first tried it back in January. At that time, it was a promising game which suffered from clunky controls, and for a Mega Man-style game that is pretty much a dealbreaker.
I revisited it recently, and i'm happy to say they have absolutely solved that problem. The animations are smoother, the controls feel a lot more responsive. It actually feels like i'm playing Mega Man X now, which remains the benchmark for precise controls in platforming games. When you take this into account, and also consider the huge amount of content, replayability and cool features the game boasts, you've got a very worthy spiritual successor to one of the best platformers of all time.

I haven't played a lot of early access but took a chance on this and have been happier than with any other gaming purchase in the last year. Right now new things are added every 2 weeks. The game is already "worth it" and is still improving. It has been exciting to see it change and evolve.
This is a great Mega Man X-alike that adds randomness to breathe new life into a stale genre. I'm not as good at it as I'd like to be but I always have a good time playing.
The graphics are getting better. At first glance they look like retro 16-bit, but when you look closely and play you'll see that they're actually HD and well-animated. They are not pixel art, but they evoke pixel art and the feelings you had playing SNES as a kid.
The controls are as tight as any old Capcom game.

Challenging and fun in most of the same ways that Megaman is, but with the randomness of a roguelike, so you can't just memorize levels and twitch your way through.
It's not quite as much randomness as some other roguelikes, which isn't a bad thing, necessarily.
Shiny graphics, with spot-on sound design. System of powerups is varied and fun, though some are so good that it's hard to play without them.
There are leaderboards and daily challenges, but I don't participate in them, so I can't say much about them.
Only real complaints are that some levels spawn with obstacles that are nearly impossible to pass without taking damage, and some are just impossible without the right powerups.
Post-release Update:
This game just gets better and better. The devs are very responsive and have fixed every major issue that has cropped up. I still wholeheartedly recommend this to fanst of Rogue-likes, Rogue-lites, and Megaman games. If you find yourself in the shaded areas of that Venn diagram, you will like this game.

I loved Sonic 4 Episode 1, but i did see multiple flaws in it that let me see why people didn't like it too much. This game makes a lot of improvements. The music is still great, the physics and mechanics have been tweaked to be much better, and with Tails in tow, you have a lot of options to get through each stage. The stages are fun, the bosses are great, especially the fights with Metal Sonic, and overall it's a great 2D Sonic game. It's still a little more like Sonic Rush than the Genesis games, but it's a little more in the middle of the two. The big problem I have is the Special Stages. I've beaten them all, and while Super Sonic leads to major catharsis factor, the stages are the most frustrating part of the game. They start off fine, like Sonic 2's stages with proper control, but you will need a guide and a lot of patience for the later ones. Here's a tip: if you approach the goal and don't have enough rings, pause before you step over the goal, and hit restart to try the stage again as much as you want. I'll give this one a 9.0 out of 10. One of the better Sonic games.

Episode 2 is a marked improvement over Episode 1, but still doesn't quite match the legacy it's trying to emulate. The difficulty is uneven, the boss fights are some of the most tedious in the Sonic franchise, and the music is repetitive to the point of being annoying. Co-op is the coolest part, but it doesn't save the game from being aggressively mediocre at best.
Level design lacks the clear purposeful simplicity of old Sonic games. It plays well enough, I suppose, but lacks the imaginative spark of creativity the series was once known for, instead coming off as hackneyed "What if we took one old level and mashed it up with this other one?" Originality is not this game's strongest suit.
Difficulty is extremely unbalanced. You can breeze through most of the game on autopilot, but every now and then you'll hit a speed bump that will have you stuck for a frustratingly long amount of time. It makes the game feel uneven and sloppy.
Most of those speed bumps will probably be the game's boss encounters, which feature excessive, flashy animation sequences that will keep you waiting. Every time you fight one of the game's bosses, you'll have to sit through a cutscene that shows them "getting ready" to fight. Some of these cutscenes can last a full minute, and you have to re-watch them every time you die. Death comes often in these boss fights, which can last upwards of five minutes (a really long time for a boss!) and offer no checkpoints. Dying on the last hit only to have to sit through a minute-long cutscene for the third time is the pits.
Even music, typically a high point for most Sonic games (even the really bad ones!) falls extremely flat. It's generic retro video game music, but does not evoke the old Sonic games in the slightest. It's too tinny, too repetitive, too annoying. Oil Desert Act 2 in particular will grate on your nerves, with a meowing synth instrument that doesn't sound like anything on earth. Classic Sonic games were trying to evoke real instruments on limited hardware, but this just sounds like hissing, scratchy square wave nonsense. Chiptunes for the sake of having chiptunes.
If there was one part of this game that felt genuinely inspired, it would be the game's two-player online co-op mode. This ends up being a legitimate improvement over co-op modes in past Sonic games, given each player gets their own separate view instead of having to share the screen. The game's flying stage, similar to Sonic 2's Sky Chase Zone, ends up being particularly harrowing in this mode. Here, Player 2 flies the plane, and is burdened with the task of getting Player 1 in to position -- a truly cooperative experience.
The game is almost worth it for the co-op alone. Almost... but not quite.
Indie roguelikes are a tried and true formulae but this game makes it feel fresh by taking all the right cues from Megaman X. Good gameplay, good aesthetic, good music, good fun.

A nice little indie production that creates an alloy of traditional JRPG and puzzle solving in the spirit of games such as Solstice for the NES.
The exploration and puzzle solving all takes place inside the massive space ship. As a maintenance droid the player possesses no weapons to defend himself and has to overcome adversity by problem solving and navigation skills. Some of the jumping puzzles can be agrevating but nothing that feels unfair.
The combat system comes into play whenever a security door or an opponent needs to be hacked. The electronic avatar of the player character Asimov possesses the capability to attack the security measures of the system he hacks. Over the course of his adventures he rescues a vide range of avatars that has lost their robotic bodies. They complement Asimovs Jack-of-all-Trades skills with their specialities.
There is not much innovation about the combat compared to some of the more popular Japanese RPGs out there but it does it job well and achieves enough strategic depth for the entertainment value in a product of this size.
The way the game is set up it is possible to solve many puzzles forcefully by hacking most of the opposition making the actual puzzle solving alot easier. A welcome function for players that dont favour jumping skills or the puzzles them selves.
Playtime is between 5 to 15 hours depending on how thorough the ship is searched.

I was genuinely surprised with this one. After what I heard from fans I knew personally, I thought it would be unpleasant. Not bad, just not fit for the DMC label.
PROS:
-The swordplay... holy crap. This is the most satisfying combo-ing (is that a word...? Is now!) in the series. In any gmae I've played! You can resume combos even after switching weapons. It's also very easy to swtich, with 3 at your disposal at any time and the other 2 just a single press on the D-pad away, meaning it's possible (in theory) to include all 5 of Dante's melee weapons in one string of attacks. They're also quite balanced and a ton of fun to use on their own.
-The grappling hook mechanic and other aspects of the game's platforming work exceedingly well. First Devil May Cry game where I actually look forward to platforming instead of wanting to rip what little hair I have out.
-I dig the look of the game. The environments look quite nice. Characters do as well. As for other aspects of the characters, we'll get to that later.
-The music isn't quite up to snuff here, but it's still good for what it wants to do. The fighting is backed up by nice and energetic tracks while the calmer moments have some decent enough atmospheric pieces.
-Voice acting is well done. As for the writing itself...
CONS:
-The story is BAD! It's basically Internet: The Video Game. All the parallels it draws are way too on-the-nose for what's supposed to be a serious game. There are other problems, but I'll not say anything to avoid spoilers.
-The writing for some characters is absolutely horrendous. I like swearing... a lot... but there's a time and place for it. DmC just throws it out there like a 12-year-old who's just starting to learn how to use the words correctly. It grates after the first couple of missions, and then keeps going on with it for the rest of the game.
-Guns are weak to the point of being absolutely useless. I only use them out of habit.
-Overall, the game is a bit on the easy side. Great for newcomers, but I've been with the series since day 1. Dante's just a bit too powerful for what the game throws at you. Series veterans should probably start the game on hard. I've been sticking to normal, again, out of habit.
MEH:
-Didn't need 3 dodge buttons. One button for basic dodge roll would have been fine. Other dodges are unnecessary.
-Devil Trigger should not include anti-gravity. It's there for when you need a momentary boost, not as an "I win" button.
-Dante is really unlikable at the start of the game. He gets better though. Overall, I like him, but...
-None of these characters really fit in a Devil May Cry game, except maybe Virgil, but that's a bit of a stretch.
-I keep forgetting there's no manual lock-on and dodge rolling into enemies. It's not a problem really, as the auto-lock goes where I want it.
VERDICT:
It's good, plain and simple. Quite good actually. I don't care about story in DMC to begin with, so the problems I have with it are just an annoyance. If they're going to do another game, keep the gameplay like this with a few tweaks and bring back the old characters. Yeah, they're bishie, but that's part of the fun.
All this being said, if you have a PS2, get DMC3. It's better overall. Otherwise, get this. The PC version of DMC3 is awful.

The game is a mish-mash of three major game types: adventure games, platformers, and...well, not a game type, but Metroid-style boss fights. I have enjoyed these things in other games: solving puzzles /opening new areas up in adventure games (a la the Space Quest or Deponia series), getting around by jumping from thing to thing to explore the world (a la Ori and the Blind Forest and older titles like Super Mario 64), and Metroid-style boss fights (a la Super Metroid, etc.). However, in Wuppo, I did not feel like any one of these gameplay types was handled well.
Adventure games typically work well when you put the player in a fairly small area, rife with vibrant things to interact with, be it characters, contraptions, inventory interaction, etc. The solution should not always be obvious, but if you listen to characters and put the hints together, you can figure out what you need to do. Wuppo puts players in large areas, requiring platforming to navigate to different screens, giving the player hints like "head underground." This means the player should be looking for digging utensils, right? Or stay close to the ground to find an entrance, right? Or find a machine or character who mines/tunnels, right? Nope. You go to the highest point in the entire region to go underground.
Your only clue in the many screens is a bird saying "this area seems important." It doesn't tell you that it's important right now or toward going underground, though. Why in the world would a person think that? The game gives you a completion percentage, and it was around 10% or so at that point, so I figured this would be an important place much later in the game, and immediately looked elsewhere for ways to get underground. This led me to wandering around aimlessly for a couple of hours, platforming my way back up again and again, lost until I finally used a walkthrough to continue. This is a poorly designed puzzle with no alternative solutions and you cannot complete the game without doing it.
After that section, required actions to progress became much clearer. However, once you get to a city, many hum-drum side-quest-like actions are needed to raise a number called "credit" for the city to 100,000 to expand the city. I found the city already too large with various largely empty screens with a few statues or signs in the background, and a bunch of wums (people) walking around. I didn't want to expand the city due to a lack of motivation, but I'll talk more about that in a moment.
Platforming can be fun, but when mixed with backtracking due to not knowing where to go became annoying. I was hopping up to the top of the jungle-y region repeatedly, randomly looking for ways underground, and had to do the same platforming over and over again. It was dull. There are also typically no enemies in the game, aside from bosses. I think enemies might worsen things, thanks to the backtracking, but imagine if Super Mario Bros didn't have enemies and there were maybe 5 or so coins to collect in a level. No time countdown, no power-ups, no dying, but numerous places to fall and have to platform your way back up again each time you make a mistake (sans rare shortcut exceptions).
The Metroid-style boss fights are often big, you shoot them with charged or automatic paint gun shots, and they can often come at you out unexpectedly or with a small hint, which is in line with Metroid as well as Resident Evil games. I actually liked these for the most part. I handled the first 9 bosses, according to the game's boss-kill tracker, and not one boss fight was like the others, which I liked. One boss underground did zoom the camera out significantly, and it was quite difficult to keep track of my character in the mess, which made hitting the boss and avoiding attacks unnecessarily difficult.
There was also a single stealth section. I needed to steal something from two people. You can only do it at night, so you need to wait until the sun sets, and if you alert the people in the room, you get thrown out and have to do it over again, waiting until the next night, or loading your last save. Stealth elements in games are actually something I love, but Wuppo handled this poorly, in my opinion. Dishes are stacked up in the room, and you have to jump over them and land close to them to avoid alerting the people in the room, but if you knock a dish off, you have to do it over. The worst part is that the thing you need to steal is sitting on a big, breakable container, and the only way to grab what you need, is to land
the breakable container. Unless you land
right, the container will fall and break. I probably spent 20+ minutes repeatedly trying to do this, loading my game every time that container fell. It was incredibly frustrating and at no point did I enjoy this part of the game. Any delightful visual charm and peaceful music was undermined by this event.
You can purchase things in the game, but money seems finite, and many of the items you can purchase are incredibly high-priced. I felt like the economy needed some work, or at least a way to grind a little cash to buy things. I normally get excited when I see shops in games; not so in Wuppo, because I never felt comfortable spending my severely limited funds.
There
a train on the west side of the world, and I won't spoil anything about it, but I thought it was charming and a neat idea, and there's a pit stop in the middle of the journey that was pleasant as well. I know it's vague, but I have to admit I liked that, and thought that was kinda innovative.
Wuppo has very little story. I would go so far as calling it a "slice of life" storyline, actually. I got just over 39% in, and the world isn't in danger, people aren't dying or kidnapped, there's no deep lore, few characters exist and each could be detailed in full in one or two brief sentences, and you are not on any huge quest. You're just trying to get a home. It's quaint and I like the idea of it, as well as its execution for a couple of hours.
Beyond that, however, the lack of story, when mixed in with the large areas without much direction on where to go, made the game eventually become very boring for me. It got so bad that I went days and even weeks without touching the game. Every time I started playing again, I would want to sleep when I wasn't really tired, and I dreaded playing the game any time I thought about it. This is definitely one of the least compelling games I've ever played in my life, and I cannot recommend it based purely on the few things I did like about it, because the negatives were overwhelming for me.

Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter developed by Yager Development. It was released in 2012. I remember watching a review about how this game was better than most of the military shooters released at the time, so I was interested in playing this game for the longest time. I never got to play it at launch, and having just finished it, I am glad I didn't buy it at the time.
It is not a terrible game. Its functional, and thoroughly boring. There is nothing original about the gameplay. I understand that this is supposed to be a narrative driven game, but that does not prevent the game from being boring because of generic the gameplay. Gears of War is a much better cover shooter, and that came out years ago.
The game is built using Unreal 2 engine, and it handles a lot like Mass Effect. What this means is, the game does not have jump, and shooting involves diving behind cover and peaking out, and taking shots at enemies. Just about every single encounter turns into this. Like most console ports at the time, the controls are not optimized for the PC. Spacebar is used for both sprinting and taking cover. I did not enjoy this in Mass Effect, and I did not enjoy this in Spec Ops.
The gunplay is weak, and the weapon variety doesn't add much to the game because other than ammo capacity, all rifles felt the same. I understand that they cannot stray too much from reality because of the military setting, but that is no excuse of the weak weapon handling. The reason I did not like the weapon handling is probably because I am playing this game in 2017, and as a Battlefield player, I find most other shooters to be not as good as Battlefield 3 and Battlefield 4.
The game tries to incorporate squad play, but the system is not very fleshed out, and I felt it was awkward to use. There are few instances where giving orders to your squad is useful, but overall it is possible to play most of the game without ever giving any squad orders. The much talked about environment interaction is basically shooting some objects during combat to take out enemies, such as shooting a window to cause a sand slide etc. Do not expect Red Faction like environment destruction.
The main selling point  of this game was the story. I am playing this game 5 years after its release, and having played other games which attempted something similar, I could see the twist coming well in advance. Like Modern Warfare 2, there is one section in the game that this game is going to be remembered for, and I could see that coming as well. That said, the story itself is not too bad, but I think there are some instances where they left things to interpretation and this doesn't provide closure. Also, the suspension of disbelief required is a little too much for me. The main character and his two friends take on what looks like the entire US army, get thrown off buildings, survive a massive truck crash, and a chopper crash with no broken bones...
It is difficult to achieve the level of engagement they were asking for, because they want to tell a story that is grounded in reality, but the gameplay just does not lend itself to that.
I purchased this game as a part of a Humble Bundle for $1, and for that price, I am not disappointed, but I really would not recommend paying any money for this game because it has no replay value, and there are so many great games out there for cheap.

Despite not completely following the formula that was established in Sonic 1, 2 & 3(and Knuckles) It's still a very functional game that perhaps is more catered to a slightly more modern audience, since the classic games play in a more 1990s sort of fashion. You can feel the difference with a lighter Sonic and feels a bit more fluid than in previous 2D games. So for long time Sonic fans you may still be thrown off by the unfaithful physics that don't reflect the old-school days of 2D Sonic, but they are a step up from what Episode I had to offer because of some added tweaks to the game engine and, and some subtle changes to Sonic in this game too, such as how he no longer uncurls out of a Spin when jumping of a slope.
So the game handles quite well in my opinion, despite not really playing like the Genesis/Mega-Drive days.
Tails controls well too, and the implementation of team based gameplay is executed well too, so I have no real issues there.
Now content is important, as Sonic 3 & Knuckles was a big game(s), and Sonic 4 Episode II on its own isn't veyr massive, and the locations of zones like in Episode I are virtually all tributes to zones from the Genesis days, but there's much more to do in Sonic 3. And since Episode II is a seperate game that you have to pay for individually (and with Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles it's easy to buy the two games together) Sonic 4 Episode II doesn't offer too much a sequel since it doesn't really expand but rather just pay a homage to Classic Sonic, so if you we're hoping to see more than what Sonic 3 & Knuckles offered, then even with both episodes combined, you won't really get that here.
However it's still a fun game that any fan of Sonic should give a go, and can even appeal to people who aren't necessarily fans of Sonic. It's not amazing, but a good game nontheless.

If you've played Sonic 4 Episode 1, you'll probably guess that this game is probably as bad as the first one, and you would be 75% correct. Sonic 4 Episode 2 is yet another dissapointing release in the never ending Dark Ages of Sonic, which is an on-going line of bad Sonic games starting from 2006, and this one has joined the bandwagon.
Instead of being based off Sonic 1, this one is based off Sonic 2 and rightly so, only because it has Tails in it.
The gameplay is not too shabby and it is actually better than the first one, but it still has some kinks. The physics are still kind of bad but not as bad as Episode 1. There's also no copying of any of the previous zones from old Sonic games, but some zones are similar to other zones seen in the Sonic series, but I can't really list them all.
The story is really hard to notice due to all of the characters refusing to talk during the entire game, in all seriousness a storyline isn't really here in this game.
This game relies way too heavily on the special Sonic + Tails moves, most of the game requires you to use those moves. Like in Oil Desert Zone act 2 or 3, the end of the act requires you to use the flying-Tails-carrying-Sonic thing for the rest of the act, and I've died a few times in that part.
The Co-op mode is ok, and suprisingly it is accurate to Sonic 2's co-op mode: You both have to stay on the same gosh darn screen.
It's still not a worthy sequel to the Sega Genesis Sonic we all know and love, but it is slightly better than episode 1. This game is really only for bored gamers waiting for something interesting to happen and for crazy Sonic fans who collect every Sonic game known in exsistance both good and bad.

While, from what I have heard, that the game is better than the first one, it is STILL by no means a good game. While the first two acts you could probably breeze through, the next two, Oil Desert and Sky Fortress, just surge in difficulty where the first two had it in small bursts. The worst part, however, is the bosses. Again, the first two bosses are not all that difficult if you have some knowledge of the mechanics of the game. The third boss in Oil Desert, however, is mostly boring climbing and occasionally waiting for Eggman to reveal his weak spot. However, the point where I stopped playing, and I am pretty sure that I cannot give this game anything other than a 'not recommended' review after having game over'd from it twice, is Sky Fortress's boss.
To put it shortly, Sky Fortress has you fighting Metal Sonic in the blue carrier from before. However, his strategy is far different from Sky Fortress Act 1. For the first portion of the fight, he will move to either the top or the bottom of the screen and fire screen-filling lasers at you.  You have to hit Metal Sonic in the cockpit, which, provided you don't completely outrun the carrier yourself, is somewhat easy. The next phase is also fairly self-explanatory: Metal Sonic will move to the right side of the screen and fire bird bots and lasers along the screen, simply avoid him and hit Metal Sonic. The last part, however, is down-right impossible at first glance. The screen fills up with missiles (apparently supposed to be in the background), and much larger missiles fly towards you, albeit rotating as they come to you. What it doesn't tell you, however, is that the one move designed to destroy stuff in the way, the team-up command, doesn't break through the missiles, but it is instead to hit Metal Sonic who is way out in front. If you can't keep up with the screen, you are thrown back to the beginning of the battle. Mind, this battle is fairly long, and, again, they don't tell you ANYTHING during the fight, except on what half of the screen the missiles take up. If you're lucky you can get multiple hits on MS in the earlier portions to speed up everything, but what's the point if you die in one hit at the end of the battle unless you have the reflexes of some kind of god or something?
There's a reason the classic games' bosses were simple, but not so simple that a monkey could simply wail on a genesis controller and win. Well... there's a reason THREE of the four classic games didn't do that. Sonic 2's bosses were kind of REALLY easy at times. So, for a game supposed to be a modern game built as a sequel to the classic quadrilogy, this fails pretty cohesively as a sequel, even if Sonic 4 Episode 1 apparently failed that much harder.

Sonic The Hedgehog 4 - Episode 2 is the second episode of Sonic 4 project, which is 2D Platformer with multiplayer, came out in 2012, two years after the first one. It ended up being the last episode in the project, with no news on Episode 3 ever since. Outside of "it's pretty much cancelled". No big differences between mobile and other versions this time around.
Owners of Episode 1 on Steam will also get Episode Metal bonus.
No complaints on technical side this time around, it supports all the needed resolutions.
Being an episode, you may think it's very short. Well, it's decend old platformer lenght. You are given 4 zones with 3 acts each, plus boss act. Add to that final level and special stages. Each act is adds long enough overall for it to be considered to be about as long as, say, Sonic 1. So don't knock this title off for being "not full game".
This time around Sonic doesn't travel by himself. The ever cute Tails the fox joins him and becomes part of the team. And he isn't just wasting space either, as the game introduces ability to call Tails to help you. He can lift you up in air, let you travel underwater or you can do a combined spin-dash. Said spin-dash breaks through special walls, destroyes everything and simply goes really fast. Yes, I said a cliche thing. You can't turn around in this mode and it will stop by itself after colliding with a wall three times. In all honesty, I don't like this move. It either will be abusive, making some sections go too easy, or will give you cheap deaths of falling into pits you couldn't possibly see before too late. Try not too use it too much.
Oh, and takling of pits. Game for once actually puts signs over bottomless pits, so you know if it will kill you or just a way to lower path. The fact that you can call Tails to save you by lifting into air with push of a single button helps you to get out of this sticky situation where you are already falling into one. Quite clever thing, if you ask me.
Now, it's not the first time you have Tails as sidekick. When he was first introduced in Sonic 2, he was giving game much of good. Second player could exploit that Tails always respawns to make bosses too easy, while AI would ruin special stages for you. He would later learn to fly in Sonic 3, also being able to lift Sonic along, but you had to grab Second Player's controller to do that and thus was only used to find rare bonuses. Sonic 2 bad sides of Tails were still there.
Then in Sonic Advance 3, with it's sidekick system, you could take Tails along with you and could easily use his ability as single-player to help you. But because you could take any different sidekick with very different abilities, game was still using them for optional things, like finding bonus items or just helping usual process.
In Sonic 4 Episode 2 though he is always your sidekick. Thus the game actively uses it and even throws challenges that requrie Tails help. For example, at the end of one of the acts in the Oil Desert you have to use Tails to hover slowly, while avoiding enemies and being pushed around by wind. By the way, flight isn't timed, instead you can "lift yourself up sllightly" only limited times.
You can't abuse Tails for bosses either, as when it comes to multiplayer, from what I know, the lives are limited for Tails. Or maybe they are shared.
In all honesty, I didn't try multiplayer out. But I think it should be real nice. Sonic can call Tails to his location, so Tails player will not feel left out that camera only follows Sonic. And yes, it has all the needed options and system to play over Internet. Maybe even too much, it's just 2-player coop of short platform game after all.
I didn't find anybody active online there. So you should just use it to play with friend, not going to find strangers. Then again, playing with friend is the way it should be done anyway.
Game also fixes some of the main complaints and just improves. Levels still have pacing, platforming and few paths. Actually, each level has one red ring hidden in it that you can collect. In other Sonic games it usually unlocks something. Here it doesn't do anything aside from giving achievement and just being something to explore levels for. They say that it had some use for upcoming Episode 3, but as it's not being developed, well, yea. Each act also tries to get something unique going for it, but there is still ntohing like darkness and carts.
Physics are good. They are still not on par with older Genesis titles, so it's not a game about rolling down the slopes. But they about as good as other modern 2D Sonic games, so there should be no complaints. Still got platforming going for it after all.
And I also should mention that this time around game doesn't feel like it tries to restrict itself. It finally feels like continuation to classic trilogy. Perhaps this one should have been the real Episode One, really. Bosses are epic, Metal Sonic makes awesome return too. This game actually does the best justice to this villian. Final boss is huge, unique and isn't easy-easy. You will even get to take down flying fortress again. And yes, there is stage where you fly on top of Tornado plane and it's more complicated than original in Sonic 2. Other zones are also unique and don't feel as much of deja vu like in Episode 1.
Shame though that some boss acts are too generous with throwing rings at you non-stop. Ah well, at least battles themselves felt enjoyable.
Graphics are great. It's all modern 3D now, using polygons for backgroudn details as well, not using that simplistic shading effect of Episode 1 either. While not requiring much of computer, it strikes some beautiful sceneries.
Same can be said of music. In Episode 1 it felt like bad experiement at some times. In Episode Two majority of it is great. It seemed to find it's own identify and provides some unique feel that you will not find in original trilogy, providing tensity too. Oil Desert Act 2 comes to mind, which has a bit of that old-school lo-fi feel, while also giving you a feeling of being in hot oily desert. Burning. Normal boss music is still too repetitive.
You can still collect 7 emeralds in special stages, which are similiar to Special Stages in Sonic 2, where you run through a tube and collect rings. No twists this time, just additional small features. That, and it's still better than Sonic 2 ones because you can actually see things before they hit you. Some of them are hard, so you will either learn to abuse "retry" button in menu or will have to do it in multiplayer.
Episode Metal allows you to go through the Episode 1 levels as Metal Sonic. No sidekick. Metal even has same shading to him there as characters in the first Episode. You will just go through one act of each of the four zones. And layout of that act is changed heavily. Could say that it's unique ones. But using elements from what you already seen before. At least they aren't too easy.
So, Sonic 4 Episode 2 is a pretty good platformer and 2D Sonic game. Better than Episode 1 for sure and actually feels more like proper Sonic 4. You should have fun with it. The only shame is that ending may feel cliffhangery for some.
A huge improvement over Episode 1, with a lot more challenge and more feautures, this game is a true sequel to the first one without a doubt. Where the hell is Episode 3 though?

Hitman has some really great features, but there are two (2) items that make impossible to recommend:
1) Time. The online-only requirement has been unreliable in the past and will be disconnected some time in the future. So it is not just the "elusive targets" that are subject to limited gameplay duration. Moreover several times (such as the lighting and shadow updates with Marrakesh) during Season One the *new features/improvements* introduced horrible bugs that the community had to track down and provide solutions for the developers to implement. The players were used as Quality Control. So, the time-sensitive content ensured the worst possible experience for dedicated players. Anyone purchasing the GOTY version now has (i assume) missed all the "elusive targets" and are paying money for the rewards without the opportunity for the gameplay included in those elusive targets - so pay to not play.
2) Trend. The corporate decision to charge extra for "bonus content" even for customers who purchased the season pass in advance. I'm not upset that they're asking $25 for DLC that reuses existing maps for *new* missions. I am concerned by the clear corporate decision to charge as much as they think they can get away with for whatever they think fans will buy; at the expense of their reputation. They can't be trusted to deliver on a Season Two Season Pass, and the "outfit bundle" clearly indicates that item (outfits/items/weapons/etc) microtransactions will be coming soon.

The short of it is that this game is a lot like sitting down to eat seconds of a good meal. You've tasted it all before (City, Asylum, etc.), but seconds are filling. The food does the job. You're able to walk away from the table without feeling hungry.
Chiefly, I recommend Arkham Origins for the story. It has a numerous plot threads but the primary story concerns the nature of the relationship between Batman and The Joker.
Batman and The Joker are cut from the same cloth. They are two sides of the same coin, and their material base is Gotham City. This alone isn't too relevatory if you've seen any of the movies or Batman:TAS. The interesting twist this game supplies is that once having established Batman and Joker as twinsies, so to speak, it digs a little deeper into their respective obsessions for one another.
The Joker, of course, plays horribly contrived games but in playing these games he attempts  to carry them to a logical end in a way that will fundamentally reveal the true character of the players. In Batman's case, Batman with little push, violia, might show that underneath his cowl is a clown with very green hair.
Fun! Right? It's okay. Batman and the Joker essentially have different answers to the same question, and since I referenced food at the start of this review, I may as well reference it again (and I think this line is used in one of the movies): how loyal do you expect a good dog to be when hungry?
The one bad day can turn someone onto many different roads. In the Joker's case, it made him into a crazy. In Batman's, the bad day riddled his being with guilt. The real question is about whether the bad day is an indicator of fate or free will. My leaning is the Joker, at bottom, believes no hungry dog is a loyal dog. It's nature. It's chaos. It's whatever you want to call it. We are all animals destined for a brutal, disappointing life. We just need a little push to reveal our true face. Batman would likely disagree. Life may be one vile task after another, but we have the choice to let it affect us in such and so a way.
Anyway, there's a lot more to say here. I jotted down some of the thoughts I had (whether they be right or wrong) after initially completeting the story of the game. There's plenty to think about and for that I give this game thumbs up.

Amazing game, Note I'm not really a fan of prison management games and I wasn't specifically looking for this kind of game(who is) before I played it, but something in this game really got me hooked into.
The graphics are 2D and very simplistic, and even though I like super awesome graphics, they are tolerable because of the art style.
What got me hooked in is the gameplay/mechanics of the game, and how a great 'sim/tycoon' game it is.
The gameplay is very simple, you manage a prison, you build it from scratch, you can set the rules, you hire the staff, guards, janitors, doctors, warden, etc. and then the prisoners come in. as time passes, if you do it right, you get more money, and you can expand your prison to handle more prisoners, and therefore you need to hire more staff and build more facilities, and your prison just goes bigger and bigger. Prisoners can try to escape, initiate riots, fight with each other, obtain contrabands, and stuffs that prisoners do in real life prisons. The fun is trying to come up with a great layout for your prison, all while managing it, handling and securing the prisoners properly, and making sure you get enough income for the prison to continue operating and expanding.
Good game, You don't have to play alot of it or play it regularly to get it's worth, you can like binge play it for hours/days and then forget about it for months. then remember it again and binge play it again, with a brand new prison.

The recommendation portion of this review is a bit tricky.  I would recommend this game... to the right people.  To people like me, I would not recommend it at all.
I am a casual gamer.  I enjoy the character progress of a good MMO through missions and such.  I enjoy the social aspect as well.  I am not a "hardcore" gamer or whatever they are calling themselves now.  This game seems far more for their type.  I learned this in under an hour of gameplay.
Character creation was fun and enjoyable.  I really felt like I was making a unique character that was solely my own.  Then I got to gameplay and the tutorials are very light.  Just, "press these buttons.  Got it?  Now go get a car.  Press these buttons.  Got it?  If so, hit K.  Ok!  Let's go straight into missions where everything is PvP!"
I never really noticed this (though it was hinted at many times) at first.  The whole thing is PvP, so you're up against whatever morality the opposing side can throw at you immediately.  In my first mission, I was given a starter gun and I spawned right next to another guy with a starter gun.  Two little machine guns in our starter car as we drove off to the way point.  We were almost there when a rocket destroyed our car.  Respawn.  Drive a different route.  Rocket destroys car.  Respawn.  Drive halfway, run on foot, try to stay incognito.  Approach waypoint, realize the enemy can see you on radar because you can see them.  There's six of them.  Nearest one has a rocket launcher.  Misses.  Run around the building, encounter second guy, also has a rocket launcher.  He kills you.
Respawn.
Drive all the way the hell around the waypoint and try your luck with the other four.  Encounter the closest one.  Oh good he also has a starter gun.  Kill him, move up.  Fourth guy?  Rocket launcher.  You put six bullet in him while he runs around.  He kills you in one shot like the rest.
Respawn.
It's at this point you realize that your fellow newbie teammate has ragequit a while ago, and you're left by yourself on your very first mission against a six man team of griefers.  On your first mission.  First.  Mission.
So if you're like me and you only have an hour or two a day to play and mostly use it to relax and enjoy yourself for a short while before the baby wakes up or what have you, this is definitely not the game for you.

What a rollercoaster it's been.
I want to emphasize already that the game is great. I love the characters, I love the world design, I love the humour (although I might be a bit biased because I'm Dutch, and a few jokes you'll only notice if you speak Dutch). I even like the combat system in contrast to what some people say. I definitely do not regret buying the game.
The reason I wanted to emphasize that it is a good game is because of one thing that I can't let go. The final bossfight. I'll try to elaborate by not giving any spoilers.
Summed up: it's really difficult, but not for the right reasons.
Difficulty in itself is not something that's bad. Just look at games like Dark Souls. The reason that it's not done correctly in this case, in my opinion anyway, is because there are elements to it that make it incredibly annoying. Firstly, there is an attack that is unavoidable. I've read somewhere that it has a pattern and that you can dodge it, but after more than two hours (yes, it actually took me two hours on the highest difficulty) I haven't been able to dodge it more than once, and that was pure luck.
Secondly, there was a lot of downtime in the fight. I had no choise but to use an exploit in the game to gain enough health to survive. If you know the game, I'm talking about
. To my knowledge there isn't another way to gain enough health than to buy loads and loads of food, which requires loads and loads of money, which requires a lot of grinding (= also a lot of downtime).
Maybe it's just me. I don't know. I do not have these complaints about any of the other bossfights.
Anyway, just know that if you're a completionist and you're going to complete Wuppo on higher difficulties, I wish you good luck.

Wuppo is a game with a cute art style and a few charming NPC interactions. Unfortunately, it's not enough to make it a compelling game. I really wanted to like it. It was clearly made with a lot of heart, but in the end it just fell flat and couldn't hold my interest.
One thing that comes up in other reviews is mention of Metroidvania game play. I think this is doing this game a huge disservice because it lacks any of the hallmarks of a Metroidvania game and it's clearly not trying to be one. If these reviews caught your interest, you will be disappointed.
I honestly wouldn't recommend Wuppo to anyone I know, so it gets a "no" from me. However, I wouldn't outright dismiss the game. It has a strong following, so others must be finding something rewarding that just wasn't doing it for me. Proceed with caution.
Pros:
Cons:

Good Game. has a good storyline, funny, puzzle, and boss battle

It's hard to file Wuppo in a genre. It's a metroidvania, bullet hell, RPG with an emphasis on story and exploration. But it doesnt' feel like any of those genres at all. There aren't many combat situations in the game, in fact combat probably takes up less than a quater of the game. Most of it will be spent exploring the world, solving puzzles, running errands and completing quests, interacting with a multitude of characters, collecting items of all sorts, and learning about the game world. Wuppo feels very relaxed, the game isn't that difficult (although many optional challenges and difficulty settings do exist), the writing is innocent and genuinely funny, and it's an overall just enjoyable experience. My only flaw with the game is that moving around the different areas of the world takes a long time, and often becomes tedious. An area select option of sorts only becomes available at the very end of the main story too which seems silly. This game is very short, but the optional content would at least double or triple your playtime. Wuppo is a great game for casual and dedicated players alike, I can't reccomend it enough.

I got this game from the Humble Monthly Bundle and had never heard of it before. I am so glad I decided to check it out! It really is a fantastic indie game that reminds me a lot of the Paper Mario games in terms of writing and world development. The art style is really cute and the soundtrack is really fun.
The gameplay is somewhat of a Metroidvania but it takes its own unique spin on things in terms of controls and inventory management. The game also doesn't hold your hand so it can be somewhat difficult to figure out what you're doing at times, but I personally really like that because it reminds me a lot of the old Nintendo games I grew up playing. I'm really tired of modern games just pointing an arrow in the direction of your next objective all the time. There's also no map so you better know your way around the world.
My biggest complaint is that your character doesn't look very unique and it can be easy to lose track of your character in certain areas of the game where there's lots of NPCs that look identical to you. My other complaint is a certain train system in the game that runs in real time and it can be a pain waiting for the train at your stop when you just want to move to the next area. Other than that, I don't have any real complaints.
Seriously though, this game is definitely worth checking out! It's a hidden gem amongst all the garbage on Steam nowadays. Pick it up at full price, on sale, or however you can get it, just buy this game and support the devs!

At the same time, the game needed more polish and was clearly rushed to make the 2013 holiday season, which is not surprising since the game takes place during the night of Santa's expedition. There were two or three times where I fell through the floor and Batman registered that he fell into the sea. The challenge ladder requires you to do them in order, which makes the predator ladder nearly impossible to complete on a single playthrough. There are also missable achievements, which are pretty infuriating if you miss them.
I never got to try the multiplayer; ther servers are dead. If you liked Arkham City and are willing to trade overall presentation quality for more, new content, then I highly recommend this game.

Well, after putting 200 hours into this game, I have to say I most definitely recommend it. I'm not sure what I can really say that hasn't been said before, so I'll just leave potential buyers with a couple thoughts.
This game is absolutely a lot of fun, but I have found, both with the original Borderlands and this one, that there are times where it can just get tedious and boring. Whenever that happens, I generally take a break for a week or so, come back, and it's back to being fun again.
Playing online adds a whole new layer of fun and difficulty, but be wary. There are a lot of people that edit and dupe OP items, or mess around with things so that you get more cool stuff, and I've found that while that can be cool, it does sort of make you feel like you've been cheated out of the play time you'd have spent getting them the legit way. I've taken to having one character I play online with, and one I play entirely offline with. That way, I've always got a completely clean character to just play the game with.
You don't have to get the DLC, but it makes the game a lot more fun. Particularly the two Ultimate Vault Hunter Upgrade packs. They raise the level cap and add more loot, which drastically increases the amount of time you can put into the game, and generally just makes things much lovelier. The DLC included in the GOTY edition are all cool, but you don't *need* them in order to enjoy the game.
And, finally, Gearbox is awesome. They are not a perfect developer, by any means, but the amount of love they've put into this franchise is just rad. I mean, it's been over three years and they're still supporting the game with updates and hot fixes. In a world where quite a few companies just stop all support for older games the moment they see fit, it's nice seeing Gearbox show that they still care about Borderlands 2.
All in all, this is a good game. I've put 200 hours into it, and honestly, I don't really see myself stopping anytime soon.

A preliminary caveat; this game is certainly worthy of a mature rating, possibly more so than virtually any "mature" rated title seen before by the author.
With that warning provided, let the buyer know two things. First, as a true "sim" game, Prison Architect goes well above the standard set by many of its peers. You are the final authority on virtually all aspects of an imprisonment complex, from utility design to cuisine management to emergency response services to inmate psychological welfare. A power outage is a problem, until it incenses the tenants to riotous anger and becomes a potential catastrophe. Don't let the simple stylized art lower expectations - you will have more than enough to deal with on a regular basis.
Second, this game does something previously unseen by the author in making a "sim" game that is actually story-driven on a fundamental level. This aspect of the game is where most lasting opinions will probably cement; from the distant vantage of a prison architect, you will be exposed to characters and situations, and you WILL care about them. Perhaps it will be heartsickness at the pain, or hope that you can be a good influence on your prison kingdom, or anger for anger's sake, or just numbness.
As odd as it may sound, though, this game is exceptionally recommended. It grabs the player by the guts, taps into both halves of their brain with surgical precision, and pulls them into an experience that will sit in the psyche for a long, long time to come. It does what so very many good orators and famous figures have throughout history by posing questions that are not merely discomfiting to contemplate, but morally demand an answer.

Unlike Sonic 4 Episode I, Sonic 4 Episode II doesn't just reuse a bunch of old things from the classic Sonic games, puts them all in one game and call it a sequel. Instead, it actually adds new things and tries to fix any problems with the first episode.
Most of the levels, besides Oil Desert Zone and Sky Fortress Zone which look like Oil Ocean Zone from Sonic 2 and Wing Fortress Zone from Sonic 2, look very original and are extremely creative and fun to look at.
The graphics in this game are a huge improvement in this game, the game itself is now is 2.5D and now everything looks a lot nicer and beautiful. Sonic's textures in the game also aren't extremely light blue like the last game and he along with everything else in the game, looks great.
Even though this game is nice, I wouldn't call it “Sonic 4” because it still doesn't feel like a direct sequel to Sonic 3, despite the game still being really good. I feel like the game should have had some more characters and stages to lengthen the game and also make the game feel alot larger than Sonic 3 was, but Sonic 4 is an episodic game so I guess both Sonic 4 episodes 1 and 2 would basically be one whole game and if you put combine all the zones in the game you get 10 zones which is close to the amount Sonic 3 & Knuckles has.
Because of all of this, I recommend you buy this game at some point and if you want to play the whole “Sonic 4 Saga” then wait for Episode I to be on sale and buy it at a lower price.

Not to say I've been playing this game long.  I only have 10 hours as of this review. However, I will have far more before I'm through.
Why gripe about characters?  It's not a biggie, honestly.  However,
playing blue Nina or red Ace, always N-Buster or A-Saber as weapons, when you can play multiplayer, is so disengaging in modern gaming.  So many games allow you to customize your color scheme at the least, if not different body parts and weapons/skills entirely like in DBZ Xenoverse.  If I could see some more unique character development options, this game would be a solid 10/10 for me.  Gameplay will always be Mega Man X Clone, so the real way to step out of the mould is with character development.
That's not to say the devs haven't done that already.  With the shops and upgrades similar to Risk of Rain, the skulls, the 5 weapons per character, and the core augments that change your appearance (without having to go to X location in Y stage to get Z core augment) they are already a step above MMX.  I can picture multiple ways some more customization could be added in without changing Nina or Ace, or a couple ways (like palette choices) to affect them for the user's preference.  Anyone else remember playing as Black Zero?  Or when Mega Man's colors changed based on the boss power equipped?
This game is solid.  I will continue playing it and look forward to where it goes.

This is a very solid entry in the dmc series.  Controls are a bit different. There's a dedicated dodge button (in addtion to jump) which is very forgiving.  Holding LT or RT when pressing the face buttons gives a different set of moves which provides a ton of room for experimenting and making your own combos.  Among other things it lets you pull enemies towards you can lets you pull yourself to them.  The variety here probably makes it the best combat system in the series.
Pros:
+ one of the best combat systems in series
+ can run at glorious 120 fps (console versions upset everyone by limiting to 30)
+ runs well (2500k and 660 ti ran constant 120+fps on high)
+ good variety of environments
Cons:
- even on Nephilim (hardest difficult for first playthrough), it's probably easier than the other 4 games; this means it doesn't demand you learn the fighting system
- quite a few pointless scenes where it just lets you walk around (no jumping or practicing moves) while others talk
- the few pre-rendered cut-scenes are still at 30fps which can be jarring, but at least they use motion blur like film

A nice old classic, but they never went back to fix some glaring technical issues.
Unless you are on a menu screen, the game crashes when alt-tabbing.
The game MUST be played fullscreen, because windowed uncaps the framerate.  Some of the game physics are tied to this framerate (enemy movement mostly), expecting 60, making many stages either insanely difficult or fully unplayable.  Fullscreen manages to cap it to 60 and allows for normal play.
Still worthwhile if you have never tried it, but it is a shame they never went back to fix these problems.

You run.
You run some more.
You try rolling down a hill, but notice that the game won't let you, because... physics?
You run some more.
And that's about it, aside from occasionally frustrating level designs.

And if you're lucky, maybe they'll even spin.
And I'll be gosh-darned if Dimps doesn't LOVE their water levels. If the first level in a Sonic game is water-based, you know something's wrong.
And believe me, something here is very, very wrong.
...And yet, even with all that said, it's still a huge step up from the first one.

20XX is a game that replaces the Megaman formula's meticulous level design with a random number generator.  Somehow, it works.
This is a game inspired QUITE heavily by the Mega Man X series to the point where veterans will be able to master the game's controls within seconds.  A multitude of game mechanics return directly, such as charging shots, dashing (and dash jumping), wall jumping up individual walls, boss weapons, and many of the upgrades from the original games.
However, 20XX does display some discipline when taking elements, removing or modifying gimmicks that induce frustration (such as blunting spikes and bottomless pits to a single point of damage as punishment) and adding several common roguelike mechanics.
By action-roguelike standards, 20XX does pull its punches, and the success of a run is not as reliant on RNG as its compatriots.  It does suffer from the common action-roguelike problem of creating difficulty through bullet hell-type enemy attack patterns, but in a normal run, bullet density will never become outright ludicrous (as it does in Rogue Legacy) and there is still some emphasis on reacting to attack patterns rather than painstakingly threading the protagonist through holes in a sea of projectiles.
The character progression in an individual run is excellent.  In addition to raw damage/health/energy numbers increasing, items can be collected to increase jump height/movement speed, add special aerial maneuevers, and drastically change the behavior of standard attacks.  Progression is significant enough that starting a new run after getting fairly far can be quite jarring, as one gradually becomes accustomed to the increased agility and utility one gains as one moves farther into a run.
As of this review, the game is still in early-access, and there are some small flaws and glitches to be encountered.  Unlike most Early-Access titles, I would recommend the game in its current state, as the price is planned to increase until release and the game is quite enjoyable as it is.

The second Arkham game I played. Numerous glitches made this game problematic - especially for PS3 users who (much like PC users with AK) were majorly shafted with several problems that were never fully solved and remain in gameplay to this day - ranging from graphic problems with lag during glide-mode all the way to Batman becoming 'stuck' during boss fights.
The 'shock gauntlets' (for lack of a better name) while an interesting gimmick for less-capable players, took away much of the challenge that City contained and lacked any option to disable them. Like Batman himself this game was much more rough-around-the-edges than what was to come; but what it did right it did well and for that it deserves appreciation.
The story, the atmosphere and the young Bruce/Batman MADE this game approachable even if you weren't familiar with the series. It is an origin story without actually being one.
The new 'random event/cop in danger' missions that crop up from time to time over the police band are a welcome distraction that feels like it could have been used in Knight. The much larger map of Knight with randomly generated numbers of foes and victims to save would have been quite a simple feature and is one of the reasons I still play Origins.
Getting back to the story - and it isn't hard to do so - the plot in Origins moves around much more quickly than City, Asylum and Knight as well. The feel of a goal - a purpose - is much more present in Origins. Gotham - for the first time in the series history - actually FEELS like a city (or at least a town) with the much larger scope and map. Also, the origins the game gives for characters and areas that are introduced through the narrative are not only plausible, they (in many ways) are more streamlined and believable than many things DC has produced to date!
The writing of this game - coupled with actors like Troy Baker - leave you wanting more even if you get stuck during that fight with firefly.
